13 Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE DTA Report 447A NR 1745 COVIDCARDTECHNOLOGYREVIEW Nathaniel de Lautour,Logan Small,AustinChamberlain, JohnHarris, Brent Martin, MattHopkins 24 July 2020 ABSTRACT This report contains a DTA review of CovidCard, a digital contact tracing system proposed for COVID-19 pandemic control in New Zealand. The system comprises a card with a Bluetooth Low Energy radio device that transmits pseudo-random numbers from a unique sequence, allowing other cards in range to detect and record its presence. In addition, there are multiple software service layers and a security architecture to enable the secure upload of contact data to a central server. We believe that CovidCard could provide benefit for contact tracing by reducing the time taken to identify close contacts, if there is sufficient user acceptance and the system proves reliable in practice. We also make some recommendations for modifications and additional testing, and finally highlight some potential security risks. COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE DTA Report 447A Defence Technology Agency Private Bag 32901 Devonport Auckland 0744 New Zealand ©Crown Copyright 2020 COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE EXECUTIVESUMMARY CovidCard is a digital contact tracing system designed to augment manual contact tracing for COVID-19 pandemic control. The system comprises a card with a Bluetooth Low Energy radio device that transmits pseudo-random numbers from a unique sequence, allowing other cards in range to detect and record its presence. In addition, there are multiple software service layers and a security architecture to enable the secure upload of contact data to a central server. The server performs a process to match cards to serial numbers based on the pseudo-random number sequences emitted. This enables contact tracers to identify the owner of a card, and the identities of people the card has come into contact with. At the request of the Department of Internal Affairs (DIA), we have carried out a review of the technology underlying the CovidCard system based on documentation provided by the developer and 12 prototype cards that were supplied for inspection and physical testing. The review was supplemented by a workshop at DTA that was attended by representatives of the CovidCard development team and DIA. In general, we were impressed with the quality of the effort put into the development of CovidCard, and in particular the attention paid to security and privacy considerations. We also note that the supplied documentation was of high quality, and that the development program has been informed by data collected during field trials. Following simulation exercises, physical tests and documentation review, we believe that memory, battery capacity, and robustness would be sufficient to meet the target design lifetime of at least one year. The security architecture of the card has been carefully designed and we believe it meets reasonable privacy expectations. However, to confirm our views we recommend that a professional security consultant be engaged to provide an additional review of the privacy and security aspects of the CovidCard system. We believe that CovidCard has the potential to detect and record close contacts to a level useful for contact tracing, but that an unknown and possibly significant number of false positive contacts will be generated. Increasing CovidCard’s detection thresholds to reduce the false positive rate is possible but this risks true positive contacts being lost. The true positive rates achieved in trials ranged from 0.63 to 1.0, while false positive rates ranged from 0.03 to 0.69. While it may be possible to improve card performance above what has been observed in trials, this would need to be demonstrated in a large-scale trial. To mitigate possible false contacts from signal strength fluctuations we recommend that contact duration be stored along with the RPE, and we have proposed two possible modifications in contact record architecture to achieve this. When the firmware, including close contact detection thresholds, is finalized we recommend that CovidCard be run for an extended period (exceeding 21 days) to verify software robustness and validate the battery life modelling. Given that cards may not always be worn on a lanyard, we recommend that additional tests be carried out to assess card performance when worn in alternative positions, such as a shirt pocket. Although these locations might not be ideal, it would enhance user acceptance and is likely to still provide a useful level of performance. Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE 1 INTRODUCTION CovidCard is a digital contact tracing system designed to augment manual contact tracing for COVID-19 pandemic control and to speed up the notification of at-risk individuals of possible exposure to SARS-CoV-2. The system comprises a card with a Bluetooth Low Energy radio device that transmits pseudo-random numbers from a unique sequence, allowing other cards in range to detect and record its presence. In addition, there are multiple software service layers and a security architecture to enable the secure upload of contact data to a central server. The server performs a process to match cards to serial numbers based on the pseudo-random number sequences emitted. This enables contact tracers to identify the owner of a card, and the identities of people the card has come into contact with. At the request of the Department of Internal Affairs (DIA), we have carried out a technical review of the proposed CovidCard system. The primary purpose of the review was to provide independent advice as to whether CovidCard would be able to perform as represented under the assumption that a population wide distribution is achieved. DTA was provided specific terms of reference for the review which included the card system design, the security architecture, and ongoing support that we could provide to the project [1]. The review was undertaken based on documentation provided by the developer, and 12 non- functional cards supplied for inspection and physical robustness testing. The material submitted for review was supplemented by a workshop at DTA that was attended by representatives of the CovidCard development team and DIA. The remainder of this report details the review covering the items listed in the terms of reference. Although we have provided feedback on the security architecture as requested we recommend that a professional security consultant be engaged to provide an additional review of these aspects of CovidCard. Note that there were a number of items specifically ruled out of scope for this review, including user acceptance, project cost, and alternative contact tracing solutions, and these issues are not considered here This report is an edited version of DTAReport 447 which was releasedto DIAin July, 2020. Parts of theoriginal report relatingto securityaresensitive andhave been removed. 2 CARDPERFORMANCE 2.1 Overview CovidCard is designed to assist COVID-19 contact tracing by recording Bluetooth Low Energy advertising signals emitted by nearby CovidCards. Each signal contains a random number known as the Ephemeral Advertising Identifier (EAI) which is drawn from a pseudo-random sequence that is unique to each card. The key and initial value needed to generate the pseudo-random sequence are uploaded from the card during production and stored on a central server. When contact records containing the EAIs are uploaded to the server, the cards can be identified by a partial reconstruction of the pseudo-random number sequences they emit. To decide whether a detection should be logged as a close contact an exposure risk metric based on the RSSI is calculated. It is based on the idea that exposure risk depends inversely on the distance, and that RSSI can be used to estimate distance. In free space conditions the signal strength varies inversely with the square of the distance. In this idealised case inferring distance from RSSI is straightforward, as long as the transmitter and receiver are calibrated. Here, CovidCard has an advantage over smartphone apps for RSSI based distance estimation DTAReport 447A COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE 1 Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE because the Bluetooth radios in the cards are identical. However, there are additional factors that strongly influence signal strength – multipath fading, antenna orientation, body attenuation – and estimating distance based on RSSI data alone is an inherently difficult problem. 2.2 CardDetection Performance When CovidCards are in the active state, they cycle between advertising (transmitting) and scanning (receiving) modes. Assuming a Packet Error Rate (PER) of 50%, the developers estimate that six detection opportunities a minute are needed to meet the criterion of 98% chance of card detection in one minute (5.3.3.1, System Overview ). The PER assumption seems reasonable and we concur with the estimate of six detection opportunities per minute to meet the 98% detection threshold. Scanning and advertising window durations intended to meet the six detections/minute criterion are discussed in sections 5.3.3.1 and 5.3.3.2 of the SystemOverview . In advertising mode, the cards will transmit an advertising signal about every 130ms. The card remains in the advertising mode for 20±1 seconds, after which it enters the scanning mode. In the scan mode the card listens for peer CovidCard packets for 290ms. We have checked and agree that these intervals enable detection of six advertising signals per minute and so meets the desired detection criterion. The performance of cards in high density environments (situations where large numbers of people are in close proximity) was considered in section 5.3.4 of the System Overview by simulation. We have not been able to directly verify the results presented but the approach and underlying assumptions seem reasonable. The conclusions reached were that the CovidCard will cope with up to 75 cards in receiver range without compromising detection performance with a 130ms advertising interval. Assuming a maximum density of about 50 people per 10 square metres, and the likely effects of body attenuation on the signal, a card density limit of 75-100 is plausible. To further increase confidence in card performance a high-density scenario could be tested as part of a field trial. 2.3 ExposureTrackingSubsystem The exposure tracking subsystem of CovidCard processes peak RSSI values, calculated over one minute intervals, for each entry in the watchlist. Exposure tracking is based on an internally calculated parameter called the Relative Proximity Estimate (RPE). The RPE is obtained by converting peak RSSI to a free space path loss estimate, and then calculating what is effectively a scaled inverse distance under the assumption of inverse square path loss. For the lifetime of a watchlist entry, the peak RPE is determined and the sum of the RPE values is accumulated. The total RPE is intended to be a measure of total exposure risk which can be used to prioritize contact tracing. Viral transmission risk is inversely dependent on the distance between two people and directly dependent on the contact duration. The exposure risk metric proposed for CovidCard seems a natural generalization of these criteria to the situation where the distance between people is varying with time. Note that this is a different approach to that taken in the Google-Apple Exposure Notification API, in which the exposure risk is dependent on attenuation, contact duration, number of days since exposure, and transmission risk [3]. The intention is to convert the RPE into a fixed-point representation, and scaling constants are to be defined to ensure that the range of RPE can be contained inside this value. These constants have not yet been defined, and the algorithm/code for calculation of RPE and accumulation of DTAReport 447A COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE 2 Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE total RPE is not given. If intermediate calculations are performed in fixed point then the impact of round off error should be considered. The decision to record a watchlist entry in the contact log will be determined by thresholds on the peak and total RPE, but final values of these thresholds have not yet been set. The intention is to do this following final field trials to meet “target performance requirements” as stated in 7.2.4Firmware Specification . The setting of these threshold values carries the risk that either valid contacts (true positives) are missed, or the cards will record too many false positives. Since this is a critical aspect of card performance, we think that additional limited trials in a variety of environments should begin as soon as possible, and that the data on which the thresholds have been based should be released for independent review. 2.4 Effect of RSSIFluctuations We note an estimated range between two devices is implicit in the calculation of the RPE (it is proportional to the inverse of the range under the assumption of inverse square path loss). However, in real environments there are reflections of the signal that combine with the direct transmission path at the receiver, and this can result in extreme fluctuations in the RSSI. While on average the RSSI declines with range, when using the peak value there is risk that close and casual contacts may not be differentiated. To illustrate this, we collected RSSI readings from Bluetooth Low Energy packets exchanged between two Raspberry Pi devices in a meeting room at DTA. The devices were suspended at a height of about 1.3mfrom two camera tripods One thousand packets each were collected at ranges from 0.5mto8mbetween the devices, with a 130msinterval between transmissions. The data collection process took about two minutes at each position. The raw RSSI data is shown in the left hand plot of Figure 1. The raw RSSI data was then filtered to simulate the effect of a 290msscan interval repeated every 20 seconds, combined with a one minute peak filter. The right hand plot in Figure 1 shows the range of peak RSSI values that could be obtained with this processing approach. There is a range because the first scan interval on the CovidCard can start at a random time in the data series. This experiment shows that there can be considerable overlap in values of peak RSSI at different ranges. Hence any metric derived solely from peak RSSI may not be able to discriminate close and casual contacts. DTAReport 447A COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE 3 Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE Figure 1: Left : Raw RSSI values measured at different distances between two Raspberry Pi devices. Right: The simulated range of peak RSSI values from CovidCard basedonthe Raspberry Pidata. We believe that providing contact duration information in the contact record may partially mitigate this issue. We suggest two possible approaches to incorporating contact duration in a contact record: a)Reduce the opcode to a 2-bit field, introducing a new 5-bit field containing the total contact duration in minutes (i.e. the number of minutes the EAI was visible), and reducing the size of the total RPE field to fit within the remaining 14 bits. b)Replace the current 16-bit field for total RPE with 8-bit fields for both the time averaged RPE and contact duration. Saving the raw RSSI values and doing contact exposure processing on the server would be preferable. However, we recognize that this is not possible within the memory constraints of the device without severely impacting on the size of the watchlist. 2.5 Sensitivity andSpecificity CovidCard can be programmed to record an encounter if the received signal satisfies criteria based on duration and strength of the signal. For contact tracing the Ministry of Health defines seven scenarios with particularly high infection risk (“close contacts”). Two of these scenarios involve inter-personal contact within two metres for15 minutes or more, and these are targets for Bluetooth contact tracing systems like CovidCard. Implicit in these close contact definitions is that transmission occurs via inhalation of droplets from an infected person, and that a partition or barrier would block transmission. CovidCard can generate false positives by the same mechanisms as smartphone apps because it is also based on Bluetooth radio signals. False positive contacts fall into two categories: •Acontact with correctly estimated range and duration where the signal was received through a physical barrier; • A contact with an underestimated range due to Bluetooth signal strength variation. DTAReport 447A COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE 4 Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE There is no way to mitigate the first of these on the card, and this is a problem inherent in all contact tracing systems based on radio signals. False contacts obtained through walls or partitions can only be resolved at the contact tracing interview stage, i.e. there is no technological solution to this problem at present. Estimating range using Bluetooth is an inherently difficult problem due to fluctuations in signal strength. Earlier this year we conducted a literature review of distance estimation using Bluetooth signals and concluded that this can be very unreliable [ 4]. Our subsequent data collection exercises performed with Raspberry Pi devices have confirmed this view. An initial trial on an early CovidCard prototype was performed at Nelson Hospital [ 5] The trial report recommended that further trials be held to refine the algorithm used to determine close contact. The report noted that an effective algorithm was essential to reduce false positives and conserve battery and memory. A number of additional trials on a CovidCard prototype were performed in May [ 6]. These validation trials aimed to collect card data in a number of real-life situations and use this data to test and refine close contact detection algorithms. In this trial, a contact was recorded on a card if two or more detections with RSSI ␀63 were received. Bluetooth data was downloaded from the cards and compared with ground truth data obtained by observer notes and video recordings, after applying a 15 minute duration threshold to both data sets. The true positive rates for card contacts in these trials ranged from 0.63 to 1.0, while the false positive rates ranged from 0.03 to 0.69 (Table 3 of [ 6]). While it may be possible to improve card performance above what was observed in trials, this would need to be demonstrated in a large-scale trial implementing an improved close contact detection algorithm. 3 SERVER-SIDEPROCESSING There are multiple aspects to the server-side processing that must be considered. The first step, after uploading readout data, is the identification of cards based on the received pseudo-random identifiers (the EAI values). The matching of EAI values with card serial numbers is performed by a search through a time-limited table of EAI values that is continuously updated by the server. The developers have not yet implemented or tested a specific algorithm for server-side card resolution. But, based on information provided at the DTA workshop, we believe that server-side card resolution is computationally tractable and could be scaled up or parallelised if needed using cloud computing resources. In the current design approach determination of exposure risk (measured by the RPE) is performed on the card. Only the total RPE is saved in a contact record, and this is very limited information with which to identify potential false positives. To give contact tracers more information that might help to identify false positives we recommend that contact duration be stored in the contact record log as well as the RPE. Two possible approaches to incorporating contact duration were described in section 2.4. Neither of the modifications suggested change the contact record size, and would enable a more detailed exposure risk assessment on the server. This could take into account the the additional factors of transmission risk and time since exposure, as implemented in the Google-Apple Exposure Notification API [3]. DTAReport 447A COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE 5 Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE 4 BATTERYLIFE 4.1 Overview It is clear from the supplied documentation that significant attention has been given to the power considerations of the CovidCard. The impact on instantaneous power consumption, battery duration and therefore indirectly, the usability of the CovidCard has been highlighted at all stages of the design. The need for such an ultra-low power device has led many architectural decisions in the design of the CovidCard. It is important to note that this power/battery assessment is based purely on a study of the CovidCard documentation since a device with fully operational firmware has not been submitted for testing. Empirical measurements have not been gathered. Given the potential consequences of mistaken power calculations, it is imperative that the power budget is accurately modelled. Such modelling commences in Section 5 3.2 of the System Overview with a description of the expected lifecycle of the CovidCard. Four distinct phases are considered: Production, Shelf life, Operation and Readout. Battery capacity is inherently determined by the form factor of the CovidCard and readily available battery chemistries/capacities. The limitations and realistic expectations of the selected battery are set out in Section 5.3.2.1 and Table 2 of the System Overview. Considering the mean annual temperatures in New Zealand, the CovidCard battery model is de-rated by 20% due to temperature and manufacturing tolerances from 800mAh to640mAh. A self-discharge estimate of 2% per annum is used throughout the usable life of the card For all phases the worst-case pessimistic view on battery capacity and power consumption is used in further modelling. These estimates are considered realistic. 4.2 Battery Life Modelling Production Given the high volume of manufacture, the production phase (specifically Initialisation) is very brief. The power model takes a worst-case consumption of 1mAh for this period. Shelf Life During storage the CovidCard is in a low power state awaiting activation. During this time, the power model assumes a maximum period of 12 months consuming 4µAof current in order to maintain the real-time clock and RAM state. The quoted values of current are in line with the Apollo Blue MCU specifications stated in the device datasheet. Operation The battery model for this phase is the most complex and comprises three different states: Battery Level Check, Sleeping and Scanning/Advertising. Battery Level Check: To enable the user to check the battery of the CovidCard a button press will initiate a LED flash. This power consumption is estimated for an eager user to be no more than 1mAh during the 12-month life cycle. In the current firmware version, the battery check procedure lights the red LED. This uses less power but is misleading to the user. Use of the green LED is far more intuitive and would not greatly impact power consumption. Sleep: To facilitate extended periods of low powered sleep during the Operation phase, the CovidCard utilises an accelerometer to detect card movement and wake the microprocessor. Section 5.1 of the FirmwareSpecification details the duty-cycle and backoff procedure selected DTAReport 447A COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE 6 Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE to enable accurate motion detection whilst minimizing accelerometer on time, even during long periods of inactivity. Given the ability to accurately detect user motion the power consumption model assumes 10 hours of active use per day, 7 days per week. A value of 4µAis predicted for the sleep state. The design of the accelerometer subsystem and assumptions stated are reasonable. Scanning/Advertising: Following subtraction of all above overheads the remaining battery capacity of526mAh can be assigned to scanning and advertising. Section 5.3.3 in the SystemOverview presents a convincing model for parameter selection of scanning and advertising. This model can be used to prove that for the parameters selected, the remaining battery capacity is sufficient to obtain contact events. This state-based simulation boosts confidence in achieving a 98% detection target with a 130ms advertising interval and 290ms scan window at an interval of 20 seconds. Readout Reasonable estimates for power consumption are given in the readout phase considering the duration a readout is expected to take, the higher power BLE radio state and the LED flashing current. Net energy usage is estimated at 1mAh per readout cycle. 4.3 Conclusion Future changes to firmware design and a lack of empirical measurements makes a definitive answer on battery duration difficult, however based on the supplied documentation, we believe that the assumptions and values pertaining to battery duration are plausible and well modelled. The estimates given for current consumption and the time spent in each phase/state are reasonable and accurately described. Notes/Suggestions •It may be possible for a determined malicious user to frequently enter higher power states, such as battery checking or readout in order to reduce battery lifetime. This is considered unlikely given the effort required to do so. •There may be other factors to consider such as battery internal resistance growth with age, however these ages are typically greater than the expected lifetime of the CovidCard. •It is likely in mass roll out that defective batteries will be encountered, these cannot be predicted and must be overcome via a replacement programme. •To enable a prediction of real battery and power consumption, a long-term programme of empirical power measurement could be undertaken on initial cards to prove expected performance. •In the current firmware version the red LED appears to be used to signal ‘Good’ battery state. If this is the case, we recommend changing to green to avoid user confusion. Note that the battery life projections depend on estimates of current drain by final production firmware, which does not yet exist and so has not been tested. But, based on the documentation provided, we believe the projected battery life and the modelling that underlies it is plausible. DTAReport 447A COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE 7 Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE 5 MEMORYCAPACITY The CovidCard is limited to the storage constraints of the included microcontroller unit (MCU). The CovidCard contains the ‘Ambiq Micro Apollo3 Blue’, specifically the part number AMA3B1KK-KBR-B0. This MCU has a total of 1MBavailable on-board storage (flash) and 384KBof available volatile memory (RAM). The MCU also contains 16KBof flash cache. The allocated storage for firmware and runtime is unknown as the firmware is not yet finalised. 5.1 Contact Log Design After activation, the CovidCard enters the Active state and the contact logging begins using the Bluetooth Low Energy Advertiser and Scanner. The size of the incoming data from the Bluetooth Scanner is variable depending on how many other cards are within Bluetooth range, unlike the Bluetooth Advertiser which transmits a static data size at a known frequency. Figure 2: CovidCardcontactlogdataflowfromScannertoReadoutasshownin section 7.2ofthe FirmwareSpecification . During contact logging, the largest use of data is in managing incoming data from the Bluetooth Scanner subsystem (shown in blue in the figure above). The Tracker subsystem (shown in orange) receives all incoming data from the Scanner and must keep an on-going watchlist for potential contacts (performed in RAM). The following Storage subsystem (shown in green) then takes confirmed contacts from the Tracker and stores them in the permanent contact log (in flash). 5.2 WatchlistMemoryCapacity The Tracker subsystem first mitigates against a flood of messages by limiting the incoming messages to 150 per scan (in the Flood/DoS protection block). The watchlist contains entries for every ‘active’ unique temporary card ID (EAI) that is being received. 32kBof storage has been allocated in the RAM for the watchlist, an upper limit of 1024 entries (at 32 octets per entry). We consider an extreme heavy-usage scenario for the CovidCard as encountering 20 new, unique EAIs per scan ( 290msevery 20 seconds), which might occur when walking through a crowded area with many cardholders. 60 watchlist entries would therefore be created every minute, resulting in 1500 new entries after 25 minutes. This exceeds the maximum 1024 watchlist entries allocated in RAM. It is not specified when an EAI is considered inactive (at which point the entry is removed from the watchlist), but it is assumed this is at most 25 minutes after the time that the EAI is first encountered (each EAI persists for 15 to 25 minutes). The Contact event detection block should therefore contain further logic to determine when a watchlist entry is DTAReport 447A COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE 8 Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE considered inactive, rather than purely relying on a 25-minute timer. If the inactivity threshold time were reduced to 15 minutes (the current duration for the definition of a close contact), this extreme example would still create 900 entries in that time. Although this extreme scenario can saturate the watchlist, we note that the entries with the oldest “last seen” time are deleted, which would minimise the risk that an active contact is removed. And the entries that are deleted are also assessed for exposure risk, meaning they may still be written to the contact log if the criteria are met. We consider a worst-case scenario for the CovidCard to be 150 incoming messages with new and unique EAIs per scan. This represents a malicious attack that would create 150 new watchlist entries per scan (one every 20 seconds), or 450 entries per minute, overwhelming the watchlist in just over two minutes. Mitigation against this type of attack may require further additions to the Flood/DoS protection block, or stricter logic on when an EAI is considered inactive. 5.3 Contact Log MemoryCapacity The Storage subsystem takes watchlist entries that are potential close contacts and encrypts and stores them within the permanent contact log in flash. 512kBof flash storage has been allocated for the contact log, an upper limit of 32,768 entries (at 16 octets per entry). Watchlist entries that are transferred to the contact log are first placed in a FIFO ring buffer in RAM, for batch-writing contacts to flash. The 512kBof flash storage allocated to the contact log is also designed as a ring buffer such that the oldest entry will be overwritten upon surpassing the memory limit. The extreme heavy-usage example given in Section 5.4 of the System Overview assumes 10 new contact events every 5 minutes for 12 hours every day. This would result in 1,440 new contact events every day, or 30,240 contact events over the 21 days, which is just within the storage limit of 32,768 entries. Hence, we consider it is extremely unlikely that the memory capacity will be exceeded under normal operation. The CovidCard also records the times when the card enters a sleep state and wakes from a sleep state into the contact log. These entries take up the same amount of storage as an exposure entry (16 octets). Continuing the extreme heavy-usage example, the CovidCard could undergo 10 minutes of inactivity to trigger a sleep state, followed by some motion or a button press to immediately trigger an active state. After 12 hours of repeated sleep-active state cycling, 144 sleep/wake entries will have been written to the contact log. After 21 days of 12 hours cycling each day, 3,024 sleep/wake contact events will have been written. In the extreme heavy-use example of 30,240 exposure events, this would overwrite the oldest 496 exposure events in the contact log. This shows that the most extreme sleep/wake cycling activity has the potential to cause exposure contact events to be lost (again, under the most extreme exposure activity). One mitigation may be to reduce the size of the sleep/wake entries in flash. 5.4 Conclusion Based on the documentation provided, we believe the memory capacity of the CovidCard is sufficient to capture contact records over the period of interest (prior 21 days from the start of the readout procedure). The current design can deal with extreme examples of use, however further thought may be needed on Flood/DoS attacks and the conditions on declaring a watchlist entry to be inactive. Also, a limit on the frequency of wake/sleep events being written to the contact log may guard against the overwriting of exposure events, which are more important data to be captured. Due to time constraints and lack of suitable equipment we were not able to perform all of these tests. Note that where there was a requirement for electrical function to be working after a test this was confirmed by verifying that the two LED modes still functioned. 6.1.1 Abrasion The polymeric material of the card outer case was identified by fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) as likely to be a styrene acrylonitrile copolymer (SAN). The abrasion (alcohol) test described in section 5.2.2 of the Hardware Specification was carried out using isopropanol and no deterioration of the printed label was observed. Three additional solvents were also trialled for interest: petroleum ether (hexanes), AVTUR (aviation kerosene), and acetone. Use of petroleum ether and AVTUR did not result in noticeable deterioration of the printed label but the acetone dissolved the card material resulting in a smearing of the etching. 6.1.2 Bending A 3-point bend test was also conducted, as this seemed like a potential failure mode when a user is sitting with the card placed in a back pocket. The card was placed between a 70mmgap, as shown in the Figure below. The card was deformed by 9.3 mm at the maximum load of 23.9kg. Once the load was removed the card returned mostly to its original state (retaining only a 1mm deformation) and remained functional. Figure 3: 3-point bendtest being performed onthe CovidCard. 6.1.3 Immersion The ingress protection test from section 5.2.3 of the Hardware Specification was carried out with the card being submerged in water at a depth of 1mfor 30 minutes. The card was still functioning after the test. After the cover was removed no water was found inside the weld line. DTAReport 447A COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE 10 Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE 6.1.4 Crushtest The crush test described in section 5.2.4 of the Hardware Specification was carried out but a load of100kNwas applied instead of the required 15kN. However, despite the excess force the card still functioned. Some slight warming of the battery area was observed immediately after but this did not persist beyond a few minutes. The card thickness was reduced from 4.2mmto 3.6mm by the crush test. 6.1.5 Impact The impact test in section 5.2.4 of the Hardware Specification was carried out by dropping a 9.9kgweight from a height of 1monto a15mmdiameter bolt placed on top of the card. The card was deformed and no longer functioned. 6.2 Commentson PlannedPhysicaltests Xenon Arc exposure more closely matches the spectra of sunlight at the earth’s surface. This method could give more useful results over the solely UV method proposed. Prescribing the exposure according to a known standard will give more weight to the results obtained. ASTM D2565 (Standard Practice for Xenon-Arc Exposure of Plastics Intended for Outdoor Applications) would be a good option as the card will be in use outdoors and polystyrene and its copolymers are susceptible to UV degradation. The use of recognised standards in the specifications will help to ensure that robust and relevant testing is undertaken. Where standards cannot be fully met or lack relevance then partial compliance or use of a subset of conditions or parameters would still be useful, if the deficiencies are noted. It is also recommended that a recognised standard of acceptance testing is used, such as the ISO 2859 or 3951 series 6.3 LanyardWearing The developers have proposed that the CovidCard be worn suspended by a lanyard on the front of the body. This aligns with the belief that maximum viral transmission risk is associated with face-to-face contact. Worn in this position maximizes RSSI for face-to-face contact, which is a key parameter in exposure risk calculation. Use of a lanyard would be precluded for machinery operators. But the card could be placed frontally in a shirt or overalls pocket, which should not significantly compromise performance. Surgeons and other health workers who perform procedures on patients may find lanyards too encumbering or dangerous to wear. Note also that lanyards have been identified as an infection control risk in hospitals and may not be appropriate for front-line medical workers for this reason alone Once again, in these situations the CovidCard could be placed in a pocket. Fitness instructors may find the lanyard inconvenient and uncomfortable to wear while taking classes. The nature of this work should not preclude the wearing of the card from a health & safety aspect, but resistance to wearing the card on a lanyard may be encountered amongst this group. DTAReport 447A COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE 11 Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE 7 SECURITYARCHITECTURE 7.1 Specification and DesignAssurance Robust security is critical to protecting user privacy in the CovidCard system. Specific security elements needed to achieve this are described in Section 2.2 of the Security Specification (the “primary security goals”). Below we consider the security of CovidCard when in the active state, the secure download procedure, and the server-side security architecture. 7.1.1 Card Operation The primary threat model considered in this section is the ability of an observer to track a specific CovidCard user. This tracking could be either following the user over time and distance or locating the user at a specific location. In both cases the attack is against the pseudonymous EAI – can an attacker predict the EAI in order to persistently identify a given user? The EAI has several measures which will make this a difficult attack, particularly with the limited range of the hardware. The random BD_ADDR, short and variable lifetime of each EAS, and destruction of previous EAS in the sequence, mean that an adversary does not have a predictable signal to attack. In most scenarios where the CovidCard is required – where the CovidCard user is mingling with other users – isolating a given card will be impractical at the software level. Another threat model is the ability of an attacker to determine the list of associates of a given CovidCard user. Given the difficulty of tracking a single user across the EAI changes, it would be substantially more difficult to attack multiple users. Afurther threat model is whether an attacker can overwhelm a given card or all cards at a specific location. This is explicitly addressed by the DoS/Flood protection. An adversary could flood a target CovidCard with replay attacks (of valid advertisements) but this would only be effective against the target card(s) while the attack is maintained. This could have the effect of masking users in a group or blinding the contact system for a specific location. The usefulness of such an attack is questionable so it can be regarded as low risk. The use of the opcode in the contact log should be used with caution for other types of events. The standard “exposure” event is required, but any other type of event could present a privacy risk. Even simple card sleep/wake events would be sufficient to develop a pattern of life for a given CovidCard user 7.1.2 Secure Download Download of contact record data takes place over a Bluetooth connection with a tablet or smartphone that runs the Secure Download Application (SDA). When new contact records are first created they are placed in a circular buffer in RAM, and when the buffer becomes full the records are written to flash memory. Contact records are encrypted before they are stored in RAM or flash using AES-CBC with a 256 bit Log Encryption Key (LEK). The LEK and the associated Log Encryption Initialization Vector (LEIV) are generated by CovidCard when it is first activated by the cardholder, and remain on the card in RAM. The log manager process erases any contact records in either RAM or flash that are older than 21 days. An attacker that gains access to the card’s RAM may be able to decrypt the contact records that are stored on the card. To enable readout the card readout mode must be first enabled by pressing and holding the activation button, after which CovidCard acts as a Bluetooth Low Energy peripheral device. The SDA initiates connection to the CovidCard and communicates using the Readout GATT DTAReport 447A COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE 12 Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE service. Before download can begin the SDA makes a Certificate Signing Request (CSR) to the CovidCard. The process of generating a CSR by the SDA and then submitting it to the Readout Authorisation Service is cryptographically very strong. It is normally applied on a lesser scale, for example in generating one-year certificates for websites, but it scales well to the frequent use here. This cryptographic certificate request passed over a secure connection is a strong and fully tested process, fundamental to network security. The strongest protection against misuse of the download process is the required physical activation on the CovidCard itself. Unless the card has been maliciously modified during manufacture, there is no way to connect to the card without the physical activation. To target a given card would require theft or interference by the attacker, or subversion of the health care system by coercing a healthcare worker. The standalone Readout Authorisation Service (RAS) provides a degree of separation from the download process. This will make the RAS a target for any attacker attempting to subvert the download process, but also allows a zero-trust connection between the Secure Download Application and the RAS. The information passed to the RAS (the identity of the Healthcare Professional and the scope of the request) provides an auditable log. This will mitigate the risk of subverting the download process by persuading a healthcare worker to extract data. 7.1.3 Server-side SecurityArchitecture The final design of the server components of the CovidCard system is still pending. These components consist of one mobile app (the Secure Download Application) and four server-based systems: the Readout Authorisation Service, the Escrow Service, the Contact Analysis Service, and the Card Registry Service. The Readout Authorisation Service and the Escrow Service require some level of public access in order to allow access for the Secure DownloadApplication. Both should be designed with the key aim of limiting access solely to the SDA. The RAS already has a secure design for communication with the SDA. The Escrow Service should additionally minimise any communication back to the SDA. Since each upload instance requires coordination of the CovidCard user and a Healthcare Professional, the Escrow Service should confirm successful upload of the contact data (for Live Readout Mode) and this confirmation should be a minimal response with no further communication. Silently accepting the upload may provide marginally more security (particularly against an attacker probing the Escrow Service) but creates a significant service risk that failed uploads are lost. The remaining server components – the Contact Analysis Service and the Card Registry Service – are not directly exposed to public access and so can be designed according to standard system security principles. When registering cards, cardholder personal data and the CovidCard Serial Number (CSN) should be uploaded to the Card Registry Service by a one-way connection. The Card Registry Service is the most valuable target for an attacker seeking information from the CovidCard system, so there should not be any access to the public. There should be no way to check the details associated with a given card, apart from a COVID-19 exposure alert. To minimise risk in this area, the CovidCard system should not allow cardholders to check or update their data. Users may withdraw from the system, or be issued a new card, as required. DTAReport 447A COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE 13 Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE 7.1.4 Conclusions We conclude that the primary security goals of the CovidCard System are sufficiently met by the security architecture. The CovidCard system separates the security operations at each stage of CovidCard use and uses dedicated encryption for each stage. This means separate encryption keys are used at each stage and so any successful cryptographic attack will only yield a fragment of the overall information. The ciphers in use are all current to accepted cryptographic standards with appropriate key lengths. Further security is provided by the use of ephemeral keys where possible, and the storage of keys in volatile memory to ensure their destruction in the case of most forms of tampering. DTA could also investigate use of the MANA computer model, or similar agent-based models, to simulate CovidCard interactions in a phase two trial. Combined with additional small-scale trials of real cards, the simulation modelling may partially substitute for a full-scale phase two trial. DTA could provide a second review of the exposure risk procedure if this is modified, either along the lines we have suggested or in another way, and/or when exposure risk thresholds are finalized. We have considered the idea of a large-scale field trial at a NZDF installation, for example, Linton military camp. This would be problematic for a number of reasons: a number of individuals would not be able to participate due to security issues; there are concerns that card data could reveal pattern of life behaviour; and that interactions of personnel in the trial would not be sufficiently representative of the population as a whole. There would also be frequent occasions where the cards would have to be placed in lockboxes, since they cannot be taken into classified environments. 9 SUMMARY& CONCLUSIONS We have carried out a review of the technology underlying the CovidCard system based on documentation provided by the developer and 12 prototype cards that were supplied for physical testing. The review was supplemented by a workshop at DTAthat was attended by representatives of the CovidCard development team and the Department of Internal affairs (DIA). Following simulation exercises, physical tests and documentation review, we believe that memory, battery capacity, and robustness would be sufficient to meet the target design lifetime of at least one year. The security architecture of the card has been carefully designed and we believe it meets reasonable privacy expectations We believe that CovidCard has the potential to detect and record close contacts to a level useful for contact tracing, but that an unknown and possibly significant number of false positive contacts will be generated. Increasing CovidCard’s detection thresholds to reduce the false positive rate is possible but this risks true positive contacts being lost. The true positive rates achieved in trials ranged from 0.63 to 1.0, while false positive rates ranged from 0.03 to 0.69. While it may be possible to improve card performance above what has been observed in trials, this would need to be demonstrated in a large-scale trial. To mitigate possible false contacts from signal strength fluctuations we recommend that contact duration be stored along with the RPE, and we have proposed two possible modifications in contact record architecture to achieve this. When the firmware, including close contact detection thresholds, is finalized we recommend that CovidCard be run for an extended period (exceeding 21 days) to verify software robustness and validate the battery life modelling. Given that cards may not always be worn on a lanyard, we recommend that additional tests be carried out to assess card performance when worn in alternative positions, such as a shirt pocket. Although these locations might not be ideal, it would enhance user acceptance and is likely to still provide a useful level of performance. DTAReport 447A COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE 16 Redacted consistent with 6(a) and 9(2)(k) Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs COMMERCIAL-IN-CONFIDENCE 10 RECOMMENDATIONS A number of recommendations for performance improvement and risk mitigation were made throughout this report. For convenience, they are itemized here: 1.The contact duration should be saved on the card along with RPE to reduce false positive risk from signal strength fluctuations. We suggested two possible approaches to incorporating contact duration in a contact record: a)Reduce the opcode to a 2-bit field, introducing a new 5-bit field containing the total contact duration in minutes (i.e. the number of minutes the EAI was visible), and reducing the size of the total RPE field to fit within the remaining 14 bits. b)Replace the current 16-bit field for total RPE with 8 bit fields for both the time averaged RPE and contact duration. 2.For further physical testing it is recommended that a recognised standard of acceptance testing is used, such as the ISO 2859 or 3951 series In addition, theASTM D2565 standard should be used for testing degradation in sunlight. 3.The Escrow Service should minimise communication back to the Secure Download Application. The Escrow Service should confirm successful upload of the contact data and this confirmation should be a minimal response with no further communication. 4.The Card Registry Service is the most valuable target for an attacker seeking information from the CovidCard system. There should be no way to check the personal data associated with a given card apart from a COVID-19 exposure alert. To minimise risk in this area, the CovidCard system should not allow cardholders to check or update their data. 5.A professional security consultant should be engaged to provide additional review of the privacy and security aspects of CovidCard. 6 7.The performance of the CovidCard system should be conclusively demonstrated in a large-scale controlled trial. This should be conducted by independent and experienced investigators, and subject to independent review. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 9 of 21 I propose that the process for children and young people has some additional requirements 56. While I believe self-identification should be available to children and young people , I propose that additional measures are in place . This ali gns with approaches taken in most other jurisdictions who have adopted a self -identification process for children and young people . Additional measures will ensure the child or young person understand s the amendment and that it is based on their own decision about their gender. The focus on consent is important to protect the child or young person from undue influence (eg from guardians ) and support their autonomy over how their gender is recognised . I propose different age categories to reflect older adolescents’ higher level of cognitive development 57. For children and young people, I propose introducing two age categories with different requirements that reflect different levels of cognitive development: 57.1 I recommend that young people aged 16 or 1 7 years can apply on their own behalf and that this must be accompanied by either : 57.1.1 written consent from their guardian; or 57.1.2 a letter of support from a suitably qualified third party . 57.2 I recommend that applications for children and young people aged 15 years and younger must be: 57.2.1 made on behalf of the child or young person , with their consent, by their guardian;14 and 57.2.2 be accompanied by a letter of support from a suitably qualified third party . 58. The additional measures for children and young people aged 15 years and under are more stringent than those for 16 and 17 year old s. This reflect s that 16 and 17 year olds are in later adolescen ce and generally have a higher level of cognitive development and can live independently from their guardians . I acknowledge that those aged 15 and under can have capacity to make informed decisions. However, this would require a case -by-case assessment, which would be difficult to set clearly in legislati on. 59. Recognising 16 and 17 year olds as more able to provide consent is consis tent with the process for changing a young person’s name under BDMRR Act . Under this process , the guardian applies on a young person’s behalf but must have the young person ’s consent if the y are aged 16 or over. It is also consistent with other legislation in New Zealand , for example , 16 is the age at which you can apply for a learner driver licence , and consent to general medical procedures. It also aligns with other jurisdictions where self-identification policies are often eased once a person turns 16 , such as in Norway, Portugal , and Belgium. 60. Note , I propose to retain the existing provisions in the BDMRR Act that enable young people aged under 18 to be treated as an adult where they are or have been in a marriage, civil union or de facto relationship. T hese young people will not need guardian consent or a letter of support from a third party.

WICS use econometric models to claim that o pex efficiencies of 50 percent are possible WICS has used an Ofwat 2004 econometric model to estimate that, after reform, larger New Zealand water entities can achieve up to a 53.3 percent efficiency impro vement to operating expenditure (opex) . To estimate the opex efficiencies, WICS combined 2003 -2004 data from the UK with recent data from N ew Zealand councils to estimate a performance baseline to measure New Zealand water entities against. To ensure comp atibility of the estimates with New Zealand’s operating environment, the gaps in efficiency between New Zealand entities and the benchmark w ere adjusted with ‘special factors’ related to regulatory, geographic and environmental factors that were considered unique to New Zealand. Based on observed efficiency gains from UK water reforms, WICS assumes that New Zealand water reforms may achieve th e same operating efficiency results – roughly a 50 percent improvement. It is important to note that these estimates are an assumed benchmark that provide s a guide to what might be possible based on experiences in the UK water sector but, as peer reviewer Farrier Swier note s, care needs to be taken as it is not possible to conclude that those efficiencies can be realised . 22F22F22F23 From observations of UK data, larger water entities – those serving populations greater than 800,000, realised larger efficiency improvements than smaller entities. The role of the third party would be to assess that the child or young person understands the amendment and that the decision is based on their own perceptions of their gender. It is important that the third party is suitably qualified to make this assessment but does not create a barrier by being difficult to access . Prescribing the third parties in regulations allows flexibility to experiment about how to achieve the right balance between prescribing third parties that can ensure a child and young person underst ands the decision and ensuring these third parties are accessible. 62. In develop ing the regulations target ed consultation will be completed with professional groups or people who may be suitable to act as the third party . Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 11 of 21 Regulation making powers are needed to give effect to my proposals 68. I propose a regulation making power to give full effect to the self -identification proposals outlined above. This power will be to enable regulations that prescribe: 68.1 the sex marker options other than the binary; 68.2 the additional requirements where a person amend s their registered sex more than once ; 68.3 the third parties who can provide a letter of support for applications for children and young people ; and 68.4 any other matters required to give effect to a self -identification process , which align with the overall intent of the proposals in this paper. There are further minor policy issues I intend to address 69. There are other, more minor, issues in the Bill to address. I am seeki ng Cabinet’s agreement that I can make decisions on the se issues . These issues include, but are not limited to: 69.1 a transition period for implementation of the self -identification provisions – up to 12 months may be required to ensure the technical infrastru cture is in place to give effect to the changes with the birth register ; 69.2 how a person’s previous re corded sex markers are treated on the birth register (eg are they closed or deleted); 69.3 clarify ing that section 33 in the BDMRR Act means that birth certifica tes are not conclusive evidence of someone’s sex or gender ; and 69.4 clarifying that where a person has amended their registered sex , previous names and sex markers must not be shown on the amended birth certificate . 70. These changes will be included in the self -identification SOP that I intend to bring to Cabinet in July 2021. Minor technical and operational improvements to the wider Bill 71. I am also seeking Cabinet agreement that I can make decisions on minor and technical change s associated with a separate SOP unrelated to self -identification. Other minor amendments will likely be needed to the Bill , which relate to the operation of and access to the Birth, Death and Marriage registers. These changes are needed to address operational issues that have been identi fied since the Bill was drafted in 2017 . These amendments will be made via a separate SOP later in the year. This SOP will not be referred to Select Committee and will be introduced at committee of the whole House stage. Addressing issues previously raised by Crown Law 72. The previous Minister of Internal Affairs cited and publicly released advice from Crown Law when they deferred the Bill in 2019. Crown Law raised that section 33 in the BDMRR Act, which states that a person’s sex should be determined by the “general law of New Zealand ,” is unclear. This provision means that birth certificates should not be the determining factor in decisions about a person’s sex and that consideration should be given to other legislation and the common law. I intend for this provision to be re - drafted, so its meaning is clarified. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 12 of 21 73. I believe that birth certificates should not be how a person’s sex is determined. In practice birth certificates are not relied on to determine access to women -only spaces (eg changing rooms or scho ols) or entitlements (eg sports teams or scholarships) and this should continue. 74. Related to this, Crown Law advised that clearer statutory guidance on how sex is determined could be beneficial (for example, what factors should be considered to determine a person’s sex). While I agree this could be useful, the matter is broader in scope than the BDMRR Act and the Internal Affairs portfolio. Work on this matter would require a cross -agency initiative as processes for determining sex are in place across numer ous institutions. Any further consideration of this matter should not delay the progress of introducing a self -identification process. Crown Law also raised the placement of people in prisons 75. Birth certificates are rarely required in legislation to determi ne someone’s sex or gender. While sex is referred to across legislation, t here is only one instance where sex on a birth certificate determines a person’s sex . This is the how the Department of Corrections (Corrections) determines the accommodation of peop le in male or female prisons. 76. Corrections determines placements in men’s and women’s prisons under the Corrections Regulations 2005 . These state that where there is doubt about if a person should be placed in a male or a female prison and a birth certificate is supplied, a person must be placed in accordance with the sex on the birth certificate . If a birth certificate is not provided, a review can be initiated where considerations include a person’s gender, safety and wellbeing, and wider considerations. Where people have a history of prior serious sexual offending against their nominated sex, the placement cannot be reviewed. 77.

15. Digital identity is central to the secure, people -centred digital delivery of services such as social prote ction, health care and finance. Digital identity has the potential to deliver significant economic and societal benefits in both the public and private sectors and through commercial market development. International studies have suggested that the potenti al benefit of enabling digital identity in a mature economy is between 0.5% and 3% of GDP (approximately $1.5 to $9 billion in NZD).3 16. Developing the digital identity ecosystem is also a critical component of achieving the Prime Minister’s commitment in th e Single Economic Market agenda towards mutual recognition of identity services with Australia. New Zealand and Australia are developing a roadmap for cross recognition of digital identities. This process can only commence once New Zealand’s requirements a re confirmed. 17. Digital identity can also enable digital trade and other cross -border transactions. One example involves the recently concluded Digital Economic Partnership Agreement (DEPA) between New Zealand, Chile and Singapore. The development of the dig ital identity ecosystem and interoperability will enable New Zealand to advance discussions on digital identity in the DEPA and other contexts as appropriate.

18 Further work is required on the development of the TF Authority’s complaints and dispute resolution operating model, before we can determine whether regulations are required to support the establishment and implementation of accessible, fair, timely , and cost -effective complaints and dispute resolution arrangements. This work will include considering what role, if any, an external alternative dispute resolution provider could play to support or complement the Authority’s compla ints investigation and compliance management functions. Complaints and dispute resolution process Figure 2 highlights key elements of the complaints and dispute resolution process provided for in the Act. Complaints must be about breaches : Under the Act the TF Authority is charged with addressing complaints received from any person that believes a TF provider has breached the provisions of the Act, the rules, the regulations , or the terms of use for the accreditation mark . The Complainant must try and reso lve a complaint directly with the TF Provider before involving the TF Authority: Complainants are expected to make reasonable efforts to resolve a complaint directly with the TF provider concerned before involving the TF Authority. This should involve usi ng a TF provider’s internal complaints resolution process and utilise any disputes resolution scheme or process that the TF provider is a party to th rough their membership of a particular industry. Preliminary Assessment : When the TF Authority receives a c omplaint it will complete a preliminary assessment. The assessment process will include providing the TF provider with the opportunity to comment on the complaint. The preliminary assessment can result in the TF Authority: • referring the complaint (in full or in part) to the Ombudsman, the Privacy Commissioner, the Inspector -General of Intelligence and Security 6 or another officeholder when, following consultation with those officeholders, the TF Authority determines the complaint falls within their jurisdi ction and would be more appropriately dealt with by them; • informing the parties to the complaint that it will not consider the complaint further and explaining its reasons ( the reasons for not further considering a complaint are outlined in section 73 of t he Act); or • deciding that a breach appears to have occurred.

Low Broad public views have been canvased through other mediums. • A good understanding of broad public views on self-identification has been developed based on: submissions received at Select Committee in 2018; considerable public debate; and related work by other agencies (eg StatsNZ’s work updating the statistical standards for gender, sex and variations of sex ch aracteristics ). The views have been taken into account in developing the policy proposals. • Referring the SOP to Select Committee will provide another opportunity for the public to provide feedback on the self -identification provisions. Young people and Māori, Pacific and ethnic communities’ views on a self - identification process have not been sought High No consultation with these communities has occurred . Medium These communities may express disappointment at not being involved in policy development , where their views would have been beneficial. •Targeted efforts will be made to reach out to young people and Māori, Pacific and ethnic communities to support them to access and engage in the Select Committee process. •Engagement will be undertaken with youn g people and Māori, Pacific, and ethnic communities as part of regulation development to explore options for culturally -inclusive sex markers and appropriate third parties who can provide the letter of support . Opposition from some individuals and groups to a self-identification model may affect the progression of the Bill High Opponents are critical that gender self -identification: •replaces a robust definition of sex; •undermines sex -based protections and will result in men accessing wom en-only spaces; and •creates opportunities for ‘predatory’ men to find ways to reach vulnerable women.Medium Groups opposed to self-identification will likely organise public campaigns that will generate significant media interest. These could delay the progress of the Bill (eg through a substantial number of Select Committee submissions) and provide misinformation about the changes it makes. Debate on this issue is likely to be divisive and could negatively impact the wellbeing of some individuals. •There is no evidence to suggest that a self-identification process will affect how people access women -only spaces (eg changing rooms) and entitlements (eg sports teams) as: o gender is already represented on passports without evidence of th is being abused; and o a birth certificate is not considered conclusive evidence of someone’s sex or gender and is not required to access women -only spaces or entitlements. •Any perceived risk that people would abuse the process is mitigated by: o the requirement to fill a statutory declaration form - falsifying a statutory declaration form is a criminal offence and can lead to imprisonment for up to three years; and o making it clearer in the Bill that birth certif icates should not be taken as conclusive evidence of someone’s sex or gender. •Communications material has been developed to manage expectations, likely questions and explain the rationale for a self -identification process. •Officials will be available to support Select Committee to make the submissions process safe for all parties and to support the wellbeing of those who want to submit. Introducing a self-identification process to amend registered sex 2 agreed that the Bill be amended to: 2.1 remove the requirement to obtain a declaration from the Family Court stating it is appropriate for a person’s registered sex to be amended; 2.2 remove the requirement for applicants to provide evidence of medical treatment that has enabled them to physically conform with the sex they want recorded on their birth certificate; 2.3 introduce a self-identification process where people apply directly to the Registrar- General of Births, Deaths and Marriages to amend their registered sex; 2.4 require an application to amend registered sex to include a statutory declaration verifying the person: 2.4.1 wants the sex marker on their birth certificate to match their identified gender; 2.4.2 intends to live as a person of this gender; and 2.4.3 understands the consequences of the application; 2.5 allow a range of sex markers reflecting genders other than the binary (male and female) and that these can be prescribed in regulations; 2 As at 30 June 2021, there were 1,059 venues operating 14,704 machines. This shows a trend for venues and machines decreasing, as venues peaked at more than 2,200 in the late 1990s and machines peaked at 25,221 in June 2003. Despite the decline in venues and machine s, total spend continues to increase. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Regulatory Impact Statement | 6 What is the policy problem or opportunity? 29. New Zealanders are spending almost a billion dollars every year at the pokies and t he level of harm associated with playing pokies is increasing - and wi ll continue to do so without Government intervention. This gambling harm has a negative effect on individuals , t heir whānau, friends and the wider community. This harm is also disproportionately affecting Māori, Pacific peoples and other population groups. 30. The key reasons for harm are the time spent gambling and the money lost. These affect people differently. In 2020 , about 4.5% of New Zealand adults self -reported some harm from their own gambling in the previous year. Gambling harm is widely believed to be underreported, in part due to the perceived stigma . 31. In addition, we know that people who have a problem with gambling on pokies are not usually identified in pubs and clubs. According to the Health and Lifestyles Survey 2020, over 60% of pokies reported that they had not any interaction with staff about their gambling. Interactions included: know my name or recognise me; monitor the pokie room; spoken to me with a concern about my gambling; given me a leaflet on gambling support services. 32. The current regulations do not ensure adequate use of some of the key levers for reducing pokies harm – controls in the gam bling venue, restrictions on machine features, and enforcement tools to drive compliance. The research and practice advice, such as the guidance issued by Te Hiringa Hauora have evolved since the Regulations were created in 2004 – and difference approaches are recommended as best practice in terms of venue management and game features. 33. S ome people are experiencing, or at risk of, a level of harm that could have been prevented or minimised. 34. A recent District Court decision has also identified that more prescriptive requirements are needed. A Christchurch patron with a n addiction to pokies , spent around $500,000 of earthquake insurance money on pokies over three years, before passing away suddenly. The manager of one of the venues he frequented was prosecuted for not identifying his problem. In a 299- day period, he’d spent over $75,000 there. On one single visit, he made 17 EFTPOS withdrawals totalling $2 ,700. Towards the end, he was there every second day. The venue missed all the signs of his addiction. 35. The decision [ Department of Internal Affairs v Suppressed [ expendexpendNZDC 11625] has shown, the need to set more prescriptive requirements for identifying gambling harm in venues. To summarise: • the venue manager was charged with failing to take reasonable steps to ensure that the venue’s harm minimisation policy was used to identify a problem gambler , • the reasonable steps included having systems to track multiple cash withdrawals and regular long play durations , • the Judge held that as these steps were not included in the harm minimisation policy, they were not self -evident requirements, and • the decision noted that these steps could be prescribed by regulations and that venue staff and gamblers would benefit from this. 36. The current ‘light touch’ regulation model, where societies and venues have been expected to develop and apply strong harm minimisation measures, has not been successful . A more prescriptive approach to harm minimisation could reduce the harm New Zealanders experience from gambling on pokies. Advocates in the harm prevention and minimisation sector, as well as local authorities, have been asking for stronger measures for some time. 37. Preventing and minimising harm is one of the purposes of the Act - and the sole purpose of the Regulations. The Act contemplates a substantially higher level of regulation in relation to Class 4 gambling than is currently used. Detailed regulation- making powers are provided for : • harm prevention and minimisation (section 313); • gaming machines (section 314); • admission to, and exclusion from, gambling venues (section 315); • exclusion of problem gamblers (section 316); and • infringement offences for the breach of any regulations (section 360). Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Regulatory Impact Statement | 7 38. The range of regulation- making powers provide an opportunity to create a stronger harm minimisation approach. Government intervention, by way of strengthening harm minimisation requirements, which could reduce the harm on individuals and their communities. In line with the scope, we could: • set more explicit direction for venues and societies ; • providing more player information on pokie games and make features less addictive; and • providing supporting offences and penalties for the regulations. What objectives are sought in relation to th e policy problem? 39. The core objective is to reduce the level of individual (and, by extension, second- hand) gambling harm being experienced from pokies in venues. Our more specific objectives , in line with the Minister’s scope decision s, are to: • make it easier for venues and societies to reduce harm ; • make pokie machines safer ; and • creates consequences for breaches of the regulations . 40. The secondary objective, for the next stage of work post -consultation, will be to ensure any proposed regulations are cost effective and not overburdening for the organisations impacted by them (societies, venues and the Regulator).

2 Focus area two: Strengthening our capability This focus area is about ensuring our people, processes and systems are all fit for purpose – aligned to our strategy and flexible enough to accommodate change. Strategic initiatives RSG’s capability initiatives reflect a strong emphasis on kaimahi development, including tools which support career progression and success planning (for example, the capability framework and workforce plan). They also identify where RSG has identified there may be gaps in terms of either capability or functions and that some work will be undertaken to more fully assess these. The development of a cross-RSG ICT roadmap is about ensuring that system groups are individually equipped with the technology resources they need now and for the future, and that every opportunity is taken to maximise existing and future systems for the benefit of all RSG. Managing risk is an important part of RSG’s role. An RSG risk tolerance policy will articulate the Group’s risk appetite and tolerance, clarifying what constitutes acceptable risk-taking so that RSG can more effectively manage risk and take advantage of opportunities as they arise.
