55 Affected employees who are not reassigned will be consulted individually about other options. If no other options are identified, notice will be given and redundancy provisions apply. Affected employees Before final decisions are announced, all potentially affected employees will be notified individually. Employees may be informed that they:  have been reconfirmed in a position and are no longer affected, or  are affected and will be considered for reassignment. Reconfirmation process Prior to announcement of the final decisions, an assessment will be made to determine if employees meet the criteria for reconfirmation. This assessment will be made by the group General Manager/Director, with support from HR, and approved by the Deputy Chief Executive, Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy. The reconfirmation process requires a comparison between existing positions and those in the new structure to determine if they are the same or nearly the same. The criteria for reconfirmation are:  the new job description is the same or nearly the same as the job the affected employee currently does;  the salary is the same;  the terms and conditions, including career prospects are no less favourable; and  the location is the same or in the same vicinity.

56 Reassignment process The purpose of the reassignment process is to place affected employees, who have not been reconfirmed into positions in the new structure, into suitable alternative positions. A suitable alternative position is one that involves duties that are not unreasonable taking into account the employee’s skills, knowledge, qualifications and experience, and where the employee could reasonably be expected to carry out those duties with a reasonable amount of training and development. A reassignment panel of the group General Manager or Director and a representative from Human Resources will consider all expressions of interest and seek to reassign employees based on a balance of:  the employee’s preference(s)  suitability for the position  placing as many employees as possible.

Reconfirmation or reassignment review process Employees have the right to seek a review of the reconfirmation decision where they do not consider that the criteria have been applied correctly. Employees who register a preference or preferences for reassignment also have the right to seek a review of the reassignment decision where they are not offered reassignment to any of the positions for which they registered a preference. Employees who do not register a preference for reassignment cannot seek a review of reassignment decisions. Any request for a review, including the grounds for the review, must be communicated in writing to the Deputy Chief Executive, Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy within 3 working days of the reconfirmation or reassignment decision being communicated. If requested, employees will be provided with the documentation associated with the reconfirmation or reassignment decision under review that relates directly to them. They will not be provided with specific information or documentation regarding other affected employees. Reviewers will be independent of the original reconfirmation or reassignment panel and will be agreed by the Deputy Chief Executive, Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy and the employee and/or their representative. Any recommendations made by the reviewer will be considered by the Deputy Chief Executive, Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy, who will decide whether any recommendations made by the reviewer will be implemented. Review decisions are final - there is no internal appeal process. Released under the Official Information Act 1982

A refreshed approach to funding during and immediately after an emergency 266. In addition to an overall shift in the investment approach to emergency management, there needs to be some specific changes to the way funds for response activities are administered and a reappraisal of which costs are eligible. The current state for funding response and immediate readiness activities 267. The current objectives of government financial support for local government during and immediately before an emergency focus on caring for directly affected people, and preventative actions to reduce immediate danger to human life or to reduce the potential consequences of an emergency. 62 Current government policy is that councils can apply for reimbursement of 100% of welfare costs they incur in caring for displaced people.63 Central government will fund 60% of other eligible activities above a threshold based on the net capital value of the council. Eligible activities include the repair of essential infrastructure like water, storm water, electrical, sewerage and gas assets as well as other council-owned structures like retaining walls and tunnels upon which essential services depend. Both these funding functions (welfare, and other response costs) are administered by NEMA. 268. Councils are responsible for most other response costs, including for example repairs to local roads. In practice, government funding is made available to councils and communities to support this response spending through a range of government agencies. Increasingly, it is also provided through event-specific bespoke government funds like the North Island Weather Events funding package. In addition, different government agencies provide funding for specific activities or sectors, ranging from support for farmers to silt removal following Cyclone Gabrielle. 269. Councils can also request reimbursement of funds that were incurred by iwi and other organisations with a formalised role in providing welfare services after an emergency. The Emergency Management Bill includes provisions for iwi and Māori organisations to be directly reimbursed for welfare costs within the criteria set at the time of the emergency. 64 We support the intent of this provision, reflecting the key role of iwi Māori organisations in providing welfare services.

58 Remaining affected employees Employees who remain affected following the Branch reassignment process will be notified of this, and the Department will work with the employee to identify other potential reassignment opportunities elsewhere in the Department. Affected employees may then apply and be considered for any potentially suitable vacancies. Affected employees will have preferential right of appointment over non-affected employees and external candidates in the event that their suitability for the position is assessed as being the same. Other options Employees not placed through reassignment are advised in writing that they are surplus and will be consulted individually about the potential for other options to be agreed. There may be vacancies within the wider Department which could be considered suitable for employees affected by this change process. Affected employees may apply and be considered for any potentially suitable vacancies. Affected employees will have preferential right of appointment over non-affected employees and external candidates in the event that their suitability for the position is assessed as being the same. Upon acceptance of appointment to another position within the Department, employees are no longer affected by the review. Where another option is agreed with the affected employee, this will be confirmed in writing and the employee will no longer be considered affected. Notice If the Department determines that no other option can be agreed, the affected employee will be provided notice in line with their employment agreement. Where a longer notice period is preferred for operational transition reasons, this may be agreed between the Department and the affected employee. During the notice period, the Department and the employee may consider any opportunities for other options that may arise. The number of DVD rental stores has declined from 500 in 2008, to 30 in 2018. Retail stores selling DVDs has declined from 590 in 2008, to 120 in 2018. Revenue from user-charges arising from the classification of DVDs have also reduced. Over the last ten years, income from classifying commercial publications such as DVDs and films for release in theatres has reduced by 66 percent. Due to the decreasing market for physical material, such as DVDs, increasing fees for the classification of physical media content may cause this classification activity to further decline. DVD distributers may not be able to sustain increased charges and there may be a flow-on effect for consumers and viewers if less content is made available. Funding for OFLC’s CVoD related activities is needed The classification of CVoD content is currently unregulated and there is no charging regime in place. This has created uneven business costs between distributors of media content such as DVDs and distributers of media content screened via online platforms. The Government is progressing an amendment to the Classification Act that will require CVoD content to be classified and allow CVoD providers to self-rate their content. The classification of CVoD content before screening will minimise the risk of harm to children and young people. It will support informed viewing choices by all New Zealanders by ensuring content has the appropriate classification, rating and advisory notes consistent with the New Zealand classification regime. The Amendment Bill is expected to be passed into law by mid-2020. CVoD providers will be able to classify their material in three ways: • using a self-classification Rating Tool designed by OFLC and co-created with industry; • by using an OFLC approved and accredited system to self-rate content; and • by submitting material to the FVLB. Further information about the Amendment Bill is available from the Department’s website. OFLC will be undertaking new activities related to regulating CVoD content. Estimates of the costs to operate the classification system Overheads (accommodation, depreciation, administration, and executive salaries not directly attributable to OFLC’s classification or information activities) represent OFLC’s main expenditure. Overall, OFLC’s largest expenditure item is personnel. In 2018/19, it cost OFLC $2.869 million to carry out its statutory functions. OFLC completed a restructure during 2017/18 which reduced its costs as far as practicable while maintaining its ability to meet its statutory obligations. OFLC’s workforce reduced by 40 percent as result of the restructure. OFLC now operates with 16 full time staff. Current fee levels are causing OFLC to project ongoing deficits. A summary of options assessed against principles is provided as Appendix D . 19 Review of options for funding the classification framework – Consultation documentCost-recovery options Which OFLC costs are covered by the cost-recovery options? The cost-recovery options discussed below refer only to the costs of Commercial classifications, including the costs of CVoD classifications. Classifications in this category make up approximately 40 percent of OFLC’s current annual budget (an estimated $1.2 million in 2020/21). For the purpose of this consultation and the setting of any subsequent charges, the following costs will be met by the Crown and are not included in the cost-recovery options: • Crown classifications; • OFLC’s information services, including a proportion of research costs; and • fee waivers for the purposes of cultural benefits. The rationale for this approach is that the New Zealand community is the principal beneficiary of those activities not included in cost-recovery proposals. Considerations of effectiveness, equity and fairness indicate that the Government should bear the costs involved, which make up approximately 60 percent of OFLC’s current annual budget (an estimated $1.806 million in 2020/21, not including the funding agreed by the Government in September 2019 for OFLC to respond to increased demand for its services following the Christchurch terror attacks). Cost-recovery for current Commercial classifications The current approach to funding Commercial classifications was established in 1993. It involves the Crown and submitters sharing the costs. The options below step back from the current approach and ask: who should pay for current Commercial classifications, and how much each party should pay? Who benefits from current Commercial classifications, and how much? A key question in considering cost-recovery options for classification is: who benefits? Considerations of equity and fairness in particular suggest that the main beneficiaries should meet the costs, although a number of other factors (for example, ability to pay) may need to be taken into account. New Zealand’s classification system creates significant benefits for distributors, consumers, and the wider community. Rating systems are widely used by commercial distributors, whether or not there is any government involvement. Rating systems provide information which helps to define and promote the distributor’s products. By doing so, they help consumers make informed choices. Consumers value rating systems for the information they provide. The wider community benefits from rating systems, particularly because they help to protect individuals from the harm which arises from people viewing material that is inappropriate for their level of maturity. If the viewer doesn’t have the psychological resources needed to take a healthy perspective on what they see, they may suffer personal harm or inflict harm on others. Government involvement in the provision of a New Zealand classification system reflects the fact that the community as a whole prefers a rating system that is different for example, more stringent, more informative, than what would be produced as a result of private arrangements between distributors and consumers. 20 Review of options for funding the classification framework – Consultation documentIncentives to keep costs low While equity and fairness may suggest that the Government and the sector should pay for the costs of classification, quantifying respective benefits can be challenging and may also be complicated by other considerations. The activities of distributors give rise to the risk of harm from media content, indicating that their share of the costs of classification should reflect this. Conversely, our classification system only exists in its present form because this is what the community wants, which supports the view that the Government should take responsibility for meeting the costs of the system. Any contribution to funding from the sector may produce benefits in terms of incentivising the provider to minimise costs. New Zealand distributors display a keen awareness of the cost of classification and a preference for those costs, or at least their contribution, being kept as low as possible. The degree of distributor influence on our system’s cost- efficiency will be enhanced by making the operations of OFLC as transparent as possible, through continued, regular review and setting of charges. Other evidence for different approaches to funding New Zealand’s classification system There is evidence that private distributors would prefer to use their own systems rather than participate in the official New Zealand system (suggesting that distributors may need to incur net costs to meet the requirements of the New Zealand system). However, this evidence is fragmented. Applications for CVoD classification fell significantly1 after a 2015 legal ruling which said that CVoD content was not covered by the Classification Act. Nevertheless, some distributors such as Google and Sony have continued to voluntarily submit CVoD items for classification. The fact that the sector and the community receive benefits from classification does not dictate what approach should be taken to cost-recovery. For example, the federal Australian equivalent to our 9 For example, a major distributor of CVoD material submitted 1480 items to OFLC for classification in the 18 months leading up to August 2015. The same distributor has submitted no items since the 2015 legal ruling.classification system is largely funded by the sector through classification fees2 and the British equivalent is 100 percent sector-funded. By comparison, the New Zealand sector is currently paying approximately 24 percent of the costs of OFLC activities. Past patterns of funding for the New Zealand system also offer minimal guidance about how responsibility for the cost of the system should be divided between the Crown and the sector. Classification costs overall have varied over the years, as has income from the sector. They do not represent a recommended approach, although all can be supported by principles-based arguments. QUESTION 5: What impact would the cost implications in the scenarios under each option have on your business or activity? 25 Review of options for funding the classification framework – Consultation documentDiscounted rates for cost-recovery (waivers and reductions) This section addresses the question: should reduced rates of cost-recovery apply to certain groups and classification activities? At present, certain categories of distributor and classification activities qualify for lower rates of cost- recovery. Current Regulations give the Chief Censor wide discretion to reduce or waive fees. For example, fees can be reduced for special interest groups and charitable organisations, and up to 75 percent of the fee can be waived in situations where the charging of the full fee would be unreasonable, unfair or unduly burdensome. In terms of volume and income foregone, these provisions are mainly applied to film festivals and groupings of films and DVDs. Film festivals may have up to 75 percent of classification fees waived on grounds of the cultural benefits to the community arising from their activities. Publications submitted as a group are required to pay only one classification fee, even though multiple items (for example, a box set of DVDs) are involved. The grouping provision recognises that classifying a group of similar items (for example, multiple episodes of a television series) takes less time than classifying the equivalent number of unrelated items such as films, and that the full fee applied to groups of DVDs and some films such as groups of short films would be unduly burdensome. The level of fee revenue forgone under current waiver and reductions provisions is projected as $399,049 in 2020/21. Table 14 Waivers and reductions Waivers and reductions Financial impact • Waivers and reductions currently impact on the amount paid by submitters for classification services. A film festival, for example, may pay $281 to have one film classified. This represents a reduction of $843 from the standard fee. • Projected income foregone in 2020/21 through cultural benefit waivers is approximately $142,000, or 35 percent of the shortfall in revenue for that year. • The operation of waiver and reduction provisions affect the quantum of costs that must be recovered either from those who don’t qualify, or from the Crown. Advantages • Waivers and reductions recognise that some media content provides significant cultural benefits and the cost of classifying some items are lower than for others or would otherwise be unduly burdensome for some providers. Disadvantages • If the sector has to pick up the costs of concessions relating to cultural benefits, cross-subsidisation would be involved (cross-subsidisation can be associated with inefficiency, inequity and lack of transparency). • Challenges in quantifying cultural benefits of media content, with associated risks of over-payment or under-payment. • The current waivers and reductions system involves significant handling costs for OFLC, the FVLB and distributors. Implementation • A system of concessionary rates could be developed for CVoD classification. • If the present system of concessionary rates is retained - no implementation issues. Cost-recovery for OFLC’s CVoD activities This section addresses the question: who should pay for OFLC’s CVoD related activities, and how much should each party pay? The arguments for Crown versus sector funding of CVoD classification are similar to those for funding classifications under the existing Regulations. The funding approaches chosen for the traditional media such as DVDs, games, films in theatres and CVoD content therefore need to be consistent. Any difference between the two approaches would need to be clearly justified. The options discussed below assess whether the Crown, the sector, or a mix should fund the classification system. Options for feedback The CVoD costs, estimated fees and levies are estimates and should be treated as indicative only. The funding levels (100 percent and 50 percent cost-recovery) chosen for scenarios are illustrative and do not represent a preferred solution. Advantages • Costs are recovered from submitters who are major beneficiaries of classification and whose activities give rise to the risk of harm from some types of media content. • Users pay the costs they give rise to. Disadvantages • The community receives significant benefits from classification over and above the private benefits to submitters, by way of harm reduction and increased information to support consumption choices but would not pay for the benefits it receives. Implementation Transition to full cost-recovery could be: • implemented as a one-off increase; or • phased in over two to three years (this option would produce budget shortfalls in the period leading up to full cost-recovery, which would need to be funded). Children and young people can change the sex on their birth certificate using the Family Court process. We recommend replacing the Family Court process with a self-identification process for children and young people. Children and young people are high users of birth certificates as a form of identity as they often do not have entitlement or access to a driver license or passport. It is important that they can feel safe using their birth certificates and feel accepted for who they are as they grow up. 57. The policy changes required to introduce self-identification for children and young people are more complex and potentially controversial. We have not had time to fully assess the implications and impacts of introducing a self-identification process for children. We are still considering the requirements for: 57.1 parent al or guardian consent – for example, ensuring we have policy around children or young people who are unable to gain consent, are wards of the state, or have multiple parents or guardians ; 57.2 differentiating requirements for different age groups – the current drafting creates a separate category for 16- or 17-year olds that may add unnecessary complexity to the process ; and 57.3 requiring letters of support, for example from a health professional – further work is required to determine what assurances we would be seeking through a letter of support and who would be best placed to provide that. 58. We are seeking an in-principle agreement to introduce a self-identification process for children and young people to change the sex on their birth certificates. We will provide further advice on the details set out above in April. Further consideration is needed on establishing a limit to the number of changes allowed 59. The select committee recommended only allowing for one change of gender (except under special circumstances). Agency feedback clearly argued against this, particularly for children, as gender is a deeply personal choice that can change over time. We will consider this issue further and provide advice in April. Self-identification has implications for Corrections regulations 60. Birth certificates are rarely used to determine someone’s sex or gender. There is only one instance we have found where changing sex on a birth certificate would have implications for other legislation. Sex on a birth certificate will not override agency discretion to determine the accommodation of prisoners 61. The Department of Corrections makes decisions about the accommodation of male and female prisoners. Currently, if a birth certificate is supplied a placement must be made in accordance with the sex listed on the certificate (unless the person seeks a review of the determination).
