Source: NZTA 21 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY ABOUT THE INQUIRY PREFACE RECOMMENDATIONS 22 Government Inquiry into the Response to the North Island Severe Weather EventsRecommendations Emergency management system design and structure Recommendation 1: Put people and their communities at the heart of an integrated emergency management system A. Legislate for and invest in an inclusive, community-led emergency management model that explicitly recognises the knowledge and capability of iwi Māori, businesses, and local communities in emergency management. B. Utilise existing community-based emergency management structures and systems, such as those built through the COVID-19 response, to ensure community participation in planning and response. C. Build networks of trained and accredited local community leaders and volunteers, which extends beyond the currently recognised volunteer groups. D. Develop and invest in a comprehensive and ongoing education and public awareness programme to ensure people have a common understanding of how to prepare for (readiness planning) and what to do in an emergency. Recommendation 2: Utilise the value of the wider government ecosystem A. Expand the New Zealand Defence Force’s role to make better use of specialist skills (such as logistics and air coordination) during a significant civil defence emergency. B. Note the Inquiry endorses the Weather Forecasting System Review to (among other matters) identify changes in access to weather data. C. Require that timely and enhanced weather and hydrological forecasting is provided to and used by all councils and government agencies. D. Note the Inquiry endorses the work of the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet (DPMC) to lift the resilience of New Zealand’s critical infrastructure. Recommendation 3: Optimise the effort of iwi Māori to benefit all people in an emergency A. Note the Inquiry endorses the 2017 Ministerial Review into Better Responses to Natural Disasters and Other Emergencies recommendations: I. “Recognise the capability that iwi bring to emergency management; II. Legislate to enable iwi to participate in planning for and responding to a natural disaster or other emergency, and to bring more clarity to their role: • Appropriate iwi representatives to be part of the Groups Coordinating Executive Group; • Appropriate iwi representatives to be included on the Group Joint Committee”. B. Empower iwi Māori who have the capacity, capability, and desire to contribute to emergency management. Recommendation 4: Invest in a refocused National Emergency Management Agency A. Legislate for and invest in the National Emergency Management Agency’s (NEMA) primary function and purpose to hold system leadership for emergency readiness and response. In making these changes: I. responsibility for leadership and coordination of critical infrastructure remains with NEMA for readiness and response only II. leadership for reduction and recovery to be referred to DPMC to request that the Hazard Risk Board considers which agency should hold functional leadership responsibility, and to ensure there is a single point of contact for critical infrastructure entities on reduction III. leadership for welfare coordination should sit with the Ministry of Social Development and NEMA’s welfare responsibilities be clarified, and IV. leadership for natural hazards and support for other emergencies remains with NEMA. B. Strengthen monitoring and assurance of the system: I. provide NEMA with the necessary authority and powers to set standards and fulfil its assurance functions II. invest in NEMA’s monitoring and assurance function to ensure roles, responsibilities, and functions at all levels of the system are performed, and III. require that organisations with responsibilities under emergency management legislation have effective business continuity plans and assets in place, and report to NEMA annually for review. Leadership, roles, and responsibilities Recommendation 5: Clarify roles in emergency management A. Explicitly clarify the roles of central, regional, and local levels of government in a national state of emergency. 23 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY ABOUT THE INQUIRY PREFACE RECOMMENDATIONS 24 Government Inquiry into the Response to the North Island Severe Weather EventsB. Clarify and strengthen, in legislation, the governance role of mayors and chairs during an emergency. C. To strengthen regional and local council governance accountability for readiness and leading response, require that: I. the chair of the Civil Defence Emergency Management Group is the chair of the regional council, or the mayor in the case of a unitary council (noting that a chair or mayor can delegate within the regional or unitary council) II. regional and local authority chief executives become the primary controller and can delegate to suitably qualified individuals, while retaining overall accountability, and III. controllers acting under delegation are employed by, or seconded to, the council, and accountable to the council through the chief executive. Recommendation 6: Increase capability and capacity in civil defence emergency management across New Zealand A. Increase command and control capability in emergency management governance, leadership, and controller roles. B. Implement a national programme for emergency management capability-building across New Zealand. C. Build a larger pool of skilled and experienced controllers, hydrologists, and other specialists, who provide expert information and can be seconded across New Zealand. D. Establish at least three full-time Emergency Management Assistance Teams (EMAT), that can be deployed to emergencies or to build wider sector capability. Management of the immediate response Recommendation 7: Build fit-for-purpose National Crisis Management Centres A. Move the National Crisis Management Centre to a new, improved, purpose-built facility. B. Identify and invest in a back-up National Crisis Management Centre in a city other than Wellington, potentially using an existing purpose-built civil defence emergency management facility. Recommendation 8: Improve real time situational awareness for authorities in emergency events A. Legislate for and invest in a single common operating platform and picture for emergency management to be adopted by every council and NEMA. B. Review the 111 system to ensure information relevant to the emergency is shared between New Zealand Police, Fire and Emergency New Zealand, and ambulance providers, and supports efficient tasking across emergency response services. Recommendation 9: Develop a comprehensive warning system for the public A. Develop a comprehensive warning system that is flexible enough to cover all natural hazards and empowers the public to act, even when technology fails. Recommendation 10: Amend the three-day self-sufficiency guidance A. Improve and promote guidance that people and communities need to be self-sufficient for at least seven days (or 14 days for isolated communities). Supply of goods and services and the place of critical infrastructure Recommendation 11: Restore power and telecommunications early and improve electricity resilience A. Ensure controllers prioritise early restoration of power and telecommunications as a key enabler of the coordination and delivery of emergency services. B. Strengthen the Electricity (Hazards from Trees) Regulations 2003 to improve the resilience of the electricity network. Recommendation 12: Recognise a wider group of critical infrastructure entities A. Formally recognise the following as necessary critical infrastructure sectors (in addition to current lifeline utilities): I. supermarkets II. waste management III. stopbank and flood protection systems IV. rural water, and V. river management systems. 25 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY ABOUT THE INQUIRY PREFACE RECOMMENDATIONS 26 Government Inquiry into the Response to the North Island Severe Weather EventsFunding settings Recommendation 13: Prioritise strategic investment in reduction and readiness activities A. Increase the appropriation for the existing contestable fund that is administered by NEMA to support a significant uplift in community readiness and resilience across New Zealand. B. Note the Inquiry endorses recommendation 13b of the report by the Future for Local Government Review: I. “In order to prioritise and deliver on wellbeing, central government makes a greater investment in local government through… significant funding to support local priorities, place-based agreements, and devolution of roles.” Recommendation 14: Update the policy settings, criteria, and process for funding and distributing response costs A. Move the administration of welfare related costs to the Ministry of Social Development as the proposed leader for welfare coordination and reassess welfare funding criteria to cover a broader definition of welfare. B. Review the current reimbursement process for distribution of non-welfare related response and immediate readiness costs to allow funds to flow more freely (with appropriate oversight). C. Allow the Director of Civil Defence Emergency Management to approve ex-gratia payments (subject to clear criteria) for those situations where individuals/groups incurred costs during an emergency. A position which is more than one level or tier below an employee’s previous position will not generally be considered a suitable alternative, however each situation will be considered on its merits based on the requirements of the new position and the employee’s skills, knowledge, qualifications and experience. Note that there are two types of reassignment:  non-contestable reassignments occur when there are an equal number of affected employees (or less employees) to suitable vacancies. Affected employees will be asked to submit an EOI to demonstrate that they have the skills required to fill a ring- fenced vacancy. Where their skills match the requirements of the vacancy they will be reassigned to that position. An interview and/or other form of assessment may also be used to identify that they have the skills required to fill a ring-fenced vacancy.  a contestable reassignment process is required when there are more affected employees than suitable vacancies. Affected employees will be asked to submit an EOI to demonstrate they have the skills required to fill the vacancy(s). An interview and/or other form of assessment may also be used to identify which employees are best suited for reassignment to available vacancies Also, in order to maximise the appointment and retention of employees through the reassignment process and to take account of overall Department needs, reassignments may be offered to positions that are not the individual’s preference. Furthermore, an employee may be offered a reassignment even if they have not submitted any preferences at all. The steps in the reassignment process are as follows: 1. Accreditation is not mandatory. While digital identity service providers do not need to become accredited to deliver a service, there are benefits. Alignment with other health and social services Rates of harmful drinking, tobacco use, other drug use and psychological distress tend to be much higher among people experiencing problem gambling (a high risk of gambling harm) and, to a lesser extent, among moderate- and low-risk gamblers , than they are among the general population. Those living in areas with a higher social deprivation score are also more likely to experience gambling harm. The service plan will continue to promote actions that better align services that prevent and minimise gambling harm with other health and social services in the 2019/20 – 2021/22 period. Where gamblers experience significant comorbidities, we will also explore options for developing more holistic packages of care. Outcomes-focused agreements The Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment has incorporated Results-Based Accountability™ principles into a streamlined contract framework that government agencies and NGOs can use to identify, measure and monitor achievement of outcomes. The Ministry implemented outcomes-focused agreements incorporating these principles for its preventing and minimising gambling harm contracts in January 2018, and expects to refine these based on learning from audit, evaluation and research in the 2019/20 –2021/22 period. Changes in gambling participation and expenditure While the overall gambling participation rates as a percentage of the population have been static over the past five years or so, the total numbers of ‘at-risk ’ gamblers in the population have increased in line with population growth. Changes in gambling participation and expenditure tend to have long-term flow-on effects on the prevalence of gambling harm and the number of people seeking help for gambling problems, although the causes of harmful gambling behaviour are complex. The overall amount gamblers spent on the four main forms of gambling in New Zealand has increased each year since 2010/11, most recently from $2.209 billion in the 2015/16 financial year to $2.334 billion in 2016/17. Adjusting for the effects of inflation and changes to the New Zealand population (aged 18 years and over), this was an overall increase of 1.1 percent over the six-year time period. Section 4.3 outlines changes in player expenditure and player expenditure forecasts, for each of the main forms of gambling. Any Ministry publication that outlines the concepts and evidence from research to inform the approach to reducing gambling harm will help raise awareness in the gambling sector of the knowledge base that informs the strategy. 2.10Strategic framework 2019/20 –2021/22 The Ministry has made relatively minor changes to the strategic plan/framework that was published in 2016/17, to better target reductions in health inequities. The strategic framework is based on an outcomes framework agreed by both the gambling industry and gambling harm services in 2012/13. The Ministry expects to revisit the strategic aim and objectives during the next levy period, to ensure they remain fit for purpose. Most submissions the Ministry received on the consultation document supported the general direction of the strategy and strategic objectives; many also commented in detail on matters that were of particular importance to them. The Ministry has made some changes to the strategic priorities and actions, with the aim of highlighting specific matters, while bearing in mind the objectives are intended to be set at a high level, and the service plan in Section 3 addresses operational matters. Overall goal of the strategic plan The Ministry is committed to a long-term approach that has not significantly changed from the approach outlined in its first six-year strategic plan in 2005. The overall goal is: Government, the gambling sector, communities and families/whānau working together to prevent and minimise gambling harm, and to reduce related health inequities. Eleven strategic objectives The following 11 strategic objectives guide the strategic direction for the actions in the service plan. Objective 1: There is a reduction in gambling-harm-related inequities between population groups (particularly Māori , Pacific and Asian peoples, as the populations that are most vulnerable to gambling harm). Objective 2: Māori have healthier futures, through the prevention and minimisation of gambling harm. Objective 3: People participate in decision-making about activities in their communities that prevent and minimise gambling harm. Objective 4: Healthy policy at the national, regional and local level prevents and minimises gambling harm. Approach to change The strategy will result in some ongoing refinement for RSG. RSG leaders are committed to managing this in a considered and transparent way, ensuring planning, implementation and evaluation of change are factored into the implementation of the strategy. This change is likely to take place over time. RSG will put people at the heart of the change; people-centric change is about ensuring the full participation of our people in the design and implementation of change initiatives. It is also important to acknowledge that change happens at an individual level, which means finding different ways to seek to involve everyone – starting with ensuring a shared understanding of why and how we are changing, what needs to happen for the change to be effective and enduring, and how we will practically implement it.On this basis, the RSG approach to managing change is likely to include some of the following: ◆Using a change methodology that puts people at the centre of the change (for example, Prosci ADKAR) ◆Ensuring RSG leaders are engaged and prepared to successfully lead and support the change ◆Engaging with everyone in RSG early – and communicating often along the way ◆Working collaboratively and sharing ideas ◆Sharing plans to get different perspectives from different stakeholders on different things ◆Learning from each other ◆Preparing RSG people well, to be ready for change ◆Celebrating successes along the way ◆Learning from experiences by listening to leaders and kaimahi 35 Our approach to change Understand the change Involve people early to understand why we are making the change, who is impacted and what is needed to support them Connecting people Working together and involving all key stakeholders is critical to ensure the needs of our people are met, and a smooth transition for everyoneAwareness Desire Knowledge Ability ReinforcementIdentify gaps Analysing the impacts from several perspectives to understand what supports, connections, and resources are needed Embedding Ask impacted people what they think and how they are feeling about the change. Continue to engage and support. Ensure benefits are realised and positive stories are shared Planning and integration Ensuring the right people and change activities are coordinated and integrated where possible, in a sequence that makes sense Engagement Engage and support our people. Our engagement will help our people understand ‘what’s in it for me’ and the end goal Readiness Check that everyone feels comfortable, things are ready to go and the right people know what’s happening

Approval of the Pūtaringamotu Riccarton Bush Bylaw 2023 We have been contacted by the Riccarton House and Bush Trust (the Trust) who need decisions from you and the Governor -General to make a new bylaw operative. The Trust is a council -controlled organisation of the Christchurch City Council. It was established by the Riccarton Bush Act 1914 (the Act) to manage 12 hectares of land gifted to the people of Canterbury. T he property includes Riccarton House and Deans Cottage, the first house built on the Canterbury Plains. The Act enables the Trust to make, alter and repeal bylaws for the operation and management of the property. Bylaws made by the Trust must be approved b y the Governor -General and gazetted before becoming operative. The Trust adopted the Pūtaringamotu Riccarton Bush Bylaw 2023 at a meeting on 28 June 2023. It is intended to replace the Riccarton Bush By -laws 1955 and is the first amendment to the trust’s b ylaws since 1955. The Cabinet Office has advised that the Governor -General can approve the Trust’s bylaw on advice from a Minister. In your role as Minister of Local Government you are considered the most appropriate Minister to advise the Governor - General on this as the Trust is a council -controlled organisation and the Department administers both the Riccarton Bush Act 1914 and the Bylaws Act 1910. This is a procedural matter of low priority that we will advise you on as resourcing allows. We are conscio us that the Trust first raised this with the Department on 31 July 2023 and resolution has been delayed because of the election and higher priority work. To avoid unreasonable further delay for the Trust we will aim to have this advice to you by May 2024. Officials have been communicating with the Trust, so it is aware that this is being actioned. As the world becomes increasingly digitised, every country around the world is having to come to terms with the emerging issues around the sharing, usage, and storage of information in a digital manner. G iven these issues are relatively new, this placed some key limitation and constraints on the Department’s analysis. These limitati ons and constraints are outlined below. The variety in comparable jurisdictions The Department consulted with a wide variety of international partners, including comparable jurisdictions such as the United Kingdom, Canada and Australia, to identify and assess intervention options. While there was broad agreement with establishing a Trust Framework, each country has to contend with certain unique features (e.g. federal structure, constitutional constraints) . This created minor differences in approaches to the implementation of a Trust Framework which meant that lessons identified, and implementation options , could not always be readily adopted in the Department’s options analysis. Sometimes assumptions had to be made regarding options in a New Zealand context, for example, as a unitary state New Zealand has national standards for identification management, whereas federal jurisdictions such as Australia need to align the identification standards and approaches of each state with a federal approach . The limi tations around consultation All stakeholders were consulted on their views regarding the challenges with digital identity services and how they thought these could be addressed, but not all stakeholders were directly consulted on the options that are prese nted in this assessment. Additionally, engagement with Māori stakeholders remains in its infancy. Iwi have shown a desire to work collaboratively with government to enhance digital iwi registration processes in line with tikanga Māori, however, it takes ti me to establish enduring relationships. As a result of these challenges, some of the options analysis is based on assumptions that proposals would match to, and deliver on, the feedback received.

Attribute: An item of information that describes something about an individual or organisation (such as an individual’s name or address, or a company’s registration number or New Zealand business number) . This definition may change as part of work to develop the Digital Identity Trust Framework. Authenticator: one or more things known and/or possessed by a user (such as a login, a code, a piece of software, or a device) . This definition may change as part of work to develop the Digital Identity Trust Framework. Credential: A record kept in digital form that: (a) is issued to an individual or an organisation by an infrastructure provider; (b) describes one or more identity or other attributes about the individual or organisation; and (c) is [usually] bound to an authenticator . This definition may change as part of work to develop the Digital Identity Trust Framework. Confirmation Service: The Confirmation Service allows organisations to validate biographic identity information against the source database/register. Retrieval Service: The Retrieval Service allows the Police and potentially the Ministry of Justice in the future, to enter biographic data and then access the photo of that individual for law enforcement purpose . RealMe services: There are two elements to the RealMe service. The RealMe login service allows people to access multiple online services with a common username and password. A RealMe verified identity allows people to securely prove who they are online when applying for services and products from participating organisations .

Balancing of community interests 54. Elected members are required to act in the best interests of their district and region, and that role requires some balancing of interests in decision- making, including taking into account minority interests. Polls are an instrument of majority rule, and the outcome will always depend on the majority’s perception of the minority interests . Consistency of council decision- making about representation arrangements 55. Currently a council can decide to establish a ward that is representative of a significant community of interest (e.g., a rural ward) and the public has no ability to overturn this decision through the use of a poll. It may, however, appeal to the Local Government Commission for a review of the decision. The ability for a poll of electors to overturn a council resolution is also unusual in the context of council decision- making. F or most council decision- making processes, the public does not have this level of influence over the decision. 56. The Māori ward poll process was identical to th at for council resolutions on which electoral system to use (STV or FPP). While these issues are both electoral, the impact of these decisions is not equal. Decisions about the electoral system apply equally to all voters, while decisions about Māori wards disproportionately affect Māori. 57. This criterion considers whether the option establishes additional barriers to Māori representation that do not apply to other communities. 58. Neither the status quo nor any of the proposed options involve fully aligning the process of creating Māori wards with the process for creating general wards through the representation review process.

Billing customers for three waters services 87. There are two possible arrangements for billing customers for three waters services: 87.1 direct billing by the water services entity; or 87.2 collection via territorial authorities. 88. These different arrangements could be used for some or all types of charges, some types of customers, during the initial period of operation of water services entities, or on an enduring basis. 89. The National Transition Unit is working towards water services entities being able to charge for all three waters services on day one (1 July 202 4). However, if this cannot be set up in time, the entities may need to use existing territorial authority billing systems for billing in the short term. Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page 15 of 41 90. A critical issue is how the collection of payments on behalf of the water services e ntity may be treated when assessing the credit rating of local authorities. Pass -through charging is unlikely to impact the financial ratios of territorial authorities, especially if only a short -term transitional measure. A pass -through arrangement where territorial authorities do not take collection risk is relatively straightforward and lik e the current Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act 2020 arrangements. 91. Pass- through arrangements would not typically be expected to compromise the balance sheet separation. However, when considered in the context of an enduring pass- through charging arrangement and the institutional and governance arrangements between local authorities and water services entities, ongoing pass - through charging could impact the balance sheet separation. 92. I recommend that the legislation should enable pass -through billing arrangements with territorial authorities, like the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act 2020. With these arrangements enabled, water services entities would be able to use them on a temporary basis. We are however proposing that these legislative provisions expire on 1 July 2034. This would not prevent water services entities negotiating directly with local authorities after that date, but local authorities would not be obliged to prov ide the services. 93. Collection via territorial authorities may be particularly desirable for stormwater charges, especially if the water services entity does not provide drinking water or wastewater services to the property. The property would pay for stormwater services provided by the water services entity through the local authorities’ rates invoice, and the relevant stormwater revenue would be transferred to the entity.

Budget Sensitive Office of the Minister of Internal Affairs and Office of the Associate Minister of Health Chair, Cabinet Social Wellbeing Committee Strategy to Prevent and Minimise Gambling Harm 201 9/20 to 20 21/22 Proposal 1 This paper reports back on and seeks approval for the Strategy to Prevent and Minimise Gambling Harm 2019/20 to 20 21/22 (attached), for changes to the Ministry of Health ’s appropriations to f und the Strategy , and for a problem gambling levy and levy rates to recover the cost of the Strategy from levy -paying gambling sectors . Executive Summary 2 Gambling harm is a significant social and economic issue. Measures to prevent and minimise gambling harm contribute to several government priorities , including supporting improved mental health and health equities and reducing child poverty. 3 The Ministry of Health (the Ministry) is responsible for the Strategy to Prevent and Minimise Gambling Harm 2019/20 to 2021/22 (the Strategy), which is the “integrated problem gambling strategy focused on public health ” described in section 317 of the Gambling Act 2003 (the Act). This is a revised Strategy prepared for 2019/20 to 2021/22. 4 The revised Strategy proposes to refocus and develop service s to better meet the needs of people affected by harmful gambling by: 4.1 improving the range of, and access to, services, facilitat ing co-design and use of consumer networks to de velop more targeted and appropriate services ; and 4.2 strengthening enablers that support these including : workforce training , addressing cultural and language barriers, use of technology, and action -oriented research and evaluation . 5 These changes strongly align with the types of service changes recommended b y He Ara Oranga , the report of the Mental Health and Addiction Inquiry. He Ar a Oranga notes harmful gambling is often associated with other forms of addiction and mental health issues . 6 The total cost for the Ministry to implement its Strategy for 2019/20 to 2021/22 , is $60.339 million. This is an increase of $5 million from the previous levy period, to invest in expanding access to , and choice of , services. The cost of the Strategy is recovered by a problem gambling levy (the levy) set by regulation at dif ferent rates on the profits of specified gambling operators, so the Strategy will be fiscally neutral over time. 7 The current levy regulations expire after 30 June 201 9. If the revised Strategy and new levy regulations are not in place from 1 July 201 9, until the date they are in place the cost of any Ministry -funded services to prevent and minimise gambling harm will not be recovered . 1wzrx7ijjr 2019-05-16 08:10:17 Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs

Supporting the Long-term Financial Sustainability of the Racing Industry Portfolio Racing On 11 September 2024, the Cabinet Economic Policy Committee: 1noted that the New Zealand racing industry, which contributed $1.9 billion to the New Zealand economy in the 2022/23 racing year and sustained 13,632 full-time equivalent jobs across the country, is almost wholly reliant on TAB NZ for funding; 2noted that while TAB NZ has a monopoly on land-based sports and racing betting, New Zealand’s gambling legislation allows offshore online gambling operators to offer sports and racing betting to New Zealand-based customers, which threatens TAB NZ’s and the racing industry’s ongoing financial sustainability; 3noted that in June 2023, TAB NZ entered a 25-year partnership agreement with global betting operator Entain, which provides for 50:50 revenue sharing for the term of the agreement, guaranteed returns to TAB NZ until 2028, and a conditional payment should the Government legislate to provide TAB NZ with an online monopoly; 4noted that while the partnership has helped in the short-term, uncertainty remains with respect to long-term distributions to the racing industry, especially after the guaranteed return period concludes; 5noted that: 5.1in July 2024, Cabinet agreed to establish a new online casino gambling regulatory system [CAB-24-MIN-0277.01]; 5.2the above decisions present indirect risks to TAB NZ’s long-term financial sustainability and the Minister for Racing intends to work with the Minister of Internal Affairs on areas of common interest between the portfolios on these matters; 6agreed to amend the Racing Industry Act 2020 to: 6.1make it illegal for any entity other than TAB NZ to offer betting on sporting or racing events to a New Zealand-based customer; 6.2repeal the Point of Consumption Charge (POCC) and associated regulations; This Bill introduces legislation to improve the financial sustainability of the New Zealand racing industry and features on the Coalition Government’s Q4 Action Plan for New Zealand. 2 The Minister for Racing proposes that the Bill is introduced on 3 December 2024 and enacted by 19 May 2025. Policy 3 On 16 September 2024, Cabinet agreed to make it illegal for any entity other than TAB NZ to offer sports and race wagering to persons in New Zealand, effectively extending TAB NZ’s land-based monopoly to online-provided wagering [CAB-24-MIN-0350]. 4 This Bill is required to maintain and improve the long-term financial sustainability of the New Zealand racing industry. The New Zealand racing industry, which is worth $1.9 billion to the New Zealand economy and employs nearly 14,000 people, is reliant on TAB NZ funding. Over 90% of their income comes from TAB NZ. TAB NZ’s distributions to the racing codes are increasingly under threat from the loss of revenue to offshore online operators, despite TAB NZ’s monopoly on land-based sports and racing betting and the cash injection from the recent TAB NZ Entain partnership. 5 In addition, Cabinet’s recently agreed proposals to establish a new online casino gambling regulatory system [CAB-24-MIN-0277 refers] presents indirect risk to TAB NZ’s long-term financial sustainability because the proposals potentially strengthen the market position of TAB NZ’s biggest competitors. 6 This Bill proposes to amend the Racing Industry Act 2020 (the Racing Act) to extend TAB NZ’s monopoly to all sports and racing betting offered online to New Zealanders. The Bill will: 6.1 make it illegal for any entity other than TAB NZ to offer betting on sports or racing events to a New Zealand-based customer; I N C O N F I D E N C E 1 44qw4kdm06 2024-12-02 08:03:34 I N C O N F I D E N C E 18.1 restrict or prohibit inducements to engage in betting; and 18.2 regulate the intensity of betting by a person using an online betting system provided by TAB NZ, including how frequently successive bets may be placed. 19 The Bill also creates a new regulation-making power to ensure TAB NZ cannot restrict otherwise lawful customers from accessing its online products without an appropriate reason. 20 It is anticipated that some aspects of the interim framework may be placed in regulations. Other instruments 21 This Bill will introduce new Ministerial powers to require additional reporting and information-gathering from TAB NZ to ensure that the Government has sufficient oversight and can respond to any future risk. Definition of Minister/department 22 The Bill does not create a new definition or amend an existing definition of Minister or Department. Commencement of legislation 23 The Bill will come into force on the day after Royal Assent. Parliamentary stages 24 The Bill is intended to be introduced on 3 December 2024 and passed by 19 May 2025. 25 The Bill is on the 2024 Legislation Programme, with a Priority 5 (to proceed to select committee by the end of 2024). It is proposed for the Bill to be referred to the Governance and Administration Select Committee for a consideration period of 4 months (December 2024 to April 2025). To support passing the Bill in this timeframe, it is proposed that the first reading occurs on 12 December 2024. Proactive Release 26 As per Cabinet Circular CO (23) 4, the Minister for Racing intends to proactively release this Cabinet paper subject to any redactions that may be justified under the Official Information Act 1982, within 30 days of decisions being made. These risks heighten the need to ensure legislative settings protect the viability of TAB NZ in order to improve the long -term financial sustainability of the racing industry . CONCLUSION The eight closed field trials demonstrated that the Bluetooth-based CovidCard contact tracing card has an ability to recall a high proportion of ground truth close contacts, and even a basic on-card contact algorithm is able to rank potential close-contacts in an order that positively correlates with ground truth ranking. Server-side prioritisation of contacts achieved no false positives in the top 10% of ranked contacts. Further work such as a larger open trial and ongoing development of post-download contact prioritisation algorithms will ensure the cards are fit-for-purpose for deployment on a national scale.

Card Technical Method The trials used Minew C10 Bluetooth Low Energy cards with custom firmware implemented by the CovidCard product development team. This firmware provided low radio operating duty cycles that satisfied the needs and power consumption constraints of the system under design.
Card advertising packet lengths were set near the maximum permitted by the technology (30 octets advertising payload; likely 50% longer than would be the case in the ultimate system) and included a static card identifier/serial number (in the range 1-255 for these trials). No privacy features (e.g., rotation of pseudonymous advertising identifiers) were implemented 5 Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs sometimes referred to as the True Positive Rate. b. False Positive Rate (FPR): the number of contacts seen by the card that were not ground truth contacts, as a proportion of card contacts. c. Spearman Rank Correlation (Rank Correlation) [3]: the measure of how strongly correlated the order of the ground truth contact list (using time multiplied by intensity to determine order) versus the order of the predicted contact list from the card (using time multiplied by RSSI). A perfect ordering match scores 1, 0 for no correlation and -1 for reversed order. Since both lists must have the same length in order to calculate the rank correlation, only the recalled (true positive) contacts were used for this metric.

Castalia report – Advice on Water Reform Opt-Out
Castalia’s interpretation of the economic literature is not consistent with the Department’s, or those of reputable economic advisors including Frontier Economics and Farrierswier . There are many examples in the literature of water service s aggregation , alongside governance and regulatory reform, leading to efficiency gains : • A Frontier Economics report for t he UK water trade association, which found that reform of the water industr y in England resulted in annual productivity growth of 2.1% or 64% over 24 years when adjusted for service quality improvements .1 • Australian water utilities are typically set targets for efficiency improvement of between 2 -4% per annum. This is in a more mature sector with less opportunity for catch -up efficiency. For example, the Western Australian Water Corporation has been set an efficiency challenge of more than 12% over the 5 years to 2025/26. • Frontier Economics, in its review of the experience with water services aggregation in Australia, Great Britain, Ireland and New Zealand (Auckland and Wellington) finds that there is “strong and consistent evidence” that reforms have led to significant improvements in productivity and efficiency.2 • The Productivi ty Commission in Australia, that service delivery reform has helped to improve efficiency and deliver significant benefits for water users3

Chair Cabinet Legislation Committee Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Bill: Approval for Introduction Proposal 1. This paper seeks approval to introduce the Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Bill which will give effect to stage two of the Local Water Done Well reform programme . This Bill holds a category 2 priority on the 2024 Legislation Programme (must be passed within the year). 2. The Bill provides for the preliminary and foundational provisions relating to the new framework proposed in Local Water Done Well which will enable councils to self- determine how they wish to transition to the new , long term water services delivery model. The enduring settings are proposed to be given effect in a further bill – the Local Government ( Water Services ) Bill - to be introduced in December 2024 . 3. I propose that the Bill is introduced on 27 May 2024 , be referred to the Finance and Expenditure Committee and be enacted by early August 2024. Policy 4. In February 2024, we fulfilled our commitments to repeal the previous government’s unpopular water services entities regime , restoring local government responsibilities for water services delivery, and halt the establishment of the 10 mega entities. Cabinet also agreed to begin work on the new policy proposals for Local Water Done Well, to be implemented in two further Bills [CAB -24-MIN -0024]. Local Water Done Well provides a new approach to local government water services delivery, with a critical emphasis on financial sustainability a nd funding for growth. 5. In March 2024, m y policy paper Local Water Done Well stage 2: Establishing the framework and transitional arrangements was approved by Cabinet. It contained the first set of proposals for the new framework . These proposals are preliminary in nature and set expectations on councils to present their intentions to transition from their current service delivery models to financially sustainable water service delivery models that meet water quality regulatory standards [ECO -24-MIN -0034]. 6. The Bill imposes requirements on councils in the near term, which will prepare them for water services delivery under the long -term settings. Requirements include foundational information disclosure, firstly through the preparation and delivery of water services delivery plans , and then later through a more formal regime if the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs and I determine that one or more councils are ready to provide enhanced information in prepar ation for the long -term economic regulatory framework. 7. To enhance flexibility during the transitional period, streamlined consultation and decision -making requirements are made available for councils who wish to establish or amend water services council- controlled organisations under Local Government Act 2002 provisions . 29e1n91k9v 2024-05-23 11:05:19 Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE
Chair Cabinet Māori -Crown Relations C ommitt ee New Plymouth District Council (Waitara Lands) Bill – progress of local bill and inclusion of Crown interests Proposal 1. This paper updates the Committee on progress of the New Plymouth District Council (Waitara Lands) Bill. It: 1.1 informs the Committee about the local Bill; 1.2 seeks Cabinet’s approval to advising the Governor -General of the inclusion of Crown interests in the local Bill, being the Crown’s underlying title to reserves in Waitara; and 1.3 seeks Cabinet’s agreement to a time -limited tax exemption of six months for the Waitara hapū entity (as defined in the local Bill as the entity representing the Waitara hapū). 2. The local Bill provides the opportunity to resolve the longstanding issues at Waitara and to make a positive contribution to the relationship between local government and Māori. Executive summary 3. The New Plymouth District Council (Waitara Lands) Bill (the local Bill) provides an opportunity for the Government to support the efforts of New Plymouth District Council (the District Council) to strengthen local government -Māori relations. The local Bill seeks to resolve the longstanding issues at Waitara which result from the confiscation of Māori land in the nineteenth century, which is today owned by the District Council (the Waitara Endowment Land) and leased to residents and businesses with perpetual rights of renewal. Proceeds from the Waitara Endowment Land may only be used at present for a limited range of activities, and the aim of the local Bill is to unlock the funds for the benefit of Ngā Manukorihi and Otaraua (the Waitara hapū) and the wider Waitara community. 4. There are two critical issues without which the Waitara hapū will not support the local Bill. This paper seeks your agreement to the steps necessary to resolve those issues. 5. First, the hapū seek the inclusion of Crown underlying title to six District Council reserves which the D istrict Council proposes to transfer to the Waitara hapū entity (upon payment of their value through a valuation mechanism in the Bill). The transfer of underlying title has been agreed by the Minister of Conservation. This paper seeks Cabinet’s agreement to advise the Governor- General of the Crown’s agreement to the inclusion of Crown interests in a local Bill. It is a procedural requirement of the Standing Orders that a message from the Governor -General to the House confirm the inclusion of Crown interests in a local Bill before the Bill may be passed. Proactively released from the Department of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 2 of 10 6. Secondly, I propose that the Waitara hapū entity be given a six -month time -limited tax exemption from the date of commencement of the local Bill. This will provide time for the Waitara hapū entity or its subsidiary to obtain a determination of its status as a charitable entity. 7. The Waitara hapū have agreed to support the Bill. My officials are working with the Waitara hapū and the District Council to finalise redrafting of the local Bill, including a preamble that tells the historical story of the Waitara hapū, and a side agreement between the Waitara hapū and the District Council that will support the implementation of the local Bill. 8. I consider that Government support for the local Bill will make a valuable contribution to improving local government -Māori relations and confer wider benefits on the Māori- Crown relationship. The local Bill represents an innovative resolution to longstanding issues by the District Council. 9. If this Bill were not to pass, the local Waitara community will miss the opportunity to benefit from $60 -80 million in funding which is unlocked by the Bill. Under the local Bill, the sums will be applied to housing development and associated growth and job creation, hapū development and hapū and community health and wellbeing initiatives, and the restoration of the Waitara River. Background 10. The local Bill broadens the purposes for which the District Council can apply re ntal income and proceeds of sale of Waitara Endowment Land. The local Bill was reported back to the House by the Māori Affairs Committee on 2 August 2017 with significant amendments from the version as introduced. Following further negotiations between the District Council and the Waitara hapū, significant changes are proposed to be made at committee of the whole House via a Supplementary Order Paper (SOP) in the name of Jonathan Young MP, the member in charge of the Bill. This local Bill will bring wider b enefits to both the Waitara community as a whole and the Māori -Crown relationship more broadly. The local Bill relates to 170 hectares of land confiscated from Te Atiawa in 1865 11. Waitara, North Taranaki, is a place of historical importance to Māori and all New Zealanders. The first shots in the New Zealand Land Wars were fired on the Pekapeka block at Waitara in 1860, due to escalating tensions regarding contested land purchases. 12. All of the land at Waitara was confiscated from Māori in 1865 under the New Zealand Settlements Act 1863. Much of the land was vested in the local authorities in 1874 and this is today owned by successor local authorities. Perpetual leases (long leases with an automatic right of renewal) were created over approximately 170 hectares o f the land (the Waitara Endowment Land) and these leases remain in place today, administered by the District Council. 13. In the 2013 census, 39.9 per cent of Waitara residents identified as Māori. Te Atiawa is the local iwi, and Waitara is home to Manukorihi and Otaraua hapū. Proactively released from the Department of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 3 of 10 Te Atiawa Treaty settlement negotiators elected not to purchase the land, leaving issues unresolved 14. In the early 2000s, the District Council resolved to make the Waitara Endowment Land available for Te Atiawa for Treaty settlement purpos es. This was disputed by leaseholders who instigated legal action against the District Council. After a lengthy court dispute, the Court of Appeal confirmed the District Council's right to sell the land. 15. For a number of reasons, Te Atiawa Treaty settlement negotiators elected not to purchase the land. This created divisions within Te Atiawa and the Waitara hapū tried to withdraw from the iwi and the Treaty settlement. Ultimately, the Treaty settlement was finalised with the Waitara hapū included but the iss ue of Waitara lands unresolved. New leadership at the District Council has prioritised resolving ownership of the Waitara Endowment Land 16. The District Council, under new leadership, has worked hard over the past 18 months to build a relationship with the Wa itara hapū and wider iwi. The Mayor and Chief Executive of the District Council see the local Bill as a way to move forward, bring benefits to the Waitara hapū and for the District Council and Waitara hapū to work together to improve wellbeing for the Waitara community. 17. The District Council perceives the local Bill as a once in a generation opportunity to resolve ownership of the Waitara Endowment Land, clean up the Waitara River and to provide opportunities for the Waitara hapū and community. They are publ icising their promotion of the local Bill in these terms among the local community. The local Bill seeks to resolve the longstanding issues at Waitara Progress 18. In 2016, the District Council promoted the local Bill sponsored by Jonathan Young, MP for New P lymouth. The local Bill as introduced transferred some land to the local iwi trust, Te Kotahitanga o Te Atiawa, and enabled leaseholders on the Waitara Endowment Land to purchase the freehold title to the same land. 19. The local Bill was referred to the Māori Affairs Committee. At the public hearings of submissions on the local Bill it became clear that neither the iwi, Te Atiawa, nor the Waitara hapū supported the local Bill. The Māori Affairs Committee recommended substantial changes, with the agreement of t he District Council, to enable more equitable outcomes for the local Waitara hapū and wider iwi. The Māori Affairs Committee report on the Bill to the House on 2 August 2017 foreshadowed further changes being necessary and noted that the Waitara hapū were due to enter further discussions with both the District Council and Taranaki Regional Council (the Regional Council). The local Bill had its second reading on 9 August 2017. Proactively released from the Department of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 4 of 10 Recent changes raise a procedural issue around the scope of the Bill which needs to be addressed 20. Further negotiations took place between the Waitara hapū and both the District Council and the Regional Council. This led to the SOP now proposed which further amends the local Bill as reported back by the Māori Affairs Committee. It remains within the intention and spirit of the Māori Affairs Committee commentary on the local Bill as reported back to the House. 21. Some of the changes proposed by SOP are out of scope of the original Notice of Intention to promote the local Bill publicised by the District Council. Standing Order 302(3) provides that no am endment may be made to a local B ill that is outside the scope of the notices advertising the intention to introduce or promote the local B ill. Jonathan Young MP has written to the House Business C ommittee asking them to waive Standing Order 302(3) to enable these changes to be made through the SOP. Additionally, from 2 November the District Council is publishing a revised Notice setting out the changes to the scope of the local Bill. The changes ar e critical to the Waitara hapū’s support for the local Bill. Unanimous agreement of the House is needed to waive Standing Order 302(3) which may be indicated by the House Business Committee. 22. I am satisfied that while these changes were not in the Māori Affairs Committee’s commentary, they are within the spirit of that report and will therefore be acceptable to the Māori Affairs Committee. The local Bill will not proceed to further House stages until the Māori Affairs Committee has endorsed the Bill’s progression. Provisions in the local Bill and the substantial Supplementary Order Paper 23. The proposed SOP substantia lly refines the local Bill. The SOP makes significant improvements to the way the local Bill seeks to provide an adequate resolution to the longstanding issues faced by the Waitara hapū while also resolving the concerns of leaseholders in the Waitara Endow ment Land. It achieves an effective balance between the interests of the Waitara hapū and leaseholders of the Waitara Endowment Land and it brings benefits to the wider community in Waitara and the Taranaki region. 24. The local Bill returns or enables the return of all District Council reserves (including some with Crown underlying title) in Waitara to the Waitara hapū and some other District Council land. It also enables leaseholders of Waitara Endowment Land to purchase the freehold title to the same land. Proactively released from the Department of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 5 of 10 25. The proceeds of sale of freehold and income from leaseholds are divided equally between the District Council and the Regional Council as follows: 25.1 The District Council’s proceeds are further divided equally between the Waitara Community Fund and the Hapū Land Fund, overseen by an independent statutory Board. The Board makes determinations as to distributions from the Waitara Community Fund, for the benefit of the Waitara community. The local Bill establishes the Hapū Land Fund Committee as a committee of t he Board. The Hapū Land Fund Committee comprises members of the Waitara hapū and determines the Board’s spending of the Hapū Land Fund which must be for the purpose of buying, developing and managing land in and adjacent to Waitara for the benefit of the W aitara hapū; and 25.2 The Regional Council’s proceeds fund the work of the Waitara River Committee, a council committee with equal membership between the Regional Council and iwi authorities of any iwi with mana whenua over the river catchment. The Waitara Rive r Committee is to distribute 70 per cent of funds toward the environmental, cultural and spiritual health and wellbeing of the Waitara River and 30 per cent toward any matter in Waitara or the lower catchment of the river within the Regional Council’s responsibility. 26. The refinements to the Bill, agreed through extensive discussions between the District Council, the Waitara hapū and Te Atiawa iwi trustees, and proposed to be implemented by the SOP include: 26.1 all of the land to be transferred in the local Bill will be transferred to the Waitara hapū rather than the iwi trustees; 26.2 the inclusion in the local Bill of all of the Council -owned reserves in Waitara, should the hapū elect to initiate the transfer; 26.3 the potential for transfer of six reserves that have a pa rtial or whole Crown underlying title to the hapū at the hapū’s election and on terms that the Crown is reimbursed for the value of the underlying title; 26.4 a time -limited tax exemption of six months for the Waitara hapū entity; 26.5 should the District Council ever sell its interests in the leased land, it must offer these rights to the hapū first. Valuation instructions for these interests have been agreed between the District Council and the hapū; and 26.6 a preamble that tells the hapū’s story of Waitara and its con nection to the whenua. 27. Both the inclusion of the Crown underlying titles and the tax exemption were critical in ensuring the hapū remained in negotiations with the District Council. For example, one of these reserves, Pukekohe Domain, is an original pā sit e and was also the location of the constabulary quartering during the New Zealand Land Wars. This site is culturally significant to both hapū and they aspire to establish a cultural base at the site. 28. The District Council and the Waitara hapū will conclude a binding side agreement to support the implementation of the local Bill. This will set out how the mechanisms in the local Bill will be applied in practice, including for example arrangements for governance of the reserves and an agreement that neither t he Waitara hapū nor the District Council will seek a change to the reserve status of land without the other’s consent. Proactively released from the Department of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 6 of 10 Outstanding issues critical to retaining hapū support for the local Bill Crown underlying title 29. The District Council has agreed to transfer title to reserve land in Waitara to the Waitara hapū. Six of the reserves are wholly or partly derived from the Crown and the Crown retains underlying title. This means that, should the District Council seek to divest its interests in the land, title r everts to the Crown. 30. The inclusion of the Crown underlying title to six reserves in Waitara enables the hapū to elect to purchase those reserves at any time in the next 172 years. Cabinet’s agreement is sought to including the Crown underlying title to the se six reserves. 31. The transfer will be fiscally neutral to the Crown as the value of the Crown underlying title will be paid by the District Council or the Waitara hapū. The underlying titles have been valued at $1.7 million. As the value is greater than in itially anticipated, one reserve will be purchased on enactment of the Bill. Agreement has been given by the Minister of Conservation for the local Bill to provide the perpetual right for the Waitara hapū to purchase the remaining five reserves. If the transfer of the five remaining reserves is made after November 2019, an updated market valuation will be required through a mechanism provided for in the Bill. 32. Under Standing Order 313, no local Bill may contain any provision that affects the rights and priv ileges of the Crown unless the Crown has given its consent. The consent of the Crown is given by a message from the Governor -General in accordance with Standing Order 167. I seek Cabinet’s agreement to advise the Governor -General that the Crown consents to the inclusion of Crown interests in this local Bill. In this case, the Crown interest is in the potential sale of the underlying Crown title to six reserves in Waitara to the Waitara hapū. Tax exemption 33. The Minister of Revenue and I have agreed that transfers of land from the District Council to the Waitara hapū entity under the arrangements in the local Bill should not be subject to income tax. The District Council as a local authority is exempt from income tax and the disposal of land by the District Council would therefore not be subject to income tax. Nevertheless, I recommend that a specific provision be included in the local Bill for the avoidance of doubt. 34. The Minister of Revenue and I have also agreed to propose to Cabinet a temporary tax exemption for transfers from the Hapū Land Fund to the Waitara hapū entity in the local Bill. The temporary tax exemption will be in place for six months from the date of commencement of the Bill. The tax exemption is critical to obtaining the support of the hapū t o the arrangements in the local Bill. It will provide a bridging mechanism, giving the Waitara hapū entity or its subsidiary enough time to obtain charitable status. Following the expiry of the six -month temporary exemption, the prevailing tax rules will apply on a go -forward basis. 35. Cabinet’s agreement is sought to account for the temporary tax exemption through the between -Budget contingency. The fiscal implications of the temporary tax exemption are likely to be small. The Hapū Land Fund is expected to total no more than $1.5 million in the initial six -month period. This would lead to maximum potential tax revenue of $0.3 million each year. Proactively released from the Department of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 7 o f 10 36. I do not consider that the temporary tax exemption risks setting a precedent. The circumstances in Waitara are uniq ue. In addition to the historical factors, the unique circumstances include that this is endowment land, so the funds provided under theBill are not obtained from rates and are not otherwise available for general use, andthat the interests of the leaseho lders are protected by the local Bill. My officials are not aware of any comparable circumstances and I consider the likelihood of similararrangements emerging is low. The proposed tax exemption is a pragmatic response tounique circumstances and does not provide a precedent for other local authorities. 37. The District Council expects that the arrangements in the local Bill will unlock fundingof $60- $80 million over the next twenty years as leaseholders purchase freehold title. The District and Regional Councils have agreed that all of this money should be used inWaitara to build the local economy and benefit the wellbeing of the Waitaracommunity. The arrangements in the local Bill would distribute this funding in the formof: 37.1 $30- $40 million to restore the health and wellbeing of the Waitara River; 37.2 $10- $20 million in a Waitara Community Fund for the general benefit of the Waitara community; and 37.3 $10- $20 million in a Hapū Land Fund for the purchase, development or management of land at Waitara. Chair Cabinet Social Wellbeing Committ ee Proposed amendments to the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification (Urgent Interim Classification of Publications and Prevention of Online Harm) Amendment Bill Proposal 1. This paper seeks agreement to amend clause 9 of the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification (Urgent Interim Classification of Publications and Prevention of Online Harm) Amendment Bill ( the Bill) . The proposed amendment w ould remove sections 119L – 119O (the filtering provisions) from the Bill. Relation to government priorities 2. The proposals in this Bill are a direct response to the Christchurch terror attack s and address some gaps and limitations in our classification legislation . Executive summary 3. The proposals in the Bill w ere developed as a direct response to the Christchurch terror attacks and address specific inefficiencies and ambiguities in our classification legislation. On 11 December 2019, Cabinet agreed to the proposals set out for the Bill [CAB -19-MIN -0672 refers]. 4. The Bill was introduced to Parliament in May 2020 and was referred to the Governance and Administration Committee (the Committee) at its First Reading on 11 February 2021. I inherited the Bill from the previous Minister of Internal Affairs and have previousl y indicated that I was open to refining the Bill’s filtering provisions depending on what came out of the Select Committee stage , given the strong views in this area . 5. Internet filtering can be a useful tool to prevent access to and mitigate harms from obje ctionable (illegal) content online. An example of this is the current Digital Child Exploitation System (DCEFS), which specifically filters child sexual abuse material. Child sexual abuse material is universally accepted as abhorrent and blocking this type of material has not been challenged. Further expansion of the categories of illegal material to be filtered needs detailed consideration to ensure the proper safeguards are there to prevent abuse of this power. 6. The current proposals leave this detail to b e determined in regulations to allow flexibility for new technologies. On balance a statutory filter provision needs more detail about the safeguards. To achieve that , the detailed work that was planned following enactment of the Bill would need to be brou ght forward. Progressing this work now would risk a further delay to the implementation of the other key regulatory and enforcement provisions of the Bill. This is consistent with the advice that I have received from my officials. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 2 of 8 7. Submitters also acknowled ged that more detail is needed before progressing the filtering provisions. T he submissions received on the Bill throughout the Select Committee stage have indicated that there is a lack of public mandate to progress with the current filtering provisions a t this time. Submissions highlighted the need to set out the specific scope of the filter in primary legislation and emphasised the need for further public consultation and community engagement . 8. These submissions are consistent with wider community feedback received during huis held on the report of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into the terrorist attack on Christchurch masjidain on 15 March 2019 . Feedback from those huis emphasised the need for greater community engagement and co -design of policie s on a wide range of areas relevant to the classification and censorship system – such as hate speech and balancing reform in that area with the right to freedom of expression, as well as greater scrutiny of the standards of media and online reporting on m inority and faith communit y issues . 9. This paper therefore, seeks agreement to remove the current filtering provisions from the Bill and investigate a voluntary approach to filtering . Background 10. In the aftermath of the Christchurch terror attacks, internet service providers (ISPs) and online content hosts worked collaboratively with Government to prevent people from spreading and accessing online footage of the attacks. While these efforts were largely effective, the experience highlighted inefficiencies and ambiguities in our censorship system for responding to objectionable online content. This Bill was developed as a direct response to the Christchurch terror attacks by addressing these inefficiencies and ambiguities in the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification Act 1993 (the FVPC Act . 11. On 11 December 2019 , Cabinet agreed to the following policy proposals in the Bill [CAB -19-MIN -0672 refers ]: 11.1 knowingly livestreaming objectionable content will become a criminal offence punishable by up to 14 years in prison; 11.2 allowing the Chief Censor to make interim classification decisions; 11.3 allowing take -down notices to be issued to require the removal of objectionable online content; 11.4 making online content hosts subj ect to a civil pecuniary penalty of up to $200,000, if they do not comply with an issued take -down notice; 11.5 ensuring ‘safe harbour’ provisions in the Harmful Digital Communications Act 2015 would not apply to objectionable online content; and 11.6 enabling the e stablishment of regulations that would allow the government to implement web -filtering of objectionable content if required. 12. The Bill updates the FVPC Act to allow for urgent prevention and mitigation of harms caused by objectionable content online. The te rm ‘objectionable’ refers to already illegal content as defined in the FVPC Act ; this includes content which “describes, depicts or expresses, or otherwise deals with matters such as sex, horror, crime, cruelty or violence in such a manner that the availab ility of publication is likely to be injurious to the public good.” It is an offence to make, possess, supply or distribute objectionable content. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 3 of 8 13. The Bill will improve the way we regulate objectionable content, including violent extremist and terrorist co ntent found online. Specifically, the Bill amends the Act to: 13.1 criminalise knowingly livestreaming objectionable content; 13.2 allow the Chief Censor to make interim classification assessments in relation to publications (both physical as well as online) likely to be found objectionable in urgent situations; 13.3 allow take -down notices to be issued to require the removal of objectionable online content; 13.4 make online content hosts subject to a civil pecuniary penalty of up to $200,000, if they do not comply with an is sued take -down notice; 13.5 ensure the ‘safe harbour’ provisions in the Harmful Digital Communications Act 2015 would not apply to objectionable online content; and 13.6 enable the establishment of regulations that would allow the Government to implement filtering o f objectionable content online if required (the filtering provisions) . 14. I inherited the Bill from the previous Minister of Internal Affairs and was keen to progress it to Select Committee stage to hear views on the filtering provisions, as there were arguments for and against. 15. The Bill was introduced to Parliament in May 2020 and was referred to the Committee at its First Reading on 11 February 2021. On 7 April 2021 I attended t he presentation of the initial briefing on the Bill and signalled to the Committee that I was particularly interested in submissions and discussions on the filtering provisions . 16. Since then, the filtering provisions have been the most submitted upon aspect of the Bill. The majority of the submissions that mentioned the filtering provisions were opposed to it. In contra st, the submissions that touched on other provisions of the Bill were mostly supportive and only recommended some minor technical changes. 17. The views expressed by submitters on the Bill align with community feedback from huis on the report of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into the terrorist attack on Christchurch masj idain on 15 March 2019 , specifically that proposals relating to freedom of expression should be developed through co -design and engagement with communities. Internet filtering can be a useful tool to prevent access and mitigate harms from objectionable co ntent online 18. In New Zealand, internet filtering already takes place without a legislative mandate or regulatory framework. This currently include s the voluntary DCEFS , which specifically filters child sexual abuse material . This filter is run by the Department of Internal Affairs ( DIA). While the DECFS is voluntary for ISPs, the majority of ISPs in New Zealand use the filter, which means that approximately 92 per cent of New Zealand internet users are protected from child sexual abuse material. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 4 of 8 19. The p roposed internet filtering provisions in the Bill provide an enabling framework and set out obligations on Government when implementing any mechanism to prevent access to other kind s of objectionable content , outside of child sexual abuse material and imag ery. The filtering provisions would not establish a filter but would give Government explicit statutory authority to explore and implement such mechanisms through regulations in the future. The filtering provisions are in clause 9 of the Bill under new sec tions 119L to 119O . 20. If established, the purpose of a filter would be to prevent access to content that is already illegal to possess or distribute. It is one of a range of tools that can be used to assist in mitigating the harms of objectionable content online. These harms can include revictimization - for example, recurring distress and trauma to victims from viewing an incident again or having others see footage of their experiences and being unintentionally exposed to this type of footage . Some of the most objectionable content on the internet is pe ddled by sites that will never respond to New Zealand’s or any other jurisdiction’s request to remove such content . A filter c ould act as a last line of defence when other approaches to remove this content ha ve failed. Submissions indicate that there is a lack of public mandate to progress with the current filtering provisions at this time 21. On 1 April 2021, written submissions closed for the Bill and the Committee received a total of 160 unique written submissi ons. The Committee received 51 submissions that specifically referred to the filtering provisions in the Bill. Out of those, four submitters supported filtering and 47 submitters were against filtering. A further 9 1 submissions, while not referenc ing the f iltering provisions specifically, were opposed to the Bill in full due to concerns that the Bill w ould impose on New Zealanders’ freedom of expression , which is the predominant reason for opposing the filter . 22. Some submitters acknowledged that there may be benefits to filtering objectionable content . However, this support was qualified by the need to clarify the detail and scope of any proposed filter. The filter being set in regulations was not seen as the best approach as there would be a lack of Parliamen tary oversight into the development of the filter, and a risk of insufficient legal safeguards. As currently drafted, the legislation is not intended to be too prescriptive in order to provide sufficient flexibility so that developments in technology do not undermine the policy intent. 23. However, s ubmitters opposed to filtering noted that there is a need for more specific detail on the scope, design and operation of the filter in the Bill. Submissions from academics, the tech nology sector , ethnic commu nity groups and interest bodies prefer that the Government consult on these aspects of any potential filter before finalising proposals and progressing legislation to implement a filter. This was reflected specifically by those in vulnerable groups that th e filtering provisions are intended to protect. There were also concerns raised about the potential infringement o n freedom of expression and the effectiveness of a filter , as it can be easily circumvented. 24. Several submissions suggested that the filter pr ovisions be removed from the Bill and be progressed as a stand -alone legislation so that there is appropriate Parliamentary decision -making and oversight of this issue. There was some commentary that any work on filtering should be considered as part of a wider review of the media regulatory landscape. There have also been suggestions of a voluntary approach like the existing DCEFS. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 5 of 8 25. I did consider options to redraft so that the filter is not set in regulations but primary legislation. However, I decided aga inst this as it would not address the issues of a lack of detail about the propose d design and operation of the filter. It would also not address concerns about the potential infringement on freedom of expression and the effectiveness of a filter. 26. While there appears to be a lack of public mandate to progress the filter, there are also additional issues to consider. This includes ensuring that the creation of a filter is fit for purpose, which would require setting out the exact scope of the filter and br oader public consultation. There is also the risk of the Bill being further delayed to allow time to determine technical specifications of the filter, which would mean other key regulatory and enforcement proposals in the Bill that are needed now would be unable to be progressed. My preferred approach is to remove the current filtering provisions from the Bill and investigate a voluntary filter 27. As noted above in paragraphs 16 to 18, filtering can be a useful tool to prevent access to and mitigate harms from objectionable content online – noting that this is content that is already illegal . However , having heard from submitters throughout the select committee process, it appears that there is strong opposition for a statutory mandated filter for objectionable content online and more work is required in this area . Therefore, my preferred approach is to remove the filtering provisions from the Bill and investigate a voluntary approach to filtering. This approach would amend clause 9, Part 7A of the Bill by removing: 27.1 section 119L: Electronic system to prevent public access to objectionable online publications; 27.2 section 119M: Establishment of electronic system; 27.3 section 119N: Approval of electronic system for operation; and 27.4 section 119O: Review of decisions and actions relating to operation of electronic system. 28. To allow for Cabinet consideration of the above proposal s, I have written to and obtained permission from the Committee Chair to exten d the report back date of the Departmental Report to 30 June 2021. The Department of Internal Affairs will continue to investigate a voluntary filter 29. There is some support for the concept of filtering objectionable content , particularly among Internet Service Providers (ISP). This is important as any filtering would work at the ISP level. I also think that there is a place for filtering as it can reduce harm for the most vulnerable, such as young people, from inadvertent access to objectionable content. However, I acknowledge that setting the filter in regulations is not the best approach. I have therefore directed my officials to investigate and provide me with advice on alternative options for progressing a voluntary approach to filtering for ISPs . A voluntary approach would align with the existing mechanism in place to filter child sexual abuse material and imagery . Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 6 of 8 30. I do not recommend removing the provisions and progressing stand -alone legislation to implement filtering objectionable content at this stage. Submitters who suggested this approach str essed that the legislation would need to set out specific details, such as the exact scope of the filter, technical capability details as well as governance and technical oversight arrangements. I anticipate these issues will be within scope of work to pro gress a voluntary filter. Stand -alone legislation to provide statutory authority to a voluntary filter can be explored in due course if there is evidence of sufficient public mandate for this to occur or a voluntary approach is unsuccessful . 31. In relation t o submissions suggesting this issue be considered within the wider media review (the review) , I note that the purpose of the review is to dev elop and establish an overarching framework for regulating and moderating media and online content. Proposals devel oped within th at broader framework may have potential cascading implications on aspects of work to progress a voluntary filter. I have been advised by my officials that they will remain mindful of possible links between proposals developed as part of the r eview and filtering options, and where appropriate align these workstreams as necessary . Next steps 32. If Cabinet approval the removal of the filtering provisions , the Bill will be amended to remove sections 119L to 119O in clause 9, Part 7A.
