Changes to financing arrangements for the Opt -Out Scenario cannot be ruled out There are other ways that access to finance by New Zealand water providers can be improved. The government ’s Opt -Out Scenario does not consider these other options. Currently, almost all three waters services are provided by local authorities. Local authorities’ borrowing limits, whether imposed by LGFA or due to ratings agency policies, are generally consider ed to impose limits on optimal investment planning in the water sector. In the Reform Scenario, the new statutory corporations will have separate balance sheets to lo cal authorities, and will be able to raise finance without being impacted by these borrowi ng limits. A number of other financing arrangements are already available for the water sector and could apply in the Opt -Out Scenario. Other financing changes could be implemented with law and other institutional reform: ▪ Central government has recently i ntroduced the Infrastructure Financing Facility 44F44F44F45 which enables finance to be raised from the private sector, ring-fenced from eligible local authorities ’ balance sheets ▪ Long -term concession contracts have been used in New Zealand (in Papakura, sig ned by Papakura Council prior to the creation of Auckland Council) under which a third -party provides water services for a fixed term (30 years in Pap akura) and collects water rates or tariffs directly from customers. Usually, the concession contract requi res the third - party to invest in and maintain the water assets and network and meet certain performance metrics . The third -party provider accesses pri vate capital markets to finance the capital investment needs (growth, renewals and maintenance) ▪ Revenue bo nds are a common way for municipal government entities in the United States to raise finance for infrastructure investment, often in the water sector . Investors in these bonds are repaid from income created by the projects the bonds fund. These are separat e from the general obligations debt raised by the municipal government .

City and Regional Deals 28 February 2025 light-touch proposal submissions
City and Regional Deals is the Government’s initiative for establishing long-term agreements between central and local government. The programme unlocks funding and resource opportunities to support councils to make improvements in their region, for example to roads, infrastructure, and the supply of quality housing.
City and Regional Deals primarily involve partnerships between local councils and central government. There is significant opportunity for collaboration from the private sector and iwi/MÄori organisations. Local government is responsible for identifying opportunities for involvement and engaging with private sector entities and MÄori organisations.
City and Regional deals will be enduring and will provide the certainty needed to attract and retain the necessary investments to deliver change. Deals make use of existing resources rather than relying solely on new funding, with central and local governments aligning our budget cycles and investment strategies to ensure resources can be used effectively.

Climate Implications of Policy Assessment
Climate Implications of Policy Assessment 195. None Population Implications 196. Vulnerable consumers, those experiencing material hardship, including disabled people, are most likely to struggle to pay their water bills. About eight percent of the population are estimated to face material hardship, but the proportion of households with people facing material hardship is likely to be less than that. Households experiencing material hardship are more likely to be younger, single parent, on a benefit as their main source of income, renters, Māori, or Pacific peoples, and people with disabilities. The proposals in this paper are intended to reduce the burden of water bills on vulnerable consumers. Human Rights 197. There are no human rights or gender implications arising from the proposals in this paper. Consultation 198. The Rural Supplies Technical Working Group highlighted the importance of being able to charge for water supplied for agricultural use on a different basis to drinking water, where both are supplied by the same scheme. This is consistent with the proposals in this paper. Targeted engagement on growth charging has also occurred with high growth territ orial authorities and the Property Council. Communications 202. The Department will also encourage an d inform the public about the opportunity to make submissions during the select committee process for the Water Services Entities Bill and the Amendment Bill. 204. My Office will play a key role in the development and rollout of communications to ensure message s are clear and appropriately tailored for the intended audiences. 205. Proactive Release 206. I intend to release this paper (subject to any redactions) to coincide with further announcements on the reforms. I note that this may occur outside of the usual timeframes in Cabinet Office circular CO (18) 4. Recommendations 207. The Minister of Local Governm ent recommends that Cabinet: 1. note that, during 2021 and early 2022, Cabinet made a series of decisions to transform the three waters service delivery system, and create four new water services entities, and that these decisions are to be given effect through an initial piece of legislation – the Water Services Entities Bill; 2. note that the Water Services Entities Bill is part of a broader, comprehensive suite of proposed legislation, including two additional bills: 2.1 a Water Services Entities Amendment Bill, which will fully implement the reforms; and 2.2 a Water Regulation Bill, to provide for a new economic regulation and consumer protection framework for the three waters system; Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page 34 of 41 3. note that this paper is seeking policy decisions on the matters to be included in the Water Services Entities Amendment Bill or the Water Regulation Bill, which are needed to fully develop and implement the new system, and operationalise the water services entities by providing them with all the necessary powers, functions and responsibilities; 4. agree to the following policy objectives for pricing of water services: 4.1 economic efficiency : prices reflect the underlying costs of services and support the financial sustainability of water services entities in the long - run; 4.2 affordability : water is an essential service and people on reticulated networks should be able to access water services regardless of their financial circumstances; 4.3 price stability : the rates of change in prices are not too high and price changes are clearly signalled in advance and smoothed over time; 4.4 cost-sharing: a key driver of the reforms is to address affordability issues, particularly for customers in smaller communities. Entities could use geographic average pricing to smooth costs across communities, thereby ensuring more affordable services for all; 4.5 horizontal equity : consumers in similar positions pay similar prices; 4.6 intergenerational equity : every generation (which can be thought of as being as small as the annual cohort of ratepayers) should be paying its fair share for assets and not requiring future generations to pay substantially more or less than their fair share through either over or under - investment. Historically, funding and w ater infrastructure investment decisions have tended to favour current over future generations; 4.7 giving effect to Te Mana o te Wai and respecting Treaty of Waitangi principles: pricing can support Te Mana o te Wai by encouraging efficient usage of water. Pricing can also engage Article 3 of the Treaty, and support equitable water service access and quality of service provision; 4.8 consistency with other government goals : pricing issues should support, or at least not undermine, government goals in other domains. For example, growth charges can have an impact on housing goals. Water services pricing can influence levels of water use which affects climate change goals including resilience and adaptation;

Commercial In Co nfidence Table 11: Citizen jury – Devon (England) Background Description Costs involved Relevance for NZ context Feasibility for different individuals and community types Risks Benefits Design choices The CJ was sponsored by the Water Quality Division of the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), the government department with responsibility for fostering sustainable rural development in England and Wales. Objective : policy on effective livestock management around water ways Necessary preconditions : “rules of procedure” provided; background information on the issue at hand provided to jurors and witnesses. Process : 13 jurors were recruited and 18 witnesses to the jury process. Jury was chaired by member of CJ project team as had most experience in chairing policy development and partnership working process in the environmental context The rules of procedure were discussed among jurors, and witnesses provided statements on this. Event held two weeks before the main jury proceedings. Main jury proceedings were held across three days in two locations; a civic space i n the city and a scientific research institute in the countryside with a working livestock farm. Jurors had a walking tour of the farm and the microbiology lab to gain extra context around the issue. - Jury verdict was built around the sequential explora tion of issues of ‘acceptability’, ‘culpability’, ‘necessity’ and ‘responsibility’ to deliver clear outcomes and recommendations. - The jury proceedings were formal with witness processes treated similarly to a legal jury. After each exploratory theme (4 o f them) jurors developed partial verdicts/responses in closed discussions The total cost to run the jury process was 19,740 pounds (in 2007 pounds). Very formal process, unclear how this would transfer to NZ without further exploration into the mechanisms used (detail not available in literature) Not clear beyond general ‘community’ involvement. Easy for participants to start to go beyond the questions asked of them due to personal thoughts and topical social affairs. Scope of issue jury is debating must be well defined to mitigate this - The need for advertising the jury, its proceedings, decisions and its support by local government poses the risk of influencing the jury’s decision (must be balanced) Good way to bring together and frame differing perspec tives from science, policy and practice into one agreed lens - Nature of jury itself enables different community members to come together on single issue – academic, scientists, policy makers, interest groups, general. Greater understanding gained by each party of each other (including between other witnesses) - A way of building confidence in the public image of policy makers - Structured process helped people to see final jury decisions as credible - In this instance the jury verdict ultimately consider ed as a formal submission to this consultation - CJ cuts across disparate domains of responsibility and expertise for the governance of environmental risks. It challenges decision makers to think more broadly about the political, moral and economic framin gs of otherwise narrowly conceived science -policy problems - CJs used to bring together both scientific and non -scientific forms of expertise - Jury is balanced in terms of age, gender, ethnicity and area of residence (urban and rural) and also expertise o r experience surrounding the issues (none to plenty of knowledge) - Acceptance and recognition that all jury members will bring their own opinion to the issue - Advertise in local media to ask for jury participants. Especially in the local newspaper as thi s is very effective. Advertise in strategic locations for participants where missing demographics e.g universities for young people
Commercial In Co nfidence Table 1: Participatory Budgeting – Example Fresno , California (USA) Background Description Costs involved Relevance for NZ context Feasibility for different individuals and community types Risks Benefits Design choices Fresno is a town of demographic divides, made worse by past planning infrastructure and zoning decisions. It employed PB to allocate funds for climate and environmental projects. Fresno has a population of about half a million. Participatory budgeting was introduced into the climate action by the local government after a series of initial meetings and sustained pressure by com munity leaders. Objective : joint allocation of $70m for climate and environmental projects. Necessary preconditions : steering group of 30 people appointed by councillors; Staff support provided by a foundation (CVCF) – partner who had good state and local contacts, dedication to stay involved and staff capacity to support Process and structures : Project eligibility & funding guidelines developed through continual feedback from community steering committee (CSC) meetings – open meetings attended by hundred s. Specifics decided on from outset were voting eligibility, process and lines of authority. City and CVCF staff assess project submissions and cut ineligible ones. Eligible projects presented to community members and community steering committee (CSC). 2 /3rd binding vote by community to accept a proposal. 4th CSC meeting – given more in -depth info on eligible projects and asked to rank. CVCF and city staff ranked and created four proposed packages – then presented at further CSC meeting. Minority communi ty also developed a 5th package on their own accord so another CSC meeting held to present this. 5th package got overwhelming support. Innovative engagement methods : town hall meetings at minority run churches with Q & A sessions Pre-engagement : public bu lletin announcements and mailed announcements to neighbourhood residents as well as town hall type church meetings early in the process (right after the decision on the involvement of the public in climate action was taken). Generally higher costs than traditional public involvement -$65k (USD) provided by city for professional facilitator, venue costs, marketing, printing costs, translation services for the 1-year process (but was said that operating funding was insufficient) - The culture of philanthropy in the US mean that there is more resource available for such projects compared to what is likely in NZ - Relies on broad -based, member led organisations that have the capacity and capability to engage large numbers of long -excluded citizens - The steeri ng group appointments by councillors is less likely to be acceptable in NZ – could be seen as ‘jobs for friends.’ Engagement with ethnic minorities through meetings in minority run churches (Q&A sessions) Ethnic minorities developing a separate eligibilit y package (which ultimately won the funding). - Key set of design principles must be used otherwise fail at implementation – Marginalised populations not always involved - Risk of PB becoming “participatory grant writing” rather than full-fledged PB when specific funding requirements have to be met - “Token” attempt at true community participation if trust not built – distrust that packages not created with community’s direct involvement - Reliance on existing community organisations to be a stable base means often same people engaging PB as those in traditional democratic participation practices - Increased trust in government - Creative solutions often more effective than elites’ ideas - Clear up -front commitment from public entity for specific $ or % of funds - Binding public vote - Delegate unconditional decision -making authority to community - Community members engaged early on to define and shape process – often rules written through steering committees - Clear and easy rules and way of community engagement - Leverage resources to target and engage typically marginalised populations - Continual encouragement of participation - Reduce barriers to participation – childcare and food at meetings, transport stipends - Small detai ls are important - e.g meeting room is comfortable, no one dominating voice in the room - Identify priorities first then projects - Longer timeline for high -quality process - Dedicated operating funds for PB process itself - Institutionalisation of PB with paid staff needed for broader implementation - Flexibility of budget: what to spend on and quantity (in US range from $75k in Long Beach to $40m in NYC). - Larger budgets improve participation rates/interest and have greater ability to address redistrib utive goals - Areas with traditionally stronger base of civil engagement and organisations more likely to have successful long term PB institutional change - Needs to be a wider part of community engagement practices so not just ‘token’ nor one-time fun ding allocation
Commercial In Co nfidence Table 3: Participatory budgeting - Paris (FR) Background Description Costs involved Relevance for NZ context Feasibility for different individuals and community types Risks Benefits Design choices In Paris, participatory budgeting was introduced in 2014 by then newly elected mayor Anne Hidalgo against the backdrop of declining voters’ participation. Politically, Paris has been known for giving little space for citizens’ participation in government. The Paris PB is the largest in scale and scope in the world . The number of people voting is increasing every year at a significant r ate. In 2014, 40,000 people voted, 67,000 in 2015, and close to 93,000 in 2016, which represents about 7% of the Parisian population. The funds involved are considerable as well. I n 2014, 17.7 million euros were allocated to 9 projects . In 2015, 67.7 milli on euros went to 8 city -wide projects and 180 boroughs projects. In 2016, 94.4 million euros went to 11 city -wide projects and 208 boroughs projects. A total of €500 million has been earmarked for PB for 2014 -2020. Objectives : to rebuild public trust by in creasing the role citizens have in governance and political decision -making . Necessary preconditions : clear rules of engagement and criteria for eligible projects; Structures : City Evaluation Committee (Mayor, elected officials, technical experts and randomly selected group of citizens ); borough -level committees to evaluate borough -level projects (similar composition). Process : There is an annual cycle repeated every year: January -February: proposals are submitted by individual Parisians or groups (no limi tation on age or nationality). This is supported by a variety of meetings, and resources are provided to help develop projects. March -April: initial evaluation of feasibility and cost and co -construction and collective discussion between citizens, NGOs and neighbourhood councils with a view to improve them April-May: finalised project submissions and their technical evaluation by City’s experts June -August: projects are assessed and approved by city - and borough -level ad -hoc Evaluation Committees August -September: selected projects are announced, and citizens are encouraged to organize public campaigns to draw voters September: two weeks for online and in -person voting by Parisians (no limitations on age or nationality) December: Winning projects are announ ced and added to the budget for the next financial year to be passed by the City Council of Paris Project implementation begins immediately in the new FY. The website has a ‘track progress’ feature for citizens to monitor this. Funding allocation informat ion only, no information found on cost to administrate. Regular repetitive programme could be replicated, however likely to involve high costs to communicate, advertise and administer. It would be worth investigating to get a better understanding of the system for voting on projects and any security measures taken to restrict voting from outside the area or multiple votes by one person. Scale is much larger than would be able to be supported by NZ LG, especially in education Participa tion is open to any resident of Paris, there are no limitations on age or nationality. This encourages participation of youth and migrants. Targeting youth and children by reserving a certain amount of budget (10 million euros) for children to vote on proj ects for youth/ children and education. This may encourage family participation in general. Targeting underrepresented and marginalised populations by reserving a certain budget (30 million euros) for projects in deprived areas. - Engagement and participat ion of marginalised populations is low because many projects are seen as “lifestyle ideas” and are not treating actual social problems - Projects do not tackle more complex/ social issues because only the investment budget is available for PB (i.e. no long -term large costs can be incurred for the city). Only a small number of ideas are in areas of solidarity, security or cleanliness. - Information overload of citizens due to the large number of ideas and amount of information they need to make an informed decision. This may discourage participation. - Work overload of the team and systems running the PB due to the need of processing and managing of a large number of ideas - Encouragement of horizontal cooperation between institutions and people - Promotion of constructive dialogue between citizens and government and among citizens - Bringing new perspectives and fresh ideas to city management and development - Better prioritisation of budgetary allocations by the government – following the citizens’ needs - Government opening up to citizens and introducing more flexibility in its processes - Citizens being educated about public budget processes - Citizens more empowered both through their better knowledge of the government, public finance and project manage ment and through gaining agency over the development of their communities - Tangible results of civic engagement in every neighbourhood - Political buy -in and commitment from the senior officials and politicians allows to leverage the necessary resources to deliver and grow the programme and raises its profile among the population and overall. - Support from the civil society helps the promotion of the initiative and increases awareness and participation. - Comprehensive promotional campaign through multip le channels (online and offline) improves awareness and engagement and ensure high participation. - Transparency of the process ensure credibility and legitimacy of the process. - Ongoing engagement with the citizens, especially after the voting, ensures t hat citizens see and understand the tangible results of the PB they were involved in. This motivates them for participation in the next round, confirms credibility of the process and inspires more participation. - While the use of new technologies is impor tant, offline activities are indispensable to galvanise participation. - Respect for deadlines and quick realisation of winning projects are critical to maintain legitimacy and accountability. - Continuity (i.e. repetition of PB every year) has impacted awareness and familiarisation and ensured PB’s becoming a popular practice.

It is estimated that $1.53 million per year wo uld need to be allocated for operating costs if the pilot was to run across all 25 wards in the City of Toronto. With a capital cost of $6.25 million for capital improvements per ward). The greater communication campaign via various media attracted a lot of participants, including from underrepresented population of you th and newcomers. More suitable for small geographic areas: in large areas residents may feel too distanced and not connected to the result/ process . Idea/ project pitching and voting for projects are competitive, which may lead to reinforcing the existing demographic divisions and inequalities

Commercial In Co nfidence Table 9: Citizen jury – Italy Background Description Costs involved Relevance for NZ context Feasibility for different individuals and community types Risks Benefits Design choices CJ 1 and 2 were conducted in 2010 in Turin. CJ 3 based in Castelfranco, a small town in Tuscany. The town is situated in the important industrial district specialised in leather treatment and processing, where more than 500 factories are located. Waste management is a crucial and divisive issue. CJ1 Objective : examined devolution and how to implement at the local level including its consequences. Specific focus on impacts on health and education systems. Process : a jury of 22 people (50/50 male and female split) met for two days in December 2010 and March 2011. Over the two days had plenary meetings (90mins each) and small assisted group discussions (60-90mins). Experts gave technical, legal, political and social advi ce and perspectives on devolution. Jurors gave recommendations at end of 2 -day process. CJ 2 Objective : examined devolution and how to implement at the local level including its consequences. Process: the same as above, the jury (made up of 14 males, 28 f emales) was not able to come to conclusive position on the matter. CJ3 Objective : planned construction of a biomass gasification plant. Process : the jury made up of 50 people (28 males and 22 females) met for 6 days over February and April 2011. Also had plenary meetings (90 -120mins) and group discussions (60 -90mins) with experts. At the end of the 6 days of deliberation they provided recommendations. Innovative engagement method : Participants were randomly selected using LAPS -University of Siena’s Random Digit Dialling (RDD) system from the resident population of the city/town where the jury was to be held. RDD system ensured a non -proportional stratified sample of participants by sex, age, education and area of residence. For CJ3, the commune estimated the cost of 48,250 euro (human resources and materials, e.g. equipment, premises). NZ Councils do not have responsibility for health and education. Adaptation to other areas possible – would need to develop a compelling case for jury involvement. Significant pre -work to enable good decisions in short time -frames (2 day sessions) CJ were run in both a large city (Turin) and a relatively small mountainous commune (Castelfranco) of 13000. - Self selective participation of community can affect the degree of accessibility for inclusion in the participatory process - Structured setting of CJ well served the purpose of accomplishment but not the purpose of learning - Heavy reliance on information experts provided to make decisions, not so much innovati ve thought, knowledge nor arguments between jurors to share and come to decisions - Facilitators and experts may get more speaking time than actual jury members - Tendency for certain jury members to dominate the conversation, may lead to group think/pres sures to adopt originally dominating viewpoint - Communication and collaboration between stakeholders may not always be constructive - If already well established community opinion on issue CJs may be used by political powers to simply re -affirm their p osition, as jury members are likely to be influenced by external community context. CJs become a political tool not true participatory democracy mechanism. - CJ3 was financed by the proponent of the pyro -gasification plant – which was a risk factor that it could manipulate the jury. (the risk did not materialise.) - The implementation of CJs leads to greater direct involvement of citizens to inform policy planning in a variety of sectors, e.g., environment, public health, social services, and urban renewal. - Despite differing degrees of participation and influence in conversations CJs were still perceived by participants as a democratic and open process where they could freely express their opinions - Overall deliberation atmosphere of CJs is cooperative - Facts given by experts on situations have tendency to change participants perceptions on issues meaning better informed decisions by community - Build trust with community as jurors feel they are directly asked for their participation, opinions and de cision on topical issues - Participants find overall experience interesting and a good learning experience - Design of the participatory setting important (task, time, roles, rules, facilitating style) to avoid unintended consequence - Participants must have equal opportunity to speak and mutual obligations of respect for other participants - Process must be democratic. Quality of process effects quality of deliberation (but is not the only factor) - Random selection of participants to be balanced with the need for differing initial opinions on the jury i.e participants may need to be targeted - Decisions made by jury must be legitimized by council - Due to reliance on experts information, experts and others heard by jury must be balanced and represent di verse stakeholders and perspectives - vetting is important – must be balance between need for efficient deliberations (structured setting/process) and the opportunity for collective learning and creative thought (unstructured setting/process) - Evaluation of CJ and it’s processes are key for learning
Commercial In Confidence CASE STUDIES Introduction In consultation with the Department of Internal Affairs we first undertook one case study on a citizen jury example ( the Victoria’s Citizens’ Jury on Obesity) and one on participatory budgeting (Participatory budgeting in Reykjavik ). Following a discussion w ith the working group we added a study on engagement with a strong need to involve Māori or Pacific people ( Out of the Shadows – Bringing Waipā’s Heritage to Life ) and a further one evidencing models for investing in the underlying relationships between lo cal government and communities with examples of soft infrastructure (Neighbourhood Empowerment Network in San Francisco ). Victoria’s Citizens’ Jury on Obesity Background The Victoria’s Citizens’ Jury on Obesity was initiated by Victorian Health Promotion F oundation (VicHealth) – a statutory authority in the Australian state of Victoria with a mandate to promote good health of all Victorians. VicHealth identified obesity as a significant health challenge impacting the Victorians (and Australians more general ly) and decided to design an innovative collaborative response to achieve a high impact and wide support. The organisation newDemocracy Foundation, which is a leading Australian research institute specializing in democratic innovation, developed and imple mented the process of citizens’ jury. One of the design objectives was to “give a random sample of everyday citizens a ‘journey of discovery’ about their food choices”. The citizens’ jury was focused only on food and the way we eat. The specific question w as formulated for the jury: “We have a problem with obesity. How can we make it easier to eat better?” The complete process took place from 28 August till 18 October 2015 and resulted in 20 “asks” (recommendations) for government, industry and the communit y to work together to tackle the obesity crisis. Specific objectives of the citizens’ jury For this jury, two objectives were central: 1 Build trust through public accountability and accessibility, and 2 Build consensus and provide recommendations how poor ea ting behaviours could be addressed. Commercial In Confidence Design choices The important design choices that made this engagement a success are: • Explanation: A lot of effort was spent at the early engagement stage to explain people why a certain plan was made , or a certain policy measure was proposed. The Discovery Bus Tours primarily aimed to show the rich local history and the immense interest of the public i n this history, which could be used to attract more visitors and boost local economy. At the same time, the proposed measures were directed at preservation and study of local history. The use of engaging language (plain English) and accessible visual produ cts is important to bring the point across. • Clear vision of what the Council wants to achieve helped to frame the discussion and engage with the Council’s proposals. • Focus on the people: The engagement campaign put people in the centre. Council staff went where people were, both to physical locations and online locations. For instance, the Council realised early on that Facebook is the main channel of communication with the residents and provided most content and communication over its Facebook account and not via other social media. In terms of physical locations, instead of inviting people to the Council’s premises, the Council’s staff went on a road tour and met people at schools, shops and other places. This approach significantly increased the outreach and draw in some residents who are usually less involved in Council’s matters (e.g. youth). • Iwi involvement was (and continues to be) critical for the project, adding the valuable perspective and credibility to the process. • Equal partnership: treating the community as equal partners in the process increases the credibility of the process and enhances engagement. • Feedback: reporting back to the community is a part of the engagement process. People need to know what happened to their submissions, what decis ions were taken and why. This may increase their willingness to participate in the future local government activities and increases trust. • Ongoing process: public engagement is an ongoing process that did not end with the adoption of the 10 -Year Plan. The Future Waipā website is being used to inform about the decisions taken and the actions of the Council. Available at: https://www.c ambridgenews.nz/2018/04/bus -trip-through -history/ Neighbourhood Empowerment Network in San Francisco Background The Neighbourhood Empowerment Network (NEN) was launched by the Mayor of San Francisco, Ed Lee, in response to the difficulties experienced by communities in New Orleans through hurricane Katrina. The analysis of the response to (and preventive measures in anticipation of) hurricane Katrina by Harvard Kennedy School of Government showed the complete breakdown of the working relationships between the residents and the government. The analysis issued several recommendations focused on increasing capacities of local residents. These recommendations were implemented by San Francisco in the form of NEN. NEN has been operating since 2007 supporting a mi x of community needs (development strategies, public health and safety and emergency management). It employs community development approach and leverages such techniques as place -based planning, human c entred design, asset -based organising and servant lead ership to engage communities and ensure the transfer of ownership back to the n eighbourhoods of their resilience. NEN has created a range of tools, programs, and technical resources that can be considered “soft infrastructure” that is necessary to support grassroots resilience building efforts that are applicable in the City of San Francisco and beyond. Specific objectives NEN aims to empower communities (neighbourhoods) to craft and implement culturally competent strategies that strengthen their capacity to negotiate times of stress and to protect the health and well - Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs
Commercial In Confidence INTRODUCTION MartinJenkins has been contracted by the Department of Internal Affairs to provide research and analysis of participatory practices in local government, in the context of the recent amendment to the Local Government Act 2002 to restore the promotion of com munity wellbeing to the statutory purpose of local government. Local government across comparable jurisdictions has evolved over recent years. The top down systems that support an elected representative system are still strong . However , there is an increas ing shift to include more active, ongoing citizen participation in local decision -making and budget setting. Many citizens are no longer content to simply vote every three or four years and leave local governance to elected members in between elections . The range and scope of participatory practices internationally is enormous, as can be seen in this ‘participedia’ https://participedia.net/ . The advent of new technologies and expectations of anywhere, anytime data and communication have presented both opportunities and challenges for local government. While on one hand technology can enable better participation, in some cases it can also exclude people and increase the division between people who are able to pa rticipate easily and those are not. Good participatory practices are designed to enable engagement from divers e groups of people to ensure that they are properly representative of local demographics . Practices strongly centred around a new technology can be difficult for older citizens to participate in , and practices with significant time demands could exclude people with multiple jobs and high family demands . There is emerging understanding in some of the international examples we looked at, that unless t here is some form of remuneration attached to participation, it can exclude large sections of society that simply cannot afford to participat e at the expense of actual or potential loss of income. This report looks at some of the literature on participato ry practices , as well as describing our own knowledge and understanding of examples we have come across. Th is is necessarily selective, as it is beyond the scope of th is project to find and document every method and incident of citizen participation , and t he methods are still evolving. We have sought to find examples where there is credible analysis of the practice , and an indication of its efficiency and effectiveness. We have found that much of the available academi c literature is focused on the theories of participation rather than on practical examples, or is about consultation and engagement, not participation. As with many emerging practices , there is a tendency to adopt the title with a loose interpretation and we have sought to identify practices tha t are truly participatory .

Available at: https://participedia.net/case/4225 Out of the Shadows – Bringing Waip ā’s Heritage to Life Background The project “ Out of the Shadows ” was a part of the Waipā District Council's campaign “What’s the story” in preparation of the draft 10 -Year Plan. The project was explicitly designed for the “pre - engagement” stage of the community engagement, meaning it engag ed people in the preparatory stage of the 10 -Year Plan. The project began in April 2017, while the submissions for the draft 10 -year Plan were closed in April 2018. The project was developed to inspire a conversation with and among the community about Waip ā's rich history and to position common Waipā ’s heritage as a guide for its common future. Waipā District Council won the Local Government New Zealand Fulton Hogan Excellence Award in 2018 for its successful campaign to highlight the district's heritage, including its role in the New Zealand Land Wars. The project has been widely discussed by local councils all around New Zealand. Specific objectives The Out of the Shadows project had many specific objectives: • to increase the knowledge of the district’s h istory by district’s residents; more generally the council also intended to raise national awareness of Waipā ’s heritage and Waipā ’s role in the New Zealand Land Wars ; • to start a community discussion about the past before talking about the future; • to creat e environment where all people are comfortable to discuss their heritage and what it meant to them knowing that all perspectives are valued; • to create a platform for local iwi to share their stories and to ensure their voices are heard and considered; • to contribute to local iwi’s economic development objectives; • to obtain informed inputs from the community for the proposed increase in heritage investment (i.e. three major heritage proposals) for the 10 -Year Plan; • to make the proposed heritage investment tra nsparent and real, including its impact. Commercial In Confidence KEY FEATURES AND SUCCESS FACTORS This section sets out the common features and success factors in effective community p articipation practices. Community participation is through different forms of a deliberative mini -public, defined by political scientist Robert Dahl as “an assembly of citizens, demographically representative of the larger population, brought together to l earn and deliberate on a topic in order to inform public opinion and decision -making.”1 Features and rationale The exact mandate and model of a participatory practice can vary. Whilst all feature a body of citizens who come together to deliberate on a given issue , this can range from providing a set of recommendations or options , through to formulating a proposal to put to popular referendum , and ultimately to making a collective decision on an identified topic that the convening body has already agreed it will accept. Their common feature is that they go beyond community consultation to a practice whereby citizens directly contribut e to decision -making. It is reported in overseas jurisdictions t hat mini -publics significantly increase tr ust in the decision making of a council. In a local government context, t he rationale underpinning mini publics is that they enable councils to engage citizens meaningfully in decision -making , and can be designed to represent the demographic or demographics whose voices a council wants to hear on the topic. Research has concluded that that a group of randomly selected citizens, when given the information, resources and time to deliberate on a given topic, can produce an informed public judgement . They can also signal real public opinion on a policy issue2. Mini-publics provide a broader model of governance, expanding from a representative democracy where deliberation and decision -making rests with elected representa tives alone, to one where decision -making is shared. Elected politicians may not necessarily reflect the communities they serve,

Commercial In Confidence NEW ZEALAND CONTEXT Local government in New Zealand differs from many other countries in several ways , and participatory processes need to be selected which are appropriate , or can be adapted to this context: • it does not operate core social services such as housing and benefit administration (although there are exceptions where, for example, Wellington City Council operate city housing on behalf of central government) • it does not have responsibility for core emer gency services such as fire, police and ambulance • it does not have responsibility for education • most of its funding is from property tax ( in many other countries it is funded by central government) • the role of Mayor is consistent across New Zealand, is ele cted by popular vote and is a functional role (some countries vary from area to area, have a system of rotation for the Mayoral role or it is elected by the Councillors and the role is ceremonial only i.e., has no voting rights or involvement in administer ing by -laws or regulations) Like other countries New Zealand is experiencing decline in local government voting participation, particularly from youth and diverse communities. This ‘voter apathy’, as it is often called, is thought to be caused by the impre ssion that there is little ability to affect outcomes. Participatory practices have emerged as a response to this, although we have been unable to find strong evidence that they have increased voter numbers yet. There is evidence that New Zealand local gov ernment has been experimenting with participatory practices, especially with planning and spending prioritisation. Examples of efforts to include citizens in participation can be seen in Auckland Council ’s co-design lab, Wellington City Council ’s trials using Loomio to develop its Alcohol Management strategy and Waip a District Council ’s approach to engagement for its Te Ārā Wai initiative. The limitation on local government adopting more participatory practices, appears to be the associated costs and the a dditional time they involve, which needs to be resourced . Changes to the Local Government Act 2002 have focused on increasing consultation for long term plans but have not fully anticipated the trajectory of public participation. The legislation is now se en by some as a barrier to more fluid, consistent participatory practices due to the: • focus on point -in-time engagement • guidance toward consultation based on pre -established council policies and positions • requirement for document -type consultation material • expectations of councils to allow people to present to them (reinforcing the engagement settings that some councils have , expect ing people to come to them to present) We note that these were all appropriate at the time of legislation and that at the time, it did a good job of setting the expectation of much stronger engagement practice around long term plan development. The comments we make on this are simply to point out that there could be more flexible expectations Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs
Commercial In Confidence OVERVIEW OF POPULAR PARTICIPATORY PRACTICES Practice Description Relevance for NZ Risks Benefits Participatory budgeting This practice allows citizens to make decisions on how funding is used. This is mostly practiced in Europe with limited examples in New Zealand but can be applied to ring - fenced funds in NZ. Takes longer and costs more. Harder for some communities to participate, especially groups that have less available time, poorer communication ability or lack tech skills. Improved levels of trust in local government, if done well. Better spend - $ on th ings that matter to community. Improved connection between local government and community. Citizen juries Decisions made by a jury that is representative – usually on a single , significant topic/issue. May not be compatible with NZ top down structures as genuine juries have full delegated decision making (as in a court ). Would only be practical in larger cities. Takes longer and costs more. Harder for lower socio - economic participants. Can produce poor decisions if training and familiarisatio n is insufficient. Difficult to get true representation without power to require it ( like court juries) Decisions are more likely to be acceptable or explainable across the full range of community groups. Improves connections between local government and all communities

Commercial In Confidence Post-engagement actions In May 2018, hearings o n the submissions were held. The submitters could present additional information, elaborate their submissions and answer questions of the Councillors. After the hearings, the Council held deliberations on the submissions. At deliberations, all submissions were considered taking into account such factors as the number of submiss ions per issue, the opinions expressed, knowledge of the district etc. After that, a workshop was held to review the financial implications resulting from deliberations. The submitters received feedback on what happened to their submission. A summary report on decision s taken during the deliberations was released and distributed through the media, the Future Waipā website and Council website and offices. In addition, a letter or email was sent to those submitters who provided input that was not included in the summary report. This individual feedback included the record of decision made on the submission. Risks Local heritage is a risky topic for engagement. On the one hand, it may be of little interest f or the residents and require a lot of promotion and education. On the other hand, it is a very sensitive and even controversial topic. For example, the Council was accused by different “sides” of telling “their” version of truth. In 2010, the Council’s pro posal for a museum and theatre complex failed and was strongly criticised. A lot of patience, understanding and cultural competence are key mitigation measures. Advice from local iwi and history experts was sought were appropriate. Investment in local heri tage is not considered the “core Council business” by some residents who strongly and very vocally opposed the campaign. The complex project with many fast -moving elements is at risk of getting messy and fail. The mitigation measure was to have very clear distribution of tasks and responsibilities and a robust time plan The cost may run high both due to the amount of materials produced and events conducted and due to the bilingualism (i.e. learning the correct pronunciation of all Māori words, creating bili ngual materials and checking them – all takes time and money). Benefits The following benefits have been identified: • Local residents and Council staff developed better knowledge and understanding of the local history, pertinent to New Zealand’s history, especially through uncovering different (Māori and Pākehā) perspectives. • The engagement linked the local history to the future planning. • The broad engagement of the community and receiving inputs from the community ensure a higher buy -in/ support for the Council’s investment plans. It was reported that the Council’s proposal to invest in Waipā heritage sites was supported by 71 per cent of submitters. Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs

It brings together diverse representatives in a deliberate manner to gain a wide range of perspectives on a variety of matters. It can be single issue or ongoing. I t doesn’t typically involve decision making. We are aware of examples of New Zealand Councils using citizen panels including Hutt City, Dunedin City and New Plymouth District Councils. Wellington City launched a citizen panel in 2013, however we were unabl e find evidence of it operating today. If not properly structured, can become a group of people taking to each other with no mechanism to influence or inform decision makers. Is usually online which can restrict some group’s participation. Quick and easy way to get feedback on ideas, issues or policies. Low cost and can be effective if proper structures for disseminating information, taking feedback into the council and providing feedback loops to the group are in place. Some councils make efforts to do this now. Can be difficult to sustain with some groups over long periods. Can miss less obvious considerations like hidden assets and infrastructure. More involvement and inclusion . Better connections between LG and hard to reach groups. Neighbourhood plans Collaborative planning for a specific area or aspect that the community prioritises. Commercial In Confidence Stakeholders involved A number of stakeholders worked together to ensure the successful outcome of the jury process: • VicHealth managed the supplier consortium, handled stakeholder relations, chaired the steering group, defined the jury’s remit, provided an overview of obesity and food in Victoria, drafted the final insights report (jointly with newDemocracy Foundation). • Multidisciplinary supplier consortium of suppliers to be key creation and delivery partners of the jury process, combining leading expertise in democratic research, large -scale deliberative facilitation, user experience design and social technologies. • newDemocracy Foundation developed and implemented the complete citizens’ jury process, starting with the selection of jurors and finishing with co -producing the insights report. • Steering group was created to include key public health organisations that would be potentially involved in implementing the jury’s recommendations. The group included key decision -makers in government, industry and the community , namely the Department of Premier and Cabinet of Victoria , the Australian Food and Grocery Council, Australian Beverages Council, Australian Medical Association Victoria, Foodbank Victoria, Coles (major superm arket chain), Melbourne city council , Obesity Policy Coalition, CHOICE (consumer advocacy group), C-PAN Deakin University and Tennis Australia. • Media partners with regional newspapers to boost awareness and legitimacy of the initiative (The Herald Sun 1.3 million readers in Victoria every week day and Sunday Herald Sun by 1.4m every Sunday) • Jury: 117 jurors started online process, 78 participated in the face -to-face event (largest scale citizens’ jury in Australia). Process Jurors were recruited using stratified random selection . First, 20,000 invitations were sent, both by regular mail and electronically, to candidates drawn from two student databases and the VoteCompass database (VoteCompass is an interactive, online voting advice application; citizen s interested in public policy events register there). These sources were chosen to ensure a varies sample and to reach the young people who are typically a low response group. In the second selection round, 117 jurors were selected to provide a representat ive sample of Victorian residents. Over a period of six weeks, the 117 jurors engaged in online deliberation in a facilitated forum. In this way, they reviewed and discussed written submissions/ evidence (64 items) presented by stakeholders, experts, indiv iduals and organisations as well as the steering group on the topic of the jury. The submissions included the readers’ poll in the Herald Sun and a youth poll. All submissions were made public. Following the online deliberations, 78 jurors met in person for face -to-face deliberations. This stage lasted two days and was facilitated by an independent engagement expert and facilitator . The main objective at this stage was to collectively produce a report with recommendations to present to the steering group. T he deliberation was held in small groups, 20 groups in total. Commercial In Confidence Stakeholders involved The main stakeholder involved was the District Council. The Council staff planned and carried out the engagement campaign. Local iwi w as involved starting from the early engagement throughout the whole process. The Waipā community as a whole can be considered as a stakeholder because the Council treated it as a partner in this process. Process of engagement The project carried out a broad community engagement programme through a variety of channels and with a great number of various elements, mixing traditional approaches with highly innovative ideas. The early engagement process started in April 2017. Sharing memories and stories was the central element of the early engagement campaign. Th e idea was to capture stories and visions of different generations, told from different perspectives, and to create a shared memory and understanding of Waipā . Council staff visited rest -homes and interviewed older residents. They also went to schools and asked their students about their hopes and dreams linked to Waipā and to memories captured. Simple cost -effective photo -booths were installed to capture memories of Waipā . Council used all imagery (photos, interviews) on its social media channels, which en couraged more people to share their stories and photos. The Council also ran print ads in local newspapers focused on key aspects of Waipā ’s history (in 2017) and on Māori history (early 2018). Discovery Bus Tours started in autumn 2017. Discovery Bus Tou rs were free bus tours, run by the Council, to heritage sites and places of historical significance, including battle sites of Land Wars of 1860s. The bus tours proved extremely popular and were all booked out within days after being announced. Initially, seven 2,5 hours bus tours were offered in 2017, and 321 people participated in them. The bus tours had a professional guide on board who encouraged passengers to share their stories and knowledge. A local iwi member welcomed passengers on sites and told th e Māori history linked to the sites and Land Wars. At the end of each tour, participants were encouraged to get involved in the community discussion around heritage and make a submission towards the 10 -Year Plan. The bus tours returned in 2018 -2019 and cov ered new areas of the Waipā district. Funding from the Ministry for Culture and Heritage was obtained for the additional bus tours in 2018 -2019. In 2018, 329 people participated in bus tours. An interactive online map was created (discoverwaipa.co.nz) to explore the Waipā district and its heritage sites as well as to discover the history around them. In October 2017, Waipā District Council was the only Council to officially commemorate the Land Wars. Local hapū, schools, community and Council representatives participated in the ceremony. After months of the broad pre -engagement, more focused engagement with the draft 10 -Year Plan started. Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs

Objective : various health policy decisions Necessary preconditions : Establishment of “rules of conduct” between jurors; an external facilitator supporting the jurors; the precise formulation of the topic, charge or question provided by organisers; s teering committees or advisory groups (in 2/3 cases) made up of policy -makers, discipline experts, advocacy group representatives, clinical practitioners, patients, caregivers. Process : recruitment of jurors (most had 12 -25 participants and three had 40 participants). Nearly two -thirds of the juries took place over 1 -2 days, usually on a weekend. Written material as well as expert presentations given to juries, after which deliberations were held. The evidence provided by expert witnesses (in two cases re source persons were used in addition to investigate any questions the jury needed addressing). Expert presentations and deliberations were guided and overseen by steering committees/ groups. They also helped to engage participants. The main method through which recommendations were developed was consensus or consensus with minority opinion or voting. Steering committees/ groups helped spread and implement findings. Innovative engagement methods : 20 different recruitment strategies were used to recruit juror s. Most common method was stratified random sampling. Other methods included: through the electoral roll, random digit dialling or commercial database of registered telephone numbers or national polling institute, non -stratified random sampling through ele ctoral roll, random digit dialling or survey response, recruitment by a market research company or a professional recruiter. In 28 cases, honorariums were offered to jurors. Facilitator fee Fee for the resource person, where used Would need to be trialled . Short duration may be workable, significant pre -work needed to ensure jury can come up to speed quickly on unfamiliar subject matter. Specific criteria for recruitment were often used to ensure marginalised or typically underrepresented groups in decisio n- making were recruited onto the jury Shorter than recommended juries may limit opportunity for constructive dialogue and some participants complained of insufficient time to explore issues, but brief daylong juries still delivered outcomes - Mixed results for recruitment strategies to get fair representation despite best efforts - Attrition important factor in bias as those who drop out tend to be those harder to recruit initially - CJs often biased (only six of the 28 studies were found to be unbiased) - Juries held in staggered fashion encountered problems associated with the disjointed nature of multiple sessions held over a long period. - Public policy process may limit use of most ideal from of CJ Ability for citizens to engage with and learn from others in their community in a structured manner - Provided the research question is tightly defined and concrete in nature, even brief one -day citizens’ juries can deliver useable outcomes to inform poli cy and practice. - CJ can enhance the citizens role, particularly in capacity building for empowered citizens - Jury length did not appear to impact on recruitment bias - CJs tend to be small enough (25 people or less) to achieve effective deliberation but still large enough to achieve diversity - CJs are relatively inexpensive compared to larger deliberation methods Special attention should be paid to recruitment, methods, independent oversight by a steering committee, jury duration, moderation and respec t for the participant volunteer - To reduce bias use stratified sampling with broad range of criteria; recruitment through market research company or by telephone, letter or door knocking ; and a substantial honorarium - Juries should be held over 4 -5 days (as recommended by the Jefferson Centre) to give participants more control over the report and provide opportunities to engage with different forms of evidence (video, witnesses, a creative writing exercise) - Hold juries in succession so not disjointed ov er long periods of time - Allow juries the opportunity to challenge the evidence presented and to seek more information to ensure diversity in witness composition in addition to jury composition - Consider withholding the topic of the jury until the jury d ay to reduce recruitment of participants with strongly held beliefs - Deliberation should be supported through the use of steering committees and independent, expert facilitators to aid interactions between jury members - Must have buy -in from policy and practice decision -makers to implement jury recommendations - May consider Pre -jury contracts binding commissioning organisations to respond to jury recommendations

Commercial In Confidence Table 13: World Cafes Background Description Costs involved Relevance for NZ context Feasibility for different individuals and community types Risks Benefits Design choices The World Café is a methodology for hosting conversations about relevant questions and themes. The ideal is that there are multiple conversations that build of f of each other to explore the issue deeply. Objectives : to explore, develop and rehabilitate own opinions through engagement with others in the community. Process : the time and place of the café as well as the topic can be announced in local media and social media. The size of the group depends on the size of the place and time available (can be from 10 to 100 participants). At the start the host defines the purpos e of the café to the participants and divides them into groups of 4 - 5 people per table. The groups will be rotating between tables in 3 -4 conversational rounds of 20 - 30 minutes. During each round, participants discuss progressively deepening questions re lated to the issue. The questions should be prepared by the hosts in advance and clearly stated to the participants at each table at the beginning of each round by a table host. Table hosts facilitates the discussion of the group and summarises the results to the next group coming to his/her table. This next group then starts off where the previous finished, learning from and building on them. At the end of the conversational rounds, groups summari se their key findings and present them to the entire group. At the end, the entire group of participants convenes to connect all of the ideas into just a few shared key points. The cost of a World Café is only as much as the host s would like to spend , so can be kept to a minimum. Generally the costs include the materials needed/desired (table cloths, markers, paper, name tags ), food and drink. World Café is a relatively simple idea and format that could easily work in a New Zealand context. While the Café label could create a preconception about the type of person who would be comfortable in that setting, it is not necessary to use that label – or indeed host it in a Café. The format could be adapted to work in a number of different environments so it could be used in contexts that are more familiar to the specific population types being targeted. Representation of underrepresented populations need to be encouraged both through the selection process and during the conversation in the cafe Can be used for a range of different topics and inputs Can be encouraged as a community -led engagement Is able to be carried out in many locations that suit the communities Set a clear context of what is discussed and why Envisage the desired outcomes and design questions and processes to ensure the café arrives to these outcomes Invest in the design of questions: the central questions need to be clear and matter to the participants Create a hospitable place, with food and drinks Use facilitators to encourage contributions from everyone (e.g. Talking Object technique is recommended) Use interactive and playful methods (e.g. use different colours for different issues and opinions, allow participants to draw on the tablecloth etc) Active listening and connecting different perspectives

Objective : To move from consultation to active involvement/ engagement of the community to jointly develop solutions. Phase 3 – The collected data was sorted and then summarised by the InstaBooth team (researchers and senior university students). On this basis, data analysis took place in a workshop of the implementation group. Workshop participants browsed the d ata and brainstormed initial themes. These themes were used to develop a draft masterplan for the town. Innovative engagement : the InstaBooth itself is an innovative form of engagement. Design Thinking used to ensure maximum and wide ranging involvement. D iscussions In Space systems – survey answers and comments displayed publicly on big screens . Blended digital and non -digital interaction tools in physical space – as described above. Exact costs not known, but the InstaBooth was funded by a grant from QUT’ s Engagement Innovation Grants (EIG) over 2014 - 2015. These grants are between AUD 10,000 and AUD 30,000 . This can work in New Zealand as it is, or can be further adapted by incorporating local design into the booth Pomona is a small town of 3000 population. The booth is portable and should be located where the issues under discussion matters. More of a way to foster debate than providing definitive answers . Questions need to be designed carefully to get necessary answers. If the engagement interfa ce of the InstaBooth is too unfamiliar, participants may have difficulty to engage. Commercial In Confidence Table 15: Neighbourhood decision making - Quarter associations and quarter contracts - Switzerland Background Description Costs involved Relevance for NZ context Feasibility for different individuals and community types Risks Benefits Design choices Switzerland has a range of informal participatory structures in addition to formal local government. Quarter association and quarter contracts are a widespread form in smaller towns and villages. Quarters are basically defined neighbourhoods. Quarter assoc iations are territorially defined non - governmental organisations and an informal form of community governance. Quarter contracts rely on citizen participation in individual quarters to identify priority projects and quarter community centres that organise social and cultural activities. Quarter association Objectives : protection of interests of the quarter residents and engagement with the local government on behalf of resident on planning issues . They see themselves as a counterpoint to the local administr ation. Necessary preconditions : legal basis in the Civil Code that made quarter associations legal entities, subject to certain requirements (e.g. regular reporting). Structures : Head committee for association elected by members. Process : Quarter statutes are passed by the members to define purpose of association and their work. Associations run own physical meeting points in their areas and websites. Association made up of members – can be admitted or resign at any time – who can be natural or legal perso ns residing in the quarter . In some cases they collect small annual membership fee. Citizens come to local association with issues, may use as an official contact point through which to contact local government . Not liable to local government but can inte ract frequently based on local policy or a memorandum of understanding . Quarter associations may also procure fuel, fertilizer etc on behalf of their members as well as run community libraries and centres. Quarter contracts Objectives : engage locals in planning processes and promote projects to locals . Structures : specific bodies that work on defining development priorities for their areas. Process : a bit similar to PB process , but with more decision making powers delegated to residents . Municipal Council designates a budget each year for (typically small) projects in a given quarter . Interested residents submit a project proposal . Project group (made up of 14 -15 quarter residents) assess project against contract aims, analyses project, contacts partners, drafts a budget and an action plan . A piloting committee (made up of mayor and another councillor, and reps from other party members on council, tenant’s association, traders association, social workers, another association and a resident – all from the quarter (area), chosen on annual basis by municipal decision) supports the project, implementation and evaluation occur. n/a Something similar could be adapted to be workable in New Zealand. It is similar to Business Improvement Districts model in use by Auckland and Wellington City Councils albeit with a more social focus. These forms are used specifically in the settlements with smaller populations (less than 30,000). Per town, there are typically several such organisations ( e.g. the town of Aarau has 21,459 population and 7 quarter associations). Strengthens sense of community Improve the knowledge of self - government, interaction with the government and project management These are forms of self - government that are complet ely self-organised. Making room for the community and support of their decisions by the local administration
Commercial In Confidence Table 16: Tables – Toronto (CA) Background Description Costs involved Relevance for NZ context Feasibility for different individuals and community types Risks Benefits Design choices Tables, or working groups, are viewed as being highly effective in that they involve citizens in both th e design and implementation of initiatives. The topics can be demographic or social. They are credited with building relationships between Council officials and the community which enabled the successful settlement of a large influx of Syrian refugees in 2015. Objectives : joint planning and implementation of initiatives Process : Tables are established on identified topics that the council seeks to advance. The local government approves the establishment of each Table, which relates to an identified priority . The Table is the responsibility of a Council Executive Leadership Team (ELT) member. This could either be in the Governance or Community Engagement Division, with strong links to the council’s social policy function. The ELT member facilitates the Table, and is responsible for ensuring appropriate connections across the ELT to drive implementation of the work of the Table. Membership of the Table is determined by the senior officer and consists of representatives from NGOs, CCOs, central government agenci es and council staff whose substantive work relates to the topic of the Table. Experts can be added to the Table as an advisory body to the Table, drawn from NGO connections and supported by them. The role of the Table is to develop strategy, support strategic implementation through developing a work plan including community engagement strategies, and to monitor and evaluate. The extent of the involvement of people with lived experience can vary fro m providing advice to co -design. The Table incorporates extensive community engagement to inform its work. No information found on costs This could be adopted for a specific purpose in New Zealand. Due to the administration and formality, it is more likel y to be of use for a nationally significant issue, or for a large council like Auckland. The tables tend to be made up of representatives from NGO’s associated with the relevant sectors – so is not typically a direct engagement. The table members then enga ge with he relevant communities. The effectiveness of the model is dependent on the skills of the facilitator. Without this: All the parties required for the shared outcomes may not be willing to participate The Table becomes a place for talking without a dvancing anything People involved in the Table are not solution focused. It brings together all parties required to advance a particular topic, connecting them to work for shared outcomes It has flexibility of membership according to requirements, and can be enhanced with additional membership of groups and individuals if they are required as the direction of the work becomes clearer It builds relationships that creating a capacity to coordinate responses to complex ‘issues of the day’ beyond the work of the Table It is embedded in the executive and driven by the leadership team so the advice provided is implemented It provides a monitoring and evaluation function. Endorsement by the local government and strong support of Tables by elected members of the local government. Participation of NGO s (rather than individual representation ) – because parties to the Table are responsible for contributing to the delivery of the work plan in their substantive role, and it is through these existing mechanisms that the Tables engage with communities.
Commercial In Confidence Table 17: Conversation station – e.g., Whanganui (NZ) Background Description Costs involved Relevance for NZ context Feasibility for different individuals and community types Risks Benefits Design choices Conversation station is an open structure for investigating culture on a personal scale in public places . Conversation stations usually investigate personal, difficult, even uncomfortable issues (e.g. euthanasia). Whanganui Distric t Council implemented one in 2018. Objective : to investigate difficult issues in an informal situation on a personal level; to investigate possibilities of public dialogue, explore social dynamics, and question who we are to each other as strangers and as members of our common society . Necessary preconditions : a large dice with discussion questions written on each side; a dialogue facilitator. Process : In a public, but fairly private space (e.g. street café) a table(s) with a large dice is set up. The dice have discussions questions written on its sides. The questions can be interchangeably personal/ social/ political. Once two persons sit down at the table(s), the facilitator invites them to start a conversation. The facilitator is not present on site, bu t is in a car nearby, able to observe and hear the dialogue. The facilitator asks people to throw the dice and discuss the question selected in this manner. The facilitator announces the end of the conversation. Currently, permanent audio has been installed that can be activated by pushing a button. It prompts people to spin a wheel to start conversation. A version of this practice is: a person (e.g. elected local government member) is sitting at the station awaiting a second person to join. Commercial In Confidence Table 20: Tools for collating citizens ideas and ranking them or ‘voting them up’ e.g., Ethelo Background Description Costs involved Relevance for NZ context Feasibility for different individuals and community types Risks Benefits Design choices Ethelo https://ethelo.com/ is an online engagement and decision - making platform. Ethelo is comprised of two entities: Ethelo Decisions - a technology company dedicated to helping organizations focus collective intelligence to make the best decisions more quickly - and Ethelo Democr acy - a non -profit society dedicated to a more effective, citizen -engaged democracy. Ethelo Decisions undertakes commercial projects to fund the development of the Ethelo technology, which is provided to Ethelo Democracy and its partners for the cost of hardware. The Ethelo algorithm was developed to enable fair outcomes in complex multi - stakeholder negotiations. Objectives : to harness the power of collective wisdom for governance and group decisions. Process : Ethelo is a patented algorithm that uses an extension of morphological analysis. It is compatible with and a complement to processes such as conjoint analysis, the Monte Carlo Method and decision trees. It incorporates a novel approach to liquid democrac y using trust networks . The algorithm combine s various decision parameters (options, issues, criteria, constraints, influence, and fairness ) and build s a space of potential outcomes . These are evaluated and ranked according to aggregated analysis of the participants. It finds outcomes with high average support and low variance in satisfaction among participants .
