The Construction Board also consults with Neighbourhood Councils on the feasib ility and costs. For example, in 2017, the Construction Board assessed 1090 ideas and left over 250 most popular ideas that also met criteria for the online vote. This stage takes three months and ends in June. The third stage is voting (in October). First, the voters need to be authenticated via the National Voters Registry (online). Voters also need to choose online, in which of the 10 districts (neighbourhoods) they will vote. Each resident has one vote. To cast a vote, a re sident divides the available budget up between his/her favourite projects. As a resident vote, he/she will see how the overall budget is reduced, and the remaining projects that are over -budget are greyed out. To prevent against bias in voting, e very time a voter clicks on the site , ideas are presented in a random order. The vote is electronic, secure and binding. Voter can go back and correct their votes several times; only the final vote counts. A dvanced security measures are utilized to protect user and website information (for instance, the technology provider does not have access to personal data). The software used for the vote is open source (Open Active Voting ). The tallying is done by the City Council, and winners are announced through a special cer emony. Results are also emailed to participants of the voting. The final decision on the implementation of projects is taken by the City Council, who committed to formally process the highest voted proposal on a monthly basis and implement them (in 2014, 6 4% of proposals were implemented). Each year around 100 -120 ideas are implemented by the City Council and Neighbourhood Councils . Execution of projects starts shortly after the voting is finalised; construction projects usually start the year following the voting (in summer). While most projects relate to construction and infrastructure (e.g. improvements to parks, playgrounds, roads) and are relatively small, there are examples of other projects. For instance, one of the early successes was an idea put for ward by a nine -year-old girl requesting more school field trips. Larger -scale projects included renovation of a small disused power station into a youth centre and an increased provision of shelters for homeless people. Engagement Reykjavik’s City Council invests heavily in the promotion of participatory budgeting. The campaign was opened in Reykjavik’s main cultural centre. Posters and billboards were used all over the city. It has used professional marketing companies and a multi -channel marketing campai gn to make people aware of the participatory budgeting process. This has included Google and Facebook ads, Twitter and advertisement on radio and TV. Comedians have been hired as the face of the process. In addition, an extensive outreach campaign took pla ce offline in places, like shopping malls, schools, retirement homes and other. The My Neighbourhood website has an automatic translation to over a dozen languages. Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs
Commercial In Confidence These engagement efforts resulted in more than 70,000 participants (overall) of My Neighbourhood – over half of Reykjavik’s population (with 450,000 unique visitors in 2014 alone!). The percentage of voters has been around 8% -9% of the population. The age profile and corresponding participation remained consistent over time. The highest participation is observed in the age group 35 -39 years at 19.5%, followed by 40 -44 year -olds at 18.5% and over 56 year -olds at 20%. Cost The project starting with private financing by two Reykjavik citizens, who are also founders of Citizens Foundation. Currently, the project management team consists of 4 people. Two project managers deal with PR, evaluate incoming ideas, and maintain communication between the citizens and the government. One communications expert works with the news. One project coordinat or oversees the execution of all projects and works in the Environmental and Planning department of the City Council. In addition, there are neighbourhood Councils’ staff, Construction Board staff and other. It is estimated that around 4 to 7 people in ea ch council/ committee that are involved in My Neighbourhood project part-time. For 2011 -2015, the cost of Better Reykjavik (of which My Neighbourhood is roughly half) was about NZD 17 million (1.3 billion Icelandic krona). The expenses included the salari es of project managers, advertising and promotional costs as well as service agreement for the online platform (2500 euro per month or NZD 4400). Risks Ensuring broad participation and especially representation may be a challenge, despite wide campaigning and creative use of media. At the moment, relatively little is known about the demographics of the participants of the budgeting process. A small recent evaluation suggested that the participation is biased towards those who are university educated, those on higher incomes and people aged 35 to 55. Citizen participants do not have ultimate decision making authority, which could lead to frustration, especially as not all proposals can be implemented by the City Council. Small budget available for allocation through the participatory budgeting may discourage participation as people feel that this budget will not create meaningful changes and that only small projects will be implemented. The large number of ideas generated places a strain on both city officials , in terms of their capacity to manage and assess them, and on the IT systems. Benefits The following benefits have been identified: • Citizens receive a voice within the policy -making process and the power to influence the outcome of budgetary issues, devel op better understanding of budgetary policies and see tangible results of their engagement. Requiring substantive amounts of time can be a barrier to participation, but enough time needs to be allowed so that people can access and understand enough information and deliberate it. In all instances, ti me frames need to be defined and explained. • Deliberation s of a citizen’s jury take place over a short intensive time period This encourages participation , as it is a short -term commitment for each individual . The recommended duration of citizens juries is four to five days but may be shorter depending on the issue at hand. Key considerations are to allow time for participants to engage and assess the evidence (including hearing witnesses , and studying written ev idence ), the oppo rtunity to receive expert advice and additional research if necessary , and sufficient time for deliberation and decision -making. Part of a wider and longer -term strategy of trust building • Participatory processes are part of wider community engagement . They work best in places with a strong culture of community engagement , and when the process, the proceedings and the final decisions are publicly available. • If the process is repeated regularly, people become more fami liar with it and participation increases, especially as the decisions taken in the process are implemented. • Evaluation and feedback mechanisms are built in to the design of the process from the beginning, and the learnings incorporated into the design of future processes

The reintroduction of wellbeings into the Local Government Act, provide s new context for the relationship between Local Government elected members and officials and the public. In this report we explore some of the ways this has been approached internationally. These differences between local government in New Zealand and its international counterparts have an impact on the type and scale of participatory practices they can adopt. In considering examples, we need to be cognisant that often local government in other counties operate at a different scale, have higher overall budgets , more diversity of expertise and increased ability to address the needs of community in a holistic manner.

Stakeholders involved NEN has a “whole community” approach to stakeholder engagement and involves all types of organisations, networks and individuals located in a specific neig hbourhood. It is an alliance of residents, neighbourhoods (neighbourhood organisations), business associations and businesses, non-profits and charitable foundations, faith -based organisations, civic agencies, government and academic institutions. Examples of ‘soft infrastructure’ NEN has developed nine programmes targeting different aspects of community resilience. Each of the programmes provides a framework for community action and a variety of resources, such as templates and guides that can be used by n eighbourhoods and smaller communities. NEN also provides technical support to communities in the form of workshops, seminars and other informational, educational and training events. In collaboration with the Institute for Civic and Community Engagement (I CCE) at San Francisco State University, the NEN created a NEN university that aims to improve local communities through resilience education. Students earn class credit for projects, such as community asset mapping and leadership training, that make commun ities more resilient and better places to live. In addition, there are two NEN Leadership Academies (one for youth) that equip participants with skills to advance resilience in their communities. NEN also facilitates the engagement between communities and its leaders (including local government). The engagement focuses on risks/ shocks that communities are likely to experience and how they can work together to develop and implement mitigating strategies. This “pre -engagement” is an investment in the relatio nships between leadership and communities and helps to higher levels of trust and reciprocity with communities, which will increase cooperation during disasters and accelerate recovery from them. Empowered Communities Program (ECP) is an umbrella programme for resilience building. ECP harnesses the expertise and resources of all stakeholders to develop and implement overall resilience plans in each neighbourhood. Under ECP, NEN provides the communities with templates for resilience plans and guides them thr ough the process to develop their own plans. NEN takes an advisory and facilitator role in this process, while the community drives the development of all plans and makes decisions on leadership and operations. NEN supports the four working groups that wer e set up in each neighbourhood: 1) children and their families; 2) seniors and people living with disabilities; 3) immigrant communities; and 4) small business and non -profit organizations. These groups meet monthly for discussions, while NEN provides tech nical/ expert advice, helps with advocacy and investment planning. The Steering Group of NEN oversees the implementation of the neighbourhood plans. The HUB Program is a part of ECP and supports community’s overall preparedness on a daily basis. Even if this is not the case, trust in politicians is low and declining. Decisions made a by a cross -section of society that the broader public can identify with may seem more acceptable or even more legitimate. The approach does require a deep theoretical shift in how the role of elected members is viewed. Research by Professor Lyn Carson of the University of Sydney Business School has further concluded that a well facilitated group of citizens can make better decisions than a group of experts as they are coming to the topic with an open mind. She also provided evidence that the approach builds trust in local government, for example where a mayor in one local authority that used deliberative dialogue increased their percentag e share of the vote at the next election, in contrast to the declining vote their party had for the position of mayor in all other parts of the state.3 Mini-publics are a stronger mechanism tha n advisory models, such as panels. Such mechanisms can contrib ute to this broader governance, particularly when they are formal mechanisms with established channels to decision makers. However, they do not transfer decision -making to the citizens. F ormal long standing mechanisms are also not accessible for all divers e communities as they may not be culturally appropriate and require members to have capacity to participate and to be comfortable engaging directly with authority. They also invest power in a small number of people, whereas m ini- publics de-politicise issue s by involving interested individuals, not advocates , and different individuals over time . Attributes of effective formal participation models The context in which participatory processes operate is important. Our r esearch confirm s a range of engagement and participation mechanisms are required for diverse voices to be heard , and to build the credibility of each mechanism . One mechanism is rarely sufficient. Within this context, c ommon themes were that participatory models: • are more effective when the council adopt s a broader view of governance , and actively supported mechanisms which engage its diverse populations meaningfully in its decision making. • are more effective when they are endorsed by the elected members, from where they derive their status and authority, but primarily work with the council organisation to ensure a link between policy and implementation • are more effective when participants are perceived as “ordinary” citizens, reflective of the community , rather than as lobby groups , and the selection process and outcomes are transparently communicated • are more credible when they allow for the participation of many individuals over time , and of different individuals and different demographics who are selected according to the voices needed for each topic
Commercial In Confidence participants . Citizens are involved in making and agreeing these “rules of engagement”. For example, in joint planning: - There is a clear understanding on the scope of the planning , the legal force of the final plan , how it will be implemented and by whom, and how this will be supervised - There are clear rules for the planning process, including the timeframe and what should be achieved, roles and responsibilities, how the plan will be agreed , including who can vote • Participatory processes are designed to be transparent to and share information with the wider community, which creates legitimacy and acceptance of the decisions . • Once a participatory process is established, citizens agree on the process and decision -making criteria . They are supported by external experts as required, and by local government staff who can provide technical expertise , an understand ing of how council operates, and a secretariat function where required . However, the council has delegated decision -making to the citizens. For example , in participatory budgeting, participants decide on appropriate proposals and projects – if council officials did this it would simply be grant giving . Participation, recruitment and selection • Once the council has decided to establish a participatory process , the purpose and the way citizens can get involved are widely promoted using a variety of media, channels and methods which are both digital and non -digital. This increases participation in collective processes such as participatory budgeting and increases the pool of people willing to serve on a citizens’ jury. It i s the first step in transparency and increases the legitimacy of the decision s taken at the end of the process . This is further enhanced when: - Participation is extended to groups who cannot vote in elections , for example young people between 14-18 and new migrants - Strategies are designed and implemented to reach marginalised and under -represented populations, and people not otherwise involved in civil society organisations. This can include special events for families and youth, multi -lingual tools, and visits to community meeting places such as places of worship • Participatory budgeting and joint planning do not normally require a selection process as usually anyone can participate. However, a selection process is required for citizens’ juries. To reduce bias and ensure a jury that is reflective of its community, participants are chosen from the positive responses by stratified random selection . Participants can be selected to match the demographic of the whole city or community , or on selected demographic s. Enablers and incentives Participatory processes should be designed and promoted so that : • Potential participants feel it is worth the ir time and effort . The greatest incentive is that it will be a fulfilling experience that will make a positive difference , with tangible results . Fundamentally this is achieved by the council communicating that it will accept the outcome of the process. Other motivating factors can include scale, for example that the funds available for allocation in a Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs
Commercial In Confidence participatory budgeting process are reasonably large , or that participation is a development opportunity, with participants learning new skills such as project management . • Barriers to participation are minimised . This can include providing stipends or an honorarium for citizens’ jurors. For participatory processes that require meetings, it can include food, childcare, transport , meeting locations that are easily accessib le (including remotely ), varied meeting times . interpreters and multi -lingual documents, and a defined time commitment . Adequate s upport for participation • The processes are well-resourced, with a commitment in advance to funding , and adequate time from council staff • Council staff are trained well in advance to be able to run an effective promotion, recruitment and selection process es, and to provide technical support throughout the participatory process . Staff also play a role in helping participants to understand how local government works. • Subject matter advice is also available from independent external experts where appropriate . For example with citizen’s juries, there should be a diverse range of experts and witnesses to support varied and balanced perspectives on the issue. Eviden ce considered must be made public to ensure transparency and increase the legitimacy and acceptance of the jury. • Citizen’s juries have a facilitator with the expertise to run a deliberative dialogue process, including supporting all participants to contribute and to critically assess complex information. This ensures participants can contribute effectively even when they have no prior knowledge or experience of the topic. The facilitator helps the group to weigh up strengths and weakn esses of options and make some decisions. Independent oversight by a steering group is also advisable to prepare the jury proceedings . This also supports a process that facilitates quality decision - making, i ncreas ing the legitimacy and recognition of the j ury. • Council staff also act as a secretariat . This may range from note -taking, to writing the outcomes document for a citizen’s jury on behalf of the citizens. This improve s the efficiency of the process and reduce s the burden on participants. For joint pl anning processes, the plan a can be written by a specially created committee of community or neighbourhood representatives. Scale and reach • Participatory budgeting in particular works best in small scale environments, so that participants have a rich understanding of the community to inform their choices , and also experience its results. • There should be transparent and regular communication and information provided to citizens during the exercise. This can be two -way: t he use of on -line too ls and open data can expand participation, with a wider group of citizens providing ideas and opinions to inform the deliberation of participants. Tools that have been used successfully include Twitter, Facebook, emails, web site, online forums, special o nline platforms and online ideation tools, and also face -to-face meetings, and physical stalls. Based on their knowledge, the jury could select witnesses they wanted to hear from. The additional evidence and the jury deliberation were made public. The decisions on what to include in the final jury report were made by supermajoritarian voting (80%+1). To ensure the minority views and dissenting voice are heard, the jurors could write minority reports that were also included in the final report. To facilitate consensus, the jurors were sometimes asked to vote on "can you live with the recommendation?" – instead of a simple “yes” or “no” to a recommendation. In total, the jury considered 110 “asks”, but settled on 20 to include in the final report. The online and offline work was organised in small groups that were regularly mixed to avoid factions. To help jurors analyse the large amount of information, the mix of synchronous (webinars) and asynchronous (example) learning approaches was used. The jurors had access to expert opinions throughout the entire process. The steering group witnessed the entire process, but jury was able to reques t periods where no observers were present. Engagement Once selected, the jurors received a welcome email and pack in the mail, orientation into online platform, the process and introductions. Technology played a key part in collaboration. An online platfor m was created specifically for this process and was used up until the face -to-face deliberations of the jurors finalized the process. In addition, facilitators used email, news groups, chat rooms, blogs, wikis and podcasts to share info and facilitate inte ractions. The jury process was highly publicised and received 126 media mentions in print, online and radio. The readers’ poll in the Herald Sun received 2580 responses and its results were presented to the jury as a submission. Costs The process reported ly cost about $370,000, which include d the commissioning of original research, international evidence reviews, research design and implementation, the publishing of a final report and a $250 honorarium for the jurors. Accommodation was offered to those tra velling from regional areas to attend the in -person deliberations. Victoria's Citizens' Jury on Obesity , in: Participedi a, available at: https://participedia.net/case/4409 Participatory budgeting in Reykjavik Background In the wake of the 2008 financial crisis in Iceland, Icelanders’ political trust plummeted from 40% in 2008 to just 11% in 2011. There was a sense of urgency in the society for more transparency of the government and a greater role for citizens in the decision -making. Against this backdrop, a not -for- profit civic technology provider Citizens Foundation was s et up. On the request from Best Party (a protest party that won municipal elections in Reykjavik in 2010), Citizens Foundation developed a platform Better Reykjavik that can be used for crowdsourcing political ideas and consultation. The platform was thoug ht a tool to rebuild the relationship between elected officials and their constituents. Later in 2010, a tool My Neighbourhood (initially called Better Neighbourhoods) was added to the platform designed specifically for annual participatory budgeting in di stricts across the city. The software is open source. The first round of participatory budgeting took place in 2011. In 2011, Reykjavik’s Better Reykjavik and My Neighbourhood projects received the European Award in the E -Democracy Awards. In 2017, they we re among the final 3 candidates for the Green Digital Charter award for “ Citizen participation & impact on society ”. It was praised by the Council of Europe as an example of how “ thousands of citizens having had a real influence on their environment. All neighbourhoods of Reykjavík have been visibly improved through the My Neighbourhood project" . Many European cities (e.g. in Norway, Slovakia) are looking replicating Icelandic experience. Specific objectives The objectives of the participatory budgeting process (and the inspiration for the custom -made software) were strongly influenced by the described political context. Design choices The design choices that made this citizens’ jury a success story can be summarised as follows: • Establish key delivery partners and clea rly outline their roles; • Independent and apolitical body to front and run the process; • Provide good levels of resourcing (including a honorarium for the jurors), structure and support around the group. This leads to high levels of engagement and dedicatio n to the process; • Consider recruiting more jurors than you actually need to allow for people who may drop out of the process or to have alternates; • Create a steering group of key decision -makers that acts as a responsive authority to the jury and will imp lement the jury’s recommendations; • Establish a clear remit (ideally a singular question) and demonstrate an authorizing environment. Stakeholders involved The main stakeholders participating in the process are: • Reykjavik C ity Council has formally accepted the platform as a collaborator and provided initial investment. It also operates the voting and provides a part of an investment budget to be allocated through the process. It implements the projects voted by the citizens. • Citizens Foundation is the technology provider. • Project Management Team at the Mayor’s office runs the Better Reykjavik project (including My Neighbourhood) on the day -to-day basis, including its promotion and engagement campaigns. • City's Construction Boa rd reviews the projects suggested for funding via the process for feasibility and cost. • Internal Audit monitors the election and does a security audit of the system each year, before, during and after the vote. • Neighbourhood Councils support the process by advising the Construction Board on the feasibility and cost. They also participate in the implementation of the projected selected. • Citizens: different groups of people participate in the discussions of projects and voting. Basically, anyone can register on the platform to submit project ideas and discuss them (the authentication process is via a verified social media account or email/ password). Authentication for voting on projects is run by the National Voter Registry, so that only those eligible to vot e in Reykjavik can participate. Voting age is 16 (which is 2 years lower than for national and local elections). Process Each year, the City Council allocated a certain amount of city’s investment budget for the allocation through participatory budgeting. Initially, it was 300 million Icelandic krona (approximately NZD 4 million, about 0.35% of the city total budget) and in 2019 amounted 450 million Icelandic krona (NZD 5.7 million, about 0.25% of the city total budget), divided between 10 districts (“neigh bourhoods”) of Reykjavik. The participatory budgeting process can be roughly divided into three stages: generating ideas, assessment and voting. The first stage starts in March with a call for ideas for improvement projects and their refining and discussin g online. The idea can be submitted to the platform by any registered participant (as mentioned, authentication with a Facebook account or email/ password suffice). The pitch needs to contain a short description and an image of the location as well as shar e the exact location on a digital map. Registered participants can like and comment on other proposed ideas, add points for or against them. The city also runs face -to-face meetings to generate ideas. The meetings are run everywhere, from shopping malls t o retirement homes to schools. The staff uses tablets and feeds the put forward straight into the online process. The first stage lasts about one month. Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs

We identified four attributes that are present within effective participation models : • draw information and perspectives in from the community • are credible with communities • are well supported and facilitated • are influential with elected members and departmen ts of the council Risks of participatory processes are: • they are more expensive than traditional decision -making processes, and the choice to spend rate payer’s money in this way can be open to criticism • if the facilitator is not skilled enough to manage the process, this can result in poor decisions • the breadth of th e topic is narrow, and the community does not set the agenda . The quality of the process is critical to ensure acceptance and legitimacy • it is highly dependent on buy -in from the governing body • trust in the council would be detrimentally affected if the g overning body did not accept the recommendations of the group. Success factors Whilst many details vary across the settings and methodologies of the participatory processes we have reviewed , there are some common factors that contribute to the ir success . We have set these out below, including s pecific success factors for citizen’s juries , participatory budgeting and joint planning . Settings • The community does not set the agenda. A topic is selected by the council and a question is carefully framed for the group to consider . However, a n important feature of the most effective participatory processes is that the council has at the outset agreed that it will accept the recommendations of the group . Communities across New Zealand are safe, resilient and thriving Regulated activities minimise harm and maximise benefits to people and communities Three Waters Reform Building an efective, afordable, resilient and sustainable three waters system (drinking water, stormwater and wastewater) will provide lasting benefits for our communities our economy, and the environment. We are responsible for leading the reform of the three waters system, and for monitoring the performance of Taumata Arowai – the new waters services regulator. The service delivery reforms involve a system-wide transformation of the way three waters services are regulated and provided to communities. A comprehensive, integrated package of reform proposals and a support package for local government have been proposed. A key system change is the active recognition and provision of te mana o wai statements that proposed water services entities will be required to embed into their operations from governance to delivery. We will support the Government in making its final decisions on the reform proposals and will implement the reforms that are agreed. We will support the Government to implement the reforms, and lead the significant work required to design and transition to the new system. This includes working with the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment to establish new economic regulation and consumer protection regimes necessary to ensure three waters services are delivered eficiently, efectively and afordably to consumers. The Department will also monitor Taumata Arowai to ensure water services are provided to standards necessary to achieve improved and more consistent public health and environmental outcomes for the benefit of all consumers and communities. Regulatory system stewardship We have developed a strategy to move our regulatory services from a focus on compliance, to a focus on regulatory system stewardship so that communities in New Zealand are safe, and the wellbeing of iwi is improved. The strategy positions our regulatory services to be at the forefront of regulatory excellence. We are concurrently implementing a new strategic direction for gambling that emphasises community wellbeing aligning to our outcomes and the Government’s wellbeing agenda. We will continue to focus our gambling advice on the regulatory settings needed to manage harm from online gambling by New Zealanders, along with improved measures to minimise harm from Class 4 Gambling (“pokie machines”). This work will ensure New Zealanders who choose to gamble are protected, especially those most vulnerable to gambling harm. 26 Department of Internal Affairs NGĀ TAKUNE RAUTAKI STRATEGIC INTENTIONS 2021-2025 Modernising content regulation and providing greater protection against online harms We will be modernising the media content regulatory system and providing greater protection against online harms through the content regulation review. The review will be supported by the Ministry for Culture and Heritage and will lead to a modern, flexible and coherent regulatory framework to address all harmful impacts of media content, regardless of the way the content is delivered. We will complete the legislative process to amend the Films, Videos and Publications Classifications Act 1993 to ensure prevention and mitigation of harms caused by objectionable publications. The Department is also progressing recommendation 41 of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into the terrorist attack on Christchurch masjidain to make further amendments to that Act in relation to racism. Embedding the Countering Violent Extremisms (CVE) Online team and reduction of online harmful content We will help facilitate the swif removal of online violent extremist content from platforms and continue to build strong working relationships with government agency partners, overseas law enforcement and technology platforms. In doing so, we will ensure New Zealanders know where and how to report online violent extremist content. This will require a community approach and trusted relationships with civil society. As our capability grows, we will explore further online prevention initiatives, in consultation with relevant government and non-government agencies. Anti-Money Laundering (AML) – implement mutual evaluation recommendations We will support the statutory review of the Anti-Money Laundering /Countering the Financing of Terrorism Act. The review will result in recommendations for regulatory and legislative change to strengthen the AML framework. We will also focus on implementing the Financial Action Taskforce Mutual Evaluations recommendations to strengthen the AML/CFT framework and our delivery of services to ensure the integrity of and public trust in New Zealand’s financial system. The Community Resilience work programme is a partnership working with local government to help better manage these risks through investing in risk reduction measures and supporting councils to manage natural hazards and the efects of climate change. The programme will provide the Government with options for reforming the Land Information Memorandum (LIM) system by which local government discloses information on natural hazard risk to property buyers and sellers. We are also contributing a community resilience perspective to the Government’s work programme on the reform of the Resource Management System and the development of the National Adaptation Plan. A community funding system that is inclusive and flexible The Department is undertaking a review of Crown community funding with the objective to support a community funding system that is more flexible, inclusive and honours Te Tiriti o Waitangi. Findings from an analysis into community funding identified the current system to be complex and ad-hoc with limited strategic direction. This has resulted in barriers for communities, ineficiencies in the system and inequitable funding outcomes. We will identify potential options for a funding system that represents the most efective investment in community development and has a long-term intergenerational impact for iwi, hapū and communities, utilising good-practice principles. This review will align with changes being considered in the distribution of Lottery funding to ensure consistency and allow for more efective outcomes across community funding. Charities Act Review We have resumed the work to modernise the Charities Act 2005 by addressing practical issues that impede the efective functioning of charities, while ensuring the necessary transparency for public trust and overall confidence in the sector. This work is expected to lead to legislative proposals in 2022. 29 Department of Internal Affairs NGĀ TAKUNE RAUTAKI STRATEGIC INTENTIONS 2021-2025 Racing industry recovery We will complete the implementation of the racing industry reforms, working alongside key industry stakeholders such as Racing New Zealand to support a sustainable racing industry. Conclusions 97. As indicated by the analysis table above, the preferred process option is option three: a self-identification process that requires a statutory declaration process without evidence of medical treatment. When compared, this option meets all the criteria (except integrity) better or much better than the status quo and is better at meeting the criteria than option two. 98. A self-identification process is worse than the status quo in respect of the integrity criterion because of the removal of any form of third party assurance that can act to mitigate fraudulent applications. However, unlike the other options, this option provides a process that is primarily based on self-identification and is likely to better meet the needs of transgender and intersex people. 99. We consider the risk of the preferred process option being used for unlawful reasons is sufficiently mitigated by the requirement for a statutory declaration and additional requirements where a person applies more than once. 100. The self-identification process is beneficial for children and young people. This option increases the accessibility and inclusivity of the process for children and young people and mitigates risk that 16 and 17 year olds may not be able to obtain guardian consent. It is flexible and recognises existing views that gender is not age restrictive and that older adolescents are more able to understand important decisions. Lastly this option supports the integrity of birth register information and the autonomy of children and young people through requirements that focus on ensuring the child or young person understands the decision and it is based on their self-identified gender. Conference support The Ministry contributes part of the funding for a biennial international gambling conference held in New Zealand and an associated international think tank. The conference will take place twice in the 2019/20 –2021/22 period, in February 2020 and 2022. The Ministry is budgeting for an $80,000 contribution towards the costs of each conference and think tank. Holding international conferences on gambling harm in New Zealand promotes the country as a world leader in preventing and minimising gambling harm. It also enables practitioners, researchers, industry representatives and government officials from around the world to meet and exchange ideas specific to gambling harm. 3.4 Intervention services The Ministry has increased the indicative budget for the 2019/20 –2021/22 period from the previous period to accommodate an increased focus on service development to address persistent gambling harm (see Table 17). Section 3.6 describes additional funding for piloting new intervention services. Within th is budget, the Ministry intends to explore the potential for more innovative intervention services. In particular, it will seek to fund or develop services that are client-centred and enhance the mana of consumers. The Ministry will base new approaches on successful regional or local models, where they exist, and will co-design them with stakeholders, and particularly with consumers. Indicative priority areas for 2019/20 to 2021/22 are to:  explore innovative ways to treat the whole person through joined-up gambling, drug, alcohol and mental health services  pilot and evaluate new service models to address gaps in current service provision . The pilots will focus on delivering both public health and intervention services across regions (particularly rural regions) and responsiveness to Māori  lay the foundations to pilot and introduce residential care and peer support into the intervention service mix in the medium term  develop the range of online self-help available  deliver services that are responsive to the needs of different population groups; in particular, those groups where there is strong evidence of inequality and inequity in gambling harm. Minor changes have been made to the Bill following consultation. 9ldr2190z0 2019-12-03 09:04:38 9(2)(h) 9(2)(h) Proactively released by the Minister for Racing IN CONFIDENCE Page 4 of 6 Binding on the Crown 19. The Racing Industry Bill will bind the Crown. Creating new agencies and amending law relating to existing agencies 20. The Bill disestablishes RITA and creates TAB NZ, with the objectives of facilitating and promoting racing and sports be tting , maximising its profits for the long -term benefit of New Zealand racing and maximising returns to sports , while ensuring harm minimisation is prioritised . The Bill also creates the RIB, a single entity responsible for the investigative and adjudicative functions of racing, while maintain ing independence between these functions. The current integrity system, the Judicial Control Authority and the Racing Integrity Unit, will be disestablis hed at the point the RIB is established. 21. TAB NZ and the RIB will be established as statutory bodies, each with board s of up to seven members appointed by the Minister for Racing . Both agencies will be required to present their statement s of intent (SOIs) and business plan s to the Minister for Racing, for tabling in Parliament. 22. The Bill transfers racing responsibilities held by RITA , to the three racing code bodies (Thoroughbred Racing New Zealand, Harness Racing New Zealand and Greyhound Racing New Zealand) . The Bill amends the accountability requirements of the codes, requiring them to submit their SOIs and business plans to the Minister, for tabling in Parliament. Allocation of decision -making powers 23. The draft legislation does not involve the allocation of decision -making powers between the executive, the courts, and tribunals. The Bill creates powers to make regulations to specify further detail related to the operation of the RIB, including the judicial committees and appeals tribunals. Associated regulat ions 24. The clauses which relate to the establishment of the RIB (clauses 33 to 41) will come into force on a date to be made by Order in Council . The following Order in Council powers are also included: 24.1 ending the statutory restriction on club property transactions without the club first obtaining code approval; and 24.2 enabling the transfer of club property to the code, with payments to the club and local community where warranted. 25. In addition, given the scale of the changes , the Bill creates powers to make regulations if required , in the following ways : 25.1 if a commissioner is appointed to resolve a significant disagreement between the codes , whose decision would be binding on those involved, levying the codes for the associated costs ; 25.2 specifying further detai l related to the operation of the RIB, including the judicial committees and appeals tribunals; 25.3 setting the level of funding for the RIB if a funding agreement cannot be reached; 9ldr2190z0 2019-12-03 09:04:38 Proactively released by the Minister for Racing IN CONFIDENCE Page 5 of 6 25.4 prescribing the independent body responsible for assessing and approving TAB NZ’s request to introduce new betting products; 25.5 setting the decision -making framework and fee arrangements for the independent body responsible for assessing and approving TAB NZ’s request to introduce new betting products ; and 25.6 prescribing a process and criteria that codes must apply when negotiating with clubs about the use of surplus venues, having due regard to any community interests in the venue. Other instruments 26. The Bill does not include any provision empowering the making of other instruments deemed to be legislative instruments or disallowable instruments . Definition of Minister/department 27. The Bill continues the definition of Department within the Racing Act . It includes the option for the Department to be the designated agency that will admin ister the levy relating to the appointment of a Commissioner in clause 1 4. Commencement of legislation 28. Except for clauses 17, 18, 33 to 41, and clause 5 in Schedule 1, the Bill will come into force on 1 July 2020. Clauses 1 7, 18 and clause 5 in Schedule 1, will come into force the day after Royal assent. Clauses 33 to 41 will come into force on a date to be determined by Order in Council. It is anticipated this will take place within 12 months of the Bill being enacted. A deferre d commencement i s required to prepare the current integrity system for the transition. Parliamentary stages 29. It is intended the Bill be introduced on or before 3 December 2019 and referred to the Transport and Infrastructure select committee, for a select committee process of four months. Given the timeframes, approval is being sought for PCO to make any technical changes to the Bill prior to introduction. The Bill must be passed on, or before, 30 June 2020. Proactive release 30. Consultation and agency feedback We have consulted with the following agencies: Department of Corrections, StatsNZ, Crown Law, Ministry for Women, Ministry of Health, Oranga Tamariki –Ministry for Children, Ministry of Education, Ministry of Social Development, Ministry of Youth Development, Ministry of Justice, Te Puni K ōkiri, Ministry for Pacific Peoples, Sport NZ, New Zealand Transport Agency, New Zealand Police, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (Immigration), Inland Revenue, Public Service Commission, Office of 7 See section 33 of the BDMRR Act and clause 22I of the Bill, which state that a person’s sex should be determined by the “general law of New Zealand.” 9(2)(f)(iv) Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 10 of 15 Ethnic Communities, Human Rights Commission, Office of the Privacy Commissioner, and Treasury. The Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet has been informed. The above agencies are generally supportive of self-identification, for example, the Office of the Privacy Commissioner stated: The Privacy Commissioner supports the proposal to introduce a self- identification process to enable a person’s gender to be recognised on their birth certificate. The Commissioner notes that the proposal would create consistency between birth certificates, and passports and driver licences which are more commonly used as identity documents and have a self-identification process for recognising gender. The Commissioner considers the proposed self- identification process to be privacy enhancing as a person is no longer required to provide sensitive medical information to change their registered sex. We have addressed many of these agencies ’ previous concerns, including around the previously proposed one-time limit on changing sex markers and the requirements for children to access self-identification. Some concerns remain around requirements for guardian consent as described in paragraphs 41 and 42 above. During consultation agencies raised new concerns about how people who were born overseas but now reside in New Zealand will access official documents that recognise their gender. For example, transgender asylum seekers or transgender M āori who were born overseas and whose birth cannot be registered in New Zealand. We recognise this is an issue but consider it outside of scope of the self-identification proposals discussed in this paper – it would not be appropriate to legislate a process to amend information for births registered overseas. We will consider if and how this matter could be resolved and provide you with further advice. As requested by your office, a summary of the agency feedback received during the development of the advice about self-identification is included at Appendix B . Communications We have provided your office with a communications plan and frequently asked questions to support work on introducing a self-identification process. We are ready to work with your office on an announcement following Cabinet of your intention to progress the Bill with self-identification and refer the self-identification SOP to Select Committee. We will provide yo u material to support this announceme nt along with the final Cabinet paper in early May 2021. We consider that an announcement soon after Cabinet approval is important. Proactive communications clearly setting out the rationale for the changes and what they involve will pre-empt and potentially mitigate opposition to self-identification. Providing information on the changes early will also be important so interested individuals and communities can prepare to engage with the changes at Select Committee. We will provide you with separate advice ahead of Cabinet on engagement to support young people and Māori, Pacific peoples and ethnic communities , who have not been heard from, to participate in the Select Committee process. For example, this could include providing written information about the Bill to iwi authorities, community organisations and media networks that have reach in these communities and with young people . Contact Tracing Technologies Prototype Research Programme key documents
Contact Tracing is a public health method which identifies persons who may have come into contact with an infected person and subsequently collects further information about these contacts. By tracing contacts and isolating them, public health authorities aim to reduce further infections in the population. Contact tracing in New Zealand is performed by our public health authorities. Sources of infection The base reproduction rate, or R0 (“R nought”), for COVID-19 is around 2.5. Each infected person infects, on average, 2.5 other people. Newly infected persons then each infect another 2.5 people, causing exponential growth in infections if left unchecked.

Cost -of-living implications 59. The proposals in this paper will require unplanned spending for a number of councils in the 2024/2025 financial year. Relative to total council spending , this will be small expenditure and have little effect on ratepayers for larger councils . It will have a more significant impact on small er councils. Financial implications Restoring polls on Māori wards 60. The permanent reinstatement of the poll mechanism for Māori wards has no notable financial implications for the Crown. Councils would need to fund the cost of standalone polls on Māori wards when a petition is received. Estimated costs for these polls are $175,000 for a council with an electoral population of 50,000. Based on previous experience, councils will factor the risk s and cost of polls into decisions on whether to attempt to establish Māori wards. 9(2)(f)(iv), 9(2)(g)(i) 9(2)(f)(iv), 9(2)(g)(i) 9(2)(f)(iv), 9(2)(g)(i) 9(2)(f)(iv), 9(2)(g)(i) Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE 9 IN CONFIDENCE Māori wards Option 1A 61. The transitional mechanism in Option 1A requiring up to 4 5 councils to hold polls in late 2024 will have financial implications for both the Crown and councils : 61.1. Between 31 and 45 councils will need to fund standalone polls (estimated cost $175,000 for a council with an electoral population of 50,000) . 61.2. Some of these councils will also need to complete expedited representation reviews. Due to the time constraints , it is likely that many councils will need to prepare two representation arrangement proposals in advance – for both possible poll outcomes. For most of the affected councils , this will be unplanned expenditure (estimated cost from $170,000 to $190,000 for a council with an electoral population of 50,000) . 61.3. The Electoral Commission will need to provide additional processing of data extracts and information technology support for a large number of polls in a compressed timeframe – the estimated cost is $84,000. Māori wards Option 1B 62. The financial implications for Option 1B are similar to 1A, except that only councils that receive a valid petition for a poll will incur the unplanned costs . Māori wards Option 2A 63. The financial implications will be less by more than half for councils that hold a poll alongside the 2025 local elections. 64. Financial implications for the Electoral Commission will be minimal under 2A . Māori wards Option 2B 65. The financial implications for Option 2B are similar to Opt ion 2A except that only councils that receive a valid petition will incur the unplanned costs . Fixing postal voting timeframes 66. This proposal has minor financial implications for councils because they will need to provide special voting facilities over a longer voting period. 67. There are cost implications for the Electoral Commission because the enrolment update campaign will need to start earlier, and the additional enrolment support will need to be in place over a longer period. CovidCard CovidCard ​ is a dedicated hardware device which performs much the same function as an app, but can potentially achieve the necessary levels of compliant adoption across broader segments of society. ​CovidCard ​ is designed to be worn on a lanyard around the neck, for both easy compliance monitoring in venues where it might be required, but also to enable optimal device function.
CovidCard Design The CovidCard​ is a Bluetooth Low Energy (Bluetooth LE) device approximately the size of a credit card. It is designed to be worn on a lanyard around the neck when you are in environments where people congregate. This includes public transport, workplaces, bars, restaurants, gyms, hospitals, large gatherings and events. Openly wearing a ​CovidCard​ contributes to easily assessing and enforcing compliant use, as required.
CovidCard does not store any personal information on the card itself, and no card data is automatically stored in the cloud or elsewhere. A card’s own broadcast identifier is cryptographically generated, and rotated approximately every fifteen minutes to ensure anonymity of the cardholder. Only the aforementioned Crown Entity has the ability to decrypt IDs and associate them with a cardholder. Cards cannot track user location as they do not contain location-aware technology such as GPS. Only 21 days of data is stored on the card and the battery for each card will only last for approximately 12 months.
CovidCard ​ detects and records close contacts using Bluetooth LE and stores this data securely on a person’s card. No contact data is automatically stored in the cloud or elsewhere and only 21 days of close contacts will be stored. Cards do not track user location as they do not contain GPS capability.
CovidCard ​ exists within a system of policies, operational management and other tools and should be considered as such. A detailed assessment of existing contact tracing capabilities is not within the scope of this document. Consideration has been given to the wider strategic context into which the ​CovidCard ​ might be deployed.
CovidCard ​ has a non-rechargeable battery with a typical 12-18 month battery life. Once the battery is depleted contact records are lost and become irretrievable as records are encrypted using a key held in volatile memory which is lost if power is lost. At that point, cards are recycled or disposed of.
CovidCard ​ has no notion of location as it does not use GPS or have a network connection. Cards simply receive and record properly-formed transmissions from other nearby cards and use this information to help determine close or casual contacts. Records of other cards are retained on the card, not on any phones, computers or servers elsewhere, for a maximum of 21 days.
CovidCard ​ is designed as a temporary solution for COVID-19. The battery on the device will only last around 12 months Deploying ​CovidCard ​ in New Zealand in advance of relaxing border restrictions is likely the time when ​CovidCard ​ is able to deliver the greatest value as this will be a time of elevated risk.
CovidCard ​ makes contact tracing faster, more accurate, and more scalable if effectively integrated with existing contact tracing efforts. The main benefits of ​CovidCard ​ are:
CovidCard ​ must be deployed in advance of any second wave of COVID-19. Otherwise, by the time we distributed cards to everyone we would have already had our second Level 4 lockdown and would have been moving down the Alert Levels again. While ​CovidCard ​ could play a role with essential workers during a Level 4 lockdown, lockdown alone can control the spread of the virus in the wider community. The time when ​CovidCard ​ should be deployed will likely be characterised by complacency in the community regarding COVID-19.
CovidCard ​ should be evaluated against its ability to meaningfully slow the spread of COVID-19. An ongoing Cochrane Review of digital contact tracing solutions identified multiple modelling studies that can inform the evaluation of the ​CovidCard ​ (including Kucharski 2020; Ferreti 2020; Hinch 2020; Plank 2020; Grice 2020; Vaithianathan 2020). Three of these studies focus specifically on the New Zealand context (Plank 2020; Grice 2020; Vaithianathan 2020).
CovidCard ​ would enable close contacts to be immediately notified and asked to self-isolate and could immediately provide contact details of close contacts to contact tracing teams. Four days, on average, can likely be saved between potential exposure and isolation, thus reducing tertiary infections. Downloading the cards of close contacts would also enable rapid isolation of second-order contacts which we consider a necessary further step if elimination is the goal.

Currently the Customer Nominated Services AISA is used to:
Currently, the contact tracing process is entirely manual: patients are asked to recall their close contacts over the last few weeks, and these are followed up with phone calls from contact tracing teams based at each district health board (DHB). Aside from being labour-intensive, the process relies on human recall, which may be unreliable particularly for interactions that occurred further into the past.
Currently, the intense physical distancing measures implemented at Alert Level 4 are acting as a strong safety net for cases not detected at the border and the case and contact management system. If the intensity of physical distancing decreases (by de-escalating to Alert Level 3 or by a decrease in compliance), this lowering of protection will induce a critical reliance on effective case management (including detection) for stopping existing transmission and any new transmission associated with a ‘leaky’ border.

How ACC may use Personal Information provided by the Registrar -General The Personal Information received by ACC from the Registrar -General may be used to: a) ensure that an individual applying for or utilising ACC services is not required to provide identity and Life Event records that the Regi strar -General holds. b) update the records of an individual upon their death. c) update the records of an individual upon a name change. d) assess or reassess the eligibility for and entitlement to public services on the marriage or civil union of an individual. e) provide additional protection to information provided by the Registrar -General where the individual concerned has an active Non -Disclosure Direction under the BDMRR Act. f) enable the prevention, detection, investigation and prosecution of offences, and the c onduct of civil proceedings including judicial review. This briefing seeks your approval to upload the final version of the Cabinet Legislation Committee paper: Rates Rebate (Specified Amounts) Order 2021 (the paper) to CabNet. The paper is attached as Appendix A . Background 2. On 29 March 2021, you agreed to adjust two key settings of the Rates Rebate Scheme(the Scheme) for the 2021-22 financial year [LG202100318 refers]. These adjustmentsreflect CPI (Consumer Price Index) inflation of 1.4 percent for the year ended 31December 2020 by: a)raising the maximum rebate available from $655 to $665; and b)raising the income abatement threshold from $26,150 to $26,510. 3. You also agreed to proceed to the Cabinet Legislation Committee, to seek approval ofan Order in Council which adjusts the two key settings of the Scheme. The Order inCouncil has been drafted by the Parliamentary Counsel Office and is provided withinAppendix A of the paper. During consultation a change was proposed to the Cabinet Paper 4. Hon Grant Robertson, Minister of Finance, Hon Carmel Sepuloni, Minister for SocialDevelopment, and Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall, Minister for Seniors were consulted on theproposals. 5. During Ministerial consultation, Minister Sepuloni asked if the proposed increase in theScheme was sufficient given the anticipated high rate increases expected this year in most councils. She also made a specific suggestion to adjust the two key settings of the Scheme using the average wage (as with Superannuation) rather than CPI. 6. The Department of Internal Affairs (the Department) notes that while the Scheme provides a modest amount of financial assistance, other cost of living subsidies (suchas the Accommodation Supplement) and adjustments to income support remain moreeffective at insulating low-income ratepayers from high rate rises . 7. The Department considers that if you were to proceed with Minister Sepuloni’s recommendation, you would need to review the Scheme at a more strategic level inthe context of other subsidies and supplements that are available to low-incom e households. This could not be completed in time for an adjustment to the Scheme totake effect on 1 July 2021. 8. Adjusting the Scheme by more than CPI would also likely exceed the currentappropriation for the 2021- 22 financial year . 9. Talking points on the adjustment level are provided to assist you in the CabinetLegislation Committee meeting on 3 June 2021 should questions arise ( Appendix B ). Next steps 10. Following your approval, the Department will upload the paper to CabNet by 27 May2021. Your Office will complete the lodgement process. 11. The Cabinet Legislation Committee is scheduled to consider the paper on 3 June 2021. 12. Cabinet and the Executive Council are scheduled to consider the Order in Council on 8 June 2021. DISCUSSION The results show that the card, even with a basic algorithm, is capable of performing recall greater than 90% of contacts in most situations. The two office trials (which were different run-throughs of the same scripts with different cards) showed similar results. There is no significant difference between the means at a 95% confidence (P = 0.63), demonstrating that the results were repeatable despite a small number of cards not being activated. As the required contact duration to be considered a close contact increases, false positive rates fall in more sparse environments (cafe) and increase in denser ones (construction, party).

The response rate for the exit survey among participants was less than anticipated (38%), and could be a reflection of the dist ribution method (daily diaries were administered via a link in an SMS, whereas the exit sur vey was fully anonymous and a link was sent out in a mass email to staff in the medical ward) Among respondents, including 16 pilot participants and 5 non-participants, 86% stated that they currently do not keep a written record of people they are near in public places, and 10% stated that they log their details into guest books of venues. The willingness to document personal close contacts using variou s methods is summarised in Table 5. Most respondents were not at all willing to keep their own personal diary on paper or on -line. Similarly, 52% were very willing to use a passive app on their smart phones, while one -third were very willing to use an ac tive app. The method with the highest proportion of respondents who were very willing to use it was a co ntact card (i.e., Bluetooth card) at 67%, which was also the method with the smallest proportion of respondents who were not at all willing to use (9.5% ). None of the respondents who were not at all willing to use a contact card actually participated in t he pilot study. This is an analytical tool to help assess the potential for policies and programmes to increase wellbeing. In the Living Standards framework there are four capitals presented. To generate the most wellbeing each capital needs to be strong and they need to work well together. The Four Capitals (natural, human social, and financial and physical) are the assets that generate wellbeing now and into the future Looking after intergenerational wellbeing means maintaining, nourishing and growing the capitals 02/19The norms, rules and institutions that inﬂ uence the way in which people live and work together and experience a sense of belonging. Includes trust, reciprocity , the rule of law , cultural and community identity , traditions and customs, common values and interests.All aspects of the natural environment that support life and human activity . Includes land, soil, water , plants and animals, minerals and energy resources.Natural Capital Social Capital Financial and human-made (produced) physical assets, usually closely associated with supporting material living conditions. Department of Internal Affairs TE MAHI KIA PAI AKE A AOTEAROA MŌ TE IWI O AOTEAROA MAKING NEW ZEALAND BETTER FOR NEW ZEALANDERS5 Tirohanga Whānui mai i te Pou Whakahaere – Overview from the Chief Executive Kia tuia te rangi ki te whenua, te whenua ki te rangi Mā te mahi tahi e rangonahia ai te whanaungatanga Mā te whanaungatanga e tō mai i te manaakitanga Nā te manaakitanga ka pupū ake te kaitiakitanga Māna e rarau ake, kātahi ka puta te kotahitanga Tau, tau, tau ana e! I am pleased to present the Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs Strategic Intentions for 2019–2023. This document outlines our priority areas for the next four years, as we aim to serve and connect people, communities and government to build a safe, prosperous and respected nation. The Department of Internal Affairs has an incredibly varied remit with many responsibilities and functions – for example, our world-leading online passports service, protecting the nation’s precious taonga, maintenance of the charities register, administration of births, deaths and marriages, censorship compliance and gambling regulation are just part of what we do. As we look to 2023, we are focusing our efforts towards progressing four broad outcomes for the benefit and wellbeing of all people. People can easily access the services and information they need We provide important services to New Zealanders throughout their lives, and we are making our services easier to access and use. We are continually working to integrate services across multiple agencies, designed around the needs of our customers – not us as a Department. Utilising our system leadership roles, the Government Chief Digital Officer and the Government Chief Privacy Officer, we drive digital transformation across the public sector, and make sure the digital world is a safe environment for New Zealanders to participate in. Iwi, hapū and communities across New Zealand are safe, resilient and thriving Communities are the cornerstone of our society and their wellbeing is vital in making New Zealand a great place to live, work and play. We regulate, to keep New Zealanders and their communities safe from harm. This will include establishing a new water regulator and strengthening our work in minimising the distribution of objectionable material. Our Office of Ethnic Communities strives to ensure diversity is celebrated, respected and embraced in New Zealand. We will also continue to support communities to lead their development and achieve their aspirations, through initiatives such as the Community-led Development Programme. People’s sense of belonging and collective memory builds an inclusive New Zealand Through Archives New Zealand and the National Library of New Zealand, we are the privileged guardians of our nation’s most precious taonga, including Te Tiriti o Waitangi. Protecting New Zealand’s heritage for now and for future generations continues to be a strong focus for us. We are investing in significant new storage infrastructure, more effective ways to manage electronic records and improvement of online access to our collections. As Crown partners to the Treaty of Waitangi, as well as guardians of the physical Treaty document, we will work to strengthen Māori/Crown relationships by engaging effectively with Māori and contributing to Maihi Karauna, the Crown’s strategy for Māori language revitalisation. Department of Internal Affairs STRATEGIC INTENTIONS 2019-20236 New Zealand is a well-functioning democracy, across central and local government We strive to support effective partnerships between central and local government, addressing regional and Government objectives and to enable the system to work cohesively. We do this by taking a collaborative approach to community resilience, supporting the urban growth agenda, and local government financing and funding. We also support members of the Executive to ensure they can carry out their duties effectively. Our outcomes are aligned with the Government’s priorities and will guide the direction of our work over the coming years. We have many areas in which we can focus our efforts, but will also need to adapt our ways of working to deliver our many diverse functions effectively for both New Zealanders and the wider public service. Within our Department, he tāngata, our people are the heart of our organisation and we will continue to make sure our Department is a place where everyone feels safe, healthy and respected. Celebrating our people, supporting their development and fostering a culture rich in wellbeing, inclusion and diversity will continue to be a priority for us – because we know our people are at their best when they can bring their whole selves to work. Our outcomes are aligned with the Government’s priorities and will guide the direction of our work over the coming years. I look forward to seeing our progress in achieving our outcomes over the next four years, and I know our people will work with a spirit of service and a commitment to making New Zealand better for New Zealanders. Our purpose remains consistent, even as the functions and services we perform evolve and develop to meet the changing needs and expectations of people and the Government. We aim to make New Zealand a better place to live and to enhance the lives of New Zealanders. We work with people, communities, and other parts of government – both central and local, to build a safe, prosperous and respected nation. Our Ministerial Portfolios We are responsible to eight Ministers, administering seven Portfolios within the single Vote Internal Affairs. The Minister of Internal Affairs is the Vote Minister and the Responsible Minister overseeing the Government’s ownership interests in the Department. Portfolios and Responsible Ministers are: Internal Affairs Hon. Tracey Martin Community and Voluntary Sector Hon. Poto Williams Ethnic Communities Hon. Jenny Salesa Government Digital Services Hon. Department of Internal Affairs STRATEGIC INTENTIONS 2019-20238 Ā Mātou Kawenga me ā Mātou Mahi – Our roles and functions The Department operates under a single Vote of $450 million (operating expenditure) to support activities under the seven Portfolios. We have a broad range of responsibilities and functions that span information and communication technologies (ICT) investment, information management, working with communities, ensuring effective regulatory frameworks are in place, supporting the Executive and local government and delivering a range of services to support and foster New Zealand’s cultural identity. Our system leadership roles include the Government Chief Digital Officer (GCDO) and the Government Chief Privacy Officer (GCPO) to lead the digital transformation of government across the State Sector. In this respect, we support our State sector colleagues to transform their services through better investment in ICT and to maintain the privacy of New Zealanders’ government-held information. We also play a system leadership role with respect to local government. We are responsible for linking central and local government more effectively to achieve improved outcomes for citizens and communities. The Department is responsible for the National Library of New Zealand and Archives New Zealand. These institutions play an important role in preserving New Zealand’s documentary heritage and ensuring a full and accurate public record is created and maintained. We are also responsible for the Office of Ethnic Communities, which supports the many diverse ethnic communities that make New Zealand their home and the benefits that diversity brings to New Zealand society. Our specific functions include: • Managing and protecting the integrity of national identity information, including life events such as births, deaths, marriages, citizenship and issuing passports • Regulating activities in several sectors including: gambling, censorship, government recordkeeping, charities, unsolicited electronic messages, anti-money laundering, private security personnel and private investigators • Providing policy advice to government on local government, ethnic communities, community and voluntary sector, fire and emergency services, identity, information and communications technology, information management, digital safety, gambling and racing • Building, preserving and making accessible New Zealand’s information, documentary heritage and public records • Providing information, resources and advice to communities to support their aspirations • Administering grant funding schemes and promoting trust and confidence in the charitable sector • Supporting the effective operation of government and the Executive • Coordinating and managing official guests of government visits to New Zealand • Supporting public and government inquiries and reviews Department of Internal Affairs TE MAHI KIA PAI AKE A AOTEAROA MŌ TE IWI O AOTEAROA MAKING NEW ZEALAND BETTER FOR NEW ZEALANDERS9 • Administering a range of statutory functions for the Minister of Local Government, including for Lake Taupō and offshore islands • Leadership in the direction and operational approach for digital across the core public service. We administer 80 pieces of legislation or regulation.1 We monitor the performance of two Crown entities (Fire and Emergency New Zealand and the Office of Film and Literature Classification) and manage the appointment process for members of a range of trusts, committees and boards. 1 The legislation administered by the Department can be found at the Department’s website at https://www.dia.govt.nz/About-Internal-Affairs---Our-portfolios--- Legislation

Digital technologies designed for population-wide deployment are new to the playbook. There is, as yet, limited evidence of how these tools may help. This is the first global pandemic since the advent of the smartphone.
Digital technologies hold some promise for accelerating symptomatic people into testing and both broadening and accelerating the quarantining of close contacts. Do both exceptionally well and the virus can be contained. Apps have been rolled out in a number of countries already but despite reasonable numbers of people downloading tools (~20% in Singapore and Australia), compliant use lags and any contribution made to manual contact tracing efforts so far is insignificant.
Digital technologies hold some promise of helping to “fight COVID-19”. In practical terms, the big potential levers are in getting people tested faster, isolating infected people quickly, and quarantining close contacts.
Digital technologies must be assessed rigorously in order to estimate the possible impact of these tools. Impact does not come from the mere existence of tools - they must be promoted, downloaded and used as intended at an absolute minimum. Any tool must work as intended and we must take a clear headed view of what our embedded assumptions are on the path to impact.
