The Strategy builds on five previous strategies and consists of a strategic framework and a t hree-year Service Plan that sets out the activities the Ministry considers are required for the 2019/20 to 2021/22 period , to make further progress towards preventing and minimising gambling harm. 24 The Ministry’s budget ed spending for 2019/20 to 2021/22 is $60.339 million (Table 1 refers) . This represents a $5 million (9%) increase compared with the average cost of the preceding three levy periods (which averag ed an appropriation of $55.539 million each) , but is less than one percent of the $7.5 billion forecast player expenditure over the same period . Table 1 Ministry of Health Budget (GST exclusive), 2019/20 to 2021/22 Service 2019/20 ($m) 2020/2 1 ($m) 2021/22 ($m) Total ($m) Public health services 6.870 6.790 6.870 20.530 Intervention services 8.413 8.415 8.415 25.243 Research and evaluation 2.060 2.219 2.350 6.629 New service and technology pilots 1.335 1.695 1.970 5.000 Ministry operating costs 0.957 0.990 0.990 2.937 Total ($m) 19.635 20.109 20.595 60.339 25 The investment in the Strategy is necessary because the gambling harm needs assessment required under the Act to inform the Strategy found that significant changes were necessary to make inroads into reducing gambling harm.1 For example, it found the number of people affected by gambling harm continues to increase in line with population growth, harm reduction impacts have plateaued over the past seven years, service use rates have declined and systemic inequities persist for the most affected at risk population groups. Key proposals for the Strategy and Service Plan 26 The Strategy propose s to refocus and revitalise activities to better meet the needs of people affected by harmful gambling and achieve further gains in gambling harm reduction . This is in line with the needs assessment and the recommendations of He Ara Oranga (see below ). Key changes include : 26.1 expand ing the mix of services to more closely match those available for addictions generally (by a dding residential care and peer support ), facilitat ing co-design and use of consumer networks to de velop more targeted and appropriate service models; 26.2 strengthen ing enablers t o su pport the se services such as workforce development, training , addressing cultural and language barriers, and the use of technology ; and 26.3 using pilots, evaluation and action research to inform decision -making . 27 The additional $5 million will be invested in piloting new service models and technology to manage and mitigate gambling harm , covering public health and intervention services co - designed with stakeholders and consumers , and seek ing to build resilience by enhancing the mana of service users . The pilots will also address service gaps and areas of systemic, persistent gambling harm and would be evaluated and supported by action research. This investment will enable current levels of se rvice to be maintained while the Ministry tests new service models and identif ies those activities that more effective ly address gambling harm . 1 Sapere Research Group. 2018. 12 agreed to extend the permitted maximum length of contracts and joint arrangements for water services from 35 to 50 years; Improving how stormwater networks are managed 13 agreed that the legislation will provide that territorial authorities are responsible for managing and maintaining stormwater networks in their city or district, including overland flow paths and urban watercourses that are both on private land and related to the operation of the stormwater network in urban areas; 14 agreed that the legislation will include provisions that require territorial authorities to: 14.1 develop a stormwater network risk management plan to identify risks and hazards related to stormwater networks; 14.2 work with private landowners as required to protect and maintain the conveyance capacity of overland flow paths and urban watercourses; 14.3 develop (as required) stormwater rules that would provide direction to private landowners on their responsibilities for maintenance and protection of the conveyance capacity of overland flow paths and urban watercourses on their land; 15 agreed that the legislation will provide for stormwater rules and rule-making powers to support the management of overland flow paths and urban watercourses on private land, including that the rules (and rule-making powers, as the case may be) will: 15.1 be made pursuant to stormwater network risk management plans; 15.2 set out landowner duties, including access to land, and notification requirements; 15.3 replace current bylaw making powers as they relate to urban stormwater networks; 16 agreed that the legislation will include requirements relating to stormwater network risk management plans, including that these plans will: 16.1 identify any hazards that relate to a stormwater network, including (without limitation) emerging or potential hazards; 16.2 assess any risks that are associated with those hazards; 16.3 identify how those risks are to be managed, controlled, monitored, or eliminated; 16.4 be provided to Taumata Arowai for review and comment, prior to being finalised; 17 agreed that the legislation will set out private landowners’ statutory rights and responsibilities in relation to overland flow paths or urban watercourses that are on their land, including provisions to the effect that: 17.1 where a landowner impairs or alters an overland flow path or watercourse, without resource consent or in breach of a stormwater rule, they would be responsible for either eliminating the impairment or meeting the costs of the territorial authority, if they do that on the landowner’s behalf; 3 I N C O N F I D E N C E 5sshjf9dn5 2024-07-31 14:52:41 I N C O N F I D E N C E CAB-24-MIN-0277.03 17.2 a private landowner would not be responsible for an impairment or alteration of a stormwater network if that impairment or alteration was caused by the act or omission of another person; 17.3 a private landowner would be required to notify the relevant territorial authority before undertaking any work that might affect the stormwater network; 18 agreed that the legislation will provide for an enabling framework for the development of service agreements, which can be used by territorial authorities, water organisations and other agencies to support the integrated management of the stormwater network; 19 agreed that the legislation will reflect the complex relationship between stormwater networks and transport corridor stormwater infrastructure, and define transport stormwater infrastructure as including the infrastructure that is owned or operated by a transport corridor manager to collect or discharge stormwater relating to a transport function of the corridor; Charging and billing for water services, by water organisations 20 agreed that the new legislation will include a suitably modified version of the current legislative framework for local government rating, to enable water organisations to identify which ratepayers should be charged for water services; 21 agreed that the legislation will require councils to share relevant billing information with water organisations (to enable the identification of ratepayers), and allow councils to charge a reasonable fee for this service; 22 agreed that the legislation can include any technical amendments that are needed to cater for situations where consumers may have to pay both water organisations and councils for water services at the same time, due to water organisations being formed part-way through a rating year; 23 agreed that the legislation will allow water organisations to charge a ‘serviceability fee’ to properties that could be, but are not, connected to the water network; Rates Rebate Scheme and associated financial implications 24 noted that: 24.1 except for ratepayers in Auckland, who pay water charges to Watercare, water costs are included as part of council rates under current arrangements; 24.2 under the current approach in the Rates Rebate Act 1973, rebates are applied to the rates bill only and not water charges (which are not considered rates and so are not eligible for the rates rebate); 24.3 if water charges are split out from rates bills and charged by new water organisations rather than councils, some recipients of a rates rebate would receive a lower rebate, even though their total expenses (rates and water) may not have changed; 25 agreed to amend the definition of ‘rates’ in the Rates Rebate Act 1973 to include water charges, so that ratepayers will not receive different levels of rebate depending on whether they are billed for water charges as part of their rates bill, or separately through a water organisation; 4 I N C O N F I D E N C E 5sshjf9dn5 2024-07-31 14:52:41 I N C O N F I D E N C E CAB-24-MIN-0277.03 26 noted that the above amendment will result in a per annum increase in the cost of the Rates Rebate Scheme, because water charges paid to Watercare would now be considered rates and would be eligible for the rebate; 27 noted that the additional costs can be met from within the existing Rates Rebate Scheme appropriation for the immediate future, meaning there is no current impact on the Crown’s fiscal forecasts; 28 noted that the Rates Rebate Scheme is a demand-based scheme that is periodically adjusted to reflect macroeconomic factors, and that the new definition of rates will capture the additional in the calculation of adjustments required over the longer term, contributing to an increase in adjustments made; 29 noted that the Treasury has been consulted on the above impact and is comfortable with the proposed amendment to the definition of ‘rates’ in the Rate Rebate Act 1973; 30 agreed that the legislation will require water organisations to provide information to the relevant council(s) on the amount of water charges paid by a consumer during the year, in order to facilitate the administration of the Rates Rebate Scheme by the council(s); Charging for growth by water organisations 31 noted that under Local Water Done Well, some councils will choose to shift their water services delivery into separate water organisations, and that those water organisations will need a specific mechanism to directly charge for new or additional demand on water infrastructure; 32 agreed that water organisations will be enabled to use the development contributions regime in the Local Government Act 2002, with the necessary modifications – as an interim measure – pending any future changes that may be made following work on development contributions settings as part of the Government’s Going for Housing Growth policy; 33 agreed that the legislation can enable a flexible approach in which: 33.1 water organisations are able to develop their own development contributions policy; 33.2 as an alternative to a separate water organisation development contributions policy, a water organisation and a council within its service area could agree to development contributions set by the water organisation being included in the council’s policy; 33.3 a council within a water organisation’s service area can administer the organisation’s development contributions policy on its behalf; 34 agreed that the legislation will include appropriate transitional arrangements, to ensure a smooth transition to charging for the growth-related costs of water services infrastructure from a council to a water organisation; 35 agreed that the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act 2020 be amended so that the Infrastructure Funding and Financing model can be used for water services infrastructure that is to be vested with a water organisation; Powers of receivers in relation to water organisations 36 noted that in situations where new water organisations achieve financial separation from their parent councils, the legislation will need to include provisions to ensure receivers can act appropriately in the event that a water organisation defaults on a debt; 5 I N C O N F I D E N C E 5sshjf9dn5 2024-07-31 14:52:41 9(2)(f)(iv) 9(2)(f)(iv) I N C O N F I D E N C E CAB-24-MIN-0277.03 37 agreed that the legislation will include provisions to: 37.1 allow the receiver to assess and collect for a given financial year both the amounts owed by the water organisation for that year and the reasonable costs incurred in collecting that amount; 37.2 prohibit the receiver from having any interest or security in water services infrastructure assets; 37.3 allow the receiver to collect the amount through water services charges assessed on consumers; Enabling exemptions from some of the minimum requirements that will apply to water organisations 38 agreed that the legislation will include a process that enables councils to seek an exemption from some of the minimum requirements that are due to apply to water organisations, as agreed by Cabinet in June 2024 [ECO-24-MIN-0106]; 39 agreed that the ability to seek and grant an exemption would apply to the following requirements only: 39.1 water organisations must be companies; 39.2 activities of water organisations will be limited to the provision of water services, and directly-related activities; 39.3 ; 39.4 only councils or consumer trusts can be shareholders of a water organisation; 40 agreed that the legislation will provide that: 40.1 councils that wish to seek an exemption would do so by submitting an application to the Secretary for Local Government, 40.2 the Secretary for Local Government would assess applications, and work with the Commerce Commission, Taumata Arowai, and Inland Revenue to provide advice to the Minister of Local Government; 40.3 the assessment and advice would be based on whether the council’s proposal for water services: 40.3.1 meets the legislative objectives of Local Water Done Well; 40.3.2 maintains the core requirements that the Minister of Local Government deems to be non-negotiable for all water organisations, including that the proposal and scope of the exemption do not involve any form of privatisation; 40.3.3 will provide water services that are financially sustainable; 40.3.4 satisfies the Minister of Local Government that the financial sustainability of water services would be put at greater risk if the exemption were not granted; 40.4 exemption approvals would be granted through an Order in Council, made on the recommendation of the Minister of Local Government; 6 I N C O N F I D E N C E 5sshjf9dn5 2024-07-31 14:52:41 9(2)(g)(i) I N C O N F I D E N C E CAB-24-MIN-0277.03 Tax exemptions for water organisations 49 agreed to grant tax-exempt status to water organisations; 50 agreed that the legislation will provide that, if a water organisation is wound up, there will be a requirement that assets must be transferred to another water organisation or to a council on wind-up; Borrowing in foreign currency 51 agreed that the legislation will explicitly allow water organisations to borrow in foreign currency, to ensure they have access to the borrowing that may be required to meet the significant costs associated with water infrastructure; 52 agreed that the legislation will also allow water organisations to enter into incidental arrangements, which allow water organisations to reduce their exposure to currency volatility; Rateability of land and assets owned by water organisations 53 agreed that the legislation will provide that land owned by water organisations should be rateable; 54 agreed that the legislation will require assets that are owned by a water organisation, but located on or under land the organisation does not own, should be rateable; 55 noted that changes are not being proposed to the bespoke arrangements for the rateability of Watercare’s land and assets that apply under the Local Government (Auckland Council) Act 2009; Civil Defence Emergency Management cost-sharing arrangements 56 agreed that the current Civil Defence Emergency Management cost-sharing arrangements with the Crown will apply directly to water organisations, to ensure financial separation of water organisations and allow them to directly seek partial reimbursement from the Crown for emergency expenses; 57 noted that further policy decisions will be required prior to the establishment of any financially independent water organisation (including Watercare) to ensure these arrangements apply appropriately to the water organisations and local authorities, with no material fiscal impacts for the Crown; Approach to consumer protection 59 noted that: 59.1 information disclosure will be part of the new economic regulation regime for local government water services, as agreed by Cabinet in June 2024 [ECO-24-MIN-0107]; 59.2 information disclosure could be used to oversee aspects of the consumer experience, and enable the Commerce Commission to learn more about how existing consumer protection settings are working in practice, and identify potential shortcomings; 8 I N C O N F I D E N C E 5sshjf9dn5 2024-07-31 14:52:41 I N C O N F I D E N C E CAB-24-MIN-0277.03 60 agreed that the legislation should clearly enable the Commerce Commission to require public reporting from water service providers on consumer protection issues, and to publicly summarise and analyse the information disclosed; 61 agreed that the legislation will also include the power for the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs to make regulations relating to consumer protection measures, to provide flexibility to consider what may be needed in the future, particularly if information disclosure reveals that issues exist; 62 agreed that regulations could be used to specify requirements relating to: 62.1 complaint processes, the provision of information, the recording of complaints, and/or reporting; 62.2 providing access to an external consumer dispute resolution process; and/or 62.3 other matters relating to consumer protections that the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs considers necessary and appropriate; 63 noted that service quality codes could be a useful consumer protection mechanism, but that the development of such codes should be sector-led in the first instance; 64 agreed that the Commerce Commission will be able to issue guidelines to water service providers on matters relating to a service quality code; 65 agreed that the legislation will enable the Commerce Commission to make a service quality code in relation to the provision of water services, where no sector-developed code exists or, in the opinion of the Commission, the purpose of Part 4 of the Commerce Act 1986 could be better met by a mandatory code; 66 agreed that, before making a mandatory service quality code, the Commerce Commission will be required to provide a report to the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs containing the reasons for doing this; Compliance and enforcement relating to consumer protections 67 noted that: 67.1 the Commerce Act 1986 contains a range of compliance, enforcement and investigation powers for use under Part 4 of that Act, including enforceable undertakings, pecuniary penalties, offences, orders, injunctions, and the ability to require information for statutory purposes; 67.2 compliance, enforcement, and investigation powers similar to those under Part 4 of the Commerce Act 1986 will be applied to the economic regulation of water services, as agreed by Cabinet in June 2024 [ECO-24-MIN-0107]; 68 agreed that the legislation will enable similar compliance and enforcement powers and mechanisms to be applied to consumer protection requirements, to ensure the Commerce Commission has access to adequate and appropriate tools, and provide consistency across regimes; 9 I N C O N F I D E N C E 5sshjf9dn5 2024-07-31 14:52:41 I N C O N F I D E N C E CAB-24-MIN-0277.03 Amendments to the Water Services Act 2021 Exemptions 75 noted that section 57 of the Water Services Act allows the Chief Executive of Taumata Arowai to grant exemptions to any drinking water supplier or class of drinking water supplier from complying with nine requirements of the Act; Local Water Done Well Stage 3: Further Decisions Portfolio Local Government On 24 July 2024, the Cabinet Economic Policy Committee: Background 1 noted that, as agreed by Cabinet in February 2024 [CAB-24-MIN-0024], the legislative strategy involved in implementing Local Water Done Well includes three pieces of legislation: 1.1 the Water Services Acts Repeal Act – passed in February 2024 – which repealed the previous government’s legislation and restored ownership and responsibility for water services to local government; 1.2 the Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Bill – introduced in May 2024 – which will establish initial components of the new framework and transitional arrangements; 1.3 the Local Government Water Services Bill – anticipated for introduction in December 2024 and enactment in mid-2025 – which will provide enduring settings and frameworks; 2 noted that policy decisions for the third Bill above are being sought through a suite of three papers, the first two of which have already been agreed: 2.1 Local Water Done Well Stage 3: Water Services Delivery System [ECO-24-MIN-0106]; Relation to government priorities 3. The Speech from the Throne, in December 2023, stated that the Government w ould repeal the “Three Waters” legislation and restore council ownership and control, with stronger central government oversight, and strict rules for water quality and ongoing investment. 4. Moving towards sustainable long -term investment in water services infrastructure through Local Water Done Well will play a critical role in supporting housing growth. 9(2)(f)(iv) IN CONFIDENCE Page 2 of 54 Executive summary 5. Local Water Done Well sets out a clear direction for financially sustainable water services, underpinned by a robust regulatory system. It puts an emphasis on meeting regulatory standards, and the transparent and sustainable performance of these services – but provides for local choice about the form of service delivery structures. 6. During June and July 2024, I am seeking decisions on three papers, which together will give effect to the third stage of the Local Water Done Well programme: 6.1 Local Water Done Well stage 3: water services delivery system [ECO-24-MIN - 0106, 19 June 2024 ]; 6.2 Local Water Done Well stage 3: water services regulatory system [ECO-24-MIN - 0107, 19 June 2024 ]; 6.3 this paper – Local Water Done Well stage 3: further decisions . 7. Background 14. In February 2024, we enacted the Water Services Acts Repeal Act 2024 . This fulfilled our commitments to repeal the previous government’s unpopular water services legislation, restore local government responsibilities for water services, and put a halt to the establishment of the 10 mega entities. 15. That was the first stage of the Local Water Done Well programme. As outlined in my February 2024 paper, Water Services Acts Repeal Bill: Approval for Introduction [CAB - 24-MIN -0024] , the policy and legislative approach for implementing the new water services system will be progressed through two further Bills . 16. In March 2024, I report ed back to the Cabinet Economic Policy Committee (ECO) with the first set of policy proposals for the replacement regime . The Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Bill was introduced in May 2024, and is expected to be enacted in August 2024. That Bill sets the early foundations for the new system, and support s and progress es some initial activities . IN CONFIDENCE Page 4 of 54 17. Through the February 2024 paper, I was invited to report back to ECO with the second set of policy proposals for the replacement regime, to inform a Bill to be passed in the second quarter of 2025. It was noted that Bill will include provisions relating to long - term requirements for financial sustainability, provide for a complete economic regulation regime, make amendments to the water quality regulato r’s empowering legislation, and make refinements to the water services delivery system settings. 18. This is the third paper of a suite of papers, i n June and July 2024, that reports back and seeks decisions on these matters. The first two papers sought agreement to: 18.1 a new approach to local government water service s delivery arrangements; 18.2 the establishment of a new economic regulation regime for local government water service providers; 18.3 some initial changes to the Water Services Act, to help reduce the regulatory compliance burden on small drinking water suppliers. 19. If agreed, the proposals in these papers will inform the development of the Local Government Water Services Bill . Once in place, this package of legislation will implement this Government’s Local Water Done Well policy , and bring about a new approach to water services delivery and regulation . We need to equip water service providers with modern and fit -for-purpose powers relating to water infrastructure and services Modernised powers to carry out work on land, control connections, and manage other issues 57. Current legislation relating to water services has often fallen behind similar legislation that applies to other utilities in New Zealand or other jurisdictions. It is generally old, often contains gaps, and is spread across multiple Acts. The application of this legislation can be challenging for some councils, particularly where they lack capability or ready access to legal advice. 58. I have identified several areas in which modernising the legislation relating to water service providers’ functions and powers would enable more effective delivery of water services. This would help to reduce costs, streamline processes, and support priori ties such as urban development. 59. I am proposing changes in the following areas: 59.1 Powers for water service providers to control connections to water services and infrastructure. These are powers that enable councils to approve connections by private individuals or businesses to water supply, wastewater and/or stormwater infrastructure, and include the ability to set design or engineering requirements. These powers are a critical part of urban development. Modernisation should reduce compliance costs by providing greater certainty and consistency. 1 Water organisations is the general term used to refer to all of the models of water service provider except where councils continue with direct ‘in -house’ delivery. The term ‘water service provider’ includes all forms of water service provider and councils. IN CONFIDENCE Page 9 of 54 59.2 Powers for water service providers to carry out work on land in relation to water services infrastructure . These are powers that are required by all kinds of utility providers (water, telecommunications, electricity, and gas) to ensure infrastructure can be constructed or maintained, particularly where it is on private property or underground. The proposed ch anges will simplify and streamline the use of these powers, while providing appropriate protections for all parties, and are important for both ongoing maintenance and new development. 59.3 A modernised approach t o the current bylaw regime relating to water services . Councils use bylaws to control water catchments (such as reservoirs), manage trade waste, and to set restrictions relating water supply or wastewater infrastructure use (for example, sprinkler use during droughts, or disposing of toxic substances in toil ets or drains). I am proposing the current system is replaced or supplemented with new, fit-for-purpose statutory provisions , including requirements for management plans and enforc ement rules . This will enable more effective and consistent management, while still addressing local issues and needs. 60. I am seeking agreement to provide in the legislation for modernised powers relating to water services infrastructure, including powers for water service providers (councils and water organisations) to: 60.1 control connections to water services infrastructure ; 60.2 carry out work on land relating to water services infrastructure .2 61. I am also seeking agreement to provide for a modernised approach to the bylaw system relating to water services. I expect t his would include statutory provisions covering the following areas. 62. Firstly, the legislation will need to enable water service providers to control drinking water catchments by specifying land within a “controlled drinking water catchment area” , which would be covered by a water catchment management plan. 63. These plans would set out arrangements for the control and protection of the area, including access , activities that might be undertaken , use of water , and restrictions or prohibitions regarding contamination of water in the area. Any rules with respect to land that is not owned or controlled by the water service provider would only be by agreement with the owner. 64. Secondly, water service providers will need to be enabled to manage trade waste . This is commercial and industrial liquid waste that is discharged into the wastewater system. I am proposing t his would be done through published trade waste plans (developed with local consultation ), and supported by a system of permits, certification and registration. Domestic customers would also be subject to this regime if discharges were beyond a normal household level (for example, a home workshop working with toxic chem icals ). 2 This is not intended to apply in relation to Crown land. Legislation relating to Crown land in general, and public conservation land, already contains mechanisms to enable access, providing the activities and access are consistent with the land’s status and legislative purposes. IN CONFIDENCE Page 10 of 54 65. Trade waste plans would set out conditions on the quality, quantity and timing of discharges , as well as testing. Local plans will allow flexibility in controlling the thresholds and conditions for discharges to meet local conditions – for example, the capacity or vulnerability of local systems. Customers will be able to seek a review of a permitting decision, possibly through the court system. 66. Each of t he above approaches will need to be underpinned by an offence regime to enable appropriate and effective enforcement. The legislation will also need to enable water service providers to manage water supply and wastewater services with offence and infringement tools. 67. I anticipate t he legislation will include necessary offences and penalties (including infringements), with penalties modelled on similar offences in other legislation .3 The Department of Internal Affairs will work with the Ministry of Justice to develop the details needed for legislative drafting. 68. The legislation will also need to provide for detailed transitional arrangements , cover ing matters such as timeframes, suspension of current mandatory bylaw revie ws during the transition period, revocation of bylaws (if relevant) , and appropriate safeguards and requirements around the forming of new management regimes (which will function as secondary legislation). 69. I am seeking delegated authority to approve matters that may arise during the course of drafting and may be required to align with the decisions in this paper . This would include approving detailed matters relating to these proposals. Supporting long -term contracting arrangements 70. Sections 136 and 137 of the LGA02 relate to contracts and joint arrangements for water services. Under these provisions, local government organisations (councils and CCOs ) can enter into contracts and joint local government arrangements with one another without restriction. However, there are limitations on the length of contracts and joint arrangements that involve third parties (such as the private sector) . 71. The maximum length of a contract or joint arrangement for water services – involving bodies that are not local government organisations – is 35 years. 72. I am not considering changes to these sections of the LGA02 – other than to ensure new water organisations are also considered to be local government organisations in future. However, I am interested in views on whether the maximum length of a contract or joint arrangement should be extended to 50 years. This woul d reflect the long lifespan of water infrastructure, and the potential opportunities to enter into longer contracts. 73. I am seeking a decision on whether the maximum length of contracts and joint arrangements relating to water services should remain at 35 years or be extended to 50 years instead. 3 For example, the Local Government Act 2002, the Resource Management Act 1991, the Water Services Act 2021, Te Ture Whenua Māori Act 1993 (where relevant) and other utilities legislation . IN CONFIDENCE Page 11 of 54 74. There are concerns about the capacity of local government organisations to effectively design and manage long -term contracts. The prevalence of information gaps on New Zealand’s water network further complicates effective design and management of longer -term contracts. 75. The current 35 -year limit is consistent with the common length of public -private partnership contracts globally (about 25 to 30 years). It is also the maximum period for which resource consent s can be granted , for taking water and discharges . This effectively puts third -party providers on the same footing for recovering capital costs as councils, which typically repay debt for a new water treatment plant over a term of between 20 and 30 years. 76. An argument can be made for extending the limit to 50 years, as this may enable certain types of public -private partnerships, such as ‘build , design and operate ’ cont racts, for high capital expenditure assets. The development costs of the asset could be recovered over a longer period or to match the economic life of the asset, which can lead to low costs per annum for providing this infrastructure. 77. Regardless of whether changes are made in this respect, I am exploring potential mechanisms for providing the local government sector with support to enter into successful long -term contracting arrangements. Support mechanisms could include guidance materi al and targeted assistance for councils. We also need mechanisms to improve how s tormwater networks are managed and help reduce risks to people and property 78. Overland flow paths and urban watercourses are an urban area's natural drainage system – providing critical ‘overflow’ capacity for the stormwater network. While stormwater network infrastructure has been designed to collect and divert stormwater from urban development, in almost all c ases it will discharge that stormwater to the nearest overland flow path or urban watercourse. 79. Private ownership, uncertainty around legal responsibilities, limited regulatory tools , and information gaps are key challenges that affect the protection and maintenance of the conveyance capacity of overland flow paths and urban watercourses . These issues are exacerbated by urban intensification and climate change. 80. Together , these challenges mean that initiatives to protect and maintain the conveyance capacity of urban watercourses are difficult to implement and more likely to be reactive than proactive. This can expose people and property to significant flood risks. A lack of proactive interventions and maintenance was identified as a contributing factor to flooding impacts on properties in the Auckland floods in January 2023. 81. Regional councils, territorial authorities, and transport corridor managers all have overlapping responsibilities for managing the impacts of stormwater in urban areas. Stormwater network infrastructure owned by other public agencies and private property o wners is often physically connected to council stormwater network s. Local context may also affect how those responsibilities are allocated. Improving the integrated management of stormwater and its impacts relies on effective coordination across those agen cies and networks. IN CONFIDENCE Page 12 of 54 82. I have identified some mechanisms to support integration between key agencies and improv e the management of overland flow paths and urban watercourses . My proposals fall into the following related areas: 82.1 specify ing territorial authority and private landowner statutory roles and responsibilities ; 82.2 enabling new planning and regulatory tools – through ‘stormwater network risk management plans ’ and ‘stormwater rules ’ to support risk-based management of overland flow paths and urban watercourses ; 82.3 enabling territorial authorit ies, regional council s, and transport corridor managers to put in place ‘service agreements ’ to support the integrated management of stormwater networks. Roles, responsibilities, and new planning and regulatory tools 83. I am proposing to include provisions in the legislation that state that territorial authorities are responsible for managing and maintaining the stormwater network in their city or district (service areas) – including overland flow paths and urban watercourses that are both on private land and related to the operation of the stormwater network in urban areas . 84. As part of this approach, the legislation w ill require territorial authorities to: 84.1 develop a stormwater network risk management plan to identify significant risks and hazards that impact on the function of critical stormwater network assets ; 84.2 work with private landowners as required to protect and maintain the conveyance capacity of overland flow paths and urban watercourses ; 84.3 develop (as required) stormwater rules that would provide direction to private landowners on their responsibilities for maintenance and protection of the conveyance capacity of overland flow paths and urban watercourses on their land . 85. The legislation w ill provide for these stormwater rules – and associated rule -making powers – to support the management of overland flow paths and urban watercourses on private land . The se would : 85.1 be made pursuant to stormwater network risk management plans ; 85.2 set out landowner duties – including access to land, and notification requirements ; 85.3 replace current bylaw -making powers as they relate to the urban stormwater network. 86. The legislation w ill also include requirements relating to stormwater network risk management plans. These plans would have an operational focus, and require stormwater network operators to : 86.1 adopt a risk -based approach to identify any hazards that would impact on critical stormwater network assets , including (without limitation) emerging or potential hazards; IN CONFIDENCE Page 13 of 54 86.2 assess any risks to the operation of the network, including any risks to people or property that are associated with those hazards; 86.3 identify how those risks are to be managed, controlled, monitored, or eliminated. 87. The intention is that the plans will improve flood risk information , to inform proactive management of hazards and risks to the operation of the stormwater network, and to people and property. They will also provide a framework for stormwater rules to support the management of overland flow paths and urban watercourses on private land . 88. Prior to being finalised, stormwater network risk management plans w ill be provided by the territorial authority to Taumata Arowai for review and comment. This w ill complement the approach to risk management plans that has been adopted for drinking water and wastewater in the Water Services Act . It would provide an opportunity for Taumata Arowai to issue guidance and align environmental standards for stormwater management to improve consistency. 89. I am also proposing the legislation w ill set out private landowners’ statutory rights and responsibilities in relation to overland flow paths or urban watercourses that are on their land. This would include provisions to the effect that: 89.1 where a landowner impairs or alters an overland flow path or watercourse, without resource consent or in breach of a stormwater rule they would be responsible for either eliminating the impairment or meeting the costs of the territorial authority, if they do that on the landowner ’s behalf; 89.2 a private landowner would not be responsible for an impairment or alteration of a stormwater network if that impairment or alteration was caused by the act or omission of another person; 89.3 a private landowner would be required to notify the relevant territorial authority before undertaking any work that might affect the stormwater network. Service agreements 90. Stormwater management has a range of interfaces and overlapping jurisdictions . This means different parties need to work together to manage their respective statutory roles and functions to support the integrated management of the stormwater network . 91. Service agreements can be a useful mechanism for managing the interactions between these parties. Many councils already use similar service level agreements to man age cross -agency interactions. T hese agreements can set out the roles and responsibilities of each party, how they will work together and share information, and a dispute resolution process. 92. I am seeking agreement that the legislation provides for an enabling framework for the development of service agreements , which can be used by territorial authorities , water organisations and other agencies to support the integrated management of the stormwater network . IN CONFIDENCE Page 14 of 54 93. The legislation will include the core features of these agreements, but their use would not be mandatory. This approach reflects the cooperative nature of the agreements, and the need to provide some flexibility for the parties to adopt arrangements that are appropriate to lo cal circumstances. Definitions 94. Finally, I consider the legislation should reflect the complex relationship between stormwater networks and transport corridor stormwater infrastructure. 95. Stormwater infrastructure in transport corridors has been developed to enable the transport functions of those corridors. To protect that transport function, particularly in relation to local roads , which (apart from Auckland) are owned and operated by territorial authorities, I am propos ing the legislation define s transport stormwater infrastructure, by recognising that the primary purpose of that infrastructure is for transport purposes. 96. The defin ition of transport stormwater infrastructure will include the infrastructure that is owned or operated by a transport corridor manager to collect or discharge stormwater relating to a transport function of the corridor . 97. The intention is that the definition recognise s and protect s the transport function and investment in this infrastructure. It w ill not include matter s related to the operation, maintenance or level of service related to transport stormwater infrastructure. While these are important issues for integrated management across those stormwater networks , I consider ‘ service agreements ’ should be the primary mechanism to ensure territorial authorities and transport corridor manage rs work effectively together within their respective statutory responsibilities . We need to consider various matters relating to c harging for water services , including ensuring water organisations can charge for growth Charg ing and billing for water services 98. In my previous paper, it was agreed that the legislation will enable water organisations to assess, set and collect water services charges – separate from their owner councils. I am now seeking agreement to further details to support and enable this approach. 99. Water charges are currently included as part of council rates (except for Watercare, which bills property owners directly). The Local Government (Rating) Act 2002 provides a framework for identifying who is liable to pay rates (that is, who is the ratepaye r), which broadly aligns with who owns the property. 100. The new legislation will need to include a suitably modified version of the current legislative framework, to enable water organisations to identify which ratepayers should be charged for water services. 101. I am not proposing any changes to the way usage charges are assessed for residential properties, or changes to the existing arrangements that apply for tenants and landlord s. Current arrangements would continue, whereby bills for water charges are raised directly with the property owner, but tenants are liable for any consumption - related component of that bill. IN CONFIDENCE Page 15 of 54 102. Water organisations will need to be able to contact their customers to communicate any new arrangements, and to bill them for water charges. I am proposing the legislation require s councils to share relevant billing information with water organisations (to enable the identification of ratepayers) , and councils are allowed to charge a reasonable fee for this service. 103. When a new water organisation is set up, there may be a period in which the obligation to provide water services has been transferred but the necessary billing systems are not yet in place. If this occurs, the council(s) and water organisation will be willing participants who have agreed to the date of transfer. It is reasonable to expect they will cooperate to develop any ‘pass -through’ billing arrangements that may be needed. 104. I do not consider the legislation needs to include transitional provisions to deal with these kinds of billing arrangements. However, there may be situations where a water organisation is formed and begins charging for services part -way through a rating ye ar. This may cause issues where rates are charged over the course of the full year, even if the component of the rates related to water charges is calculated based on the part of the year the council provides water services. This may mean that a consumer i s paying for water charges to both a council and a water organisation at the same time. 105. I am seeking agreement that the legislation can include any technical amendments that are needed to cater for these situations . Unconnected properties 106. There is a question about whether properties should attract water cha rges where there is no active connection to the water supply. Under current arrangements, the treatment of these properties differs from council to council. In most cases, though, unconnected prop erties that are ‘serviceable’ by the network are charged water - related rates. 107. I am proposing the legislation allows water organisations to charge a ‘serviceability fee’ to properties that could be, but are not, connected to the water network. This fee is for the option to connect to the water network, recognis ing that the owners of these properties receive a benefit from the network through increased property values, and from any fire hydrants located nearby. Interaction with the Rates Rebate Scheme 108. The Rates Rebate Scheme provides support to low -income owner -occupiers. Just over 100,000 households currently receive a rates rebate, about 78 percent of which receive New Zealand Superannuation. The level of subsidy available to a household depends on bo th their income and their rates bill. 109. Councils administer the Rates Rebate Scheme, and the rebates are funded by the Crown . The a ctual costs of the Scheme fluctuate based on demand , and the Department of Internal Affairs has a statutory obligation to reimburse councils for any rebates granted to eligible ratepayers. C osts for the 2022/23 year were $65.3 million and an appropriation of up to $78 million per year is in place for 2023/24 and outyears. 110. Except for ratepayers in Auckland, who pay water charges to Watercare, water costs are included as part of rates under the current arrangements. The water charges that Watercare issues are not considered rates and so are not eligible for the rates rebate. IN CONFIDENCE Page 16 of 54 111. When water charges are split out from rates bills, some recipients of a rates rebate would receive a lower rebate, even though their total expenses (rates and water) may not have changed. This is because under current legislation the rebate would be applie d to the rates bill only, and not the water charges. 112. I am seeking agreement to amend the definition of rates in the Rates Rebate Act 1973 to include water charges. This will mean ratepayers will not receive different levels of rebate depending on whether they are billed for water charges as part of their rates bill, or separately th rough a water organisation. 113. I am advised th is amendment will result in a per annum increase in the cost of the Rates Rebate Scheme. This reflects that the Crown would need to fund additional rates rebates for Auckland ratepayers, as water charges paid to Watercare would now be considered rates and would be eligible for the rebate . The additional costs can be met from within the existing appropriation for the immediate future, meaning no immediate changes to the Crown’s fiscal forecasts are required . However, as the scheme is periodically adjusted for macroeconomic factors, such as CPI, the new definition of rates will impact adjustments required over the longer term. 114. The proposal will create an additional administrative burden on councils – who currently administer the Rates Rebate Scheme – as they would have to assess water charges as well as rates bills. To mitigate this, I am proposing that water organisations should be required to share information on the amount of water charges paid by consumer s during the rating year , with the administering council . This would enable a streamlined application and assessment process for eligible ratepayers and councils . Charging for growth by water organisations 115. Under Local Water Done Well, some councils will choose to shift their water services delivery into separate water organisations. As agreed in my previous paper, these water organisations will be given the power to set their water charges directly and indep endently. 116. Water organisations will need a specific mechanism to directly charge for new or additional demand on water infrastructure. This will help to achieve financial sustainability, through funding appropriately for growth and keeping water charges to existing r atepayers lower than otherwise. It would also support the Government’s housing and urban development objectives. 117. Wider work is underway by officials from the Minist ry of Housing and Urban Development and the Department of Internal Affairs to improve infrastructure funding settings as part of the Government’s Going for Housing Growth policy . . 118. Until any future policy and legislative changes are made in this respect, I am proposing –as an interim measure – that water organisations should be enabled to use the development contributions regime in the L GA02 , with the necessary modifications. 119. I am seeking agreement that the legislation can enable a flexible approach in which: 119.1 water organisations are able to develop their own development contributions policy; 9(2)(b)(ii) 9(2)(f)(iv) IN CONFIDENCE Page 17 of 54 119.2 as an alternative to a separate water organisation development contributions policy, a water organisation and a council within its service area could agree to development contributions set by the water organisation being included in the council ’s policy; 119.3 a council within a water organisation’s service area can administer the organisation’s development contributions policy on its behalf . 120. There will need to be appropriate transitional arrangements , to ensure a smooth transition to charging for the growth -related costs of water services infrastructure from a council to a water organisation . 121. I am also proposing that the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act 2020 be amended so that the Infrastructure Funding and Financing model can be used for water services infrastructure that is to be vested with a water organisation . I note that amendments to this Act to enable it to be used by water organisations will be progressed as part of the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act Amendment Bill, and not as part of the Local Government Water Services Bill. 122. I am not proposing that water organisations will be able to charge financial contributions under the Resource Management Act 1991 (RMA) . Financial contributions are an unsuitable funding tool for water organisations. It is more appropriate to allow water organisations to recover the costs attributable to growth by charging development contributions instead. Debt collection and powers of receivers relating to water organisations 123. In my previous paper, I noted that water organisations will need the ability to collect overdue amounts. It was agreed that the legislation will include provisions to the effect that those organisations should rely on commerc ial debt practices to address this. 124. I also noted that additional options were being explored, and I would provide further advice in this paper. 125. I am not recommending that water organisations have stronger powers to collect overdue amounts from customers. However, I consider it would be desirable for the legislation to include provisions that deal with situations in which a water organisation itself defaults on a debt. 126. The LGA02 and Receiverships Act 1993 contain longstanding provisions that allow a receiver to be appointed where a council defaults on a debt. Among other things, a receiver may collect rates to repay the debt. These provisions are a modification of standa rd receivership arrangements that include safeguards reflecting the special character of local authorities – for example, a receiver may not act in a way that interferes with services that are essential to public health and safety. They are necessary to pr ovide lenders confidence that, if a local authority defaults on a debt, the lender can recoup the loan. IN CONFIDENCE Page 18 of 54 127. The Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Bill contains similar provisions that apply directly to Watercare if it defaults on a debt. These are needed as financial separation of Watercare and Auckland Council will mean that receivers w ill no longer be able to rely on the powers granted to them under the LGA02 to collect Watercare debts from Auckland Council ratepayers. The receiver will be able to levy water services charges on consumers rather than collect rates, as rating is not possi ble for Watercare. 128. New water organisations that achieve financial separation from their parent councils will need similar provisions to ensure receivers can act appropriately in the event that a water organisation defaults on a debt. I am proposing the legislation includes provisions that would: 128.1 allow the receiver to assess and collect for a given financial year both the amounts owed by the water organisation for that year and the reasonable costs incurred in collecting that amount ; 128.2 prohibit the receiver from having any interest or security in water services infrastructure assets; 128.3 allow the receiver to collect the amount through water services charges assessed on consumers. Other matters relating to water organisations Enabling e xemptions to be sought from some of the minimum requirements that will apply to water organisations 129. In my June 2024 paper [ECO -24-MIN -0106] , it was agreed the legislation will include a set of minimum requirements that w ill apply to all water service providers – including water organisations, and councils that continue with ‘in -house’ delivery. It was also agreed there will be additional requirements for water organisations , and further requirements for water organisations that involve consumer trusts . 130. I am aware t here may be situations in which a council ’s preferred water service delivery arrangements may not meet some of these requirements. For example, one council has already approached me about transferring their water services and assets to an existing, locally owned co -operative in their region. The co -operative owns and operates the region’s electricity distribution network and a fibre o ptic communications network. 131. The council in question sees several benefits arising from their proposal, including preservation of community ownership and a reflection of the district’s distinct community identity, as well as significant benefits from an economic regulation perspective as the lines company is already a regulated entity. This solution shows an innovative approach from a council that is considering alternative options to achieve financial sustainability and accelerate their ability to respond to economic regulation. Howev er, the solution itself does not meet all of the minimum criteria that have been agreed for future water organisations, such as activities of water organisations will be limited to the provision of water services, and directly -related activities [ECO -24-MIN- 0106]. IN CONFIDENCE Page 19 of 54 132. As important part of Local Water Done Well is providing councils with the flexibility to identify and establish the deliver y arrangements that work for them . However, I also recognis e there are some minimum requirements and expectations that are non - negotiable. This is particularly the case with regard to privatisation, which will not be permitted under any circumstances , as well as requirements for financial sustainability and meeting regulatory standards . 133. To achieve an appropriate balance between these factors , I am proposing the legislation includes a process that enables councils to seek an exemption from some of the minimum requirements that are due to apply to water organisations. This approach w ill allow for a case -by-case consideration of each proposal, and maintain a clear set of requirements for water organisations in legislation. 134. Having a clear process will introduce flexibility into the water organisation requirements and give councils a broader scope to develop their future service delivery arrangements. The flexibility can be balanced by: 134.1 limiting the requirements that are eligible for an exemption; 134.2 ensuring the appropriate level of approval for exemptions; 134.3 the assessment criteria and process associated with considering exemptions. 135. I am proposing that the ability to seek and grant an exemption w ill apply to the following legislative requirements , only : 135.1 water organisations must be companies; 135.2 activities of water organisations will be limited to the provision of water services, and directly -related activities; 135.3 ; 135.4 only councils or consumer trusts can be shareholders of a water organisation. 136. The legislation w ill place further limits on exemptions to ensure that no form of privatisation is permitted. This w ill let councils develop proposals , similar to the energy trust model seen in consumer -owned power distribution companies. 137. Councils w ill be required to submit exemption applications to the Secretary for Local Government (the Chief Executive of the Department of Internal Affairs ). The Secretary will assess applications, and work with the Commerce Commission, Taumata Arowai and Inland Revenue to provide advice to the Minister of Local Government . 138. The assessment , advice and final recommendations will be based on whether the council’s proposal for water services: 138.1 meets the legislative objectives of Local Water Done Well; 138.2 maintains the core requirements that are non-negotiable bottom lines for all water organisations , including that the proposal and scope of the exemption do not involve any form of privatisation; 138.3 will provide water services that are financially sustainable; 9(2)(g)(i) 9(2)(g)(i) IN CONFIDENCE Page 20 of 54 138.4 satisfies me th at the financial sustainability of water services would be put at greater risk if the exemption were not granted . 139. Exemption approvals w ill be granted through Order in Council, made on the recommendation of the Minister of Local Government . This w ill provide an appropriate level of Cabinet oversight of decisions that involve exempting councils from statutory requirements – as well as public transparency about the outcome of those decisions. 140. The exemptions process w ill include the ability to – as the case may be : 140.1 grant an exemption from a requirement through Order in Council; 140.2 modify a requirement if a full exemption is not needed; 140.3 impose additional conditions on water organisations; 140.4 decline the exemption application. 141. Councils that have an exemption application approved and then go on to rely on that exemption when forming a new water organisation will be required to provide information on this matter on their websites. Transitional tax issues 145. Currently water services are mostly supplied by councils, which are all primarily exempt from income tax under the Income Tax Act 2007. It is expected that in future some councils will transfer water infrastructure assets, and responsibility to supply water services, to new water organisations. 146. If councils decide to transfer water services, they will need to consider existing legislation that applies with respect to tax obligations and employees . In the absence of any amendment to tax legislation, this may have tax implications for both the council and water organisation. 147. The general tax policy approach to facilitating restructuring in response to changes in Government policy is to provide specific transitional tax relief in legislation, with the broad policy objective of enabling reform to be carried out on a tax -neutral b asis and to remove any tax consequences arising solely from the restructure. 9(2)(b)(ii), 9(2)(f)(iv) IN CONFIDENCE Page 21 of 54 148. Consistent with this approach, I am proposing the legislation includes new provisions that treat the transferor and transferee as the same person for the purposes of the Income Tax Act 2007 and Goods and Services Tax Act 1985. This would apply when council s transfer water services to a water organisation, or when water services are transferred from a single -council water organisation to a multi -council water organisation. This will allow those transfers to occur without triggering income tax or GST conseque nces and provide a tax neutral result. 149. This is a situation that has been dealt with a number of times in the past, such as the transfer of electricity services in 1992, and the amalgamation of district health boards into Health New Zealand in 2022. 150. A feature of these examples was that the transfers were mandatory and had to happen within a set period. There is no mandated transfer in the case of water services. I am therefore recommending making the new tax relief provisions available for a period of five years from enactment, as they are intended to be transitional provisions only.4 Tax status of water organisations 151. Councils are tax -exempt, but are able to form CCOs that are subject to income tax. One of the reasons CCOs pay tax is because they may be operating in areas where they are competing with private enterprise s – meaning they should be subject to the same conditions, including being subject to income tax, to allow their performance relative to private enterprise to be compared. 152. This will not be the case for water organisations, as water services are inherently a monopoly market with a sole provider. 153. Water organisations will either be owned by one or more councils, one or more consumer trusts, or potentially a combination of the two. I expect councils considering whether or not to transfer water services into a new water organisation will take tax status into account, as income from water services delivered in -house by councils is not taxable. 154. I consider the new water organisations are similar to public -purpose Crown -controlled companies (e.g., Crown Infrastructure Partners, City Rail Link Limited). An income tax exemption is provided to these companies if the entity : 154.1 is solely owned by the Crown, or majority owned by the Crown with only local authorit ies or other tax -exempt entities as its other shareholders; 154.2 is not engaged primarily in a commercial activity with a profit -making objective. 155. These criteria are applied because the purpose of the exemption is to: 155.1 reduce compliance costs for the entity without reducing government revenue or creating economic distortions (meaning there should not be any private sector investors involved to benefit from the exemption ); 155.2 to exempt entities whose primary purposes are to assist in carrying out the Government’s social objectives, rather than to make profits. 4 General tax rules would continue to apply to any transactions after that timeframe, including existing rules contained in Schedule 9 of the LGA02 . IN CONFIDENCE Page 22 of 54 156. I am proposing to g rant tax -exempt status to water organisations . I consider water organisations satisfy the criteria above. While it may be the case that the y will seek to make a profit from their day -to-day operations, this will be for the purpose of funding capital expenditure on water infrastructure. 157. The prohibition on distributions to shareholders – discussed below – ensures that private individuals will not be able to receive a private pecuniary benefit or profit from the income tax exemption. 158. Additionally, if a water organisation is wound up, there will need to be a requirement that assets must be transferred to another water organisation or to a council on wind - up. This ensures that a taxable consumer trust or private shareholder would not receive any of the water organisation’s assets (including any untaxed accumulated gains). 159. If a council applies for an exemption from a minimum requirement for water organisations (see previous section) , their tax status may be affected if they no longer meet the criteria discussed above. Ability to borrow in foreign currency 160. The LGA02 prohibits councils from borrowing in foreign currency, but is silent on whether CCOs are able to do so. In 2011, a legislative amendment was made to allow Auckland Council, and thereby Watercare, to borrow in foreign currency due to its large bo rrowing programmes. 161. Many water organisations (which may include a form of CCO) will need to borrow significant amounts to meet infrastructure costs. As the total amount of borrowing required for water infrastructure is expected to exceed the amount of New Zealand - based lendin g available ), I am proposing the legislation explicitly allows water organisations to borrow in foreign currency. 162. Water organisations would also be allowed to enter into incidental arrangements, such as derivatives and hedges, which allow water organisations to reduce their exposure to currency volatility. Rateability of land and assets owned by water organisations 163. I am proposing that land transferred to water organisations should be rateable. I propose the legislation requires land owned by water organisations, and assets that are owned by the organisation but located on or under land the organisation does not own, should be rateable. This aligns with the way that land and assets of other network providers, such as electricity and telecommunications, are rated. 164. Councils will have the option to remit those rates if they decide that the water organisation, which they will likely be shareholders in, should not have to pay them. 9(2)(g)(i) IN CONFIDENCE Page 23 of 54 165. Under the Local Government (Auckland Council) Act 2009, Watercare has bespoke arrangements for rateability of its land and assets. Watercare is not required to pay rates on assets it owns, if those assets are on land that it does not own. Watercare is required to pay rates on land that it owns; however, the rates are subject to a special calculation. These rules relating to land and assets are concessionary towards Watercare and were agree d as part of the negotiations during the formation of the Auckland Co uncil in 2010. I am not recommending changes to these rules for Watercare or extending them to other water organisations. Civil Defence Emergency Management cost -sharing arrangements 166. I am proposing the current Civil Defence Emergency Management cost -sharing arrangements with the Crown would apply directly to water organisations. This will ensure financial separation of water organisations and allow them to directly seek partial reimbur sement from the Crown for emergency expenses. 167. The Civil Defence Emergency Management Act 2002 (CDEM Act) enables the Crown, without further appropriation, to reimburse or pay a local authority for expenses it incurs because of an emergency, as long as the criteria in a Government policy in force befor e the emergency occurred are met. This provision of the CDEM Act will need to be amended to also refer directly to water organisations. 168. Objectives and principles for government financial support are in the National Civil Defence Emergency Management Plan Order 2015 (the National Plan), which is secondary legislation. The National Plan will also need to be amended to include water organisat ions. 169. The current financial arrangements (set by Cabinet) are in Section 33 of the Guide to the National Plan. These arrangements include that, above a threshold, the Crown will partially reimburse local authorities at 60 percent for certain essential infrastruc ture recovery repairs following an emergency (the 60/40 cost -sharing arrangements). 170. 171. For instance, the threshold that needs to be met before eligibility for reimbursement is based on a fixed percentage of the capital value of the area of the local authority. How the threshold is calculated will need to be reconsidered to ensure it is appropriate for both water organisations and local authorities after water infrastructure assets have been transferred, and remains fiscally neutral overall for the Crown. 172. I am seeking agreement that these further policy decisions are delegated to myself, the Minister of Finance, and the Minister for Emergency Management and Recovery.

I am seeking agreement to a set of pricing objectives – building on previous considerations and outcomes noted by Cabinet 45. In the 18 October 2021 paper, Further decisions on the three waters reforms [CAB -21- MIN -0419], a range of pricing outcomes were set out, but not explicitly agreed by Cabinet. From those outcomes I have developed the following objectives to inform our decisions on pricing and charging. 46. My proposed objectives are: 46.1 Economic efficiency : price s reflect the underlying costs of services and support the financial sustainability of water services entities in the long -run. 46.2 Affordability : water is an essential service and people on reticulated networks should have access to water services regardless of their financial circumstances. 46.3 Price stability : the rates of change in prices are not too high and price changes are clearly signalled in advance and smoothed over time. Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page 8 of 41 46.4 Cost -sharing : a key driver of the reforms is to address affordability issues, particularly for customers in smaller communities. Entities could use geographic average pricing to smooth costs across communities, thereby ensuring more affordable services for all. 46.5 Horizontal equity : consumers in similar positions pay similar prices. 46.6 Intergenerational equity : every generation (which can be thought of as being as small as the annual cohort of ratepayers) should be paying its fair share for assets and not requiring future generations to pay substantially more or less than their fair share through either over or under -investment. Historically, funding and water infrastructure investment decisions have tended to favour current over future generations. 46.7 Giving effect to Te Mana o te Wai and respecting Treaty of Waitangi principles : pricing can support Te Mana o te Wai by encouraging efficient usage of water. Pricing c an also engage Article 3 of the Treaty and support equitable water service access and quality of service provision. 46.8 Consistency with other government goals : pricing issues should support, or at least not undermine, government goals in other domains. For example, growth charges can have an impact on housing goals. Water services pricing can influence levels of water use which affects climate change goals including resilience and adaptation. The Government policy statement is an important tool for achieving this objective. 47. The 18 October 2021 paper also referred to vertical equity, whereby consumers with a higher ability to pay (or more assets) pay progressively more than those with less ability to pay. On further consideration, I consider that a means -tested system for generating water bills would be overly complex, expensive to operate and lead to further distortions in pricing. Under the status quo, rating valuations have been used as a proxy for ability to pay but can create inequities as the value of a pro perty is not always well correlated to the wealth or income of the owner. Using means -testing or rating valuations would result in complex price structures that do not always relate well to the actual costs of service provision. 48. For these reasons I prefer affordability, rather than vertical equity, as an objective. I consider the needs of financially distressed consumers in Part B of this paper. Not all the above objectives will be reflected directly in legislation and different policy tools will be used to achieve different objectives.

ICT incident response The Department plays a role in supporting all-of-government responses to cybersecurity and privacy incidents, as well as the COVID-19 pandemic. We will continue to lead responses to all-of-government ICT supplier outages and incidents, provide advice and assurance to Ministers on digital aspects of responses, and assist agencies leading responses by communicating advice and providing support as needed. Local government works collectively to address national objectives At a system level… Our Ue te Hīnātore - Local Government Branch aims to achieve a collaborative systems-wide, public service approach in which central and local government work together for the benefit of people, communities, business and the environment. Central to our system stewardship role are our Partnership Directors. They have strengthened connections with the sector by building direct relationships with local government chief executives and mayors. They also continue to navigate and make pathways for understanding with local government and iwi / Māori. This positive change is critical for the implementation of the Government reform agenda of the Three Waters Reform, Climate Change, the Resource Management Act Reform and the Future for Local Government Review. Future for Local Government Review The Minister of Local Government has established an independent review into the Future for Local Government in response to major reforms under way that will impact the sector. The Review is intended to identify how our system of local democracy and governance needs to evolve to be fit for the future. The Review will run to 30 April 2023. As part of our role as stewards of the local government system, we need to ensure that the reforms afecting local government are integrated and support a coherent system framework, including in its current state and any transition to a future state. This role requires the provision of policy advice to Ministers on the key strategic issues facing the local government sector, building productive partnerships with local government to achieve the Government’s policy objectives for the sector, and collaborating with other central government agencies to ensure their work on local government is consistent. Following the major milestones of the Review the Department will undertake work to consider whether and how to progress the Review’s recommendations. Governance and democracy reform The regulatory framework for local government elections needs reform to ensure there is an enduring system in place. The Department will progress a programme of reform that is informed by the Future for Local Government Review. We anticipate that the Future for Local Government Review may also identify other areas of the local authority governance framework where reform should be prioritised. The Department will also complete the work currently under way to make improvements to the process for establishing Māori wards and constituencies. 37 Department of Internal Affairs NGĀ TAKUNE RAUTAKI STRATEGIC INTENTIONS 2021-2025

I propose we introduce a statutory rates remission process or Māori land under deve lopment. Currently local authorites have considerable discreton over their rate remission policies or Māori land and may not include development remissions in their policies. 41. A statutory remission process will provide owners o Māori land a right to apply or a rat e remission when land is under development, without having to rely on the local authority’s policy. However, the decision about whether a remission is granted, or how long it is granted, and on what conditons it is granted, will remain with the local authority. This will allow local authorites to apply a natonally consistent approach to their decisions, without each council having to develop its own policy or land under development. 42. Providing rate remissions during development will allow scarce capital to be devoted to deve loping land, rather than paying rates. Once development is completed, the remission would cease and the land would be rateable in the same manner as any other land. In the long run this will be benefcial to local authorites as it strengthens both their ratng base and their community. 43. During the development process owners are incurring the costs o development. How ever, the benefts that come rom development, either by occupying the property or housing, or generatng income i the development is or commercial purposes, are unlikely to commence untl development is complete or well advanced. Managing cash fows through the development period is challenging or any land owner and will usually be more so or Māori landowners given the restrictons on mortgaging their propertes to obtain development fnance. 44. This would be in additon to, rather than in place o , the existng remission policies, whi ch potentally cover a wider range o maters than land development. However, in relaton to remissions or development, the statutory obligatons I propose would take precedence over the local authority’s current policies. 45. The power would be an administratve power, provided to the chie executve o each loc al authority.
