Rates arrears are a signifcant disincentve to Māori landowners engaging with and deve loping their land. The presence o large rates arrears on Māori land inhibits constructve relatonships between local authorites, iwi and Māori landowners. 26. Successors to interests in a block o Māori land that is in arrears efectvely inherit the arr ears. In the case o general land, i the owner passes away with debts in excess o their assets, the land would be sold and estate creditors sufer the shortall. In the case o Māori land, because o the constraints on its sale, rates arrears are shared among cur rent and uture owners. This presents an impediment to the next generaton o owners developing their whenua. 27. Local authorites have no statutory authority to write of rates. The LGA02 provides that elected members o a local authority can be held personally liable i the “local authority has intentonally or negligently ailed to en orce the collecton o money it is law ully enttled to receive”. 7The combined efect o these arrangements provides a power ul disincentve or local authorites to write of rates arrears. 28. The consequence is that local authorites tend to allow uncollected rates to acc umulate, with penaltes accruing, untl they are prevented by statute rom commencing collecton acton. Rates are not statute barred rom collecton untl six years afer the last payment date or the various rates instalments or the year. By the tme a rate is statute barred, or every $1,000 originally assessed, with accumulated penaltes the outstanding debt will have grown to $3,452. Since Māori land is over - represented in propertes in arrears, this tends to disproportonately infate the size o the r ates arrears actually incurred on Māori land. 29. Currently the only tool local authorites have to manage arrears are rates remissions. Rem ited rates are shown in the rates records as having been paid by the local authority. Local authorites can be reluctant to remit rates because that can be seen as condoning non-payment. 30. While my main concern is with the efect o rates arrears on the development o Māori land, I can see no reason why this power should be constrained only to Māori land. There may be rare cases where collecton o rates on general land is impractcal. In those cases, writng of rates may be more help ul than allowing rates arrears to accumulate untl they are statute barred rom collecton. 7 Sectons 44 to 46, Local Government Act 2002. IN CONFI ENCE Background Māori and 7. Māori land is governed by TTWM Act. The preamble to that Act includes the statement “it is desirable to recognise that land is a taonga tuku iho o special signifcance to Maori people and, or that reason, to promote the retenton o that land in the hands o its owners, their whanau, and their hapū, and to protect wāhi tapu: and to acilitate the occupaton, development, and utlisaton o that land or the beneft o its owners, their whanau, and their hapū”. 8. TTWM Act places a number o restrictons on the ability o owners to deal with Māori land. The land may not be sold without the approval o the Māori Land Court, which is required to prioritse ownership remaining with people with an ancestral relatonship with the land. This makes it impractcal to mortgage the land and precludes the land being sold on the general land market. 9. Māori land is approximately fve per cent (about 1.4 million hectares) o the New Zea land land area and is predominately concentrated in the mid to upper North Island. Māori land is commonly held by multple owners (some blocks have more than 1,000 owners). There are about 2.7 million interests in 27,212 Māori reehold land blocks. The average Māori land block is 52 hectares with 100 owners. Multple ownership creates additonal costs and challenges in achieving consensus or acton, including collectng unds to pay rates. 10. Māori reehold land tends to be more isolated, in smaller holdings and, less ‘useable’ than general land: 80 per cent o Māori reehold land is classifed as being o lower quality and only 17 per cent o Māori reehold land is considered suitable or arable use. Up to 20 per cent o land is considered landlocked, and about 16,000 (60 per cent) o Māori land ttles are smaller than fve hectares, with approximately 11,000 (40 per cent) being smaller than one hectare. Around a third o the total indigenous vegetaton on private land is on Māori land, with approximately 25 per cent o Māori land having indigenous orest cover. 11. At the same tme there are many examples o Māori land having been developed into succe ss ul arming units or being used or commercial orestry. Notwithstanding, it has been identfed, through detailed whenua block by block analysis, that there is an opportunity to improve the per ormance o Māori land. This could result in estmated benefts o $1.407 billion (present value (PV) $387 million) - $2.064 billion (PV $650 million) over 40 years, increasing livelihoods and wellbeing derived rom this land. 1 12. While much Māori land is in rural setngs, there are signifcant areas o Māori land in some urban communites, especially Tauranga, Rotorua, and Taupō and in many smaller communites. Some o this land has been subdivided into house sites while some remains in large blocks that could, i the owners wished and were able, be substantally developed. In those locatons vacant Māori land has the potental to prov ide homes or its owners. The Whenua Māori programme 13. IN CONFI ENCE Making unused Māori and non-rateab e 31. I propose that Māori land ratng units that are entrely unused and land that is subject toa Ngā Whenua Rāhui kawenata8be made non-rateable. At the tme this occurred, existng arrears on that land would be writen-of. 32. To support the implementaton o this proposal, I propose as a working defniton that unused l and be defned as: Unused land:  includes land that is un ccupied r is used similarly t a reserve r c nservat n area, despite any pers nal visits t the land r any pers nal c llect n f kai r cultural r medicinal material fr m the land; and  excludes land that is leased r that is used f r agricultural, h rtcultural, apicultural, c mmercial f restry, residental, c mmercial, industrial r c mmunity actvity. 33. I expect the fnancial impact o this proposal on local authorites to be low. This type o Māo ri land is the type on which rates collecton is worst. Since the owners derive no economic beneft rom this land, it generates no income to pay rates. 34. Much Māori land is unused. Unused land occurs in diverse situatons, both urban and rura l and varying in size between large propertes covering hundreds o hectares and small house lots. 35. In some cases there is no legal or practcal access to the land. The land may be land locked, or access may be by an un ormed road or by sea with no sa e landing places. In other cases rate arrears are likely to build up as the owners derive no income or beneft rom the land that would enable or just y the payment o rates. A partcular issuew ith Māori land is the ratng treatment o land subject to Ngā Whenua Rāhui kawenata. These covenants cover approximately 1/8th o all Māori land, and require the owners to preserve the land in its natural state. This can provide a range o benefts to Māori landowners and to the public good by preserving indigenous biodiversity and mātauranga Māori on Māori land . 36. While the write-of power proposed above may reduce this problem, its use is stll depe ndent upon the local authority exercising its discreton. Making unused land non- rateable provides a much stronger springboard or enabling owners to develop their land with less ear that rates arrears will be an impediment to that development. 37. Since all propertes, irrespectve o their ratng status, pay water, sewer and re use col lecton rates where they are assessed, making unused urban Māori land non- rateable would stll leave those propertes liable or those rates. The rates arrears on those propertes would be reduced, but not eliminated. 38. I have considered other optons or this aspect o the proposals. We could limit an exe mpton o this nature only to land that has no legal or ormed road access. However, the impediments to access make this land the most difcult land to develop. While this would provide relie to Māori land owners rom being charged rates on land they can obtain no economic beneft rom, it would be the least efectve opton in promotng our goal o encouraging Māori land development. 8 A Ngā Whenua Rāhui kawenata is a covenant between the owners o Māori land and the Crown to manage a block o Māori land to preserve and protect the natural and historic values o the land, or the spiritual and cultural values which Māori associate with the land. This paper seeks Cabinet policy approval to amend the Local Government (Ratng) Act 200 2 (the Ratng Act) to beter enable Māori land owners to develop and use their land, including or housing, and to modernise provisions in the Ratng Act relatng to Māori reehold land (Māori land). Executvesummary 2. The proposals in this paper represent the next step in our programme o whānau deve lopment through whenua. We have previously agreed to invest $56.1 million over our years in a whenua Māori programme to assist owners o Māori land to develop that land. My proposals to address this are to:  provide local authorites with a power to write-of arrears; and  make unused Māori land (including Māori land protected by a Ngā Whenua Rahui kawenata) non-rateable. 5. Authorised or lodgement Hon Nanaia Mahuta Minister o Local Government Mini ta Whanaketanga Māori Page 19 f 21 95fdor4ymq 2020-02-17 11:56:23 Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Appendix A: Financial implications of proposals for local authorities Proposal Implications Writing off arrears. This proposal is an enabling proposal. Local authorities will not be required to write-off rates, but may choose to do so. Therefore , the financial effects will depend upon t he decisions local authorities make. Important ly, The Department of Internal Affairs expects t hat the proposal will be used to write off rates earlier than would otherwise occur, so t hat the proposal will affect the time at which rates are written off, rather t han t he amount of rates written off. Therefore, there would be no loss of income to local authorities. There would also be a cash flow advantage to local authorities, in that an earlier writing-off of rates will result in an earlier recovery of GST input tax which the local authority has paid to the Inland revenue department when t he rates were originally invoiced. Making unused land and land subject to Nga Whenua Rahui kawenata non-rateable. This type of Maori land is the class of Maori land on which rates collection is the poorest. It includes, but is not limited to, landlocked and inaccessible Maori land. Owners are reluctant to pay rates on this land because t hey derive no economic benefits from the land and are likely to perceive themselves as not receiving benefit from council services. It is likely that local authorities do receive a small amount of income from t his land, so there would be a small financial cost to local authorities of making t his land non-rateable. There would also be an administrative cost to local authorities in identifying unused land and adjusting rating records to apply t he new law. In the cases where a Nga Whenua Rahui kawenata applied to part of a rating unit, the local authority would have to contract its valuation service provider to split the value of t he property between the rateable and non-rateable part of t he property. This would be a desktop exercise, so would have a low cost to process (likely less than $200 per affected rating unit). A key objective of the proposed transition provisions for the Bill would be to provide local authorities with sufficient time to use existing staff resources to carry out this work. Rates remissions for land This is an enabling provision. Local authorities will not be required to under development remit rates when development occurs but may choose to do so. Therefore , the financial effects will depend upon the decisions local authorities make. There is a small risk that if a local authority remits rates, and a development does not proceed, the local authority will be unable to recover t he remitted rates. Treating multiple Maori land blocks as one for rating purposes The amount of uniform charges assessed for each rating unit varies from council to council, and can vary within different parts of a council district. Charges in the order of $1,000 per rating unit are common. While the impact on the rates for individual properties is significant, the likely impact of this proposal on local authority incomes is low, because it will take time for owners of Maori land to take advantage of t he opportun ity presented , and many properties are not suited to development. IN CONFI ENCE Supportng the deve opment of housing on Māori and 51. A key objectve o the Whenua Māori Programme is to promote the use o Māori land byi ts owners or housing. Ratng issues are requently identfed as one o the barriers to housing on Māori land. 52. I recommend allowing the practce o apportoning rates on a Māori land ratng unit betw een diferent homes and treatng those apportonments as a single ratng unit or the purposes o the rates rebate scheme. This will put owners o homes on Māori land on a level playing feld with other homeowners when it comes to accessing the rates rebate scheme. 53. Apportonment will make it easier or individual home owners to pay the rates or their home s and or local authorites to collect rates on homes on Māori land. I propose that once rates are apportoned, liability or rates on the home rests only with the home owner. 54. Strict applicaton o the law means that the owners have to make a collectve arr angement among themselves to collect rates rom the various home occupants on the property, pay it over to the local authority, and manage among themselves the issues that arise where some owners are unable or unwilling to contribute their share. There are many Māori land sites with multple homes on them. The extreme case ofcials have identfed is a site with 187 homes on it. Sites with 10 or more homes are not uncommon. Frequently owners o Māori land aspire not only to build individual homes but communites o homes on their land, where the size o the site permits it. 55. The current rules around the defniton o a ratng unit ocus on the individual ttle as ther atng unit. Where multple homes exist on one ttle, legally local authorites should keep them in one rate account. An excepton occurs where an occupaton order has been made under s 328 o TTWM Act. Such an order provides the owner in whose avour the order is made “ exclusive use and occupaton o the whole or any part o that land as a site or a house”. 56. I do not regard reliance on occupaton orders as a conclusive soluton to the admi nistratve problems in ratng multple homes on Māori land. Applicants have to incur costs in making such applicatons and may not be success ul. The Court may only make an order i it is satsfed “that there is a sufcient degree o support or the applicaton among the owners”. With multple owners who may be geographically spread ar and wide, obtaining the necessary owner support or an order may be logistcally impossible. 57. I note that currently there is no obligaton on the Māori Land Court to not y the rel evant territorial authority when an occupaton order is made or changed. I propose a minor amendment to TTWM Act to require the Court to not y the territorial authority o any new or changed occupaton orders so that the territorial authority can ulfl its obligatons under the Ratng Valuatons Act 1998. Including purpose statements 75. I propose that both the LGA02 and the Rating Act be amended to include the purpose statement of TTWM Act as the purpose of their specific provisions relating to Maori land rating. The purpose statement for the TTWM Act states "it is desirable to recognise that land is a taonga tuku iho of special significance to Maori people and, for that reason, to promote the retention of that land in the hands of its owners, their whanau, and their hapu, and to protect wahi tapu: and to facilitate the occupation, development, and utilisation of that land for the benefit of its owners, their whanau, and their hapu." 76. Inclusion of purpose statements in statutes is an important way for Parliament to signal what legislation is intended to achieve. Section 5(1) of the Interpretation Act 1999 states "The meaning of an enactment must be ascertained from its text and in the light of its purpose". Hence purpose statements can assist users and the Courts in determining the meaning of particular statutory provisions. 77. While the absence of purpose statements has not directly contributed to the current problems with the rating legislation , I consider inclusion of purpose statements will encourage users of the legislation to think about the application of the specific provisions relating to Maori land in a constructive manner. 78. I intend, subject to advice from Parliamentary Counsel, that this would be done by adding a further clause to the overall purpose of the Rating Act and to the purpose of local authority revenue and finance policies. IN CONFIDEN CE Proactively released by the Minister for the Community and Voluntary Sector Office of the Minister for the Community and Voluntary Sector Chair Cabinet Legislation Committee Charities Amendment Bill: Approval for Introduction Proposal 1 I am seeking Cabinet’s agreement to introduce the Charities Amendment Bill. The Charities Amendment Bill is intended to be introduced in September 2022 and passed by June 2023. Executive Summary 2 This paper seeks Cabinet’s agreement to introduce the Charities Amendment Bill (the Bill). The Bill summarises a suite of proposed chang es to the Charities Act 2005 (the Act) to modernise the Act and ensure it supports charities to thrive, while ensuring sufficient public transparency. 3 The Bill makes legislative amendments, and includes the provisions to: 3.1 Enable reduced financial reporting requirements for very small charities to mitigate compliance burden; 3.2 Clarify who an officer is and their role, and measures to improve governance; 3.3 Clarify and improve compliance and enforcement under the Act; 3.4 Increase the transparency and fairness of regulatory decision -making by the Chief Executive of the Department of Internal Affairs and the Charities Registration Board 1; and 3.5 Introduce a simpler appeals mechanism by e mpowering the Taxation Review Authority to hear appeals under the Act. 4 Subject to Cabinet’s agreement, I intend to introduce the Bill in September 2022. I expect that the Government will refer the Bill to be scrutinised by the Social Services and Community committee later this year. I expect that the Bill will be passed by June 2023, subject to other Government priorities. 1 Under the Charities Act, regulatory functions are split between two bodies, the independent Charities Registration Board and the Chief Executive of the Department of Internal Affairs . While the Board is responsible for all registration and deregistration decisions, it delegates most decisions to Charities Services (under delegat ion from the Chief Executive under the Act). IN CONFIDENCE Allocation of decision -making powers 22 The Bill will expand the TRA , an existing tribunal, to take on a new function to hear appeals under the Charities Act . This new function requires the allocation of several decision -making powers including confirming, modifying, or reversing the decision of the original decision -maker; exercising powers of the original decision maker; making orders ; regulating its procedures ; conducting hearings ; hearing evidence; awarding costs; and stating cases for the High Court. These powers are consistent with the current powers of the TRA . 23 The Bill provides the Chief Executive of the Department of Internal Affairs with a power to exempt very small charities in tier 4 from meeting the XRB standard for reporting. The power could only be used to exempt charities that are defined by financial thresholds in regulations. The financial thresholds will then be subject to my recommendation as the Minister for the Community and Voluntary Sector. Associated regulations 24 Regulations associated with the TRA may be made to enable the procedures for appeals to an Authority under the Charities Act. These regulations will include notice of claim requirements, filing fees and directions hearing procedures. These regulations will be completed within 12 months of enacting the Bill, to align with the commencement date of the appeals provisi ons. The drafting task of developing these regulations will be small as the policy and drafting on the procedures for appeals has already been completed. 25 Regulations may be created for reducing reporting requirements for very small charities. These regulations w ould include setting maximum financial thresholds that will determine whether a charity qualifies as a very small tier 4 chari ty. These financial thresholds will relate to the total amount of assets, and the total annual operating expenditure, o f any given charitable entity. I currently consider that appropriate thresholds to determine what a very small charity would be total assets of less than $30,000 and total expenditure of less than $10,000. The timing for the development of th ese regulations is largely dependent on the outcome of the XRB’s consultation. If regulations are made to reduce reporting requirements, these will require consultation with the sector. Other instruments 26 The Bill does not include any other instruments. Definition of Minister/department 27 The Bill does not contain or alter a definition of Minister, Department or Chief Executive of a department. IN CONFIDENCE Proactively released by the Minister for the Community and Voluntary Sector 11 Charities currently report to one of four tiers developed by the XRB. The four tiers are based on the charities’ annual expenses or operating expenditure of its previous two financi al years. Each tier has its own standard with more rigorous reporting required from larger charities, while smaller charities can use more simplified reporting. 12 Even the current simplified reporting can be burdensome for the smallest charities , which are often volunteer -run and time poor. To minimise the compliance burden while balancing the benefit of transparent reporting, Cabinet has agreed to provide the ability to exempt very small charities from reporting to the XRB standard. These charities would instead report basic financial information in their annual return [CAB -22-MIN -0021]. 13 The XRB are aware of the compliance burden on small charities and are currently consulting on proposed changes to Tier 3 and 4 not-for-profit reporting . The objective of this work aligns with Cabinet’s agreement to reduce the compliance burde n on small charities. 14 However, findings from the XRB consultation will not be available until after the consultation period, which ends on 30 September 2022. I have therefore included the exemption power in the Bill, in the instance the outcome of the XRB consultation does not align with this policy change. My officials will continue to work with XRB on developments following their consultation. Financial implications 15 Th is paper does not seek new funding . As part of Budget 2022, the Government announced funding to expand the Taxation Review Authority to hear charities appeals and fund the associated legal costs expected with a more accessible appeals body. Budget 2022 funding was also secured to cover fees for the two new Charities Registration Board members, and one FTE to support the enhanced regulatory decision -making processes. IN CONFIDENCE Proactively released by the Minister for the Community and Voluntary Sector Background The Bill will modernise the Charities Act 2005 5 The Charities Act 2005 (the Act) provides a registration, reporting and monitoring system for entities that carry out charitable purposes and therefore have a public benefit. Registering for charitable status brings several benefits, including eligibility for tax exemptions and funding opportunities. 6 The Act is a key piece of legislation for the not- for-profit sector. The charitable sector is diverse, ranging from large iwi organisations, churches and education providers to local providers of social services, toy libraries and sports clubs. Since the Act was introduced in 2005, the sector’s operating environment has changed; including the disestablishment of the Charities Commission in 2012 and changes to the financial reporting requirements for charitable entities in 2015. 7 Cabinet commissioned work to modernise the Act in 2018 to ensure it was fit -for- purpose and suited the needs of the charitable sector [SWC -18-MIN -0058]. 2 The fundamentals of the Act were noted to be sound. In March 2021, Cabinet agreed to a rescoping of the programme to focus primarily on making practical improvements to the Act [SWC -21-MIN -0017]. Policy There are several policy proposals given effect to in the Bill 8 In February 2022, Cabinet agreed to policy proposals (outlined in Table 1 ) to amend the Act to support charities to thrive, while ensuring sufficient public transparency [CAB -22-MIN -0021]. The Bill gives effect to the legislative changes agreed to by Cabinet and is attached as Appendix A . Cabinet also authorised me to make minor and technical changes that align with the policy intent. These are also included in the table below. Table 1: Summary of proposals in the Charities Amendment Bill Proposal objective Proposal detail Reducing financial reporting requirements for small charities to mitigate compliance burden Provide the Chief Executive of the Department of Internal Affairs with a power to exempt very small charities in tier 4 from meeting the External Reporting Board (XRB) standard for financial reporting where the compl iance burden is disproportionate to the level of transparency needed from these charities See clause 19 2 The fundamentals of the Act were noted to be sound. IN CONFIDENCE25.In line with coalition agreements, I propose councils that do not disestablish or rescind a decision to establish Māori wards will have to follow a binding poll process. 26. I consider that there are two key variables for possible polls on Māori wards: 26.1. Timing: Whether the outcome of any polls should apply from the 2025 or 2028 local elections; and 26.2. Prompt: Whether polls should be imposed on councils or occur only if communities effectively petition their councils . 27. I have considered four options to meet the coalition agreements that reflect different combinations of decisions on timing (2025 or 2028 local elections) and prompt (petition or no petition) : • Option 1A: the outcome of polls take effect at the 2025 local elections after a mandatory poll in late 2024; • Option 1B: the outcome of polls take effect at the 2025 local electionsfollowing a petitions process in late 2024 and polls in early 2025; • Option 2A: the outcome of polls take effect at the 2028 local elections after a mandatory poll at the 2025 local elections ; and • Option 2B: the outcome of polls take effect at the 2028 local elections following a petitions process in early 2025 and polls at the 2025 local elections . 28. T hese options and their risks are detailed below. 29. Option 2A is my preference. This option has l ower cost s for councils, as poll s held alongside the 2025 elections will be less expensive than standalone polls. This option also carries less implementation risk, as councils will have more time to implement the poll results and reconfigure their representation arrangements prior to them taking effect . However, this choice means the poll outcome will apply later, from the 2028 elections . 30. A list of the 45 councils that will be affected by these proposals and four councilsthat I consider should not have to hold a poll is attached at Appendix C. Option 1A: the outcome of polls take effect at the 2025 local elections after a mandatory poll in late 2024 31. This option would require councils to hold a poll in late 2024 if the y did not hold one when originally establishing Māori wards since 2020. The result of this poll would be binding and determine if a council has a Māori ward (s) for the 2025 elections. These polls will take councils approximately three months to conduct. 32. Following mandatory polls in late 2024, some councils will need to complete arepresentation review prior to election processes starting in April 2025. This doesnot allow enough time for the standard representation review process . I propose Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE 5 IN CONFIDENCE that, if the poll results mean a representation review is required, councils be allowed to complete a truncated representation review. This shortened representation review process will remove the Local Government Commission’s appeal function. Councils will make the final decisions on their representation arrangements. 33. Remov ing the appeal function carries some risk that councils may fail to comply with legislative provisions, as well as risks of missed opportunities for enhancing effective representation of communities , or of incumbent councillors manipulating representation arrangements. To mitigate the non- compliance aspect, I propose that the Commission be given a legislated role to provide technical guidance to councils going through this shortened representation review process. These councils will also be required to carry out a standard representation review in the next term of local government. 34. A ‘no’ outcome in the polls will have different effects for the two categories of councils : 34.1. Councils that established Māori wards without having held a poll would have a choice to either use their previous representation arrangements from before the establishment of Māori wards ( if viable to us e 2015 or 2018 population figures) or complete the truncated representation review process described above . 34.2. Councils that resolved to establish Māori wards in the 2022– 2025 local government term would be able to keep their current representation arrangements or undertake the truncated representation review process. These councils will also have to complete a truncated representation review if the outcome of the poll is ‘yes’. Option 1B: the outcome of polls take effect at the 2025 local elections following a petitions process in late 2024 and polls in early 2025 35. For the 45 councils that have resolved to establish Māori wards since 2020, without holding a poll, this option would allow electors to petition their council in late 2024 to hold a poll in early 2025. The results of these polls would be reflected at the 2025 local elections. 36. Because of the timeframes of this option, councils would not have time to undertake a representation review and would instead only have time to make a resolution on their representation arrangements. This removes: 36.1. the public submissions process; and 36.2. the Local Government Commission appeals process. 37. Councils would have approximately six weeks to make their final decisions by early April 2025, shortly before election processes begin. 38. This option has significant risk due to the tight timeframes for petitions, polls , and representation arrangement decisions , and there being no community consultation on representation arrangements. Impact analysis Regulatory impact statement s 74. The Department of Internal Affairs Regulatory Impact Analysis panel (the panel) has reviewed the completed RIA in accordance with the quality assurance criteria in the CabGuide and considers that the information and analysis in: • The RIS Changing timelines to enable local elections to be delivered(Appendix A) meets the quality assurance criteria. • The RIS Binding polls on the establishment of Māori wards (Appendix B) partially meets the quality assurance criteria. 75. The panel made the following statement about the information and analysis in theRIS Binding polls on the establishment of Māori wards : 75.1. “The RIA was developed within a very tight, ministerially set, timeframe to deal with the implementation of Government a coalition commitment to undo legislative changes made by the previous government. These factors 9(2)(f)(iv) 9(2)(h) 9(2)(h) Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE 11 IN CONFIDENCE limited the analysis and consultation that could be undertaken and the evidence available. They also required the policy problem and objectives that underlie the commitment to be ‘ backfilled ’. 75.2. While these limitations are acknowledged in the RIA, their consequences could be stated more clearly and explicitly addressed. 75.3. While the panel found the identification of policy objectives related to the stated policy problem, and the development and use of criteria based on those objectives to be useful, there was insufficient analysis of the relative value of Māori wards as a mechanism for meeting effective representation objectives. As a result, the panel did not feel the application of the criteria provided a compelling assessment of the policy commitment against the status quo. 75.4. In relation to the transitional application of the poll provisions to existing Māori ward decisions, the panel did not believe the use of similar criteria was appropriate to assessing process and timing options to achieve the Government’s objective. The panel did not find the Department’s preference for the status quo to be useful in this context and felt more explicit exploration of the relative cost, timing, and process implications of the options considered (for instance, the impact on the integrity of representation reviews) would have enabled a more useful comparison of the relative merits of the other options. 75.5. On this basis, the panel felt that the RIA failed to fully meet the “complete’ and “convincing” criteria prescribed by Cabinet. The context within which the proposals were developed also precluded any meaningful consultation with affected parties. This is acknowledged in the RIA which does include some evidence of stakeholder views from previous consideration of the underlying issues. ” Climate implications of policy assessment 76. The Climate Implications of Policy Assessment (CIPA) team ha s been consulted and confirms that the CIPA requirements do not apply to these proposals as the threshold for significance is not met. Population implications Restoring polls on Māori wards 77. The changes to Māori ward processes specifically affect electors of Māori descent who have chosen, or may choose in the future, to be on the Māori electoral roll. Prior to the 2021 legislation changes, Māori were typically underrepresented in local government compared to their proportion of the general population. Survey data from Local Government New Zealand indicated that after the 2019 local elections approximately 13.5% of local government elected Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE 12 IN CONFIDENCE members (comprising mayors, councillors, local board members and community board members) were Māori, compared to 16.5% of the wider population in the 2018 Census. Following the 2022 local elections , the percentage of elected members who identify as M āori is now estimated at 21.6%. Fixing postal voting timeframes 78. Extending the voting period would particularly benefit rural voters and Māori communities and could raise the rate of voter participation in local elections . Human rights 79. More work needs to be done to determine if the proposals in this paper are consistent with the rights and freedoms affirmed in the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990 and the Human Rights Act 1993. Reinstating polls on the establishment of Māori wards may raise issues of discrimination on the basis of ethnicity. A final determination will be possible when the legislation is drafted. Use of external resources 80. No external resources were used during the development of these proposals . Consultation 81. The following agencies were consulted during the development of these proposals : the Ministry of Justice, the Electoral Commission, Statistics NZ, Land Information New Zealand, officials from the Local Government Commission, Parliamentary Counsel Office, Te Arawhiti , and Te Puni K ōkiri. The Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet (Policy Advisory Group) and the Treasury were informed. Only officials from the Local Government Commission were consulted on Options 1B and 2A in this paper. 82. The Ministry of Justice has raised concerns about the remov al under Option 1A and 1B of the role of the Local Government Commission in hearing appeals in the proposed truncated representation review process . 83. Statistics NZ ha s raised concerns about the ability under Option 1A and Option 1B for councils to roll back to pre- Māori ward representation reviews because of population data accuracy issues and difficulties where statistical boundaries have changed in the meantime. Department of Internal Affairs officials are currently working with St ats NZ officials to see how this risk can be mitigated. 84. Due to the time constraints, consultation with the local government sector has been very limited so far. L ocal Government New Zealand ( LGNZ ), Taituarā, election service providers, and NZ Post (and their business division Datam) have been consulted on the proposed changes to election timeframes and are supportive of these changes . 85. There has been no public consultation and no consultation with iwi and Māori. Legislative timeframes mean this will not be possible before the Bill is introduced. Māori wards provide for dedicated, elected representation for New Zealanders on the Māori electoral roll . 48. Legally privileged – An urgency application has been filed in the Waitangi Tribunal regarding these policies . As part of a broader claim relating to policies in the Coalition Government’s 100 -Day Plan, it asserts that restoring binding polls on Māori wards breaches the Treaty and its principles. The Tribunal is currently considering whether the claim is suitable for an urgent hearing. Fixing postal voting timeframes Background 49. Under the Local Electoral Act 2001 there is a 22.5- day voting period for postal voting in local elections. Under the Local Electoral Regulations 2001, all postal voting papers must be delivered in the first six days of the voting period. Responsibility for meeting this statutory requirement sits with local electoral officers. NZ Post provides almost all the postal services for local elections. 50. NZ Post has struggled to deliver voting papers within the six -day window in recent elections. NZ Post has now informed the Department of Internal Affairs that it will take up to two weeks to complete nationwide delivery of voting papers for local elections for the 2025 and future local elections. This creates a risk that some voters will not have a reasonable opportunity to cast their vote. Proposal: Adjust statutory timeframes of local elections processes 51. I propose extending the voting period so that the delivery period for postal papers can increase from six to 14 calendar days. The statutory date for the close of voting will remain as the second Saturday in October every three years. 52. The extra time will come from shifting a number of statutory timeframes for local elections , including a slightly shortened nomination period and shifting the cut -off date for electors to be included on the printed roll earlier. 53. At the same time as extending the delivery period to enable people to receive their votes, I propose some other small adjustments to statutory dates to address some lingering issues in the local electoral timeframe. This will allow more time to print voting papers, and starting the mailout earlier in the week so any mistakes identified do not have to be fixed over a weekend. These timeframes would also apply to by -elections and polls, where applicable. Further policy decisions may be required 54. The policy proposals above have been developed under time constraints in order to meet the goal of having these changes apply from the 2025 local elections. It is likely that I will need to seek a number of further policy decisions from Cabinet at the same time as seeking approval to introduce this Bill. IN-CONFIDENCE 10 To mitigate the risks around spoofing, D aon’s technology includes 3D facial liveness detection . This is intended to ensure that the face presented is a genuine live and present individual. 5.4. Key stage limitation To reduce the risk of a brute force attempt, limits are in place at each stage of the process . An individual in a session may only make a limited number of attempts to enter correct identity details matching those contained within an identity document , and may only make a limited number of attempts at the passive liveness challenge before they are subject to a 72 hour lock out. The limited number of attempts within the process reduces malicious attempt s to spoof liveness and to learn from previous failed attempts. Any individual who fails to confirm their identity within these session limitations will have to try again later after the lockout period has elapsed , if allowed by the requesting organisation, or use another method such as presenting their physical identity documents in person at a requesting organisation’s offices. 6. Collection 6.1. Notice Prior to the collection of any information within the Identity Check service the individual is provided with the following privacy information. “The Department of Internal Affairs needs your information to confirm your identity. Find out more about how your information will be used in the privacy statement .”. The privacy statement and Terms of Use are displayed on the DIA interface. The privacy statement varies depending on the requesting organisation utilising the Identity Check service. The privacy statement details : • how information provided will be used by DIA. • that information will be shared with and by Waka Kotah i if the individual chooses to verify their identity using their driver licence . • that metadata will be shared with the requesting organisation in all circumstances . • that the passive liveness confirmation , result from the identity document photograph comparison and identity document confirmation will be shared with the requesting organisation with the individual ’s consent. • if appropriate, that the selfie will be shared with the requesting organisation with the individual’s consent. • how to request a copy of information held by DIA. • how the requesting organisation will use information provided by DIA including a link to their privacy statement. The individual is also provided a link to the Terms of Use for the Identity Check service which include s an acknowledgement of the privacy statement. IN-CONFIDENCE 11 6.2. Collection whilst using the service The individual is asked to provide details of their identity document . They select the document they would like to use then provide the following information as contained on the document: • document number • document version number (driver licence only) • name • date of birth . Once it has been confirmed that the information provided is valid and the document meets the validity requirement and is not lost or stolen , the individual is asked to provide access to their device’s camera to take a live photo when prompted. If they do not provide access, then they will not be able to proceed to use the Identity Check service. Prior to the passive liveness check commencing a sample of the ambient light is made . If the light conditions are not sufficient the individual is advised to move to another location. The next stage is a passive liveness check, the individual is provided instructions on how to complete the passive liveness check. When the individual is ready to begin they will push a button to start, and a live photo is collected . A still photograph (selfie) is extracted from one of the frames within the live photo along with a series of other comparison frames. The individual is not able to review the selfie. The selfie and comparison frames are processed by the liveness engine. The selfie is also compare d to the document image held by DIA or Waka Kotahi. If the individual fails the passive liveness check, they can reattempt the passive liveness check a further four times. Therefore, one session may result in multiple sets of comparison frames and selfies being captured. 6.3. Collection of driver licence information from Waka Kotahi If the individual selects to use their New Zealand driver licence for their identification, then DIA will first confirm the provided driver licence information with Waka Kotahi using the Driver Licence Verification Service.

IN-CONFIDENCE 14 8. Accuracy 8.1. Ability to compare accurately The facial recognition algorithm is provided by Dao n and configured by DIA based on recommendations by Daon’s biometric experts. Information related to the accuracy of the algorithm as independently assessed by NIST through their FRVT program is available at https://pages.nist.gov/frvt/html/frvt11.html . The configuration of the system is weighted towards providing a negative comparison result if there is any doubt to ensure robust evidence of identity. The NIST results indicate with a configured threshold to accept 1 in 1 million chance of a false accept, they see a false reject of 1 in every 108 attemp ts. As DIA allow multiples attempts , this would approach closer to 1 in 428,000 chance of a false reject in three attempts. In real world operation m any factors affect the effectiveness of facial recognition systems. Lighting conditions, like variations in light and shadow, can distort facial features and make details less visible. The angle and pose of the face also matter, as non -frontal or obstructe d views can be challenging. Changes in appearance due to age ing, weight fluctuations, and cosmetic alterations can complicate matching. Movement during image capture or in real- time can blur facial images, reducing system effectiveness. Additionally, image quality, resolution, noise, and compression artifacts can hinder accurate extraction and analysis of facial features. Considering these factors is crucial for developing reliable facial recognition technologies. The Identity Check process and thresholds attempt to account for these factors through customer interaction and tuning. DIA has completed testing of the facial recognition algorithm with real users. While the sample size was limited the results reflected those of the NIST testing . 8.2. Passive Liveness detection The passive liveness algorithm is provided by Daon and configured by DIA based on recommendations by Daon’s biometric experts. The effectiveness of the algorithm has independently been reviewed by iBeta. iBeta is nationally accredited as a test lab by the National Voluntary Lab Accreditation Program (NVLAP Testing Lab Code 200962) to the requirements of ISO/IEC 17025:2017 (General requirements for the competence of testing and calibration laboratories). They are an expert in the field of biometrics. The iBeta results showed the systems performed 100% accurately during their testing. DIA has completed testing of the liveness algorithm with real users. W hile the sample size was limited the results reflected those of the iBeta test. 8.3. Human oversight There is currently no ongoing human oversight as part of the photograph comparison process. However, DIA are currently exploring the need to set up a project to review the previous comparisons completed over a period. This work is intended to input into the enhancement roadmap for the product, for example if people wearing glasses are unable to use the service successfully more often instruction may be provided to remove an individual’s glasses before utilising the service. 8.4. Impact of errors on individuals The Identity Check service aims to create a convenient way for individuals to access services online where they wouldn’t otherwise be able to. Disclosure of New Zealand driver licence information to DIA If the individual selects to use their New Zealand driver licence for verification , then Waka Kotahi will confirm the validity of the driver licence information to DIA when requested . The T erms of Use will detail that by using the service to validate against a driver licence , that the individual has provided consent for their driver licence information to be confirmed using the Waka Kotahi Driver Licence Verification Service. Section 200(2) of the L TA authorises the disclosure of driver licence photographs by Waka Kotahi to DIA if it is within the course of a person’s official duties as an employee of DIA to verify the identity of an individual. The driver licence photograph will be disclosed by Waka Kotahi to DIA on request upon the successful confirmation of the licence details . DIA use two APIs to request information about the driver licence automatically. The initial API will be used to confirm the validity of the driver licence details to DIA . When requested from Waka Kotahi, another API will then provide the photograph of the driver related to the requested driver licence. 9.6. Disclosure of information to requesting organisations with consent At the start of the Identity Check process the individual is advised how the service works and what they will need to do. They are asked to provide consent to share the results with the requesting organisation for the purposes of verifying their identity. The individual must make an active step to check the consent box before they are able to proceed. The IICA provides authorisation for disclosing the New Zealand passport information in the form of confirmation of the match . The consent of the individual will be required as the authority to disclose their driver licence information in the form of confirmation of the match . If the individual selects to share their results with the requesting organisation, then DIA provide s to the requesting organisation the following: • the transaction number • confirmation the individual passed the liveness check • confirmation of a successful result from the identity document photograph comparison • the full name • the date of birth • if applicable, the selfie . The fields shared with the requesting organisation are strictly limited to the information fields listed above . At no stage are the details and images held within the passport or driver licence databases released to the requesting organisation . The small number of fields being disclosed links back to the Identity Check service’s purpose, that being providing identity verification for a requesting organisation Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs

Disclosure of metadata When a n individual uses the Identity Check service, details of their actions are captured in the metadata. The full details of the metadata will not be released to the requesting organisation by DIA. However, DIA will provide to the requesting organisation details on a per transaction basis about the time and date and whether during the transaction the individual : • completed the transaction successfully • had an unsupported browser or device • exceeded the timeout period • exceeded the number of possible attempts to complete the liveness check • chose to exit the Identity Check service • did not authorise the sharing • had an unsuccessful Identity Check transaction due to failing the liveness check, identity document photo graph comparison , or identity document data match. The disclosure of this information is not optional if the individual chooses to proceed to use the Identity Check service. The information is disclosed to a requesting organisation to enable the requesting organisation to evaluate how the service is functioning and any pain points that need to be addressed. The information is shared at a transaction level rather than at a summary level. This enable s a requesting organisation to augment the Identity Check information with other information, regarding the individual , to evaluate trends and issues relating to specific groups of individuals e.g., individual s who are purchasing a particular product and are more likely to have an unsupported browser or device. 9.8. Daon , by default , do not have access to any information within Identity Check as the solution is hosted at Datacom within a DIA owned and managed tenancy . The only scenario where Daon may have access to personal information is when a defect occurs and DIA request support. In this scenario the access is limited to copies of logs or other information provided by DIA to Daon to support the resolution of the issue . Information provided to Daon is kept to the absolute minimum required for defect resolution. Daon must keep the information confidential in all other circumstances . The exception to this is where the disclosure is: • required by law • to the courts of any competent jurisdiction • to any government regulatory or financial authority . Prior to making a disclosure Daon must consult with DIA. 9.12. Disclosure s to law enforcement agencies DIA may voluntarily disclose, or be compelled to disclose , personal information in the Identity Check service to law enforcement agencies such as NZ Police or the Serious Fraud Office . Live photos Live photos are only held until the selfie and comparison frames have been created. These are then automatically destroyed. 11.2. Successful verifications If successful verification of identity has occurred , then the selfie(s) , comparison frames and liveness confirmation are held for 31 days within the Daon solution hosted by Datacom New Zealand. The information is retained for this period to enable a requesting organisation to query DIA in the event of an investigation or suspected offence. There is currently no Disposal Authority under the Public Records Act that explicitly details the handling of the Identity Check information by DIA. However, DIA are in in the process of having the Disposal Authority created and this is currently in consultation with the Chief Archivist. 11.3. Unsuccessful verifications If the individual is unable to successfully verify their identity , then the selfie(s) , comparison frames , liveness confirmation and identity document photograph comparison result will not be retained as standard. However, DIA may choose as part of an evaluation period to retain these items for up to 31 days if investigating issues around the performance of the Identity Check service. There is currently no Disposal Authority under the Public Records Act that explicitly details the handling of the Identity Check information by DIA . However, DIA are in in the process of having the Disposal Authority created and this is currently in consultation with the Chief Archivist. 11.4. They are also required to cooperate in the prevention or limitation of the breach. 12.2. Correction of personal information DIA’s existing Privacy Act request process will continue to be utilised for the correction of information. However, due to the nature of the Identity Check service it is unlikely that any requested corrections will be made to the information held within the Identity Check service as it is accurate at the time of collection. The requesting organisation is responsible for the processes where individual’s wish to retake or change their selfie after it has been provided by DIA. IN-CONFIDENCE 4 1. Executive Summary 1.1. Introduction The Identity Check service is provided by DIA Service Delivery and Operation s to provide quick and convenient identity verification. Individuals are directed to the service from other organisations needing to confirm the individual’s identity . Given that people are seeking services it is critical that barriers to access services are reduced. One such barrier for applicants is establishing their identity. The Identity Check service leverages technology to provide remote identity verification, without individuals being required to visit a requesting organisation’s premise s or to have a RealMe Account. The tool uses facial recognition technology and evidence of passive liveness (to prove that the captured live photo is a person and is not, for example , a deep fake ). At the start of the Identity Check process the individual is advised how the service works and what they will need to do. They are asked to provide consent to share the results with the requesting organisation for the purposes of verifying their identity. An individual using the Identity Check service is required to complete two initial steps : • Provision of their identity document information • Completion of a passive liveness check. The identity document details are compared to the information held in the relevant identity document database . Then the liveness check is completed using a series of comparison frames from the live photo captured. A still photograph (selfie) is also automatically extracted from the live photo , and the selfie captured is compared to the photograph held in the relevant identity document database. Currently , supported identity documents are New Zealand passports and New Zealand driver licences. When an individual is using a New Zealand passport as their identity document, the confirmation to the requesting organisation is authorised under the I ICA. When an individual uses a New Zealand driver licence as their identity document, the details are confirmed to DIA with the consent of the individual using Waka Kotahi NZ Transport Agency’s Driver Licence Verification Service. When the identity document details (from either their passport or driver licence ) match the information provided and a successful passive liveness check and photographic comparison has been completed , then the following information is provided to the requesting organisation: • the transaction number • confirmation the individual passed the passive liveness check • confirmation of a successful result from the identity document photograph comparison • the full name • the date of birth • if applicable, the selfie . 1.2. Assuming all planned controls are implemented and functioning effectively , there are no zone one risks and t wo zone two risks . IN-CONFIDENCE 6 2. Project S ummary 2.1. Problem Statement The Identity Check service is provided by DIA Service Delivery and Operation s to provide quick and convenient verification of an individual’s identity . Individual s are directed to the service from other organisations needing to confirm the individual’s identity . Given the individuals using the service are seeking services , it is critical that barriers to access services are reduced. One such barrier for individuals is establishing evidence of identity. If an individual wishes to obtain services from a requesting organisation , the individual may currently be required to visit the requesting organisation in person to confirm their identity through the provision of physical identity documents , prior to being able to obtain services . A key component of organisations being able to take services fully online is the requirement to be able to confirm an individual’s identity online . The purpose of the Identity Check service is to increase the ability for individuals to complete all interactions online. Organisations utilising Identity Check are required as part of their contract with DIA to provide at least one other method for individuals to confirm their identity. Individuals must still be able to confirm their identity in person if the y desire. 2.2. Identity Check Service The Identity Check service is provided by DIA Service Delivery and Operations . Individual s are directed to the service from requesting organisations . This release of the Identity Check service will enable verification that the individual using the device is the same person as the individual whose identity document details were provided . The individual ’s details, passive liveness confirmation and photograph comparison result are sent to the requesting organisation with consent from the individual . Certain requesting organisations will also be provided with the individual’s selfie with their consent , where the requesting organisation has a business purpose for receipt, such as inclusion of the selfie on a physical card being issued. The Identity Check service currently allows verification of an individual’s identity using either a New Zealand passport or New Zealand driver licence . The individual chooses which identity document they wish to use . If a New Zealand passport is used it must be current or less than two years expired , and not be reported lost or stolen. If a New Zealand driver licence is utilised it must be current and not reported lost or stolen. The service is underpinned by a passive liveness and facial recognition solution provided by Daon and hosted in a DIA tenancy at Datacom New Zealand. Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs
IN-CONFIDENCE 7 3. PIA Scope This PIA covers : • confirming the identity of individuals using their New Zealand passport or New Zealand driver licence . • provision of the individual ’s details, passive liveness confirmation , and photograph comparison result to the requesting organisation with the consent of the individual. • provision of the individual’s selfie to the requesting organisation with the consent of the individual . • delivery of the Identity Check service direct to the requesting organisation. This PIA does not cover : • consideration of how the requesting organisation will utilise the individual ’s details and selfie once confirmed by DIA. • the processes used by the requesting organisation for confirming the identity of individual s who do not utilise or are unsuccessful in using the Identity Check service. 4. Applicable Legislation 4.1. Privacy legislation The Identity Check service is primarily intended for use by individuals within New Zealand and the service will be provided by a New Zealand Government agency therefore the New Zealand Privacy Act 2020 will apply. Currently the terms of use prohibit use of Identity Check by individuals outside of New Zealand. Therefore, this limit s exposure to additional overseas privacy legislation. 4.2. Identity Information Confirmation Act 2012 The IICA governs the use of confirmation services. The IICA defines a confirmation service as one which confirms identity information of an individual to : • contribute to the prevention of a crime (particularly identity -related crimes) and • ensure that agencies can use and, if necessary, record confirmed identity related information. Identity information is defined in the IICA as including New Zealand passport related information but not New Zealand driver licence information. The IICA is not a complete code and information that is not covered by it can still be shared, but that sharing needs to be lawful in its own right. Where there is an inconsistency between the IICA and other relevant legislation, including the Privacy Ac t and the Passports Act 1992, the IICA prevails (s21 of the IICA). This means where the IICA applies, it needs to be complied with where it deviates from the requirements of that other legislation . Because the purpose of the Identity Check s ervice is to confirm the identity of the individual for a requesting organisation’s purposes, it falls within the definition of a confirmation service when a New Zealand passport is used for verification purposes . Therefore, where the IICA applies (the sharing of passport details, other personal information and the result of the identity verification) the IICA needs to be complied with. Where other personal information is shared that sits outside the IICA (the driver licenc e confirmation ), sharing needs to be lawful in some other way, for example, by being authorised in accordance with the Privacy Act . Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs
IN-CONFIDENCE 8 4.3. Land Transport Act 1998 The Land Transport Act 1998 (LTA) sets out the responsibilities and general requirements for all individual s in the land transport system and associated agencies such as Waka Kotahi. The LTA includes a requirement that all drivers must be licensed. It also governs the issuance and management of driver licences and the licensing system. The LTA requires that d river licences have a photographic image of the holder (s28(5)) . Whilst there are tight restrictions on the access to d river licence images (s200), the LTA expressly provides for the use of d river licence images for the purpose of verification of a person’s identity by DIA (s200(2) ). Therefore, the LTA directly provides for a service, such as Identity Check , that permits DIA to use driver licence photo graph s to verify the identity of a particular individual when facilitating an identity verification service for other organisatio ns. IN-CONFIDENCE 9 5. Architecture 5.1. High level process The Identity Check service involves an identity verification workflow which includes several key stages : • the individual consents to the results being shared with the requesting organisation. • the individual chooses the type of identity document they would like to use to confirm their identity. • the individual enters their identity document details as contained on their identity document. • the identity document details are either retrieved from the New Zealand passport database or queried with NZTA and confirmed to match those provided. • a live photo is captured of the individual. • a still photograph (selfie) and a series of comparison frames are taken from the live photo and used to complete a passive liveness challenge to provide assurance that the live photo is of a live and present individual . • the selfie is compared to the photograph held in relat ion to the identity document provided . A back -end record stores each attempted Identity Check verification and the outcomes of each stage. If multiple live photos are captured as part of the process , each series of selfies and comparison frames will be stored. The live photo is not stored. Where a successful verification is made the Identity Document Federated ID is stored . 5.2. IN-CONFIDENCE Full Impact Statement Template | 1 Coversheet : Progressing Digital Identity : Establishing a Trust Framework Advising agencies Department of Internal Affairs Decision sought Approval to proceed with the preferred option Proposing Ministers Minister for Government Digital Services Minister of Internal Affairs Summary: Problem and Proposed Approach Problem Definition What problem or opportunity does this proposal seek to address? Why is Government intervention required? New Zealand lacks consistently applied standards and processes for sharing, storing and using personal and organisational information in a digital environment. As a result, systems and services have been developed in an unstructured and inconsis tent manner that creates inefficiencies, increases security and privacy risks and hinders interoperability. This is undermining consumer trust and confidence in digital identity1 services at a time when more and more transactions are taking place online, a nd the ability to share information digitally to assert one’s information is becoming increasingly vital to daily life and a key foundation for the economy. A governance and compliance regime is required to ensure that those who are providing digital ident ity services consistently meet legislation and standards for using, storing and sharing personal and organisational information. This will imbue the ecosystem with consistency and trust, encourage uptake, enable the flow of information, improve user experi ence, reduce identity theft, and position the digital identity ecosystem to realise the significant social and economic benefits digital identity services can provide. Summary of Preferred Option or Conclusion (if no preferred option) How will the agency’s preferred approach work to bring about the desired change? Why is this the preferred option? Why is it feasible? Is the preferred approach likely to be reflected in the Cabinet paper? The preferred government intervention, as outlined in the Cabinet paper, is the implementation of a regulatory framework to ensure minimum standards are consistently applied across the digital identity ecosystem . This intervention would include : •The establishment of a Digital Identity Trust Framework (Trust Frame work) to set the rules (standards, legislation) for those participat ing in New Zealand’s digital identity ecosystem. •The establishment of a governance board to exercise control over the Trust Framework and to update and maintain its rules as required . 1 Digital identity is defined as ‘user -initiated, digitally -enabled sharing of personal and organisational information’. IN-CONFIDENCE Page 1 of 10 Responses to claims made by Castalia Claim Response Investment estimates “WICS’ modelling is entirely based on a top -down, New Zealand -wide assumption that a massive nationwide investment programme is necessary for all council water services. This is despite WDC and all other local authorities submitting detailed bottom -up information about planne d capital investment. ” (page 11) This is incorrect. The WICS modelling takes information councils provided (through the Request for Information process) on asset values , lives and valuations and projects future renewals investment based on industry -standard rates of economic depreciation, making adjustments for differences in input costs (e.g., relative wages and material costs) between New Zealand and the UK. It uses council -supplied populati on growth projections to estimate the future capital costs of providing for growth. In assessing the likely costs of meeting water quality and environmental standards, WICS uses council population density, topography and other geographic variables to model the likely scale of investment required based on what water services providers that operate across the United Kingdom, and which share similar population and geographic characteristics, have made to achieve current levels of compliance with EU standards. The applicability of these standards to New Zealand was reviewed by Beca New Zealand who found that the investment projections from the WICS modelling may well underestimate the necessary investment costs given the pressures of managing and delivering impr ovement and asset renewals backlogs simultaneously, the higher seismic risk profile of New Zealand, and cost pressures associated with climate change and iwi/Māori aspirations that are not quantified in the WICS investment projections. “WICS makes no adju stment for the overlapping nature of growth and replacement investment ” (page 12) The replacement investment represents the cost of replacing the asset base with a modern equivalent of that asset whilst providing the same or higher level of service in the long run. Growth investment to meet new demand will increase the asset base, therefore, increasing (rather than reducing) the future replacement need. WICS has also performed sensitivity analysis through Montecarlo modelling using the investment unconstrained numbers provided by the council in the RFI. The Scotland comparator model has been used to derive one side of the investment range and it displayed the s trongest relationship (R2 of 64% ) between considered variables and made use of bottom -up investment and geographic information . Arguably this model best captures the geography and topography of New Zealand (e.g. central belt with Greater Glasgow & Edinburgh and Lothian as a proxy for the Auckland region, and more northern rural areas as a proxy for the northland areas in New Zealand). This paper seeks Cabinet Legislation Committee approval for the introduction of the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification (Commercial Video on -Demand) Amendment Bill (the Bill). Policy 2. The policy relating to the content of th e Bill was agreed by Cabinet on 2 September 2019 [CAB -19-MIN -0445]. The Bill was given a priority of Category 3 for the 2019 Legislation Programme, and Cabinet has indicated an intention to have it introduced into the House in 2019 [CAB -19-MIN -0445 refers] . The Bill is attached as Appendix A . 3. The purpose of the Bill is to address a regulatory gap where Commercial Video on - Demand (CVoD) content is not currently subject to mandatory classification requirements prior to being made available in New Zealand. 4. The Bill will enable CVoD content to be rated and labelled in the same way that films are already regulated under the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification Act 1993 (the Act) . Regulated CVoD providers will be required to label content by: 4.1 self-rating content using their own systems that have been approved by the Office of Film and Literature Classification (the Classification Office) ; 4.2 self-rating content using the Classification Office’s online tool and resources; or 4.3 submitting content to the F ilm and Video Labelling Body (the Labelling Body) for rating and labelling, with certain content to be referred to the Classification Office for classification where appropriate . 5. Nothing in the Bill will prevent the Chief Censor from ‘calling in’ CVoD cont ent for classification on an as -necessary basis , in accordance with the powers afforded by section 13(3) of the Act. This is consistent with the treatment of all publications in New Zealand. 6. Cabinet also authorised me to take remaining policy decisions necessary to enable final drafting of the Bill. The final Bill provides that only CVoD providers who are specified in a Schedule to the Bill will be subject to the new requirements. This Schedule will be ame ndable by Order in Council upon the recommendation of the Minister of Internal Affairs. The principal consideration for whether a CVoD provider should be specified in the Schedule will be the potential for ‘risk of harm’, as established by assessment again st three criteria prescribed in the Bill.
