We consider that this cannot wait until the broader reform to be address ed, as the broader reform will likely take at least 18 to 24 months to complete and is de pendent on Government priorities. We refined our three objectives for assessing our recommended approach following consultation feedback and further analysis 196. We assess ed the proposed CVoD provider criteria and pro posed labelling exemptions for targeted consultation against the three objectives of fair and appropriate, clear for industry and regulators, and cost -effective (refer to para 166). 197. In light of feedback that w e received from submissions on these objectives, as well as our further analysis of the CVoD definition, we refined our objectives to: a)Proportionate to risk of harm : Our recommended approach should consider where the most benefit to New Zealanders will be from having trusted classifications t o help them make informed viewing choices. It should also consider where the potential for most harm would be from having insufficient consumer information ; b)Clear for industry, regulators and consumers: Our recommended approach needs to be clear on which providers are covered by the new requirements. Providers that are regulated should clearly understand their obligations, classifications should be clear and consistent to benefit consumers; and c)Cost -effectiv e and proport ionate to provider size: Our recommended approach should consider compliance and implementatio n requirements for both providers and regulators (e.g. ease of compliance, regulation and administration). It should not unduly act as a barrier to c ompetition . Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Impact Statement Template | 49 Our recommended approach to clarify the CVoD definition and providers 198. Our findings confirmed the need to have a clear definition for CVoD content and a clear process to identify which providers would be required to label their content. Our recommendations to clarify these two matters are as follows : a)Define CVoD content to focus on video on -demand content that is accessed by users in New Zealand through payment of a fee or as a reward (e.g. as part of a bundle offered by Spark). This will include subscripti on and transaction -based video on -demand services. It will exclude free and advertisement -based video on - demand services , which will be considered as part of the broader review work programme ; and b)Set a Schedule to the Classification Act that will specify which providers of CVoD content are required to label content. Specifying providers in a Schedule provides clarity for all parties 199. We think the best way to make it clear which providers are regulated (and required to label their content) is by listing the m in a Schedule. Amending the Schedule will be done via Order in Council (OIC) with the final decision being made by the Governor -General, upon recommendation from the Minister of Internal Affairs. Amending the Schedule will be done on an as-needed basis a nd the Minister will need to consult the Chief Censor before making recommendation s. 200. There needs to be a basis for determining whether a provider should be added (or removed) from the Schedule. Findings from our targeted consultation hav e helped us shape what we think should be key considerations in this process. The key consideration should be the perceived ‘ risk of harm ’ to consumers due to CVoD content being available without appropriate labels under the Classification Act 201. The main ob jective for this c hange to the Classification Act is to ensure that New Zealand consumers have enough trusted information to make informed viewing choices. This helps mitigate the potential risk of harm to consumers, including children and young people, fr om viewing inappro priate content. 202. We recommend that the principal consideration for whether a provider should be included or excluded in the Schedule should b e the potential ‘risk of harm’ to consumers due to CVoD content not being appropriate ly labelled under the Classif ication Act . 203. To determine this , the Minister should consider the following criteria when amending the Schedule: a)Market presence: refers to a provider’s existing or expected share of th e CVoD market in New Zealand . Existing market presence can be indicate d through a survey asking consumers which CVoD providers they use. Such a survey was commissioned by OFLC during September 2019 (outlined in para 187). Based on the outcomes of this survey, providers could be considered to have a ‘sizeable’ market presence if approximately 10 per cent or more of survey respondents indicated they use that provider’s service. However, this assessment is limited as it is ba sed on a single data point and therefore can be considered indicative only. Other useful sources of data that may be used to consider market presence include providers’ user numbers, and their revenues from providing their services in New Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Impact Statement Template | 50 Zealand. However , this data is highly commercially sensitive and may be difficult to obtain. Evaluating market presence may also include consideration of whether the provider is registered for GST in New Zealand, but this will not be a determining factor as previously pr oposed (refer to para 1 68b). The various ways that existing market presence can be determined, and the limitations involved in each, demonstrate the difficulties in establishing a definitive market presence for each provider currently operating in New Zealand. W e will continue to work with providers on implementation and will seek their views to ascertain th e best met hodology for sizing market presence. However, we do not propose including any specific or fixed thresholds for market presence. This approach will allow flexibility for the Minister to consider several data sources . It will also enable the Minist er to cons ider the market presence criterion alongside the other two criteria outlined below when making a recommendation to amend the Schedule . In addition to considering existing market presence , the m arket presence criterion will also consider a provide r’s expect ed market presence in New Zealand . This will enable the Minister to recommend adding a provider to the Schedule in anticipation of their likely high market impact in New Zealand. It reflects a likelihood that providers tha t have a large market presence overseas will also reach a sizeable presence in New Zealand ; and b)Compliance and commitment to another classification framework in New Zealand: considers whether a provider is using a classification framework that provides consistent and appropriat e information to consumers, as well as the extent and reliability of their commitment to that framework. For example, t his enables the Minister to consider whether a provider is satisfactorily complying under the BSA’s regime , and whether this compliance is evidence of a reliable com mitment to informing consumers about potentially harmful content through providing clear and consistent labelling of that content . This consideration addresses concerns outlined by industry about compliance under two regimes . IN-CONFIDENCE Page 2 of 8 Purpose 1. Following Cabinet decisions in June 2024 [CAB-24-MIN -0228 refers ], this briefing seeks decisions to enable us to prepare drafting instructions for the consumer trust mode l in the Local Government Water Services Bill (Bill 3) . 2. We propose that the legislation should provide for high -level principles, and set out required contents of the trust deed, while the trust deed will contain the detailed operative provisions. The legislati on will ensure that c onsumer trusts operate within the same parameters as other water services providers. The trust deeds will be modelled on the energy trusts approach . This will provide local flexibility in the design of consumer trusts and ensure that minimum requirements are met. 3. We propose t he legislation include s: 3.1 requirements for the contents of a trust deed; 3.2 requirements for the Secretary for Local Government (the Secretary) to approv e a trust deed ; 3.3 provisions that enable Ministerial p owers of assistance and intervention in Part 10 of the Local Government Act 2002 (LGA 02) to apply to consumer trusts (as well as the water organisations they own) ; and 3.4 regulation -making power s if additional rules are needed . Local Water Done Well provides for a consumer trust model of water services ownership 4. Under Local Water Done Well policy setting s, councils may establish consumer trust s to own water organisation s. This may be a complete transfer of water services into a consumer trust, or a mixed owne rship model retaining partial council ownership . 5. A consumer trust will represent the interests of the consumers of the water organisation in which it has an ownership interest. The water organisation must be a company unless an exemption is given . Trustee s will be responsible for : 5.1 Appointing, monitoring, and removing board members ; 5.2 Issuing the statement of expectation for the water organisation (if the trust has a majority ownership share ); and 5.3 Monitoring the organisation’s performance . 6. Once a trust is vested with the trustees, the settlor council/councils will no longer have an interest in a water organisation . The interest will be held by consumers who become the beneficiaries of the trust. A consumer trust with majority ownership of a water organisation will have effective control of water services and assets. 7. The primary accountability mechanism for trustees will be elections by local water consumers , including commercial customers , on the basis of one vote per account . 8. Bill 3 will set out requirements for a consumer trust that will need to be reflected in the trust deed. The requirements are modelled off the approach for energy trusts. In addition to meeting the specific legislative requirements, general trust law will apply. Using this mo del, councils will be able to develop the required trust deed. IN-CONFIDENCE Page 4 of 15 The current regulatory and operational environment for digital identity carries risks for users and government 18. On 5 November 2018, Cabinet considered the paper Developing Options for a New Approach to Digital Identity [DEV -18-MIN -0242, CAB -18-0541], and agreed that the government will continue working with citizens, agencies and the private sector to: • develop options for a new approach to digital identity, including the long -term role of government and the private sector in the provision of digital identity services; and • identify regulatory gaps. 19. Cabinet invited the Minister for Gover nment Digital Services and the Minister of Internal Affairs to report back to Cabinet Economic Development Committee by October 2020 on the outcomes of this work. However, Cabinet also made provision to provide interim papers on significant issues. 20. We have identified three regulatory and operational gaps that obstruct innovation and the development and adoption of digital identity services: • people have limited control over how their information is used and growing concerns that they are unnecessarily expose d to privacy and security risks; • a lack of efficiency and coordination between organisations in the public and private sectors, making user -consented information sharing more difficult and resulting in services that cannot work with each other in a truste d way; and • a lack of governance and structure resulting in inconsistent laws and standards (including statutory limitations on what attributes and data sets can be shared) and their uneven application in both the public and private sectors. 21. Focus group res earch shows Māori have lower levels of trust than other groups over government holding and sharing information about them. Participants in the focus groups attributed this distrust to the misuse and abuse of Māori data, creating biased assumptions of Māori and a narrative not informed by Māori. There is a need to actively promote Māori involvement in digital identity and work through concerns Māori have. 22. Additionally, the inconsistent application of data privacy, identification and security standards can le ad to systematic issues and breaches. This poses risks to both customers and businesses, undermining trust and confidence in the digital identity ecosystem further and slowing adoption. 23. We recommend the immediate creation of a Trust Framework in order to address these gaps, and to ensure secure and trusted access to digital identity services in New Zealand. Comparable jurisdictions (countries such as Australia, Canada and the United Kingdom which do not have single identity registries) are choosing to deve lop trust frameworks to address regulatory gaps similar to ours. An analysis of international initiatives and approaches has informed the Trust Framework recommendations in this paper. 24. Officials have regularly engaged with a working group with members from a wide variety of relevant public and private sector stakeholders (as outlined in the Consultation section) to test , support and inform the analysis and evidence base for regulatory gaps and solutions. The working group are broadly supportive of the imple mentation of a Trust Framework.
IN-CONFIDENCE Page 4 of 8 Trustees should not be directors on the board of the water organisation 17. We propose that consumer trust s should be prohibited from appointing trustees as directors on the board of the water organisation. 18. This would provid e appropriate separat ion of governance and management roles for a water organisation. The prohibition will also prevent the conflicts of interest that would arise if a trustee also holds a water organisation board position. 19. We do not propose extending this prohibition to councillors and mayors given the separation that will exist between a water organisation and councils under the consumer trust model. The prohibition will apply to all owners, so in a mixed ownership model th e prohibition will apply to both councillors and trustees. A council should be unable to interfere in the business of a consumer trust 20. We propose that Bill 3 should expressly provide that settlor councils cannot intervene in the affairs of a trust once it is settled. 21. Under trust law, it is possible for a settlor to design the trust deed in a way that gives them an oversight role. This would allow a council, as settlor of a trust, to define a role for itself in the trust deed, such as the power to appoint a nd remove trustees. We propose a legislative prohibition on the settlor council including any role for itself in the operation of the trust to ensure appropriate separation . Transfer restrictions should apply when a consumer t rust is being wound up 22. The provisions relating to the transfer of assets will apply on the wind up of a trust. Ordinary trust law will apply, subject to any legislative restrictions in Bill 3. 23. We consider that Bill 3 should be clear that the restrictions on transferability of ownership interests will include a requirement that water services and assets must be transferred to another water organisation or to a council upon the wind up of a consumer trust. The Trusts Act 2019 also requires that the trust deed state how the trust p roperty is to be distributed upon wind up. Under both provisions, settlor councils will have to stipulate the distribution restriction. The Secretary for Local Government should approve a trust deed 24. We propose that Secretary must approve the trust deed be fore a consumer trust is settled to ensure that minimum legislative standards are met. 25. We also propose that any amendment to a trust deed must also be approved by the Secretary. Under the Trust s Act 2019, the variation of a trust deed requires the unanimo us consent of beneficiaries or a court decision. Regulation -making powers should be available if they prove necessary 26. We propose that Bill 3 should include regulation -making powers as a back -stop power if any unexpected issues should arise. Consumer trust election rules should be made in the trust deed with backup regulation -making powers 27. The trust deed will provide for trustee elections under our proposed approach . IN-CONFIDENCE Page 5 of 15 Covid -19 has highlighted the importance of digital identity for ensuring access to essential services 25. Physical distancing requirements have made it more difficult for people to access essential public and private sector s ervices (e.g. welfare payments, doctor visits), whilst placing strain on agency resources. As a result, digital capability is becoming a greater priority for public and private sector entities. Examples of how digital identity services can help the Covid -19 recovery include: • supporting a mobile and transitionary workforce by making it easier for workers (e.g. returning health care professionals) to prove their qualifications and eligibility to work; • making it easier for people that rely on government servic es to prove their eligibility through secure sharing of personal information (e.g. name, date of birth, Inland Revenue number, bank account, residency status); • providing digital alternatives to requirements that identity documents be certified in person b y an approved practitioner (e.g. establishing a business relationship with a customer under the Anti -Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009 or for conveyancing property under the Land Transfer Act 2017); and • facilitating the develo pment and maturation of open banking services. 26. There is an opportunity to combine innovation in the public and private sectors with the public sector’s information and resources to provide trusted, integrated, people -centred digital services. Covid -19 has accelerated demand for and innovation in the private market for digital identity services. The absence of an agreed set of rules to assure the trustworthiness of digital identity services is a key barrier. A Trust Framework will establish a regulatory fram ework to provide this assurance. Establishment of the Trust Framework A trust framework is a regulatory framework that will set out rules for the delivery of digital identity services 27. The Trust Framework would consist of five component parts where it: • defines the roles of participants involved in providing digital identity services, such as information providers (e.g. passports, utility companies ) and relying parties (services that rel y on the asserted information, such as liquor stores relying on a date of birth), so that it is clear which entities should be accredited ; • sets out rules that accredited participants must follow, with a focus on identification, privacy and security requir ements that are based on laws and standards that are either existing or in development ; • establishes a body to accredit the participants that have demonstrated they can adhere to the rules of the Trust Framework ;4 • makes the rules of the Trust Framework legally enforceable upon all accredited participants, who will be audited to ensure the rules are complied with ; and

There is potential for agglomeration efficiencies and for networks to achieve some scale benefits based on prox imity alone. This means that the “asset optimisation” (that is, the ability to consolidate water networks between towns ) is likely to be much lower p.19 Castalia’s analysis does not take into account Scotland’s rural and island communities. IN-CONFIDENCE Page 7 of 10 Claim Response Economies of scale are not available in water services from amalgamations at the level WICS claims WICS claims that the 50 percent capex efficiency gain emerges when water entities achieve a population of 800,000 or more. It also claims that entities servi ng a minimum population of 59,000 increase capex efficiency as they approach the 800,000 population number. This claim has no basis in the economic literature. INTERNET & WEBSITE FILTER
INTRODUCTION The global COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted an opportunity for improved practices for tracing close contacts of known or probable cases of the virus in New Zealand. Our proposed solution is a Bluetooth Low Energy card (CovidCard) that detects and logs other cards within a close (~10m) radius of itself. The efficacy of the cards for recording close contacts was tested using “closed” validation trials where the cards were worn by participants who then acted a role in a directed scene, or were closely monitored in a closed environment. This report summarises all of the trials, the methodology used to evaluate the CovidCard performance, and presents results of the cards’ ability to record close contacts.

Identity Check is a quick and secure online identity validation tool. Consent is provided, passport or driver licence details added, and a photo provided to confirm identity. No personal data are shared with third parties. Instead, government records are checked to ensure a match to the data provided. Results show a 94 percent success rate.
Identity Check is a safe and secure online identity verification service, developed by Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs.
Identity Check is a secure online identity verification service that enables you to use photo ID you already have, safely and securely online. Identity Check confirms the identity information provided by a user online against New Zealand Passport or Driver Licence official records.
Identity Check protects the private information of its users in several ways.
Identity Check service helps New Zealanders by providing easier, more secure ways of accessing services
Identity Check uses facial recognition, a type of biometric technology. While biometric technology offers security and efficiency benefits, concerns have been raised around fairness or bias in the system. In response to these concerns, DIA commissioned the Identity Check bias evaluation in 2024.
Identity Check was developed to make it easier for people to safely verify their identity online, often a first step in accessing a service.
Identity Check works by confirming the identity information provided by a user online against the New Zealand Passport or Driver Licence databases.

Identity theft - What is identity theft?
Identity theft can damage your personal and financial reputation. This can have serious impact on your life, if you can no longer prove who you are and what is yours.
Identity theft is when someone uses your personal information to pretend to be you. This could be done to commit identity crimes such as taking out loans or accumulating speeding tickets, avoiding arrest or court orders by appearing to be a different person. It could also involve maliciously impersonating you, perhaps to make it appear that you believe or think something controversial.

The Inquiry heard and observed that, as elected leaders, mayors felt the pressure and weight of responsibility in the lead up to and during an emergency. There was, however, inconsistent understanding about their role and governance responsibilities once a state of emergency had been declared. We heard that controllers who did not have senior management experience were less aware of the governance roles of elected officials. We also heard that local and group controller responsibilities and accountability lines are ambiguous, convoluted, and not clearly understood. Mayors 104. Local authority mayors and chairs (or a delegated elected official) serve on the regional CDEM Group and are responsible for declaring a state of local emergency. During an emergency response they retain their usual governance responsibilities and accountability to communities. However, during an emergency there is variation in what the mayors’ governance function looks like in practice. This lack of shared understanding left some mayors feeling disempowered or superfluous. The governance role of mayors and chairs, as outlined in NEMA guidance, should be strengthened, and clarified in legislation. “Presently the Chair and Mayors are the governance on the CDEM Joint Committee and are responsible for all decisions, yet once a State of Emergency has been declared we effectively become redundant! All decisions are then made by the Group Controller or his offsider. So surely there must be a way to retain the governance, for checks and balances?” —Mayor of Wairoa, Craig Little 105. Mayors need to be clear on the specifics of their local governance roles and how to best serve their communities during an emergency. This includes how they work with, and are supported by, the controller and other key roles, including the Public Information Management function. 106. Mayors are a known name and face in their communities and can provide a high level of trusted reassurance during an emergency. People look to their mayor or regional council chair for information and leadership. They need to be visible and provide good quality, timely, accurate communication to their communities and media, and respond proactively to mis- or disinformation. 107. Some mayors leaned into this leadership role during the severe weather events. They offered strategic communications, leveraged community contact networks, updated their local communities and wider audiences on what was happening, gathered intelligence on local needs and situational development from their local communities, and shared information with the controller to inform tasking decisions. However, the approach of mayors was not consistent across regions, and they received differing levels of support from the Public Information Management function. Ame ndments to the Classification Act will be required to give effect to proposed legislative changes. It is intended that the changes will be in effect by July 2020, with the Bill being passed into legislation by early 2020. This is however largely dependent on the House programme and priorities. 234. We acknowledge that it would be ideal to give OFLC , the Labelling B ody and regulated bodies (CVoD providers) enough time to ensure their systems are updated to comply with new system requirements. 235. OFLC and the Label ling Body will be responsible for ongoing operation of the new arrangements. The DIA will continue to play an enforcement role under the Act and will work with OFLC to ensure a smooth implementation of new arrangements. 6.2 What are the implementation ris ks? 236. We note that the ease of implementing this option depends on a few factors like the readiness of the self -classification tool and how quickly CVoD providers can update their systems to the standard requirements. This was highlighted by submissions stating the need for providers to be given enough time to update t heir systems, should this option be progressed. Given this is a Ministerial priority with relatively short timeframes, officials would continue to work closely with OFLC and providers to ensure the tool is fit for purpose, and that providers are given enou gh information to prepare for when requirements come into effect. 237. The underlying assumption is that content providers will be willing and able to implement the required self -classification int o their systems and processes. Overseas based providers do hav e the option of pulling out of our market entirely if they are not satisfied with their legislative obligations. We do not believe this to be particularly likely but has been considered as a ris k. 238. Risks will be mitigated through continuous and proactive communication with OFLC and providers. Ensuring everybody is informed will allow issues with implementation to be dealt with early and proactively.

Impact and options for implementation of Three Water transfer arrangements for Council Controlled Organisations that provide water related services
Impact of block tariffs on vulnerable consumers 68. Water services entities may consider the use of block tariffs or low usage charges to try and improve affordability of water. For example, under a block tariff, the first 10 cubic metres of water is priced relatively low, but then the next 10 cubic metres is charged at a higher price. 69. This type of pricing structure rewards all households with low consumption patterns with low prices, but this means that higher consumption households end up paying much more regardless of their ability to pay. 70. However, vulnerable households are sometimes large and possibly overcrowded. This means they sometimes consume more water, even if the amount per person is relatively low. A block tariff in a large household could lead to undesirable rationing behaviour and have a negative impact on people with specific medical conditions who require large quantities of water. Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page 12 of 41 71. Decisions around the use of block tariffs or low usage charges will be made by each water services entity as part of its funding and pricing plan. However, due to the significant impact these pricing structures can have on vulnerable households, I recommen d creating a regulation -making power that would enable the Government to limit or prohibit or limit the use of low usage or block tariffs for residential customers, if it were necessary. I propose that these regulation- making powers only come into effect from 1 July 2027 to avoid disruption in the initial stages of the reform.
Impact of volumetric pricing on vulnerable consumers 61. As part of setting pricing and charging plans, water services entities may consider using volumetric charges for a portion of the overall charge residential consumers pay. With volumetric (or variable) pricing, consumers pay based on the volume of water they use. Volumetric pricing is one means water services entities could use to give effect to Te Mana of te Wai as it incentivises more efficient use of water and water conservation. More than half of households already pay some form of volumetric charge. Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page 11 of 41 62. The use of volumetric charges can have negative impacts on vulnerable consumers. Preliminary data (from Watercare) suggests that the biggest predictor of household water usage is the number of occupants in the household. Larger households also generally tend to have lower incomes. In addition when water costs are collected through volumetric charges, the cost is typically passed on to tenants who are much more likely to be in financial hardship. 63. A very high proportion of volumetric charges is not necessarily required in order to achieve efficiency gains, because there are substantial fixed costs in supplying drinking water. 64. As an example, Kāpiti Coast District Council introduced a combination of water meters and recovering about 45 percent of its drinking water costs from volumetric charges to achieve a reduction in water usage of about 25 percent. Tauranga City Council achieved similar levels of water savings to Kāpiti but has a tariff structure t hat recovers more than 90 percent of its drinking water costs from volumetric charges. At the other extreme, Christchurch City Council introduced water meters but no volumetric charges and has seen relatively little improvement in water conservation. It is now planning to introduce a volumetric charge for households with high water usage patterns. 65. Decisions around the use of volumetric pricing will be made by each water services entity as part of their funding and pricing plan, taking into account the pricing principles and consultation with their community. It is possible some entities may set a high ratio of volumetric pricing but balance the impact of this on vulnerable consumers in other ways. 66. Given the significant impact volumetric pricing can have on low income households, I recommend there should be the ability to limit, through regulation, th e ratio between fixed and volumetric water revenues. This would enable the Government to put a cap on the total amount recovered through volumetric charges for residential customers if this were considered necessary in order to protect vulnerable consumers . 67. As a point of clarification, this regulation would not limit the volumetric charges on the bill for any individual consumer. There would be no cap on their volumetric charges. The restriction only refers to the proportion of total charges recovered by the water services entity, which is an average across all residential consumers.
Impact on sports funding 102. The impact on funding for sports should also be acknowledged. The loss of the Point of Consumption Charge (approximately $2.1m per annum to sports organisations) will see a fall in revenue for National Sporting Organisations (NSOs). It is anticipated that the monopoly will, however, see an uplift for sports but this is not guaranteed. 103. In addition, the monopoly will also likely cause a decrease in the revenue received by NSOs and racing codes from BIUC charges for the use of their racing and sports information from offshore providers. If New Zealanders are unable to bet with offshore provider s, it can be expected the value of BIUC agreements with NSOs and racing codes will drop . We are unaware of what this decrease in value may be, however the degree of this decrease for any NSO will likely depend on the proportion of New Zealanders who bet with that offshore provider, as opposed to overseas bettors on any given sport or racing type. 104. Despite this impact , the racing codes (who collected $22.8 million the 2022 financial year from BIUC agreements via TAB NZ acting as an agent for them) support the monopoly proposal. However, the financial impact on NSOs is uncertain and likely to depend on the individual sports . Stakeholder Views/Public Consultation /Public consultation 105. This specific option has never been consulted with the public and stakeholders. Ideally, consultation would be undertaken . However, due to the constraints and limitations listed earlier, there is no opportunity for this to occur. 106. However, the issue of regulation of online gambling and sports and racing betting has been actively discussed for some years and the previous Government announced in May 2023 in agreed in principle to TAB NZ having an online monopoly, subject to further work being undertaken. From this , we anticipate there are likely to be a range of views on the options. For example, offshore operators are likely to favour a regulated online gambling market they can legitimately enter and participate in , and oppose TAB NZ being given an online sports and racing betting monopoly, and/or a raised POCC rate.

Implementation Two aspects of the strategy implementation are worth noting: the extensive use of pilots to test new service and design models, and a joint work programme with DIA to address areas of mutual interest related to gambling harm. Extensive use of pilots The Ministry intends to follow an open process to develop, pilot, evaluate and implement the proposals in the strategy. In response to significant interest from stakeholders, the Ministry will hold a series of workshops to determine the size, location and characteristics of the pilots, before inviting specific proposals through a procurement process. Requests for proposals would set out more detailed funding proposals. Historically, the Ministry has offered this form of funding through a competitive tender, such as those for the research innovation rounds held under previous strategies. However, the Ministry wish es to test the opportunity for greater collaboration on some pilots, to make more effective use of resources. Pilots may include both public health and intervention components, and the Ministry will evaluate all pilots to inform future service provision. Joint work programme with the Department of Internal Affairs The proposed strategy involves areas in which DIA and the Ministry have mutual responsibilities or interests: for example, areas in which the policy or regulatory settings are outside the direct control of the Ministry , or where the Ministry ’s work requires input from DIA, which administers the Act and the broader regulatory and policy framework. One example is work that looks at the potential to trial and evaluate an enhanced MVE database that supports facial recognition and other administration service improvement for excludees and affected others. The Ministry would work through the details of such a project with DIA and industry, and potentially other affected stakeholders, to ensure the design was robust and likely to be effective. To provide visibility for this type of work, the two departments are establishing a joint work programme covering the priority areas. In 1907 the Colonial Secretary's Office was renamed the Department of Internal Affairs when New Zealand became a Dominion. By now it was acknowledged to be the appropriate home for new government functions which were not substantial enough to justify a separate administrative structure and did not fit conveniently into another agency. This role has continued to the present day, as new tasks have been taken on and long-established ones have been transferred elsewhere.

In collaboration with DIA, the Ministry aims to identify and use opportunities for diverse perspectives to clarify what gambling harm minimisation means for different parts of the health sector and to work with the health sector to implement the strategy through the future service plan. The proposed service plan provides more detail about the Ministry ’s response to the recommendations identified in the Sapere needs assessment. 2.7 Outcomes monitoring The Ministry has reviewed progress towards gambling harm reduction outcomes to assess what has been achieved over time in gambling harm minimisation. This review complemented the needs assessment discussed above and provides information about the nature of gambling harm in New Zealand and changes over time. Research shows that while the proportion of the population at risk of gambling harm, as measured by the PGSI is at the lowest levels seen for 25 years, the level of harm in the overall population has remained relatively stable for the last five to seven years (at about 5%) (Abbott et al 2018; Thimasarn-Anwar et al 2017). This plateau effect has also been observed overseas (Abbott 2017 ). Similarly, the number of people presenting for gambling support and treatment has not increased in line with population growth. Yet this figure represents only a small fraction of the estimated numbers affected by gambling harm. In fact, the overall number of ‘at risk ’ gamblers in the population has increased in line with population growth. Importantly, while inequalities between population groups by age, social deprivation, gender and ethnicity have reduced in absolute terms, in relative terms, disparities in exposure to gambling and experience of gambling-related harm persist and have been relatively static over the past five years. A refocusing and revitalisation of activities is warranted The outcomes review and the needs assessment together suggest that, while there has been some success in reducing gambling harm since the first strategy in 2005, in the past few years, the number of people affected by gambling harm has been growing. We need to refocus and revitalise gambling harm responses in the service plans if we are to make further gains in reducing gambling harm and health inequalities and inequity in the experience of gambling harm by a range of population groups , particularly Māori and Pacific peoples . Economies of scale are n ot available in water services from amalgamations at the level WICS claims Castalia has previously advised DIA, LGNZ and the Joint Steering Commi ttee that the economies of scale claimed in WICS’ 2020 slidedecks from administrative amalgamations were Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs CONFIDENTIAL 20 Castalia implau sible . In New Zealand, only minor economies of scale are achievable through institutional reform , and these will be mostly in management and proc urement (not infrastructure capex). 13F13F13F14 Castalia showed that economies of scale are unlikely to be availa ble in New Zealand on the basis of the evidence presented by WICS, Frontier Economics and in the economic literature relied on by the government . The findings in Castalia’s 2020 Economies of Scale report ha ve not been rebutted . WICS claims that the 50 perc ent capex efficiency gain emerges when water entities achieve a population of 800,000 or more. It also claims that entities serving a minimum population of 59,000 increase capex efficiency as they approach the 800,000 population number. This claim has no b asis in the economic literature. In fact, the literature that looks at the specific question of whether economies of scale are available from administrative amalgamations find that there are none except in highly specific circumstances, not present in New Zealand . Economies of scale estimate is based on non- credible evidence When preparing the 2020 Economies of Scale report, Casta lia reviewed the WICS 2020 slidedecks . Access to the underlying models and assumptions was refused . In the 2020 Economies of Sca le report , we were advised 14F14F14F15 that the economies of scale assumption was based on England, Wales and Scotland observations. However, we now know that the supporting evidence for the 53 percent capex efficiency is a single Scottish observation from 2002-2021. 15F15F15F16 WICS economies o f scale claims are rejected by peer reviewers FarrierSwier FarrierSwier peer -reviewed WICS’ approach and had access to the underlying models . It found that “WICS analysis cannot be used to definitively conclude that amal gamation in and of itself will lead to material efficiency gains in New Zealand” . 16F16F16F17 Its review did not assess whether the outputs from the WICS analysis are reasonable or free from error. 17F17F17F18 FarrierSwier also state “significant care should b e taken when relying on the capital efficiency gaps estimated by WICS. This is particularly important , given the significant step up in investment forecast for the 30 -year period and the role that the capex efficiency assumption plays when estimating benef its from amalgamation and as sociated reform.” Like Castalia, FarrierSwier express concern with the sensitivity analysis approach. Diseconomies of scale not considered Diseconomies of scale can emerge from administrative amalgamations in water services. This was not considered in WIC S’ modelling. A big question should always be ‘how does the public view this’ . Dan Corry Chief Executive, New Philanthropy Capital (former Senior Advisor to the UK Prime Minister, 2007–10) In the end, regulatory outcomes have to be something the public accept as fair. If you don’t have that, whatever nice theories you have, the system collapses. A big question should always be ‘how does the public view this?’ Dan Corry Chief Executive, New Philanthropy Capital (former Senior Advisor to the UK Prime Minister, 2007–10) Strategic context RSG – and other regulators – are operating in an environment where change is the ‘new normal’ and can occur rapidly and unexpectedly. COVID -19 has prompted governments and businesses alike to reflect on how agile and adaptable they are, whether their digital platforms and services are fit for purpose, and how well they are operating in an increasingly global context. Challenges facing regulators include disruptive trends relating to the speed and scale at which technology innovations can effect change across whole sectors, the degree to which people’s views have become more polarised – informed by social media – and power imbalances caused when industry expertise exceeds that of the regulator. In New Zealand, health and economic outcomes are being viewed as interrelated and there is a growing concern about harms to communities – and the disproportionate effects of these on some communities in particular. In this regard, there is an increasing and strongly felt desire for regulators to address inequitable outcomes for hapū, iwi and Māori. There has been a significant maturing of regulatory practice and professionalism in recent years, resulting in a much greater understanding of the need for many regulators to have and maintain a ‘social licence’ , to be able to anticipate and respond to industry changes (which affect their ability to regulate effectively) and to be able to show that they are making a measurable difference. For some this is easier than others. Concepts of regulatory stewardship – what adopting a whole-of-system, lifecycle view of regulation, and taking a proactive, collaborative approach, to the monitoring and care of the regulatory system(s) within which they have policy or operational responsibilities means for specific systems and regulators is increasingly well defined and understood. One size does not fit all. Related to this, many regulators are challenging the traditional siloed ways of working and are looking for partners or collaborators with whom they can identify new and more innovative interventions using different tools and approaches. 9

Increasing the total number of clinically relevant close contacts identified The full extent to which contacts are missed by manual contact tracing efforts is not well understood. In New Zealand, the current manual contact tracing system has been able to track up to 50% of self-reported known close contacts within 7 days, with the target of reaching 80% of self-reported known close contacts within 4 days. ​Modeling efforts assume a high percentage of close contacts will be traced (also referred to as tracing fraction), ranging from 75% (Ferretti 2020) to 95-100% (Kucharski 2020 and Hinch 2020), while others (Vaithianathan 2020) illustrate the impact of a range of percentages of contacts traced (25-100%). Importantly, there is a difference between assumed tracing fractions (percentage of all close contacts, known or unknown, traced) and realized tracing fractions (percentage of self-reported known close contacts ultimately traced).

Inequalities and inequity in health Some people experience differences in health that are not only avoidable but also unfair and unjust. Equity recognises that people with different levels of advantage require different approaches and resources to get equitable health outcomes. We usually refer to differences in health experience occurring between population groups as ‘health inequalities ’. A ‘health inequity ’ is an inequality that we can attribute to social, cultural and economic factors, rather than biomedical ones. Inequalities and inequity in health occur between groups because of a range of well-recognised socioeconomic, cultural and biological factors. The most common factors are sex, age, social deprivation, ethnicity and education. Similarly, the components of the service plan for the next three years focus on each service area (public health, intervention services, and research and evaluation) to support the plan ’s key actions and priorities. Interim Government Response to Social Services and Community Committee report Petition 2017/91 of Jenn Hooper: Develop Changing Places facilities
Interim Government Response to the Report of the Social Services and Community Committee on Petition 2017/91 of Jenn Hooper Proposal 1. The paper seeks approval for the attached interim Government response to the Social Services and Community Committee’s report on Petition 2017/91 of Jenn Hooper. 2. It also seeks Cabinet’s agreement for the Department of Internal Affairs to consult with Local Government New Zealand and the Society of Local Government Managers on the recommendations of the Committee, before a final response is lodged with the Cabinet Office. Background 3. Petition 2017/91 of Jenn Hooper was referred to the Committee on 12 April 2018. The petition requested, “That the House of Representatives encourage the Government to support the development of a nationwide network of Changing Places facilities.” 4. Changing Places facilities are high-specification bathrooms designed and built to cater to the needs of people with significant physical impairments. Features include mechanical hoists and adult-sized changing tables, and more space around items such as toilets and sinks, as well as wide doors. In partnership with Hamilton City Council and sponsors, in early 2019 Ms Hooper oversaw the construction of the first changing places facility in New Zealand at Hamilton Gardens. A second changing place bathroom has just been completed at Westfield Mall in Newmarket, Auckland. 5. On 7 August 2019 the Committee heard from the Department of Internal Affairs (the Department), the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE), the Ministry of Health (MoH) and the Office for Disability Issues (ODI). 6. In their oral submission to the Committee, MoH recognised that initiatives such as Changing Places bathrooms provide clear benefits to the disability community. They supported the intent of the petition, but do not have any responsibility for regulation, funding or delivery of public toilets. ODI supported this comment. MBIE noted that they provide written guidelines for minimum performance building standards. The Department in its oral submission noted that local authorities in New Zealand provide public toilets under section 125 of the Local Government Act 2002. The Department administers the governance framework under which local authorities operate. On this basis, the Department considered that the local government sector itself, through Local Government New Zealand, would be best placed to oversee the development of a network of fully accessible bathrooms if agreed. Proactively released by the Minister for Local Government IN CONFIDENCE IN CONFIDENCE Page 2 of 4 Committee report and recommendations 7. The Committee presented its report to the House on 4 June 2020. The Committee made three recommendations, which support the substance of the Petition. The Committee recommended the Government:  develop a nationwide network of bathroom facilities for those with extensive and complex disabilities that is based on the population density of towns and cities;  make available capital funding to support smaller local councils to develop fully accessible bathroom facilities and purchase the required equipment; and  require the Ministry of Health and all District Health Boards to review and make changes to policies that result in some outpatients or visitors with extensive and complex disabilities being changed on the floor of standard accessible toilets. The delay of the dissolution of Parliament means a response is due earlier than anticipated 8. Standing Order 252 requires the Government response to be tabled within 60 working days of the Committee report. 9. The House was due to be dissolved on 12 August for the 2020 election, providing for a response back to the Committee 15 days after Parliament resumed, in approximately early November. The extension of Parliament has meant the response will be instead due on 27 August. The Government is focussed on the COVID response, and consequently, a substantive cross-portfolio response cannot be achieved within the remaining timeframe. 10. To meet standing order requirements, I therefore recommend Cabinet agree to the interim response attached as Appendix A . 11. A substantive response responding to the three recommendations will be made in 2021. Financial implications 12. There are no immediate financial implications from tabling the interim Government response. I will address any financial implications when I report back to you with the final response. Legislative implications 13. There are no legislative implications arising directly from the interim Government response. However, once further work on the Committee’s recommendations is undertaken, legislative change may be proposed. Again, I will report back to you on this in the final response. Population Implications 14. There are no immediate population implications arising from the interim Government response. I will address any implications when I report back to you with the final response. Proactively released by the Minister for Local Government IN CONFIDENCE IN CONFIDENCE Page 3 of 4 Human Rights 15. There are no immediate human rights implications arising from the interim Government response. I will address any implications when I report back to you with the final response. Disability perspective 16. Physical and mental wellbeing is one of the top five priorities for Budget 2020. The Petition of Jenn Hooper fits within the wellbeing priorities. There are no immediate disability implications arising directly from the interim Government response. I will address the disability perspective more when I report back to you with the final response. Consultation 17. The Department of Internal Affairs has consulted with the following agencies in developing the interim Government response: Ministry of Health, the Office for Disability Issues and the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment. 18. The Department considers that input from representatives from the local government sector will be necessary to provide a comprehensive response to the Committee’s first recommendation. I therefore seek your agreement for the Department to consult with Local Government New Zealand and the Society of Local Government Managers in developing the Government response. Communications and proactive release 19. As this is an interim Government response I do not intend to issue a media release. These will be developed in conjunction with the final response. Recommendations The Minister of Local Government recommends that the Committee: 1. note on 4 June 2020 the Social Services and Community Committee released its report Petition of Jenn Hooper: Develop Changing Places facilities ; 2. note that under Standing Order 252 the delay of the dissolution of Parliament means that Government response to the report is due earlier than originally expected, and must be presented to the House by 27 August 2020; 3. agree that an interim Government response be provided now which notes that a substantive response will be provided in 2021; 4. approve the interim Government response, attached as Appendix A , which gives effect to recommendation 3 above; and 5. authorise the Department of Internal Affairs to consult with Local Government New Zealand and the Society of Local Government Managers in the preparation of the substantive response, as required.

International studies have suggested that the potential benefit of enabling trusted digital identity in a mature economy is between 0.5% and 3% of GD P equivalent. The Department anticipates that the approximate value of digital identity to the New Zealand economy is u p to $1.5 billion NZD of GDP equivalent per annum. Interpreting the annual/quarterly data
Intervention In the 2017/18 year, over 5,400 people sought help from Ministry-funded services, for problems due to their own or someone else ’s gambling. Most of these people were in crisis. If brief interventions in non-clinical settings are included in this analysis, the total increases to more than 10,5 00 people. In the three years 2015/16 to 2017/18, there was a slight decrease in the total numbers of reported interventions. The decline over the period is attributable to fewer new clients coming forward. The numbers of existing clients receiving interventions has been relatively static over the period. Going further back, the number of people seeking interventions has been relatively stable for five to seven years. Similarly, the proportion of people reporting some form of harmful gambling behaviour in the HLS surveys remained static, at approximately 5 percent of the population, between 2012 and 2018. 14 Importantly, these static rates belie the fact that the actual number of people affected by harmful gambling is increasing in line with population growth, and intervention services growth is flat. Similarly, needs assessment and outcomes monitoring reports show that only 16 percent of potential clients for gambling support services (that is, people whose reported harm results in a moderate to high PGSI score) actually access or present at these services. This low service use is also evident for other forms of addiction. Improving intervention and service use rates remains a challenge. It will require further work to address systemic or persistent barriers to access and inequities based on ethnicity or socioeconomic factors. Accessibility for Māori , Pacific and other vulnerable grou ps Analysis of Ministry gambling service administrative data for 2017/18 and 2016/17 shows that the number of gamblers seeking treatment continues to decline, despite the increase in real numbers of people experiencing gambling harm. Introduction This Government is committed to putting the wellbeing of current and future generations of New Zealanders at the centre of our work. Physical and mental wellbeing is one of the top five priorities for Budget 2020. This work includes improving the terms on which individuals and groups take part in society. Background The Social Services and Community Committee (the Committee) met between 2 May 2018 and 3 June 2020 to consider the petition of Jenn Hooper. On 7 August 2019, the Committee heard from the Department of Internal Affairs, the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, the Ministry of Health, and the Ministry of Social Development. On 4 June 2020 the Committee released its report with three recommendations that support the substance of the Petition. The Committee recommended the Government:  develop a nationwide network of bathroom facilities for those with extensive and complex disabilities that is based on the population density of towns and cities;  make available capital funding to support smaller local councils to develop fully accessible bathroom facilities and purchase the required equipment; and  require the Ministry of Health and all District Health Boards to review and make changes to policies that result in some outpatients or visitors with extensive and complex disabilities being changed on the floor of standard accessible toilets. Government Response The Government has examined the recommendations and notes this is an important issue requiring full consideration across government agencies with disability, Health and Local Government implications. The House was due to be dissolved on 12 August for the 2020 election, providing for a response back to the Committee 15 days after Parliament resumed, in approximately early November. The extension of Parliament has meant the response will be instead due on 27 August. A substantive cross-portfolio response cannot be achieved within the remaining timeframe. To this end we propose to produce a substantive response in early 2021, but have requested that the Department of Internal Affairs begin consultation with Local Government New Zealand in the meantime. Introduction from Suzanne Doig, Deputy Chief Executive, Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy I would like to present to you the final decisions of our organisational change process. I appreciate the feedback you have provided during the consultation period and the thought that went into this. It helped refine our thinking and test our assumptions and rationale for what was proposed. I would also like to thank everyone for your professionalism and for the manaakitanga you have extended to each other over the past weeks. These decisions have not been made lightly and I would like to acknowledge all those who are affected by the final decisions that have been made. Why change is necessary Late last year, the Minister of Finance announced an ongoing Fiscal Sustainability Programme to embed a culture of responsible spending across government, requiring us to make permanent baseline reductions from the 2024/25 financial year. In Budget 2024, the Government implemented a reduction of 7.0% in the Department’s permanent baseline, after Ministers asked us to find more than the initial 6.5% savings requested of us. Te Tari identified initiatives to enable us to meet that target. The initiatives broadly covered reducing costs, reducing discretionary spending and finding more efficient ways to deliver our mahi. While the majority of initiatives did not affect our people, some did and resulted in this organisational change that impacts positions and kaimahi. Final decisions have been made This document outlines the final decisions for the Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy Branch organisational change, as well as the implementation plan for putting those changes in place. We carefully considered all the feedback received over the consultation period, and now the leadership team and I will be implementing the new structure as outlined in the consultation document with some adjustments. We received 74 submissions of which 14 were group submissions. The common theme of the feedback across all groups was for the retention of roles, as there are concerns that the reduction in staffing will mean that other people, teams or groups will need to pick up work. I acknowledge this, but I am clear that the reduction in capacity means that we will have to deprioritise some work and focus our mahi more narrowly where possible. We also received submissions proposing alternative changes such as reporting line changes, merging/consolidation of teams, disestablishing vacant positions so we can retain filled positions that were proposed to be disestablished, and the need for new additional resourcing. We have made some changes as a result, but in most cases we were not able to accommodate 7 Section Two: Branch Context and Background The Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy organisational change consultation process began on 22 April 2024. The financial environment we are currently in requires us to operate within reduced Crown- funded baselines from 1 July 2024. Opportunities we identified to cut spending in non- personnel related costs did not go far enough to meet the cost savings required for the Government’s Fiscal Sustainability Programme and the additional emerging cost pressures we are experiencing as a Branch. We therefore had to propose some organisational structure changes to meet the spending reduction required. The following principles were used to form the consultation proposal: 1. Firstly, closing down vacant positions where possible, some of which have been deliberately held vacant in recent months in anticipation of baseline reductions. 2. Consolidating management structures and leadership positions where possible, while still ensuring the right level of technical and kaimahi oversight. 3. Ensuring the right level of capability is retained to deliver the core requirements of the mahi we are accountable for. You will be familiar by now with how the nature of our funding across the Branch varies; some areas are Crown-funded, while others are funded through third-party revenue managed through memorandum accounts, or other forms of cost recovery. We can only count reductions in Crown-funded expenditure towards the baseline reductions required of the Department. As many of you noted through the consultation process, the changes proposed for Toi Hiranga amount to more than the 6.5% initially sought by the government. That is because many parts of the Branch were already facing significant inflationary cost pressures (for example, the average salary at Te Tari Taiwhenua increased by over 11% from 2021 to 2023;1 salary increases almost always need to be funded from existing baselines). While groups in the Branch have been absorbing these inflationary costs through savings such as reduced contractor use, reduced travel, and recruitment delays, we had reached the point where we could no longer afford all the roles in the current structure. This has been factored into the final decisions, but we have not drawn a distinction in this final decision document between ‘unfunded roles’ and roles disestablished to meet baseline reduction requirements. As mentioned earlier, I know the concern remains that the reduced staffing capacity will have flow on effects for kaimahi both within the teams and across the Branch. I reiterate there will be no expectation for kaimahi to do the job of multiple people. The reduction in capacity will mean that work will need to be deprioritised.
