Crown entities We monitor two Crown entities and are responsible for managing the Government’s relationship with them. The Office of Film and Literature Classification is an independent Crown entity under the Crown Entities Act 2004. This means it performs its functions at “arm’s length” from the Government. The office has two primary functions: • To classify publications such as films, books or computer files which may need to be restricted or banned • To provide information about classification decisions and about the classification system as a whole Fire and Emergency New Zealand (FENZ) is a Crown agent under the Crown Entities Act 2004. This means it is required to follow government policies. It is responsible for the delivery of both rural and urban fire and emergency services throughout New Zealand. FENZ is responsible for over 14,000 staff and is therefore one of the largest organisations in the State sector. Risk and assurance We need to integrate and embed risk management explicitly across our organisation. Everyone can contribute directly to good risk management. Our risk management framework ensures that risk management is consistent, repeatable and in line with international standards. It provides evidence of how well business risks are being managed, opportunities are being taken and the business is performing. The Department has administrative responsibility for approximately 50 Acts (plus an additional 62 historic Local Legislation Acts) and about 90 pieces of secondary legislation. We also have functional regulatory roles or share responsibility under six other pieces of legislation. The Chief Executive of the Department of Internal Affairs also holds the role of Government Chief Digital Officer (GCDO), a system leadership position. The GCDO is designated as a system leader under section 56 of the Public Service Act 2020, leading the digital transformation of government across the public sector. As the public service lead for Digital, the GCDO is responsible for setting the direction for and supporting the development of a modern, efficient and adaptive public service that operates as a unified whole. We also play a system leadership role for local government. We link central and local government more effectively to achieve improved outcomes for citizens and communities. The Department is the home of the National Library of New Zealand and Archives New Zealand, which act as the memory of society and the memory of government, respectively. These institutions play an important role in preserving New Zealand’s documentary heritage and ensuring a full and accurate public record is created and maintained. In particular: »The Chief Archivist has a system leadership and regulatory role in administering the Public Records Act 2005, which establishes the statutory framework for information and records management across the public sector »The National Librarian has a system leadership role in the preservation, protection, development and accessibility of New Zealand’s documentary heritage. Our wider functions Our wider functions include: »Managing and protecting the integrity of national identity information. This includes life events such as births, deaths and marriages, citizenship and issuing passports »Regulating activities in several sectors, including gambling, online child exploitation material and violent extremism material. We also regulate government record- keeping, charities, unsolicited electronic messages, money laundering and financing of terrorism, private security personnel and private investigators »Providing policy advice to the Government on: local government, the community and voluntary sector, fire and emergency services, identity, digitising government, National Library and public records management, digital safety, gambling and racing 22 – Nature and scope of functions 8 Strategic Intentions – Ngā Takune Rautaki 2024-2028 »Providing information, resources and advice to communities to support their aspirations »Administering grant funding schemes, as well as promoting trust and confidence in the charitable sector »Supporting Ministers to ensure the Executive Government operates efficiently and effectively. Our strategic direction 1 At the time of developing the RSG strategy the wording of this outcome was yet to be finalised.Background In 2018, the Regulatory Services Group (RSG) embarked upon a strategic journey which resulted in a fundamental shift from regime to system leadership. This new strategic direction was designed to enable RSG to effectively deliver on its stewardship responsibilities in a future that anticipated rapid change and significant digitalisation. RSG is continuing its transformation journey through the development of the RSG Strategy to: ◆Realise RSG ’s ambition to be highly effective regulators ◆Articulate RSG’s vision and the outcomes it aims to deliver for New Zealanders ◆Realise RSG ’s ambition to provide leadership to the systems it regulates (current and future) ◆Enable RSG to be future-focused, innovative and adaptable in how it delivers services ◆Collaborate across the RSG regulatory systems to leverage learnings, experience and expertise ◆Build a culture of growing kaimahi (staff) and leadership capability and make RSG a great place to work ◆Articulate compelling and measurable markers of success.Alongside the strategy, a three-year work programme has been developed, setting out the key initiatives that will be undertaken across RSG. The RSG strategy is strongly aligned to the DIA Tō Tātou Mahi outcomes: Hapū, iwi, and communities across New Zealand are safe, resilient and thriving … and … The wellbeing of hapū, iwi and Māori is improved through a strong and enduring Māori-Crown partnership that is equitable and positive1 The RSG strategy aims to maximise the effectiveness of RSG’s current and future regulatory systems through establishing a shared view of what regulatory excellence looks like and enabling systems to consistently excel. The strategy sits across existing (and yet-to-be- developed) system group operating models. Each system group has a clear outcome focus and will have its own operating model which sets out how it undertakes its regulatory work. The first two issues from Crown Law relate to determining a person’s sex under the law  The Crown Law advice did not express significant concern about the self-identification clauses. Its main query was whether there could be more guidance on how sex and gender is determined by the law generally.  Both the Bill and the Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Act have a provision stating that a person’s sex should be determined by reference to the general law of New Zealand. Crown law raised two issues about this: oThe scope of application of the ‘general law of New Zealand’. Who is required to determine sex by reference to the ‘general law of New Zealand’? oThe distinction between registered sex (e.g. in a birth record), and sex for other purposes. Do we want sex for all purposes to be determined by what is on a birth record?  As noted by Crown Law, it is not clear how sex is determined by the general law of New Zealand. It advised that clearer guidance in the Bill could be beneficial.  We agree that providing clearer guidance for determining sex or gender may be warranted but this work is broader than the Internal Affairs Portfolio. The third issue from Crown Law is about the consequences of a self-identification model on the placement of transgender people in prison  Corrections Regulation 65(3) states that if a person in prison supplies a copy of their birth certificate they must be placed in a prison that accords with the sex on this document. This overrides all other considerations, including a history of sexual offending.  Crown Law suggested Corrections consider modifying the regulations as the self-identification process would remove judicial oversight for changing sex on a birth certificate. The concern was that men, particularly those who have committed sexual offences, would take advantage of the self-identification process to change their recorded sex and be placed in a female prison. A new BDMRR Bill would provide an opportunity for consultation with M āori about access to births, deaths, marriages and civil union registers (BDM registers) to ensure that the Crown is fulfilling its obligations under Te Tiriti o Waitangi. This is important as there was no targeted consultation with M āori in the development of the BDMRR Bill. 5. We are aware that the BDMRR Bill does not incorporate M āori perspectives of identity effectively. For example, the current access provisions can be a barrier to whakapapa research for iwi authorities and individuals. Iwi authorities have a strong interest in being able to identify people who whakapapa to their iwi as this data helps them to provide support and plan for iwi development. Individuals have an interest in knowing their whakapapa, so they can claim support, participate in iwi-related matters, connect with others (whakawhanaungatanga) and affirm their identity. Through the BDM registers the Department directly impacts M āori knowledge of their whakapapa. Because of this, and as the Department’s Letters of Commitment with Tūhoe and Ngāti Kahungunu ki Te Wairoa directly reference access to BDM registers, further consultation with iwi is recommended. …and operational improvements identified since the original Bill was introduced in 2017 6. A new BDMRR Bill would enable additional legislative changes to address operational issues identified since the BDMRR Bill was drafted in 2017. Changes could be made to ensure the BDMRR Act is channel neutral. Work that is underway to enable digital channels and digital identity verification, could be complemented with work to promote equity of access for those who have difficulty using digital technology. This briefing sets out opportunities to modernise the legislation that sits behind New Zealand’s identity services. It also provides you with information about the ongoing operational and regulatory stewardship work to maintain our identity systems. 2. We propose a meeting with you to discuss a three-year policy work programme for the Internal Affairs portfolio. This briefing informs that discussion. Executive summary 3. You are responsible for the legislation which sets the requirements for maintaining New Zealand’s primary identity records. As we move into an increasin gly connected and digital world, we need to modernis e our systems for recording, storing, accessing and confirming the identity information held by the Department. There is work that we need to continue across legislation, systems and operations to ensure they remain fit for purpose. 4. The first piece of work we would like to discuss with you concerns the Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Bill (the BDMRR Bill). The BDMRR Bill was introduced in 2017 to improve the way people can digitally access information held on the registers of births, deaths, marriages and relationships. It was deferred in 2019 after the Select Committee expanded the scope of changes in the Bill to include amendments to the process for changing the sex recorded on a birth certificate. 5. It is important that work on modernising the Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Act 1995 (the BDMRR Act) is continued as soon as possible to realise the benefits of the systems modernisation work . You could choose to also consider changes to the way sex is recorded on birth certificates to allow for greater consultation on this issue and further work on the recording of gender identity on official documents. There is strong public engagement and interest in changes regarding sex and gender, but these can be pursued separately from the system modernisations. 6. Other legislative amendments may also be required to support operational and systems change. This will include supporting digital identity work, continuing to update our systems and practices, and may include work to support changes under the Adoption Act 1955 (which is administered by the Ministry of Justice) . You are responsible for the legislation governing primary identity records 7. As the Minister of Internal Affairs, you are responsible for the legislation which sets the requirements for many of New Zealand’s identity records. Together the identity related legislation within your portfolio allows for the: a) registering of births, deaths, marriages, civil unions, adoptions and name changes; b) granting and recognising citizenship; c) issuing passports; and d) digital sharing of identity credentials through RealMe, the all-of-government system providing authentication and identity assertion services . You are responsible for the direction of policy development, reviews of legislation and, under some legislation, you have direct decision-making responsibilities. The Department is the kaipupuri, or guardian, of New Zealand’s identity records, and administrator of the legislation. You have received a briefing on your role regarding the Citizenship Act 19771. You will be briefed separately about the operation of the Civil Registration system (which includes births, deaths, marriages, relationships and passports) . 9. The Department of Internal Affairs (the Department) holds the registers of births, deaths, marriages and civil unions . The registers are administered by the Registrar- General of Births, Deaths and Marriages (the Registrar-General), who is appointed under the BDMRR Act. The Registrar-General is also responsible for operational policy developed under this Act. 10. The identity services the Department provides are critical for enabling people in New Zealand to establish their identity in order to access services and take part in society. Our records allow people to establish their right to publicly funded services and benefits and apply for citizenship in New Zealand or another country. Many other government agencies and organisations rely on t he Department’s records to establish the identity and identity history of people accessing services. 11. In 2019 Cabinet approved funding for a programme to adapt many of the Department’s identity services to today’s digital world through a programme called Te Ara Manaaki. Te Ara Manaaki is moving all the data and services managed by the Department from outdated, increasingly risky databases on to one, integrated platform. Work on Te Ara Manaaki is well advanced, but the potential of the new system to deliver better outcomes for New Zealanders cannot be fulfilled without legislative reform. Identity systems and legislation need to be modernised over this term of government 12. New Zealand does not have a national identity document or a single system that records the identity of every person with the right to remain permanently in New Zealand. As a proxy for an identity document, people in New Zealand use a range of official documents to verify their identity, such as a birth certificate, driver licence, passport or marriage certificate. In many situations, someone will use a combination of these documents. 13. Policy work is needed to ensure that New Zealand ’s legislation governing identity data: a) is ready for a digital future; b) upholds the Crown’s obligations under Te Tiriti o Waitangi; and c) serves the needs of all New Zealanders.

Outcome: Oranga hapū, iwi and Māori is improved through an enduring, equitable and positive Māori-Crown partnership Tūāpapa - Whāia te hīnātore o te mauri atua, hei oranga mō te mauri tāngata The pursuit of environmental sustenance and potential, enhances the wellbeing and life essence of people and place. Intermediate Outcomes • Mātauranga Māori is respected and valued • Māori, iwi and hapu aspirations, interests and rights are understood and respected This outcome derives from concepts in the Māori account of Ranginui and Papatūānuku. At the heart of this statement is the word “mauri” or the life force, linking the mauri of our environment with the mauri of people and place. This is consistent with the view shared in Māoridom that if the land and waters are well, so too are the people and community they live in. Making the link between the land and waters, people and community, and wellbeing will guide our engagement with hapū, iwi and Māori on outcomes and Treaty rights and interests. This concept of oranga or wellbeing also aligns well with our other outcomes. Incorporating these concepts into our strategic framework signals our commitment to lifing our capability to engage with te ao Māori. Success will mean that by 2030 we will see: • te ao Māori capabilities in Te Tari Taiwhenua are lifed • mātauranga Māori is respected, valued and protected • Māori, iwi and hapū aspirations, interests and rights are understood and reflected in our work programmes • strengthened Treaty partnership with Māori through a mix of co-design, management and governance • Te Tari Taiwhenua can report on outcomes and impact for Māori. Outcome: Communities across New Zealand are safe, resilient and thriving Intermediate Outcomes • Regulated activities minimise harm and maximise benefits to people and communities • Māori are supported to realise their aspirations • Communities are supported to develop and prosper The Department is good at responding to events and incidents that impact on communities and in providing practical support. In the future, we will proactively identify and work with iwi, hapū and communities to build their own capability to make decisions locally for greatest impact on what afects them. The unique characteristics of diverse communities means that a “one size fits all” approach is unlikely to be successful. 19 Department of Internal Affairs NGĀ TAKUNE RAUTAKI STRATEGIC INTENTIONS 2021-2025
Outcome: People can easily access services and information Intermediate Outcomes • People’s identity can be easily and securely verified • Barriers to digital inclusion are reduced • People’s access to government is enhanced • Taonga tuku iho rights are protected The Department is eficient at processing peoples’ requests for services and information. In the future, we will go beyond just service provision to enable people to get to the outcome they need to fully participate in and benefit from New Zealand society (eg from delivering passports to enabling travel). With greater control over their own data individuals will be able to opt in to more all-of-government or cross- government services and systems. They will receive faster and more eficient provision, including greater automation, while also respecting privacy and security. Ensuring that the opportunities and gains of digital service provision are realised is important, but equally vital is ensuring services and information are accessible to all and that barriers to inclusion are reduced over time. Success will mean that by 2030 we will see: • people having more control of their data, which is accessed with their consent • people’s circumstances driving automated, transparent public sector services • the public sector operating of standardised, interoperable, and common digital systems • all people having access to high-performing infrastructure services • all New Zealanders having what they need in an increasingly digital world to fully participate in and benefit from New Zealand society. 22 Department of Internal Affairs NGĀ TAKUNE RAUTAKI STRATEGIC INTENTIONS 2021-2025

How MBIE may use Personal Information provided by DIA The Personal Information received by MBIE from DIA may be used to: a) ensure that an individual applying for or utilising MBIE services is not required to provide identity and Life Event records that DIA h olds. b) update an individual’s I mmigration New Zealand records . c) update new passport information for N ew Zealand citizens to ensure identities are accurately maintained . d) enable the prevention, detection, investigation and prosecution of offences, and the conduct of civil proceedings including judicial review. e) identify an individual applying for an Electronic Identity Credential. 3. Waiver to 28 -day rule •A waiver to the 28 -day rule is being sought because addressing the issue at such a late stage impacted the original timeframe to have the regulations in place by 15 June 2023. •A waiver is being sought on the grounds that the re gulations need to come into effect by 15 June 2023 to comply with the statutory obligations in the Act, and that the regulations primarily provide a benefit, which is to operationalise a process that supports a small proportion of the population to amend their birth certificate. Additional requirements for 16 - and 17 - year -olds •The process and requirements for 16 - and 17 - year -olds is not within scope of the regulations being considered today. They are also not unusually restrictive compared to other jurisdictions that have enacted a self-identification process. For instance, the State of Victoria in Australia requires 16 - and 17 - year -olds to have guardian consent. Digital Identity: Establishing a Trust Framework Portfolio Government Digital Services / Internal Affairs On 2 July 2020, the Cabinet Government Administration and Expenditure Review Committee: 1 noted that digital identity is a key enabler of digital transformation across the public sector and the economy, and is a foundation in Rautaki mō tētahi Rāngai Kāwanatanga Matihiko , the Strategy for a Digital Public Service; 2 noted that demand for digital identity services has increased during the Covid-19 pandemic, which has prompted the acceleration of the creation of a Digital Identity Trust Framework (Trust Framework) to support New Zealand’s economic recovery; 3 noted that digital identity has the potential to deliver significant economic and societal benefits with the potential benefit of enabling digital identity in a mature economy estimated to be worth between 0.5 percent and 3 percent of GDP (approximately $1.5 to $9 billion in NZD); 4 noted that there are regulatory and operational gaps in the provision of digital identity services, including the lack of a regulatory regime; 5 noted that the establishment of a Trust Framework in legislation is proposed to address the regulatory and operational gaps, with an interim Trust Framework to be established while the legislation is developed; 6 noted that establishing a Trust Framework in New Zealand will help deliver on the Prime Minister’s commitment under the Single Economic Market agenda for mutual recognition of digital identity services with Australia; 7 agreed to the establishment of an interim Trust Framework consisting of: 7.1 an interim Trust Framework team, established within the Department of Internal Affairs, who will develop and test the Trust Framework rules; and 7.2 a transitionary governance group, including representatives from the Government Chief Digital Officer, the Government Chief Information Security Officer, the Government Chief Data Steward, the Office of the Privacy Commissioner and Māori to approve the Trust Framework rules; Page 1 of 2 Proposal to amend long -term plan requirements for specified councils We are consulting on a proposed temporary change to the Local Government Act 2002 (LGA) allowing specified council s to decide on mak ing voluntary buyouts to owners of properties that have been severely impacted by weather events in 2023, without having to amend their long -term plan s (LTPs) as required by the LGA. The change will also clarify that the exemption provided to specified councils by clause 8 of the Severe Weather Emergency Recovery (Local Government) Order 2023 applies to decisions about FOSAL buyouts and a LTP amendment is not required. We are preparing an Order in Council (Order), unde r the Severe Weather Emergency Recovery Legislation Act 2023 (SWERL A), to clarify that Auckland Council, Central Hawke’s Bay District Council, Gisborne District Council, Hastings District Council, Thames -Coromandel District Council, Wairoa District Council, Hawke’s Bay Regional Council (the specified councils) are not required to amend their LTP to accommodate buyouts . Section 97 of the LGA prevents a council from starting a new significant activity or significantly changing existing service levels if these were not included in the council’s LTP . Given their scale and costs, land purchases could be a new significant activity for the specified councils above or would significantly impact some of the council’s existing services. Public consultation on this pr oposal and the draft Order will be open on 2 4-31 August 2023. Why is this change necessary ? The proposed Order is needed to enable the specified local authorities to act quickly on making buyout offers to property owners severely impacted by recent weather events . It would provide certainty f or these specified homeowners and communities , many of who m have been unable to occupy their properties for several months . It would also ensure that the process to resolve the future of damaged and at -risk land progresses without additional delays . Temporarily suspending the requirement to amend the LTP for the buyout process provides regulatory relief to the specified councils . There is also limited benefit in requiring the specified councils to complete the LTP amendment process with the information currently available. Background to the issues requiring an Order in Council Under section 97 of the LGA , councils may not commence a new significant activity or significantly change service levels of an existing activity if these were not provided for in the council’s LTP. This would require councils to go through a LTP amendment process before undertaking a ny new activities or changing service levels.

Page 1 of 3 Proposal to amend e ight c ouncils’ long - term planning requirements : We are consulting on a proposed temporary change to the following councils’ planning requirements in response to the effects of Cyclones Hale and Gabrielle and heavy rain events early this year: • Central Hawke’s Bay District Council; • Far North District Co uncil; • Gisborne District Council; • Hastings District Council; • Hawke’s Bay Regional Council; • Kaipara District Council; • Napier City Council; and • Wairoa District Council. We are preparing an Order in Council (Order), under the Severe Weather Emergenc y Recovery Legislation Act 2023 (SWERL Act), to allow for a three -year plan instead of the statutory 10 -year long -term plan. This would be a temporary change to support local authorities during the recovery from the recent extreme weather events. The draft Order is attached for you to review. We have provided some supporting information on the proposal below, including an explanation of why this Order is considered necessary. Public consultation on this proposal will be open on 25 July - 4 August 2023. If you have any feedback or questions on this proposal, please send it to LGCycloneRecovery@dia.govt.nz. Why is this change necessary ? To be able to do long -term planning, councils must have a detailed understanding of the present situation of their communities. This includes knowing the condition of infrastructure like roading and the funding available for their maintenance and operation . Councils are still assessing the extent of the damage from severe weather. They still need to confirm the funding required, when that funding will be needed and when that funding will be received. Given the very limited information, planning for the nex t 10 years is likely to be inaccurate. Without the proposed change, c ouncils would have to develop and consult on long -term plans that do not reflect the longer -term impacts arising from the weather events. In addition, c ouncil staff who would normally wor k on the preparation of a long -term plan are deployed on recovery efforts. Requiring councils to do a long -term plan means having to pull these people out of this task, which at this point has a higher priority. However, planning is still very important. A recovery -focused, three -year plan would strike a balance between the need for planning and the uncertainties arising from the weather events. A similar measure was taken following the Canterbury and Kaikōura earthquakes.
Page 1 of 3 Understanding Ministers’ Expenses (after 2014) Information on the expenses disclosed by the Department of Internal Affairs for members of the Executive. Statutory framewor k Members of the Executive (Ministers of the Crown) require financial resources and support services to fulfil their responsibilities and to service the public efficiently and effectively . Under the provisions of the Members of Parliament (Remuneration and Services ) Act 2013, services for Ministers are determined variously by the Remune ration Authority, the Speaker of the House of Representatives and the Minister Responsible for Ministerial Services. Where no additional or alternative provision is made for Ministers under the Remuneration Authority’s, or the Minister Responsible for Ministerial Services’ determinations, Ministers’ entitlements are as for those members of Parliament who are also not ministers.

Page 10 of 26 60. In the limited situations described above, we consider the Crown intervention bodies should be able to initiate merger investigations and the development of proposals, by entities that woul d potentially benefit from merging. This would occur through a recommendation to the regional representative group by the relevant Crown intervention body. In these circumstances, it would also be desirable for there to be a lower threshold for a merger proceeding. I consider 50 per cent of each regional representative group would need to agree to the merger for it to go ahead. Entity financing arrangements 61. In my earlier paper, I noted a consequence of moving to a 10 -entity model is that some entities will have weaker standalone credit profiles (due to these entities’ more concentrated assets, less diversified customer base, and weaker financial ratios), and that this may limit their borrowing capacity and raise their borrowing costs. Smaller entities might find it more challenging to raise competitively priced debt from banks and capital markets due to the weaker credit quality and financial resilience of some entities, and the increased number of borrowers in the market. 62. Reflecting the above, Cabinet invited me to report back with advice and proposals for suitable financing mechanisms, including consideration of mechanisms that vary from entity to entity, and a backstop central financing facility that could operate on a near commercial basis, enable the pooling of risk and provision of credit enhancement, and achieve economies of scale and market access benefits [CAB -23-MIN -0143]. 63. Officials have since undertaken further work to better understand the credit quality and financial resilience of the proposed water services entities, and the implications for their ability to access cost -effective finance.

Page 11 of 14 Appendix A: Current harm minimisation r egulations The Gambling Act 2003 provides for a substantial level of regulation in relation to Class 4 gambling: • harm prevention and minimisation (section 313); • gaming machines (section 314); • admission to, and exclusion from, gam bling venues (section 315); • exclusion of problem gamblers (section 316) ; and • infringement offences for the breach of any regulations (section 360). The table below shows the key requirements for Class 4 gambling in the current Gambling (Harm Prevention and Minimisation) Regulations 2004 (note: administrative clauses 1– 3 are not shown) . Table: Key requirements in the current Harm Minimisation regulations Regulation 4. Venues that are declared unsuitable to be a Class 4 venue. Regulation 5. No ATMs are permitted in the gambling area of a venue. Regulation 6. Stake and prize limits for C lass 4 gambling. Regulation 7. Gaming machine must display certain messages at the election of the player, specifically: • game information (odds, average winnings, player spend rates) • player information (duration, amount spent, net wins/losses). Regulation 8. Gaming machine must include feature that interrupts play every 30 minutes and provide player information (duration, amount spent, net wins/losses). Machine must include a feature that automatically pays out any winnings and credits to the player, if they do not wish to continue. Regulation 9. Jackpot advertising cannot be visible from outside the venue. Regulation 10. Any advertising related to a venue must not convey the impression that there is a gaming machine jackpot at the venue. Regulation 11. The following must be available: • pamphlets containing information about the odds of winning on gaming machines and the characteristics of problem gambling, including the recognised signs of harmful gambling and how to seek advice; and • visible s ignage that clearly encourage players to gamble only at levels they can afford and contains advice about how to seek assistance for problem gambling. Regulation 12. There is always a staff member who has received problem gambling awareness training at the venue at all times when gambling is available. A trained staff member must be able to approach a player and provide appropriate information about problem gambling. Reducing Pokies Harm: Approval to Consult Portfolio Internal Affairs On 9 March 2022, the Cabinet Social Wellbeing Committee (SWC): 1 noted that Class 4 gambling (‘pokies’ in pubs, clubs and TAB NZ venues) is the most harmful form of land-based gambling in New Zealand, with approximately one in five pokie players being considered at-risk gamblers and nearly $1 billion lost on pokie machines per annum; 2 noted that the current Gambling (Harm Prevention and Minimisation) Regulations 2004 have some gaps that could easily be addressed to do more to reduce harmful pokies gambling and improve the enforceability of the regulations; 3 noted that the Gambling Act 2003 contemplates a substantially more detailed approach to regulation of Class 4 gambling and there is an opportunity to develop a much stronger harm reduction approach; 4 agreed to the release of the discussion document, Reducing Pokies Harm , attached to the submission under SWC-22-SUB-0029, which outlines some regulatory proposals to better reduce harm in three key areas (the gambling venue, the gaming machine, and compliance tools); 5 noted that the Minister for Internal Affairs intends to return to SWC by 30 September 2022 with proposals to amend the current regulations; 6 noted that work to minimise harm from pokies gambling is part of the broader work programme underway to prevent and minimise harm from gambling. Page 11 of 26 65.2 establishing a dedicated ‘Water Services Funding Agency ’, which could operate on a similar basis to the LGFA; and 65.3 direct l ending by the Crown (as the last resort) . 66. Several of the se options present challenges that would need to be overcome to provide confidence that the required funding can be raised: 66.1 LGFA option : Ther e would be transitional advantages (such as simpler debt settlement processes with councils) and potential longer -term advantages in water services entities ’ borrowing via a modified LGFA. However, there are significant barriers to progressing this option, because of the requirement for unanimous agreement by shareholding councils. The different risk profiles of councils and water services entities, and the weaker initial financial positions of some of the entities, also complicates this option. 66.2 A dedicated Water Services Funding Agency (WSFA) : This would operate on a similar basis to the LGFA , by pooling risk and achieving scale and market access benefits. This option could be enabled through legislation, but any decision to establish a WSFA would require further Cabinet consideration. The existence of a credible WSFA backstop ‘option’ gives the Crown greater leverage when engaging with banks, institutional lenders and the LGFA for private -market financing solutions. If required, this option would be preferable to the Crown providing direct lending to entities,

Page 12 of 26 70. Due to the technical nature of the legislative provisions to give effect to this option, and the implications for Crown support, I seek authorisation from Cabinet for the Minister of Finance and I to approve policy and technical matters that may arise during legislative drafting. 71. The Minister of Finance and I consider the Treasury should play a stronger role in leading the development and implementation of a financing strategy for the entities, given the Crown’s likely role in ensuring suitable financing mechanisms are in place for the entities upon establishment. This will require the Treasury, and the National Transition Unit within the Department of Internal Affairs, to work closely together – given the interdependencies with other aspects of the transition programme (such as determi ning the amount of the payments water services entities will make to local authorities in respect of water infrastructure debt). 72. Further work on financing strategy will require market engagement to test lender appetite for the different options with banks and other institutional lenders, including the LGFA. This work will include further consideration of the LGFA and WSFA options. In considering Entity A’s financing arrangements, officials will work closely with the establishment board and chief executive to ensure any solution works for Entity A, and the other nine entities. 73. The tight timeframes for entity establishment mean it will be necessary to move swiftly to ensure suitable arrangements are in place by the proposed 1 July 2024 ‘go live’ date for Entity A , and for any other entities that will ‘go live’ at that time or s hortly after. To enable this, I seek authorisation for the Minister of Finance and I to make further policy and technical decisions required to identify and execute the preferred funding options. Page 14 of 14 Appendix D: Population impacts Who is more likely to experience gambling harm? Māori are more likely to experience gambling harm, especially from pokies Māori make up 30% of all high- risk gamblers despite only making up 16.5% of the overall adult population. Some level of gambling harm was experienced by 38% of Māori pokie players compared to 12% of non -Māori pokie players. Māori are also over five times more likely to be high risk gamblers than the general population, suggesting that Māori are more likely to experience gambling harm as a result of their own gambling, or someone else’s. This is a result of numerous causes, including the number of gaming m achines and venues in areas of high deprivation areas where Māori are more likely to live, as well as reflecting the wider inequities faced by Māori. Pacific peoples also face disproportionate gambling harm Although Pacific peoples are less likely to part icipate in gambling (63% in comparison to the national average of 69.3%), they experience higher rates of harmful gambling (3.8% compared to the national average of 1.6%). Pacific peoples have the lowest median income ($23,300) compared to other population groups and are more likely to live in higher deprivation areas and therefore have greater access to pokie machines. This proximity can lead to increased time and money spent gambling. Asian communities are also at greater risk Research also shows that some Asian communities disproportionately experience gambling harm. The proportion of Asians who gamble is relatively low when compared to Māori, Pacific people and European/Other; however, those who do gamble are more likely to experience harm compared to E uropean/Other. The 2016 Health and Lifestyles Survey found that Asian people were more likely to be moderate risk/problem gamblers (5.9%) compared with people of European/Other ethnicity (1.1%). For women , pokies can be a ‘double- edged sword’ Although being male has generally been considered a risk -factor for gambling harm, recent studies have shown that when New Zealand women gamble, it is to a similar extent to men. Gambling on pokies in local communities appears to offer women especially respite, distraction, comfort and time- out from family, while placing them at a heightened risk of experiencing problems and harm. For disabled people, the impacts are not known Little is known regarding the extent to which disabled people experience gambling - related harm. This is an area that is not well covered in current research.

It highlights the importance of decision -making proximate to affected communities, long -term strategic planning and high- quality, responsive, resilient and sustainable water management throughout New Zealand. Key to the framework is bolstered central government oversight, which will ensure efficiency and accountability within the sector. We have encouraged collaboration where possible, while leaving decision -making at a local level, as l ocal decision makers know their communities best. Page 2 of 10 8. While all public wastewater treatment plants have resource consents, approximately 20 percent of plants are currently operating on expired consents and have been doing so for an average of four years and almost 60 percent of these plants will come up for consent renewal in the next 10 years. 9. Wastewater standards will directly address this infrastructure challenge by reducing regulatory burden; delivering much greater standardisation of treatment systems and related infrastructure; enabling cost efficiencies in the design, consenting, build and operation of wastewater systems; and providing councils with greater certainty of costs through standardisation and longer -term consent durations. 10. Based on case study, cost savings of up to 40 percent for consenting processes could be realised, depending on the type of plant and consents required. Moving from shorter -term consents to mandatory 35 -year duration consents will mean that reconsenting costs are not incurred as frequently. Further cost efficiencies will be achieved through infrastructure design solutions that will introduce greater standardisation. 11. The Local Government (Water Services) Bill (the Bill) will introduce a new approach to wastewater standards, in terms of the standards themselves and how they are made. The Bill proposes that the wastewater standards are a single standard rather than a minimum (or maximum) that must be implemented by regional councils in resource consents and cannot be exceeded, apart from on an ‘exceptions’ basis. 12. The Bill also proposes to align the process for making wastewater and stormwater environmental performance standards with the process for making drinking water standards. This will involve the standards being made through an Order in Council (as regulation s), on the recommendation of the Minister of Local Government. Stormwater standards will be made at a later date . 13. The intention is to make the new standards as soon as possible after the enabling legislation is passed so that the many councils that have treatment plants requiring consent renewals can accrue certainty and cost effectiveness benefits from the new standa rds. 14. The introduction of wastewater environmental performance standards is the first stage of a new wastewater regulatory system. Once the wastewater standards are in place this will enable the second stage of wastewater regulatory reform – the introduction of infrastructure design solutions. 15. ‘Infrastructure design solutions’ are a new tool provided for in the Bill that will help to further reduce the costs of design and consenting of wastewater treatment plants – in particular for the smaller -scale plants that make up approximately 50 percent of council -owned wastewater treatment plants in New Zealand. 16. I have requested that the Authority work at pace to ensure the Order in Council relating to the standards is made as a priority by . The proposed standards will cover discharge of wastewater to land, discharge of wastewater to water, beneficial reuse of biosolids, and risk -based monitoring and reporting requirements for wastewater network overflows. 17. To expedite this process, I am seeking delegated authority to issue drafting instructions to Parliamentary Counsel Office to prepare the draft Order in Council, after public consultation is completed. 9(2)(g)(i) Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE
Page 2 of 12 Purpose 1. In August 2024, Cabinet agreed that the National Engineering Design Standards (NEDS) should be a mandatory requirement for water services providers [ECO-24-MIN 0129 refers]. This briefing sets out our proposed approach to implement the NEDS. Background Scope and purpose of the National Engineering Design Standards 2. The proposed National Engineering Design Standards (NEDS) provide technical standards for design and construction of drinking, wastewater and stormwater reticulation network infrastructure (water services network infrastructure). 3. The NEDS are intended to provide a consistent set of design standards to developers, contractors, water service providers (currently councils and CCOs) and regulatory engineers on how to design, construct and commission “public”1 three waters water services network infrastructure. 4. Currently, the technical standards for design and construction are set out in council engineering codes of practice (codes). These codes provide guidance to developers and contractors on the design and construction of water services network infrastructure. 5. The codes also provide guidance on products that will meet the standards and requirements. This "approved products" register (e.g. pipes and inlets) is a key feature of the codes, and functions in a similar way to approved products under the Building Code. The approved products register also supports developers and contractors to practically implement councils’ codes. 6. Developers and contractors must demonstrate that the water services network infrastructure they are proposing to vest in the council (e.g. the transfer of ownership and ongoing maintenance and renewal obligations of those assets,) or connect to the “public” three waters network, meets the technical standards in the relevant code. Councils also use the technical standards in the codes to guide the maintenance, renewal, upgrade or decommissioning of the new or existing public water services network infrastructure. 7. Currently, there are up to 45 different engineering codes in use nationally. Although there is a degree of commonality between codes, the differences between regional, city, and district requirements for reticulation networks have created small, fragmented markets, and hindered the mobility of suppliers, potentially leading to higher costs than necessary. 8. The current arrangements also create challenges for councils. Where they can, councils do work with others or 'borrow' standards but reviewing and updating councils’ engineering codes is an ongoing task that requires significant expertise and resource. This is significant challenge for smaller councils. 1 In this context this includes three waters network as defined in the Water Services Act 2021. This includes drinking water, wastewater and stormwater network infrastructure that is owned and operated by a water services provider, which could include Council, Water Services Organisation or a Government Department. Page 2 of 2 As part of its cyclone recovery efforts, Auckland Council intends to start making buyout offers t o the owners of Category 3 propert ies under the Future of Severely Affected Land (FOSAL) programme before the end of 2023. However, there are concerns that FOSAL purchases would trigger section 97 of the LGA. The Department of Internal Affairs (DIA) considers that this is likely , due to estimates of the costs involved and the number of properties affec ted. DIA would also like to clarify that the existing exemption for the specified councils outside of Auckland continues to apply. Having to amend the LTP requires consultation using the special consultative procedure and an audit review of both the consultation document for the amendment and the final amendment itself. Satisfying these requirements would take a considerable amount of time, effectively delaying the work on FOSAL purchases. Proceeding without complying with these requirements would expose the effected local authorities to the risk of its decision being challenged in the Courts for not being consistent with section 97. DIA investigated different options to support the specified councils in providing certainty to impacted property owners as soon as possible. Of these options, the proposed Order will enable the effected councils to act sooner on its buyout decisions without exposing themselves to unnecessary legal risks. What would the proposed Order include? The proposed Order would exempt the specified councils from section 97 of the LGA until 30 June 2024. The purpose of this amendment is to enable the specified councils to make decisions on whether to make voluntary buyouts to property owners for properties that have been severely impacted by severe weather ev ents in 2023, without having to go through the prescribed process for amending its LTP. The specified councils would not be exempted from all consultation requirements in the LGA. The specified council s would still be required to consult in a way that c omplies with the LGA. The proposed Order would not require a particular consultation procedure to be followed. It is for each Council to determine what form of consultation is appropriate in the circumstances.

Page 2 of 26 Executive summary 8. On 11 April 2023, Cabinet considered my paper Refocusing the water services reforms: strategy and urgent decisions [ CAB- 23-MIN -0143 ]. This was the first in a series of papers reporting back on options and proposals to refocus the reforms, to achieve our intentions to deliver more affordable water services and infrastructure. 9. Through that paper, I obtained agreement to a new strategic and legislative approach, and to key changes to the reform model – including increasing the number of water services entities from four to 10, and amending the establishment timeframes. 10. At that time, I noted that a second paper would follow in May 2023 to provide further advice on some matters. In this paper, I am seeking to confirm the detailed proposals relating to: 10.1 the approach to the entity ‘go live’ dates – including confirming that the Auckland and Northl and Water Services Entity would ‘go live’ on 1 July 2024 ; and the timing for establishing the other entities and applying economic regulation ; 10.2 community priority statements – which would be new instruments (distinct from Te Mana o te Wai statements) to provide communities with an avenue to communicate their interests in a body of water, and their priorities for how the environmental impacts of the entities’ activities on that body of water might be managed ; 10.3 a legislative process to support and guide locally -led, voluntary mergers between entities – to recognise that, in time, councils and communities in higher- cost regions may wish to see the benefits of further amalgamation; 10.4 entity financing arrangements – including provid ing in legislation for the establishment of a backstop financing mechanism, through the establishment of a dedicated Water Services Funding Agency ; 10.5 shared services arrangement s – including providing in legislation for the responsible Minister to be able to di rect water services entities where collaboration or a whole of sector approach is required, and seeking agreement to the establishment of a digital shared service , which would be owned and governed by the entities . 11. As discussed in the April 2023 paper, leg islation is required to give effect to most of the decisions in that paper – as well as the decisions in this follow- up paper. In recognition that this legislation needs to be progressed quickly, I am seek ing approval to include a Water Services Entities Amendment Bill on the 2023 legislation programme, with a priority category two – must be passed before the 2023 general election. 12. Drafting is already underway for this Bill. I am seeking agreement to issue the remaining instructions – on the matters in this paper – as soon as possible. 13. I am intending to submit a third paper in June 2023 on matters that do not need to be included in the proposed legislation – but are still necessary to give effect to the new model . This will consider the implications of the change in approach on programme funding, implementation , and the reforms more broadly –
Page 2 of 3 Planning for the next three inste ad of 10 years will reduce the burden on these councils. By focusing on recovery, a three -year plan would offer their communities more useful information and strategic direction than a 10 -year plan could. It will provide a basis for financial planning, and future council decisions. It would deliver accountability to communities. In addition, the consultation requirements related to Long Term Plans will be carried over to the proposed three -year plan. This preserves the interests of stakeholders and ensures that council planning can capture the views of stakeholders. Councils would also be encouraged to plan for the longer -term implications of decisions in the three -year plan, where practicable. Background to the issues requiring an Order in Council Under the Local Government Act 2002 (LGA 2002), local authorities must always have a long - term plan covering 10 consecutive years. Councils prepare and adopt a long -term plan every three years, in consultation with their communities. They are required to adopt a 20 24-34 long -term plan by 30 June 2024, to come into effect on 1 July 2024. Severe weather events early this year have resulted in high pressures on council resources from recovery efforts and uncertainty on the scale of infrastructure damage and recovery funding. These constraints are impeding these councils' ability to meet their planning obligations under the LGA 2002. Given these challenges, we consider that the proposed O rder achieves the purpose of the SWERL Act. Its purpose is to assist councils and communities to respond to, and recover from, the impacts of severe weather events. It also ensures that activities normally undertaken by councils and their communities, such as planning, continue to be undertaken. DIA investigated different options for long -term planning to support these councils achieve uninterrupted recovery and functional plans. Of these options, the proposed Order will require the least council resources while still providing future direction and a basis for decision -making in the me dium -term, despite the uncertainties over infrastructure damage and recovery funding. It also retains community consultation on the councils’ intended direction for the next three years. What would the proposed three -year plan include? Under the draft Order, the three -year plan will provide most of the same information as a long -term plan, but for at least three instead of ten years. Councils will be allowed to forecast further if they wish. The three -year plan will identify key challeng es for the coming years, describe the councils’ intentions to deal with these, and discuss how this will be funded. The plan will also discuss things that are expected to have a significant impact on councils during the next three years, including levels o f service to be delivered during the recovery. Councils will still need to prepare and adopt an annual plan for each financial year, with the three -year plan acting as the annual plan for 2024 -25. The proposed Order does not include audit requirements for the three -year plan, as this is impractical given the quality of the information available at this time and the content of the plan. Annual reports will continue to be audited.

The Scheme is not the only form of accommodation support • The Rates Rebate Scheme is one of a suite of policy instruments designed to support households to meet their living costs. • Other cost of living subsidies (such as the Accommodation Supplement) and adjustments to income support remain more effective at insulating low -income ratepayers from rate rises than the Rate Rebate Scheme. Th ese mechanisms are also more effective at addressing equity concerns between renters and homeowners. In response to questions What are the financial implications on the appropriation? • In 2023 -24, the Scheme is estimated to co st $70 million. This estimate is within the appropriation of $70 million for the 2023 -24 financial year. • It is difficult to predict the impact that the increase in the cost of living will have on the uptake of the Scheme, so the Department will monitor th e appropriation through 2023 -24. • In the last three years, the appropriation for the Scheme has increased by $14 million. For this reason, the uptake will be closely monitored, and remedial action will be taken if necessary. Any increased uptake of the Sche me will be accounted for in the October or March baseline updates. How will people find out about the adjustments to the Scheme? • The adjustments to the key settings will be published in the New Zealand Gazette . • I will also issue a press release. • The Depart ment will inform councils and key interest groups, such as Grey Power and Age Concern, of the adjustments to the Scheme. • Details of the adjustments will also be shown on the Department’s Rates Rebate webpage. Why not adjust the Scheme by using the average wage (as with Superannuation) rather than with increases to the Consumer Price Index (CPI)? • If I was to adjust the Scheme using the average wage, we would need to review the Scheme at a more strategic level . • This would need to be a comprehensive re view in the context of other subsidies and supplements that are currently available to low -income households. • Such a review could not be completed in time for an adjustment to the Sche me to take effect on 1 July 2023 . • Adjusting the Scheme with average wag e growth would also likely exceed the current appropr iation for 2023 -24. Why does the adjustment need Cabinet approval every year? • In 2008, Cabinet decided that the two key settings of the Scheme should be adjusted each year to reflect the increase in CPI for the previous calendar year. I expect to provide the proposed Order to the Cabinet Legislation Committee (LEG) in (following the enactment of the Local Government (Water Services) Bill) to seek authorisation for submission to the Executive Council. Background Why are national wastewater standards needed? 19. Much of the wastewater infrastructure in New Zealand was built 30 to 40 years ago and is approaching the end of its useful life. Around 50 percent of New Zealand’s wastewater treatment plants service populations of 1000 or less, meaning the costs are disproportionately spread across a smaller ratepayer base. 20. A 2021 report prepared by the New Zealand Infrastructure Commission – Te Waihanga looked at the cost of consenting infrastructure projects in New Zealand. 1 The report found the cost of consenting to be considerably higher in the waste and water sectors, which was largely driven by the amount of expert advice and intensive engagement required. The report also found that the most significant indirect costs we re those associated with delay. Funding is often set aside for infrastructure upgrades, yet unable to be used due to significant delays in the consenting stage. The cost of construction and availability of resource may change considerably in the meantime, resulting in higher costs. 21. New Zealand lacks a national approach to managing wastewater discharges and overflows, as well as to monitoring and reporting. The current system: results in expensive and inconsistent bespoke arrangements for wastewater discharge consents and consent conditions, with a lack of certainty for network operators when they plan and fund individual plants; adds expense and time to consent processes involving multiple rounds of engagement; and disincentivises councils from addressing wastewater overflows, due to inconsistent definitions and approaches that impact the management of the scale and frequency of overflows. 22. Approximately 60 percent of wastewater treatment plants will require reconsenting in the next 10 years, including approximately 20 percent of plants already operating on expired consents. Implementing improvements to consenting processes now will ensure the benefits can be quickly realised by a large number of wastewater network operators, the majority of whom are councils. What benefits will the wastewater standards provide? 23. Establishing national wastewater standards will set clear requirements that must be met by wastewater infrastructure. The standards will provide a framework which broadly takes into account the receiving environment (e.g. ocean, freshwater, high and low mixing environments, and land). 24. This enables some flexibility for councils to make decisions locally about where they should discharge wastewater (e.g. water or land), and then apply the relevant standard in their consent application. The standards will provide a clear consenting pathway for each wastewater network.
Page 3 of 10 Local Government ( Water Services ) Bill policy dec isions 17. While the Bill goes through its select committee process , further policy proposals for Local Water Done Well are due to be considered by Cabinet in June and July 2024. They will be presented in the Local Government ( Water Services ) Bill and will provide for the long -term replacement regime , including new service delivery models, the planning framework, economic regulation , consumer protection and refinements to the current water service regulatory system settings. These will all be underpinned by the requirements to achieve financial sustainability and will be supported by an updated assistance and intervention regime . Overview of the Bill ’s key components 18. The Local Government (Water Services Preliminary Arrangements) Bill will set up the preliminary arrangements for councils to transition from their current arrangements to their future, financially sustainable models. 19. The Bill contains three substantive parts : 19.1 Part 2 includes requirements for councils to submit water services delivery plans within 12 months of the Act coming into force. These plans will provide information on councils ’ current water services arrangements and detail a strategy for how they will achieve the delivery of financially sustainable and resilient water services (subpart 1) . Cabinet has previously agreed that Councils can use repurposed Better Off funding to support the implementation of Local Water Done Well, which will include using some of their existing funding to support the development of water services delivery plans [ECO -24-MIN -0034] ; 19.2 bespoke Ministerial powers in relation to the statutory deadlines and requirements of the water services delivery plans (subpart 2); and 19.3 provision for certain councils to be required to provide further information in relation to water services. This information will be collected by the Commerce Commission and be used to inform long -term economic regulation. Councils will be subject to this enhanced requirement via an Order in Council upon Ministerial recommendation (subpart 3) . 19.4 Part 3 provides for streamlined consultation and decision -making processes which territorial authorities may voluntarily take up if they wish to establish or amend water services council- controlled organisations. These streamlined requirements compl ement and modify the relevant provisions in the Local Government Act 2002 . 19.5 Part 4 provides the legislative provisions for a financially separate Watercare . The Bill: 19.5.1 places a statutory prohibition o n financial support from Auckland Council to Watercare; 19.5.2 imposes the statutory obligation to continue to provide water supply and wastewater services on Watercare, together with statutory protections from privatisation; 19.5.3 gives the Minister of Local Government powers to appoint a Crown Review Team, Crown Monitor, or Crown Manager to Watercare in the event of a significant problem; 29e1n91k9v 2024-05-23 11:05:19 Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE

The NEDS would enable a national approach to standards and requirement for the design and construction of water services network infrastructure (e.g. similar sized manhole covers for drains across New Zealand). While the transition from the existing codes to the NEDS will be challenging, councils and the water sector have been calling for national standards for water for many years. 10. The National Transition Unit (NTU) under the previous three waters reform was progressing work on NEDS and had developed and consulted on four NEDS for drinking water networks, wastewater gravity networks, wastewater pumped systems, and stormwater networks. The four draft NEDS were circulated to the sector in September 2023.While sector feedback was received and recorded, the draft NEDS were not updated and finalised. 11. We provided you with advice [LG20242359] on the cost of finalising the four draft NEDS, so that they would be available as a voluntary standard, which was estimated to be around $150K - $200K. While we believe this still reflects the costs to finalise the existing drafts, further work and costs will be incurred to provide for the additional requirements to implement the mandatory NEDS. Proposed Approach to implement National Engineering Design Standards 12. The following sets out our proposed approach to establish the regulatory power to implement mandatory NEDS. Water service providers (councils or water services organisations) will be required to incorporate the NEDS into their engineering codes of practice (as they apply to water services water services network infrastructure). Subject to transitional arrangements discussed below, the NEDS will replace all locally developed engineering codes of practice. Page 3 of 26 Background 14. Earlier this year, I was asked to report back to Cabinet with options to refocus the water services reforms, looking particularly at three priority areas: 14.1 the number of entities and their boundaries; 14.2 how Māori rights and interests are reflected in the new system; 14.3 the timing and sequencing of implementation. 15. On 11 April 2023, Cabinet considered the first of a series of paper s reporting back on these areas, Refocusing the water services reforms: strategy and urgent decisions [CAB- 23-MIN- 0143]. 16. In that paper, I explained that, while there continues to be a strong rationale for reform, it ha s become clear that the four-entity reform model presents challenges for community acceptability . There continue to be concerns across local communities that this model for water service delivery results in loss of local influen ce and voice. 17. To help address this issue, I obtained agreement to proceed with a new model, in which there will be 10 water services entities instead of four. The new entities will be more closely based around existing regions, and every territorial autho rity owner will be represented on the regional representative group. This approach will better align the entities to communities of interest, thereby strengthening local representation and influence . 18. I also explained that moving to a model involving more entities would have a number of implications, and mean s we will forgo some of the economic benefits associated with the four -entity model . However, there are ways to recoup some of the scale economies that might otherwise be lost due to smaller entities, such as through financing mechanisms and shared services/functions across entities . 19. Further work has been undertaken to develop proposals on entity financing mechanisms and shared services arrangements. I am seeking decisions on these proposals through this paper. 20. I am also seeking to confirm the detailed proposals on the other matters that were signalled in my previous paper – where these need to be given effect through legislation. The remaining areas will be included in a third paper, in June 2023, cove ring implementation and financial implications. Page 3 of 4 • The Rates Rebate Act 1973 (the Act), specifies that adjustments to the key settings of the Scheme should be made by way of Order in Council by substituting any amount for any amount specified in subsection 1 of the Act. • Adjusting the two key settings of the Scheme each year ensures that Cabinet is responsive to cost of living changes. What impact will the Future for Local Government review have on the Scheme? • The review is wide -ranging in scope and has proposed that a ‘ke y shift’ is required to support more equitable funding and may identify specific mechanisms for supporting low-income households. • The review’s equitable funding ‘shift’ and other feedback on the Scheme’s efficacy present an opportunity for me to assess th e strategic issues of the Scheme. • Whilst this is ongoing, maintenance of the Scheme as is proposed in this paper remains prudent. • My officials have informed me that they will be assessing the strategic issues facing the Scheme in the latter half of this year and will report back to me with any recommendations to consider in the context of the Future for Local Government review. What impact will the Water Services Reform Programme have on the Scheme? • Clause 22 new section 318 of the Water Services Leg islation Bill 2023 would amend the definition of rates to include water service entities charges. • Amending the Act to include water charges is likely to be fiscally neutral, except in Auckland where the council currently ‘tops up’ the central government f unded rebate as if Watercare bills were a rate. This costs Auckland Council about $500,000 per year. • The changes are planned to come into effect in July 2024 when the water services entities go live, and so at this stage will have no impact on the uptake o f the Scheme for the 2023/24 rating year. What impact will the high level of inflation have on the Scheme? • Adjusting the settings of the Scheme to reflect the high level of inflation will help provide support to recipients with the impacts of the increase in the cost of living. • The adjustment to the key settings of the Scheme reflects the increase of 7.2 per cent of the CPI. The Scheme’s appropriation takes this into account and the total cost of rebates paid for 2023/24 is expected to fall with in it. • The adjustment of the Scheme is consistent with the raise in Superannuation for 2023, which was also at the same percentage. This briefing seeks your agreement to adjust the 2023/24 maximum rates rebate and income abatement threshold for the Rates Rebate Scheme (the Scheme) in line with the 7.2 percent increase in the Consumer Price Index (CPl).1 Background 2. The Scheme allows low-income ratepayers to access a rebate on their council rates. 3. Applicants apply for a rebate directly to their council and, if successful, they either have their rebate applied to their rates account or are paid a cash refund if their rate:s have been paid in full. The Department of Internal Affairs (the Department) then reimburses the council. 4. Eligible applicants include: 4.1 residents who are ratepayers for the property to which the rebate is being claimed; and 4.2 residents who own a non-separately rated unit in a retirement village, and who contribute to the outgoings of the retirement village; and 4.3 on Maori land, residents of individual houses on the same block (upon request). 5. The applicant's income used in the assessment is that earned from the previous tax year. For example, a person applying for a rebate in the year from 1 July 2023 to 30 June 2024 is assessed on their income for the financial year ending 31 March 2023:. The definition of income also includes an applicant's partner's income. Adjustment history 6. In 2008, Cabinet agreed that the maximum rebate and income abatement threshold should be adjusted annually, in line with movements in the CPI for the previous calendar year [CAB Min (08) 14/ 1 (32) refers]. The maximum rebate available and the income abatement threshold have been adjusted in most years since 2008. 2 7. In 2022/23, you agreed to adjust the Scheme's key settings by 5.9 percent, in line with CPI. The maximum rebate increased from $665 to $700, and the maximum income abatement threshold increased from $26,510 to $28,080, as stated in section 3(1) of the Rates Rebate Act 1973 (the Act). Previously identified issues with the Rates Rebates Scheme 8. In December 2022, we informed you that the Department has been preparing to provide advice to you to address identified issues with the Scheme. Given the complexity and overlapping mandate with other government departments, and the full work programme of the Branch, this has not been a priority. We expect to finalise our advice providing options through the Briefing to the Incoming Minister at the end of this year. 1 The CPI number is the percentage movement in the all groups index for the calendar year. 2 There was no adjustment made to the maximum rebate available for the 2016/17 rating year. The CPI for the year ended 31 December 2015 was 0.1 per cent which was too low to result in an adjustment to the maximum rebate available, rounded to the nearest $10.
