Amendments to the Water Services Act 2021 20. On 15 April 2024, Cabinet approved the policy proposals tabled by the Minister Responsible for RMA Reform in the paper First Resource Management Act Amendment Bill: Addressing a Small Number of Time Critical Changes [CAB -24-MIN -121.01]. Cabinet agreed for the amendment of the Resource Management Act 1991 (RMA) to exclude the hierarchy of obligations contained in the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management 2020 (NPS -FM) from resource consent applications and consenting decision -making processes. That Bill is due to be enacted by the end of 2024. 21. Te Mana o te Wai informs how the NPS -FM is implemented. Te Mana o te Wai imposes a hierarchy of obligations that prioritise the health and wellbeing of water first over the health and needs of people and the ability of people and communities to provide for their social, economic and cultural well -being. 22. I received advice on the implications of excluding the hierarchy of obligations in the NPS-FM on Taumata Arowai - the Water Services Regulator when setting wastewater standards and on councils when issuing consents for wastewater treatment plants. Under th e Water Services Act 2021, Taumata Arowai must give effect to Te Mana o te Wai when undertaking any function, power or duty and may develop wastewater environmental performance standards. Taumata Arowai have begun developing wastewater standards consistent with the current provisions. These standards are expected to be operational from mid -2025 and will apply when new consents are issued. If the hierarchy of obligations is removed from consenting decisions but is in place when the standards are formulated, councils will still be bound by the likely higher standard. 23. I was authorised by Cabinet to determine if amendments to the Water Services Act 2021 are required to ensure consistency with the proposed changes to the RMA, specifically whether the Te Mana o te Wai hierarchy of obligations should be disapplied to the setting of the wastewater standards. Interim amendments to the Water Services Act 2021 are recommended to ensure that Taumata Arowai do not apply the hierarchy of obligations when developing wastewater standards. This will mean that councils will be able to issue consents consistent with the Government’s new approach to the NPS -FM. I expect to provide a longer -term solution through the Local Government (Water Services) Bill which will address the regulatory settings for Taumata Arowai in more detail. 24. I have asked officials to instruct Parliamentary Counsel Office to draft minor and transitional amendments to the Water Services Act 2021, to align the Government’s approach to hierarchy of obligations relating to Te Mana o te Wai. This is consistent with the Cabinet decisions referred to above. 29e1n91k9v 2024-05-23 11:05:19 Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE
Page 4 of 10 25. Councils will still need to get consents for their wastewater networks/treatment plants, but the process will be much simpler as regional councils will not need to create bespoke sets of consent conditions for each network/plant. Instead, all parties will know the requirements from the outset and once granted, all consents that the standards apply to will be for a 35 -year period. This standardisation and longer consent duration will eliminate some consenting costs as many plants are currently granted with s hort to medium term consent durations. It will also enable greater certainty of costs for councils in the management of their wastewater networks and in consenting processes. 26. Wastewater standards provide an opportunity to: give clear environmental performance expectations to communities for wastewater infrastructure; streamline consent processes; provide certainty to councils as network owners about the costs of infrastructure investments and upgrades; ta ke advantage of economies of scale in plant design, procurement and operator capability / training; make compliance and enforcement more achievable and transparent; and enable performance benchmarking, to drive improved efficiencies and environmental outco mes over time. There will be further benefits once infrastructure design solutions are in place 27. The Bill provides for a new discretionary regulatory tool – ‘infrastructure design solutions’ which will support the use of modular infrastructure for waste water treatment plants. The solutions will set out the design and operating requirements for standardised modular wastewater treatment plants or components that are deemed to meet the wastewater standards. The infrastructure design solutions will be simila r to Acceptable Solutions, such as those relating to drinking water (under the Water Services Act 2021), and under the Building Act 2004. 28. Infrastructure design solutions will result in faster consenting processes and potentially significant cost savings, and over time will enable network operators to standardise the design and procurement of infrastructure, and enable modular, off -the-shelf solutions to be installed. 29. The infrastructure design solutions are initially likely to focus on small treatment plants. They are not in the scope of consultation on proposed wastewater standards. They will be developed and publicly consulted on once enabled through legislation as part of the implementation of the standards. What cost efficiencies will be achieved? 30. The proposed wastewater standards are expected to deliver significant cost-efficiencies that may include reduced consenting costs of up to 40 percent based on case study. This includes reductions in costs associated with the consenting process including staff time, technical assessments, feasibility assessments, legal costs and consultation and engagement costs. 31. In some cases, there may also be reductions to capital upgrade costs and ongoing operating costs such as staff training and maintenance. The cost savings on an individual plant will depend on specific circumstances, such as the type or size of the plant, t reatment processes, and options for where the plant discharges. However, over time, further costs savings are expected as materials are standardised, and modular options are available that comply with wastewater standards. The NEDS will apply to following parties and circumstances:  private developers or contractors seeking to vest (transfer ownership and responsibility for operation and maintenance of water services network infrastructure) to water services providers;  private developers or contractors proposing to connect water services network infrastructure to the “public” network; and  the maintenance, renewal, upgrade or decommissioning of new or existing public water services network infrastructure by water services providers. 17. The NEDS standards and requirements will sit alongside any other statutory requirements that may apply to water services providers, developers, or contractors. This could include the Resource Management Act 1991, the Building Act 2004, or relevant Health and Safety requirements. Oversight and administration of the National Engineering Design Standards 18. We are proposing that the Water Services Authority – Taumata Arowai (the Authority) should provide for the oversight and administration of the NEDS. 19. Our view is that there is synergy between the existing functions of the Authority to set standards and approve process and products across all water services network infrastructure. We think that consolidating the NEDS with those other standards will enable all those standards to be more effective and the process for their development more efficient. Further cost -efficiencies are expected once infrastructure design solutions are in place by enabling standardised wastewater treatment plants or components of treatment plants to be commissioned and delivered faster. 33. Additional information about potential cost -efficiencies is provided in the discussion document, the interim Regulatory Impact Statement (attached as Appendix B )and attached factsheets: Wastewater and Stormwater Environmental Performance Standards, and Infrastructure Design Solutions (Appendix C ). What will the standards cover? 34. I am proposing to set four sets of draft wastewater standards. The standards will cover discharge to water, discharge to land, beneficial re -use of biosolids, and risk -based monitoring and reporting requirements for wastewater network overflows. 35. The proposed standards will target cost -effective ways to manage wastewater plants and networks while protecting public health and the environment. The initial tranche of standards focuses on the main contaminants from wastewater treatment plants. 36. The standards will also take particular account of small wastewater treatment plants (serving populations of less than 1,000). This is because approximately half of New Zealand’s treatment plants service populations of this size. These plants have characte ristics that are different to those that service larger towns and cities. 37. The wastewater standards proposals are only intended to apply to wastewater treatment arrangements that service communities (that is, treatment plants and significant reticulated networks). The standards may apply to all public networks (owned by a territo rial authority or its service delivery arm such as a council- controlled organisation, a government department, or the New Zealand Defence Force). 38. The proposals are not intended to apply to privately owned networks, onsite systems that treat wastewater within the same property boundary, or small wastewater systems that service schools or camping grounds (such as those operated by the Department of Co nservation or the Ministry of Education). Treatment arrangements of this nature will be excluded as part of the drafting when the Order in Council for the wastewater standards are prepared. Nature of the standards 39. Under the current legislation, any standards are ‘minimum’ standards, which means a regional council considering an application for a resource consent that relates to a wastewater network could not grant a consent with conditions that are less restrictive than the standards. They could impose conditions over and above the standard. 40. In July 2024, Cabinet agreed to amend the Water Services Act 2021 and Resource Management Act 1991 (the RMA) to make changes to how wastewater standards will be implemented through resource consents [CAB -24-MIN -0277.3 refers]. The Minister of Local Governm ent was authorised to work with the Minister Responsible for RMA Reform (and other Ministers) to develop the appropriate policy approach and the necessary legislative changes. 41. These changes will be implemented through the Local Government (Water Services) Bill (the Bill). The Bill proposes wastewater standards are a single standard rather than a minimum (or maximum) that must be implemented by regional councils in resource consents and cannot be exceeded, apart from on an “exceptions” basis. We think there are significant benefits for a regulatory system (both for regulators and those who are regulated) from consolidating the national oversight, performance monitoring and standard setting for wastewater, and stormwater water services network infrastructure within one regulator - the Authority. 21. For water service providers and the water services industry, a consistent regulatory approach for three waters networks will provide clarity and certainty on network standards and requirements. Those standards and requirements will need to be consistent with the Authority’s renewed mandate, to ensure that costs are proportionate. 22. Consolidating all the three waters standard setting in the Authority will build stronger and more effective relationships with water sector. Through its work on wastewater standards, the Authority is already building those relationships, and these can be leveraged to support the development and implementation of the NEDS. 23. However, we acknowledge that administering the NEDS will require the Authority to broaden its capacity and capability from predominately science-based regulation to include engineering-based regulation. While these capabilities are already required to deliver infrastructure design solutions for wastewater treatment, the inclusion of this new function for the Authority will require an uplift in that standard setting capacity and capacity. 24. In considering whether the Authority should administer the NEDS, we evaluated whether this task would be better allocated to Crown Infrastructure Partners (CIP). While the content requirements of the NEDS fall within their capabilities and it has synergies with their wider infrastructure and procurement roles, they do not have the same level of focus or connection to three waters services that the Authority has. 25. We also note that as CIP transitions to become the future National Infrastructure Agency, they will go through a period of transition and establishment as they build their full set of functions, and there is a risk that progress on the NEDS could be reprioritised as wider priorities are reallocated across the infrastructure sector (e.g. the reprioritisation of the NES on infrastructure) and subsequently delayed. 26. However, while we are proposing that the Authority should have the legislative accountability for administering the NEDS, we think that it is important that the development of the NEDS is aligned with wider network infrastructure standards. To provide that assurance, we propose that CIP should provide a technical review of the NEDS ahead of wider consultation (discussed below). Page 5 of 14 level of regulation in relation to Class 4 gambling in terms of both topic s covered and the level of prescription, providing the opportunity for a much stronger harm reduction approach. 24 New Zealand takes a public health approach to reducing harm from gambling. My officials assessed the Regulations against best practice approaches for harm minimisation and identified some key gaps. The current regulations do not adequately use some of the key levers for reducing pokies harm – controls in the gam bling venue, restrict ions on machine features, and enforcement tools to drive compliance. For example, the current regulations: • do not specify procedures for harm minimisation policies, such as how and when venue staff should check on players ; • have few restrictions on the gaming features known to attract players and encourage continuous play; and • have no associated infringement offences. 25 The legislative framework provides an opportunity to create a stronger harm minimisation approach. The matters to be covered in the discuss ion document , outlined in the next section, are expected to be relatively uncontroversial, although stakeholders will likely have different views on the optimal approach. Overview of the Discussion Document 26 I am seeking agreement to consult with stakeholders and the public on their views on ways to strengthen the requirements in the Regulations, through the discussion document , Reducing Pokies Harm , attached to this paper as Appendix B. 27 Comparing the current regulations against best practice approaches to harm reduction has identified the areas where improvements are needed and will be most effective. This resulted in three focus areas summarised below. • The venue : Government has not stipulated specific actions that venues must undertake. Staff who work at pubs and clubs lack the tools to identify problem gambling and intervene effectively. The mechanisms and criteria for intervening are either not prescribed or not clearly prescribed in organisation’s harm minimisation policies and practices . Training and record- keeping requirements need addressing . • The machines: The number , nature and impact of gaming machine features designed to keep people playing has increased significantly as technology has developed. There are considerable opportunities to reduce harm through restricting game features and jackpot branding . • Enforcement : Few of the chargeable offences and infringement offences in the Act relate to breaches of harm minimisation requirements, and there are no enforcement options for breaches of the current regulations. A strong enforcement toolkit needs a spectrum of responses, including proportionate, lower -level options for small to moderate breaches . Page 6 of 10 What engagement has informed the development of the standards so far? 42. The Authority has engaged with engineering and environmental industry experts and key stakeholders to ensure the proposed standards represent a cost effective and proportionate approach to consenting. A technical review group, made up of territorial author ities and regional councils, industry experts, members of the Water Services Authority Board and Māori Adv isory Group, has also provided the Authority with external assurance. 43. This engagement will result in a set of standards that: reflect appropriate treatment limits for treatment plants set by councils; are applicable to all plants, including those serving 1,000 or fewer people; and support efficient and cost -effective consent ing that balances risk and benefit while enabling effective environmental and public health protections. 44. The Authority has also engaged with a number of councils in their capacity as network operators, and with a number of regional councils as consenting authorities. This engagement has allowed the priorities and concerns of these councils to be incorporated in the proposed standards. 45. Feedback from smaller councils included concerns about affordability and ensuring that wastewater standards are tailored to the specific characteristics of their plants. Page 6 of 12 27.1 minimum technical standards for the design, construction and operational performance of three water network (reticulation) infrastructure; 27.2 information requirements (e.g. data standards) - these could be included directly in the NEDS or could reference other national asset data standards to reduce disruption; and 27.3 requirements for vesting water services network infrastructure and for connections to the network. 28. The technical standards will be performance based and the NEDS will include commentary and guidance on how to implement the standards and/or requirements. Variations 29. Although providing national consistency is a primary objective of the NEDS, there will be a need to enable some regional or local variations to the standards to reflect geographic, climatic and geological differences between regions that impact network performance. Potential examples of where a variation could be required include: 29.1 higher water volumes in areas subject to more extreme rainfall; 29.2 higher seismic design requirements in areas more susceptible to earthquakes; and 29.3 specific construction requirements where there may be specific soil types or geological conditions (e.g. potentially liquefiable soils). Approved products 30. A key feature of councils’ existing codes is the identification of “approved products” that are deemed to meet the standards and requirements in the codes. The inclusion of approved products mirrors the approach taken in the Building Code and provides a practical and cost-effective pathway for developers and contractors to determine what types of water services network infrastructure will meet the codes’ requirements for vesting or connecting to the network. 31. While providing for certification of approved products centrally by the Authority would have benefits in the current New Zealand context, it would be both costly and time consuming to certify all the products that are currently in use. This could cause significant disruption for both water services providers, the wider development community and suppliers. 32. To address those issues, we propose that we adapt the existing approach that is used to identify that building products meet the requirements of the New Zealand Building Code2. Under this model, the Authority can (subject to accreditation criteria) appoint “product approval bodies”. The “product approval bodies” would evaluate products against performance requirements of the NEDS and approve those products as suitable to be vested and/or connected to the public three waters network. Page 6 of 14 IN-CONFIDENCE Taumata Arowai Assurance of ongoing supply of drinking water in the Wellington Region On 21 February 2024, we sent a letter to Wellington Water asking for a risk mitigation plan to ensure there will not be an imminent risk to the ongoing supply of drinking water across the 2024/25 summer period . On 15 March 2024, Taumata A rowai received a reply from Wellington Water and its council owners. On 22 March 2024 , we wrote again to Wellington Water letting them know that the response did not set out a robust, measurable plan against which Wellington Water and its owner councils co uld be held to account. We requested specific information by 28 March 2024, advising that if satisfactory information was not supplied , Taumata Arowai would consider using more directive tools. We will provide you with a briefing by 4 April 2024 setting out what has been provided by Wellington Water and our assessment of their plan to avoid a severe water shortage next year. Clutha District Council’s Lawrence supply Taumata Arowai has been reviewing Clutha District Council’s Drinking Water Safety Plans, including the plan for the Lawrence drinking water supply. The Lawrence supply takes water from Phoenix Dam, which is treated using filtration, chlorination, and ultraviolet disinfection before being distributed to 430 consumers. The review of the Lawrence supply included a site visit that identified several concerns. These include highly coloured water and signs of cattle activity in the dam, insufficient infrastructure to monitor the supply, key treatment processes not working effectively (with mu ltiple activated alarms), and signs of rodent activity (coupled with open water channels) inside the treatment plant. We met with the Clutha District Mayor and Chief Executive on 20 March 2024, and followed up with a letter on 21 March 2024 . Clutha Distric t Council issued a boil water notice for the Lawrence supply on 22 March 2024 . In our letter to the Clutha District Council on 21 March 2024, we asked Clutha to provide a plan of how they intend to manage the risks identified by 27 March 2024 . We will prov ide further update s to you if there are ongoing concerns. Virus prevalence in Canterbury groundwaters project In November 2022, Christchurch City Council applied for an exemption to the contact time rule in the drinking water rules. This rule requires wate r to be held in a tank after chlorine is added, to allow time for it to kill any viruses. The exemption was not granted because it was for a process that is for primary disinfection, and exemptions can only be granted for residual (secondary) disinfection. The cost to the council to comply with this rule is hundreds of thousands of dollars, but the level of virus risk in the Canterbury groundwaters is not well understood. The Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs has delegated authority to progress drafting for this amendment [CAB -22-MIN- 0207]. Confirming proposals for community priority statements 41. In the April 2023 paper, I noted that proposals are being developed for a new instrument, which would give community groups who have an interest in a water body an opportunity to make statements to their entity about their priorities for that body. I committed to report back with detailed proposals in this follow- up paper. 42. I am proposing that provisions for ‘community priority statements’ would be included in the legislation. These new instruments will provide communities with an avenue to communicate their interests in a body of water , and their priorities for how the environmental impacts of the entities’ activities on that body of water might be managed . These statements would be a valuable source of information for the entities, when it comes to their planning and engagement processes , and decisions about investment in infrastructure . 43. I am proposing the legislation clarifies that co mmunity priority statements c an be made by any legal person 1, providing that person has a local connection with the water body and entity service area . National- level bodies would not be able to make one of these statements, unless they can demonstrate a local presence and connection. 44. The statements must relate to a water body in the entity’s service area , and the person providing the statement must state the interest they have in the body of water. The statements would focus on priorities relating to the body of water, and are not a vehicle for c ustomers to comment on service provision or pricing. The re are separate consultation and engagement mechanisms to gather feedback on those matters . 45. I am proposing that the s tatements would be submitted to entities’ regional representative groups . They could then consider the themes raised in these statements when providing direction to the entities, and commenting on planning documents (under Schedule 3 of the Water Services Entities Act). 46. Regional representative groups may wish to seek advice and support from the consumer forums that must be established by the entities (under the Act) , particularly if they need help to manage a large volume of statements . The legislative role of the consumer forums would be expanded to include responsibilities to advise regional representative groups and the entities on any community priority statements they have received.

Cost -of-living implications 52. The proposals in the discussion document are intended to lead to cost savings for councils who operate wastewater treatment plants, and for regional councils who are responsible for consenting, and ultimately for communities and ratepayers. Where the standards apply to Crown network operators, cost efficiencies are also likely to be achieved. 53. As well as reductions in consenting costs there may also be reductions to capital upgrade costs and ongoing operating costs such as staff training and maintenance. The costs savings on an individual plant will depend on specific circumstances, such as the type or size of the plant, treatment processes, and options for where the plant discharges. However, over time, further costs savings are expected as materials are standardised, and modular options are available that comply with wastewater standards. Financial implications 54. There are no Crown financial implications associated with this proposal. Legislative implications 55. The proposals in this Cabinet paper have no implications for primary legislation. Page 7 of 12 Authority would maintain a register of product approval bodies, and approved products. 33. While a product approval body could be an industry provider, we anticipate that (at least initially) they will primarily be water service providers. Water service providers are also best placed to monitor the ongoing performance of “approved products”. 34. We think it is likely that most, if not all, of the existing approved products will meet the NEDS requirement, given that the initial drafts have been drawn from best practice approaches in existing councils’ engineering codes of practice. This will reduce the potential disruption on suppliers and the sector of introducing the NEDS. 35. The national register of "approved products" (maintained by the Authority) will support water service providers to identify other suitable products that are used in other regions. We think that over time, the current regional differences in approved products will reduce as “approved products” are adopted nationally. 36. To ensure that new products can be identified and deployed quickly, provision should also be made in NEDS, to enable alternative solutions (like the approach in the building code), where the developers or contractors and water service providers can agree to adopt alternative processes or approaches that meet the NEDS performance standards. Review, consultation and adoption 37. We are proposing that Water Services Authority may review the NEDS at any time to respond to new approaches or issues but that a review should occur at least every five years. When reviewing the NEDS, the Authority should be required to consult with the public, industry bodies, the economic regulator and other relevant infrastructure agencies 38. The NEDS will need to be developed with appropriate technical and sector input, and reviewed regularly as new engineering methodology and products are developed. Our engagement with the water sector has highlighted the importance of ensuring that both the industry and waters services providers are well represented on any technical reference groups that may be established to support the development of the NEDS. 39. As we have noted above, through its work on wastewater standards, the Authority is already building relationships with the water sector. We think it is already well placed to establish the industry and water sector technical reference groups needed to support the development and implementation of the NEDS. 40. To ensure that there is appropriate oversight of the NEDS, we propose that their development should be subject to the same requirements as the drinking water standards and wastewater standards, which includes an Order in Council process (including the preparation of a regulatory impact assessment). Page 7 of 26 47. In addition, I am proposing the legislation is amended so that the chief executive of a water services entity would have to set out how the entity will respond to community priority statements. This would occur through an annual consumer engagement stocktake, which is an existing mechanism for the entity to report on consumer and community views. These annual stocktakes would include reporting on matters such as the number of community priority statements that have been submitted, key themes, and actions the entity will take or has taken in response to them. 48. It is important to note that there is no change to the legislative requirements to give effect to Te Mana o te Wai, or the ability of mana whenua to make Te Mana o te Wai statements under the Water Services Entities Act. The proposed new instrument is distinct from the Te Mana o te Wai statement. 49. Under the Act, Te Mana o te Wai statements for water services may be provided to a water services entity by ma na whenua whose rohe or takiwā includes a water body in the service area , or whose interests in the service area are recognised in a Treaty settlement a ct. Under my new proposals, Māori communities or individuals who are not mana whenua would also be able to provide a community priority statement (for example , a community group who undertake planting or restoration work on a relevant water body ). 50. Under the Act, all persons performing or exercising duties, functions, or powers under the A ct must give effect to Te Mana o te Wai, to the extent Te Mana o te Wai applies to those duties, functions or powers. Entities must also respond to Te Mana o te Wai statements issued to them by mana whenua. 51. The requirement to give effect to Te Mana o te Wai is a requirement that has been in place in the resource management system since 2014. Te Mana o te Wai statements are a structured way to enable water services entities to give effect to Te Mana o te Wai, as they make investment decisions in areas like wastewater services where mana whenua have long -standing interests. Te Mana o te Wai statements also provide a strong link to enabl e the entities to be work well with their Treaty partners , and to support Treaty settlement obligations that exist at place ( such as Waikato river settlements). 52. Community priority statements will not have the same legal weighting as Te Mana o te Wai statements, but will be a valuable input that I expect regional representative groups, entity boards and chief executives to consider. 53. The other difference is that an entity has to include information on actions it plans to take, or has taken, in response to a Te Mana o te Wai statement in its planning and reporting documents (for example, statement of intent or asset management plan). Responses to community priority statements would be included in the annual consumer engagement stocktake. As these statements are provided to regional representative groups, they may take the themes raised into account when setting the strategic direction of the entity . Page 8 of 10 “The panel considers that the information and analysis summarised in the interim RIS partially meets the quality assurance criteria. The interim RIS accompanies a public consultation document on proposed national wastewater environmental performance standards (wastewater standards). The consultation document seeks views on standards covering specific areas (discharge of wastewater to la nd and water, reuse of biosolids, and monitoring and reporting requirements for wastewater network overflows). The interim RIS sets out analysis that narrows the scope of the wastewater standards to these areas. The interim RIS sets out assumptions and limitations on analysis. This includes having wastewater standards in place as soon as practicable after enactment of the Local Government (Water Services) Bill. This has impacted the assessment of the scope of the standards that can be implemented in the time available. The interim RIS also notes challenges with quantifying the savings from introducing wastewater standards. While efforts have been made to quantify savings, these are based on assumptions and will depend on the details of the wastewater standards. Updated analysis of potential savings that is based on the details of the proposed standards will be important for final policy decisions. The interim RIS partially meets the convincing criteria. It would have been improved with further information on what aspects of the current process for consenting wastewater treatment plants are working effectively and how these have been considered in developing the proposed standards. This information would be useful for final policy decisions. The interim RIS indicates a good level of early consultation on the details of the standards, which will be supported by the planned consultation process. However, the panel considers the interim RIS is only partially consulted because narrowing the scope of the standards to specific areas has not been widely consulted. The interim RIS is clear and complete given the stage in the policy process.” 59. This means gambling harm from pokie machines is experienced by those who are least resilient to impacts such as emotional and psychological distress, damage to relationships, child neglect, debt, family poverty, study and employment issues. The least resilient are less likely to be able to access services, and more likely to have other related health concerns such as those related to alcohol and smoking. 45 There is also a strong correlation between gambling on pokies and family violence, and a link to fraud and other related crimes. Women and children are particularly vulnerable to the strain caused by gambling harm. 46 Little is known regarding the extent to which disabled people experience gambling -related harm. Page 8 of 26 54. It is my intention that the two instruments are distinct and complementary. It is important that the mana of Te Mana o te Wai statements is protected and upheld in the legislative framework for these reforms, and the way in which the future entities and regulators conduct their business. Community priority statements have been designed to be distinct from Te Mana o te Wai statements , and are a separate mechanism. The distinction between the two mechanisms recognises the special taonga of water for mana whenua. Confirming details for a locally -led, voluntary merger process 55. As indicated in my previous paper, I consider it would be desirable to provide for a legislative process that allows water services entit ies to merge. This recognises that, in time, councils and communities in higher -cost regions may wish to see the benefits of further amalgamation, in terms of greater investment, increased efficiencies and service standards , and lower charges. 56. I expect this to be a locally -led process , with merger proposals formally initiated by regional representative groups . They could involve two or more existing entities merging to form a new entity. Mergers would proceed if agreed by 75 per cent of the regional representative group s (the threshold for their other decisions under the Act) . As described below, these decisions would be informed by the details contained in a merger proposal, and community consultation. 57. The legislation would need to include a few procedural requirements relating to the merger process, to ensure there is clarity to the entities, their customers and staff, council owners, mana whenua, and financial institutions about what is involved. 58. I am proposing there would be several steps in this process , involving the following components: 58.1 Step 1: Internal investigation s by a n entity of the merits of a merger . This would include informal discussions with the other entity (or entities) about this proposal, and reaching an agreement on whether to proceed to the next step. These initial investigations could be prompted by various s ources – including suggestions by an entity board, its owners, and/or consumers. It could also be suggested by one of the statutory assistance and intervention bodies under the Water Services Entities Act (Crown Observer, Crown Review Team, or Crown Manage r) or through the system -wide review processes in that Act. 58.2 Step 2: Formal initiation of a merger proposal. This would be done by agreement by the regional representative group. It would involve formal identification of the other entity (or entities) that would be party to the merger – and an obligation on that entity to consider the proposal. It would also include notifying the responsible Minister and monitor (under the Water Services Entities Act) of the proposal; public notification; and notifying any other entities with which there are service agreements in place. Part B – Game features 55. Part B considers how gambling harm can be reduced at its source, by reducing harm associated with the gaming machine experience. 56. The proposals selected for Part B of the discussion document may help improve at -risk users’ ability to control their gambling, reduce spending and time spent gambling. 57. The proposals are based on (a) information to address the fallacy of having any ‘control’ in the game, and (b) removing some of the key ‘reinforcing’ features that keep people gambling. Option s Description and discussion 11. Pokies machines could be required to display more information (such as: return to player; volatility of games; harm minimisation messages). RTP (return to player) ratio of games The r atio refers to the level of loss a player should expect on average when playing a particular game. Most games in NZ are set at the higher end of the 78% to 92% requirements (e.g. near 92%, or $0.08 lost for a single game bet of $1). Providing information on this aspect of the game is not likely to assist players when choosing between different games or machines. However, being informed (and reminded) of the level of loss they should expect when they gamble on a machine could assist with better decision- making, for those that struggle to control thei r gambling. Volatility of games The likelihood of winning as well as the likely size of wins. A highly volatile game gives a low chance of winning, but wins are likely to be large. A low volatility game gives a high chance of winning, but wins are likely to be low. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Regulatory Impact Statement | 12 Being informed about volatility of games may help at -risk players make decisions, especially those who are chasing losses, and assessing the likelihood of regaining those losses. Harm minimisation messaging Currently gaming machines are required to periodically provide information about how much money has been gambled and how much has been lost. This provides potentially useful information to the person using the machine, but also a break. Stronger messaging suggesting a break (or even offering to stop the game for a period) could be used. Messaging could also be made more prominent. 12. Display losses as losses Stop partial losses being presented as wins . Th at is, a user might gamble $2.50 on a single game and have a return of $0.50 – but this will usually be presented as a $0.50 win, even though the user has lost $2. Providing information about the amount that was lost, instead of presenting the amount of the user’s own money they didn’t lose on a gamble as a win, could help at -risk users understand and better assess their chances of winning or losing. 13. Prevent the ability to make multi -row bets Multiple lines operate together to disguise losses as wins. Preventing multi -row bets could reduce harm by not disguising losses and might make EGMs less attractive and reduce the speed at which money is spent . 14. Reduce maximum stake of $2.50 The current maximum stake of $2.50 is relatively low compared to s ome other jurisdictions but c onsideration could be given to reducing the maximum stake – for instance $2, $1.50, or $1. This would likely reduce the level of harmful gambling but could impact on people who currently gamble without harm, making gaming machines gambling less attractive for that group. 15. Prevent or limit the number of “free spins” Research shows that gamblers prefer to play EGMs with free spi ns. Free spins have been associated with loss of control over time and money spent gambling. Free spins have also been explicitly linked to the notion of getting ‘value for money’ which was attractive both to social and problem gamblers. Preventing or limiting free spins may reduce the attractiveness of the EGM to problem gamblers, as well as others. 16. Maximum number of games in an hour Pokies machines have a maximum number of games that could be pl ayed in an hour . This could lead players to take a break from playing. 17. More information and restrictions on jackpots Pokie machines could be required to provide information about how much of any stake is being used for jackpots . Maximum jackpot size could be reduced. Signage showing jackpot levels could be prohibited. 58. Some of our initial thinking on the Part B proposals, below, has been provided in the discussion document for validation or feedback : • These options could lead to reductions in time/money spent gambling and/or breaks in play, so gamblers get out of the ‘ gambling zone’. • Some changes could take longer to implement depending on the complexity (e.g. whether both current and new machines must comply with the new regulations, or just new machines). • Any software changes would need to consider and be consistent with international gaming machine standards. • Cost is dependent on specific changes. Changes to machine features will incur software costs – which will vary depending on the option and rollout requirements. • Pokie machines are becoming increasingly addictive due to technological developments and game features will become ever more sophisticated. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Regulatory Impact Statement | 13 • Changes to game features will have an impact on reducing gambling harm, but the size of the impact is uncertain. • Some people engage with technical information such as odds / volatility more than others.

Paying for water services 52. I recommend that residential property owners continue to be liable for water services payments, including for both fixed costs (costs of connection and maintaining the service) and consumption related charges. Currently, property owners pay rates, which include a component for three waters services. In Auckland, Watercare charges property owners for its drinking and wastewater services. 53. In situations where residential properties are occupied by tenants, Section 39 of the Residential Tenancies Act 1986 provi des for the landlord to be responsible for all outgoings that are incurred whether the property is occupied, such as general rates. The same section also provides that the tenant is responsible for all outgoings that are exclusively attributable to the ten ant’s occupation of the premises, including charges for water provided to the premises based on consumption. 54. I am not recommending changes to the Residential Tenancies Act 1986. I consider it appropriate that landlords should pay the fixed costs of water s ervices. These are a cost of property ownership that, in turn, may be reflected in the level of rent charged. Landlords should be able to pass on any variable cost directly to tenants. 55. I recommend that the property owner should be liable to the water services entity for the entire water bill, including consumption charges. This reflects the status quo in places that currently have volumetric water charging. My reasons for this approach are that: 55.1 requiring charges to be split between landlords and tenants would result in complex billing arrangements, and increased administrative costs that would be passed on to all consumers; Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page 10 of 41 55.2 water is an essential service and water servic es entities will not be allowed to disconnect service for non- payment. In general, property owners are good at paying their rates, with only one to two percent of rates bills unpaid. Tenants will have varying abilities to pay, and invoicing them directly f or consumption charges would result in higher collection and bad debt costs for the entities; 55.3 other things being equal, property -owning landlords should realise an equivalent reduction in their rates bill when water bills are split out from rates (though t his is dependent on decisions by territorial authorities); 55.4 landlords can pass waters services costs through to tenants via rents. 56. For commercial properties, there are a variety of arrangements depending on lease terms. I propose replicating the relevant provisions of the Local Government (Rating) Act 2002 (with suitable modification), which outline when lessees are liable for rates instead of the property owner. Trade waste charges are billed to the business generating the waste rather than the property owners. 57. I also propose replicating the relevant provisions of the Local Government (Rating) Act 2002 (with suitable modification), which outline who is responsible for paying rates for Māori freehold land.

Utaina! Audio-Visual preservation programme Utaina! is the collaborative programme between Archives New Zealand, the National Library and Ngā Taonga Sound & Vision to preserve the audio-visual (AV) heritage content of significance to the nation. Magnetic media used to capture defining moments in our nation’s history and experiences of New Zealanders through the decades is ageing and the equipment required to play it back is now rare or obsolete. Utaina! will transfer AV taonga from media such as open reel tape, VHS video tapes and compact cassettes into digital formats that both support long-term preservation and ofer greater opportunities for access by New Zealanders. 31 Department of Internal Affairs NGĀ TAKUNE RAUTAKI STRATEGIC INTENTIONS 2021-2025 A culture of reading enhances literacy and knowledge Developing literate citizens Research shows that reading can transform people’s lives. Three national reading initiatives are underway at the National Library to grow a nation of readers. The Communities of Readers initiative “Pūtoi Rito” was made possible with support from the Te Puna Foundation. Pūtoi Rito is working with four to six communities where there are significant inequities in access to books, libraries and reading role models. Community-led, the goal is to weave a whāriki of support to inspire a love of reading among tamariki and rangatahi. The newly established Te Awhi Rito New Zealand Reading Ambassador is a national role model advocating the importance of reading in the lives of young New Zealanders. Te Puna Foundation and other partners provided substantial support to make this role possible. The National Library also leads the He Pā Rito initiative, a cross-sectoral national conversation on the value and impact of reading. Pilots The Ministry proposes to fund a range of new pilot service models that address inequity related public health and intervention services. Examples include cultural models/services, language support, online services, public health messaging and access for isolated communities. Pilot costs are based on current full time equivalent (FTE) personnel costs at about $100,000 per year. The Ministry plans between three and five pilots of various sizes each year in the second and thi rd years, but a smaller number in the first year (2019/20), to allow for phasing. The Ministry does not currently know the exact size or number of these pilots; therefore, a more precise costing is not practical. The Ministry will meet the pilot evaluation costs from the research evaluation allocation. Technology The Ministry proposes to allocate a fund to support technology-related innovation. There is a strong consensus from both industry and service providers that the strategy should provide for greater use of technolog y to mitigate and manage gambling harm. The Ministry could use this fund to build on an established activity – such as potentially funding a database with facial recognition capabilities, or trialling venue management modules – or to develop online support tools or pilot tools to monitor and manage or limit player exposure to gambling harm. The Ministry will evaluate all trials. Peer support Peer support is a model that has been proven overseas and in New Zealand for other forms of addiction ( ‘peer’ in this context means a person who has had a similar kind of relevant experience to other people that has had a significant impact on their lives) . The formal evidence for peer support in mental health and addiction is growing, and shows high satisfaction from consumers of services. Outcomes from peer services are as good as if not better than conventional services, yet there currently are no funded peer support positions within gambling harm services. The Ministry proposes to encourage training for and trial the introduction of peer services during this levy period. Costs are based on providing support for workforce development/training in each year, plus funding additional peer support positions in years two and three . The Ministry has taken into account a range of factors, including current FTE costs and average peer support workers ’ salaries and training costs. There are a few ways in which the Ministry could support this aim; however, its preference is for a limited number of workforce development scholarships. The Ministry has not yet determined the workforce development component costs for this, as more investigation into potential demand and timing is necessary. Currently agreed funding declines from $19.845 million in 2021/22, to $11.655 million in 2022/23, and $1.500 million in 2023/24 and outyears. 30. We analyse d other regulated water utilities , including in Australia , to determine whether there was a clear relationship between asset level per connected citizen and population d ensity . Australia has some similarities with New Zealand in that its population is highly urbanised, but overall population density is quite low, because towns are far from each other. Preferred weighting 42 There is no “correct ” weighting option ; each is a subjective judgment about how to best apportion payments to each sector. There was broad support for the 30/70 weighting option from the NCGM sector, two service providers, one local government and some gambling industry stakeholders. Gambling operators preferred weightings that limited their own levy liabilities. Casinos, the New Zealand Racing Board , the New Zealand Lotteries Commission and one local government stakeholder indicated support for the 10/90 weighting. 43 The Ministry notes there is now a stronger evidence -based case to increase the weighting on expenditure . A broad range of submissions on the draft Strategy called for a greater weighting on expenditure, arguing it is a more current indicator of exposure to harm than presentations, which tend to be more subjective and reflect harm that has manifested as a crisis. 44 Ministry officials consider that any weighting from 5/95 to 30/70 would meet the statutory weighting provisions, but note there is strong support for increasing the weight ing on expenditure to 30 percent (the 30/70 option). This support came from the NCGM sector , service providers and most other stakeholders. Casinos, the Racing Board and the Lotteries Commission all supported the status quo 10/90 option, which also limits their levy liability compared to the 30/70 option. The Gambling Commission also supports the 30/70 option an d could see no justification for either 5/95 or 10/90 options . 45 We have considered this advice and the information and analysis in the Cost Recovery Impact Statement attached to this paper. The Strategy includes public health, intervention, research and evaluation components, but ultimately it is intended to prevent and minimise gambling harm. There is now stronger evidence that a high weighting on presentations does not provide a fair allocation based on harm . Presentations tend to account for much , but not all , of the acute harm such as high risk problem gambling , but do not reflect any of the low to moderate harm that represents about half of all gambling harm . Player expenditure is more likely to attribute to a sector their share of this low to moderate harm and the non-intervention service components of the Strategy. 46 While lowering the weighting on presentations might discourage diligent host responsibility , there are regulatory provisions in the Act that minimise th is risk. In any case, this risk is not a satisfactory reason for any sector not to pay a reasonable share of the budget. In our view, the 10/90 and 20/80 options both push the NCGM sector’s share of the budget too far above that sector’s share of 2017/18 expenditure while at the same time pushing the New Zealand Lotteries Commission’s share of the budget too far below its share of presentations. We consider the 30/70 weighting represents a suitable balance to enable the Strategy ’s costs to be spread fairly across all levy-paying sectors. 47 We recommend that the Committee agree s to a 30/70 weighting for the problem gambling levy, for the period 2019/20 to 2021/22 . Price shocks and rate of increase of prices 117. Cabinet has previously expressed the desire to manage price shocks for consumers and communities [CAB -21-MIN -0269]. Price shocks can create affordability issues, particularly when consumers are not expecting a price increase. 118. Changes to household water bills will occur in two ways: 118.1 Changes to pricing structures : the wide variety in tariff structures across the 67 territorial authorities means that changes to simplify and harmonise tariff structures will result in changes in bills for individual consumers. There will be both increases and decreases to individual household bills from almost a ny changes in tariff structure, even if the overall level of revenue collected remains the same; and 118.2 Changes to price levels : changes to the actual level of prices, driven by the need to make up for historic under -investment. 119. In the longer -term, the proposed approach to economic regulation will help to mitigate the risk of price shocks through the ability of the economic regulator to use revenue smoothing. However, this smoothing occurs at the aggregate level and does not rule out relative price changes between different groups of consumers necessary to achieve horizontal equity and other objectives. 120. It is likely some of the pricing principles proposed above (‘full cost recovery’ and ‘non - discrimination’) support price stability, once they are fully implemented. Full cost recovery also reduces the risk that prices include a monopoly profit, as monopoly profits are not part of the underlying cost structure and any surpluses are required to be reinvested. 121. There is a risk that, in the absence of any other constraints, some prices could increase significantly in the short -term, especially where there has been significant historic under -pricing and/or large cross -subsidies. s 9(2)(h) s 9(2)(h) s 9(2)(h) Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page 21 of 41 122. Officials are still in the process of collecting detailed information on current costs and prices for three waters services. The quality of this information is variable, in part because of the large variation in prices across territorial authorities, and because the revenue raised from water charges does not necessarily match the expenditure on water services. 123. The process of discovering current costs and charges is a major undertaking and will significantly increase transparency of existing charges, including existing inequities. Revealing the existing costs and associated charges for water services is likely to create a shock for some ratepayers, particularly if those costs have been funded through general rates. 124. While some price increases are likely to be both necessary and desirable to address historic underinvestment, there are three different but related regulatory powers (tools) that could be used to reduce price increases and changes in bills in the first few years: 124.1 A power to freeze existing tariff structures . This would be very effective at limiting changes in bills at the individual property level, if combined with a limit on price changes. But it would also have the effect of delaying the achievement of almost all other pricing objectives, other than price stability; 124.2 A power to regulate the rate of change in individual prices would limit price changes and generally keep the average bill stable. However, it would not be effective at reducing changes in the bills of all properties, unless combined with some sort of control of the tariff structure. It would also be ineffective for any new prices that may arise from a new tariff structure; and 124.3 A power to regulate the overall level of revenue from a particular service or customer group would enable changes in tariff structure while limiting the increase in average bills. There would still be winners and losers from the changes in tariff structures. 125. I recommend that the legislation include a regulation -making power to freeze tariff structures, limit price increases, and regulate the overall level of revenue for particular services or classes consumer. This power would be limited to the regulation of household prices. This regulation -making power would expire on the commencem ent of the first economic regulatory period, likely 1 July 2027. The economic regulator would need to be consulted on the making of these regulations. 126. Cabinet previously noted the work on collecting detailed pricing information from local authorities and i nvited me to report back on the outcomes of that work in June 2022 [CAB -21-MIN -0269]. My officials currently only have data on a small group of territorial authorities. I propose delaying this report back until November 2022 when they will have data on all 67 territorial authorities. This report back will also include proposals on the most appropriate way to use, or not use, these regulation -making powers to manage price shocks before the commencement of economic regulation. 127. 127.1 s 9(2)(f)(iv) s 9(2)(f)(iv) Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page 22 of 41 127.2

This briefing provides you with advice on mixed -use rural water schemes, and opportunities to further reduce regulatory compliance costs for these schemes. Mixed -use rural water schemes 2. There are around 100 mixed -use rural water supply schemes across New Zealand. The schemes provide rural communities with both drinking water, and water for commercial farming purposes . The schemes are essential to rural econom ies and the health and wellbeing of rural communities . 3. Many of the schemes were established in the 1970s and 1980s with central government funding from the then Ministry of Works, sweat equity and sometimes financial contributions from local farmers, and agreements with local authorities to operate and maintain the schemes (often with ratepayer funding support) 4. Many of the schemes were initially established as stock water schemes, and over time they have expanded to provide drinking water to households, townships, and community facilities (such as halls, schools and churches) .1 5. Typical characteristics of mixed -use rural schemes, such as those in the Clutha District , include : 5.1 their supply of treated water at an agreed quantity for both human drinking and farming purposes, often based on restricted volume (trickle feed) to point s of storage on consumer properties ; 5.2 their supply of relatively large volumes water for farming purposes and small volumes for human drinking ; 5.3 the involvement of farmers in their governance and operation , often through scheme management committees, who work in close collaboration with council staff in their ongoing operation and maintenance ; 5.4 unclear legal ownership, though in districts such as Clutha the schemes are accounted for on the council’s balance sheet , operated by council staff and managed through the council’s long term planning process ; 5.5 their costs are generally paid for through a mix of variable water charges (based on agreed daily volumes of water) and rates ; and 5.6 their regulation by Taumata Arowai on the same basis as other council drinking wate r schemes . The mixed -use schemes face financial challenges and need investment to modernise ageing infrastructure 6. The mixed -use schemes face issues similar to those faced more generally by small rural district councils, including : 6.1 the need for capital investment to : 6.1.1 replace and modernise aging infrastructure, much of which was built in the 1970s or earlier ;

Internal Affairs Local Government briefing Hon Simeon Brown Minister of Local Government Title: The role of Taumata Arowai in wastewater and stormwater regulation and standard setting Date: 14 March 2024 Key issues You have asked officials for advice on the scope of Taumata Arowai's functions that pertain to stormwater and wastewater. We note that these functions have not yet come into force and so there is no data supporting the efficacy of the current arrangements. You have also indicated that you may wish to reconsider the placement of centralised stormwater and wastewater functions . Officials will work with other agencies to prepare a subsequent briefing providing options for changes to the current system.
