Contact for telephone discussions (if required) Name Position Contact Number f12Ha> Ben Leggett Manager, Monitoring and I Stewardsh ip Bex Sullivan Acting Executive Director, Policy, legislation and 9(2)(a) I Stewardship Return electronic document to: Jessica.duckworth~dia.govt.nz Cohesion document reference I0=3W2D U3RAJSR2-121301344 1-26 Ministerial database reference LG20241008 IN CONFIDENCE Suggested 1st contact ✓ Page 1 of 10 The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Purpose 1. This briefing provides information about the role of Taumata Arowai in stormwater and wastewater regulation, as well as the options that were considered to arrive at the current settings. 2. A second briefing which considers the costs and benefits of Taumata Arowai retaining stormwater and wastewater functions as well as options for the reallocation of functions will be provided, should you wish, following this briefing. Background 3. The potential impact of poorly managed wastewater and stormwater on public health and the environment is significant . Urban water is the poorest quality in the country. Community views have changed since much of the infrastructure was built and consented , and sewage overflows on urban beaches are no longer acceptable. Poorly managed stormwater can exacerbate impacts of flooding or extreme weather events, as well as pollute local rivers or coastal environments . 4. Infrastructure is aging and in many parts of New Zealand has outlived its useful life. A large proportion of the network requires upgrades and greater investment in maintenance . Resource consenting arrangements and the corresponding monitoring or enforcement by regional councils are not transparent or consistent. Very little information is made available about whether wastewater infrastructure complies with consents, and much of our stormwater infrastructure is unconsented. At present, around 15 percent of wastewater treatment plants are operating on expired consents. We also know wastewater infrastructur e is facing a wave of reconsenting, with 70 percent of consents needing renewal by 2034. 5. The system for managing and regulating stormwater and wastewater networks spans multiple agencies who have related and overlapping roles and responsibilities . A diagram of regulatory responsibilities can be found in Appendix A. Taumata Arowai was given a role in this system in an effort to address transparency issues through public reporting, and consistency of regulation through the setting of national baseline standards and performance measures . Taumata Arowai is not the primary actor in stormwater and wastewater management 6. It is worth noting that while Taumata Arowai has gained functions related to stormwater and wastewater, its functions are limited. Primary regulatory responsibility remains with regional councils and is managed mostly through consenting processes . 7. The functions held by Taumata Arowai are closely related to, and overlap with, the resource management and planning systems. The regulatory responsibility for stormwater and wastewater remains primarily with local government . The Ministry for the Environment (MfE) continues to play a role in the environmental management aspects of wastewater and stormwater networks through providing national direction and standards . Taumata Arowai has a limited role in the stormwater and wastewater regulatory system 8. The stormwater and wastewater functions Taumata Arowai holds are: 8.1 Setting national baseline standards and performan ce measures; 8.2 Holding and updating a register of networks and network operators; IN CONFIDENCE Page2of 10 The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua 8.3 Reporting on the performance of networks and network operators in a way that allows comparisons between networks; 8.4 Coordination between other parts of the system and providing support and guidance to network operators. 9. Taumata Arowai has yet to establish its stormwater and wastewater functions. A timeline for the stand-up of these functions is attached in Appendix 8. Setting baseline standards 10. As mentioned above, Taumata Arowai is responsible for developing and consulting on wastewater and stormwater environmental standards. Standards set by Taumata Arowai are related to, but different from, those set by MfE as they are intended to supplement existing environmental standards, through setting standards on the performance of networks, not just on network outputs (e.g. standards around leakage rates, rather than around end of pipe discharge). The standards that Taumata Arowai produce are more able to be responsive to system needs than those produced in National Environmental Standards {NES), being easier to update, and being directly related to the performance information produced by operators. Setting performance measures 11. Taumata Arowai is also responsible for developing and publishing performance measures and targets for stormwater and wastewater networks. These measures will allow uniform data collection and reporting and can help to develop nationally consistent minimum standards. 12. Example measures include compliance against resource consents, as well as general asset management information . The measures will be phased in across multiple years, and the information received from network operators will be summarised in an annual report for the public. Over time, the information Taumata Arowai collects through mandatory reporting will provide comparisons, trends and examples of good practice. 13. Performance measures will allow operators and regulators to ascertain compliance with standards in a way that: 13.1 should improve operators' understanding of performance; 13.2 increase certainty around monitoring for both operators and regulators; and 13.3 increase transparency, aiding in consumers' understanding of performance. 14. Currently there are no nationally consistent performance measures for stormwater and wastewater operators, making national oversight impossible , as well as preventing any comparative understanding of performance or effectiveness of regulatory tools. 15. These functions increase the public accountability of network operators to their consumers and ratepayers and increase the accountability of regional councils giving additional incentive to monitor compliance. This comparative reporting also helps build public and sector understanding of best practise and allows for future benchmarking. System coordination 16. Taumata Arowai also has a system coordination role. National oversight and increased transparency around network performance means that Taumata Arowai will have the ability to support and provide guidance to operators, as well as identify system issues, capability gaps, and providing insight into the efficacy of settings for other actors in the IN CONFIDENCE Page 3 of 10 The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua system. The role of Taumata Arowai as a water regulator means it has existing relationships with MfE, regional councils, and territorial authorities, giving it the ability to share information and feedback on the efficacy of existing system settings to inform policies developed by other actors and Ministers. 17. Additionally, Taumata Arowai has indicated its intention to monitor regional councils' regulatory performance to get a better understanding of how regional councils are ensuring compliance and over time. Taumata Arowai has no infringement powers for stormwater and wastewater network non-compliance 18. Taumata Arowai's functions with regards to stormwater and wastewater network non­ compliance are limited to reporting requirements, which support transparenc y and public trust, as well as supporting regional councils to better regulate network owners and suppliers. Specifically, it's regulatory responsibilities are: 18.1 maintaining public registers of wastewater and stormwater network operators; 18.2 annual reporting on operators' general performance and environmental performance to enable comparison between network operators; 18.3 producing the Annual Network Performance Report; 18.4 identifying and monitoring matters that affect the safety of drinking water, and the environmental performance of wastewater and stormwater networks; 18.5 providing oversight of, and information to central and local government in relation to the development of and compliance with, operations, standards, regulations, and other statutory requirements for wastewater and stormwater. Taumata Arowai has some general system support functions 19. Similarly to drinking water systems, the water reforms previously recognised a general lack of capability in New Zealand when it comes to wastewater and stormwater management expertise . In view of this, Taumata Arowai has general functions intended to support the functioning of the system as a whole. Functions specific to wastewater and stormwater include: 19.1 developing advice and guidance to enhance sector capability; 19.2 facilitating, promoting, or supporting research, education, and training, to support the environmental performance, management, and regulation of wastewater and stormwater networks , including: 19.2.1 organising campaigns and promotional activities to raise awareness; 19.2.2 supporting and contribute to useful research to inform decision making; 19.2.3 working with education providers and sector to ensure fit-for-purpose training is available to build sector capability. 19.3 identifying, preparing or promoting national guidelines and best practices that relate to wastewater and stormwater networks and network operators. Other agencies also have standard setting functions 20. A diagram outlining roles and responsibilities is attached in Appendix A. MfE is responsible for establishing National Direction under the RMA, in the form of National IN CONFIDENCE Page 4of 10 The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Environmental Standards (NES) and National Policy Statements (NPS), or regulations. National Direction sets out how specific resources should be managed to protect the environment, strengthen the economy, and enable social and cultural wellbeing, where there are benefits of having a nationally consistent approach. The National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management 2020 (NPS-FM) potentially has the greatest implications for wastewater and water quality aspects for stormwater management. 21. The NPS-FM does not set specific standards for affected parties to meet, but rather provides an overarching approach to regulation and environmental management . Standards set by other parties should be in line with and informed by the NPS-FM, including standards developed by Taumata Arowai and Regional councils in their relative roles. It is worth noting that work is being done which looks at the settings and impacts of the NPS-FM, with the possibility that aspects of it will change. MfE is the agency leading this work. 22. Regional councils are responsible for establishing and implement ing objectives, policies and rules for natural resource management under the RMA, including for wastewater and stormwater discharges. They process resource consent applications to ensure regional requirements are met and adverse effects are avoided, remedied or mitigated. Regional councils must implement National Direction, and they are currently amending their freshwater plans to give effect to the NPS-FM. After standards under the Water Services Act are made, regional councils must ensure any consents granted are not contrary to those standards. 23. The economic regulator is also likely to have some functions related to standard and performance measures. In its role to ascertain the financial sustainability of supplier asset management plan performanc e measures which support an understanding of levels of service that will need to be developed. Work is on-going on the scope of the economic regulator and what its functions pertaining to stormwater and wastewater infrastructure will look like. We expect that information gathered by Taumata Arowai about network performance will be useful to the economic regulator when developing operational policies. Other options that were considered at the time of allocating stormwater and wastewater functions 24. To address the system issues identified earlier in this paper, Taumata Arowai was given new functions created to address the regulatory gap resulting in inconsistent and sometimes ineffective regulation of stormwater and wastewater networks . 25. The functions given to Taumata Arowai are directly related to increasing transparency around network performance and gaining national oversight of the function of the wider system. Several options were considered for where responsibilities should sit 26. Three agencies were considered as options for where the new functions would be best placed. These were: 26.1 Taumata Arowai; 26.2 Ministry for the Environment ; and 26.3 the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). IN CONFIDENCE Page5of 10 The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua 27. It is important to note that at the time these considerations were taking place, work had not started on the role of the economic regulator. 28. Taumata Arowai was found to be the preferred option as the stormwater and wastewater functions fit most closely with the other functions of Taumata ArowaiJ including its role in increasing sector capability and public trust. 29. The wastewater and stormwater functions allocated to Taumata Arowai have strong synergies with the drinking water functions they hold, and will utilise many of the same systems, approaches and scientific and technical expertise. Co-locating these functions was deemed to enable skills and knowledge to be pooled, shared and developed further, helping create a centre of expertise for the broader system. This approach also addresses the problem of limited capability within the sector by centralising the pool of expertise. 30. Locating stormwater and wastewater functions within Taumata Arowai was also found to provide an opportunity to develop a well-integrated, consistent approach to three waters regulation, and a more capable regulator. 31. An independent report also found it is more cost-effective, as fewer staff are needed to deliver the functions in a single regulator, compared with locating them in MfE or the EPA. The synergies between these functions provide the opportunity to leverage the skills and expertise that already sit within the drinking water regulator. MfE was considered as an option 32. While MfE have related functions , the additional functions did not fit in well with MfE's mostly policy-based functions and would have required MfE to set up new functions and develop new capability. 33. MfE has historically focused on the quality of freshwater at a catchment level, across all discharge types, rather than on wastewater and stormwater infrastructure. This has meant it has not had the expertise or given priority to work on three waters infrastructure which is an area that requires dedicated oversight, given the sheer size of the sector (both in dollar value and complexity spread across all councils), and impact it has on both ratepayers and their urban water quality. 34. Subsequently, MfE has developed a greater focus on implementation and has progressed policy work on compliance and monitoring in the resource management system. However, as it pertains to the regulation of wastewater and stormwater network s, MfE continues to respond to issues as they arise, and there no framework for regular review of regional council performance . The EPA was considered as an option 35. The EPA was not considered to be a good fit primarily because its core responsibil ities do not easily align with the stormwater and wastewater functions. Placing the stormwater and wastewater functions alongside the EPA's current roles and responsibilities would mean that the functions would primarily be used in the context of environmental protection rather than to support a coherent catchment level water system. It would also potentially lose some of the public health focus from the system. 36. The placement of the functions in the EPA would require adding in new capabilities into the agency and was the second most expensive option considered in the independent report (MfE being the most expensive option). IN CONFIDENCE Page 6of 10 The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Taumata Arowai are currently in the process of developing standards 37. Taumata Arowai is currently working to stand up its wastewater and stormwater functions starting with updating public registers, developing standards, and introducing performance measures {which were consulted on in late 2022). A timeline of the development and set up of the wastewater and stormwater functions are attached in Appendix B. The role of the economic regulator 38. The economic regulator was not considered through the options analysis as the scope of the economic regulator was not settled when the above considerations were made. 39. Work is on-going as to the scope of the economic regulator, led by the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment. It is possible that there may be some overlap between the wastewater and stormwater functions Taumata Arowai currently holds and the functions of the economic regulator. This is contingent on the decision being made to include stormwater and wastewater functions in the scope of the economic regulator. 40. The suitability of the placement of the stormwater and wastewater functions currently held by Taumata Arowai within the economic regulator will be considered in the next briefing. There is an opportunity to re-examine allocation of environmental regulation functions for stormwater and wastewater 41. As Taumata Arowai are yet to establish their stormwater and wastewater functions, it is too early to assess whether the expected value and benefits of placing these functions with Taumata Arowai has been realised, or if they are better placed elsewhere . 42. However, there is merit in having centralised oversight within the environmental system that provides coordination, a degree of consistency and considers the environmental impacts of three waters infrastructure. For these reasons, we believe it is worth retaining Taumata Arowai's performance measures, system oversight and coordination functions related to stormwater and wastewater. It is particularly important that there is a centralised place for these oversight and performance measurement functions , given the current variation in how regional councils operate and execute their regulatory responsibil ities. 43. There may be opportunity to look at whether standards setting functions could be consolidated or streamlined across Taumata Arowai and MfE, as part of the policy development for your next Bill, the Local Government Water Services Bill (Bill 3). Next steps 44. If directed, officials will work with other agencies to develop alternative options for the placement of some or all of Taumata Arowai's wastewater and stormwater functions. Consultation 45. We have worked with both Taumata Arowai and MfE in the development of this briefing, in the presentation of their suite of functions and considerations that led to their respective allocation of regulatory functions . The Department is making some changes to modernise RealMe with the login service recently being re -platformed to a Microsoft cloud -based solution. The shift away from the custom -built RealMe login service will reduce operating costs and the need for ongoing investments to upgrade expiring components. It is expected that Microsoft will continue investing in the product to suppor t future improvements to user experience and security. However, RealMe login is only one component of RealMe services, and much wider changes will be needed to realise the value of digital identity and drive system change. 23. RealMe services are currently funded at approximately $2 2 million per annum (including operating and capital expenditure) until June 2022 and However , additional investment is needed to develop modernised digital identity services that realise the potential benefits . Comparable jurisdictions such as Australia are investing significantly in digital identity.3 The current approach of multiple time -limited funding requests for RealMe services will also need to change as it has undermined certainty about long term service provision , which in turn, impacted the ability of agencies and organisations to develop their services using RealMe. 24. However, government needs to do more than investing in digital identity services to realise the bene fits. People need to be able to access information or attributes about themselves and reuse them to obtain more services digitally. 25. Government has a key role in this as it holds a wide range of identity -related information and attributes about people. There are multiple examples of attributes where there could be significant benefits for people, the economy and government if investment and other changes are made (including legislation in some cases) to make these available. These include attributes related to: 25.1 driver licencing information, which people commonly use to verify their identity, particularly where they do not have a passport ; 25.2 immigration to help prove the identity and eligibility of non -New Zealand citizens within New Zealand ; 25.3 health to support access to services and to enable health professionals to prove their qualifications and skills (including health records such as vaccinations, and registrations such as the Health Provider Inde x held by the Ministry of Health) ; 25.4 education to support access to learning or access to services dependent on the outcome of learning already completed (such as the Record of Achievement administered by the New Zealand Qualifications Authority and other re cords associated to the National Student Number held by the Ministry of Education) ; 25.5 eligibility to make it easier to access services (such as people’s concession entitlements held by the Ministry of Social Development) ; and 25.6 business and employment, so people can represent themselves professionally or represent their organisation when undertaking activities such as compliance (including occupational licences and authorisation to represent an organisation held by the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Emplo yment). 26. Such information will need to be of utility for both users and receiving organisations, to encourage their participation in the digital identity system. Government will also need to change how it receives information as it is a significant user of identity services to determine who people are and their eligibility to access services (in this capacity, government is a ‘relying party’).

Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs AN AGREEMENT made BETWEEN THE SECRETARY FOR INTERNAL AFFAIRS, (hereinafter referred to as "the Secretary") of the one part AND hereinafter referred to as "Cardholder") of the other part
Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs CONFIDENTIAL 10 Castalia 1 Introduction The New Zealand government is proposing to reform the drinking, waste and storm water (three waters) sector. It proposes to amalgamate the three wa ters services of the 67 local authorities into four regional public corporations . The government is proposing to amalgamate WDC ’s water services into a new statutory corporation called “Entity A” together with the water services of Far North District Counc il, Kaipara District Council and Watercare Services Limited , owned by Auckland Council (the Refo rm Scenario). The government has presented the only alternative to the Reform Scenario as being a situation where WDC remain s as a standalone water service prov ider under council control (the Opt-Out Scenario ). This report analyses the evidence underpinning both the Reform Scenario and the Opt-Out Scenario as follows : ▪ The Reform Scenario is analysed , and its underlying assumptions tested to determine whether th e stated level of household bills is robust (section 2) . Specifically the analysis reviews : – The estimates of the required level of assets for the Reform Scenario (section 2.1) – The estimated efficiencies apparently available in the Re form Scenario (section 2.2) – Other aspects of the methodology that raise questions (section 2.3) . ▪ The Opt-Out Scenario is analysed and its underlying assumptions tested to determine whether the stated level of household bills is robust (section 3) ▪ Finally, the risks and costs to the WDC community with the Reform Scenario are examined (section 4). 2 Government ’s Reform Scenario produces implausible household bill estimates The Reform Proposal predicts household bills for 2051 . The WICS analysis rests on two key assumptions : First, th at the capital stock invested in New Zealand water services needs to increase by a very large amount . Second, that the Reform Scenario will del iver large efficiency gains compared to the Opt -Out Scenario . In our view , WIC S’ assumed scale of required increa se in capital stock , and of the achievable efficiency gains under the reforms, are both implausible. 2.1 Required investment estimate is overstated The government’s case for reform rests on a claim that New Zealand water services require a significant capital investment over the next 30 years. The government relies on WICS advice and analysis to set the level of investment for the Reform Scenario from 2021 to 2051. WICS ’ modelling is entirely based on a top -down , New Zealand -wide assum ption that a massive natio nwide investment programme is necessary for all council water services . This is Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs CONFIDENTIAL 11 Castalia despite WDC and all other local authorities submitt ing detailed bottom -up information about planned capital investment . Capital investment is needed in some parts of New Zeala nd now and in the next 30 years to meet the dema nds of growth and due to historical deferred and underinvestment . There have been high -profile asset failures. However, it is not clear that the investment is needed in all places, at the scale WICS claim. WICS are selective in estimating the nationwide re quired investment amount. WICS also use inappropriate Scottish comparators to support its claim that New Zealand needs to invest at equivalent levels. WICS ’ estimate of required investment is significantly higher than the levels of investment that asset -owner WDC has estimated will be required. WICS used projected investment requirements across three investment types that include replacement or renewal investment, enhancement investment, and growth investment projections. These projections are based on assumptions relating to asset lives, replace ment costs, inflation, population density, and projected connections growth. 2.1.1 WICS approach to estimating required investment is unsound In order to estimate the requir ed investment, WICS uses English and Scottish comparators. WICS allocated New Zealand -wide investment requirements for councils based on statistical relationship s and observed experiences in England and Scotland. The total investment required is made up of two key components that include ‘enhancement and growth’ and ‘asset replacement and ref urbishment’ . WICS model led the required investment using three approaches . WICS then cross -check ed the modelled investment against information gathered from councils ’ RFI re sponses . The modelled investment from the three approaches, plus investment specif ied in council s’ RFI responses are summari sed in Table 2.1. WICS took three steps with each of its three modelling approaches : ▪ Step 1 is to ap ply econometric models to predict New Zealand’s investment needs ▪ Step 2 is to manually adjust the Step 1 est imate for differences in growth ▪ Step 3 is to apply a cap of $70,000 to reflect an assumption about the ability to pay for the investment. With a dedica ted economic regulator collecting a wider range of standardised financial performance information and with Taumata Arowai collecting performance information, WDC will be able to better assess the performance of its water services. This is likely to lead to improv ements in performance over time. 3.2.3 WDC management and operational competence likely to improve with competition between entities for staff The government has noted that larger , corporat e water entities are likely to improve management and operational compete nce. If this is the case, then one should expect WDC to also lift competence of its management and operations . This is because WDC will have to match the working conditions at the larger corporate entities, leading to improvements in performance ove r time. 3.3 WDC can increase access to finance to lower short - term costs WICS base assum ption is that WDC’s financing headroom is 2.5 times revenue. In fact, the Local Government Funding Authority has approved WDC (and other local authorities with a credit rat ing of A+ or above) to borrow up to 2.8 times revenues 43F43F43F44. Furthermore, the Opt-Out Scenario assumes that WDC can make no improvements to its financing arrangements . Efficient use of f inanc e can lower costs of service Efficient financing is an important co nsideration in investment planning for water utilities. The term of loans should ideally match the useful life of the asset the loans are financing. If the loan is repaid over a shorter period of time, then water bills after the loan is repaid will be lowe r than they otherwise would be. WICS assumes that amalgamated entities have greater access to financing and can make more efficient use of finance to lower the cost of service. We tested the change in average cost per household for 2051 across different f inancing option scenarios for both WDC in the Opt -Out Scenario and for the Reform Scenario ( amalgamated entity ). Table 3.1 and Table 3.2 show that a significant proportion of the claimed reduction in averag e cost per household for the Opt- Out Scenario compared to the Reform Scenario is due to changing the financ ing requirements.

Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs CONFIDENTIAL 5 Castalia Executive summary The government is proposing to reform the drinking, waste and storm water (three waters) sector . The reform will involve amalgamating the water services of the 67 local authorities into four new r egional statutory corporations , with centr alised management and a new governance structure . The structure will have indirect Board appointment rights for local authorities to be shared with mana whenua representatives. The government proposes to amalgamat e Whangārei District Council (WDC) into a new statutory corporation called “Entity A” together with the water services of Far North District Council, Kaipara District Council and Watercare Services Limited (owned by Auckland Council ) (the Reform Scenario). The government has given WDC two choices, join the Reform Scenario or Opt -Out. WDC, along with other local authorities, has been asked by the government to consider the evidence and whether the government’s proposal to reform the water sector will delive r benefits to its residents. The government also committed to providing Whangārei with $38 million in funding under the “better off” package, a n additional $5 million for stranded overhead costs under the “no worse off” package, and further comp ensation for any loss in WDC’s debt headroom. These amounts are to be part-funded from the balance sheet of the new entity. Key question: will the Reform Scenario deliver the claimed benefits? The key question for this report is whether the benefits for W DC that are claimed by the government are robust, and whether the Whangārei communi ty is likely to be better off with the Reform Scenario. The Reform Scenario uses analysis provided by Water Industry Commission for Scotland (WICS), the Scottish government’ s regulator of its monopoly water provider Scottish Water. The WICS analysis and mo delling underpins the case for reform. The government has relied on WICS for the claims that significant capital investment is needed in the New Zealand water sector, and th at amalgamation in to four separate entities with accompanying institutional changes is the only way to achieve the cost -efficiencies to make the reform affordable . The g overnment is promising that household bills will be four times lower in Reform Scenario than in Opt-Out The government is promising that the Reform Scenario will deliver household bills that are more than four times lower than the bills that would exist in the Opt-Out Scenario . The government claims that the Reform Scenario will deliver Whan gārei residents: ▪ Household bills that average $ 803 by 2051 ▪ Improvements in service delivery and affordability ▪ Improvement in the ability to raise finance In contrast, the government’s WICS analysis claims that if WDC provides water services as a n opt-out provider, household bills will rise to $4,055 by 2051. Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Overview Your manifesto document Local Water Done Well sets out a clear direction for financially sustainable water services, underpinned by a strong regulatory regime. The regulatory environment for water services delivery include swater quality and environmental regulation, economic regulation and consumer protection . This slide pack provides an overview of the existing regulatory environment, opportunities to strengthen the regulatory regime, and an approach to stand up interim economic regulation over the next 12 months. The contents of this pack are: •Overview: recap of features of Local Water Done Well that support the stand up of the future regulatory environment •Section 1: Economic regulation and Part 4 of the Commerce Act •Section 2: Proposed interim arrangements for economic regulation • IN CONFIDENCE 2 9(2)(f)(iv) Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Regulatory Context IN CONFIDENCE 3Water services delivery by councils has a number of issues, including: • In many places, investment in water services has not been prioritised and has been diverted to other priorities ; • Many ratepayers not being informed on how much of their rates are being spent on water services; and • It is often difficult for ratepayers and communities to make informed submissions on council proposals for water infrastructure and funding, or to hold their councils to account for ‘poor’ decisions . Water services regulation already has water quality standards and some environmental standards ,but no economic regulation. There are currently few requirements on councils for the management of infrastructure, and none for infrastructure investment. There are requirements for councils to prepare an infrastructure strategy as part of their long -term plans, as provided for in the Local Government Act 2002. Existing requirements under the Act have not resulted in adequate investment in, or the substantial management of, water services infrastructure by councils. This is because while these plans are review ed by auditors, they are not reviewed by regulators and they cannot ‘require’ investment. Evidence from overseas jurisdictions and other utility sectors in New Zealand indicates that economic regulation is indispensable for a well -functioning water services delivery system. It plays a crucial role in safeguarding and improving the long -term interests of consumers, and providing incentives and regulatory oversight to improve performance. We can provide you with an overview of economic regulation regimes in other jurisdictions. Multiple agencies will be involved in achieving comprehensive regulation of water services. Their work needs to be well connected to ensure a cohesive and effective approach to regulation. •Department of Internal Affairs – interim monitor and agency to provide support to councils in the development and assessment of their Water Services Delivery Plans; •Taumata Arowai – the water quality regulator; •Commerce Commission – long term economic regulator; and •Regional Councils – in regulation of environmental impacts . Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Features ofLocal Water Done Well IN CONFIDENCE 4Effective regulation of water services is critical to improved delivery. Local Water Done Well provides for this – by putting a greater focus on investment levels, revenue sufficiency, and sustainable performance of water services, and introducing more transparency and direction to councils. Many of the features of your manifesto policy will set in place the foundations for a strengthened regulatory regime The requirement for councils to prepare plans for how they will transition water services delivery to new models that meet requirements for investment and financial sustainability, is an important step to setting up a future economic regulation reg ime and continuing to build on drinking water and environmental regulation (quality regulation). The development of investment rules and criteria for assessing financial sustainability of the plans will be particularly important. Other features of Local Water Done Well also support the stand up of the future regulatory regime: •The Minister of Local Government signing off councils’ plans once satisfied they meet requirements. The Government will not mandate any specific model for water services onto councils. •A regulatory backstop to ensure councils deliver a viable plan that can deliver on outcomes for water quality, infrastructure investment and financial sustainability. •Repeal of the Water Services Economic Efficiency and Consumer Protection Act 2023 and instead regulation of water services delivery under Part 4 of the Commerce Act 1986. •The Water Infrastructure Regulator will set quality standards for water infrastructure. Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Section 2: Economic Regulation and Part 4 of the Commerce Act Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs A comprehensive approach to economic regulation is critical to the successful delivery of water services, as outlined in Loca l Water Done Well. Economic regulation aims for efficient market and supplier operations, along with consumer protection, particularly in industries with limited competition or when businesses wield substantial market power, such as in the water industry. It also supports the achievement of various health, economic, and social goals and ensures the delivery of services at a quality and resilience level that aligns with consumer and broader community expectations. Without economic regulation the monopoly nature of water services delivery would be detrimental to consumers, as the providers would have the ability to charge higher prices than in a competitive market. In the context of water services delivery, the key questions in the economic regulation space: How does the water supplier optimise operations for efficiency, resilience and sustainability? What measures are in place to ensure fair pricing? How does the supplier guarantee compliance with service quality and other standards? Economic r egulatory tools include: •Requiring public disclosure of certain information to understand the performance of those delivering water services; •Benchmarking, monitoring, analysing and reporting publicly on performance; •Regulating the revenues and quality of service, including the ability to require ringfencing of revenue for specific services ; •Setting minimum standards for service quality that must be met; •Reviewing/approving asset management plans and funding & pricing plans; •Setting and enforcing a service quality code to improve the quality of water services; and •Enforcing and monitoring consumer complaints processes and monitoring the consumer dispute resolution service. Regulation for water services regulation would be added into Part 4 of the Commerce Act 1986 and would be implemented from within the Commerce Commission (and the Water Services Economic Efficiency and Consumer Protection Act 2023 repealed ). The Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) is the lead agency for policy advice on economic regulation, and will be briefing the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs next week on this topic. Our initial view is that ifPart 4 of the Commerce Act is used, it should be amended to make water services a regulated sector. There are some features of water services that may require more bespoke requirements, and further advice can be provided on these .Economic regulation of water services IN CONFIDENCE 6 Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Overview Part 4 of the Commerce Act provides for the Commerce Commission to regulate the price and quality of goods and services for the benefit of consumers in markets where there is little or no competition. The Act sets out the particular goods and services that are subject to regulation and the legislative rules governing that regulation. Current industries regulated under Part 4 include electricity lines services, gas pipeline services and certain airports serv ices. The telecommunications and dairy sectors are governed by their own respective legislation. Who decides which sectors are regulated under Part 4? •Parliament decided that electricity lines services, gas pipeline services and certain airports should be regulated under Part 4. •Regulation under Part 4 may also be imposed by the Governor -General on the recommendation of the Minister of Commerce following a Part 4 inquiry by the Commission. However, while a this is technically feasible route to regulation, this process is not considered suitable for water services. •A Part 4 inquiry would consume significant resources to collect and analyse evidence, take considerable time, and the outcome of the process would be uncertain (e.g., at the end of the process the Commission may recommend not to proceed with regulation). •In making a recommendation to proceed with regulation, the Commission needs to consider the benefit to consumers through lower prices or improved quality would be greater than the costs of regulation, which include the cost of setting up and administering a new regulatory regime (which consumers would ultimately pay for through charges). •The size and structure of the industry in question will have a material bearing on this assessment of costs and benefits, wit h the costs of regulating many smaller suppliers operating with a variety of corporate and non -corporate structures potentially posing challenges to a regulator. •In the current circumstances, the most effective and efficient mechanism for ensuring regulation would be for Parliament to pass legislation to place the regulation of water services under Part 4 of the Commerce Act.Part 4 of the Commerce Act 1986 IN CONFIDENCE 7 Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs IN CONFIDENCE 8 9(2)(f)(iv) Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Differences between Part 4 and the WSEECP Act 2023 IN CONFIDENCE 9•The economic regulation parts of the WSEECP Act 2023 (as distinct from the consumer protection parts) have much in common with Part 4. •The purpose statement and statutory objectives within the WSEECP Act are based on those in Part 4, with modifications made to reflect that water entities were to be publicly owned and prohibited from paying dividends. •If Council -owned water organisations were structured as companies with shareholdings and had the potential to pay dividends now or in future, then they would look a lot like existing companies regulated under Part 4. Many electricity distribution businesses have council ownership, for example. •The general regulatory approach provided for in the WSEECP Act 2023 is similar to that in Part 4 of the Commerce Act, including provision for information disclosure, quality -only regulation and price -quality regulation. The Act also provides envisages similar role and process for developing and applying input methodologies. •However, the WSEECP Act 2023 included a broader range of regulatory tools than what is available under Part 4 and generic competition and consumer law, reflecting the unique characteristics of the water sector. For example, the WSEECP Act included tools such as performance requirements that are broader than the Part 4 approach of setting quality standards. The WSEECP also provided for the Commission to ‘ring -fence’ a portion of an entity’s allowable return that would then be held in reserve in case of any unexpected investment requirements, thereby ensuring entities have the minimum required level of cash to finance their operations. Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs •Part 4 was designed to be flexible and adaptable to the regulation of a wide range of entities and is expected to be suitable for regulating water services. However, the effectiveness and efficiency of regulation will be very dependent on the structure of the industry. Other things being equal, regulation of a fragmented sector with many small suppliers and diverse corporate and non -corporate forms is likely to be less effective and more costly than regulation of water services organisations organised into more conventional corporate structures operating at a scale suitable for the industry. •Further, there are some unique features of water services that may better suit a bespoke approach to regulation not easily provided for under Part 4 of the Commerce Act. •There is a track record for industry specific regulation in New Zealand, including for example in the telecommunications industry. Sector -specific regulation in the form of Part 7 of the Telecommunications Act was brought in to remedy specific issues with customer service, fault service levels, and billing in the retail telecommunications sector. •The benefits of sector -specific economic regulation and consumer protection regulation could include: •allowing the legislation to be designed in a way that reflects the unique characteristics of the entities compared with other monopoly businesses regulated under Part 4 and generic consumer law, particularly that water services will be council -owned and potentially delivered through a wide range of non -standard corporate and non -corporate forms •certain regulatory approaches used under Part 4 may not be effective or practical when applied to the council water services providers, given they will operate differently and face different incentives to other regulated businesses •bespoke regulation may better reflect the need for significant improvements in efficiency. For example, Part 4 does not allow for comparative benchmarking, which could be a useful tool in driving efficiency improvements in the industry. •standalone regulation would enable a broader approach to setting performance requirements than the Part 4 approach of setting quality standards •a standalone regime could be used to place restrictions on distributions of surplus, or to ring -fence funds, until such time that certain quality - or service -standards had been achieved •it could provide for the specific consumer consultation requirements, which could then inform the setting of performance requirements, quality standards and minimum service levels. •These benefits are nuanced and the relative merits of general or specific regulation are unlikely to be clear cut.Whether to use Part 4 or sector -specific regulation IN CONFIDENC E 10 Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Section 3: Proposed interim arrangements Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Local Water Done Well outlines a requirement for councils to submit a Water Services Delivery Plan (plan) for how they will transition their water services that meets water quality and infrastructure investment rules. These plans, and the analysis that will underpin the plans, will be an important step to setting up a future economic regulation regime and continuing to build on drinking water and environmental regulation. The development of investment rules and criteria for assessing financial sustainability of the plans will be particularly important. There is an opportunity to use this process to support improvements in the information base, and to pave the way toward economic regulation. Content of the plans We recommend that the first plan has two component parts, with the relevant weighting to the sections dependent on whether councils are considering amending their existing delivery model or pursuing a new model, and how quickly they wish to stand up a new model: 1. Councils’ initial plans for: •Intended delivery model: oE.g. direct ownership and management of services, council -controlled organisation (CCO), joint CCO with other councils; existing approach or new. oTimeframe and establishment plan - implementation plan and timetable to transition to the new model ( eg to stand -up CCO+s, or amendments to existing processes) and market capacity and local workforce assessment to deliver proposed model. •Infrastructure investment pathway – full accounting of the state of current assets (where known) and where they are in their lifecycle. •Funding pathways: oFinancial sustainability plan - proposed approach to pricing and charging consumers, and approach to finance and debt. What prices they will change their consumers? How will these charges be kept separate from the rest of the rates that consumers pay? oAsset management programme - proposed investment path, including maintenance, replacement and renewal, building for growth and building to improve quality for consumers. 2. Baseline performance information: •Key financials and other required information (to be developed alongside the Commerce Commission). •Performance against current regulatory requirements ( eg Water Quality Plan - how they will meet water quality requirements as per those issued by Taumata Arowai ). •Performance against sustainable financing performance. Water Services Delivery Plans IN CONFIDENCE 12 Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Getting to a system of full economic regulation will take time to develop and implement. There are a number of key components that need to be stood up, for example the development, consultation and implementation of input methodologies. This typically takes several years, regardless of other future legislation that the Government may choose to implement. We recommend that interim economic arrangements are put in place to support improvements in the quality of information on assets, costs, and enhancing the transparency and accountability of water services. As the steward of local government, DIA is well positioned to help facilitate and organise an interim economic regulation regime, alongside MBIE and the Commerce Commission. DIA could build on existing monitoring frameworks and work alongside councils as they develop their Water Services Plans, to begin to build the information base that will support key indicators for future economic regulation (with the Commerce Commission). Crown Infrastructure Partners will also have a key role in the interim and future arrangements. As an interim step, Crown Infrastructure Parters could monitor the execution and delivery of capital plans. A staged transition to economic regulation A staged transition to economic regulation could commence with lighter -touch requirements in the first 12 months (e.g. a focus on the level of adherence to infrastructure investment rules/the evidence that needs to be demonstrated for water services delivery plans), that are increased over time to achieve consistent information disclosure. There are several benefits to taking a staged transition to economic regulation. The staged approach allows: •Time to build the information base, while using the information as it is developed to understand current performance and areas of risk. •Considered development of the new policy settings and for local authorities to respond to these and implement changes. •An opportunity to incrementally build requirements for councils. Given the phasing, this also may support higher enforcement of requirements at each step – a scale of enhanced monitoring of some councils could be included on the basis of their earlier reporting. •May provide more space for the economic regulator to define the relevant regulations without path dependency on the measures that have already been set. •A greater opportunity to work with local authorities through the transition.Commencing economic regulation IN CONFIDENCE 13 Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Information disclosure is a key step to commencing economic regulation IN CONFIDENCE 14Information disclosure from councils is critical to development and implementation of economic regulation. In particular, information disclosure is needed early to inform the development of methodologies to establish price quality regulation (or similar). We recommend starting with information disclosure as a regulatory tool while councils develop their water services delivery plans. There are several options you can explore for improving transparency and quality of information during this interim period, including: • Specifying information that must be included in water services delivery plans; • An option to repeat the Request for Information process that DIA led previously in 2019 -20 where councils were asked to provide information on their assets (potentially co -developed with regulators and expert advisory group); • Potentially introducing new planning and/or reporting requirements for water services under the Local Government Act 2002; and • Placing statutory obligations on council officers to sign -off on the quality of information. To address gaps in information to inform economic regulation, we propose that DIA work alongside the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment and the Commerce Commission to establish what information can be collected through council water service delivery plans. If you agree, the following steps will form the approach to transition: •We will advise you on a process to set the expectations and requirements for Water Services Delivery Plans (working with Taumata Arowai , MBIE and the Commerce Commission). •As part of this process, we will work with MBIE and the Commerce Commission to specify information disclosure requirements for councils. •The first Water Services Delivery Plans will be used to set expectations and to capture base line performance and financial information to inform establishment of economic regulation plus setting early expectations for performance .

The bottom line is, our communities have different needs. A one -size-fits-all approach to meeting those needs simply won’t work. This is what Local Water Done Well is all about. • The Coalition Government strongly believes in empowering communities and supporting local governance in managing and delivering water services. Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 7 of 13 • We believe that communities are best placed to make decisions about things that directly affect them – like the future of their water assets, and ensuring sustainable, high -quality management of water services. • And sitting atop all of this, we believe in setting clear expectations and bottom lines. This means stronger support and oversight from Central Government, to promote efficiency and accountability within the sector. Today’s announcement is another step forward in delivering on these fundamental elements of Local Water Done Well – and empowering local government to lead the way in delivering the changes required for their communities. • Cabinet has agreed to the first set of policies that will establish the Local Water Done Well framework and the transitional arrangements for the new water services system. • This includes streamlined processes for setting up water services council -controlled organisations, new requirements for councils to develop Water Services Delivery Plans, and steps towards future economic regulation. • The policies will be introduced through legislation to be passed by mid -2024, as part of the second stage of our implementation plan. • The third stage, which I expect to share key information about around the middle of this year, will form part of third Bill that will establish the enduring settings and begin the transition to the new system. •

Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua IN-CONFIDENCE Page 2 of 10 Purpose 1. This briefing provides advice on the water service delivery plans (the Plans) that councils will need to submit on their preferred water services delivery model . 2. We are seeking your decision on whether to receive further advice on a one - or two - phased approach to the Plans, and identifies other key considerations ahead of policy decisions being sought in January 2024. Background 3. Local Water Done Well (LWDW) requires councils to submit Plans within 12 months of repeal of the Water Services Entities Act 2022 for how they will transition their water services to a new model , that meets quality standards and is financially sustainable . A range of specific parameters for the Plans – including the need to meet infrastructure investment rules, and direct ministerial approval – were outlined. 4. We provided initial advice to you on the water services regulatory context on 1 December 2023. This advice is attached at Appendix A for your convenience. This advice noted that: 4.1 Historically councils have faced a number of challenges with water services, including incomplete information about the true cost of delivering water services, the state of water infrastructure, competing priorities, and providing transparency to communities on the investment in water assets relative to need ; 4.2 Effective regulation of water services is critical to improved delivery; 4.3 Water services regulation already has water quality standards and some environmental standards but no economic regulation ; and 4.4 Multiple agencies will be involved in achieving comprehensive regulation of water services. 5. Alongside overviews of water quality, economic and interim regulation, the previous advice also set out our understanding of what the Plans need to achieve: 5.1 Set expectations for the transition of water services by councils to meet quality and financial sustainability requirements; 5.2 Provide oversight of council planning to meet safe drinking water standards, ensure sufficient investment in maintenance and replacement of assets, considering future access and growth, and that they are pricing and borrowing sufficiently to fund their investment path; and 5.3 To inform the use of any regulatory backstop powers to ensure councils deliver a viable plan that can deliver on outcomes for water quality, infrastructure investment and financial sustainability . 6. This advice also noted that: 6.1 The Plans could require information on both councils’ initial plans for delivery (including intended delivery model, and infrastructure and funding pathways) and baseline performance information (including financial information, and performance against current regulatory requirements and other measures). 6.2 Information gathered through the Plans will contribute to the design of economic regulation and other policy settings ; and Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua IN-CONFIDENCE Page 3 of 10 6.3 An indica tive process for developing requirements for the Plans and guidance for councils, and subsequent submission and assessment timeframes. 7. At present, there is no legislative framework to require provision of the Plans . Based on previous experience with respect to long -term plans, we expect councils will prefer a clear legislative framework setting out any requirements for the Plans, and as such we recommend that a requirement for councils to complete the Plans is set out in the replacement legislation. 8. Your recent Cabinet paper [CAB -23-MIN -0479] outlined the proposed approach to progress a new water services legislative regime, in two phases. This advice signalled that the framework necessary to set out the Plans would need to be included in a first replacement Bill , in order to set clear requirements quickly for councils. Broad factors relevant to the plans 9. Councils will be starting in different places with respect to their future water service delivery model. We expect some councils will broadly retain their existing arrangements with some amendments to meet new requirements (for example financial ring -fencing and sustainability ). These c ouncils may be able to leverage existing planning material , with some modifications, from their long-term plans. 10. However, c ouncils seeking to progress a more substantial change to their service delivery organising structures will require more lead in time and focus on their establishment efforts . Councils opting to use financially -independent council - controlled organisations (CCOs) , when available, w ould need to undertake additional implementation planning for the transfer of services , revenue and assets to the new organisation. This will be more complex for multi -council organisations that will also need to negotiate and agree across councils on key parameters of the CCO (for example share allocations, funding and pricing approaches ) to inform establishment. 11. The development of the Plans will be a new activity for all councils . While c ouncils will need to adjust and plan for meeting any requirements over time, compliance in the immediate term may pose a problem . Larger councils may be able to pivot resources to absorb this work, but some smaller councils may face significant capacity constraints. Councils will likely need to undertake public consultation on their Plans, reducing the time available to them to develop materials. 12. LWDW describes greater transparency and strengthened planning and reporting for water services. These Plans would represent a n initial step towards achieving this, but the longer -term planning and reporting framework for water will need to be integrated with broader local government planning and reporting. A range of intersections will need to be worked through, including : 12.1 Reporting and oversight material required by the Commerce Commission to enable economic regulation (including transitional arrangements) , regulation of financial ringfencing, and any information required to inform the use of regulatory backstop powers ; 12.2 The existing local authority planning and accountability regime , includ ing how to incorporate accountability to central government within a system that is predicated on accountability to communities ; 12.3 What a ‘fit for purpose’ planning and reporting framework would look like for a range of water services delivery models ; and Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua IN-CONFIDENCE Page 4 of 10 12.4 Questions about whether councils need to consult communities before submitting a Plan to central government, and whether subsequent modifications to a Plan will mean long -term plans need to be amended. 13. Reflecting their joint delivery intentions, some councils may seek to provide Plans together as a region. This approach poses no immediate issues and the Department will work to enable this, though we note some careful consideration of this will need to be considered when developing the regulatory backstop powers that may be informed, in part, by the Plans. 14. It should be noted that, besides the availability of new financially independent CCO vehicles, or other novel organisational arrangements, there is no legislative barrier to councils transitioning their water services to more sustainable models in the near term (for example, using existing CCO provisions in the Local Government Act). We expect some councils may wish to set up new organisations for water before all replacement legislation is passed, or before they complete their Plans. Where this happens, councils will be looking for clarity from the outset on the process for developing and approving Plans. Options for how the Plans should be delivered 15. In developing the approach to the Plans, there is a need to strike a balance between : 15.1 driving progress , with a fast transition of models, infrastructure investment lifting in the near term, and financial sustainability achieved sooner ; and 15.2 ensuring a supported transition for councils , that is responsive to their individual situations, provides a path to full compliance over time , and which does not set unreasonable expectations and planning burden on them in a short period of time . Require councils to deliver all content in a single plan, as articulated in LWDW 16. Councils could be required to meet all the requirements outlined in LWDW in a single plan within the original 12 -month deadline . This option would most closely align with LWDW . This would al low a more straightforward a ssessment of whether a council’s Plan represents a more financially sustainable and viable model, as all supporting analysis regarding infrastructure investment pipeline, price paths and plans to meet regulatory standards would be compiled. 17. However, councils may experience significant issues in complying with the request within the time available, and this may be faster than all councils are able to achieve. This approach would also pose issues for the policy development process (for example, developing appropriate infrastructure investment rules for councils to respond to) , and the legislative timeframes to give effect to these . A two -stage approach would allow the requirements to be built up over time 18. Alternatively, a two-step approach to the parameters and requirements of the Plans could be considered. In this model: 18.1 The first step would set out the foundational settings for the Plans, including that councils would be required to provide them and indicative content. These requirements would apply to a draft Plan that councils would need to submit for review . Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua IN-CONFIDENCE Page 5 of 10 18.2 The second step would then build on and significantly tighten these settings, including increasing accountability to, and introducing ‘regulatory backstop ’ powers for, central government . These requirements would expect to apply to the final Plans councils would need to submit for approval . 19. An indicati ve approach to what would be required at each step is attached at Appendix B. 20. The Department recommends that a two -stage approach be taken to the Plans. Th is option would enable more flexibility for councils who wish to move quickly to new service delivery models , while also reliev ing some pressure on councils to deliver complete plans several months after completing their long -term plan . The submission of a draft Plan within 12 months would continue to set expectations for the transition, and provide oversight of council planning for yourself and agencies through the process. 21. Some councils may seek to move quickly, and prefer to meet all requirements in a single plan . As noted, it may require time for the full regulatory regime , and the rules councils will need to meet, to be issued. The Department will work to provide as much confidence as is possible in what will be required of councils early, to help enable this flexibility . There is further optionality within a two -stage approach 22. Within what has been proposed in Appendix B, there are opportunities to require some elements earlier (or later) as preferred. For example, setting and reporting against performance measures could be brought forward for inclusion in t he draft Plans . Conversely, some elements could only be required for the final Plans, for example funding and pric e path information. 23. There may also be value in not committing to the form of the second st age at this time. As noted previously, t he Plans are one part of the regulatory and oversight framework for water services that is currently being developed . In retaining flexibility, and not committing to the remaining specific requirements outlined in LWDW, there may be opportunities for reconsidering and potentially streamlining planning and reporting requirements and reducing the compliance burden on councils. Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua IN-CONFIDENCE Page 2 of 7 Purpose 1. This paper provides advice on: 1.1 the potential tax impacts of Cabinet’s decision to not prohibit water organisations from making distributions; and 1.2 the interactions between exemptions from minimum requirements and the tax status of water organisations. 2. Ministers’ decisions on these matters will inform the drafting instructions for the Local Government (Water Services) Bill (Bill 3). Background 3. In June and July this year , Cabinet approved a series of papers which set out the policy detail of Local Water Done Well, including: 3.1 restor ing council ownership and control of water services; 3.2 establish ing clear outcomes -based rules and minimum requirements for water services; 3.3 strengthen ing the regulatory regime through new economic and improved water quality regulation; and 3.4 provid ing a framework for new water organisation s designed specifically for water services. 4. In the third and final paper, Cabinet agreed (CAB -24-MIN -0277.03) that water organisations should be granted tax -exempt status. This proposed income tax exemption was recommended on the assumption that water organisations would not be able to provide distributions to shareholders, which had been proposed in the paper. 5. Cabinet also agreed that councils could apply for an exemption from some of the minimum requirements applying to water organisations. The Cabinet paper noted that granting such an exemption could affect the water organisation’s tax status. 6. Due to the outstanding tax issues , Cabinet authorised the Minister of Finance, Minister of Local Government, and Minister of Revenue to make further decisions during the course of legislative drafting in relation to how any tax implications associated with water organisations, distributions made by water organisa tions, and the exemption process for water organisations may be addressed. 7. Cabinet invited the Minister of Local Government to report back to the Cabinet Legislation Committee on any substantive decisions made under the delegated authority when approval to introduce the bill is sought . Why tax status is important 8. New Zealand’s tax settings reflect the principle that tax should apply to a wide definition of income (broad -base) so that less tax needs to be collected (low rate) from each source. Tax exemptions put pressure on tax rates as they inherently reduce the total amount of potential income that is available to be taxed. Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua IN-CONFIDENCE Page 3 of 7 9. The income tax exemption proposed for water organisations was justified on the basis that: 9.1 private sector investors would not be able to benefit from the tax exemption , due to the prohibition on distributions and restrictions on shareholders ; and 9.2 these organisations will have a primary public -policy purpose of undertaking water -related activities in a monopoly market , rather than a profit -making activity in competition with the private sector. 10. As water organisations will be able to make distributions to shareholders, and taking into account the potential outcomes arising from exemptions from minimum requirements, we have modified our positions for consistency. 11. In developing a response to these issues , consideration has been given to both the impact this may have on the tax base and the precedent it may set in relation to other entities in similar circumstances. Tax status of water organisation s that meet all minimum requirements 12. As previously advised [ LG20242706 ], allowing water organisations to make distributions means the tax status of the shareholders should be considered when determining the tax status of the water organisation. 13. Under the minimum requirements, shareholders of water organisations can either be councils or consumer trusts. Councils are broadly exempt from income tax1; the income they derive, primarily through rates, is used for the benefit of their communities. 14. However, a consumer trust would be a taxable entity and would face no such restrictions on how it used the income it receives . A consumer trust can achieve income tax-exempt status by applying for and maintaining charitable status. As previously advised [ LG20242705 ], we believe consumer trusts created to hold shares in water organisations will easily fall within the “other purposes beneficial to the community” category of charitable organisations. This would both grant the water organisation a tax exemption and ensure that it only provides public, and not private, benefits. 15. Nevertheless, there may be good reasons that a consumer trust would not want to apply for charitable status. One reason could be if the council establishing the water organisation wanted the shareholding consumer trust to distribute income back to consumers in the same fashion that an energy trust does. Energy trusts are not able to gain charitable status, in part because of the intent to provide private benefits back to consumers , normally through a discount on lines charges . 16. It is important that the shareholders of a tax -exempt entity are also tax -exempt if there are no restrictions on distributions . Tax exemptions are primarily provided for specific public purposes.
