This briefing provides advice on a 'single standard approach' to wastewater environmental performance standards (wastewater standards), where, once made by Taumata Arowai, the requirements in the standard would be implemented through resource consents. Stricter or higher requirements would only be included in a resource consent by a consent authority (regional councils) in exceptional cases.1 Since your last briefing outlining a minimum and maximum range approach [LG20242842 refers] officials have continued to develop the policy approach in relation to setting a single national standard. 2. This briefing outlines: 2.1 the approach taken in other jurisdictions and how wastewater standards operate; 2.2 how a similar approach might be implemented in New Zealand (including the implications for legislation, and whether changes might be required); 2.3 whether other changes could be made to incentivise use of modular design treatment plants as part of standard-setting; 2.4 how the approach would be explored and implemented through Taumata Arowai's work programme; and 2.5 initiatives that could be pursued in the broader resource management system to achieve further regulatory efficiencies for wastewater treatment plants. Background 3. Taumata Arowai is currently developing wastewater standards covering core areas in resource consents for wastewater treatment plants. You have requested advice on your preference for a single standard rather than a minimum and maximum range approach , and information on how that could be achieved. The wastewater standards will apply to all receiving environments but will be particularly applicable for discharges to water. A single standard is consistent with international best practice and is the preferred approach 4. In previous advice we explored what a minimum and maximum range approach to wastewater standards might look like [LG20242842 refers]. 5. Either a minimum -maximum range approach to standards or a single standard approach are possible in legislative and operational terms: 1 A single standard approach would include tiers of standards based on characteristics such as population serviced by a plant or mixing level of a water body it discharges to. IN-CONFIDENCE Page 2 of 11 Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs> 5.1 while both would require further work as part of Taumata Arowai's work programme, in terms of the technical work it is much more complex to set a minimum -maximum range; 5.2 both will require legislative change to the RMA, and probably the WSA, to be confident the approach can and would be implemented across the regulatory system. 6. On balance our advice is that a single standard is the better approach for the reasons outlined below. 7. A single standard approach is consistent with international best practice2• Taumata Arowai's technical experts could not identify any other jurisdiction where a maximum standard approach was adopted. They advised that in other jurisdictions where a standard is set, plants are generally consented to a national standard. That is, it is not a 'minimum standard', it is the standard. 8. In this sense a discharge standard operates like the drinking water standards which set treatment requirements that suppliers are expected to meet. Requirements for higher levels of treatment are generally only set in exceptional cases, for example, where a wastewater plant discharges to a pristine or particularly sensitive water body. 9. In system terms, a single standard is a better fit with the existing RMA regime. While it will deliver standardisation in approach to resource consenting, together with the flow on standardisation of infrastructure and procurement, there will still be potential for consent authorities (regional councils) to set conditions in consents that are stricter than the standard. However, this ability will be limited through legislative change so stricter or higher requirements would only possible on an exceptions basis defined in legislation. 10. Taken overall, a single standard approach will allow for standardisation of treatment systems and related infrastructure, material cost efficiencies in the design, build and operation of wastewater systems and greater certainty for councils in terms of infrastructure and budget planning. The single standard approach will also allow for greater certainty, consistency, and cost control across the wastewater treatment plant consenting system. As with a minimum and maximum range approach, these outcomes are aligned with the objectives of Local Water Done Well. 11. The problematic areas for a minimum -maximum range approach are related to the "maximum" standard which regional councils would not be able to go beyond when setting a resource consent. Taking expert advice, we have not been able to identify another jurisdictions that takes this approach. In system terms it is likely to present challenges for regional councils and network operators depending on how the maximum standard is configured for the following reasons: 11.1 there will be cases where a maximum standard will be inflexible to (or be perceived to be) inflexible to the water quality of a water body. Under the RMA, water quality, together with community expectations about what it should be, is the primary driver for consent limits rather than standardisation of 2 Taumata Arowai sought advice from technical experts with experience in overseas jurisdictions such as the United Kingdom and the European Union where wastewate r standards have been in place for over 30 years. IN-CONFIDENCE Page 3 of ll Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairsinfrastructure. In a subset of cases, higher treatment than the maximum standard maybe required to deliver the right outcomes for the water body; 11.1 there is a risk a maximum standard will have unintended consequences, and will not provide flexibility where a wastewater operator voluntarily treats wastewater to a higher standard than in the resource consent (for example, to provide for reuse of wastewater), and inadvertently breaches their resource consent because wastewater is "too good" to discharge to water. 12. For iwi/Maori there may be a perception that a maximum standard would cut across the health of the water body and their role as kaitiaki, by hardwiring in a maximum level of treatment that could lead to greater pollution than their aspirations. There may also be greater implications for those Treaty settlements which have catchment­ related requirements (such as the Waikato-Waipa or Whanganui settlements). 13. In order to progress a single wastewater standard approach, legislative change will be required to ensure consenting authorities implement a single standard approach in resource consents. You may also wish to consider including provisions in the WSA allowing Taumata Arowai to specify infrastructure and operating requirements that, if implemented by a wastewater operator, will meet the treatment requirements in the standard. Broader changes to the resource management framework might also be possible to streamline consenting pathways. These matters are dealt with in the remainder of this briefing. Realising the benefits of a single standard approach Regulatory efficiencies could be achieved where wastewater treatment plant design and consenting processes were aligned to a new wastewater standard 14. There is a significant opportunity for economies of scale and cost savings across the system if an end-to end modular design-consent-build approach was adopted for lower-risk wastewater treatment plants for small communities (i.e. less than 1,000 people), aligned to comply with a new wastewater standard. These are likely to be smaller-scale plants in provincial or rural areas with less complex treatment processes and will not generally include those with industrial discharges. 15. An example is where an oxidation pond may be currently used to treat wastewater. This is common throughout New Zealand, but treatment outcomes are highly variable and, as a consequence, these arrangements often breach resource consents. Reconsenting of oxidation ponds could occur with integration of a modular plant to lift treatment outcomes. This approach to upgrading plants is being implemented by some territorial authorities. Wastewater standards would incentivise the approach across New Zealand. 16. Of the 294 wastewater treatment plants that will require reconsenting in the next decade, 150 service populations of 1,000 people or less. These plants make up around 50 percent of the total number of council-owned wastewater plants in New Zealand. 17. While there will be local differences, industry estimates of the costs of the design, consent and construction of those plants are up to $25 million for plants servicing less than 1,000 people. It is estimated that, in some cases, up to half of those costs relate to design and consenting issues. In contrast, a modular off-the-shelf wastewater treatment plant that was designed to meet the standard could be 'constructed' and be operational for around $10-20 million. IN-CONFIDENCE Page 4 of 11 Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs18. Modular, standardi sed approaches to the provision of wastewater treatment are common internationally , but barriers to their adoption in New Zealand include: 18.1 no consistent approache s to consenting wastewater treatment plants; 18.2 councils operating in silos and rely on local consultants leading to bespoke design; and 18.3 lack of capability/confidence to procurement of standardised solutions internationally . 19. With the bow wave of wastewater treatment plants needing to be reconsented (and upgraded} in the next 10 years, the development of a 'pipeline' of plants that could be commissioned and the use of modular design could drive these costs down further (LG 20242359 refers]. 20. Wastewater standards under the WSA are linked in legislation to resource consenting under the RMA. Section 104 (2D) of the RMA specifies that a consent authority, when considering an application for a resource consent that relates to a wastewater network (as defined in the WSA): • must not grant the consent contrary to a wastewater environmental performan ce standard made under section 138 of that Act; and • must include, as a condition of granting the consent, requirements that are no less restrictive than is necessary to give effect to the wastewater environmental performance standard. IN-CONFIDENCE Page 5 of 11 Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs22. Taumata Arowai was given powers to make wastewater standards under the WSA. Once the wastewater standards are in place, resource consents must not be granted contrary to, or less restrictive than, a standard. However, a consent authority may currently impose conditions that require higher treatment requirements. 23. Despite the recent legislative changes to both the RMA and the WSA to remove the Te Mana o te Wai hierarchy of obligations from resource consenting processes and the development of wastewater standards, there are still provisions that allow a proposed wastewater standard to be exceeded in consenting decisions. For example, where regional council policy requirements go beyond national policy requirements (e.g. by directing all wastewater discharges to land, as is proposed in the Northland Regional Council freshwater plans), and where regional plans and policy statements and some iwi management plans have embedded Te Mana o te Wai in their planning documents and the hierarchy remains operational. 24. To be able to implement the changes outlined proposed in this briefing relating to a single standard, legislative changes to the WSA and RMA legislation will be needed to: 24.1 provide more directive provisions that ensure regional councils cannot set additional or higher requirements than the standard (allowing for some specific exceptions); 24.2 allow Taumata Arowai to be able to set infrastructure and operating requirements that, if implemented by a wastewater operator, will meet the treatment requirements in the standard -this could be used to specify design solutions such as integration of modular plants with existing oxidation ponds; and 24.3 allow an easier consenting path or 'pre-consented option' for lower-risk small-scale modular wastewater treatment plants that met the standard. 25. These changes are critical to support councils in addressing challenges in the reconsenting the bow wave of wastewater treatment plants. Around 70 percent of wastewater treatment plants will require reconsenting in the next 10 years, with the most challenging issues where plants discharge to freshwater or low mixing environments like estuaries or bays close to the coast. 26. This does not mean lower environmental requirements for discharges to fresh water or coastal water. It means that a consistent approach to consenting the discharge of wastewater from treatment plants will be provided, which reduces the regulatory burden by targeting key weaknesses in the existing resource management regime. 27. Further work will be needed to develop and agree the appropriate policy approach and nature of the legislative changes. In your July Cabinet paper you are seeking the following legislative changes: 27 .1 delegated authority to work with and agree the appropriate approach with the Minister Responsible for RMA Reform to progress these changes; 27.2 once changes to WSA and RMA have been agreed, delegated authority for you to authorise issuing of drafting instructions to include these changes in the Local Government Water Services Bill. 28. Your Cabinet paper has been drafted in line with the points in paragraph 27, and is currently with Ministers and departments for consultation. If you agree, your Cabinet paper could also be amended to authorise changes to the WSA to allow Taumata Arowai to be able to set infrastructure and operating requirements that, if implemented by a wastewater operator, will meet the treatment requirements in a wastewater standard. Taumata Arowai has started work on developing the wastewater standards 30. Taumata Arowai's work programme is already focused on a single standard approach of this nature, by identifying the approach taken in other jurisdictions, and considering how they might need to be adapted to the New Zealand context. 31. To ensure the outcomes in this briefing are achieved, further work could be commissioned to identify: 31.1 what, in practice, are the situations in other jurisdictions where wastewater plants have needed to be consented above a national standard on an exceptions basis -this evidence would be used to develop changes to the RMA to ensure regional councils cannot set additional or higher requirements than the standard except on an exceptions basis that would be specified in legislation; and 31.2 infrastructure design and operating requirements that, if implemented by a wastewater operator, would meet the treatment requirements in the standard - for example, modular or package plants. This information could be used to specify or incentivise standardisation in infrastructure as part of the wastewater standard. 32. Draft recommendations on the wastewater standards will be available in the coming months that will be tested with two groups: 32.1 a technical advisory group made up of councils and industry experts who will provide advice on whether the standards are technically fit for purpose -that is, do they target the appropriate contaminants and are workable for infrastructure requirements and consenting processes; and 32.2 a reference group that will provide confidence about the regulatory impact of standards (for example, whether they promote cost efficiencies in the system) and their overall fit with Local Water Done Well priorities. 33. Taumata Arowai can discuss the composition and membership of these groups with you. Members of your Technical Advisory Group could also be included on one or both of these groups to provide continuity across work programmes. The wastewater standard and changes proposed above go a long way to improving regulatory efficiencies, but more could be done in the resource management system 34. Role of bylaws 12. Currently local authorities have the ability to regulate the activities of their water services consumers and third parties through broad bylaw -making powers under the Local Government Act 2002 (LGA02) , with offences and enforcement powers set out directly in the Act. There are also some relevant provisions in the Local Government Act 1974 and the Health Act 1956 .1 13. As part of the Local Water Done Well model, the enabling legislative framework for water organisations will need to allow for them to exercise some of these regulatory powers. 14. Bylaws are one of the few tools available to local authorities to manage relationships with their water services consumers. They cover a wide range of matters, including: 14.1 consumer responsibilities; 14.2 infrastructure design standards; 14.3 prohibition of certain discharges; 14.4 demand management (water restrictions); 14.5 charges; and 14.6 establishing local authorities’ rights to access water systems and read meters. 15. Bylaws can also regulate actions of third parties in relation to activities that may affect water services . For example, they can make it illegal to discharge certain substances into stormwater drains, control who can access drinking water catchment areas, and regulate work on or around networks.

The next steps section at the end of this briefing outlines the likely work involved. Key messages 3. Under the Water Services Act 2021 (the Act), all drinking water suppliers (except domestic self-suppliers) are covered by the regulatory system, and required to provide safe drinking water. This was considered the most effective and straightforward way of protecting public health, and responding to the concerns raised in the Inquiry into Havelock North Drinking Water. The new regulatory regime has been designed to tailor regulatory settings to the size, risk profile, and complexity of supplies. 4. We understand you may be interested in reconsidering this approach, to reduce the potential 'regulatory burden' that may be incurred by smaller suppliers. This is something that has been advocated by some stakeholders, and by members of the National Party and ACT Party. 5. You could consider excluding some smaller suppliers from being regulated, based on the number of people they serve. We have outlined two possible options: a threshold of 25 people (option 1); and a threshold of 100 people, but only for lower-risk supplies (option 2). 6. Our initial view is that option 1 could be a pragmatic way to make the regulatory system less burdensome with a level of risk that could be tolerable -providing Taumata Arowai is able to provide support to unregulated suppliers (that want it). We would like to do further work to develop and test this option. We do not recommend option 2, as this would carry much greater risk and be more difficult to implement. 7. We have also outlined a further option (option 3), which we suggest is progressed in parallel with option 1. This involves minimising the requirements that apply to other smaller suppliers, and giving these suppliers a longer timeframe to be compliant with the Act (beyond the current 2028 deadline). 8. To provide a basis for considering which -if any -of these options you might like to progress further, we have provided an overview of what being regulated is likely to mean in practice for smaller suppliers. This helps to indicate how much of a 'burden' they might face if no changes are made. 9. Taumata Arowai is required to regulate in a way that is proportionate to the scale, complexity and risk profile of drinking water supplies. This means many smaller suppliers will be subject to minimal obligations, and will receive advice and support - both to comply, and if emergencies arise. Regulatory approach under the Water Services Act 2021, and why it was introduced 13. Under the Water Services Act 2021: 13.1 all drinking water suppliers -except domestic self-suppliers -are covered by the regulatory system; and 13.2 all drinking water suppliers are required to provide safe drinking water. 14. This approach was taken in response to significant concerns raised through the Inquiry into Havelock North Drinking Water, and other work, about the previous drinking water regulatory regime in the Health Act. There were concerns that regime was failing to provide assurances that water supplies were safe and reliable. 15. The new regulatory approach sought to address two core issues with the previous arrangements: some suppliers were not being regulated effectively , and others were not regulated at all. 16. Advice in 2019 estimated that around 800,000 people were receiving drinking water from suppliers that were not regulated under the Health Act. The regulation of networked supplies was fragmented and weak, and many suppliers were effectively unregulated.1 17. Under the Water Services Act, all suppliers were brought into the regulatory system. The 2019 Cabinet paper that sought the relevant policy decisions noted that: ... the proposed approach would address many of the serious shortcomings with the current system, and provide New Zealanders and international visitors with the confidence that our drinking water supplies are safe and reliable. However, it involves a judgement call about how far to extend the regulatory perimeter, and the pros and cons of different options. We have approached the design of the reform proposals from the perspective that everyone should receive safe drinking water, but recognise that this will impose costs in the regulatory system that will be passed on to consumers.1 1 This included network supplies to fewer than 100 people. It also included several kinds of 'specified self­ supply', many of which were institutions and facilities serving a lot of people (such as schools, campgrounds, universities, airports, and defence properties) . 2 "Strengthen ing the regulation of drinking water, wastewater and stormwater", Minister of Local Government , Minister of Health, and Minster for the Environmen t (July 2019). IN CONFIDENCE Page3of12 Proactively released by the Department of Internal AffairsThe Department of Internal Affairs Taumata Arowai 18. This approach was considered the most effective and straightforward way of protecting public health and addressing widespread compliance issues -in suppliers of all size and type. Historically, there have been long-standing problems with non­ compliance as the size of the supply decreases. 19. It reflects that most consumers cannot assess the quality or safety of the water they drink, and have little or no choice about who supplies their water services. They have to put their trust in those responsible for supplying and regulating those services. 20. The Act requires suppliers to provide safe drinking water. It reflects that an essential principle of drinking water safety is that suppliers must 'own' the safety of the water. 21. In practice, this means all suppliers need to identify and manage risks to their supplies, ensuring they can deliver safe drinking water on a consistent basis.3 22. Domestic self-suppliers are excluded from the Act because they are responsible for the supplies to their own properties, and therefore have the ability and incentive to manage risks to those supplies themselves. What does being regulated mean for smaller suppliers? What do the smaller suppliers look /Ike? 23. Approximately 14 percent of people in New Zealand receive drinking water from suppliers that are not local or central government. This includes: 23.1 Private suppliers that provide drinking water to a larger, often fluctuating, number of people, such as vacation hotspots, supplies used by water carriers, campgrounds, and rural schools. 23.2 Private suppliers that provide drinking water to more than one household or dwelling. 23.3 Domestic self-suppliers, who are not regulated under the Act. 24. Many smaller supplies are located in remote communities, with poor infrastructure (including reliable electricity supplies necessary to run pumping, treatment and monitoring equipment) , limited access and greater distances to health services, and disproportionate exposure to severe weather events and their impacts. 25. Some smaller supplies, such as marae, campgrounds and community halls, have fluctuating populations and provide civil defence support in emergencies . This occurred in the aftermath of Cyclone Gabrielle in 2023. Others could be characterised as shared domestic supplies providing household water; for example, where a farm supplies neighbouring properties, or a drinking water source is shared between adjacent holiday homes. 3 This marked an important change from the previous legislative requirement to "take all practicable steps" to comply. That approach was highly problematic, as suppliers were deemed compliant If they started implementing a water safety plan. In effect this meant they could be technically compliant with the law, even though the water being supplied was not demonstrably safe. IN CONFIDENCE Page4of12 Proactively released by the Department of Internal AffairsThe Departme nt of Internal Affairs Taumata Arowai How are smaller suppliers regulated, and what ore they required to do? 26. Smaller suppliers (who were not previously registered) have until November 2025 to register with Taumata Arowai -through a free online self-service portal. They then have a further three years to become compliant with the full requirements in the Act and relevant secondary legislation (including the Drinking Water Quality Assurance Rules and Drinking Water Standards). 27. During the transition period -to November 2028 -smaller suppliers are: 27.1 subject to a basic obligation to provide safe drinking water that complies with Drinking Water Standards; and 27.2 required to comply with any direction or compliance order issued by Taumata Arowai. 28. The Act does not distinguish drinking water suppliers by size, although it requires regulatory mechanisms to be proportionate to the scale, complexity, and risk profile of each supply. Instead, the stratification of supplies into different groups by size (or other characteristics) occurs through secondary legislation made by Taumata Arowai, particularly the Drinking Water Quality Assurance Rules. 29. These Rules group 'smaller' supplies into two categories : 29.1 'Very small community' supplies that provide drinking water to up to 25 consumers. (Approximately 150 private supplies of this size have registered with Taumata Arowai, to date.) 29.2 'Small' networked supplies that provide drinking water to 26 to 100 consumers. (Approximately 200 private supplies of this size have registered.) 30. There are also 'medium' networked supplies that provide drinking water to 101 to 500 consumers, and 'large' networked supplies covering more than 500 consumers. These are primarily council owned and operated supplies. 31. The population thresholds in the Rules were chosen to align with previous Ministry of Health thresholds that suppliers were familiar with under the Health Act. Under that regime, suppliers to 25 or fewer people had minimal regulatory requirements outside of registering with the Ministry of Health. Very few supplies in this category did register as drinking water suppliers. How much of a 'compliance burden' might there be for smaller suppliers, and how is Taumata Arowai mitigating this? 32. Taumata Arowai regulates in a way that is proportionate to the scale, complexity, and risk profile of drinking water supplies. Regulatory resources are limited, and targeted to larger suppliers displaying risk. Typically, these supplies are more complex. At the small-to-medium end, Taumata Arowai will tailor any regulatory engagement to suit the needs of the supplier and community, alongside any indications of heightened public health risk. 33. Currently under the Drinking Water Quality Assurance Rules, the only obligations on drinking water supplies providing water to up to 25 people are to: 33.1 test twice a year for E. coli, using an accredited laboratory to perform the testing analysis; and IN CONFIDENCE Page So/ 12 Proactively released by the Department of Internal AffairsThe Department of Internal Affairs Taumata Arowai 33.2 make the results available to the owners and occupiers of all properties connected to the supply. 34. If the testing detects E. coli or other determinands that exceed maximum acceptable values, the Act requires a supplier to take certain actions, including: notifying Taumata Arowai, taking action to rectify the situation, and taking all practicable steps to advise affected consumers of the situation and what they should do to protect their health. 4 35. Once small suppliers register with Taumata Arowai, they must prepare a drinking water safety plan, which records the risks and hazards that impact a supply's drinking water and how they will be managed. Taumata Arowai has published guidance and templates to make it easy to make a plan and manage the risks associated with supplying drinking water. 36. 'Acceptable solutions' allow some suppliers to use off-the-shelf, end-point treatment systems (rather than centralised treatment that tends to be more expensive, labour­ intensive and require a higher level of maintenance) .5 37. For a single household, an end-point treatment system that meets acceptable solution requirements is estimated to cost $4,450. For a larger supply, such as a sports club or marae, this increases to an estimated $7,150. The costs are influenced by a range of factors, such as existing water supply configurations, location, and availability of tradespeople. 38. Suppliers that adopt an acceptable solution do not have to prepare a separate drinking water safety plan assessing the hazards and risks affecting their supplies. 39. There are currently three acceptable solutions, which relate to: 39.1 drinking water suppliers that abstract water from springs and bores; 39.2 mixed-use rural supplies (where at least 50% of the water supplied is intended to be used for agricultural or horticultural purposes); or 39.3 supplies that rely on roof water. 40. Taumata Arowai will take an engagement -led and educational approach to support smaller supplies coming into the regime. This will mean working with communities to understand their risks and needs, and to help them to build their capability. It will build off work already done through groups such as the Rural Supplies Technical Working Group, and the Marae and Papakainga Technical Advisory Group. 41. This approach will enable Taumata Arowai to further understand what the level of risk in these small supplies is, and therefore the most appropriate regulatory settings and interventions. 4 There have been over 800 notifications from laboratories where unregistered supplies have exceeded the maximum acceptab le levels of contaminants in drinking water since Taumata Arowai became the water services regulator in November 2021. 5 The acceptable solutions have been developed in collaboration with sector reference groups with experience of various supply types across New Zealand, including the rural sector. IN CONFIDENCE Page6of 12 Proactively released by the Department of Internal AffairsThe Department of Internal Affairs Taumata Arowai Options for reducing the 'regulatory burden' on smaller drinking water suppliers Relevant policy considerations 42. Following consideration of advice on smaller suppliers in December 2023 [LG202301363], you indicated an interest in reconsidering the regulatory approach to water suppliers in the Water Services Act. You asked for further advice on amending the 'thresholds ' for regulation. 43. We understand your main interest is in reducing the potential regulatory burden that could apply to smaller suppliers. The main option for achieving this could be to exclude some suppliers (in addition to domestic self-suppliers) from the application of the Water Services Act -based on the number of people they supply ('population threshold'). 44. Two variations of this option are outlined below. Both options are likely to require changes to the Act. Our initial view is that: 44.1 Option 1 could be a pragmatic way to make the regulatory system less burdensome, with an overall level of risk that could be tolerable -providing Taumata Arowai was still able to provide support to unregulated suppliers. We would like to do further work to develop and test this option. 44.2 We do not recommend proceeding with option 2, as this would carry much greater risk and be more difficult to implement . 45. We note that it is sometimes suggested that thresholds could relate to the number of connected properties or 'end-point users' being supplied. For example, members of the National Party and the ACT Party have previously suggested excluding supplies to 30 end-point users from the Bill/Act. (This is not terminology that has been used in legislation. The Department has interpreted it as referring to 30 connected properties, rather than 30 people.) 46. Taumata Arowai does not recommend using the number of connections as a basis for setting thresholds. This does not reflect the considerable variations in the number of people who use a connection (which could range from a person in a sole household to hundreds of people in a community facility). It would be difficult to implement and does not align with any legislative approaches that have been used previously. 47. We have also included a third option, which involves changing the regulatory approach and/or timeframes that will apply to smaller suppliers (not amending 'thresholds', as such). This may be more straightforward to implement and require less legislative change -and be a potentially useful addition to any attempts to make the regulatory system less burdensome. We suggest this work on this option is progressed in parallel with option 1. 48. Subject to your direction on these initial options, further work would be undertaken. We have outlined this in the next steps section. It would consider factors like how to design and implement the option(s), costs, benefits and risks, the detailed legislative amendments required, and implications for Taumata Arowai. 49. It would also involve engagement and testing with policy agencies with an interest in this matter, particularly the Ministry of Health, and others in the health sector. The IN CONFIDENCE Page 7of12 Proactively released by the Department of Internal AffairsThe Department of Internal Aff.3irs Taumata Arowai Ministry is responsible for policy relating to public health and interests in drinking water. 50. A key factor when considering any potential changes to the current legislative settings would be the appropriate balance between public health/safety and regulatory requirements. There would be a trade-off between protecting public health­ something that is prioritised under the current settings -and reducing the compliance costs/burden on small suppliers. 51. Placing less emphasis on regulating smaller suppliers may mean there is a greater public health risk associated with these supplies, and raise further equity issues in small, rural communities (without council supplies). It also means Taumata Arowai, and local authorities, have limited ability to identify these supplies, and offer support when required in emergency situations and in providing tailored advice. 52. Continuing to require small supplies to register and undertake limited testing (paired with bespoke support and capacity building) would help to build a picture of where these supplies are located, the risks they face, and any localised source water issues. 53. This information would support Taumata Arowai and local authorities to ensure communities have reliable access to safe drinking water if existing suppliers face significant problems (as required in the Local Government Act 2002). Not collecting this data is more likely to adversely affect remote communities and those facing climate resilience challenges. 54. That said, removing certain small suppliers from the requirement to register and undertake limited testing does not mean Taumata Arowai could not continue to provide education and tools to support suppliers to keep their water safe. There are also provisions in the Act that seek to ensure domestic self-suppliers are warned of potential water contamination issues, which could be applied to other non-regulated suppliers. 55. Taking a different approach to small supplies would provide opportunities for Taumata Arowai to place greater emphasis and focus on the larger and/or higher risk suppliers. Option 1: very small suppliers -to 25 people and below -are not regulated, and Taumata Arowal develops education material to be used on a voluntary basis 56. Under this option, all very small supplies -to 25 people and below -would be excluded from duties and requirements in the Water Services Act. This threshold would align with how very small community supplies are defined in the Drinking Water Quality Assurance Rules. 57. The public health risks associated with this change could be mitigated by Taumata Arowai providing online guidance and education material to support these supplies in providing safe drinking water. Adherence to this material would be voluntary and they would not be regulated. 58. This would be similar to the approach that is currently taken to domestic self-suppliers. It would recognise that very small suppliers have been subject to minimal regulation to date. 59. Taumata Arowai recommends this option should focus on exempting supplies characterised as shared domestic supplies -for example, those supplying neighbou ring IN CONFIDENCE PogeBo/12 Proactively released by the Department of Internal AffairsThe Department of Internal Affairs Taumata Arowai properties. This would mean arrangements where a farm or holiday home supplies drinking water to a small number of neighbouring properties would not be regulated. 60. Taumata Arowai would continue to regulate small public supplies (for instance, some rural schools) and those supplying water for commercial -style use, such as campgrounds and aged care facilities. 61. Because private supplies of this size have not been regulated, very little is known about them -either in terms of how many supplies there are, their customer and risk profile, or how difficult it may or may not be for them to comply with the new regulatory environment. This makes it difficult to estimate how much impact this option would have in practice, if implement ed (potentially making it difficult to prepare a regulatory impact assessment that contains this data). 62. If there was an interest in knowing more about these supplies -without them being 'regulated' as such -they could still be required to register with Taumata Arowai, but exempt from further requirements under the Act or secondary legislation. This would mean Taumata Arowai can collect basic information about these supplies, to inform emergency preparedness and assist local authorities to carry out assessments under the Local Government Act. Option 2: some small suppliers are not regulated -If they are lower-risk suppliers, serving under 100 people [NOT RECOMMENDED] 63. Under this option, the threshold for exclusion could be extended to suppliers to a higher number of people -for example, a threshold of 100 people. 64. We have included this option to indicate alternative considerations, but do not suggest it is taken further. It would be a higher risk approach than option 1, and is likely to raise far more challenges. However, if you were interested in th is option, we have outlined some of the factors and limitations that would need to be worked through. 65. We would suggest it is limited to privately owned and operated schemes for domestic dwellings, where the number of people being supplied is relatively low and stable. As above, Taumata Arowai would recommend publicly operated and commercial suppliers continue to be regulated. 66. We do not consider this exclusion should be extended to smaller council or other public supplies, or to supplies that are serving higher risk communities or where the numbers of people drinking the water is highly variable. 67. There are risks with small supplies of this nature, particularly around excluding supplies that provide drinking water to vulnerable communities -for example, rural schools, residential care facilities and community drinking water stations. Small supplies with fluctuating population s are also at higher risk. Campsites, marae, community halls and planned events fall into this category.6 68. We note that this kind of approach would be a departure from the recommendations of the Inquiry into Havelock North Drinking Water, and take settings back to the situation that existed prior to the 2008 changes to the Health Act. 6 Note that even if these supplies were not excluded from the application of the Water Services Act, they would still have the ability to seek an exemption from Taumata Arowai -as per the provisions in section 57 of the Act. IN CONFIDENCE Page 9of 12 Proactively released by the Department of Internal AffairsThe Department of Internal Affairs Taumata Arowai 69. There could be significant implications, unintended consequences, and potential gaps, which would need to be explored further. For example, we would need to consider what would happen to these suppliers in emergency situations- ifTaumata Arowai did not have a role/mandate to provide support, and neither the Ministry of Health nor local authorities are resourced or required to do this. 70. We would also provide further advice on the exact thresholds that could apply and how these might be set in legislation . Setting a limit of 100 people would be similar to the 'neighbourhood drinking water supply' under the Health Act. We understand the performance of suppliers of this size was not reported on by the Ministry of Health under that previous regime. Option 3: make it easier and less burdensome for smaller suppliers to comply, by extending the timeframes and reducing the regulatory requirements 71. This option could be an alternative to changing the thresholds, or it could be delivered in conjunction with either of the above options. As noted earlier, we suggest it is developed alongside option 1, as it would help to make the overall regulatory system less burdensome on smaller suppliers {not captured by any other exclusions). 72. This option would not involve changes to who is regulated -all drinking water suppliers (other than domestic self-suppliers) would continue to be covered by the Act. However, we would consider how to further reduce or minimise the requirements that apply to smaller suppliers -in the legislation and/or in how Taumata Arowai applies its regulatory approach. 73. This would align with the current situation, in which Taumata Arowai is enabled and required to take a proportionate, risk-based approach. Taumata Arowai could be given greater flexibility and discretion when it comes to regulating smaller (lower risk) suppliers. 74. With this option, there would continue to be a strong emphasis on the importance of public health and drinking water safety for all suppliers, but there would be greater recognition that only a relatively 'light touch' is likely to be warranted for very small supplies. It may be more straightforward to design and deliver than legislative changes to the 'thresholds' affecting the sizes and types of supply being regulated. 75. One particular area that could be modified -and where the 'burden' on small suppliers could be reduced -relates to drinking water safety plans. There are opportunit ies to amend the Act to make the requirements about what is included in these plans less prescriptive. Taumata Arowai could be given discretion to determine which supplies require a plan, and what they need to cover. 76. Amendments to the legislation could also be proposed to provide smaller suppliers with a longer timeframe in which to register with Taumata Arowai and to comply with the other requirements. This would give Taumata Arowai more time to provide guidance to smaller suppliers, and give those suppliers more time to understand the new regime and what it means for them. Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government 11 Organisational Capability Applicants will need to provide information specified by the TF Authority to demonstrate that the organisation seeking accreditation : •has the organisational capability including the people, policies, processes and systems required to deliver TF accredited services; •is financially sustainable; •can meet the standards prescribed in rules to deliver the service or services to one of the service levels provided for in regulations (refer to the following section for further information on service levels and the associated levels of assu rance they provide); and •has arrangements in place to provide a complaints and dispute resolution process that meets the requirements specified in regulation (further information on these requirements are outlined in the complaints and disputes resolution section of this paper). Fit and Proper Person Requirements Applicants will be required to grant permission for the TF Authority to validate information provided by the applicant to support a fit and proper person assessment of the applicant and any officer s responsible for the governance and management of the TF provider. This will include permission for the Authority to request a Police vetting check.5 The applicant would also need to provide information that demonstrate s the TF provider has appropriate policies and procedures in place to ensure employees entrusted with the delivery of accredited services meet fit and proper person requirements prescribed by the Authority. Assessment criteria The Act enables the TF Authority to accredit a provider if it is satisfied that they meet the requirements in sections 23 to 25 of the Act, any criteria for the assessment of applications, and any other requirements set by regulations. 5 The New Zealan d Police may release any information they hold if relevant to the purpose of the vetting request. This may include : •Conviction History Report . •Infringement/demerit reports . •Active charges and warrants to arrest . •Charges that did not result in a conviction including those that were acquitted, discharged without conviction, diverted, or withdrawn . •Any interaction had with New Zealand Police considered relevant to the role being vetted, including investigations that did not result in prosecution . •Information regarding family harm where the applicant was the victim, offender or witness to an incident or offence, primarily in cases where the role being vetted for takes place in the applicant's home environment where exposure to physical or verbal viole nce could place vulnerable persons at emotional or physical risk . •Information subject to name suppression where that information is necessary to the purpose of the vet. Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government 12 We propose that that the regulations provide for the TF Authority t o use the following criteria to assess applications for accreditation . There is sufficient evidence to satisfy the Authority that the applicant : •is a company that is incorporated in New Zealand, an incorporated society registered in New Zealand, or a New Z ealand Crown entity or government department; •will deliver one or more of the digital identity services specified in regulations established under the Act; •has the capability to meet the service standards specified in the rules to an appropriate level of a ssurance; •has demonstrated it will provide an internal complaints and disputes resolution process that meets regulatory requirements; •and officers responsible for the governance and management of the TF provider are fit and proper persons that can be entru sted with the delivery of digital identity services; •has policies and processes in place to ensure its employees entrusted with the delivery of accredited services meet fit and proper person standards prescribed by the Authority; •has demonstrated that it i s financially sustainable; and •has provided all the information specified in s ection 25 and addressed to the TF Authority’s satisfaction any issues of concern arising from any past practises as an identity services provider that have be en the subject of an investigation by the Privacy Commission or the Authority, or resulted in a decision to previously decline, suspend or cancel an accreditation. Duration Accreditation will be for a two -year period The Act provides that the accreditation of a TF provider or service expires at the end of the relevant period set by regulations (section 30(2) ). We propose that the regulations specify that a service accreditation ends two years (24 months) after the date it is granted by the TF Authority . We have considered options ranging from annual through to five yearly and indefinite accreditation. In proposing a two -year accreditation period, we have sought to balance the need to provide the TF Authority, users and relying parties with appropriate assurance that TF providers are meeting accreditation service standards against the compliance costs associated with renewal requirements. We consider a two -year accreditation period is appropriate given we are introdu cing a new regulatory system and there are likely to be changes in service standards given the rapidly evolving nature of the industry. We anticipate the rules will be updated in response to technology advances and commercial practice changes. Providers wi ll, need to demonstrate they are able to meet changes in service standards. Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government 13 We note that the Act allows for regulations to establish different expiry periods for different types of TF provider, different types of service and different levels of service. Du ring the Trust Framework’s establishment phase, we consider that a standard two -year period should apply to everyone. We anticipate that this is a matter the TF Authority may wish to review based on its experience administering the regulatory system two to three years after commencement. Renewal TF providers will be able to renew their service accreditations The Act includes provisions covering the accreditation renewal process (s ection 31). In effect when TF providers apply for renewal, they will need to demonstrate that they continue to meet the accreditation requirements and standards specified in the Act, rules and regulations, unless different requirements for renewal applications are established in regulations. We propose that the TF Board consider i ntroducing regulations that refine the renewal application requirements when developing the next tranche of regulations. The aim will be to establish a renewal application process that provides the TF Authority with assurance that TF providers can continue to meet accreditation requirements, in particular any changes that have been introduced since an applicant’s original accreditation, while minimising renewal application compliance costs. Accreditation mark Users and relying parties will be able to identi fy an accredited service through an accreditation mark If approved, a TF provider will be able to deliver the accredited service or services under the Trust Framework and display an accreditation mark that would apply to each accredited service. The accred itation mark that would be applied to each specific accredited service is an important distinguishing factor, as some organisations with accredited services could also provide non -accredited services, which do not display the accreditation mark. Display of the accreditation mark will help users in making decisions about who they want to share their personal information with. If they chose to use a TF provider’s accredited service, they will know that the: •service meets the technical standards set out in the rules that apply to that service; •service is delivered to a prescribed service level (as specified in the rules and regulations and discussed further in the next section of this paper); and •TF provider has undergone an assessment for security and privacy and will give the user control over the identity information they choose to share. To reduce the risk of a user or relying party misunderstanding whether a TF provider is delivering an accredited service, we propose that the regulations specify that the TF Authority will only allow accreditation marks to be displayed against specific services, rather than being displayed as a ‘generic’ accreditation by the organisation. Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government 15 5. Service Levels Overview As part of the accreditation process, the regulations will enable providers’ systems and processes to be assessed by the TF Authority to determine what level of service they can provide when delivering information, binding, and/or authentication services. Each of the ser vices will have four service levels. The service level indicates the capability that a TF provider can deliver their associated service to. Service levels will indicate to prospective users and relying parties what level of assurance a given service may a chieve. Levels of assurance are specific to attributes (or pieces of information about a person), not the service or organisation. Therefore, the service level will indicate to other people the capability of an accredited service and the expected level of assurance that service can provide. Proposed regulations The regulations will provide for the service levels that will apply to the delivery of information, binding, and authentication services. The requirements and standards TF providers will need to mee t to achieve a given service level will be set out in the rules. The rules will require compliance with the New Zealand Identification Management Standards (NZIMS ), which will be incorporated by reference. The levels of assurance set out in the NZIMS will form part of the requirements prescribed for each service level. Further details on the service levels contained in the New Zealand Identification Management Stan dards are available via this link: https://www.digital.govt.nz/standards - and-guidance/identification -mana gement/identification -management -standards/applying - the-standards/ Benefits In practice, service levels will help relying parties understand the outcome of assessment processes without having to know what the process was . They will give relying parties and other digital service providers an understanding of how robust the TF provider’s processes are. Establishing the service level through the accreditation process will also allow TF providers who rely on other providers f or information, binding , or authentication services to understand what level of assurance that provider can deliver. This increases the level of trust that relying parties and other TF providers have in the Trust Framework. Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government 17 6. Complaints and dispute resolution Overview Part 6 of the Act establishes processes for dealing with complaints and disputes. It enables any person to complain to the TF Authority if they believe a TF provider has breached the TF rules, regulations, terms of use of accreditation marks, or provisions of the Act. The Act ( section 28) also provides for regulations that set out requirements for TF providers to provide and operate their own internal complaints and disputes resolution processes. These processes can be used as a first port of call by complainants to address and resolve issues directly with the TF provider. Any complaints not resolved using this internal system can then be referred to the TF Authority for consideration. This approach is consistent with the principles established in the Act that gui de the TF Authority’s approach to complaints management , which are that : •processes for complaints should be fair, accessible and have particular regard to tikanga Māori; •complaints should be resolved in a timely and efficient manner; and •complaints should be resolved at a level appropriate to the seriousness and nature of the complaint. Proposed regulations – TF Provider internal complaints process We propose that the regulations require that every TF provider must: •receive and consider complaints about any service provided by it, including complaints that the provider has failed to comply with the TF rules, regulations, terms of use of accreditation marks, or other requirements arising from provisions in the Act; •establish and maintain p olicies and procedures for dealing with such complaints fairly, promptly and without undue formality; •publicise its complaints policies and procedures to users, prospective users, relying parties and other stakeholders with an interest in its services; and •ensure that complainants are aware that in the event they are dissatisfied with the outcome of the internal complaints process they may lodge a formal complaint with the TF Authority. The ability of an applicant to comply with these requirements will be a ssessed when they apply for accreditation. Potential future regulations for a dispute resolution scheme The Act also allows for the development of regulations to establish requirements and criteria that would enable the TF Authority to recommend a dispute resolution scheme for the Minister’s approval. Any scheme would need to complement and operate alongside the TF Authority’s complaints process which can lead to the TF Authority applying a range of remedies where it finds a TF Provider has breached legisla tive requirements. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs 1 Departmental D isclosure Statement Films, Videos, and Publications Classification (Commercial Video on -Demand) Amendment Bill The departmental disclosure statement for a government Bill seeks to bring together in one place a range of information to support and enhance the Parliamentary and public scrutiny of that Bill. It identifies: •the general policy intent of the Bill and other background policy material ; •some of the key quality assurance products and processes used to develop and test the content of the Bill; •the presence of certain significant powers or features in the Bill that m ight be of particular Parliamentary or public interest and warrant an explanation . This disclosure statement was prepared by the Department of Internal Affairs . Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs 2 Contents Contents ................................ ................................ ................................ .................... 2 Part One: General Policy Statement ................................ ................................ .......... 3 Part Two: Background Material and Policy Information ................................ ............. 5 Part Three: Testing of Legislative Content ................................ ................................ . 8 Part Four: Significant Legislative Features ................................ .............................. 10 Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs 3 Part One: General Policy Statement The objective of this Bill is to reduce t he potential for harm to consumers from viewing inappropriate content . The Bill will do this by requiring that commercial video on -demand (CVoD ) content that is made available in New Zealand display s appropriate and consistent labelling , if the provider of that content is specified in the Schedule to the Bill . This labelling will provide information about that content’s rating and description so that consumers can make an informed decision on whether to view it. Providers of commercial (subscription and transactional) video on -demand content are displaying inconsistent ratings and descriptive note s (or no ratings at all) for content available on their platforms. This is because of the gap in current legislation where on -demand online content in New Zealand is not subject to mandatory rating requirements, as ‘films’ for cinematic or DVD release ar e. This Bill will ensure that consumers see more consistent ratings a nd descriptive notes across the main CVoD platforms in New Zealand. The Bill will amend the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification Act 1993 (the Act) to clearly address the identified regulatory gap . Key changes the Bill will implement are : Requ irements for specified CVoD providers to label content before it is available in New Zealand Providers of CVoD content will be required to comply by •following the current process for the labelling of film. This involves providing content to the Film and Video Labelling Body (the labelling body) for rating and labelling. The labelling body will refer certain content to the Office of Film and Literature Classification (the Classification Office) for classifi cation , before issuing a label ; or •self-rating content that they supply using systems which have been approved by the Classification Office. This can be achieved either by using the Classification Office’s rating tool or using their own system, with approval from the Classification Office. Once content is labelled under the Act, that label will be included in a public regi ster and must be used by any other provider providing that content. These labelling decisions can be reconsidered by the Classification Office where necessary. Establishment of criteria and process to identify and list regulated providers Providers that are required to comply under the new requirements will be listed in a schedule of the Act. The schedule can be amended by an Order in Council , with the final decision being made by the Governor -General on the recommendation of the Minister of Internal Affairs. The Minister will need to consult the Chief Censor before making a recommendation to amend the schedule . The Minister will also need to consider the potential ‘risk of harm’ to consu mers from CVoD content being made available without appropriate labels before making a recommendation to amend the Schedule . The Bill sets the following criteria that the Minister must consider in determining the potential ‘risk of harm ’: •Market presence: the share of the New Zealand market that a provider currently has or is expected to have ; and •Compliance with and commitment to another classification framework established in New Zealand: whether a provider is using a classification framework that provides consistent and appropriate information to consumers, as well as the extent and reliability of its commitment to that framework; and Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs 4 •Nature of content: the nature of content being offered by a provider, and the potential of this content to cause harm to consumers. Updated functions of Classification Office The Bill will update the functions of the Classification Office to ens ure th at the new requirements for CVoD content are clearly withi n the scope of its operational work. The Classification Office will have the following new functions and powers: •providing an online rating tool that specified CVoD providers may use to rate and label content they provide ; and •approving any Self-Rating Systems which are developed by specified CVoD providers to rate and label their content; and •reviewing and monitoring the operation and outputs of both the online rating -tool and the any self-rating systems. Amendment to definition of ‘Film’ t o clarify that it includes video on-demand content Video on -demand content falls within the existing definition of a publication, but it does not clearly fall within the definition of a film (which is a subset of publications). The Bill replaces the defini tion of ‘film’ in the Act to clarify that it includes video on -demand content (CVoD is a subset of video on -demand content this is provided to consumers on a subscription or transaction basis ). Clarifying that video on -demand content is a film means that the requirements in relation to classifying and rating films will apply to any video on -demand content that is not specifically exempted from those requirements. The Classification Office’s powers in respect of publications (e.g. complaints pro cess, enforcement provisions and offences and penalties ) will also apply. Anticipated introduction of new fees for use of CVoD rating and labelling tools The new regime introduced by the Bill will also permit new fees to be set for the use and review of CVoD rating and labelling tools . Fees under the Act are set in the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification (Fees) Regulations 1994 . Work is underway to update the fees framework , including the level of the CVoD fees for specified CVoD providers. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs 9(2)(a) 9(2)(a) 9(2)(a) Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 2 of 8 Purpose 1. In December you requested from officials, information on international policy initiatives to comprehensively regulate online content. There is growing international concern over the risk of harm posed by online media content 2. Similar to NZ, other jurisdictions are also grappling with outdated media content regulatory systems that do not have the flexibility to respond to new forms of media and the risk of harm they pose. Previously, the dominant view has been that user- generated content should be largely left unregulated to protect freedom of expression . This view holds that freedom of expression needs to be given paramount protection to reap the benefits of the internet’s user participation framework. These benefits include increasing public access to information, allowing public political discussion to occur at national and global levels, and giving greater political voice to marginalised group. 3. Recent high-profile cases of serious harm arising from content hosted on online social networks have propelled growing international debate over the responsibilities of online platforms and governments to regulate harmful online content. These high- profile cases include the streaming of the 15 March 2019 Christchurch Terror Attack, allegations of foreign election interference, COVID-19 misinformation, the 20 21 storming of the United States Capitol and violations of data privacy 4. There is also growing recognition that characteristics of the online environment amplify the volume, speed, and reach of harmful media content, which increases the risk of online media content causing harm to individuals, society and democratic institutions compared to traditional media . These characteristics or the online environment include:  People are less inhibited when communicating online leading them to be more likely to create and share harmful media content. This is because social and cultural constraints on speech do not operate online to the extent they do offline. Contributing to this disinhibition effect is the relative anonymity of online content creators and sharers. In addition, the decoupling of content creators and content distributors weakens accountability, contributing to the disinhibition effect;  Social bots and fake profiles1 are being used amplify the spread of harmful content; and  Social interests and commercial incentives are in conflict - the business incentives of online platforms are, in some cases, misaligned with protecting users and the broader public from harm. The business models of online platforms are structured around maximising audience engagement for advertising revenue. For this reason, recommendation systems2 usually prioritise pages which are visited most often and have the greatest time spent on them. Content that elicits an emotional response, such as outrage, disgust and anger

Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Page 2 of 17 Purpose 1. This briefing seeks your agreement on a first tranche of policy related to introducing a self-identification process for recognising gender on birth certificates through the Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Bill (the Bill). Executiv e summary 2. It is important that transgender1 and intersex2 people are able to have their gender recognised on their birth certificates. Birth certificates are often used as a form of identity verification. If the sex recorded does not align with their gender, they risk being ‘outed’ as transgender or intersex. These experiences have a detrimental effect on the mental health and wellbeing of transgender and intersex people . 3. The Family Court process for changing sex on a birth certificate is difficult to access for many people due to cost or the intrusiveness of the medical requirement. We recommend making the change more accessible by introducing a self-identification process . This paper sets out the policy decisions required to introduce a self- identific ation process. 4. Self-identification would remove the requirement for a Family Court declaration and for evidence of medical treatment and would enable people to apply directly to the Registrar-General with a statutory declaration form. 5. We think the self-i dentification process should be available for children and young people . Further work is required, however, to determine how we do that and ensure any change is in the best interest of the child or young person. We seek an in-principle decision on this and will provide further advice in April 2021 . 6. There are risks, which will require mitigation measures, to progressing these policies in the Bill. These include: 6.1 a lack of consultation with Māori, Pacific peoples, and other ethnic communities; 6.2 organised opposition to a self -identification process; and 6.3 not addressing broader questions about sex and gender. 7. Agencies that we have consulted are supportive of introducing a self-identification process. However, they have had significant feedback on some of the specific policies we are considering. Background 8. You have indicated you would like to replace the Family Court process to change the sex on a birth certificate with a self-identification process. Self-identification was introduced to the Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Bill (the Bill) in 2018 at the recommendation of the select committee.

There are issues with the Bill’s self -identification provisions 9. You have indicated your preferred option is to progress the Bill with the self- identification provisions inserted by Select Committee in 2018 . The self-identification provisions update the process for changing the sex recorded on a birth certificate to an administrative process based on self-identification. This will benefit transgender and Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 3 of 10 intersex New Zealanders and make it easier for them to obtain a birth certificate that aligns with their gender identity. However, issues with the self-identification provisions have been identified since the Bill was deferred in 2019. First, the terminology used for sex/gender markers may not meet all people’s needs 10. The sex/gender marker options in the self-identification provisions include female, male, intersex or X – unspecified . ‘Intersex’ is not an appropriate term to include as most intersex people identify as men or women. The marker reinforces the idea that information recorded should be based on biology as opposed to a person’s gender identity. This could be considered out of step with human rights discourse and not respectful of intersex people’s right to self -determination. 11. The marker options are also not inclusive of people who identify as non-binary. While Select Committee included the option of ‘X -unspecified’ to recognise non -binary gender identities, this is unlikely to be non- binary people’s preferred term. 12. Since the Bill was deferred, Statistics New Zealand have reviewed the statistical standards for sex and gender, with updated standards expected to be finalised in March 2021. Further work could be done so the current marker options for birth certificates align with Statistics New Zealand’s findings . Second, c ontinuing to use a ‘sex’ field on birth certificates can be confusing 13. A person’s chose n marker would appear under the ‘sex’ field on birth certificates. This conflates sex and gender identity and could reinforce that the information under this field should be based on biology. For clarity , further consideration could be given to the terminology used for this category. Third, recording sex and gender on birth certificates may not be best practice 14. Recording sex or gender on birth certificates could be considered out of step with international human rights discourse, which recommends that official identity documents exclude the registration of this information. However, this discourse also recommends that where official identity documents include sex or gender, this information is based on an accessible self-identification process. We will consider how to resolve the above issues 15. We will give further consideration on how to resolve the above issues with the self- identification provisions. As part of this we will develop options for the scope of any work to address these issues, considering what could reasonably be completed so the Bill can be enacted in late 2021 or early 2022. 16. We are aware of general views for and against self-i dentification, which have been well canvassed in the process to date. However, we recognise any work to address the above issues would benefit from a better understanding of specific population groups ’ views, such as M āori, Pasifika, and intersex people. We will consider how to incorporate a targeted consultation process into any work on the self-identification provisions. We will provide you with further advice on the scope of work on the self- identification provisions and approaches to targeted consultation by May 2021. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Regulatory Impact Statement | 19 Appendix: Class 4 Venue requirements of the Gambling Act 2003 and the Gambling (Harm Prevention and Minimisation) Regulations 2004 The Gambling Act 2003 and the Gambling (Harm Prevention and Minimisation) Regulations 2004 require: 1. The venue has a policy for identifying problem gamblers. The venue manager, or person acting on their behalf, must take all reasonable steps to ensure that the policy is used to identify actual or potential problem gamblers ( Section 308). Failure to do so may result in a fine of up to $5,000. 2. There is always a staff member who has received problem gambling awareness training at the venue whenever gambling is available. A trained staff member must be able to approach a player and provide appropriate information about problem gambling ( Reg 12). 3. A notice is displayed in the gambling area advising customers that you have such a policy and that a copy of the policy will be made available on request ( Section 308). Failure to supply a copy of this policy when requested may result in the venue manager being fined up to $5,000. 4. Once a problem gambler has been identified, or there are reasonable grounds to believe that the person is a problem gambler, staff must approach that person and offer information or advice about problem gambling ( Section 309). That information or advice must include a description of the self - exclusion procedure ( Section 309(2) ). 5. After offering the advice and information an exclusion order may be issued by the venue manager (or person acting on their behalf). This prohibits the person from entering the gambling area for a period of up to two years ( Section 309(3) ). 6. An exclusion order must be issued promptly if a person has identified themselves as being a problem gambler and has requested that the venue prohibit them from entering the gambling area ( Section 310). A venue manager (or person acting on their behalf) that fails to issue a self -exclusion order when requested commits an offence and is liable for a fine of up to $5,000. 7. Staff must take all reasonable steps (including issuing an exclusion order) to provide continued assistance on an on- going basis to a person they believe is a problem gambler after the initial approach if the person’s ongoing behaviour means there are still reasonable grounds to believe the person is a problem gambler ( Section 309A ). 8. Excluded persons must not be permitted to enter the gambling area and must be removed if they do so (Section 311). A venue manager (or person acting on their behalf) who allows an excluded person to enter the gambling area or fails to remove an excluded person may commit an offence and is liable for a fine of up to $5,000 ( Section 312). 9. The venue manager must keep a record of exclusion orders ( Section 312A ), including: • The person’s name and date of birth (if provided); and • Whether the person self -excluded, or received a venue- initiated exclusion; and • The date which the exclusion order was issued and the date of expiry; and • Any conditions imposed on the person’s re- entry into the venue. 10. No one aged 18 or under can gamble at the venue ( Section 302). Offences may result in a fine of up to $5,000. 11. Providing credit for gambling is prohibited ( Section 15). 12. No ATMs are permitted in the gambling area of a venue ( Reg 5). 13. Class 4 operator s must ensure that: maximum amount single play stake (for stand- alone or linked machine) does not exceed $2.50; maximum prize single play prize does not exceed $500, and; maximum single play jackpot prize a linked gaming machine does not exceed $1,000 ( Reg 6 ). 14. Gaming machines must display certain messages at the election of the player, specifically: game information (odds, average winnings, player spend rates), player information (duration, amount spent, net wins/losses). Machine must also display correct time ( Reg 7). 15. Gaming machines must include feature that interrupts play every 30 minutes and provides player information (duration, amount spent, net wins/losses). Machine must include a feature that automatically pays out any winnings and credits to the player, if they do not wish to continue ( Reg 8). 16. No advertising relating to a gaming machine jackpot s can be published either outside the venue, or inside the venue in a way that is visible or audible to persons outside the venue ( Reg 9 and 10). 17. The following must be available to players ( Reg 11): • Pamphlets containing information about the odds of winning on gaming machines and the characteristics of problem gambling, including the recognised signs of harmful gambling and how to seek advice; and • Signage that is clearly visible that encourage players to gamble only at levels they can afford and contains advice about how to seek assistance for problem gambling.
