Second, councils will have 12 months from the enactment of the Transitional Provisions Bill to prepare Water Services Delivery Plans to show how you plan to deliver financially sustainable water services. • Water Services Delivery Plans will also include information about current water services. • The purpose of the Plans is for councils – individually or jointly – to publicly demonstrate their intention and commitment to deliver water services in ways that are financially sustainable, meet regulatory quality standards for water network infrastructu re and water quality, and unlock housing growth. • Through the development of these Plans, councils will provide an assessment of their water infrastructure, how much they need to invest, and how they plan to finance and deliver it through their preferred service delivery model. • Ringfencing of water services and revenue from other council activities is a key feature of the Plans. • Importantly, the Plans will be a way for you to provide transparency to your communities about the costs and financing of water services and empower you to make decisions about managing and delivering high -quality water services that reflect your local nee ds and circumstances. • The Plans will also support you to have conversations with other councils about joint plans for water services delivery. 9(2)(g)(i) Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 9 of 13 • The Government expects those discussions will, in many cases, progress to proposals for new council controlled or council owned water organisations to provide water services, the amalgamation of water services with those of other councils, or other shared services arrangements. • My expectation is that those discussions and decisions are already happening at a local level, and should include mana whenua. • As you’ll be aware, I have also asked my officials to support these early discussions that you may be having about your possible future service delivery arrangements. • There are couple of key things I wanted to emphasise today about the Plans: o Plans can be developed by individual councils, or jointly where groups of councils are planning to jointly establish a water organisation o Plans are one -off, transitional documents. They have no regulatory function – LTPs continue to be councils’ primary planning and accountability document. o Plans must include drinking water, wastewater and stormwater – but councils have flexibility about transferring stormwater in proposed new service delivery arrangements. o It will be up to councils to determine how best to engage with their communities as part of the Plan development process. o Plans must demonstrate how water services and their funding will be ringfenced from other council activities. • The Department will be providing information and guidance to councils to support the development of Plans. The third area that Cabinet has agreed are steps towards a future economic regulation regime as part of Local Water Done Well. • Economic regulation is a key feature of Local Water Done Well and is intended to ensure consumers pay efficient, cost -reflective prices for water services, that those services are delivered to an acceptable quality and that water services providers are investing sufficiently in their infrastructure. • Development of an economic regulation system for water services will be led by the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment,

Section 3: Implementing the preferred option How will it be implemented? 101. The BDMRR Act will be amended to give effect to the self-identification process. The Bill that re-enacts the Act is awaiting second reading. Provisions that would introduce a self-identification process are already in the Bill as reported back by Select Committee. It is intended that these self-identification provisions will be amended through a supplementary order paper, which will be referred to Select Committee for further consideration. At Select Committee, the public will be able to comment on the self- dentification process. It is intended that the Bill, with the self-identification provisions, will be passed in early 2022. 102. The Department is working with Te Puni Kōkiri, the Ministry for Pacific Peoples, and the Office for Ethnic Communities to encourage participation in the select committee process by young people, Māori, Pacific peoples and ethnic communities. An engagement plan is being developed to support this work. This will include providing written information about the Bill to Iwi authorities, community organisations and media networks that have reach in these communities. 103. The Department will undertake work to update our systems, processes and application forms to implement the new self-identification process. It is possible that this will take up to 12 months, so delayed commencement of the provisions may be required. We are considering if transitional arrangements are required for any people who may have begun the Family Court process at the time of commencement. 104. The Department will undertake consultation and regulation development to determine:  the number and terminology of non-binary sex markers;  the third parties who can provide the letter of support for applications for children and young people; and  the extra requirements for where a person applies more than once. 105. The Department will work with the Department of Corrections on necessary amendments to the Corrections Regulations 2005. The Department will also work with the Ministry of Justice and organisations that support transgender and intersex people Official recognition of transgender and intersex people’s gender will have positive impacts on their wellbeing and therefore will benefit wider society. Total monetised benefits Unknown Non-monetised benefits Medium-high Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Regulatory Impact Statement | 28 to notify affected people and the courts of the change. We will work across government to update relevant websites. 106. Improvements to the process may trigger an increase in applications. The Department is aware of this and will prepare for this as part of implementation. 107. The Department is considering how to include a range of non-binary and culturally specific markers into its applications and IT systems. We will also need to build in flexibility to allow the systems to adapt with evolving gender terminology. Monitoring, Evaluation, and Review 108. To ensure the objectives of changing to a self-identification process are being met, the process will be reviewed five years from commencement of the Bill. As part of this the Minister must consult the Human Rights Commissioner, the transgender and intersex communities and any other persons and organisations considered appropriate. 109. Ahead of this formal review, the Department will survey applicants in the first few years after implementation to understand if the new process is meeting their needs. It is open to other stakeholders to contact the Department directly to raise any concerns they have with the new process. Depending on this feedback and these surveys the formal review could be brought forward. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Self-Identification Changes 1995 Act 2018 Bill 2021 SOP Status Quo in Act: Family Court process Current Bill: Self-identification as proposed by 2018 Select Committee SOP: Preferred self-identification clauses Application Process (Adult) Application to amend registered sex is made to the Family Court. Medical evidence is required. The Family Court judge decides if the application is successful . Application to amend registered sex is made to the Registrar-General. A statutory declaration is required. The applicant decides what sex appears on their birth certificate in line with what best reflects their gender. Medical Evidence Evidence of medical treatment is required in the application. What constitutes medical evidence is decided by the judge. This can range from hormone therapy to gender affirming surgery. Medical evidence requirement removed and replaced with statutory declaration process. Statutory Declaration N/AThe applicant is required to state that they: want the sex marker on their birth certificate to match their identified gender; intend to continue to identify as a person of this gender; and understand the consequences of the application. Citizenship Eligibility Overseas-born citizens and permanent residents are included in the definition of ‘eligible person.’ The definition of ‘eligible person’ should exclude anyone whose birth is registered overseas. Statutory Review N/AA statutory review of self-identification provisions is to be undertaken five years after they are enacted. Available Sex Markers Binary sex markers only: Male Female An ‘indeterminate’ marker is available for intersex people born with a variation of sex characteristics. Non-binary sex markers available: Male Female Intersex X (unspecified)Different sex markers available: Male Female Non-binary marker options to be set in regulations Multiple Amendments to Sex Marker No set limit. However, a de facto limitation exists via: requiring satisfactory evidence that the applicant will maintain their nominated sex. only two sex marker options are available.Only one amendment to registered sex unless the Registered General is satisfied that there are special circumstances. Applicants reverting back to their sex assigned at birth may do so without meeting the special circumstances criteria. More than one amendment to registered sex is allowed. Applicants who make more than one amendment may need to meet additional requirements, to be set in regulations. Applicants reverting back to their sex assigned at birth are exempt from meeting these additional requirements. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Self-Identification Changes – Process for Under 18s Status Quo in Act: Family Court process Current Bill: Self-identification as proposed by 2018 Select Committee SOP: Self-identification Age Categories All children and young people aged under 18 apply via the same process. Children and young people aged under 16 form one age category. 16- and 17-year-olds form a second age category. 16- and 17-year-olds who are or have been in a marriage, civil union, or de facto relationship can apply as adults. 16- and 17-year-olds Application ProcessThe guardian of an eligible child applies to the Family Court. Eligible 16- or 17-year-olds make a statutory declaration. The Court must be satisfied that: the guardian intends to raise the child as the nominated sex; and there is expert evidence that shows medical treatment affirming the nominated sex has or will be undertaken. Additional requirements: Guardian consent. Health professional’s recommendation.Additional requirements: Guardian consent; OR Letter of support from a third party (to be set in regulations). Under 16s Application Process Same as above. Guardian of an eligible child makes a statutory declaration. Guardian consent is an inferred requirement based on the application process. Additional requirements: Health professional’s recommendation.Additional requirements: Letter of support from a third party (to be stipulated in regulations). N/AAt age 18, children whose guardian has amended their nominated sex on their behalf must re-confirm that this is the sex they wish to keep on their birth certificate. Not applicable because multiple amendments to registered sex are allowed. Further minor and technical decisions to be made: Gender self-identification’s impact on sex as determined by the general law of New Zealand: Clause 22I of the BDMRR Bill provides that “sex of every person must continue to be determined by reference to the general law of New Zealand”. This clause will be reworded to clarify that sex on a birth certificate should not be taken as conclusive evidence of a person’s sex. Estimated time to implement self-identification: Up to 12 months may be required to ensure the technical infrastructure of the birth register is in place. Treatment of previous sex markers on birth certificates and the birth register: Where a person amends their sex marker their previous name and sex are not displayed on their birth certificate. This is important as it stops a person being outed as transgender. Previous markers will be closed rather than deleted on the birth register.Summary of changes to be stipulated in regulations: Non-binary sex marker terminology. Additional requirements to be met if an applicant is amending their registered sex more than once. Who constitutes a third party and can provide a letter of support for under 18s amending their registered sex. Document 9 Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 2 of 15 Purpose This briefing seeks your agreement to a second tranche of policy proposals on introducing a self-identification process for recognising gender on birth certificates through the Births, Deaths, Marriages, and Relationships Registration Bill (the Bill) . This briefing also provides you with the draft Cabinet paper, Introducing a self- identification process to recognise gender on birth certificates (Appendix A ), for you r feedback and ministerial consultation. Executive summary You have agreed to seek Cabinet agreement to introduce a self-identification process to enable people to have their gender recognised on birth certificates. This briefing provides you with the associated draft Cabinet paper for your feedback and ministerial consultation. You have agreed to a first tranche of policy proposals (IA202100332 refers). This briefing seeks your agreement to a second tranche of policy proposals. These include: 4.1 setting in regulations a range of markers to recognise non-binary genders; 4.2 allowing people to amend their registered sex more than once, but with additional requirements for subsequent applications; 4.3 establishing different age categories with different requirements for applications for children and young people; 4.4 that most applications for children and young people need to be accompanied by a letter of support from a third party; and 4.5 guardian consent requirements for children and young people. Subject to your agreement on the above proposals and feedback on the draft Cabinet paper, we propose the Cabinet paper is considered by the Cabinet Social Wellbeing Committee on 12 May 2021. Background You have agreed to introduce a self-identification process to enable transgender1 and intersex2 people to amend their sex on their birth certificate.3 Provisions that would enable a self-identification process were added to the Bill at the recommendation of Select Committee in 2018. Cabinet approval of self-identification was not obtained at this time and is now required to progress the Bill with a self-identification process. We are proposing several changes to the self-identification provisions as reported back by Select Committee. These changes will be made via a Supplementary Order Paper (SOP). You have agreed to seek Cabinet agreement in May to introduce a self- identification process and the policy decisions needed to draft the SOP. 1 The term ‘transgender’ is used in this paper to refer to all people whose gender differs from their assigned sex at birth – this includes people who identify outside of the male/female binary who may use a range of terms to describe their gender including “non -binary”. 2 ‘Intersex’ is an umbrella term for people born with a variation of sex characteristics (such as sexual anatomy, reproductive organs, hormonal and/or chromosome patterns). Intersex people are born with sex characteristics that are more diverse than narrow medical definitions of male or female bodies. Like anyone else, an intersex person may grow to identify with a different gender. 3 To enable this the birth register must be updated. We are not proposing any changes to how sex is registered at birth. Gender is not known at birth, so the information collected will continue to be based on sex. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 3 of 15 You recently agreed to a first tranche of policy proposals on introducing self- identification (IA202100332 refers), including: 8.1 requiring applicants to compete a statutory declaration; 8.2 removing the intersex marker option from the Bill; 8.3 excluding anyone whose birth cannot be registered in New Zealand from the definition of eligible person; and 8.4 requiring a statutory review of the self-identification provisions five years after enactment. This briefing seeks your agreement to a second tranche of policy proposals that cover: 9.1 the number and terminology for a range of sex marker options; 9.2 the number of times a person can amend registered sex; and 9.3 the process for amending registered sex for children and young people. The first and second tranche of policy approvals are reflected in the draft Cabinet paper. Further policy approvals required to introduce a self-identification process 11. This section outlines the remaining policy approvals required to introduce self- identification. Provide sex marker options that are inclusive of non-binary genders Status Quo The Family Court process allows people to show the binary sex markers on their birth certificate: female or male. Select Committee’s recommendation The Select Committee sought to add the option “X (unspecified)” to be inclusive of people who identify other than the binary (female and male) . Department’s advice – setting in regulations a range of markers to recognise non-binary genders We proposed replacing the umbrella term “X (unspecified)” as it fails to adequately represent all non-binary genders . We instead recommended a mechanism to enable a more inclusive and flexible process where a range of genders can be agreed and used by applicants. You agreed in principle to making one or more sex markers available for non-binary gende rs and that these will be set in regulations or operational policy (IA202100332 refers). We recommend allowing a range of non-binary sex markers that are set in regulations. Consultation can be completed when developing regulations to determine the number of and terminology used for these markers. Consultation can be used to gauge transgender and intersex perspectives and the perspectives of specific population groups, such as young people and Māori, Pacific and ethnic communities. This could include exploring culturally- inclusive markers such as takatāpui (Māori), fa’afafine (Samoan), or fakaleitī (Tongan). Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 4 of 15 Setting the non-binary markers in regulations will future-proof the legislation. Gender theory and terminology evolves rapidly, and regulations can be more easily reviewed and updated than primary legislation to ensure they meet the needs of transgender and intersex people. While setting the markers in operational policy would have been easier to review and update than regulations we do not recommend this option. It would require enabling the Registrar-General to set the markers following a public consultation process. This would be a new type of decision-making power for the Regist rar-General , whereas the Executive routinely makes these types of decisions. There is a high level of public interest in this issue, which means that markers would be better determined by publicly elected members of the Executive. Setting the markers in regulation will also be more transparent, as the process and available markers will be clearly established in secondary legislation. Setting the markers in operational policy would also be costlier in the short to medium term. To assist the Regist rar-General, a new process and capability would need to be built that replicates the Department’s existing policy development capability. Development of non-binary markers would be better incorporated into the usual government regulatory process. The number of times a person can amend registered sex Status Quo Under the Family Court process, it would be rare but not impossible for a person to amend their registered sex more than once . While there is no limit on the number of times a person can apply, the requirements lend themselves to the amendment being permanent (eg the court must be satisfied a person intends to maintain their nominated sex). Select Committee’s recommendation The Select Committee recommended that under a self-identification process only one change be allowed unless the Regist rar-General is satisfied that there are special circumstances. The exception to this rule is that if a person wants to revert to their sex at birth, they may do so at any time. Department’s advice – allow for people to amend their registered sex more than once, but with additional requirements for subsequent applications 12. We recommend that people can amend their registered sex more than once. Gender can be fluid and how a person identifies may change over time. Allowing only one amendment would be out of step with a true self-i dentification model. If a person’s gender changes and they cannot amend their registered sex to reflect this, they no longer have control of how their gender is officially recognised. 13. We understand th at Select Committee recommended allowing only one amendment except in special circumstances to mitigate the risk of identity fraud. Where a person amends their registered sex their previous name and sex are not displayed on their birth certificate. This means a person cannot be easily linked to their previous identity, Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 6 of 15 Select Committee’s recommendation Select Committee’s recommended process is different depending on the age of the child or young person: 27.1 16 or 17 year olds - can apply on their own behalf with written consent from their guardian; and 27.2 15 years and under - applications must be made on behalf of the child or young person by their guardian. The process only differs in who makes the application. Both age groups require guardian consent and a recommendation from a health professional. Department’s advice - different age categories to reflect older adolescent’s higher level of cognitive development We agree with the age categories recommended by Select Committee. These categories reflect that 16 and 17 year olds are generally more able to provide consent and can live independently from a guardian . This is consistent with other legislation in New Zealand (eg at 16 years old a young person can consent to general medical procedures). It also aligns with other jurisdictions that ease self-identification policies once a person turns 16 (eg in Norway any person 16 years of age and over can amend their recorded gender, no guardian consent is required). We recommend that the age categories have different requirements to reflect the different levels of cognitive development: 30.1 16 or 17 year olds - can apply on their own behalf with either : 30.1.1 written consent from their guardian; or 30.1.2 a letter of support by a third party. 30.2 15 years and under - applications must be: 30.2.1 made on behalf of the child or young person by their guardian; and 30.2.2 be accompanied by a letter of support from a third party. Requiring third party assurance Status Quo The Family Court process requires the guardian making the application for a child or young person to provide evidence the child has undergone or will undergo medical treatment to enable them to assume their nominated sex. The purpose of the medical evidence is to assess a child or young person’s physical confirmation or ability to physically conform with their preferred sex. This requirement medicalises a deeply personal expression of self-identity and is out of step with a self- identification process. Select Committee’s recommendation Select Committee recommended that applications for all children and young people be accompanied by a recommendation from a health professional. The recommendation from the health professional is to provide assurance that the child or young person Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 7 of 15 understands the consequences of the application and that the change is in their best interests. It would not be about current or planned medical treatment. The health professionals able to provide a recommendation would be medical practitioners, health practitioners registered with the P sychologists Board or the Nursing Council of New Zealand, councillors represented by certain bodies and registered social workers. Department’s advice – most applications need to be accompanied by a letter of support from a third party We recommend that applications be accompanied by a letter of support from a third party, with the classes of persons that can act as third parties to be prescribed in regulations. After consulting with other agencies, w e recommend that the role of the third party is different to that recommended by Select Committee with a stronger focus on informed consent. The third party would be assessing that the child or young person understands the change and that the decision is based on their own perceptions of their gender. This focus on consent is more aligned with a self-identification process as it acts to protect the child or young person from undue influence (eg from guardians) and supports their autonomy over their gender. Given there is no need for gender affirming care under self-identification, people outside of the health sector may be able to assess if a child or young person understands the change. In addition, restricting the third party to certain professions could mean the letter of support is difficult to access and out of step with the aim of reducing barriers to changing registered sex. We recommend the classes of people who can provide the letter of support are prescribed in regulations. This will provide time for further analysis on what classes of people will be suitable to act as a third party . In developing the regulations targeted consultation should be completed with potential professional groups or classes of people. These could include health professionals and people outside of the health sector, such as councillors or people who may know the child or young person well. The views of children and young people should also be sought on this matter. Parent or guardian consent Status Quo Under the Family Court process all applications for children and young people aged 18 years and under need to be made by their guardians. There is no clear process in the BDMRR Act where there are disputes between guardians or where guardians refuse to apply on behalf of their child. Select Committee’s recommendation Select Committee recommendations require guardian consent for all age groups . However, Select Committee clarified that the Family Court can assist with disputes between guardians or where guardians refuse to apply on behalf of their 16 or 17 year old. In these situations, an application may be made to the Family Court to settle the dispute under the Care of Children Act 2004. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 8 of 15 Guardian is defined as all the guardians of a person (eg both parents jointly) unless: 41.1 one guardian is unavailable; 41.2 one guardian has applied to the Family Court, and the court has consented to the child or young person’s sex marker being amended; or 41.3 if all guardians are unavailable the Chief Executive of Oranga Tamariki is the guardian. Department’s advice – guardian consent is not always necessary for 16 and 17 year olds As above, we recommend that guardians apply on behalf of children and young people aged 15 years and under . To reflect their maturity, we recommend that guardian consent is not necessary for young people aged 16 and 17, if they instead supply a letter of support from a third party. Enabling 16 and 17 year olds to apply with only a letter of support, partly mitigates concerns raised by other agencies about guardians not being accepting of their child’s gender identity and refusing consent. It also mitigates concerns about young people who feel uncomfortable talking to their guardians about their gender,5 or who are estranged from their guardians.6 There may be a concern that the above risks are not being mitigated for children and young people 15 years and under. We consider that guardian consent is still important for this age group. Not requiring guardian consent for this age group would be inconsistent with the process to change names under the Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Act (BDMRR Act) and other legislation (eg at 15 years a young person needs parental consent to leave school early under the Education and Training Act 2020). It could also be considered out of ste p with a guardian’s responsibilities under the Care of Children Act for their child’s development and for helping their child determine important decisions. The Ministry of Social Development noted that requiring guardian consent could allow guardians to exercise their responsibility in ways that negatively impact a child or young person’s wellbeing. The Counting Ourselves survey found that participants who had an unsupportive family were more likely to have attempted suicide in the last 12 months. We understand this is a concern, but not requiring guardian consent would be a significant change. Guardians will often be integral to supporting a child or young person to amend their birth certificate. At this stage, we recommend that the guardian consent requirement for those 15 years and under is maintained. You agreed to a statutory review of the self- identification provisions five years after enactment (IA202100332 refers). As part of this, any negative consequences of requiring guardian consent can be reviewed. Department’s advice – keep Select Committee’s definition of guardian We recommended keeping Select Committee’s definition of guardian – that means all guardians jointly except in special circumstances. Guardians acting jointly is consistent with obligations under the Care of Children Act 2004 . As part of the statutory review 5 The Youth19 survey found that only a third of transgender and gender diverse participants had told their parents or caregivers they were transgender or gender diverse. 6 The Counting Ourselves survey found that 8 per cent of respondents had been kicked out of home because they were transgender Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 9 of 15 five years after enactment (IA202100332 refers) consideration can be given to any negative consequences of requiring guardians to act jointly. Department’s advice – keep the Family Court mechanism to resolve disputes We recommend keeping Select Committee’s provision that clarifies that the Registrar- General can uphold Family Court decisions on disputes between guardians or where guardians refuse consent for 16 and 17 year olds amending registered sex. There is likely to be a reduced need for this provision as 16 and 17 year olds can apply with only a letter of support from a third party. However, there may still be scenarios where this is useful (eg where the young person has trouble accessing a third party and their guardians refuse consent). Regulation making powers are needed to give effect to the above proposals Regulation making powers are needed to give full effect to the self-identification proposals outlined above. We recommend a regulation making power that will enable regulations that prescribe: 49.1 the sex marker options other than the binary; 49.2 the additional requirements where a person amends their registered sex more than once; 49.3 the third parties who can provide a letter of support for applications for children and young people; and 49.4 any other matters required to give effect to a self-identification process, which align with the overall intent of the proposals in this paper. Self-identification has implications for Department of Corrections regulations We previously advised that there is only one instance where changing registered sex will have implications on other legislation. This is a Department of Corrections (Corrections ) regulation that requires that where a person supplies their birth certificate they must be placed in a prison that aligns with the sex recorded. This is out of step with the BDMRR Act and the Bill, which infer that birth certificate s should not be concl usive evidence of a person’s sex .7

Server-side Algorithm Performance The main evaluation process only performs the bare-minimum of server-side processing: reidentifying the encrypted IDs to the card serial number, and filtering contacts to only those that meet the current definition of a ‘close contact’ (i.e. within two metres for at least fifteen minutes). As discussed above, there is potential to further increase the accuracy of the overall system by ranking the list of contacts provided by the card. Across all trials and ground truth contacts the card achieves 90% recall and 36% false positive rate, and although many of our false positive contacts meet the definition of a ‘casual contact’, it would be preferable to be able to prioritise close contacts over casual ones.

Sharing information digitally remains challenging Information could remain siloed because businesses and organisations do not choose to participate in the Trust Framework The flow of information is impeded, and the potential benefits of digital identity are not realised Business and organisations are enthusiastic for government intervention to address the issue of silos Public sector and private sector service providers assume this risk. Officials are working closely with businesses and organisations to ensure their needs and requirements are met by the Trust Framework and encourage their participation. This is considered a moderate risk. Business and organisations have expressed enthusi asm for government led intervention but the full costs, policies and processes of participating in a Framework have yet to be determined Service delivery does little to improve customer experience People may not actually use the digital identity services that are more secure and private, simply because others are more convenient. Uptake remains low People prioritise service delivery Public sector and private sector service providers assume this risk. Service delivery remains the responsibility of service providers and not the Trust Framework, though bring ing consistency and trust into the digital identity ecosystem will enable service providers to improve their delivery. Unclear Costs become excessive for government and/or private sector The actu al costs of compliance testing turns out to be significantly higher than the initial indicative costs. This would affect Government in phase one (2020 -22) as government is covering the cost of this testing. In phase two (2022 -25) the entity seeking accredi tation, whether public or private, will likely assume this cost. The Trust Framework requires more resources than anticipated to set up and/or maintain, increasing overall costs for government. Budgets are undermined Costs discourage participation in the Trust Framework Reasonable costs will encourage participation Government assumes the risk with regard to the cost of testing. In order to mitigate this risk, government will cover the cost of compliance testing during phase one of the Trust Framework (2020 -2022) and work with partners to test and developed compliance processes in such a manner that compliance testing costs remain reasonable and appropriate going forward. Some trials (particularly construction and party01) had a high proportion of false positives compared to the others, however: ●Cardholders with only a few ground-truth contacts would have a high false positive rate if even one false positive was found. This could have been mitigated by weighting results on the number of ground truth contacts for each cardholder. ●The basic on-card algorithm prioritises high recall since missed contacts cannot be later recovered, but there is an opportunity for filtering out or de-prioritising potential false positives after downloading and reidentifying contacts, using factors such as: ○Time of day ○Density of contacts at the time a contact was recorded ○Overall duration of contact ●The ground truth, especially for the unscripted trials, were largely entered by one person per trial. Although distances (​intensity ​<=3) were typically consistent when spot-checked, the approach to rating of “contact events” (​intensity ​=4) differed by scorer. 8 Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs With greater consistency in scoring methodology the card contact algorithm could be tuned differently and decrease the likelihood of false positives in practice. ●Other yet-to-be tested algorithms for filtering events into a contact list on the card could potentially yield lower false positive rates.

Stakeholder Views/ Public consultation 62. The public and stakeholders were not consulted on the options. However, the issue of regulation of online gambling and sports and racing wagering has been actively discussed for some years and the previous Government announced in May 2 023 in agreed in principle to TAB NZ having an online monopoly, subject to further work being undertaken. 63. We anticipate from conversations with stakeholders , there are likely to be a range of views on the options. For example, offshore operators are likely in favour of a regulated 44qw4kdm06 2024-12-02 07:59:45 Regulatory Impact Assessment | 21 online gambling market they can legitimately enter and participate in. They would likely express disappointment TAB NZ is given an online sports and racing betting monopoly. Previous consultation also indicated they would not be in favour of a raised POCC rate. 64. TAB NZ and the racing codes are highly supportive of TAB NZ having an online monopoly. While not having been directly consulted on the overall package in Option 2, some other elements of the package have been signalled with them and we believe they will be generally supportive of the option/package. TAB NZ has also expressed its desire to have the POCC rate raised. 65. Sport NZ supports extending TAB NZ's online wagering monopoly to protect community interests and minimise gambling harm. However, while the racing codes support the monopoly, the views of individual NSOs are not known. The financial impact on specific NSOs is uncertain and likely to depend on the individual sports. Option One – Counterfactual 66. Option 1 would keep New Zealand’s gambling market model the same as it is now. Although TAB NZ would be the only authorised operator of betting products in New Zealand, there would be no legal barriers for offshore online operators to offer their sports and race betting products to New Zealanders, or for New Zealanders to play on offshore sites , provided they do not advertise here . 67. As noted, under the counterfactual option, t he Governments online casino regulation regime would be put in place coming into force at this stage in 202 6. While there will not be a direct impact on the way TAB NZ operates under the online casino proposal, the changes are likely to strengthen the position of some of TAB NZ’s closest competitors in New Zealand who are able to advertise as part of licensing conditions . 68. Given these factors, we consider under the counterfactual , it is highly likely offshore competition will further erode the revenue of TAB NZ – although the rate and severity of this decline are unknown. 69. The other risks of the counterfactual are: • there continues to a large “grey” market – a “grey” market means that offshore operators are neither regulated nor operating illegally. Spending on offshore online gambling (i.e. the grey market) is expected to continue to increase over time. The advertising ban is only partially effective, and it will remain almost impossible to enforce for e.g. through advertising at overseas sports events broadcast in New Zealand ; • TAB NZ’s long -term revenue sustainability remains at risk - in turn, this risks the racing industry’s long -term viability, and could impact jobs, especially in rural communities; and in the short -term the additional payments provided for in the Entain partnership agreement for an online monopoly of $100 million and ;
Stakeholder/ Public consultation 118. Targeted consultation was conducted in April 2021 to operationalise the POCC. Consultation highlighted the need for a reasonable rate of POCC that would not unfairly inflate offshore betting providers’ tax burdens compared to domestic providers. Consultation on a 10 % rate (the current rate) highlighted support for a lower rate amongst offshore operators, whereas TAB NZ TAB NZ reiterated its view that the current rate is too low in a letter to the former Minister for Racing in October 2022. Additional assumption specific to this option 119. Some operators will continue to pay an increased POCC – If the POCC is increased, some operators will continue to pay and returns to the racing industry will increase. However, depending on the rate of increase , some operators may decide to stop paying but continue to operate in the market offering better odds than TAB NZ, or leave the market entirely. Both outcomes would impact returns to the racing industry.

Statutes Ame ndment Bill (for information only) The Statute Amendment Bill (Bill) is the legislative mechanism for technical, short and non - controversial amendments to existing legislation. The Bills are used to correct drafting errors and omissions, as well as to mak e minor technical changes to legislation and do not introduce policy change. Amendments may only progress with the unanimous support of the House of Representatives. Accordingly, all parliamentary parties are consulted on proposed amendments prior to their inclusion in such a Bill. In 2023, the Bill did not receive unanimous support in the House and did not proceed. Recently, the Ministry of Justice, as the administering agency, has supported its Minister to undertake parliamentary consultation. The Bill no w has the unanimous support required to proceed. Impact on Local Government legislation In April 2023, the then Minister of Local Government agreed minor and technical amendments could be made under the Statutes Amendment Bill to the: • Local Government Act 2002; • Local Government Rating Act 2002; and • Water Services Act 2021. The amendments are to: • section 90D of the Local Government Rating Act 2002 and Schedule 10 of the Local Government Act 2002 – to move section 90D to Schedule 10 of the Local Government Act 2002 to bring all annual report requirements for local authorities into one place; • sectio n 25(3)(a) of the Water Services Act 2021 – to remove the word “the” before “drinking water supply” to make the section consistent with section 25(3)(c) and 25(3)(e); • section 25(3) of the Water Services Act 2021 – to update example 1 in section 25(3) by removing the word “the” before “drinking water supply” to make it consistent with the other examples provided; 9(2)(a) Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs

Summary This would not achieve the objective of a consistent and trusted digital identity ecosystem. In a scenario where there is no government intervention, a private sector response that would address the aforementioned issues in a comprehensive fashion is highly unlikely to emerge and the private sector would continue to develop its own rules and standards without government direction . The challenges within the digital identity ecosystem would remain unchanged, but would be increasingly exacerbated by the ongoing digital transformation occurring in all spheres of life – a trend recently accelerated by the Covid -19 pandemic. Trust in di gital identity services would remain low, information would remain siloed, and the flow of information impeded. Furthermore, without intervention the digital identity ecosystem in New Zealand would not be positioned to realise the significant opportunities trusted digital identity could offer. This may help to support the achievement of a more consistent and trusted digital identity ecosystem, but there remain many uncertainties about the ability and willingness of service providers to comply. This may help to support the achievement of a more consistent and trusted digital identity ecosystem, but there remain many uncertainties about the ability and willingness of service providers to comply. This would achieve the objective of a consistent and trusted di gital identity ecosystem. A government -led intervention such as this would imbue the ecosystem with consistency and trust, encourage uptake, enable the flow of information, and position the digital identity ecosystem to realise the significant social and e conomic benefits digital identity services can provide. This option could be established in the near term. Phase one of the Trust Framework (2020 -22), in which a small number of participants are informally linked to the Trust Framework, will allow for the testing of policies/processes and the mitigation of risks before the Trust Framework is established in legislation, giving it legal enforceability and enabling more participants into the trusted ecosystem. This phasing approach would al so allow for the Trust Framework to be scaled and transformed in the future, if required. This could be established at a reasonable cost. Estimated costs to government approximately $1 -2 million per annum. As a result of these factors, option 3 is the Department’s preferred option. This would achieve the objective of a consistent and trusted digital identity ecosystem . This option would almost certainly address the underlying deficiencies of the digital identity ecosystem and, unlike Option 3, it would be legally enforceable from the outset. It would not be established in a timely manner. It would take years to set up this regime, ensuring that the challenges in the digital identity ecosystem remain unaddressed for some time. The costs associated with this option would be higher than any of the other options. Estimated at $2 -4 million per annum. It is possible that the size and costs of this option might be unnecessarily out of proportion with demand, once the regime is finally implemented . Undertaking such a comprehensive approach from the outset might lead to a situation where the costs of the regime outweigh the benefits. While it may be suitable to move to a comprehensive regime like this in the future, the Department does not judge this to be the most suitable starting point for the Trust Framework. The Department notes that option 3 has the potential to scale into a larger, more comprehensive regime like this is the future, if required. PROACTIVELY RELEASED

Develop and refine guidelines/train -the-trainers training to promote host responsibility in other gamb ling environments (including online environments) so operators can identify potentially harmful gambling behaviour and take effective action to prevent and minimise gambling harm and create safer gambling environments . Underlying principles: closer to home/k a aro mai kit e kāinga Good health begins at home and in communities, so it makes sense to promote the development and implementation of regulatory and policy settings that create safer gambling environments, particularly for people and communities at greater risk of moderate to high levels of gambling harm. This involves enabling systemic changes to innovate and deliver more effective services that will minimise and prevent gambling harm, to keep people and communities well and to reduce the level of gambling harm people experience. Objective 9: Services raise awareness about the range and signs of gambling harms that affect individuals, families/whānau and communities Families and whānau of problem gamblers can be badly affected by gambling harm. The Ministry therefore places great importance on improving health literacy, to drive behavioural change by helping families and whānau to recognise and address issues associated with gambling harm and to apply appropriate self-help or help-seeking behaviours. The Ministry will continue to work with HPA and other relevant organisations to target at-risk and vulnerable communities to increase awareness, reduce gambling harm and encourage associated positive behaviours. These are typically communities with a high social deprivation score, who are at increased risk because of increased access to NCGMs and vulnerable because they lack access to resources that would help improve their resiliency. The Ministry of Health will use evaluation activities, the consumer network and results-based accountability reporting to ensure that all organisations are working in the right way, with the right people. The Ministry expects the services it funds to have a robust health equity, cultural competency and health literacy focus, as well as input from consumer networks once established. It also expects service providers to build relationships with other relevant organisations and communities in the areas in which they operate. This is one way of sharing relevant information and increasing the overall awareness of gambling harm and indicators of potentially harmful gambling. Services need to better address the cultural and language differences of their target audiences. The Ministry expects that the proposed co-design approach and use of consumer networks will give consumers from vulnerable communities a stronger voice in the design and evaluation of services. 32 STRATEGY TO PREVENT AND MI NIMISE GAMBLING HARM 2019/20 TO 2021/22 Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs

Support for vulnerable consumers unable to pay water bills 58. Some consumers of water services will be households with inadequate income and resources to support their basic needs, including water services. Households experiencing material hardship will likely include occupants that are younger, single parents, on be nefits as their main source of income, Māori and Pacific peoples, people with disabilities, larger households, and renters. 59. Currently, there appears to be a very large range in average annual water charges across councils sampled by the Department of Inter nal Affairs, from a low of about $135 to a high of about $1,900. The average is about $1,300 across the sample. Auckland’s average is $1,400. In future, this range is expected to narrow as entities implement more standardised approaches to pricing, including possible geographic averaging across districts. At the low end of the range, prices almost certainly are below the long -run cost of service provision and do not cover economic depreciation. 60. The c ombined cost of water bills and rates bills should not materially change when water services entities are initially set up, other things being equal. Over time, they should be more affordable than if the same level of services were to continue to be provid ed by councils. Rates bills should reduce to offset water being separately billed, unless territorial authorities decide to increase their revenues for other reasons.

THE STRUCTURE OF THE DEPARTMENT
TRIALS Over a two-week period in May 2020 during alert level 2 of COVID-19 restrictions in New Zealand [1], eight validation trials were performed. These trials aimed to cover a wide range of natural situations, prioritising scenarios the technical team felt covered the most challenging environments for recalling close contacts that also had high potential for spreading an infectious disease. Scenarios were also prioritised if they were in the public interest (such as large gatherings/parties which were subject to additional restrictions during New Zealand’s alert levels), or covered a wide range of situations (e.g. queuing, one-on-one meetings, casual contact, etc.). Seven of the trials covered five scenarios: office, cafe, construction site, taxi, and a house party. One scenario was repeated twice (office), and one scenario was broken into two trials for ease of evaluation (house party). There was one additional trial - proximity - that was also performed but was evaluated separately as it was designed to test specific aspects of the card’s performance. The proximity trial methodology and results are included in Appendix 1.

Helpline and web-based services Helpline and web-based services provide:  information  access to intervention services for people unable to access face- to-face services  referral to other gambling harm service providers  information on self-help, peer- to-peer support options and assessment guides. Currently the Ministry funds two forms of telephone-based support, as follows.  The Gambling Helpline provides a free 24 /7 service, and is a first contact point for people in crisis as a result of harmful gambling. It also provides a back-up for other services that are not available 24/7, and ensures coverage in rural areas, where there are no face- to-face services. This is critical to the Ministry ’s service delivery model.  The Asian Gambling Helpline is a limited service for the Asian community, provided by the PGF, and is funded out of psychosocial interventions and support services. Submissions from health groups and service providers, particularly those serving Pacific and Asian communities, called for more language-appropriate support. Suggestions included translating key information into common languages online, and extending the hours and range of interpreter languages available. The Ministry will explore ways to extend the reach of these frontline services with Asian and Pacific providers and the consumer network. It will also explore ways to increase the general helpline referral rate: currently only 0.8 percent of calls are referred to a treatment provider. Psychosocial interventions and support Psychosocial intervention and support services include a range of interventions delivered to individuals or groups in a variety of settings (including prisons). People affected by a family or whānau member’ s gambling can access the same range of services that is available to the gamblers themselves. Table 18: Research and evaluation budget (GST exclusive), 2019/20– 2021/22 Service area 2019/20 2020/21 2021/22 Total ($m) ($m) ($m) ($m) Research 1.485 1.499 1.500 4.484 Evaluation (including outcomes reporting) 0.575 0.720 0.850 2.145 Total ($m) 2.060 2.219 2.350 6.629 The research and evaluation work programme Strategic priority areas for 2019/20 –21/22 The strategic priority areas are:  ongoing monitoring of the incidence of gambling behaviour and associated levels of harm through the Health and Lifestyle Survey to maintain a longitudinal time-series and inform strategic-level outcomes monitoring  researching gambling-related health inequities experienced by vulnerable at-risk populations, particularly M āori, Pacific peoples, Asian peoples and youth/children, including the barriers to service use and what might be done to remove them  examining the convergence of gaming and gambling on the design and delivery of new products (eg, NZLC ’s online ‘ instant win ’ and other online offerings from a variety of sources) , along with their effects on gambling participation in the population and on harm, in particular for vulnerable populations such as children and youth  examining the effect of ‘sinking- lid’ policies on gambling harm reduction , as well as the socioeconomic distribution of gambling machines and venues in New Zealand and the social trade-offs involved  investigating the development and use of internet-based forms of gambling  increasing the use of process and outcomes evaluations with new intervention service delivery models, including the use of new technology. Table 19: Structured p articipation in decision making using decision making tools e.g., CONSUL – Madrid Decide (ES) Background Description Costs involved Relevance for NZ context Feasibility for different individuals and community types Risks Benefits Design choices Madrid Decide was started in 2015 as a counter to the growing political mistrust caused by the austerity measures in Spain. It has since become a platform – CONSUL http://consulproject.org/en/ - developed by the municipality in Madrid, for pub lic participation. It is now used in 33 countries. Decide Madrid received the public service prize from the United Nations in 2018 . Objectives : for citizens to comment on proposed ordinances and make suggestions for changes to those ordinances ; to increase the transparency of the government and e -participation. Process : The software was developed and funded by Madrid’s City Council. The website based on the software has five sections: debates, proposals, voting, processes (collaborative legislation) , and pa rticipatory budgeting. The intensity of participation in decision making depends on the level of verification. All citizens of Madrid (age 16+) are allowed to participate on the site. Registered users who provide only a username, email address, and passwo rd can participate in discussions, create proposals, and create expenditure projects. Users who provide the previous information and verify their residence and provide a mobile phone number can participate in discussions, create proposals, create expenditu re projects, vote for proposals, and vote for expenditure projects in the support phase. Users who provide the previous information and also fully verifies their account in person at a Citizen Assistance Office or via mail, can also vote for proposals in the final decision phase . Platform users participate in the drafting and modification of regulations and give their opinions on those regulations. The opinions will be considered by the City Council. The comments are considered by th e different government sectors for the final drafting of the ordinances. Platform users can join the discussion of any of the draft ordinances or policies. The public interaction is done through different users commenting online on the ordinance and on oth er users’ comments. Users can upvote or downvote another user’s comment. All discussions and votes are available for the public to see when anyone visits the website. Proposals which gain support from one per cent of the census population are then put to a binding public vote. In addition, several face -to-face deliberative spaces (i.e. local forums, physical voting booths) were set up to support the platform and to cater to the different needs of stakeholders involved . The tool could support a participator y budgeting process in New Zealand – it is currently used in many local governments around the world. Special engagement campaign for youth and women (under - represented voters) was conducted. No proof that this practice leads to improved decisions or decis ion-making or that the trust in government grows Citizens and communities used to face-to-face interactions and other processes may be resistant to the participation in the process. Citizens give their input on local policies and regulations affecting their lives . Many different citizens have commented on many different ordinances and made suggestions for improvements (the site has 400,000 registered users – 6% of Madrid population ). Table 5: Objective 5 priorities for action Objective 5: People understand and acknowledge the range of gambling harms that affect individuals, families/whānau and communities Priorities for action Short -to medium -term priorities Long -term priorities Ensure education and messaging and actions cover the full spectrum of harm, including low to medium problem gambling. Increase participation in the development of, and exposure to, culturally and linguistically appropriate campaigns and communications that provide information to people on the health and social risks and signs of harmful gambling and what to do to mitigate these risks and obtain help. Identify ways to provide effective support to people who are seeking to independently moderate or manage their gambling behaviour (or the behaviour of their famil ies and whānau) in some way and provide that support . Continue to enhance the links between gambling harm services and other social and health services to ensure that services work together to support people experiencing gambl ing harm and their famil ies and whānau. This will include trialling collective impact and co llaborative approaches. Enhance communication and referral processes to ensure that other services that offer support to people experiencing harm from gambling address the needs of a referred client (and their family and whānau) . Continue to identify and monitor protective and resiliency factors for gambling harm . Develop and pilot initiatives that build protective factors, life skills and resilience for people who gamble . Increase the links between services to prevent and minimise gambling harm and b roader mental health promotion life skills and resiliency programmes . Support community -based life skills and resiliency programmes that help people to make healthy choices that prevent and minimise gambling harm . Underlying principles: people-powered/m ā te iwi hei kawe The health system plays an important role in health literacy – providing people with the information they need to fully understand issues to do with health and wellness, including how to be healthy, access health services and manage their own health care. To improve health literacy, service providers need to work in partnership with service users, supporting and encouraging them to be ‘health smart ’. Objective 6: A skilled workforce is developed to deliver effective services The Ministry expects the gambling harm workforce to be diverse and have a robust health equity, cultural competency and health literacy focus. T o deliver cost-effective, responsive and holistic services, alignment with other relevant services, particularly those in the wider public health, mental health and addiction fields, is essential. The Ministry has worked with the gambling harm sector to identify the core competencies (including cultural competencies) required for the public health STRATEGY TO PREVENT AND MINIMISE GAMBLIN G HARM 2019/20 TO 20 21/22 27 Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs
Table 9: Objective 9 priorities for action Objective 9: Services raise awareness about the range and signs of gambling harms that affect individuals, families/whānau and communities Priorities for action Short -to medium -term priorities Long -term priorities Target p romotional activities to reduce gambling harm and increase awareness of the range and signs of gambling harms at high -risk communities. Work to increase access to services among people experiencing gambling harm and their families and whānau, including in rural areas. Develop tools and protocols to support the primary health care sector and other community services to include screening, brief assessment and brief and early intervention for gambling harm as part of general health screening and day -to-day delivery . Underlying principles: people-powered/m ā te iwi hei kawe The health system plays an important role in providing people with the information they need to fully understand issues around health and wellness, including how to be healthy, access health services and manage their own health (health literacy). To improve health literacy, services need to work in partnership with service users, supporting and encouraging them to be ‘health smart ’ and to mitigate language and cultural barriers to accessing information. In this partnership between providers and users, different groups of people will need different forms of support, depending on factors such as: age; ethnicity; different worldviews, expectations and religious beliefs; location; and existing conditions or disabilities. Gambling harm can be associated with mental illness, other addictions and substance abuse, family violence and a range of other social issues. Enhancing awareness of the signs of harmful gambling, and opportunities for screening, among services that address these other health and social issues will help enhance the accessibility of services to prevent and minimise gambling harm. Objective 10: People access effective treatment and support services at the right time and place Provision of high-quality, effective and accessible services to prevent and minimise gambling harm requires staff who are appropriately qualified and services that are culturally relevant to the communities they serve. Access to intervention services should be available in all areas where there is access to gambling venues. Continuing to provide dedicated Māori, Pacific and Asian services is crucial to help reduce gambling-harm-related inequity and inequality. The Ministry will increase the emphasis on including consumer perspectives in service design and delivery (informed by research and evaluation). It will also explore culture-specific delivery models (where cost-effective) with consumer networks and service providers. Talking Points for Cabinet Legislation Committee on 27 July 2023: Approval to introduce voting age Bill
Talking Points │Water Services Legislation Repeal Bill for Cabinet meeting Overview • As part of the Government’s 100 -day commitment, the Water Services Entities Act 2022 and Water Services Economic Efficiency and Consumer Protection Act 2023 will be repealed [CAB -23-MIN -0479 refers] . • It is my intent for Cabinet to consider the Repeal Bill in the week of 5 February 2024, Cabinet endorsement on 12 February 2024 and the introduction to the House on 13 February 2024 .
Talking points - Repeal Bill • The Repeal B ill will repeal the: o Water Services Entities Act 2022 (including the Water Services Entities Amendment Act 2023 and the Water Services Legislation Act 2023 ). o Water Services Economic Efficiency and Consumer Protection Act 2023, which is administered by the Ministry for Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE). • The Minister for Commerce and Consumer Protection has agreed to th e inclusion of the Water Services Economic Efficiency and Consumer Protection Act in this Repeal Bill . • The Repeal Bill will: o end the 10 -entity model that was part of the water services Acts and reinstate previous legislation relating to water services that was in place, including legislation that was amended by the Water Services Entities Amendment Act 2023 and Water Services Le gislation Act 2023; o disestablish the Northland and Auckland Water Services Entity , its establishment board, and the chief executive of that entity. Employment arrangements with this entity will be terminated, and the employee will be entitled to any redundancy arrangements they may have in their contract; o will transfer any residual assets, liabilities, and information of that entity to the Department of Internal Affairs; o remove the statutory obligation to make an Order in Council setting the dates for establishment of water services entities. The Repeal Bill proposes that this provision commences on the date of introduction of th e Repeal Bill. • The Bill will retain technical amendments that improve the regulation of water services by Taumata Arowai, including the Taumata Arowai -the Water Services Regulator Act 2020, the Water Services Act 2021, and related Acts. • The Bill will repeal out of date Local Acts.

Taumata Arowai SPE and proposed response
Taumata Arowai Taumata Arowai is a new Crown entity, established on 1 March 2021, through the Taumata Arowai – Water Services Regulator Act 2020. It will not become fully operational until the Water Services Bill has been passed (expected in the second half of 2021). Taumata Arowai’s objectives relate to: • protecting and promoting drinking water safety and related public health outcomes • efectively administering the drinking water regulatory system • building and maintaining capability among drinking water suppliers and across the wider industry • giving efect to Te Mana o te Wai, to the extent that Te Mana o te Wai applies to the functions and duties of Taumata Arowai • providing oversight of environmental performance of wastewater and stormwater networks • promoting public understanding of the environmental performance of wastewater and storm-water networks.

Taxi The taxi trial (taxi00, n=3) was a short (15 minute) scripted trial to check that passengers in a small vehicle would be seen as close contacts by the card. There was no expectation of consecutive sets of passengers being recorded by each other since pickups may be many kilometres apart; however, we would expect all passengers to show on the driver’s card. There were two passengers alternated seating positions: one in front and one in back; both in back; as well as front/back seating positions for a single passenger. The three participants (n=3) wore a single card around their neck, IDs 100 (driver), 106 and 107 (passengers).

Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs Appendix A: Timeline for the Overseas Published Collections (OPC) The Overseas Published Collections (OPC) form part of the National Library's General Collection, which is a current use collection. The OPC contains mostly English language books purchased for general interest reading, with an emphasis on the arts and the humanities and general information for a public library readership. Some books that were no longer needed by public libraries were accepted into the OPC prior to 1990. 2018 • Plans to exit Wai re re House, a regional repository, triggered a review of the OPC to reduce the volume of the collections in line with the Library's Collections Policy. • Minister of Internal Affairs, Tracey Martin, approved the removal, over time, of all publications from the OPC, excluding those in subject areas identified as collecting priorities in the Overseas Collecting Plan. 2019 • National Librarian Bill Macnaught announced the start of a project to rehome books from the OPC. The first lists of books for review are published on the Library's website. 2020 • Internet Archive offers to take all books remaining after the review for digitisation to provide free access from their global digital library and to preserve the physical copies. • Mr Macnaught begins discussions with the Chief Executive of Copyright Licensing New Zealand (CLNZ) about a possible agreement with Internet Archive and suitable mitigations to allay copyright concerns of rights holders. • Book Guardians Aotearoa formed in response to the OPC project. • Around 50,000 books donated to Lions and Rotary for a special one-off fund raiser. • Rachel Esson appointed Te Pouhuaki National Librarian in December. 2021 • The National Library applies for a licence from ManatO Taonga Ministry for Culture and Heritage to export parts of the OPC to Internet Archive that may be subject to the Protected Objects Act 1975. This licence is granted but has not used due to decisions taken subsequently. • By April about 50 percent of the OPC titles had been reviewed with input from Library stakeholders, with 3,082 books transferred to libraries in the New Zealand library network. Some books were transferred to the Alexander Turnbull Library's research collections. A smaller, more focused collection of overseas publications was retained in the National Library's General Collections (approximately 10 percent of the OPC). • In July the library announced its agreement with Internet Archive for all books left at the end of the OPC review to be donated for digitisation and preservation. • Organisations including Tohatoha Aotearoa Commons, Internet New Zealand, Museums Aotearoa, the Council of New Zealand University Librarians, LIANZA, PLNZ and the NZ Open Source Society express strong support for the initiative. • The library is approached by the Publishers Association New Zealand {PANZ) and the New Zealand Society of Authors (NZSA) with concerns about copyright related to the UNCLASS IFIED Page5 of 7 Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs
Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs Purpose 1. This briefing updates you on the background and development of a removal and disposal policy for the National Library. It describes how we intend to engage with stakeholders and the connections the policy has to the Overseas Published Collections (OPC). Background The need for a removal and disposal policy 2. Under the National Library Act 2003, the National Librarian must obtain the approval of the Minister of Internal Affairs to remove any documents from the collections (s9(3)). The 2003 Act also introduced the legislative requirement that the Alexander Turnbull Library collections are kept in perpetuity (s12(a)). 3. The National Library has three broad collections -the general collections, the research collections, and the schools collection. The schools collection is already covered by a disposal policy introduced in 2020. However, the general collections, maintained to support current research needs, and the research collections, maintained to support long-term research needs and required to be kept in perpetuity, are not covered by a removal and disposal policy. 4. This policy is intended to provide the National Library with clear parameters for when items can be recommended for removal from its research and general collections by the Minister of Internal Affairs, and how they will be disposed of. It also covers process principles the National Library needs to follow when considering removal and disposal to support clarity and transparency around decision-making and to provide assurance for stakeholders. 5. There are a range of circumstances where items are considered for removal from the National Library's general and research collections. For example, if they have been identified as violating an individual's privacy, or where they are part of a collection that is best housed elsewhere in New Zealand. In addition, it is good collection management practice to ensure items in collections developed for their short-term utility and never intended for permanent retention are disposed of once that purpose no longer exists. Our approach to feedback and engagement: Ensuring good expert and stakeholder input 6. A Removal and Disposal Advisory Group has been set up to advise our team during the development of this operational policy. Advisory Group members bring both their own expertise and the views of their organisations to the discussions. 7. The Advisory Group comprises representatives from the Library and Information Association New Zealand Aotearoa (LIANZA); Te Ropu Whakahau (the leading national body that represents Maori engaged in libraries, culture, knowledge, information, communication, and systems technology); the New Zealand Historical Association (NZHA); the Professional Historians' Association of New Zealand/Aotearoa (PHANZA); Auckland Museum; and the Council of NZ University Libraries (CONZUL). The Advisory Group is currently providing advice and input into the draft policy. 8. The Advisory Group has meet twice, providing input as the policy was being drafted and providing feedback on the first draft. They have also had opportunity to advise the Library on key stakeholders to engage with during the policy's development. Te Tiriti o Waitangi / Treaty of Waitangi Implications
Te Tiriti o Waitangi/Treaty of Waitangi Implications 48 The proposals in this paper have no impacts relating to Te Tiriti o Waitangi/the Treaty of Waitangi beyond the impacts on all eligible 16‐ and 17‐year‐olds. However, we note there is a higher proportion of Māori in the 16‐ and 17‐year‐old age group, compared to older population groupings. There fore, the changes in this paper would provide for slightly more accurate electoral participation through voting and candidacy. It would support the Crown’s obligation to provide for equal treatment for Māori and non‐Māori under Ko te Tuatoru/Article 3.

Te Āhuatanga me te Hōkai o ngā Mahi Nature and Scope of Functions Our Purpose Tō Tātou Whāinga The Department of Internal Afairs serves and Ko tā Te Tari Taiwhenua he whakarato me te connects people, communities and government to hono i ngā iwi, ngā hapori me te kāwanatanga ki build a safe, prosperous and respected nation. te hanga motu haumaru, tōnui, whai mana hoki. The Department’s purpose remains consistent, even as the functions and services we perform evolve and develop. We aim to make New Zealand a better place to live and work with people, communities, and other parts of government – both central and local, to enhance the lives of the people who live in New Zealand. Our ministerial portfolios We are responsible to six Ministers, administering seven portfolios within the single Vote Internal Afairs. The Minister of Internal Afairs is the Vote Minister and the Responsible Minister overseeing the Government’s ownership interests in the Department. Portfolios and Responsible Ministers are: Internal Afairs Hon Jan Tinetti Community and Voluntary Sector Hon Priyanca Radhakrishnan Diversity, Inclusion and Ethnic Communities Hon Priyanca Radhakrishnan Digital Economy and Communications Hon Dr David Clark Local Government Hon Nanaia Mahuta Ministerial Services Rt Hon Jacinda Ardern Racing Hon Grant Robertson 10 Department of Internal Affairs NGĀ TAKUNE RAUTAKI STRATEGIC INTENTIONS 2021-2025 Our roles and functions The Department operates under a single Vote of approximately $972 million to support activities under the seven portfolios. The Department has a broad range of responsibilities and functions that span Information and Communications Technology (ICT) investment, information management, working with communities, ensuring efective regulatory frameworks are in place, supporting the executive and local government, and delivering a range of services to support and foster social cohesion, inclusion and a sense of belonging. The Department is the home of the Government Chief Digital Oficer (GCDO) and the Government Chief Privacy Oficer (GCPO) and leads the digital transformation of government across the state sector. In this respect, we support our state sector colleagues to meet the needs of New Zealanders and the Government through better investment in ICT and to maintain the privacy and security of New Zealanders’ information. The Department is the home of the National Library of New Zealand and Archives New Zealand, which act as the memory of society and the memory of government respectively. These institutions play an important role in preserving New Zealand’s documentary heritage and ensuring a full and accurate public record is created and maintained. 11 Department of Internal Affairs NGĀ TAKUNE RAUTAKI STRATEGIC INTENTIONS 2021-2025
