The Customer Nominated Services Approved Information sharing Agreement (AISA) enables a better customer experience and a more efficient approach to the authorised sharing of information between government agencies. The AISA reduces multiple requests for the same information by different government agencies and removes the need to provide physical copies of information. It also improves the quality and consistency of information that agencies hold about an individual and makes it easier to detect issues such as identity fraud.

The Death Approved Information sharing Agreement (AISA) facilitates access to information about deaths. The AISA assists with the provision of public services by facilitating access to accurate death information for organisations. It also provides for updating records about individuals associated with the deceased individual so that their records are also accurate. Organisations may take subsequent actions based on the update of records relating to the deceased individual or associated persons, such as the granting of benefits or entitlements, if that is the agreed purpose for receiving the information.

The Department is working on an All-of-Government (AoG) Roadmap to modernise government digital services across New Zealand. This includes a digital investment plan to support its implementation.The goal is to improve how New Zealanders experience digital government services, and to deliver greater efficiencies and productivity. By using reusable digital components, interoperable data, strong digital security foundations, and essential capabilities (such as digital skills and new funding models), customer experiences and efficiency will improve. The Roadmap has a rolling three-year horizon and will be updated regularly to reflect government priorities and available resourcing.Digitising government services offers significant opportunities to deliver more efficient, effective, and responsive public services, reduce bureaucracy, and ensure discipline in public spending. Digital done well can help people and businesses quickly and conveniently access government services and information.

The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Appendix A: How the Rates Rebate Scheme works 1. Four factors affect the overall cost of the Rates Rebate Scheme (the Scheme) to the Crown. These are: the Scheme’s key settings (the maximum rebate available and the income abatement threshold); the level of rates charged by councils; the uptake of the Scheme; and the incomes of residential ratepayers. Of these, only the Scheme’s key settings are within the Government’s control. 2. Applicants apply for a rebate directly to their council and, if successful, either havetheir rebate applied to their rates account or are paid a cash refund if their rates havebeen paid in full. The Department of Internal Affairs then reimburses the council. 3. Eligible applicants include: residents who are ratepayers for the property to which the rebate is beingclaimed; and residents who own a non-separately rated unit in a retirement village, and who contribute to the outgoings of the retirement village. 4. Based on the rates proposed to take effect f rom 1 July 2021, the level of rebate an eligible applicant receives is determined by the following: the applicant must pay the first $160 of the rates on the property; the potential rebate is two-thirds of the remaining rates, up to the maximumamount; from 1 July 2021, if the applicant and the applicant’s partner, and/or joint home owner living at the property, have income in excess of $26,510 gross per annum, the rebate is reduced by $1 for every $8 of income above that amount (the abatement threshold); for every dependant, the abatement threshold increases by $500; and from 1 July 2021, the rebate will be capped at a maximum of $665. 5. The applicant’s income used in the assessment is that earned from the previous tax year. For example, a person applying for a rebate in the year from 1 July 2021 – 30 June 2022 is assessed on their income for the financial year ending 31 March 2021. 6. The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Appendix B: Talking points for the Cabinet Legislation Committee meeting on 3 June 2021  I have agreed to adjust key settings of the Rates Rebate Scheme and seek approval for an Order in Council to amend the Rates Rebate Act 1973. The Scheme assists low-income ratepayers  Ratepayers apply to their council for the rebate. Councils then process the applications and are reimbursed by the Department of Internal Affairs.  In 2008 Cabinet agreed that regular adjustments to the Rates Rebate Act must be made to account for inflation.  The proposed 2021-22 adjustments reflect the 1.4 per cent upward movement in the All Groups Index of the Consumer Price Index in the 2020 calendar year.  The maximum rebate available will increase from $655 to $665.  The income abatement threshold will increase from $26,150 to $26,510.  The proposed adjustments will take effect from 1 July 2021. The Scheme is not the only form of accommodation support  The Rates Rebate Scheme is one of a suite of policy instruments designed to support households to meet their living costs.  Other cost of living subsidies (such as the Accommodation Supplement) and adjustments to income support remain more effective at insulating low-income ratepayers from rate rises than the Rate Rebate Scheme. These mechanisms are also more effective at addressing equity concerns between renters and homeowners. I recommend that Cabinet agrees to adjust the key settings of the Rates Rebate Act  As I have noted, the Rates Rebate Scheme assists thousands of low-income ratepayers to meet their living costs.  Keeping the key settings at current levels will have negative effects on the value of the rebate to its recipients: o If the maximum rebate and income threshold remain static, inflation will diminish the value of the rebate to recipients. o If adjustments are not made every year, fewer people will meet the income threshold to qualify for the rebate. This will further diminish the intended impact of the Scheme for low-income households. o After a period of non-adjustment, the cost of restoring the key settings to a desirable level could be considerable.  Proceeding with the adjustments will also lower the risk of negative public reactions, particularly from senior citizen interest groups such as Age Concern and Grey Power. Senior citizens are the largest group of beneficiaries of the Scheme. IN-CONFIDENCE Page 5 of 7 Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government
The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Appendix C: Draft Press Release Media release <insert date> Annual adjustments to the Rates Rebate Scheme will assist low-income homeowners The Minister of Local Government, Hon Nanaia Mahuta, has announced an increase to the Rates Rebate Scheme which will help ensure many low-income New Zealanders are able to pay their rates demands this coming financial year. From tomorrow, 1 July 2021, the maximum rebate will increase from $655 to $665. The income abatement threshold will rise from $26,150 to $26,510. Application forms are available from your local council and can also be downloaded from the New Zealand Government website ( www.govt.nz ) and then submitted to your local council. “The changes I have announced today mean that the rebate keeps up with the cost of living and will come as a relief to those individuals and families requiring assistance to meet the cost of their rates demands. ” The Rates Rebate Scheme is a partial refund for people who pay rates to their council. It exists to provide financial relief for low-income New Zealanders owning their own home. “If you have any questions about your eligib ility or that of a family member, I encourage you to get in touch with your local council or retirement village operator” says Minister Mahuta. The Local Government (Rating of Whenua Māori) Amendment Act 2021 was passed earlier this year and introduced pro visions to better recognise the communal ownership of Māori land, and situations where multiple houses are situated on one block of Māori land. Individual home owners on Māori land can now establish separate rate accounts for their houses, which (in the case of low-income applicants) will give them access to the Scheme. “This wi ll be hugely beneficial for low- income Māori, and I encourage anyone who may benefit to contact their council for more info rmation” s ays Minister Mahuta. The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Purpose 1. This briefing seeks your agreement to adjust the 2021/2022 maximum rates rebate and income abatement threshold for the Rates Rebate Scheme (the Scheme) in linewith inflation. Background 2. The Scheme allows low-income ratepayers to access a rebate on their council rates.More detail about how the Scheme works is included as Appendix A . 3. In 2008, Cabinet agreed that the maximum rebate and income abatement thresholdshould be adjusted annually, in line with movements in the Consumer Price Index (CPI)for the previous calendar year [CAB Min (08) 14/ 1 (32) refers]. The maximum rebate available and the income abatement threshold have been adjusted in most years since 2008. 1 The Scheme's key settings were adjusted in 2020/21 4. In 2020/21, you agreed to adjust the Scheme's key settings by 1.9 per cent, in line with inflation. The maximum rebate increased from $640 to $655, and the maximumincome abatement threshold increased from $25,660 to $26,150, as stated in section3(1) of the Rates Rebate Act 1973 (the Act). Changes to the Rating of Whenua Māori 5. The Local Government (Rating of Whenua Māori) Amendment Bill (the Bill) is currently progressing through Parliament. If enacted, one of the provisions of the Bill allowslocal authorities to establish separate rating accounts for individual homeowners, in circumstances where there are multiple houses on a single block of Māori land. If the houses are chosen to be rated individually, the occupant of the house becomes responsible for the rates on the house. This allows these ratepayers to apply for the Scheme, which they previously did not have access to. 6. There is no comprehensive dataset on the amount of housing on Māori land. This means the Department cannot be certain about the number of additional claims on the rates rebate scheme. However, the Department considers that the number ofclaims resulting from the Bill is unlikely to have a material impact on the appropriation. Comment The maximum rebate and income abatement threshold should be adjusted to reflect inflation 7. Inflation for the year ended 31 December 2020 was 1.4 per cent. On this basis, the revised settings would be:  a maximum rebate of $665; and  an income abatement threshold of $26,510. 1There was no adjustment made to the maximum rebate available for the 2016/17 rating year. The CPI for the year ended 31 December 2015 was 0.1 per cent which was too low to result in an adjustment to the maximum rebate available, rounded to the nearest $10. The Department of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua RESPONDING TO QUESTIONS What are the financial implications on the appropriation?  In 2021-22, the Scheme is estimated to cost $54.3 million. This estimate is above the appropriation of $53.5 million for the 2021-22 financial year .  It is difficult to predict the impact that the COVID-19 lockdown and recovery period will have on the uptake of the Scheme, so the Department of Internal Affairs will monitor the appropriation through 2021- 22.  This estimate includes those now eligible through the Rating of Whenua Māori legislative change .  The Department of Internal Affairs’ appropriation for the Scheme has historically been underspent but is nearing its limit. The uptake will be closely monitored, and remedial action will be taken if necessary.  Any increased uptake of the Scheme will be accounted for in the October or March baseline updates. How will people find out about the adjustments to the Scheme?  The adjustments to the key settings will be published in the New Zealand Gazette.  I intend to issue a media release.  The Department of Internal Affairs will inform councils and key interest groups, such as Grey Power and Age Concern, of the adjustments to the Scheme.  Details of the adjustments will also be shown on the Department’s Rates Rebate webpage. Why not adjust the Scheme by using the average wage (as with Superannuation) rather than CPI?  If I were to adjust the Scheme using the average wage we would need to review the Scheme at a more strategic level.  This would need to be a comprehensive review in the context of other subsidies and supplements that are currently available to low-income households.  This could not be completed in time for an adjustment to the Scheme to take effect on 1 July 2021.  Adjusting the Scheme with average wage growth would also likely exceed the current appropriation in 2021-22. What impacts will the Future for Local Government review have on the Scheme?  The review is wide-ranging in scope and could consider rates affordability, as well as specific mechanisms for supporting low-income households .  Whilst this is ongoing, maintenance of the Scheme as is proposed in this paper is still prudent . What impacts will the three waters reform have on the Scheme?  At this stage, no changes are required to the Scheme due to the reform programme. I will receive further advice next year in advance of any financing proposals that could impact the Scheme. IN-CONFIDENCE Page 6 of 7 Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government

It lost its general oversight of freshwater fisheries in 1907, but retained this function in Rotorua, Taupo and (latterly) Southern Lakes districts until 1987. The deer control operations of the 1930s to 1950s, and the struggle to save the black robin and other endangered species in the 1970s and the 1980s, excited enormous media interest. Germany passed the Network Enforcement Act (NetzDG) in June 2017, which makes commercial social networks with at least two million users, liable for hate speech that violates German law. The NetzDG Act followed rampant online hate speech during the European migrant crisis3, which was linked to hate crimes in the physical world. The German Government initially sought to encourage social media companies t o voluntarily apply German hate speech laws on their platforms. However, the German Government ultimately determined that the voluntary efforts of social media companies were inadequate, and sanctions were needed to enforce platforms compliance with German hate speech laws.4 16. Online platforms in scope must set up user-friendly complaint mechanisms to report illegal hate speech. Online platforms face significant fines if they do not remove manifestly illegal content within twenty-four hours of notice and other illegal content with a week of notice. 17. NetzDG has drawn criticism for its potential to stifle free speech, including from the former United Nations Special Rapporteur on the Promotion and Protection of the Right to Freedom of Opinion and Expression. The main criticism is that it bestows significant control on private companies over decisions affecting free speech – as companies must make determinations over what is illegal content without law enforcement. This has led to concern that NetzDG will lead to excessive removal of

Background When individuals apply for public services from New Zealand government agencies, they are frequently asked to provide evidence of their identity or other aspects of their entitlement to the public services. The relevant evidence may be supplied in the form of physical documentation (e.g. a birth certificate), but in a number of cases agencies have set up authorised arrangements to permit specific information to be shared agency to agency. These arrangements are largely information matching agreements, and the limitations of th ese instrument s have led to an environment with many agreements that are narrow, expensive to administer and difficult to adjust in response to changing needs . DIA is leading the development of a small number of AISAs which are intended to replace the existing authorised arrangements and allow new purposes to better meet the needs of individuals and Partner agencies. This AISA covers the sharing of Personal Information with Partner s for the purposes of providing ‘Customer Nominated Services’. Customer Nominated Services are public services provided by the parties that individuals wish to utilise. The parties do not require the individual’s information until the individual has initiated access to the public service. Studylink is an example of a Customer Nominated Service because eligible individuals are able to apply for a student loan, but uptake of the public service is not compulsory. The individual does not always need to consent to all the information sharing as some sharing is mandated or permitted by legisl ation , and will therefore occur by virtue of a n individual ’s decision to utilise a particular public service. Customer Nominated Services AISA 16/03/2020 PUBLIC LY AVAILABLE 11 of 51 4. Objectives and p urpose s of this Agreement 4.1. Objectives The objectives of this Agreement are to: a) gain customer service efficiencies and reduce the compliance load for individuals associated with provision of Personal Information through facilitating increased collaboration between parties ; b) verify aspects of an individual’s identity or entitlement of a n individual applying for or receiving public services ; c) enable updating of records when an individual’s circumstances change ; d) enable the prevention, detection, investigation and prosecution of offences, and the conduct of civil proceedings including judicial review; and e) apply Privacy by Design princi ples to the development and operation of the information sharing . 4.2. Purpose s The purpose s of this information shar ing are to: a) notify an individual of public services they may be eligible to access ; b) verify an individual’s identity; c) ensur e that an individual is not required to provide to a party identity or Life Event records that DIA or the Registrar -General already holds , when applying for or utilising public services ; d) ensure eligibility and entitlement requirements are met when an individual is applying for or receiving public services; e) enable cleansing and updating of records upon the change in circumstances of an individual ; f) enable parties to provide additional protection to the Personal Information shared by the Registrar -General where the individual has an active Non-Disclosure Direction ; and g) enable the prevention, detection, investigation and prosecution of offences, and the conduct of civil proceedings , including judicial review . 5. Exemptions to information privacy principles For the purposes of this Agreement , Information Privacy Principles (IPPs) 2, 10 and 11 which are set out in Section 6 of the Privacy Act 1993 are exempted (by the Order in Council) as follows:  IPP 2: Source of Personal Information It is not a breach of information privacy principle 2 for a party to collect Personal Information from , or within, a party in accordance with this Agreement and for one or more of the purposes specified in Clause 4.2.  IPP 10: Limits on the Use of Personal Information It is not a breach of information privacy principle 10 for Personal Information collected by , or within, a party to be utilised in accordance with this Agreement and for one or more of the purposes specified in Clauses 8. Customer Nominated Services AISA 16/03/2020 PUBLIC LY AVAILABLE 12 of 51  IPP 11: Li mits on Disclosure of Personal Information It is not a breach of information privacy principle 11 for a party to disclose Personal Information to a party , or within, a party in accordance with this Agreement and for one or more of the purposes specified in Clause 4.2. It is also not a breach of information privacy principle 11 for a party to disclose Personal Information to a party as part of making a request for Personal Information . 6. The public s ervices f acilitate d The public services that this Agreement is intended to facilitate are the: (a) accurate and efficient assessment of eligibility for and entitlement to receive public services that an individual appl ies for or decide s to utilise ; (b) accurate and efficient delivery of public services that an individual appl ies for or decide s to utilise ; and (c) the prevention, detection, investigation and prosecution of offences, and the conduct of civil proceedings including judicial review. 7. Type of Personal Information to be shared Parties may share Personal Information about an identifiable individual under this Agreement . Information that is not about an identifiable individual will not be shared under this Agreement . Personal Information may only be shared under this Agreement where DIA / the Registrar -General is either the providing or receiving party. Current council consultation and decision-making requirements prevent councils from responding quickly to changing circumstances. Current legislation is out of date and what should be simple processes are instead taking up councils' time and reducing operating efficiency. Council reporting is not consistent across groups of activities and not done in a way that drives public accountability and easy assessmen t of council performance. Councils struggle to make local regulations and enforce them effectively with tools such as infringement fees. Councils are failing to generate efficiency gains that can be achieved through shared services. Council expenditure using rates revenue has caused excessive increases to costs on ratepayers. Councils struggle to recover costs effectively to ease rates burdens and are not providing sufficient information for cases where costs recovery would not be viable. Insurance/ risk financing is impacting ratepayers. Council borrowing limits are constrain ing on high-growth councils. This instead encourages funding through rates revenue increases. There is a disconnect between elected members and council staff regarding access to information requirements and the ability for members to effectively represent their constituents. Elected members and local communities may have participation and engagemen t with council processes impacted by the conduct of council business inside business hours. Refocus the purpose of local government to guide council decision­ making, distinguish between the roles of central governme nt, local governmen t and the private sector, and help manage community expectations of core council services. Implemen t options to enable councils to adapt quickly to changing circumstances, and to save time and money while balancing democratic principles. Update local governmen t processes and modernise the law. Establish effective performance reporting and drive council accountability for communities. Provide councils with appropriate, modern tools for making and enforcing local regulations effectively. Consideration of greater delegation for councils to set infringement fees. Improve local government financial sustainability and consider options for balancing efficiency gains with local authorities over service levels and costs. Limit council expenditure on nice-to-haves and consider options to protect ratepayers from excessive rates increases Remove legal constraints on cost recovery for councils (where fees have been set in statute) and require counci ls to demonstrate how they are recovering costs for certain activities, thereby supporting councils to ease the rates burden. Improve risk management practices (including approaches to insurance) and support a collective approach to insurance to minimise its impact on rates. Increase borrowing limits for high-growth councils and improve the range of council funding tools beyond rates, thereby improving council activity funding and helping high-growth councils to invest appropria tely. Review access to information for elected members , codes of conduct, conflicts of interest. Consider options to balance freedom of expression with the orderly conduct of council business and allowing councillors to effectively represent local communities. Ensure chief executives are aware of other commitments that elected members have on their time when considering council business and scheduling meetings. Changes to the purpose of local government (removing the four well-beings, refocusing the purpose statemen t, and reinstating core services) are being proposed in the first system improvemen ts bill. considered as part of work to strengthen the emergency management system. Regulatory relief (relating to service delivery reviews, public notice requireme nts, and lending approval) is being proposed in the first system improvemen ts bill. Limitations affecting the analysis of transitional arrangements for holding binding polls on Māori wards established since 2021 The Minister of Local Government has decided to consider the following four options relating to councils that have established a Māori ward without a poll since the 2021 legislative amendments, and have not chosen to rescind their decision or disestablish their Māori wards : All councils that established or resolved to establish Māori wards since 2020 without a poll must e ither: • hold a poll in early 2024, with the results of the poll to apply from the 2025 elections (with variation in how resulting representation reviews are undertaken) ; • hold a poll in early 2025 if a valid petition is received from electors in late 2024 with the results of any polls taking effect at the 2025 local elections (with variation in how resulting representation decisions are undertaken) ; • hold a poll at the 2025 local elections, with the results of the poll to apply from the 2028 local elections; or • hold a poll at the 2025 local elections , if a valid petition is received from electors in early 2025. The results of the poll will apply from the 2028 elections. Options outside of the four outlined above have not been considered . The Ministry will continue to support intervention practitioners to:  register as health practitioners permitted to practise within a relevant scope of practice under the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003, or  register with or be endorsed by DAPAANZ as having demonstrated the relevant specific competencies, or  be equivalently registered with another relevant health professional body and hold at least six months’ post-qualification experience as an addiction practitioner. A key focus is to align the gambling harm intervention workforce with the wider addiction workforce. Research shows that alcohol and other drug problems are often an issue for those experiencing harm from gambling. Adopting workforce standards with comparable standards across the broader addiction workforce will provide greater career mobility and pathways and help build a more resilient and sustainable workforce. As noted in the discussion of public health, Māori, Pacific and Asian stakeholders and service provider submissions noted the need for more effective workforce training, includin g training in cultural competence and the importance of understanding the different worldviews of potential clients. Adverse Actions Section 96Q of the Privacy Act 1993 requires parties to provide written notice to individuals before any “ Adverse Action” is taken against them on the basis of Personal Information shared under an information sharing agreement, and give those individuals 10 working days to dispute the information received. Parties will dispense with the notice requirements under sectio n 96Q if they have reasonable grounds to suspect a n offence has been committed, is being committed or will be committed and that the Personal Information is relevant to the prevention, detection, investigation or the prosecution of the offence , where advan ce notification to a suspect would be likely to prejudice the investigation or prosecution of an alleged offender or offence . Overview of operational processes The first time information is shared with each par ty relating to an individual , DIA / the Registrar - Gene ral will automatically allocate the individual a unique Partner Specific Customer Identifier (PSCID) in relation to the requesting party . The PSCID will be used going forwards by the parties when conversing about the identified individual with that party. The operational processes associated with this Agreement will vary depending on the transfer mechanism utilised. Possible transfer options , depending on the circumstance, are likely to include:  API based transfer ;  Direct system access ;  Email ;  Paper based transfer ; and  Bulk transfer . As a first step of information sharing under this Agreement , a one off bulk exchange of information collected prior may occur to allow the receiving party to do a one - off update of their records for one or more of the purposes specified in Clauses 8. The operational procedures detail the operational processes for providing and receiving information for each party. 12. Safeguards to protect privacy 12.1. Staff The following safeguards exist to protect the privacy of individuals and ensure that any interference with their privacy is minimised: a) All parties to this Agreement , including their staff , will abide by the Public Sector Standards of Integrity and Conduct. b) The staff of all parties to this Agreement performing the services set out in this Agreement will hold all necessary statutory powers and delegations required for the provision of those services , and will comply with relevant operational policy and procedures. 12.2. Information handling The following safeguards exist to protect the privacy of individuals and ensure that any interference with their privacy is minimised: Customer Nominated Services AISA 16/03/2020 PUBLIC LY AVAILABLE 15 of 51 a) No party to this Agreement will provide the raw Personal Information obtained under this Agreement to other agencies or any other third party including other parties to this Agreement except as required by law or in order to comply with a court order. For the avoidance of doubt this does not prevent a party that has updated their information based on Personal Information received under this Agreement from disclosing their information. b) Processes and procedures exist within each party to ensure that information sent under this Agreement is transferred separately from information transferred under other agreements . c) Processes and procedures exist within each party to ensure that the Personal Information is only used for the purposes specified in th is Agreement and remains protected. d) Processes and procedures exist within each party to ensure that the Personal Information is not held longer than required. e) Parties may put constraints and / or caveats on information provided under this Agreement. This i ncludes but is not limited to, any constraints and / or caveats that are required to comply with protections imposed by any law or statute other than the Privacy Act, or to take account of legal privilege as defined in the Evidence Act 2006. f) Each party is responsible for ensuring constraints and / or caveats are compl ied with upon receipt or disclosure of information shared under this Agreement. g) Each party will handle Adverse Action s they may take in accordance with Clause 9. h) The PSCID will not be used as a unique identifier by any party other than DIA and the Registrar -General. i) If the individual the information relates to is resident in the U nited Kingdom or Europe and the receiving party is subject to the UK Data Protection Act 2018 or the European General Data Protection Regulation (EU) 2016/679 , then the receiving party will provide a copy of their privacy notice to the individual concerned on receipt of the information. j) No party is obliged to provide any of the requested information to be shared under this Agreement. k) DIA’s access to and use of photographic images of driver licence holders under this agreement is enabled by section 200(2) of the LTA. Employees of DIA acting in the course of their official duties may access or use photographic image s of driver licence holders to verify the identity of a particular individual. 12.3. Accuracy The following safeguards exist to protect the privacy of individuals and ensure that any interference with their privacy is minimised: a) Parties will use reasonable ende avours to ensure that the information provided to other parties is the most up - to- date information available at the time it is provided. b) Appropriate mechanisms and standard procedures are implemented by each party to verify that Personal Information shared under this Agreement is of an adequate standard and quality. c) Where it is known that information has previously been shared under this Agreement then updates as a result of a request for correction by the individual (including, where applicable and reasonable, any statement requested by the individual to be attached to the information) must be communicated to the previous receiving party, as far as reasonably practicable. This does not apply to information supplied for the purposes of issuing a PSCID . Customer Nominated Services AISA 16/03/2020 PUBLIC LY AVAILABLE 16 of 51 12.4. Privacy Act requests The following safeguards exist to protect the privacy of individuals and ensure that any interference with their privacy is minimised: a) Each party will be responsible for responding to Privacy Act requests relating to Personal Informa tion held by that party as appropriate in the circumstances. 12.5. Privacy Breach The following safeguards exist to protect the privacy of individuals and ensure that any interference with their privacy is minimised: a) Where any party has reasonable cause to belie ve than an actual or suspected breach of an IPP, not exempted by this Agreement , has occurred , an inspection and/or internal investigation process will be applied utilising the identifying party’s standard processes. b) Where a breach of any IPP has occurred , in relation to information shared under this Agreement, and not exempted by this Agreement, the identifying party will notify DIA’s Privacy Officer as soon as possible. c) All relevant parties shall ensure that reasonable assistance is provided to any inves tigation into an actual or suspected Privacy Breach in relation to information shared under this Agreement. d) Where a DIA investigation confirms actions amounting to a notifiable Privacy Breach in relation to information shared under this Agreement, in accor dance with legislation the Privacy Commissioner and individuals will be notified by DIA as required. e) Any party may suspend sharing under this Agreement to allow time for a Privacy Breach to be remedied. 12.6. Audit The following safeguards exist to protect the p rivacy of individuals and ensure that any interference with their privacy is minimised: a) To ensure safeguards are operating as intended and are sufficient to protect the privacy of individuals, each party will conduct regular internal first line assurance and internal audit s of the operation of this Agreement . 12.7. Security The following safeguards exist to protect the privacy of individuals and ensure that any interference with their privacy is minimised: a) All information shared under this Agreement will be appropriately secured when at rest and in transit in accordance with the New Zealand Information Security Manual (NZISM) . b) Where a Security Breach is suspected or there is concern that a breach may occur , the identifying party’s internal investigation proc esses will be applied. c) Where a Security Breach is found to have occurred in relation to information shared under this Agreement , the identifying party will notify DIA ’s Chief Security Officer as soon as possible. The Rates Rebate Scheme provides support to low-income owner -occupiers 72. The current Rates Rebate Scheme provides support to lo -income owner -occupiers. Just over 100,000 households cur rently receive a rates rebate, about 78 percent of which are recipients of New Zealand Superannuation. The level of subsidy available to a household depends on both their income and their rates bill. When water charges are split out from rates bills, some recipients of a rates rebate would receive a lower rebate, even though their total expenses (rates and water) may not have changed. 73. The Department of Internal Affairs estimates that about a third of the current recipients of rates rebates (34,000 households) could be affected by the splitting off of water bills. They would be the higher income recipients of rates rebates (those with a househo ld income greater than about $27,000 per annum). The Department’s analysis suggests that eligible households with a single person on superannuation would be unaffected, but that eligible households with couples on superannuation will fall into the affected group. 74. I propose to deal with this by amending the Rates Rebate Act 1973 to include water bills as part of the definition of rates. This would have the advantage of leaving current beneficiaries of the Scheme no worse off than they would have been without the three waters reforms. It would however create an additional administrative burden on the territorial authorities, who currently administer the Scheme, as they would have to assess water charges as well as rates bills. Amending the Rates Rebate Act 1973 will have a very small fiscal impact for the Crown, as Auckland Council currently tops up rebates as if Watercare bills were a rate. After the reforms, the Crown would need to meet the additional cost of topping up the rebates for Aucklanders, at a cost of around $500,000 per year. This amount is less than the underspend in the current appropriation, but the Treasury has advised that this is a discretionary policy decision and so the costs will need to be met from the between -Budget contingency. 75. I am also proposing to enable the water services entities to share billing information directly with territorial authorities, where the recipient of the bill has applied for a rates rebate. This would enable a streamlined application process for beneficiaries of the scheme

The Strategy What’s changing This strategy outlines the next steps for how RSG’s existing regulatory systems will move beyond simply being co-located to being jointly focused on driving regulatory excellence. RSG aspires to be a place where: ◆The public’s confidence in DIA as a trustworthy government agency grows even stronger, as DIA will be associated with successful regulatory outcomes ◆Government can home any regulatory system with confidence that it will stay on a pathway to growing effectiveness, capability and reliability ◆DIA’s kaimahi will flourish in the regulatory craft and go on to grow the capabilities of DIA and other regulatory agencies What’s not changing Some things in the strategy are not new. The core objectives of the strategic journey embarked upon in 2018 remain relevant: System leadership – lifting the focus up and out ◆Engaging, leading and influencing the wider ecosystems that our system groups are part of ◆Establishing relationships and partnerships; taking opportunities to collaborate or leveraging connectionsThe how… The strategy will enable this by: Ensuring each system is empowered and supported to be effective ◆Organisational design that maximises the benefit of centralised functions, and distributes others – to enable innovation and agility ◆Establishing communities of practice and practice leadership ◆Turning data, evidence and information into insights using robust ICT platforms Getting things done ◆Embedding robust governance mechanisms; improving project management and business change ◆Improving systems and processes; effective decision-making; performance evaluation The RSG strategy builds on these and describes what’s important to get right in the next few years to be better system regulators. This strategy also introduces an enhanced emphasis on outcomes for hapū, iwi and Māori, including actively seeking out opportunities to work collaboratively – and on harnessing data and evaluation to build our evidence base, improve our interventions and support others to make informed decisions. The cafe trial had lower recall rates than all the other trials, on investigation there were three cardholders that were the main contributors to these poor results. One cardholder (wearing card IDs 46 and 47) was seated alone at a table with their back to a table of three other cardholders. This cardholder was within two metres of the table at all times, met the intensity threshold being used for ground truth (​intensity​=3), but presented low transmission risk and the card had poor RSSI values which were filtered out with the basic card algorithm. This effect could have been reduced if only one card had been used per participant and instead involved a greater number of participants in the same scenario. With multiple cards there are more “people” occupying a space that can otherwise only physically be occupied by one. An additional participant at the same table in this scenario would have had a lower intensity score with respect to the table next to them. Also, if a higher intensity rating had been used for analysis (​intensity ​=4) the back-turned participant would not have been counted as a contact. Unfortunately, the “contact event” scores (​intensity ​=4) were not accurate because actual contact events were often fleeting and were not consistently rated.

About the Film and Video Labelling Body The FVLB is an incorporated society and a registered charity comprised of industry representatives. The FVLB manages unrestricted physical content by assigning ratings to content with an M or lower rating. The FVLB issues labels for unrestricted and restricted physical media content. The FVLB has been appointed by the Minister of Internal Affairs, to carry out the labelling function. The FVLB’s main sources of income are from rating films and DVDs submitted to it and issuing labels. The FVLB sets the level of the charge for labels and fees for its activities. The FVLB’s fee structure is reviewed annually by its Board and was last amended in 2016. The FVLB’s fees are available here: http://www.fvlb.org.nz/nz/pages/ forms.html2. As the FVLB has responsibility for setting its own fees the funding options in this consultation apply only to OFLC. However, there may be financial implications for the FVLB, which is likely to be involved in delivering the classification system applying to CVoD. 1 The Chief Censor has the ability to request or call in an unclassified publication in order for it to be classified (this is usually the result of complaints from members of the public). 2 FVLB fees: http://www.fvlb.org.nz/nz/pages/forms.html.Part I - New Zealand’s classification system New Zealand’s classification system exists to support people to make informed choices about the media content they view and to minimise the availability of harmful material. New Zealand’s current classification system is set out in the two pieces of legislation below: • The Classification Act regulates how games, films and other publications are classified. The Classification Act seeks to prevent harm to the public by restricting the availability of harmful material based on the extent, manner and degree of sex, horror, crime, cruelty and violence in a manner consistent with the right to freedom of expression. The application of the Classification Act that is most familiar to the public are the rating labels such as G, PG, M, R16, R18 for DVDs, video games, and theatre releases. These ratings and classifications are issued under the Classification Act by the Film and Video Labelling Body (FVLB) and OFLC. • The Broadcasting Act, 1989 requires classification of free-to-air and pay television and creates a system of broadcasting standards. There are 11 areas specified in the Broadcasting Act from which standards have been developed and people can complain to a broadcaster if they think these standards have been breached. The Broadcasting Act is familiar to the public through the G, PG and AO labels for free-to-air and G, PG, M 16 and 18 for pay television. The options in this consultation only affect the Classification Act and the Regulations issued under the Classification Act. About the Office of Film and Literature Classification OFLC is responsible for regulating the classification framework set out in the Classification Act. Under the Classification Act OFLC: • manages restricted content (classified as R13, R15, R16, R18 or objectionable) and produces classifications to inform consumer choices; 7 Review of options for funding the classification framework – Consultation documentAbout the Review The Government is reviewing options for funding the classification system in two stages. This consultation is Stage 1 of the Review. Stage 2 of the Review is developing and implementing a new charging regime. A mixed funding model of annual Government funding and user-charges currently financially supports OFLC and the classification framework provided for by the Classification Act. This model was established in 1993. Since then, there have been significant changes in the media content environment. The funding model is being revisited to assess if there is a more effective way of funding classification activities than the status quo. Funding levels for the classification framework are also being considered as part of the Review. Funding levels also need to be set for OFLC’s new CVoD activities. Objectives The Review’s objective is to identify and implement a funding model that financially supports OFLC to enable New Zealanders to make informed viewing choices and minimise the availability of harmful media content. Scope The Review’s focus is on OFLC’s charges for the classification of media content for commercial purposes and its new activities related to CVoD content. Also in scope are urgent, special, reduced fees and waivers for charitable organisations and individuals. The Review is not seeking to recover the costs of items submitted by government agencies for classification.Important terms used in this document Throughout this document, we draw a distinction between the two main categories of classification: Commercial classifications and Crown classifications. Commercial classifications - items submitted for classification under Section 12 of the Classification Act. Broadly speaking, these are mainstream commercial products distributed by commercial distributors or screened at film festivals. Crown classifications - items submitted by government agencies under Sections 13 and 29 of the Classification Act for classification. These are typically not mainstream commercial products; many are privately owned such as images on computers. 8 Review of options for funding the classification framework – Consultation documentReview timeline It is anticipated that changes arising from this Review will be implemented alongside the Films, Videos, Publications and Classification (CVoD) Amendment Bill (Amendment Bill) that is extending the Classification Act to CVoD providers and content. The Amendment Bill and new charges are anticipated to take effect from mid-2020. Table 2: Crown appropriation for OFLC 30 June 1995 – 30 June 2023 10 Review of options for funding the classification framework – Consultation documentSection 13 classifications are almost always submissions for classification from the Crown. There is considerable variation in the volumes of Section 12 and 13 submissions from year-to-year. Historically, the Government has shared the costs of submitting publications for classification under Section 12 of the Classification Act with submitters. The level of subsidisation by the Government of the classification of commercial publications has varied depending on the volume of Crown and commercial submissions. The Chief Executive of New Zealand Customs, the Police, the Secretary of Internal Affairs, and the Courts may submit publications under Sections 13 and 29 of the Classification Act to OFLC for a decision on that publication’s classification. These Government agencies prevent people using the Internet and other means to share objectionable material. These Government agencies do not pay a fee per submission for the classification of their material, as the Crown appropriation covers costs arising from the classification of enforcement material. Most Section 13 and 29 classifications involve items which are typically not mainstream commercial products. A high proportion are privately owned.Regulations state the fees to be paid by commercial organisations, and the circumstances and fees for discounted rates There are user-charges for OFLC’s existing classification activities. OFLC’s current fees are prescribed by the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification (Fees) Regulations 1994. Fees are charged for: • Section 12 classification of publications such as films, film trailers and posters, DVDs, some games and books/magazines; • applications for exemptions from the provisions of the Classification Act where any publication has been classified as a restricted or objectionable publication; • applications for classification under Section 13(1)(c) from individuals who do not have a commercial interest in the material; and • reviews of decisions by OFLC regarding the classification of any publication. Figure 1: Classifications from third parties and the Crown 11 Review of options for funding the classification framework – Consultation documentThe Regulations also prescribe the circumstances and fees payable for persons and organisations with special interest that may be eligible for a special or reduced fee. The Regulations provide for reduced fees for societies, organisations or individuals that conduct activities of a charitable, philanthropic, religious, educational, recreational, cultural, or social nature. The Chief Censor must be satisfied that the primary objective of the organisation or society, or individual is not private gain. The current levels of people presenting for services are substantively lower than expected, representing only 16 percent of the number estimated to be affected by moderate to severe gambling harm.6 Early intervention It is apparent that a number of New Zealanders who would benefit from gambling harm intervention are not seeking help . Likely causes for this (identified in submissions to this consultation from health and service providers) are the high level of stigma associated with gambling harm and societal attitudes towards gambling, as well as cultural, language and other barriers. While it is necessary to address the needs of those who have already developed a serious gambling problem and who need specialist help, it is clear that earlier prevention-focused interventions could help individuals and their families , whānau and communities to avoid developing harmful gambling behaviours and associated higher risks of harm. This approach aligns closely with public health programmes in the mental health and addictions areas of alcohol, tobacco and drug use, and family , whānau and partner violence prevention. The data from any single trial was too small to effectively train a model, so summarised data from all card contacts was collected together into a single file containing all 938 card contacts. The summarised data was one line per card contact containing: ​total contact duration, maximum RSSI, mean RSSI, maximum and mean duration of non-reidentified events (i.e. at most 15 minutes as per card ID rotation), maximum and mean intensity*duration, a count of the number of card advertisements seen, and a boolean value indicating whether the contact was a close contact as identified from our ground truth. A Random Forest model (using 100 base estimators) was evaluated using ten-times ten-fold cross-validation. During cross-validation the dataset was randomly split into ten equally-sized subsets (folds), and the model trained using nine folds and tested using the remaining held-out fold. This was repeated for every fold. The whole process was then repeated ten times (100 folds evaluated) so that results were not adversely affected by a particular random selection of folds.

The dynamics of adoption and compliant usage are critically important to understand. A population level deployment of a symptom checker increases in usefulness proportionately with usage and can quickly reach a sample size that is useful. Conversely, a contact tracing app depends on extremely high levels of adoption because everyone needs the app for it to work - it is subject to a network effect - and modest levels of adoption render it useless.

The economic regulator would have a role in implementing legislated pricing principles and regulations 98. The economic regulator would be able to issue guidance, input methodologies, and/or determinations to the water services entities on how to implement the pr icing principles and any regulations. The choice of instrument(s) would be at the economic regulator’s discretion. The regulator could also cover off issues such as appropriate transitional measures, if the water services entity is not immediately able to fully implement the principle or regulations. Determinations and guidance could also deal with relatively rare situations where there may be tensions or trade -offs between the principles. 99. I am also proposing to give the economic regulator the ability to is sue guidance, input methodologies, and/or determinations on other pricing matters not covered by principles or regulations, so long as this is consistent with the overall statutory scheme and contributes to the purpose of economic regulation. This would gi ve the economic regulator a flexible suite of tools for effectively regulating water services entities. 100. As outlined above, the economic regulator would also have the power to alter tariffs if it determined that a water services entity was not implementing the pricing principles or regulations appropriately. Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page 17 of 41 Geographic averaging of prices can contribute to affordability at a community level 101. In the 18 October 2021 Cabinet paper, a possible pricing outcome of cost- sharing was set out, with the example of geographic averaging of prices. A key driver of the reforms is to address affordability issues, particularly for customers in smaller communities. The overall reform process will improve affordability by reducing costs through the efficiency gains that will be realised from service aggregation, improved financing, and improved incentives from independent governance and economic regulation. Entities can also use geographically averaged pricing to smooth and share costs across communities, thereby contributing to more affordable services for all. 102. Geographic averaging can occur at a few different levels: 102.1 Within a network: this is generally used by electricity distribution companies for their local networks. 102.2 Within a territorial authority district: some territorial authorities will already have implemented geographical averaging at this le vel for ease of administration and to promote greater pricing transparency. Averaging within a district may require averaging across different networks and between urban and rural communities. 102.3 Within the service area of a water services entity: this has th e advantage of improving affordability for smaller communities. Through consultation, some territorial authorities have come out strongly against this level of geographic averaging because it represents a transfer between territorial authorities with diffe rent historic approaches to three waters infrastructure investments. Rural territorial authorities generally support it and the sector is generally expecting this level of geographic averaging. 103. Geographic averaging would not occur at a national level as th is would require financial transfers between water services entities. 104. The legislation would enable water services entities, in consultation with their regional representative groups, to make decisions about geographic averaging (consistent with any Government policy statement). The economic regulator would not be able to override geographic averaging but would be able to provide guidance on its implementation. 105. There would be some exceptions to geographic averaging, including: 105.1 where communities have sought a higher level of service than is provided elsewhere in the water services area, or where communities receive a lower level of service than what is generally provided in the water services area; 105.2 new growth areas (where there i s a levy in place under the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act 2020, discussed with growth charging from paragraph 174 below); 105.3 Water infrastructure contributions (growth charges, discussed from paragraph 161 below); and Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN CONFIDENCE Page 18 of 41 105.4 failing drinking water supplies (water services entities will have a duty to ensure communities have access to drinking water if existing suppliers are facing significant problems). To avoid this being ‘gamed’ by private suppliers, they should not automati cally receive geographically averaged prices if the water services entity steps in and provides a drinking water supply on either a temporary or permanent basis. 106. I also propose that the Government policy statement may be used, if considered necessary, to provide for geographic averaging of prices. This could only require geographic averaging for residential customers and only for drinking and wastewater services. T he exceptions set out above would also apply. The proposed pricing formula for stormwater charging (set out from paragraph 1433 below) already enables geographic averaging. It is unlikely to be practical to begin any form of p rice harmonisation before 2027. For this reason, the Government policy statement will not be able to provide any direction on geographic price averaging before 2027. 107. Achieving geographic averaging would first require harmonising tariff structures, as far as possible, and then harmonising the actual price levels within those structures. There will need to be a long lead in time to achieve geographic averaging without causing significant price increases in some locations. The Government policy statement would have the flexibility to set out the overall requirement for geographic averaging, as well as detail on the transition to that goal. This would enable price changes to be smoothed over time and meet the legislated pricing principles. Part D: Transition and removal of cross -subsidies 108. The non- discrimination pricing principle would remove cross -subsidies between different sectors and user groups. While the exact level of cross -subsidisation between different groups is not known in detail, some indicative data has been compiled. RISK EXAMPLES POTENTIAL OUTCOMES ASSUMPTIONS MITIGATION MEASURES ASESSMENT Costs become excessive for governmen t and/or private sector The actual costs of compliance testing turns out to be significantly higher than the initial indicative costs. This would affect Government in phase one (2020 -22) as government is covering the cost of this testing. In phase two (2022 -25) the entity seeking accreditation, whether public or private, w ill likely assume this cost. The Trust Framework requires more resources than anticipated to set up and/or maintain, increasing overall costs for government . Costs to upgrade systems to meet Trust Framework requirements are significantly higher than originally estimated , adding additional strain to the budget of the private or public sector entity seeking to join the Trust Framework . Budgets are undermined Costs discourage participation in the Trust Framework Reasonable costs will encourage participation Government assumes th e risk with regard to the cost of testing . In order to mitigate this risk, government will cover the cost of compliance testing during p hase one of the Trust Framework (2020 -2022) and work wi th partners to test and develop compliance processes in such a manner that compliance testing costs remain reasonable and appropriate going forward . The entity undergoing compliance testing assumes the cost of upgrading their systems. In the case of public sector entities, government can mitigate this through budget planning, however, private sector entities remain responsible for their own budgets. The mitigation measures will ensure this is a low probability risk.

I propose that all water services entity charges will be set out annually with the publication of a detailed tariff list. The tariff list would be based on the funding and pricing plan. The tarif f list is likely to cover the following services: 84.1 Water supply charges: these could vary with the type of service (for example, on-demand urban water supply vs. rural trickle feed), the type of water (drinking water or not), and the capacity of the connection. They may also be a mixture of fixed and volumetric charges. The use of volumetric/variable charges will not be mandated. 84.2 Wastewater charges: these could also be a mixture of fixed and volumetric (or assessed/proxy) charges, that are likely to vary with the capacity of the connection. The use of volumetric charges will not be mandated. 84.3 Trade waste charges: more detailed information on trade waste is set out in the companion paper Policy proposals f or three waters service delivery legislative settings. 84.4 Stormwater charges: the approach to stormwater charges is set out in more detail from paragraph 143 below. 84.5 Growth charges: the approach to growth charges is set out in more detail from paragraph 1611 below. 84.6 Connection charges and other miscellaneous charges. 85. Some charges and prices may be set by reference to hourly rates. Other charges may be sufficiently unusual or customised that they are not published on the tariff list. 86. The economic regulator would have the power to direct the water services entity to directly alter the funding and pricing plan or the tariff list (without any consultation requirements) if the economic regulator determined that the plan or tariff lis t was inconsistent with the pricing principles and regulations, or any other constraints set by the regulator. The proximity trial (proximity00) was a distance/signal-strength test to capture the signal strength of the cards at different distances with different placements of the cards. The floor of an empty office was marked with lines at one-metre intervals. Participants wore five cards: on a lanyard around their neck, on a clip at their hip, on a clip on their chest pocket, on a band around their arm, and inside a wallet/bag that was held at roughly waist height. Each participant stood at either end of the course, walked to the opposite end and back passing each other in the middle. The participants then stood at their ends for two minutes, before one taking a step towards the other, waiting two minutes, then the other stepping forward. Over the twenty minutes they progressed towards each other in two minute/one metre intervals before meeting in the middle (where they stood together for two minutes).

The ranking process does not affect the recall of the overall CovidCard system since we are not removing potential contacts from the list. The machine learning model could be used to remove false positives (rather than pushing them to the bottom of the ranked list), however this will potentially remove real contacts as well. 9 Proactively Released by the Department of Internal Affairs FURTHER WORK A valuable next step for production testing is to run a larger field trial in a more ‘open’ environment. A larger open trial would provide a more realistic context for evaluation of false positive rates: in many of the closed trials participants were close contacts, or in close proximity (i.e. casual contacts) with almost every other participant - so “false positives” detected by the card were actually real-world “near misses”. The main challenge with running a large open trial is the accurate collection of ground truth (such that the closed or scripted trials allow), which exponentially increases in time to collect as the number of participants increases. This could be mitigated by asking participants to complete ground truth for their own interactions, although this may also introduce error into the ground truth data.

The regulations will be developed in two phases. The first set of regulations (covered in this discussion paper ) outline the necessary legal and procedural requirements to initially stand up the regulatory system. They will cover: • Accreditation Services: Definition of the types of services that will be subject to accreditation under the Act . • Accreditation Process : Accreditation requirements, application assessment criteria, and accreditation duration. • Service Levels: Establishment of d ifferent service levels that providers can meet when delivering accredited services. • Complaints and Disputes Resolution: The internal complaints and dispute resolution process requirements TF providers need to meet. • Recordkeeping : The information to be ret ained by TF providers and the period they are required to retain that information. • Reporting : The reporting requirements that will apply to TF providers. We anticipate a second set of regulations will be developed and recommended to the Minister for the Digital Economy and Communications by the TF Board in 2024 to address any necessary cost recovery arrangements and other operational matters required to fra me the TF Authority’s administration of the scheme. Th ese regulations may include: • Cost Recovery: The establishment of fees for the partial recovery of the TF Authority’s ongoing costs for administering the Trust Framework, including consideration of accre ditation applications or renewals . It is anticipated that the TF Authority’s initial establishment and first two years of operating costs will be met from Crown funding without a contribution from fees . • Disputes Resolution Scheme: The establishment of any requirements and criteria that the TF Authority must meet should it want to recommend a disputes resolution scheme , together with any proposed fees to recover costs associated with the provision of complaints and dispute resolution services . The establishme nt of a fees regime will be considered in conjunction with the development of the TF Authority’s complaints and disputes resolution operating model, which will consider the role, if any, of an external dispute resolution service provider. • Third Party Asse ssors : Arrangements for the certification of third -party assessors to carry out functions relating to the accreditation of providers, including appointment criteria, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements. • Other Operational Matters: Any other operationa l matters that the TF Board considers should be established in regulation s to provide greater certainty to both the Authority and regulated parties on compliance requirements and ensure the cost-effective management of the regulatory system by the TF Author ity. The regulations, for example, will cover any changes to accreditation renewal requirements and compliance order forms. Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government

The security controls limit the effectiveness of any potential on-card algorithm for ranking contacts because the card will only see a contact for at most fifteen minutes before it appears as a new, entirely different, contact ID. Therefore, the best place to rank contacts is once the card data has been downloaded and re-identified back to card serial numbers as server-side processing: once re-identified, contact data can be aggregated to overall contact duration, and assessed for other factors such as time-of-day, and number of concurrent contacts. Ranking post-download also allows for the opportunity to present card data to a human for more nuanced ranking, and for re-prioritising automatically if contact definitions or contact tracing requirements change.

The ​CovidCard ​ could address health and economic inequities. First, the ​CovidCard ​ does not require any level of technical expertise so it is user friendly for people unfamiliar with technology or smartphones. Second, the CovidCard is not reliant on existing communications infrastructure such as mobile networks or internet connectivity. Third, it is envisioned the CovidCard will come at no cost to individuals, removing the direct financial barrier. Fourth, the CovidCard could enable targeted lockdown (with recursive contact tracing) so there will be a limited economic impact on most people. Fifth, the development, testing and implementation of CovidCard is being conducted in partnership with Māori to ensure the solution is responsive to Māori, is compliant with principles of Māori data sovereignty and uploads Te Tiriti o Waitangi principles. 3.7. Trust, security and privacy The concerns voiced during our consultations were mostly focused on privacy, security and the use of data. There are cost pressures associated with implementing the three waters reform programme 16. In June 2020, Cabinet established the $710 million Three Waters Infrastructure Investment and Service Delivery Reform Programme tagged operating contingency, a portion of which remains unallocated. In Budget 2021, a Transforming Three Waters Service Delive ry for New Zealanders: Transition and Implementation tagged operating contingency of $296 million was established to provide for establishment and transition costs. 17. Decisions to allocate funding for three waters reform establishment and transition costs were made early in the policy process, prior to the full suite of proposals being developed and their financial implications being understood. This has given rise to several cost pressures. 18. The October 2021 decision to proceed with reform means there is now more certainty regarding the three waters reform work programme through to 1 July 2024 and beyond. Following further detailed planning, the Department of Internal Affairs now needs to increase its capacity and capability to deliver and implement the refo rm programme. This includes a significant policy and legislative programme, a large programme of entity establishment and transition activity, ministerial services, and ongoing engagement, communications and public information activity. 19. Other notable cost pressures relate to key judgements about the best approach to transition, in particular the scope and level of support available to iwi/Māori and the local government sector to participate meaningfully in the transition process. This is an area where additional investment can help to de-risk the transition process and ensure entities are set up with the best chance of success. 20.

In water services, geography is impor tant for the cost and quality o f service. Denser urban areas tend to have lower average costs of service . Water services with more dispersed customers have to distribute drinking water, and pump wastewater over longer distances with more pipes, dispersed t reatment infrastructure and higher costs. Aside from some high -level discussion of available water sources, and similar populat ions, WICS has not investigated why Scotland’s geography is a good predictor of New Zealand’s water investment needs. The total land area and the geographical distribution of the population s are very different. WICS incorrectly assumes that lower population density in New Zealand implies lower levels of urbani sation . Table 2.2 illustrates how New Zealand’s population is more urbani sed than Scotland ’s, but despite thi s, New Zealand still has a lower population density. A larger majority of New Zealand’s population live in urban areas and the urban population is more likely to grow in New Zealand as compared t o Scotland.

Films, Videos, and Publications (Urgent Interim Classification of Publications and Prevention of Online Harm) Amendment Bill: Approval for Introduction Portfolio Internal Affairs On 5 May 2020, the Cabinet Legislation Committee: 1 noted that in December 2019, the Cabinet Social Wellbeing Committee took the following decisions: 1.1 knowingly livestreaming objectionable content will become a criminal offence punishable by up to 14 years in prison; 1.2 allowing the Chief Censor to make interim classification decisions; 1.3 allowing take-down notices to be issued to require the removal of objectionable online content; 1.4 making online content hosts subject to a civil pecuniary penalty of up to $200,000, if they do not comply with an issued take-down notice; 1.5 ensuring ‘safe harbour’ provisions in the Harmful Digital Communications Act 2015 would not apply to objectionable online content; and 1.6 enabling the establishment of regulations that would allow the government to implement web-filtering of objectionable content if required; [SWC-19-MIN-0204] 2 noted that the Films, Videos, and Publications (Urgent Interim Classification of Publications and Prevention of Online Harm) Amendment Bill: 2.1 gives effect to the above decisions; 2.2 holds a category 2 priority on the 2020 Legislation Programme; 3 agreed that the Bill include a liability exemption for staff and employees of Internet Service Providers and online content hosts, who in the execution of their duties, or acting on the instruction of the Government, are tasked with removing objectionable content;
