This paper seeks approval for the introduction of the Films, Videos, and Publications (Urgent Interim Classification of Publications and Prevention of Online Harm) Amendment Bill (the Bill). 2. This paper also seeks policy approval to extend the current liability exemptions for staff and employees of online content hosts and internet service providers (ISPs). Under this proposal they would be exempted from liability when executing their duties, or acting on the instruction of the Government, to remove objectionable content from their respective platforms. Policy 3. Cabinet agreed to the policy proposals contained in the Bill on 16 December 2019 [CAB-19-MIN-0672 refers]. The Bill was given a priority of Category 2 (must be passed this year) for the 2020 Legislation Programme and Cabinet has indicated an intention to have it introduced into the House by March 2020 [SWC-19-MIN-0204 refers]. 4. Under the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification Act 1993 (the Act), it is an offence to make, possess, supply or distribute an objectionable publication (including digital content). Such an offence is based on whether the availability of a given publication or digital content is likely to be injurious to the public good. 5. The Bill will improve the way we regulate objectionable content, including violent extremist and terrorist content found online. Specifically, the Bill amends the Act to: 5.1 criminalise knowingly livestreaming objectionable content; 5.2 allow the Chief Censor to make interim classification assessments in relation to publications (both physical as well as online) likely to be found objectionable in urgent situations; 5.3 allow take-down notices to be issued to require the removal of objectionable online content; 5.4 make online content hosts subject to a civil pecuniary penalty of up to $200,000, if they do not comply with an issued take-down notice; 5.5 ensure ‘safe harbour’ provisions in the Harmful Digital Communications Act 2015 would not apply to objectionable online content; and 5.6 enable the establishment of regulations that would allow the Government to implement web-filtering of objectionable content if required. 6. Under the Bill, the definition of online content hosts has been aligned to that contained in the Harmful Digital Communications Act 2015. The definition covers persons who have control over electronic retrieval systems, such as a website or an online application, but excludes ISPs. Page 1 of 6 a59heeqbzw 2020-06-08 12:12:03 Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Policy approval for extension of liability exemptions to ISPs and online content hosts 7. As per Cabinet’s direction, [CAB-19-MIN-0672 refers], officials undertook targeted engagement on an exposure draft of the Bill with key industry groups including telecommunication companies, ISPs, technology companies and representatives as well as Government agencies. 8. As a result of this consultation, I seek policy approval to one further proposed change, to extend the current liability exemptions for staff and employees of online content hosts and ISPs. Under this proposal these people would be exempted from liability when executing their duties, or acting on the instruction of the Government, to remove objectionable content from their respective platforms. This ensures a consistent approach to liability exemptions under the Act. 9. Several industry stakeholders raised concerns about the Act making them criminally liable when identifying, moderating and removing objectionable content, either in the execution of their duties or acting on Government instructions. Possessing, distributing and supplying objectionable material is a criminal offence under the Act. While the Act provides a defence to service providers when handling objectionable material, it only applies in restricted situations. The current defence would not apply where service providers may be required to search for variations of the content and forward links onto other service providers and online content hosts for the purpose of speedily removing objectionable content across different platforms (as was required in the wake of the March 15 terror attacks). Industry stakeholders suggested making it clear that in such situations, staff and employees of ISPs and online content hosts are exempt from liability. 10. This exemption currently applies to Government and Office of Film and Literature Classification (OFLC) officials tasked with removing objectionable content. The extension of this exemption as proposed, would ensure a consistent approach by exempting service providers and online contents when removing all objectionable content, and not just those subject to an interim classification assessment. Regulatory impact analysis 11. A Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA) was prepared to support Cabinet’s decision to proceed with these proposals in December 2019 [CAB-19-MIN-0672 refers]. 12. The Quality Assurance panel (the Panel) that evaluated the RIA concluded that it partially met Treasury’s Quality Assurance criteria. 13. The Panel concluded that the RIA is complete and includes all necessary information. Consultation with stakeholders was focussed primarily on the regulatory proposals, due to the time and scope constraints on the analysis. Discussions from consultation resulted in refining the proposals and a commitment to release an exposure draft of the Bill. Climate implications of policy assessment 14. The Ministry for the Environment CIPA team have been consulted on this Cabinet paper and confirm the CIPA requirement does not apply. Page 2 of 6 a59heeqbzw 2020-06-08 12:12:03 Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Compliance 15. The Bill complies with: 15.1 the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi; 15.2 the rights and freedoms contained in the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990 and the Human Rights Act 1993; 15.3 disclosure statement requirements (a copy of that statement is attached to this paper); 15.4 the principles and guidelines set out in the Privacy Act 1993; 15.5 the relevant international standards and guidelines; and 15.6 the Legislation Guidelines (2018 edition), which are maintained by the Legislation Design and Advisory Committee. Consultation Officials from the Department of Internal Affairs led engagement on the policy proposals contained in this Bill 16. The Department of Internal Affairs led targeted consultation on these policy proposals with key industry, community, and civil society stakeholders from 23 October to 4 November 2019. This engagement process involved seven workshops across the country, including specific workshops with youth. Attendees at the main workshops included representatives from major online content hosts, ISPs, community groups, and civil society organisations. In total, approximately 200 people attended the workshops. Stakeholders were also invited to submit written feedback, of which 17 were received. There was no formal consultation with iwi or hapū on proposals in the Bill before policy decisions were made. Following engagement on policy proposals, an exposure draft of the Bill was circulated to key stakeholders 17. Further to the direction of Cabinet [CAB-19-MIN-0672 refers], an exposure draft of the Bill served as a basis for a targeted consultation on the legislative amendments with key industry groups including telecommunication companies, internet service providers, technology companies, a civil society group, and Government agencies. Stakeholders provided written feedback on the exposure draft and several stakeholders met with officials to discuss the exposure draft. 18. Stakeholder feedback focused on terminology used in the Bill, the clarification of operational provisions, and comment on the establishment and operation of the filtering system. Stakeholders also commented on the quantum of penalty for failing to comply with a take-down notice as being potentially too low. 19. The filtering provisions of the Bill attracted a significant proportion of feedback. Stakeholders commented that it was important to ensure sufficient legislative safeguards existed to prevent improper use of the filter system. These safeguards will also ensure that the system was used in a transparent and accountable manner and is subject to appropriate oversight. Issues relating to the filter remain likely to be of interest to industry, communities and civil society groups throughout the legislative process. Page 3 of 6 a59heeqbzw 2020-06-08 12:12:03 Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE 20. Following stakeholder feedback, the Bill has been strengthened to more explicitly provide for appropriate checks and balances relating to the filter. Changes include lifting several provisions from regulations into the primary legislation, for example, clarifying that the filter only applied to objectionable material and identifying the full range of stakeholders that must be consulted on the design of the filter. 21. Stakeholder feedback also resulted in the clarification of terminology and operational sections in the Bill. Several minor changes were made to address potential inconsistencies between operational provisions. 22. Some agencies also queried whether the current proposed penalty level of a maximum of $200,000 for non-compliance with a take-down notice is sufficient. The penalty would apply to each take-down notice issued. 23. I consider that the proposed penalty level to be appropriate as it is commensurate with current penalty levels in the Act. However, officials will consider submissions on this subject and provide advice to me during the select committee process. If there is a strong case for adjusting these penalty levels, I will return to Cabinet for policy approval to adjust penalty levels and look to amend the Bill during its passage through the House. 24. The Bill was also referred to the Legislation Design and Advisory Committee (LDAC). LDAC made several recommendations relating to the Bill, including: 24.1 ensuring the policy objective is clearly defined and discernible; 24.2 ensuring the legislation is consistent with fundamental rights and freedoms, and any limits are appropriate and no more than “reasonable limits” that can be “demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society”; and 24.3 ensuring an appropriate division between what matters are included in primary legislation and what matters are included in secondary legislation. 25. LDAC’s feedback was considered when revising the Bill. 26. The Government coalition and confidence and supply partners have been consulted on the Bill. 27. The following agencies were also consulted on this Cabinet paper: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, Ministry of Justice, Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, Ministry for Culture and Heritage, New Zealand Police, New Zealand Customs, OFLC, the Treasury, Office of Ethnic Communities, Te Puni Kōkiri, Ministry for Women, Office for Disability Issues, Ministry for Pacific Peoples, and Ministry of Social Development. Binding on the Crown 28. The Act is binding on the Crown. Creating new agencies or amending law relating to existing agencies 29. The Bill will not create any new agencies. 30. The Bill will amend the law relating to OFLC and will enable it to issue interim classification decisions on publications that are likely to be objectionable. 31. The Bill will not remove any existing powers held by OFLC or the Chief Censor. Page 4 of 6 a59heeqbzw 2020-06-08 12:12:03 Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Allocation of decision-making powers 32. The Bill does not involve the allocation of decision-making powers between the Executive, the Courts and Tribunals. Associated regulations 33. The Bill contains new regulation-making powers to implement and support the establishment of an electronic system to identify and prevent access to objectionable online publications. Definition of Minister/Department 34. The Bill does not create a new definition of Minister or Department. Commencement of legislation 35. The Bill will commence by 30 April 2021. Consistent with this determination, I intend to introduce the Bill once Parliament resumes normal business. 38. This includes provision for: 49.1 Specific requirements that are so important and enduring that they need to be enshrined in primary legislation, such as the legal mandate to charge consumers for water services, and the principles to inform the development of funding and pricing plans of water services entities. Part B: Charging for water services and protections for vulnerable consumers 50. Our reform of three waters service delivery will result in better and more affordable water services than if their operation were to remain with councils. That said, there will continue to be households that will struggle to meet the costs of water services together with their other needs. The transition to more standardised prices and removal of historic subsidies and inequities will also result in gains and losses for different groups. 51. For this reason, I begin my discussion of pricing and charging by considering who should be charged for water services and what needs to be done to protect vulnerable consumers. In Part D, I discuss specific matters related to transition, and the provisions necessary to smooth pricing and reduce price shocks for all consumers.

The Local G overnment Electoral Legislation Bill proposes new obligations on councils to review Māori representation 3 The Bill improves the processes by which individuals and communities are represented through, and can participate in, local government elec tions. The Bill amends the Local Electoral Act 2001, the Local Government Act 2002, and the Local Government (Auckland Council) Act 2009. The key policy areas for the Bill are: 3.1 establishing a fit -for-purpose process for councils to review their representation arrangements , including Māori representation; 3.2 improving governance flexibility at Auckland Council; 3.3 updating the process for tied elections; and 3.4 enabling all candidates to s ubmit electronic nominations. 4 Reviews of representation arrangements must occur at least every six years. In each term of local government, approximately half of all local authorities must review their representation arrangements . 5 The Bill changes the rep resentation review process to require councils to consider Māori representation as a mandatory component of those reviews unless they have already established Māori wards. When presented with new - previously unseen - contact data the model is able to produce a probability that the new data belongs to a real close contact. A list of contacts from a given card can be ordered by the probabilities to produce a ranked list, ideally with close contacts near the top of the list and casual contacts closer to the bottom.

The Bluetooth card accu rately identified the same contacts as the UWB devices in this pilot. However, this is unsurprising given the lack of specificity built -in to the card firmware which led to the detection of a wide definition of close contacts (e.g. likely more than 2m). As such, these resul ts should be interpreted with caution as the performance of the card must be tested in a controlled setting with a strong ground truth. Such settings will facilitate robust tests of the precision of the close contact identification capabi lity. 3.5.2 Concordance between Bluetooth cards and self -report daily diaries In this pilot, we aimed to establish whether the Bluetooth cards would capture close contacts, but we did not aim to evaluate effectiveness beyond its ability to capture any close c ontacts. In Figure 3 we qualitatively compare the median number of close contacts between self -report diaries and the Bluetooth . The median number of close co ntacts recorded per day o ver the study period was 18 for the Bluetooth card s compared to only 3 or the self -report surveys. On the weekend, days 3 and 4, the number of participants decreased with minimal staffing. Accordingly, the number of possible close contacts also decreased. This is reflected in the Bluetooth card data, as the median number of close contacts on the weekend was nearly half the median number reported on weekdays, days 2 and 5. The differences in the median close contacts per participant between self -report daily diaries and Bluetooth card data should be interpreted with caution: 1) not all participants completed diaries each day, tho ugh Bluetooth cards were r ecording contacts each day; 2) the duration of the contact for each interaction captured by Bluetooth cards was assumed to be one minute, but it could have been much less; 3) diaries were reported by participants about all close c ontacts, regardless of whether those close contacts were definitively participants in the pilot. While known non - participant close contacts were removed from the analysis, if the close contact was unknown, then their data was retained; and 4) there were n o filtering close contact algorithm installed on the Bluetooth card, meaning that the cards may have at times applied a much wider definition of a close contact than the daily surveys (e.g., greater than 2m away). This work commenced with a small-scale field trial conducted May 7-12​th​ in Nelson Hospital using a “Prototype 0” version of the ​CovidCard ​. This was followed by a series of closed and controlled scenario tests conducted May 14-29​th​ in the Waikato region. These tests used “Prototype 1” cards which could be updated, enabling iterative card embedded software (firmware) development. These closed tests simulated common interactions across a range of scenarios including an office environment, a cafe/restaurant, a construction site, taxi/Uber trips and a house party/social function. The tests have provided a strong real-world dataset to support the evaluation of the CovidCard’s ​ contact identification performance relative to a robust observed reality (ground truth), derived through a combination of video capture and detailed trial observer records.

Ensuring that services and functions continue to enhance wellbeing over time requires anticipating how the environment we operate in may change, and positions ourselves to best meet the opportunities and challenges that arise. Building digital public services is at the forefront of our thinking so Government is as joined-up, and people centric as it can be. The Department of Internal Affairs has made great progress in making its services easier to use and more accessible and in supporting other government agencies in realising their digital ambitions. Meeting the challenges of regulation in the digital world and addressing barriers to digital inclusion will be a focus of attention in coming years. Ensuring that Government acts as a cohesive system is important and the Department will play an important role in system leadership for both central and local government. More effectively linking central and local government to address national objectives in areas such as community resilience and infrastructure is an important part of the Department’s work. The Department’s many and varied services will continue to provide value, including support for the Executive, registration of life events, community advice and development, public recordkeeping, library services, preserving and making accessible our documentary heritage, administration of grants, and enforcement and compliance across several regulatory regimes, including digital safety, gambling, financial transactions and charities. I believe that we are well placed to make good progress towards further developing services and activities to maximise their benefit to people, communities and the Government. I look forward to continuing to work closely with the Department as it delivers its roles and functions for the people and Government of New Zealand. Statement of Responsibility I am satisfied that the information on strategic intentions prepared by the Department of Internal Affairs is consistent with the policies and performance expectations of the Government. Hon. Tracey Martin Minister of Internal Affairs October 2019

Timetable for establishing the other entities and applying economic regulation 34. I have also been consider ing the approach to determining and communicating the ‘go live’ timetable and process for the other new entities . 35. One option would be to include a timetable of ‘go live’ dates in the Amendment B ill. However, this would be an inflexible approach, which would require a change to primary legislation if any of the dates needed to be amended during the establishment period. 36. My preference is to retain some flexibility around the dates , and to use an Order in Council process instead of primary legislation. The ‘go live’ timeframes would reflect when each entity and its council owners are ready for this to occur – based on them demonstrating this ‘readiness’ in a number of critical areas . All of the entities would have to ‘go live’ by 1 July 2026, at the latest, which is the ‘backstop’ date agreed by Cabinet in the April 2023 paper. 37. I am proposin g to develop and communicate the process that would enable an entity to ‘go live’, including which factors would need to be demonstrated for this to occur. Given all of the work that will be required to get each entity and council ready, and the impact on staff involved in the transfer, there would need to be a minimum notice period between agreeing the ‘go live’ date and the day on which the entity will begin operating . This will give everyone involved sufficient time to prepare , and time for staff to be transferred . 38. I note that some councils have already indicated they would like their entity to ‘g o live ’ on 1 July 2024, as was originally anticipated. T here are practical constraints that may make it difficult to establish a large number of entities at once, though, and not all of the councils within an entity service area may be prepared for th is. I am, however, seeking to accommodate some of these request s so New Zealanders can enjoy the benefits of reform quickly, across a number of regions. 9(2)(f)(iv) 9(2)(f)(iv) Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs IN CONFIDENCE

I am pleased to present Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Afairs Strategic Intentions for 2021- 2025. This document outlines our priorities for the next four years, as we aim to serve and connect people, communities and government to build a safe, prosperous and respected nation. The Department has a wide range of duties and responsibilities. We are focusing our intentions on making progress towards achieving five broad outcomes for the benefit of people, communities and the government. • Oranga hapū, iwi, and Māori is improved through an enduring, equitable and positive Māori-Crown partnership • Communities across New Zealand are safe, resilient and thriving • People’s sense of belonging and collective memory builds an inclusive New Zealand • New Zealand is a well-functioning democracy across central and local government • People can easily access services and information Some of the major initiatives we have planned or under way include: Three Waters Reforms, a system-wide transformation of the way three waters services are regulated and provided to communities. We will support the Government to implement the final decisions on the reforms, and lead the significant work required to design and transition to a new system. An independent review into the Future for Local Government in response to major reforms in the sector. Title: The Films, Videos, and Publications Classifications Amendment Bill – Standardising classification for Commercial Video on -Demand content – with Supplementary A nalysis ( 25 November 2019 ) Authoring agency : Department of Internal Affairs Location : https://www.dia.govt.nz/Resource -material -Regulatory -Impact -Statements -Index Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs 6 2.3.1. If so, did the RIA Team in the Treasury provide an independent opinion on the quality of any of these regulatory impact statement s? YES For the RIA dated 9 August 2019, the Quality Assurance panel provided the following statement: • The panel considers that the RIA does not meet the Quality Assurance criteria. • The panel considers that the RIA is clearly written, and is transparent about the constraints on the analysis, and about many of the gaps in the analysis. Overall, the panel co nsiders that there is sufficient analysis for Ministers to make an informed decision not to pursue Option 1 but does not provide sufficient analysis to inform the decision about whether Option 2 (the preferred option) or Option 3 is the best way of achievi ng the Government’s objectives. Our concerns are summarised under the quality assurance criteria of complete and convincing, and consulted. Complete and convincing • There is limited analysis of the size of the problem, particularly the magnitude of the risk from misclassifying content and the degree to which other information offered by commercial video on demand providers (e.g. in the synopsis and genre label that a consumer sees before viewing) mitigates the risk. There is also limited evidence that the problem needs addressing now, instead of waiting for the intended wider review. • The RIA does not establish the criteria which will be used to determine which providers will be regulated, and whether consideration will be given to exempting small or niche pro viders. Other options could have been considered. For example, encouraging providers to join the voluntary system, with the chance that regulation might follow if that was unsuccessful. • Information about impacts of options is light. Two examples are: o Little information about the costs to providers, and the extent to which costs will be passed onto consumers – whether through higher prices or reductions in content (lower -profitability minority audience content might be at greater risk). o Whether Option 2 woul d increase, rather than decrease, inconsistency of classification when considered across all household video content – a point raised in submissions. • The RIA identifies risks of non -compliance with Option 3 but is not convincing that these risks will not a lso manifest for Option 2. The RIA could have assessed what factors might lead providers to comply and had an implementation plan for gaining compliance. Consulted • The RIA generally summarises and responds to the feedback from public consultation well. Consultation elicited many issues, and providers said they required more information before they could estimate the cost of options and the time required to implement them. Further, targeted, consultation would likely help, and ultimately result in sufficient analysis to inform Ministers’ decisions.

This information can be found in Appendix A: Approach to Working Through Expressions of Interest and Alternative Opportunities for Affected Kaimahi toward the back of this document. 9(2)(a) 61 Section Six: Change protocol Introduction This protocol sets out the approach to managing the implementation of the structural changes arising from the Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy Organisational Change. This Protocol is consistent with all individual employment agreements and the Collective Agreement (including the Section 8. Management of Change provisions) between the Public Service Association and the Department of Internal Affairs, which are available to view on 1840. Principles The process is designed to:  ensure a fair and transparent process;  maximise the placement of employees into available positions;  ensure minimum disruption to ‘business as usual’;  observe the provisions contained in the relevant employment agreements and organisational policy; and  minimise uncertainty for employees. Who does this protocol apply to? The protocol applies to all permanent employees of the department including:  permanent fulltime and part-time employees  employees currently on all forms of leave including leave without pay and parental leave. For employees currently seconded to other positions the process will apply to their permanent substantive position. Fixed term (temporary) or casual employees are not covered by this protocol even though their position may be affected by the restructure. In this case the relevant provision of their employment agreement will apply. Overview Employees are affected if their current position is being disestablished or changed significantly. If there is no significant change to their position, and there are the same number, or fewer, employees than positions in the new structure, employees will be reconfirmed. Employees who are not reconfirmed will be considered for reassignment. This involves considering whether affected employees’ skills can be matched to alternative positions that require similar skills in the new structure. Affected employees who are not reassigned will be consulted individually about other options. 62 If no other options are identified, notice will be given, and redundancy provisions apply. Affected employees Employees who have been identified as being affected by organisational change will be consulted over the implementation process, and the employees will have a preferential right of appointment to vacancies within the Branch. Before final decisions are announced, all potentially affected employees will be notified individually. Employees will be informed if they:  have been reconfirmed in a position and are no longer affected, or  are affected and will be considered for reassignment. Reconfirmation process Prior to announcement of the final decisions, an assessment will be made to determine if employees meet the criteria for reconfirmation. This assessment will be made by the General Manager or Director (Tier 3 leader) for the group, with support from Human Resources and approved by the Deputy Chief Executive, Toi Hiranga l Regulation and Policy. Reconfirmation is where an employee’s existing job is compared to jobs in the new structure to determine whether they are the same or nearly the same. The criteria for reconfirmation are:  the new job description is the same or nearly the same as the job the affected employee currently does  the salary band is the same  the terms and conditions, including career prospects are no less favourable  the location is the same or in the same vicinity.

Treaty settlements and engagement with iwi/Māori1 • I have instructed officials at the Department of Internal Affairs to engage with iwi to discuss the proposed amendments to the: o Waikato -Tainui Raupatu Claims (Waikato River) Settlement Act 2010; o Te Arawa River Iwi Waikato River Act 2010; and o Te Awa Tupua (Whanganui Claims Settlement) Act 2017. • The engagement follows advice the Department received from Te Arawhiti and Te Puni Kōkiri during the department consultation. • It is necessary to engage with iwi as the amendments will change Treaty Settlement Acts. Transitional arrangements for local authorities • The Repeal B ill contain s provisions to amend the Local Government Act s, specifically the Local Government Act 2002 to reinstate local authority ownership and responsibility for the delivery of water services, including the maintenance and upgrade of water assets. • The transitional provisions will allow local authorities to include water services in their 2024 -34 long -term plans and proposed charge s for water services to be collected through rates . This planning provision is currently prohibited beyond 1 July 2026 for most local authorities and prohibited for councils in Northland and Auckland Council beyond 1 July 2024. • By including transitional provisions, including a provision for a local authority to seek an Order in Council to defer setting their long -term plans until 2025, t he Repeal Bill provide s local authorities with much needed legislative certainty for their long -term plans, by providing an extension to the legislated adoption date of 30 June 2024. • The Repeal Bill also includes a clause to enable local authorities to delay the statutory review of bylaws that relate to water services. It has been necessary to include this transition clause as local authorities with water services bylaws excluded them from work programmes following the changes introduced by the water services legislation. • I am informed that with the imminent return of water services to local authorities, the current obligations set out in the Local Government Act 2002, without transitional arrangements will place undue pressure on local authorities. • The Repeal Bill will require all water services bylaws to be reviewed by 30 June 2026. • I gave offic ials at t he Department of Internal Affairs permission to undertak e limited engage ment with the sector experts to ensure the long -term plan provisions will help local authorities meet their statutory duties . • As a result of feedback from Taituar ā, drafting instructions have been issued to enable local authorities to continue with to implement policies where development contributions are linked to long -term plans.

Trust Framework for Digital Identity
Trust Framework legislation
Trust Framework parameters Use of the Trust Framework is opt -in; personal information will not be held in a centralised database Public consultation during Parliament’s consideration of the Digital Identify Services Trust Framework Bill in late 2021 highlighted some concern that the Trust Framework may be seeking to establish a mandatory and centralised identity regime. Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government 6 The proposed system will be decentralised with no new powers for the Government to collect or share people's information without their consent. One of the key obj ectives of the Trust Framework is to support and enable users to choose what information about themselves is being shared with third parties. Also, it will not be compulsory for people to use Trust Framework accredited digital identity services, or even t o use any digital identity services at all. To ensure access, people will still be able to apply for government services in -person using paper -based systems, providing physical credentials to show who they are. Operation of the Trust Framework will involve user -controlled data sharing The current lack of regulation in the provision of New Zealand’s digital identity services means individual services are often provided directly to an individual with varying levels of security depending on the strength of the service provider’s systems and processes. Access to, and sharing of, information is primarily controlled by the service, rather than the user. However, under the Trust Framework individuals will be able to access, claim, and share their own information th rough accredited digital identity services (identified by accreditation marks). This will occur as part of a standardised process to ensure personal identity data is handled securely and according to the users’ requests, as outlined in Figure 1 on page 8. Government services The Trust Framework will apply to Crown entities and government departments as well as iwi, private sector , and other non -government organisations that seek accreditation The Act and its associated rules and regulations will apply to C rown entities and government departments that choose to opt -in and deliver services under the Trust Framework , alongside iwi, private sector , and other non -government organisations . As Figure 1 below shows , in addition to being relying parties, some Crown entities and government departments may also seek accreditation to provide accredited services. For some, this may be limited to being an accredited information provider. For others, it could include choosing to provid e other accredited services as ‘’infrastructure providers.” Crown entities and government departments that wish to provide accredited services will need to meet the requirements specified in the Act, associated rules and regulations. For example, the identity verification service RealM e will continue to be provided by the Department of Internal Affairs . To be offered as an accredited service, however, the Department will need to meet the accreditation requirements. International Alignment In 2018, the Government committed to a programm e led by the Department to develop options for a new approach to digital identity. That programme investigated how the Government could set up the right rules and environment to take advantage of new technologies, offering a modern approach to meet the evo lving needs and expectations of New Zealanders in the digital identity landscape. Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government 7 Throughout 2019 and 2020, the Department undertook extensive research and engaged with key stakeholders, including equivalent agencies internationally. New Zealand is not the only country in the process of implementing legislation to modernise its digital identity system. The Trust Framework will align with similar trust frameworks being developed in Australia, Canada and the United Kingdom, and will be a key foundation in the Government’s commitment to achieving mutual recognition of digital identity services with Australia under the Single Economic Market agenda.3 Enabling Regulations The regulations will complement the technical and operational service -related requirements established in the Trust Framework rules that apply to TF providers and their delivery of accredited services. It is our intention that the regulations will provide a flexible way for Trust Framework processes to evolve over time as the digital identity sy stem matures and technology develops . The development of the rules and regulations will be informed by eight principles to ensure they are —people -centred; privacy enabling; security enhancing; enabling of Te Ao Māori approaches to identity; sustainable; interoperable; and open and transparent.4 Further Information Appendix A provides a glossary of key terms used in this paper. Trusted citizenship and identity documents contribute to sense of belonging Digital identity The Department is working with the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment, Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet, and Statistics NZ to develop a strategy to enable Aotearoa New Zealand to flourish and prosper in the digital world. This strategy is built around three themes: mahi ake (growth), mahi tahi (inclusion), and mahi tika (trust). Central to this is the work we are doing to progress the development of an approach to digital identity whereby people can have more control of their data, which is accessed with their consent. A regulatory regime that will accredit digital identity services against standards-based rules for security, privacy, identification management and interoperability will improve individual, private sector and government trust and confidence in the digital identity system. We will also support a new approach to guide government investments in digital identity technologies. Māori, iwi and hapu aspirations, interests and rights are understood and respected Supporting iwi, hapū and communities to lead their own development and manage their taonga as kaitiaki We strive to provide whānau, hapū and iwi with easy access to collections, taonga and mātauranga held by National Library and Archives New Zealand. We also intend to understand and respond to their aspirations for caring for their own mātauranga. This may include enabling taonga to stay in communities to allow iwi and Māori to carry out their roles as kaitiaki. Whānau, hapū and iwi have a desire to develop their own capability to ensure the future conservation and preservation of their taonga and mātauranga, in a way that is led and driven by them. We are working to establish internship opportunities that go beyond research to ofer skills growth and development experiences. We are also working to reduce barriers to access so that whānau, hapū and iwi can actively work with their taonga and mātauranga. This includes developing a Māori-led academic ofering on conservation and preservation of taonga. Iwi and hapū can access whakapapa information The Department will work with iwi to understand their needs and expectations for collecting, storing and sharing iwi afiliation information, and are actively considering options that would provide the ability for Māori to self-assert whakapapa when registering a birth. If the Department were able to collect whakapapa data as part of birth registration, people could formally assert their iwi and hapū afiliations, and iwi and Māori authorities could have access to that self-assertion data for their own purposes. This will support the Department in contributing to an improved Māori-Crown relationship by contributing to the recognition of data sovereignty and considering better ways to support iwi afiliation. 23 Department of Internal Affairs NGĀ TAKUNE RAUTAKI STRATEGIC INTENTIONS 2021-2025 Engagement with Māori on digital and technology Māori participation in the digital and technology sector is critically low. Tō Tātou Mōhiohio me Matihiko – Improving our systems to enable seamless, simple and fit for purpose services The Department continues to invest in delivering digitally enabled services that meet the expectations and needs of New Zealanders, at the same time as maintaining and modernising our existing digital assets. We are addressing these challenges through cloud computing and “as a service” solutions that improve our agility, consolidating the overall number of applications we have and applying iterative delivery and customer-centred design approaches. The next four years will focus on shifing to native cloud digital platforms to provide the digital foundations for our future services. Key investments in service delivery areas will be leveraging customer relationship management, data and analytics, and system integration capability. These will be supported by continuing investment in cloud-based collaboration and corporate systems to enable internal productivity and flexibility. We will also continue the momentum of the Te Hāpai O programme, which was initiated in 2019/20. Te Hāpai O will secure better tools to provide joined up, transparent, fit-for-purpose services and enable our people to deliver great outcomes for Aotearoa. This includes continuing the implementation of our new finance system, Rehutai, which will extend the strategic finance functionality to support human resource and recruitment management, and also replace the Department’s payroll system. Te Ara Vaka strategy implementation The successful implementation of the Te Ara Vaka strategy across the Department will ensure the inclusion of Pasifika perspectives by design and the creation of safe spaces to talanoa about Aotearoa’s Pasifika history. It will strengthen our workforce, with greater Pasifika representation in senior leadership roles (tiers 1-4), with equal pay across the sector, and the recognition of cultural capability as a specialised skillset. The continued investment in the Te Ara Vaka strategy will make it easier for our Pasifika customers to use our services and support the Department to build stronger communities enabling them to be resilient, thriving and self-suficient. Investment and asset performance Our assets support our ability to delivery successfully against our strategic intentions. The Long-Term Investment Plan 2019-2029 has set out our commitment and direction for investment and asset management. It defines the principles that underpin our investment and asset management practices. This has informed the four-year capital plan, which is a rolling plan of our capital intentions that is updated twice a year. The Department plans to review and renew the Long-Term Investment Plan within the next 12 months. The four-year capital plan is focused on keeping existing systems and infrastructure working well. The Department has little capacity for further transformative investment at the present time and will have to prioritise carefully to make best use of existing resources. Opportunities, and the risks that come with them, can ofen require trade-ofs, while continuing to maintain core services to New Zealanders. To maximse our coverage and impact we need the right information, technology and systems to enable our people to work in an integrated and flexible way. Technology plays an important role in connecting our people, enabling us to operate as one connected organisation across our work locations. Tō Tātou Rōpū – improving our workplace environments Te Tari Taiwhenua owns 11 buildings across Aotearoa in Auckland, Taupō, Whanganui, Wellington, Christchurch and Dunedin. These include Archival and Library facilities, a Harbourmaster site and two properties that are used as ministerial residences. We will continue delivery of a four-year, $60 million programme following long-term under-investment in these owned buildings. Several buildings, assets and components have reached or passed their useful physical and/or economic life. The programme responds to a recognised significant risk to service delivery and the health and safety of our people. We will also establish a workplace and occupancy strategy to accommodate the growth and changing needs of our rōpū across Te Tari Taiwhenua. This will be achieved by establishing a working group, consulting with the wider organisation, and providing and implementing occupancy strategy recommendations. Tō Tātou Rōpū – environmental sustainability at DIA We are supporting the directive of the Carbon Neutral Government Programme to achieve carbon neutrality by 2025 with the establishment of an in-house sustainability programme. With the help of an external specialist we will capture, analyse and report our emissions data, establishing a baseline reading. We will then set our emissions reduction targets for the next four years and develop a plan to achieve these targets. The programme will identify ways to reduce our consumption of energy and fuel across all areas of the organisation. We will communicate these findings and engage with groups across the Department to implement a strategy to reduce carbon emissions. The programme is being supported by energy eficient upgrades to our owned buildings as part of the Forward Works Programme. This includes initiatives such as replacing fluorescent bulbs with LED lighting, and upgrading HVAC and lif systems to lower-energy usage models. To reduce CO2 emissions from our vehicle fleet we are developing a transition plan for the move to electric vehicles, including installing charging infrastructure at relevant sites, as well as looking at optimising our fleet size. This will be achieved through a system replacement and a focus on changing our culture and people’s behaviours. This three-year project will enable staf to apply good information management practices irrespective of where they work or what business tools and systems they use. This paper seeks authorisation to submit the Fire and Emergency New Zealand (Fire Safety, Evacuation Procedures, and Evacuation Schemes) Amendment Regulations 2021 (the Amendment Regulations ) (Appendix A ) to the Executive Council . Executive Summary 2. Stand ards New Zealand has published the New Zealand Standard for Automatic Fire Sprinkler Systems, NZS 4541:2020 (the updated sprinkler standard), which provides the rules for design ing, install ing, and maint aining automatic sprinkler systems. 3. The updated sprinkler standard does not include a requirement for hand operated fire - fighting equipment to be installed, which is an important part of fire safety equipment, when automatic sprinklers are present in a building . 4. The proposed regulations will: 4.1 add the updated sprinkler standard, to the Fire and Emergency New Zealand (Fire Safety, Evacuation Procedures, and Evacuation Schemes) Regulations 2018 (Fire Safety Regulations) ; and 4.2 require hand operated fire -fighting equipment that is compliant with the New Zealand Standard for Hand Operated Fire -fighting Equipment, NZS 4541:2020, to be installed in buildings where the automatic sprinkler system complies with the updated sprinkler standard. 5. The proposed changes ensure the minimum levels of fire safety currently required by the Fire Safety Regulations are maintained and apply to new or altered buildings . 6. The vast majority of buildings are unaffected by these changes. Building code requirements and existing evacuation schemes are also unaffected. Fire Safety Regulations need to be updated 7. The Fire Safety Regulations prescribe the minimum requirements for an automatic sprinkler system1 installed in a relevant building2. The Fire Safety Regulations require an automatic sprinkler system to comply with one of the listed New Zealand Standards for Automatic Sprinkler Systems, when it is installed. 1 An automatic sprinkler system is a fire -suppression or fire -control device that activate s when the air reaches a certain temperature. 2 The definition of ‘relevant building’ captures buildings that present comparatively greater risk to occupants in the event of fire, than buildings used for other purposes 45p64zrr3b 2021-07-06 12:56:01Document 1 Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 2 of 8 The Fire Safety Regulations should include a reference to the updated sprinkler standard 8. On 6 May 2020, Standards New Zealand published the updated sprinkler standard , which provides an integrated set of rules for the design, installation, and maintenance of automatic sprinkler systems, so these systems protect against the loss of life andminimise property damage from fire. The updated sprinkler standard is no t currently listed in the Fire Safety Regulations. 9. Adding a reference in the Fire Safety Regulations to the updated sprinkler standard will ensure that buildings with automatic sprinkler systems installed to the specifications inthe updated sprinkler standard are included in the Fire and Emergency New Zealand (Fire and Emergency) regulatory regime. The updated sprinkler standard does not require hand operated fire -fighting equipment to be installed ; the Fire Safety Regulations shoul d require this 10. Hand operated fire -fighting e quipment , such as fire extinguishers, fire hoses and fire blankets , supplement the components of sprinkler systems that are a fixed part of the building and fill the performance gaps where sprinklers may fall short. 11. The updated spr inkler standard removed requirements for hand operated fire -fighting equipment to be installed . This means b uildings constructed or upgraded to the updated sprinkler standard may not have the same level of fire protection as buildings constructed to an ear lier version of this Standard. 12. Standards New Zealand acknowledge that hand operated fire-fighting equipment is an important feature in buildings but decided that it was out of place in the automatic sprinkler standard . Instead, the New Zealand Standard for Hand Operated Fire -Fighting Equipment, NZS 4503:2005, should be cited for this type of equipment. Consequently, the updated sprinkler standard does not require hand operated fire -fighting equipment to be installed. 13. Where an automatic sprinkler system complies with the updated sprinkler standard, there should be a requirement for hand operated fire -fighting equipment to be installed . This will maintain the current minimum fire safety requirements in all relevant buildings with automatic sprinkler systems (old and new ). Further information on when the fire safety regime requires building owners to install an automatic sprinkler system and hand operated fire -fighting equipment is provided in Appendix B . Building Code requirements and existing evacuation schemes are not affected by these changes 14. These changes will not affect obligations and exemptions relating to automatic sprinkler systems and hand operated fire -fighting equipment under the Building Code. Existing relevant buildings that already have an approved evacuation scheme will notbe affected by these change s. Fire Safety Regulations should include the updated sprinkler standard and require hand operated fire -fighting equipment be installed 15. I recommend that regulation 24 of the Fire Safety Regulations is amended to : 15.1 refer to the updated sprinkler standard. This will ensure that automatic sprinkler systems installed to this updated Standard are included in the Fire and Emergency regulatory regime. 45p64zrr3b 2021-07-06 12:56:01 Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 3 of 8 15.2 include a requirement that where the automatic sprinkler system complies with the updated sprinkler standard, hand operated fire -fighting equipment must be installed . The amendments to the Fire and Emergency New Zealand (Fire Safety, Evacuation Procedures, and Evacuation Schemes) Regulations 2018 will be publicly notified in the Gazette on 17 June 2021. Relation to government priorities 2 This relates to the Government’s priorities from the Prime Minister’s Statement of “providing strong and responsible leadership as we rebuild from Cyclone Gabrielle”. The Government intends to announce the establishment of a charitable trust... 3 Cyclone Gabrielle, along with other recent extreme weather events at the start of 2023, has ca used significant damage to many communities. Millions of dollars have already been donated to a wide range of organisations working on the immediate response to Cyclone Gabrielle recovery. 4 The Government can complement existing donation appeals by establishing a charit able trust called the Cyclone Gabrielle Appeal Trust. The Trust will manage the Cyclone Gabrielle Appeal Fund and make decisions on how donations to the Fund will be distributed. One of the benefits of the Trust is that it will be able to proactively seek out and manage overseas, philanthropic, and corporate donations, which can often come with ‘strings attached’ (for example the donation must go to a certain project or outcome) that more locally-oriented fundraisers may struggle to accommodate. There is also an opportunity to orient the Fund towards medium-term recovery needs, to complement the sterling work of the Red Cross, mayoral relief funds and large corporate partners such as Stuff and NZME – along with many more local fundraisers – in raising money to deal with the immediate response phase. 5 Establishing the Trust will help with ensuring that donation money goes to the areas hardest hit by Cyclone Gabrielle. Money collected by mayoral relief funds and regional community trusts will likely only be able to used in that region, and more populated, wealthier regions will be in a better position to raise money. If the Government appoints trustees and advisors tasked with taking a broader and needs-based view of recovery, it can ensure that donation money is more equitably matched to need. 1 UNCLASSIFIED 6ihp9o9dtn 2023-04-14 15:09:38 Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs

Recommendation 1: Commenc ing the self -identification provisions 12 mon ths after enactment , but allow an Order -in-Council to change the date 13. A Bill is enacted (becomes an Act) when it has passed through all the Parliamentary stages and has received Royal assent (given by the Governor -General) . The term commencement refers to the date provisions in the Act take effect . Commencement dates can be set for an entire Act, or for specific sections . 14. The Bill is currently drafted to commence the day after it receives Royal assent. This is often the default decision if there are no specific reasons for delaying commencement. 15. We recommend commencing the self-identification provisions 12 months after the Bill receives Royal assent , but also provide that the commencement date can be change d by Order -in-Council. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 4 of 8 Rationale for delaying co mmencement of the self -identification provisions We are confident the technical updates could be implemented within 12 months… 16. Delayed commencement would provide the necessary time to update our IT systems. We need to update the IT system that records birt h registration details, and all the downstream systems we operate that receive, verify or share birth registration information. The proposed timeframe allows for careful scoping to capture all the necessary changes across our systems , and ensures the vendor that we engage with to maintain our systems can resource the work to make the changes. We estimate that these updates would take up to 12 months to complete. …but we are less certain about timeframes for implementing regulations, so w e recommend including the option of seeking an Order -in-Council 17. A delay will also enable us to develop necessary regulations for the self -identification provisions. This includes taking time to consult on key issues, including: 17.1 which sex markers other than the binary will be available; 17.2 who would be authorised to provide a letter supporting applications for children and young people ; and 17.3 additional requirements where a person applies to amend their registered sex more than once. 18. Given the complexity and sensitivity of this work, there is a risk that developing the regulations may not be complete d within 12 months of enacting the Bill. Including the option of changing the commencement date by an Order -in-Council would allow more time if its needed . Transgender and intersex communities might be disappointed in the delay, but the extra time is needed and gives them more opportunity to contribute to the regulations 19. Some transgender and intersex advocates might be disappointed by the delay, especially given the delays in progressing the Bill. However, this delay is necessary to introduce a self -identification process. We can provide messaging about the reasons for the delays , including your commitment to consult on the necessary regulations with these communities. Recommendation 2: Retain records of previous amendment s to registered sex 20. When a person amend s their registered sex, the Births, Deaths, Marriages, and Relationships Registration Act 1995 (the BDMRR Act) restricts access to search for that person’s previously registered sex on their birth record. The Bill carries these restrictions forward (with some alterations) in clauses 110 , 112 and 116 . 21. The restrictions are intended to protect people’s privacy, preventing them from b eing ‘outed’ as transgender or intersex. The limited conditions where information can be shared includ e measures to protect against the misuse of birth certificates to create multiple identities . Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 5 of 8 22. Clause 22F of the Bill provides a different policy for when people amend their registered sex back to what was recorded at birth. Instead of restricting access, this provision requires the Registrar -General to delete the record of the initial amendment to the registered sex. In effect, the person’s birth record wo uld look like it had not been amended since birth. 23. We disagree with th e approach in clause 22F . We recommend keeping the record s of all amendments to registered sex on the birth re cord , but restrict ing access in line with clauses 110 , 112 and 116 . Rational e for retaining the records of previous amendment s 24. Deleting records of any amendment to registered sex could make it more difficult to detect when people are using birth certificates to create multiple identities. Someone could have a birth certificate derived from a record that has been deleted . Government agencies , including law enforcement agencies, would not be able to see whether people had used the birth records to create alternate identities . 25. We do not think this would create a privacy concern. Information about previous amendments to registered sex would be restricted. 26. In general, the registers should accurately reflect changes over time, with privacy risks addressed by managing access to the records. This is the approach to adoption records, an d records of people who are under witness protection – both of which have very significant privacy interests . Recommendation 3: Clarifying that a birth certificate is not conclusive evidence of a person’s sex 27. Section 33 of the BDMRR Act provides that a per son’s sex should be determined by reference to the “general law of New Zealand.” The Select Committee recommended retain ing this provision in clause 22I of the Bill. 28. We interpret this provision to mean that birth certificates should not be considered conc lusive evidence of a person’s sex. We recommend re -drafting clause 22I to clarify this meaning . We would remov e the reference to the “general law of New Zealand ”, and instead indicat e that: 28.1 birth certificates should not be the determining factor in decisions about a person’s sex ; and 28.2 consideration should be given to other legislation and the common law. 29. Should you agree , we will work with PCO to develop how this provision is worded. Rationale for redrafting clause 22I 30. Crown Law previously advised that it is unclear what determining sex by the “general law of New Zealand” entails . Crown Law also noted that the drafting of clause 22I makes it unclear whether the policy intent is to “maintain the distinction between sex recorded on a birth certificate and sex for other purposes ”. (i.e. whether it is intended that information on birth certificates should be conclusive evidence of a person’s sex ). Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 6 of 8 31. As discussed with you previously, we recommend maintaining the existing position that birth certificates should not provide conclusive evidence of a person’s sex . This was set out in the Cabinet paper, Introducing a self -identification process to recognise gender on birth certificates .3 The proposed redraft would clarify this position. 32. We are working with Corrections on a n amendment to th e relevant regulation s before the self-identification process commences . Clarifying the provision could help mitigate some stakeholder concerns with a self - identification process 33. Re-drafting the provision will make the legislation more accessible and help people understand that birth certificates should not be the basis for determining a person’s sex. The legislation would provide clarity for organisation s about not rely ing on birth certificates to determin e a person’s access to women -only places or services . This provides assurance that t here is little risk of information on birth certificates allow ing men to access women -only places or services . 34. Some stakeholders may think we should go a step further and adopt Crown Law’s advice that statutory guidance about how sex is de termined could be beneficial (for example, what factors should be considered to determine a person’s sex). As previously advised4, developing statutory guidance for how sex should be determined generally would be broader in scope than the BDMRR Act and the Internal Affairs portfolio. It would require a cross -agency initiative as processes for determining sex are in place across numerous institutions. Recommendation 4: Clarifying that, where a person has amende d their registered sex and their name, their previous name will not appear on the birth certificate 35. Under regulations , where a person changes their name, the previous name would be printed on their birth certificate. Section 64(1)(a) of the BDMRR Act and claus e 84(3) of the Bill provide an exception to this rule : where a person has amended their registered sex, their previous name is not included on the birth certificate. This helps to avoid outing a person as transgender or intersex .5 36. However, t he way the rele vant provision is drafted in the Bill requires clarification. The Human Rights Commission advised that the provision is not entirely clear and risked misinterpretation – they recommended drafting a more explicit provision . 3 See paragraph 8 of the Cabinet paper. 4 See paragraph 37 of IA202100068 – Next steps for progressing the Births, Deaths, Marriages, and Relationships Registration Bill . 5 E.g, if a person whose name was ‘Gary’ amended their registered sex from ‘male’ to ‘female’, and changed their name to ‘Audrey’, the fact they used to be called ‘Gary’ would be omitted. I seek Cabinet’s agreement to introduce a self -identification process to enable a person’s gender to be recognised on their birth certificate . I intend to introduce th e self-identification process through the Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Bill. Executive summary 2. Since 1995 people have been able to amend their sex on their birth certificate. The process requires provid ing evidence of medical treatment to a Family Court judge who determines if an amendment to the birth register, and subsequently a birth certificate, can be made. 3. This process was considered progressive 26 years ago but is now in need of improvement. It is not inclusive and fails to support people’s autonomy over how their gender is recognised . The Family Court process medicalises a deeply personal expression of self -identity and is perceived as inaccessible for many people. 4. There is an opportunity to replace the Family Court process through the Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Regis tration Bill (the Bill) . The Select Committee that consider ed the Bill proposed a new process where people would complete a statutory declaration to have their gender recognised on their birth certificate – a self - identification process. 5. Changing to a se lf-identification process will give transgender1 and intersex2 New Zealanders greater control over how their gender is officially recognised . It will enable transgender and intersex New Zealanders to use their birth certificate to access services (such as setting up a bank account or enrolling a child in school) with less risk of being ‘outed’ or experiencing discrimination. It will help contribute to transgender and intersex people’s wellbeing and sense of belonging . 6. This paper seeks agreement to introduce a self -identification process . It also proposes changes to the Bill to ensure self-identification will reflect the needs of transgender and intersex communities as much as possible. This includes, for example, making self - identification available to child ren and young people as well as adults. 7. These changes will be reflected in a supplementary order paper (SOP). I intend to refer this SOP to Select Committee to provide an opportunity for the public to engage on the self-identification process . 1 The ter m ‘transgender’ is used in this paper to refer to all people whose gender differs from their assigned sex at birth – this includes people who identify outside of the male/female binary who may use a range of terms to describe their gender including “non -binary”. 2 ‘Intersex’ is an umbrella term for people born with a variation of sex characteristics (such as sexual anatomy, reproductive organs, hormonal and/or chromosome patterns). Intersex people are born with sex characteristics that are more diverse than narrow medical definitions of male or female bodies. Like anyone else, an intersex person may grow to identify with a different gender. Document 2 Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 2 of 21 8. I am not pro posing any changes to how sex is registered at birth. Gender is not known at birth and the information collected will continue to be based on sex. My proposals relate to amending how gender is recognised on birth certificates only. I am not proposing chang es to how other agencies and organisations determine a person’s sex or gender , if that is necessary . I intend to maintain the policy position that birth certificates do not provide conclusive evidence of a person’s sex or gender . Background Sex and gender are different 9. Gender is distinct from sex . Gender refers to a person’s social and personal identity as a male, female, or another gender . Sex refers to a person’s physiological features that characterise people as male , female or intersex . A person’s gender is not always the same as their sex . 10. Society is changing to recognise the difference between sex and gender and that a person’s gender may not be the same as their sex. In line with this shift, there is an increasing expectation that the Government should enable people to declare their gender on their official docum entation . Amending registered sex is a way fo r people to have their gender officially recognised 11. A person’s s ex is re gistered at birth. Since 1995 people have been able to amend their registered sex, which is printed on their birth certificate , under the Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Act ( BDMRR Act ). 12. Under the current process, applicants need to provide evidence of medical treatment , which is then assessed by a Family Court judge who determines if the amendment can be made. While this process is about amending sex information, its existence recognises that a person’s gender can be different to their sex. It is a mechanism for people to have th eir gender recognised. My proposal to introduce a self -identification process for amending registered sex will make much needed improvements to this process. 13. I am aware that using a sex marker to represent gender conflates sex and gender . This is a compr omise I support to ensure there are no further delays to implementing a self - identification process. Creating a separate gender marker on birth certificates has wider cost and timing implications for data collection and IT systems changes across government . In addition, the presentation of both sex and gender on birth certificates raises issues associated with outing a person as transgender or intersex. Improvements to the process to amend registered sex have previously been considered 14. The Bill was introduc ed in 2017 to re -enact the BDMRR Act to modernise its drafting, and enable people to search online for birth, death and marriage records. The Select Committee considering the Bill recommended new provisions to replace the process for amending registered se x in 2018 . They proposed a process where people completed a statutory declaration to have their gender recognised on their birth certificate – a self -identification process. 15. The Bill was then deferred in February 2019 and is awaiting its second reading. In announcing their decision to defer the Bill, the previous Minister of Internal Affairs cited concern that the public had not been consulted on the self -identification provision s. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs IN-CONFIDENCE Page 3 of 21 Introducing a self -identification process through the Bill 16. I intend to re sume progress on the Bill and to enact it this year if possible with a self - identification process to recognise gender on birth certificates . Cabinet did not approve the introduction of a self -identification process following Select Committee in 2018. I wa nt to carry forward the Select Committee’s recommendation and am now seeking Cabinet agreement to the self -identification provisions. 17. I would also like to make changes to the self -identification provisions as they are drafted, to ensure they reflect the ne eds of the transgender and intersex communities. These changes will be reflected in a SOP. I intend to refer this SOP to Select Committee at the Bill’s second reading to provide an opportunity for the public to share their views on the self -identification provisions. 18. I am not proposing any changes to how sex is registered at birth.3 Gender is not known at birth and the information collected will continue to be based on sex. 19. My proposals relate to amending how gender is recognised on birth certificates only . I am not proposing changes to how other agencies and organisations determine a person’s sex or gender. Under the BDMRR Act, birth certificates are not intended to provide conclusive evidence of someone’s sex or gender.4 I intend to maintain this policy position. There is a strong case for introducing a self -identification process The Family Court process to amend registered sex in the BDMRR Act needs reform 20. The Family Court proce ss to amend registered sex is not inclusive and fails to support people’s au tonomy over how their gender is recognised . It medicalises a deeply personal expression of self -identity and is inaccessible 21. The process medicalises a deeply personal expression of self -identity and is out of step with gender being about how a person perceives themselves. The process requires applicants to provide evidence they have undertaken medical treatment to physically conform with the sex they want recorded . The medical evidence is assessed by a Family Court judge who decides wheth er the application should be supported. 22. The medical evidence requirement excludes those who cannot or choose not to undertake medical treatment. For children and young people , the requirement could be seen to encourage medical treatment at a young age. This process was considered progressive in 1995 but is now seen as outdated and inconsistent with global developments. 23. The Family Court process is perceived to be costly , intimidating and difficult to navigate , making it inaccessible for many people . Countin g Ourselves , a 2019 survey of transgender and non -binary people in New Zealand, found that 83 per cent of respondents “did not have the correct gender marker on their birth certificate. ” This is also reflected by the low number of applications to the Family Court to amend registered sex .

Background 4. On 4 March 2023, you agreed to adjust two key settings of the Scheme for the 2023-24 rating year: the income abatement threshold and the maximum rebate paid. The adjustments reflect the increase in inflation of 7.2 percent in the All Groups Index of the Consumers Price Index for the year ended 31 December 2022 by: 4.1 increasing the maximum rebate from $700 to $750; and 4.2 increasing the income abatement threshold from $28,080 to $30,100. 5. The Cabinet agreement to the adjustment is subject to the Budget Moratorium 2023. The Moratorium started on 11 April 2023 and will end on 18 May 2023, when the Minister of Finance announces the Budget for 2023. The adjustment cannot be agreed by Cabinet between these dates. 6. You previously agreed to proceed to the Cabinet Legislation Committee (LEG), to seek approval of an Order in Council which adjusts the two key settings of the Scheme. The Parliamentary Counsel Office has drafted the Order in Council which is provided within Appendix A. Comment No issues were raised during consultation on the Cabinet paper 7. Gerra rd Carter Commit tee Secretary Present: (see over) 40x4x3jx48 2021-07-14 13:07:53 I N C O N F I D E N C E 1 Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government I N C O N F I D E N C E Present: Officials present from: Hon Andrew Little (Chair) Offi ce of the Prime Minister Hon David Parker Officials Committee for LEG Hon Nanaia Mahuta Hon Kris Faafoi LEG-21-MIN-0080 40x4x3jx48 2021-07-14 13:07:53 I N C O N F I D E N C E 2 Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN-CONFIDENCE Ofce of the Minister of Local Government Chair Cabinet Legislaton Commitee Rates Rebate (Specifed Amounts) Order 2021 Proposal 1. I propose that the Commitee authorise the submission of the Rates Rebate (Specifed Amount s) Order 2021 (the Order) ( Appendix A ) to the Executve Council. Policy 2. The Order prescribes an amendment to secton 3(1) of the Rates Rebate Act 1973 (the Act) to increase the maximum rebate and the income abatement threshold of the Rates Rebate Scheme (the Scheme) from 1 July 2021. 3. The Order increases: 3.1. the maximum annual rebate from $655 to $665; and 3.2. the income abatement threshold from $26,150 to $26,510 per annum. 4. These changes refect the 1.4 per cent movement of the Consumer Price Index (CPI) All Groups Index for the 2020 calendar year. Background The Scheme assists low-income ratepayers to meet the cost of rates 5. The Scheme was introduced by the Act. The amount of rebate provided to a household is det ermined by a formula based on total household income, level of rates, and the number of household dependents. 6. To be eligible for a rebate, the applicant must be usually resident at, and the ratepayer for, the property for which the rebate is being claimed. 7. Eligibility for a rebate is based on income for the previous tax year. Applicatons to the Sche m e for the 2021-22 ratng year will be based on income earned in the year up to 31 March 2021. 8. The Scheme is administered by territorial authorites and the Department of Internal Afair s (the Department). Territorial authorites accept and process applicatons to the Scheme and provide the rebate to recipients. The Department reimburses territorial authorites for the cost of rebates. The Act allows changes to the Scheme’s key setngs 40x4x3jx48 2021-07-14 13:06:44 Proactively released by the Minister of Local Government IN-CONFIDENCE 9. Secton 3(1) of the Act states the maximum rebate and the income abatement threshold. Secton 3(2) of the Act enables the maximum rebate and the income abatement threshold to be amended by way of Order in Council. 10.In 2008, the Government agreed that the maximum rebate and income abatement thre shold of the Scheme would be increased by Order in Council on 1 July each year. The amount of the increase would refect the upward movement of the CPI for the previous calendar year [Cab Min (08) 14/1(32) refers]. Uptake and forecast costs (excluding GST) of the Scheme 11.The cu r rent appropriaton for the Scheme is based on forecasts that include projected annual price and volume changes as a result of adjustng the maximum rebate and income threshold for infaton. 12.The total cost of the Scheme for 2019-20, the most recently completed fnancial year, was $50.7 million. For 2020-2021 the Department expects to receive $52.4 million worth of claims. 13.For 2021-22, the estmated uptake for the Scheme is $54.3 million. This estmate is abov e the current appropriaton of $53.5 million. It is difcult to predict the impact that the COVID-19 lockdown and recovery period will have on the uptake of the Scheme, so the Department will monitor the appropriaton through 2021-22. 14.If a change to the appropriaton is required over the 2021-22 fnancial year, this will be made through the October 2021 or March 2022 Budget baseline update processes in consultaton with the Minister of Finance [MCT-19MIN-0038 refers].
