UNCLASSIFIED Background 7. OFLC regulates the classification system and manages restricted content. Under the Classification Act, OFLC’s functions are: 7.1 to classify publications such as computer files, films and books; 7.2 to conduct research into the impacts of the media content regulatory regime; and 7.3 provide information about classification, the Classification Act, and how OFLC operates . Snapshot of OFLC’s financial positio n and outlook 8. 2019 [CAB-19-MIN-0498 refers ]; and 0445 refers ]. OFLC’s revenue sources comprise a Crown appropriation , third -party fees , and a small amount of interest income. OFLC has recorded deficits since 2009. Prior to 2019/20 , deficits were met from cash reserves built up in previous years. The deficits are attributed to the decline of the physical media industry3, outdated third -party fee levels , and until 2019/20 a static Crown appropriation. 9. OFLC’s existing third -party fee levels have not been re viewed since 1996 and are no longer fit -for-purpose . Over the last ten years, OFLC’s third -party income has reduced by 55 percent due to the decreasing DVD market . There is now a small DVD and physical media market that will only generate limited income. In 2018/19, OFLC received $0.496 million (19 percent) of its total revenue from third -party fees. 10. Cabinet has recently agreed the following additional funding for OFLC: • one-off funding for 2019/20 of $0.765 million to support OFLC’s operating and minor capital expenditure [ CAB-19-MIN-0174.21 refers ]; • $0.674 million in 2019/20, and increasing the baseline appropriation from $1.960 million to $2.428 million from 2020/21 onwards , to respond to increased demand for its servi ces following the Christchurch t error attacks on 15 March • up to $0.600 million for 2019/20 for OFLC to develop a self -rating system for CVoD providers to self -classify content available on their platforms [CAB -19-MIN- 11. During 2017/18 , OFLC restructured its personnel to focus more on education and information activities . OFLC is operating at a lean level to meet its statutory functions. The media content regulatory regime is changing 12. There is a gap in the legislative framework that does not require CVoD content to be classified/rated before it is screened in New Zealand . The Classification Act is being extended through the Films, Videos, Publications and Classification (CVoD) Amendment Bill (the CVoD Amendment Bill) to regulate CVoD content . The CVoD Amendment Bill wil l require the classification /rating and display of online labels (G, PG, M, R16, R18) for online content prior to its screening in New Zealand . 3 Films for cinematic release, DVDs and some games . UNCLASSIFIED Context 6. Over the past two and a half years, the Minister of Local Government has been leading a cross -government review of the system for regulating and managing drinking water, wastewater and stormwat er (the Three Waters Review). A group of Three Waters Ministers1 has met regularly to discuss and provide input into this work. A large group of agencies, led and coordinated by the Department of Internal Affairs, have provided advice to these Ministers. 7. Cabinet has considered, and made a series of decisions on, a series of papers relating to the Three Waters Review: 7.1 Review of three waters infrastructure: key findings and next steps (April 2018). 7.2 Future state of the three waters system: regulation and service delivery (November 2018). 7.3 A Plan for Three Waters Reform (July 2019). 7.4 Strengthening the regulation of drinking water, wastewater and stormwater (July 2019) – supported by a Regulatory Impact A ssessme nt. 7.5 Institutional arrangements for a drinking water regulator (September 2019) – supported by a Regulatory Impact A ssessment and business case . 7.6 Three waters service delivery and funding arrangements: approach to reform (January 2020). 8. The current paper , Investing in water infrastructure to accelerate reform and support economic recovery post COVID -19 (May 2020) , builds on and is informed by previous decisions made by Cabinet, as well as d iscussions with Three Waters Ministers about service delivery reform and infrastructure investment , and stakeholder engagement . The key decisions that are relevant to the current paper are outlined in this document . There has been no indication that these decisions need to be reconsidered. Problem definition 9. The problem definition is well established in previous Cabinet papers , regulatory impact analyses, and briefing material . Several of the Cabinet papers explored the problems and challenges facing the three waters system in considerable detail. The Regulatory Impact A ssessment , Strengthening the regulation of drinking water, wastewater and stormwater (July 2019) , also included an o verview of the key problems . 10. Some of these problems are already being addressed through significant legislative changes to the drinking wate r regulatory framework, and the creation of a new Water Services Regulator – Taumata Arowai. The proposed programme of reforms to the service delivery system is intended to address many of the other problems, as well as supporting the long -term effectiven ess and efficiency of Taumata Arowai and the new drinking water regulatory framework. 1 Three Waters Ministers include the Ministers of/for: Local Government; Health; Environment; Infrastructure; Rural Communities; Conservation; Climate Change; Commerce and Consumer Affairs; and Urban Development . The shortfall will need to be funded by the Crown, the sector , or a mix of both . 20. Cost-recovery from the sector is not sought for the following: • costs arising from classifications for the Crown’s enforcement activities ; • OFLC’s information service, including a portion of the research costs ; • a portion of costs arising fr om the classification of material for cultural purposes, and for special interest groups and charitable trusts ; and • the costs of OFLC responding to increased demands for its services following the Christchurch terror attacks. 21. The New Zealand community is the principal beneficiary of these activities, and I consider that the costs involved (approximately $ 2.328 million from 2020/21 ) should continue to be met by the Crown. 22. Cost-recovery from the sector , the Crown or from both are appropriate option s for the following: • costs arising from commercial classifications ; • a portion of OFLC’s research costs ; and • a portion of costs arising from the classification of material for cultural purposes, and for special interest groups and charitable trusts . 23. These activities will incur estimated costs to OFLC of $1. 2 million in 2020/21 . Consultation approach 24. A public consultation is planned from 13 December 2019 to 2 February 2020 . The Department is available to meet with stakeholders if request ed. Options in the public consultation document 25. The public consultation document is organised into two parts. Part 1 outlines the current classification system, OFLC’s operating environment , and provides estimates of the costs to operate the classification system. Part 2 p rovides options for cost -recovery and funding mechanisms. Part 2 also includes potential financial implications for cost - recovery from the sector set at different levels. Principles for assessing the cost -recovery options and mechanisms have been develope d using the Treasury’s Guidelines for Setting Charges in the Public Sector and the Controller and Auditor General’s advice Charging Fees for Public Sector Goods and Services ,and are included as Part 2 of the consultation document. 26. Cost-recovery options: full, partial or no cost -recovery 27. Through th e planned consultation , I am looking for feedback on an appropriate level of cost-recovery from the sector . The current approach to funding classification decisions was established in 199 6. It i nvolves the Crown and submitters sharing the costs. There is no agreed basis for how the costs are shared between the Crown and submitters . Page 4 of 9

Films, Videos, and Publications Classification (Commercial Video on Demand) Amendment Bill: Approval for Introduction Portfolio Internal Affairs Purpose This paper seeks approval for the introduction of the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification (Commercial Video on-Demand) Amendment Bill (the Bill). Previous ConsiderationOn 2 September 2019, Cabinet agreed to amend the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification Act 1993 (the Act) to incorporate Commercial Video on-Demand (CVoD) into New Zealand’s media classification regime. [CAB-19-MIN-0445] Summary The purpose of the Bill is to address a regulatory gap where CVoD content is not currently subject to mandatory classification requirements prior to being made available in New Zealand. The Bill will enable CVoD content to be rated and labelled in the same way that films are already regulated under the Act. Regulated CVoD providers will be required to label content by: self-rating content using their own systems that have been approved by the Office of Film and Literature Classification (the Classification Office); self-rating content using the Classification Office’s online tool and resources; or submitting content to the Film and Video Labelling Body (the Labelling Body) for rating and labelling, with certain content to be referred to the Classification Office for classification where appropriate. UNCLASSIFIED Office of the Minister for the Community and Voluntary Sector Cabinet Social Outcomes Committee Policy proposals for regulations to enable appeals to the Taxation and Charities Review Authority Proposal 1 I am seeking Cabinet agreement to policy proposals for regulations for appeals under the Charities Act 2005. Relation to government priorities 2 This is a matter that requires Cabinet approval now to ensure necessary regulations are in pl ace for when the Taxation and Charities Review Authority start s hearing charities appeals on 5 July 2024 . Executive Summary 3 This paper seeks Cabinet agreement to policy proposals to provide for new regulations under the Charities Act 2005 to support the Taxation and Charities Review Authority (the Authority) to hear charities appeals. 4 From 5 July 2024, charities will be able to appeal decisions related to their registration under the Charities Act 2005 to an expanded Taxation Review Authority (renam ed as the Taxation and Charities Review Authority ).1 Setting limited matters in regulations will support the core objective of access to justice while recognising other considerations such as the public and private benefit s generated by appeals , and alignment of the Authority with the wider tribunal system. 5 The proposals include: 5.1 a single fee of $200 to file an appeal including provision to waive the fee in specific circumstances (this proposal supports access to justice while recognising the public and private benefit s from appealing decisions ); and 5.2 procedural matters to ensure the Authority’s processes run seamlessly end- to-end and align with the wider tribunal system. 6 Targeted consultation between November 2023 and January 2024 confirmed that submitters ’ main concern was that the appeals process is as accessible as possible . Some submitters noted that a small filing fee would be reasonable for appellants to contribute to the cost burden of running the tribunal , while t axpayers’ larger contribut ion recognises the public benefit in an appeals process . 1 Entities and individuals (for example, officers of a charity) can appeal decisions by the Charities Registration Board and some decisions by the Chief Executive of the Department of Internal Affairs as set out in section 58A of the Charities Amendment Act 2023 . For Cabinet mat erial and any public service departmental advice use this copyright statement © Crown Copyright, Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) UNCLASSIFIED Page 1 of 13 In Confidence Office of the Minister for the Digital Economy and Communications Chair, Cabinet Economic Development Committee Ta rgeted engagement on developing Digital Identity Services Trust Framework Regulations Proposal 1. I seek Cabinet’s approval for the Department of Internal Affairs (the Department) to release the document, Digital Identity Services Trust Framework Regulations : A discussion paper (attached as Appendix A), for targeted engagement with key stakeholders . Relation to government priorities 2. The proposed regulations canvassed in the discussion paper would set out legal and process requirements to enable the Digital Identity Services TrustFramework (the Trust Framework) to be established. Establishing the TrustFramework will be an enabler of digital transformation across the public sector and the economy and is a foundation in the Government’s development of a Digital Strategy for Aotearoa. Executive summary 3. The Digital Identity Services Trust Framework Act 2023 (the Act) received Royal assent on 5 April 2023 and will come into force on 1 July 2024. The Trust Framework will regulate the provision of accredited digital identity services, so that users can securely share digital information about themselves to accessonline services. 4. Under the Trust Framework individuals will be able to access, claim and sharetheir own information through accredited digital identity services. This will occuras part of a standardised process to ensure personal identity data is beinghandled securely and according to the users’ requests. It will give users morecontrol over their own data, including what they choose to share aboutthemselves and who they share it with. 5. I propose that the Department lead a targeted engagement process on the regulations . This will in clude engagement with the Data Iwi Leaders Group and Te Mana Raraunga (the Māori Data Sovereignty Network ), the Pacific Data Sovereignty Network, key financial institutions , data infrastructure providers , industry peak bodies , citizen and consumer rights groups and government agencies . 6. Officials will seek targeted stakeholders ’ views on the establish ment of regulations covering: the types of digital identity services that may be accredited, accreditation requirements, accreditation service levels, T rust Framework provider (TF provider ) service levels, and TF provider record keeping and reporting requirements. Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government UNCLASSIFIED Page 2 of 13 7. To enable these regulations to be developed and come into force by the Act’s commencement date of 1 July 2024, the Department needs to progress the consultation process before the forthcoming general election. I seek agreement for the Department to release the attached discussion paper for targeted engagement on the initial set of regulations over a four -week period commencing 23 August and ending 20 September 2023. 8. I consider the risk of targeted engagement over this period is low because of the cross- party consensus on the need for the Trust Framework, the constructive relationship with stakeholders on this work, the technical and procedural nature of the proposed regulations which are grounded in good practi ce, and because the framework is opt -in. 9. In the event the regulations do not come into force by 1 July 2024, the TF Authority will be unable to accredit TF providers and their services or effectively regulate their activities. This means the delivery of the anticipated benefits associated with introducing the Trust Framework will be delayed. Background The Act will commence on 1 July 2024, unless brought into force earlier by Order in Council 10. The purposes of the Digital Identity Services Trust Framework Act 2023 are: 10.1 To establish a legal framework for the provision of secure and trusted digital identity services for individuals and organisations; and 10.2 To establish governance and accreditation functions that are transparent and incorporate te ao Māori approaches to identity. 11. The Trust Framework enabled by the Act will establish a set of technical and security requirements which will protect the privacy and security of an individual’s information when it is shared within the trusted environment. The requirements will apply to those organisations that choose to opt -in to the Trust Framework to deliver accredited services. 12. The anticipated benefits of the framework include: 12.1 Enabling user -controlled access to, and sharing of, personal information; 12.2 Minimising identity theft and privacy breaches ; 12.3 Improving information sharing efficiency ; 12.4 Reducing unnecessary sharing of information; and 12.5 Improving access to online and face to face services that require the provision of identity and other personal information. 13. Under the Trust Framework individuals will be able to access, claim, and share their own information through accredited digital identity services (identified byaccreditation marks). This will occur as part of a standardised process to ensurepersonal identity data is being handled securely and according to the users’requests, as outlined in the diagram in Appendix B. Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government UNCLASSIFIED Page 3 of 13 Secondary legislation in the form of rules and regulations will enable the establishment of the Trust Framework 14. Regular and timely updates of trust framework regulatory requirements will benecessary to keep pace with changes in a rapidly evolving technology -centred sector. Consequently, the Act enables many of the regulatory requirements to besecondary legislation as either r ules or r egulations . 15. The rules will establish the technical service requirements that T F providers will need to meet when designing and delivering accredited services. The rules have already been the subject of early consultation with key stakeholders and willundergo a further final round of consultation in the first quarter of 2024. The rules cover: identification management, privacy and confidentiality, security and risk,information and data management and information sharing and facilitatingarrangements. 16. The regulations will complement the rules by establishing broader legal andadministrative process requirements that either need to be met by regulatedparties or clarify how the TF Board and TF Authority will manage aspects of the regulatory system. The Privacy Act 2020 continues to apply to the collection, use and retention of all personal information under the Trust Framework. 17. While the M āori Advisory Group appointments have been made, the TF Board appointments have not yet been completed and the TF Authority is not yetestablished. The Department will engage with both the Māori Advisory Group and the TF Board once established through the regulation development process . 18. The regulations will be developed in two phases. The first set of regulations –which are addressed in the attached discussion paper – cover the necessary legal and procedural requirements to initially stand up the regulatory system , including: 18.1 The types of digital identity services that may be accredited; 18.2 TF provider accreditation process, including accreditation requirements, application assessment criteria and accreditation periods ; 18.3 TF service levels that providers can meet when delivering accredited services; 18.4 TF provider internal complaints process requirements ; 18.5 TF provider record- keeping requirements; and 18.6 TF provider reporting requirements . 19. It is anticipated that the development of second set of regulations will be recommended to the Minister for the Digital Economy and Communications by the TF Board in 2024 to: 19.1 Enable the introduction of fees to recover TF Authority costs associated with administering the accreditation process and the wider Trust Framework ; Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government UNCLASSIFIED Page 4 of 13 19.2 Establish requirements and criteria that would enable the TF Authority to recommend enhancements to the dispute resolution scheme provided under the Act ; 19.3 Enable arrangements for the appointment and oversight of third -party assessors that the TF Authority may choose to certify to carry out accreditati on functions on its behalf; and 19.4 Address other operational matters required to frame the TF Authority’s administration of the scheme. Proposed regulations Accredited services 20. The discussion paper proposes that the regulations specify that the following services can be delivered by TF providers as accredited services under the Act: 20.1 Digital Identity Information Service: provides an assessment of the accuracy of personal or organisational information; 20.2 Digital Identity Binding Service: ensures the connection of personal or organisational information to an individual or organisation; 20.3 Digital Identity Authentication Service: ensures the connection of a user to an authenticator and secures the sharing of personal or organisational information between Trust Framework participants by ensuring the authenticator(s) are held and controlled by an authorised holder ; 20.4 Digital Identity Credential Service: combines bound information and an authenticator to establish and maintain a reusable credential ; and 20.5 Digital Identity Facilitation Service (s): assists users to share credentials with Relying Parties. Accreditation requirements 21. Under the Act the TF Authority undertakes the accreditation of potential TF providers. The TF Authority will be appointed by the Chief Executive of the Department of Internal Affairs and be accountable to the responsible Minister . The discussion paper sets out the requirements that applicants for accreditation will need to meet, along with the assessment criteria the TF Authority will apply to applications . 22. The applicant will need to be a company incorporated in New Zealand, an Incorporated Society registered in New Zealand, a New Zealand C rown entity or a government department that intends to deliver one or more digital identity services. The organisation will need to demonstrate it is financially sustainable and can: 22.1 meet the service standards specified in the r ules; 22.2 provide an internal complaints process ; 22.3 meet fit and proper person requirements; and Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government UNCLASSIFIED Page 5 of 13 22.4 address to the TF Authority’s satisfaction any issues of concern arising from any past practises as an identity services provider that have be en the subject of an investigation by the Privacy Commission or the TF Authority, or resulted in a decision to previously decline, suspend or cancel an accreditation. Length of accreditation period 23. The discussion paper proposes that the regulations establish an accreditation period of two years . A two-year accreditation period is considered appropriate given we are introducing a new regulatory system and there are likely to bechanges to the service standards providers need to meet in response to therapidly evolving nature of the industry. Accreditation Mark 24. The proposed regulations will enable TF providers to display an accreditation mark against each of their accredited services. This will help users and providersknow that a provider’s service meets the standards for that service as set out inthe rules. Service Levels 25. The proposed regulations will also include provision for establishing service levels that TF providers meet when delivering information services, binding services and/or authentication services. Service levels will not apply to credential and facilitation services as the r ules will establish a single standard for them which a provider must meet for accreditation purposes. 26. This feature of the regulatory system is intended to help relying parties and otherdigital service provider s understand how r obust a TF provider ’s processes are, facilitate cooperation between providers by reducing the time required to assess the other party’s processes, and increase trust in the regulatory framework. Complaints process 27. The proposed regulations will set out requirements for each TF provider to operate their own complaints processes. Any complaints not resolved directly with the TF provider can be referred to the Authorit y to address as provided for in the Act . The requirement for TF providers to initially address complaints is good practi ce and will help encourage the resolution of complaints at the source wherever possible. It should also reduce the TF Authority’s workload . 28. Any complaints received by the TF Authority will be subject to a preliminary triaging process that enables it to identify comp laints about matters that already fall within the jurisdiction of the Ombudsman, the Privacy Commissioner; theInspector -General of Intelligence and Security or another officeholder for onward referral to them . This will enable the Authority to focus on complai nts where there may be a breach of the requirements established by the Act or the associated rules and regulations. 29. The discussion document seeks feedback on the complaints process, particularly the internal complaints requirements TF providers would need to meet, andwhether this is a suitable mechanism to addressing complaints in the first instance. Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government UNCLASSIFIED Page 6 of 13 Record keeping requirements 30. The discussion paper sets out proposals for regulations on record keeping that will require TF providers to collect and retain information about their activities, store it in a secure database, and provide the TF Authority with access to those records at all reasonable times upon request. The regulations will require the T F provider s to retain information necessary to provide assurance that they have delivered accredited services aligned with the requirements specified in the rules and regulations. Reporting 31. The discussion paper proposes that the regulations establish annual reporting requirements for TF providers to help enable the TF Authority to monitor and assess their performance and that of the regulatory system. It proposes that the annual reporting requirements will cover organisational governance and management arrangements, information on service transactions, compliance and delivery, complaints and disputes resolution, f raud events, and each provider ’s financial performance. 32. In addition , it proposes that the regulations require providers to report separately and as soon as practical any actual or suspected fraud events and other events that adversely affect confidentiality, the integrity or availability of the digital identity service and have caused or present a risk of serious harm. This will helpensure the TF Authority is aware of significant events and is able to intervene or assist where necessary. Cost recovery 33. The discussion paper confirms that the TF Authority’s initial establishment and the first two years of operating costs will be met from Crown funding without acontribution from fees. Consequently , early entrants will not need to pay an initial accreditation fee. Later entrants and TF providers seeking to renew accreditations will incur a fee if cost recovery regulations are introduced. Fees are proposed to be introduced after two years once more information is availableabout the potential number of providers in the market. Timing of engagement on the discussion paper 34. To enable these regulations to be developed and come into force by the Act’scommencement date of 1 July 2024, the targeted stakeholder engagementprocess should take place before the forthcoming general election. Once engagement is completed, further Cabinet policy decisions to inform drafting instructions and Cabinet approval of the regulations are still required. 35. I have considered the risks associated with undertaking the engagement process prior to the forthcoming General Election and consider them to be low as: 35.1 There is broad cross -party and stakeholder support for the establishment of the Trust Framework , which was demonstrated during the passage of the Bill; Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government UNCLASSIFIED Page 7 of 13 35.2 The key non- government stakeholders we are proposing to consult have already been engaged in the development of the associated rules and have a real interest in considering the associated regulatory requirements ; 35.3 The regulatory system is an ‘ opt-in’ arrangement which means parties are not obliged to meet TF regulatory requirements unless they choose to do so; and 35.4 The regulatory proposals are administrative in nature and reflect good practi ce in other regulatory systems . 36. In the event the consultation process does not take place prior to the election,officials advise that it would be unlikely that regulations will be ready before the Act’s commencement date of 1 July 2024. Therefore, the TF Authority would be unable to accredit TF providers and their services and effectively regulate theiractivities and the delivery of the anticipated benefits associated with introducing the Trust Framework will be delayed. Officials advise me that they are working through mitigations in the event of this occurring. Proposed targeted engagement 37. The Department will facilitate a targeted engagement process on the proposedregulations with the following non- government organisation stakeholders that have also been consulted on the development of the rules. This will include: 37.1 Māori peak bodies , including the Data Iwi Leaders Group and Te Mana Raraunga (the Māori Data Sovereignty Network ); 37.2 The Pacific Data Sovereignty Network; 37.3 Financial peak bodies and institutions including the Financial Services Council, NZ Bankers Association, Payments NZ and FinTech NZ ; 37.4 Infrastructure providers including MATTR, Centrality, J NCTN, Sush Mobile, and Ahau; 37.5 Industry peak bodies including Digital Identity NZ, NZ Tech, and Internet NZ; and 37.6 Citizen and consumer groups including the Privacy Foundation and Consumer NZ. 38. The Department will also continue to consult with the Privacy Commissioner onthe regulations and with other government agencies that have an interest in theestablishment of the regulatory system and the delivery of online services. Thiswill extend beyond the agencies it has consulted during the development of the discussion paper to include Te Aka Whai Ora – Maori Health Authority and agencies with an interest in digital inclusion and human rights including the Ministry for Disabled People, the Office for Seniors and the Human RightsCommission. 39. The Department will circulate the discussion paper directly to these stakeholdersand invite them to provide feedback by 20 September 2023. To support the Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government UNCLASSIFIED Page 8 of 13 engagement , the Department will also facilitate meetings to discuss the proposals . Relationship to the draft C ustomer and Product Data Bill (Consumer data right) 40. The Trust Framework and enabling rules and regulations will complement the draft C ustomer and Product Data Bill (Commerce and Consumer Affairs portfolio) which has been the subject of recent public consultation. 41. The proposed Bill intends to give consumers the ability to access and share data that is held about them with trusted third parties in a safe and secure manner.The Bill will also mean businesses have to make information about their productsavailable in a manner that will enable easy product comparison and switching.The Trust Framework will support this outcome by enabling people to securelyaccess and share their verified identity and related personal information digitally. 42. Officials from the Minist ry of Business, Innovation and Employment and the Department will continue to work together to ensure the alignment of bothregulatory systems . This will include assessing opportunities to reduce implementation and compliance costs potentially through the accreditation process along with other areas . Treaty of Waitangi/Tiriti o Waitangi Implications 43. The Act includes provisions to recognise and respect the Crown’s responsibilityto give effect to the principles of te Tiriti o Waitangi. The legis lation recognises Māori interests in the protection and use of digital identity and provides for te aoMāori approaches to be incorporated into the Trust Framework governance and decision making. Ways of embedding te ao Māori and te Tiriti o Waitangiperspectives and requirements in the regulations will be addressed during the targeted engagement process with the TF Board, the M āori Advisory Group, Data Iwi Leaders Group and Te Mana Raraunga. Cost of Living Implications 44. The introduction of the regulations proposed in the attached discussion paper will not have a direct or immediate impact on the cost of living. In the mediumterm the establishment and operation of the Trust Framework is expected to improve security leading to increased confidence in the use of the digital identi ty services system . This is expected to le ad to: 44.1 a reduction in costs incurred due to a reduction in fraud ulent activity ; 44.2 time and cost savings realised by users through the increased use of online services that enable them to access services remotely ; and 44.3 savings to R elying Parties through an anticipated reduction in transaction costs. Financial Implications 45. There are no immediate financial implications associated with initiating theengagement process on the development of the regulations. Population Implications 51. Research has identified several groups are at higher risk of not being digitally included in New Zealand including seniors, disabled people, people living in rural communities, and families with children living in low socioeconomic communities . Māori are also less likely to be digitally included than the wider population. 52. Several factors imp act on digital inclusion rates including motivation, access, skills, and trust. The development of the Trust Framework will help address the trust factor directly by enhancing security and enabling users to have greater control over the way their data is accessed and shared through accredited digitalidentity services . The framework is aligned with the Government’s Digital Inclu sion Blueprint that aims to remove barriers to access for at -risk groups in the population and ensure everyone can access and use online information, products and services. 1 1 The Digital Inclusion Blueprint – Te Mahere mō te Whakaurunga Matihiko 9(2)(f)(iv) Proactively released by the Minister for Digitising Government UNCLASSIFIED Page 10 of 13 Human Rights 53. UNCLASSIFIED …which replicates a charitable trust established after Christchurch Earthquake 6 Following the devastating 2011 Christchurch Earthquake, the Government quickly esta blished a charitable trust to complement existing donation appeals. The Christchurch Earthquake Appeal Trust (CEAT) raised approximately $95 million in donations. Most of the funding was collected in the first year of the appeal, 2011. 7 CEAT funded a range of projects. Some of the bigger grants given out were $3 mill ion to the rebuild and restoration of Isaac Theatre Royal and $7.47 million for water attractions at the new Christchurch City Council Recreation and Sports Centre in the eastern suburbs. CEAT currently has around $500,000 left to distribute. CEAT expects to make a final allocation in June this year, at which stage, with no funds left to distribute, the trustees will wind up the trust. Establishment phase includes bank account, website, trust deed, trustees and regis tration as a charity 8 The Trust is currently being established. The name has been confirmed, officials are working on a t rust deed and charitable status (which enables donors to claim a tax rebate), and working with Westpac and Clemenger BBDO on establishing a bank account, website, multiple channels for donations, and other details of how the donation appeal process will work. The pertinent clauses of the draft Trust Deed are set out in Appendix A and closely follow the language of relevant legislation such as the Charities Act 2005. 9 It is important that the charitable trust also be registered as a charity under the Charit ies Act (a separate process) as it is this status which allows donors to claim a tax rebate on their donations. All relevant agencies are working to expedite the required registrations in time for launch. 10 I am proposing three trustees, which replicates CEAT. One would be the Chief Execut i ve of the Department of Internal Affairs (who will be the ‘original trustee’ for purposes of establishment), with two others one of whom will be Māori. 11 I am recommending that decision-making authority on the appointment of the truste es, alongside other decisions about the administration of the trust, be given to the Minister of Finance, Minister of Internal Affairs and Minister for the Community and Voluntary Sector. It is proposed that these Ministers will also have authority to act on establishing a larger Advisory Board with local knowledge and expertise of the affected regions, which replicates the CEAT model. 12 I propose that the Department provide secretariat support to the Trust and, in conjunct ion with Treasury as necessary, receive and hold donations on behalf of the Trust. Underlying principles: closer to home/ka aro mai ke te kāinga Good health begins at home and in communities. Public health and population-based strategies can help to better identify and prevent long-term conditions, provide earlier interventions, shape environments and make better quality healthier choices easier for all New Zealanders. Objective 5: People understand and acknowledge the range of gambling harms that affect individuals, families/whānau and communities This objective acknowledges that people need to have the life skills and resilience to make healthy choices that prevent and minimise gambling harm. The Ministry recognises that, for most people, gambling is a recreational activity that is enjoyed safely and in moderation. However, a significant minority of people struggle with gambling. Certain groups , including Māori, Pacific peoples, Asian communities, youth, migrants and older people are particularly vulnerable to gambling harm for a variety of reasons. For example, some ethnic groups who have not been exposed to large-scale, commercial gambling previously are particularly vulnerable to such forms of gambling harm. The Ministry will continue to design public health programmes, and allocate resources, for vulnerable groups in the population, including resources to raise awareness and develop resilient life skills to prevent or minimise gambling harm. The Ministry will continue to provide information to support making healthy choices at individual and community levels. This includes raising awareness about how to recognise low to moderate levels of gambling harm, the support available and the actions people can take to mitigate these risks and address this harm. The Ministry will develop and draw on learning from projects that promote related life and financial skills and resilience, such as S orted Whānau, for their potential application to people exposed to or at risk of gambling harm. The proposed co-design approach and use of consumer networks and peer support will give consumers (people with lived experience of gambling harm), including those from vulnerable communities, a stronger voice in the design and delivery of these activities. 26 STRATEGY TO PREVENT AND MI NIMISE GAMBLING HARM 2019/20 TO 2021/22 Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs

Upgrading our tools with digital contact tracing Digital contact tracing has typically been considered in the form of an app. The Singaporean approach (TraceTogether) and the Apple/ Google Exposure API are the most notable app frameworks. The required rate of compliant adoption for any digital contact tracing technology is in excess of 60% . A compliant adoption rate of 40%, which is well beyond that achieved by any 2 contact tracing app globally thus far, would still only detect 16% of encounters. The goal for any digital contact tracing initiative really needs to target coverage of 80% of the most high risk encounters - bars, restaurants, public transport, private parties etc.

Vulnerable Communities / Disproportionately impacted communitiesA broad group of people living in the same place or having a particular characteristic in common. Includes, but not restricted to, elderly, aged care facilities, disabled persons, rural communities, Māori, Pacific and ethnic communities. Controller A statutory role under the CDEM Act that is appointed at national, regional, and local levels. Control Control (authority across agencies) is executed horizontally and is the authority to direct tasks to another agency, and to coordinate that agency’s actions so they are integrated with the wider response. Control authority is established in legislation or in an emergency plan. This control is to task a certain agency towards a certain outcome (achieve a managed evacuation for example). It is not control over resources (personnel, vehicles, assets). Coordinating Executive Group (CEG)A statutory committee that is made up of senior officials from each member local authority, Police, Fire and Emergency New Zealand, a provider of health and disability services, and other co-opted members. It is responsible for implementing decisions of the CDEM Group. Coordinated Incident Management System (CIMS)The Coordinated Incident Management System (CIMS) is a framework of principles, structures, functions, processes, and terminology that agencies can apply in in both emergency and non-emergency incidents. Coordination Bringing together agencies and resources to ensure unified, consistent, and effective response. Command and control assist with coordination by defining authority between and within agencies. 155Term Definition Councils / local governmentCollectively refers to regional councils, unitary councils, district councils and city councils. Also known as local authorities. Critical Infrastructure Entity (Lifeline utility in the CDEM Act)Any organisation named or described in Schedule 1 of the CDEM Act. This includes airports, ports, railways, and providers of gas, electricity, water, wastewater or sewerage, storm water, telecommunications, roading networks and petroleum products. Declaration A formal announcement of the beginning of a state of condition made under the CDEM Act. [Refer state of emergency]. Departmental Agency In the context of this paper, Departmental Agency refers to NEMA. It is an operationally autonomous agency with its own chief executive, hosted by the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet (DPMC). Displaced people People who have had to leave their homes as a result of an emergency event and were provided shelter and accommodation under section 73 (1) in the National Civil Defence Emergency Management Plan Order 2015. Emergency Coordination Centre (ECC)Operates at a regional level to control one or more Emergency Operation Centres. Emergency Operation Centre (EOC)A facility, usually operated by a local authority, which is a coordination and control centre for local emergency response and support. The term is used in CIMS, and CDEM guidance, but not in the CDEM Act. Emergency In general, an emergency is a situation that poses an immediate risk to life, health, property, or the environment that requires a significant and coordinated response. It has a specific meaning under section 4 of the CDEM Act as it is relevant to the decision to declare a ‘state of emergency’. Emergency Management SystemThe overall system that includes civil defence and emergency management agencies, policies, legislation, regulations, capability, funding, operations, mindset, and culture. Emergency Management Assistance TeamAn Emergency Management Assistance Team (EMAT) is a team that can be deployed to share capability and add surge capacity with the emergency management system. Essential workers Staff who work for essential businesses such as hospitals, rest homes, supermarkets, lifeline utilities or critical infrastructure, or emergency management agencies. WATER SERVICES POLICY AND LEGISLATION
WDC, and other local authorities already outsource operatio nal capability to scale providers Many New Zealand water companies already outsource operational capability to specialist providers . Several large -scale providers deliver services across all of New Zealand , such as Downer, CityCare Water and Veolia (a glob al specialist water services company). Other large - scale providers operate on a regional basis, s uch as Watercare (which provides services around Auckland) . Outsource d services amount to around 20 percent of WDC’s annual opex costs. Outsource providers already achieve economies of scope and scale across regions and New Zealand. This is because outsource d service providers can offer specialist expertise on a contracted basis, where full-time employment of staff may not be warranted. Outsource providers also compete with one another for council contracts. This ensures prices tend towards costs and it incentivises efficiency improvements. Cost reductions of up to 50 percent in the already competitive outsource service provider market is implausible. 0 50 100 150 200 250 300 350WaterWastewater Cost ($) per connected propertyAuckland (Watercare) Whangarei (WDC) Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs CONFIDENTIAL 24 Castalia 2.3 WICS anal ytical approach has other methodological flaws WICS’ analytical approach has a range of ot her flaws. WICS uses an unconventional method that back -solves the revenue path Typical best practice for calculating the cost of service and tariff levels for wate r utilities and other regulated services in developed and developing countries is to use t he “building blocks approach ”. The building blocks approach is used by the New Zealand Commerce Commission for a range of regulated infrastructure industries, Austral ian water economic regulators such as IPART and Essential Services Commission , and by Ofwat in the UK. The building blocks approach reveals a more accurate cost of service, and therefore the revenues required to meet costs. However, WICS uses a novel meth od to estimate household bill levels. The projected revenues which result in the “household bills” are calculated based on a hard coded revenue path. Typically, a model used to predict costs (and therefore revenues required to cover costs) should determine the revenue path as an output of the model , informed by the assumptions . Howe ver, the revenue path is back solved and has been hard -coded to align with the debt ratios (250 percent of revenue for the Opt -Out Scenario) . Key discretionary assumptions made b y WICS inevitably lead to the Reform Scenario demonstrating superior results WICS modelling approach uses a number of key discretionary assumptions that are highly favourable for the Reform Scenario and highly unfavourable for the Opt -Out Scenario . With such assumptions, it was inevitable that WICS modelling would reach the conclu sions that it did. The model assumes that capex efficiency can only begin to be reali sed if the council’s population size is greater than 59,000 . The efficiency factor increases progressively to 50% when a threshold of 800,000 population is crossed . This ‘limit ’ set by WICS automatically assumes that many councils, including WDC, will not realize any efficiency gains , while every amalgamated entity will realize efficiency gains of over 50%. Further, t he net investment profile is modelled differently in the Reform Scenario compared to the Opt -Out Scenario . In the Reform Scenario, WICS has only included the large investment requirements after 2031 . Yet, in the Opt -Out Scenario, WICS included the large investment requirements from 2021 . The effect is that, in the Reform scenario, the benefits of the new investment are delayed by up to a decade, while the costs arrive just in time to be reduced by the maximum efficiency gains assumed in the model. We note that 2031 is the first year when the WICS model allows maximum efficiency gains to be realised. The figure below demonstrates the effect of WICS’ time -profil e adjustment on the Reform Scenario . The solid black line shows WICS’ state d new investment path, while the blue dashed line shows what that path would have been without the manual adjustment WICS made to the time -profile of the investment. For illustrative purposes, the black dashed line also shows what the new investment path looks like before WICS applies efficiency gains .
WICS are comparing undepreciated replacement cost values for Scottish Water to depreciated replacement cost values for Whangārei p.14 The asset value per connected citizen number used for Scottish Water is derived from detailed asset replacement analysis undertaken by Scottish Water. It is correct that these numbers are the true replacement cost and do not account for depreciation as thi s is the best reflection of the cost of replacing the asset at the end of its useful life.
WICS does not disclose the relative contribution of these factors to the total 50 percent efficiency gain. p.18 Each of these factors cannot be considered in isolation or separated out and, even if such an exercise could be completed, it would likely be materially different for different entities. Different water entities adopt different approaches to delivering the standards set by regulators. In the UK, there have been partnerships, fully outsourced arrangement, fully in house arrangements and alliances. But the end results have been broadly similar.
WICS has made use of local authorities’ own estimates of required investment in several ways: • The bottom end of the range of the investment used for modelling purposes used the councils’ unconstrained views (as provided in the RFI) plus economic depreciation. • The further Montecarlo sensitivity anal ysis also used the investment figures provided by councils with no additional adjustment.
WICS makes no adjustment for the ove rlapping nature of growth and replacement investment We note that, in practice, when enhancement and growth investment takes place, the new upgraded assets often replace at least some ageing assets , thus reduci ng the need for replacement expenditure. WICS ’ approach appears to have made no adjustment for this, since the total investment is calculated as the simple sum of ‘enhancement and growth' and ‘asset replacement and refurbishment’ , and the estimates for the two categories are derived separately, with no consideration of interaction between the two. This means that WICS’ total investment estimate will be overstated. WICS ’ preferred model appears highly selective WICS’ models in approaches ‘1’ (Great Britain comparative) and ‘3’ (comparing asset values) produce a level of enhancement and growth investment in Step 1 that is broadly consistent with councils’ RFI responses. Yet despite the consistency with councils’ own estimates of investment , WICS ’ preferred model is approach ‘2’ . Approach ‘2’ reports si gnificantly higher required levels of investment.

Water New Zealand Water Journal Article The WSA are finalising an article for the September 2024 issue of the Water Journal published by Water New Zealand. The article focuses on their proportionate regulatory approach and uses the recent Tokomaru lead Maximum Acceptable Value exceedances as an example of efforts to engage and support drinking water suppliers in a range of scenarios. A sidebar to the main article is about the importance of water suppliers using flushed samples of water for routine metal testing which was a key learning from the Tokomaru incident. Multi -barrier project update By 22 August 2024, the WSA intend to send emails to drinking water suppliers who have confirmed that they have adopted a long- term plan extension or deferral under the Water Services Acts Repeal Act 2024. These emails will provide confirmation to drinking water suppliers that the timeframes have been adjusted to acknowledge their funding situation and to identify the appropriate pathway to compliance. Working with Whanganui District Council to clarify sampling requirements On 16 August 2024, the WSA identified media comments from the Whanganui District Council (W hanganui DC noting the resourcing challenges associated with meeting daily sampling requirements. The article paraphrases a staff member’s report that the sampling requirements stem from the WSA Drinking Water Quality Assurance Rules (the Rules). As there is no requirement in the Rules to undertake daily sampling, their regional team have reached out to Whanganui DC to understand the process the council is undertaking and whether there is a misunderstanding of the Rules. Whanganui DC have confirmed that WDC staff are undertaking more sampling than is required by the WSA and the Rules. All sampling has previously been conducted by in- house staff at a low cost. However, Whanganui DC understand that recent organisational changes have meant that the staff previously carrying out this sampling are no longer available for this work. WSA will continue to work with WDC staff to consider what is the best approach for their supplies to manage their risk in a way that is proportionate and cost effective. The WSA will also write to the Whanganui DC Chief Executive to note our outreach conversations and clarify the sampling requirements that are a result of the Rules. Update on Morrinsville Water Treatment Plant Since our update to your office on 16 August 2024, Matamata- Piako District Council (MPDC) advised that their back -up bores and water treatment plants were performing well to meet the current demands in Morrinsville. MPDC were able to continue to treat wate r to standards, while advising residents to conserve water. This meant MPDC was able to maintain a sufficiency of supply while working on restoring the treatment process at the main plant to full capacity. Ways of working In implementing the proposed operating model, our ways of working will accordingly be based on the following principles:  We will set out longer term priorities through the Regulatory Systems strategy;  We will look to implement the strategy through the use of quarterly, annual and multi-year work programmes that reflect the multi-disciplinary professional inputs needed;  In our planning, we will be driven primarily by our agreed strategic priorities, but will be responsive to emerging intelligence and emerging risk;  At an operational level, our choice and direction of interventions will be very deliberate and driven by intelligence and risk, as well as robust regulatory practice, using an evidence base to identify and fix the problems that are going to actually make a difference in light of what we know about the regulatory system. Importantly, this will also include active and deliberate decisions about what work we are choosing not to do;  We will have a collective approach to planning our work, moving away from a siloed approach focussed on our own responsibilities, and moving to planning both short and longer term work alongside those who support and complement our work;  The Regulatory Services Systems Leadership Group will apply effective governance and accountability over our work programmes, reviewing on a quarterly and annual basis what we have achieved and what we have yet to achieve – and considering what we may need to do to facilitate work programmes that are lagging;  We will look to actively build constructive relationships with key stakeholders, both as a source of intelligence but also as a key channel of influence to create a lifting platform of compliance amongst regulated parties;  We will support our kaimahi with robust operational policy that guides them in the practical application of their regulatory work.

We have identified four options for achieving t he objective of trusted, consistent and sustainable digital identity ecosystem . Scope When developing these options, the Department did not consider: • The implementation of unique national identifiers . There was no social licence for such a system and such a development would not align with principle 12 (Unique Identifiers) of The Privacy Act 1993. • Non-consented information sharing . The Department has defined digital identity as ‘ the user -initiated, digitally -enabled sharing of personal and organisational information’ and the promotion of non -consented information sharing would be contrary to this . Options were, however, based on the assumption s that: • The current digital identity ecosystem is unstructured, inconsistent and inefficient; and, as a result, it is a low trust environment. • Establishing and consistently applying rules to the digital identity ecosystem would instil greater trust in digital identity services. Option 1 – A non-regulatory Trust Frame work: establish a team within a government agency to develop a set of best practice rules and standards for digital identity services. A cross -agency governance group would be responsible for maintaining and updating the rules . We have options to strengthen regulatory requirements 48. One harm minimisation intervention is not enough to reduce harm, a combination of measures is needed across complementary areas. 49. A suite of proposals, spanning three focus areas (venue, machines and enforcement tools ) has been created. The key information being sought through the discussion document is : • the potential impacts of the proposals, or any alternatives offered, on reducing an individual’s harm from pokies whilst they are in a venue; Societies and venues: • Problem gamblers are not always identified or approached by venue staff, as they often have to make their own judgements about: • how long is too long to be sitting uninterrupted at a pokie machine • how many ATM or EFTPOS withdrawals a patron can safely make • how they keep track of patrons’ ATM withdrawals at a venue • the intensity of the gambler’s pokie use • what behaviour or events to note in the venue’s records • when t o involve a manager at the venue • how to intervene, such as the type of questions to ask a person about their gambling. • Venues can provide ATMs on site, just not in the gaming room. • Previously excluded gamblers can re- enter once their stipulated time expires, regardless of whether they have sought help. • Gambling rooms are normally private, with dim lighting and comfortable seating ( the ideal environment for gamblers to get in “the gaming zone” and continue to play). • Gamblers can play without considering how much they want to spend. • Training is varied as societies can devise the problem gambling training themselves , if they meet minimum content requirements . • Only one person is required to be trained, but the responsibilities for supervising the gaming room are often shared by many staff. Machines and Jackpots: • Much of the harm -focused ‘player information’ is only displayed if the player elects to see it. • EGMs display a loss as a win. • Many features included in the EGM games are known to cause harmful gambling or gambling addiction (e.g. free- spins, multi- bets). • The current play -interruption feature, after 30 minutes, still allows the player to continue. • Jackpots can be advertised within the venue . • Jackpots are creating some adverse and aggressive behaviours . • Jackpots are a significant drawcard, as the prize is twice the amount that can be won from an EGM game. But there is no relationship between the EGM being played and the jackpot. Enfor cement: • There are no offences and infringement fees that relate to the requirements in the current harm minimisation regulations. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Regulatory Impact Statement | 10 • the nature of any impacts on different population groups ; and • the level and type of operational implications for societies and venues. 50. We are particularly interested in feedback and information on: • what proposals are most important or effective; • any alternative or operational solutions ; • potential implementation issues ; • unintended consequences ; and • acceptability to the industry and to gamblers. Part A – The Venue 51. Part A considers ways to strengthen harm minimisation practices by being more explicit about required procedures, actions and environments. 52. The proposals selected for Part A of the discussion document may help improve identification of harmful gambling, through: increased monitoring of the gaming room, record- keeping of a specified range of signs of potential harm, and standardised content for training of staff . 53. The proposals are largely based on research and best prac tice guidelines and so directly target some of the known issues in identifying and approaching at -risk or problem gamblers . Options Description and discussion 1. Regular sweeps of gambling room Venues could be required to monitor the gambling area at set intervals (regular sweeps) to ensure patrons are not displaying signs of gambling harm . This would also enable staff to notice and record the duration of gamblers play, supporting option 3 below . Feedback on how often these sweeps should be will be useful. 2. Approach person who exceeds a specified period of gambling Venue staff could be required to talk to a person who has been gambling for a specified period (e.g. two hours) . Feedback on the frequency and type of interaction prescribed will be useful. 3. Recording specified events and signs Class 4 venues could be required to record a specified range of har m-related events and signs . This would work well in conjunction with option 1, regular sweeps of the gaming room. 4. Records required for use of Management Service Providers (MSPs) Societies could be required to keep records on their use of cont racting MSPs to deliver services to venues on behalf of the society . It is common for societies to use a MSP to discharge a range of the society’s obligations, including services related to harm minimisation, particularly harm minimisation training for venue staff and compliance checks of venue performance, including venue harm minimisation performance. Societies’ record keeping of their use of MSPs could provide for a more consistent oversight of harm minimisation activities. 5. No ATMs inside premises with a gambling venue There could be no access to ATMs from inside a venue, only fr om outside. 6. Requirem ents for excluded gamblers to complete before they can return to a venue Excluded gamblers could be required to seek help bef ore they can return to a venue. 7. Venue design requirements Venue design could be considered in how gambling harm coul d be prevented or minimised. This relates to changes to reduce the opaque nature of the gambling room and its ‘cosiness’ , to reduce factors that support being ‘in the zone’. For example, requirements could cover the level of light required in the room, the maximum sound level for the machines, having ‘ stand at’ machines instead of seated, etc. Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Regulatory Impact Statement | 11 8. Mandatory pre- commitment on machines All gamblers could be required to pre- com mit to the amount of money or time they intend to spend prior to gambling . 9. Standardised content for harmful gambling awareness training Standardised content for harmful gambling awareness training coul d be established. 10. All staff supervising gambling must be trained All staff who have a role in supervising the gambling room coul d be required to be trained. 54. Some of our initial thinking on the Part A proposals, below, has been provided in the discussion document for validation or feedback : • The options directly target some of the key known issues in identifying and approaching at - risk or problem gamblers. • Split duties of staff in venues (i.e. monitoring gaming machines and selling and serving food and alcohol) and high turnover of staff working in hospitality industry may have an impact on implementation. • Some monetary cost to Class 4 sector to implement (i.e. training and ongoing time requirements for observing and recording) . • Some operational updating of systems and practices required by the regulator to determine new internal regulatory criteria, communication to sector and business implementation. • What happens at one venue may only be part of a person’s overall gambling activity . • Greater prescription in identifying harmful gambling behaviour and consistent/improved record keeping, should largely look the same across all venues . • Gambling host responsibility should more closely resemble alcohol host responsibility . • Proposals s till rel y heavily on human intervention, so some variation possible in implementation.

We will provide you with further advice about this matter and the timeframe for resolving it in April. Other minor and technical changes to the self-identification provisions are required 64. There are other, more minor, changes required to the drafting of the self- identification provisions in the Bill. We will draft the Cabinet paper to seek agreement for you to make decisions on these matters prior to their inclusion in the self-identification SOP. We will provide further advice on these matters in April. They include, but are not limited to: 64.1 Transition period for implementation of the self-identification clauses: Up to 12 months may be required to ensure the technical infrastructure is in place to give effect to self-identification within the Births, Deaths and Marriages register; and 64.2 Clarification of how sex is determined in reference to the general l aw of New Zealand: Clause 22I of the Bill provides that “sex of every person must continue to be determined by reference to the general law of New Zealand.” Crown Law advised that this clause did not make the policy intention clear as to whether sex under the general law was distinct from registered sex. We recommend rewording this clause to better reflect that they are distinct and that sex on a birth certificate should not be taken as conclusive evidence of a person’s sex. Risks in adopting a self-identification process and mitigations There will not be time to consult with interested community stakeholders on the self- identification provisions 65. Given the proposed timeframe, there is not time to undertake broad community consultation in the development of the supplementary order paper. Self- identification has been a very public issue since it was introduced to the Bill in 2018. Since then, several public events have been held and material published about it. We believe we have a sufficient understanding of the general views relating to self- identification that would not be significantly advanced by more consultation on high-level issues as opposed to legislative drafting. 66. The lack of consultation can also be partly mitigated by, for example, reviewing submissions on the Bill from 2018 (which were primarily about self-identification) and drawing from Stats NZ’s work on updating the statistical standards for gender and sex identity. The select committee process will also provide an opportunity for community stakeholders to provide feedback on the self-identification provisions. 9(2)(f)(iv) Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Page 12 of 17 Māori, Pacific peoples’ and ethnic communities’ views on a self-identification process have not been sought 67. Given the timeframe for the Bill there will not be an opportunity to explore options for more culturally-inclusive markers such as takatāpui (Māori), fa’afafine (Samoan), or fakaleitī (Tongan) through community consultation . We also have not had time to seek the views of our ethnic communities. 68. We understand there is range of views among Pacific peoples, Māori and ethnic communities about the treatment of gender. One challenge is that we anticipate diverging views on self-identification within these communities which emphasises the importance of including their voice in our policy development. 69. We are exploring ways to meaningfully engage with these communities prior to and during the select committee process. We are developing an engagement plan and are seeking input from other relevant agencies as to who we should engage with and what the best way to do that is given our limited timeframes and resource. There is opposition from some individuals and groups to a self-identification process 70. Opponents to introducing a self-identification process argue that self-identification: 70.1 replaces a robust and shared biological definition of sex with a socially constructed notion based on gender; 70.2 undermines sex-based protections in society and will result in men impinging on women- only spaces including changing rooms, women’s refuges, gyms, hostels and prisons, and accessing woman-only resources and services such as single-sex schools or sports teams; 70.3 creates oppor tunities for ‘predatory’ men to find ways to abuse such access to reach vulnerable women. 71. There is no evidence to suggest that the concerns outlined above will occur. People can have their gender identity represented on their passports and driver licence already and we are not aware of any evidence of that being abused. A birth certificate is also not considered conclusive evidence of someone’s sex or gender and is not required to access women-only spaces such as changing rooms or refuges. Enabling a self-identification process would not have any direct effect on accessing women-only spaces. 72. Any perceived risk that people would change the sex marker on their birth certificates without intending to live as the corresponding gender is mitigated by: 72.1 the requirement to fill a statutory declaration form. Falsifying a statutory declaration form is a criminal offence and can lead to imprisonment for up to three years; and 72.2 making it clear in the Bill that birth certificates should not be taken as conclusive evidence of someone’s sex. 73. Debate on this issue will likely be divisive. Groups opposed to replacing the Family Court process with a self-identification process will likely organise public campaigns which may generate significant media interest. To manage opposition to the self- identification provisions, we have developed messaging and communications material that aims to: Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Page 13 of 17 73.1 provide the rationale for progressing the Bill; 73.2 provide clarity around the reasons for adopting a self-identification approach; and 73.3 clearly set out the uses of a birth certificate and the situations where it is not required, for example, to access women’s bathrooms, refuges, gyms, hostels, or sports teams or single-sex schools. This process does not address all the questions that will be raised about sex and gender 74. Introducing a self-identification process is a positive step towards making New Zealand more inclusive for our transgender and intersex communities. It is worth noting, however, that it will not address some of the bigger questions that may be raised about the treatment of sex and gender in New Zealand. For example: 74.1 Should all references to sex in New Zealand legislation be replaced with gender? 74.2 Do we need to have sex and gender information on a birth certificate at all? 74.3 Should non-residents (including migrants and asylum seekers) have access to a formal gender recognition process and official identity documentation? 75. These questions are outside the scope of the BDMRR Bill (and in some cases are outside your responsibilities in the Internal Affairs portfolio) or cannot be addressed within the timeframes of enacting the Bill this year. Agency feedback 76. We have consulted with other agencies about our advice on self-identification. We received feedback from the Ministries of Education, Health, Justice and Social Development; Oranga Tamariki; Ministries for Women and Pacific Peoples; Te Puni Kōkiri ; the Department of Corrections; Waka Kotahi New Zealand Transport Agency; the Office of Ethnic Communities; Statistics New Zealand; Crown Law; and Te Kawa Mataaho Public Service Commission. 77. While these agencies are generally supportive of the policy intention to change to a self-identification process, there was significant feedback on some of the specific policies involved. 78. The common concerns were: 78.1 Lack of targeted consultation – There was general concern that Māori, Pacific peoples and ethnic communities would not be consulted prior to seeking Cabinet decisions. This included concern that the sex markers woul d not be culturally inclusive, but also a general concern that the impacts of the whole policy on these communities would not be considered; 78.2 The one-time limit on changing a sex marker – Most agencies argued that a person’s gender changes over time and that they should be able to change the marker on their birth certificate more than once. There was particular concern about limiting the number of times children and young people could change their marker; Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs Page 14 of 17 78.3 Minors not being able to make a change without guardian consent – The Ministry of Health and Oranga Tamariki expressed concern about requiring parent or guardian consent for minors. For example, this would prevent access for minors who are estranged from their parent or guardian; and 78.4 Use of sex and gender as interchangeable terms – as discussed above, we are proposing to recognise gender on a birth certificate using a sex marker. This is a pragmatic approach in the timeframe available, but it does lead to some confusion and conflation of sex and gender. We will endeavour to make this as clear as possible in our advice and the Cabinet paper. 79. Agency feedback has informed our recommendation to delay decisions around the self-identification process for children and young people. Further work is required, particularly with Oranga Tamariki and the Ministry of Health to ensure the process reflects the best interest of children and young people. 80. We are also working with Te Puni Kōkiri, the Ministry for Pacific Peoples and the Office of Ethnic Communities to determine how we might engage prior to select committee, and how we can encourage or facilitate participation in the select committee process by these communities. Both mechanisms we are considering for how we determine the non-binary markers for birth certificates will also provide further opportunities to engage with these communities (see para 40 above). 81. Along with seeking further feedback from the agencies above, we will seek views from the Office of the Privacy Commissioner, Office of the Children’s Commission, the Ministry of Youth Development, and Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori – Māori Language Commission. Wellington Accommodation Payment. Commencing on 1 November 2009, Ministers not accommodated in a Crown-owned Official Residence are being transitioned to the Wellington Accommodation Payment. Under the new arrangement the Department will cease to lease properties for Ministerial residences as current leases expire. Instead, Ministers who make their own accommodation arrangements will now receive a payment of $37,500 per year, unless they choose to stay in the same accommodation that they occupied prior to becoming a Minister, in which case they receive payment of $30,000 per year instead.

We are not proposing a final set of new arrangements yet, as this is an interim RIS to support the decision to release the discussion document . As such, it is not practicable to develop a detailed plan for implementation and any transitional arrangements. 71. However, we can say that: • the earliest that any regulatory changes can commence would be late 2022; • the Department will be responsible for the introduction, ongoing operation and enforcement of the regulatory changes ; • Class 4 operators and venues will be responsible for meeting the new obligations from a specified date(s); and • depending on the type and nature of regulatory changes progressed: - transitional arrangements may be required (e.g. if changes to gaming machines features are among the final proposals ); - societies (either themselves or through a third party) may have to deliver new or refresher training ; and - societies may incur costs for EGM provider software design and updates . 72. Alongside the Regulator , and as part of our implementation strategy, we would hope to have support from societies and gambling harm service providers for implementation.

When New Zealand became a British colony in 1840, the Colonial Secretary's Office was the first department to be established. Although 15 separate public service agencies were created within a few months, the Colonial Secretary continued to be the Governor's chief aide, and his office was the hub of the colony's administration. Until 1848 it dealt with all correspondence between the Governor and his employees, and between officials and the public.
