The Agreement will replace a series of other agreements : • Agreement to provide birth and death information (Mortality Review Committe es); • AIA Services NZ Limited Information Supply Agreement; • Cigna Insurance Limited Information Sharing Agreement; • Domain Name Commission Information Supply Agreement; • Forsyth Barr Limited Information Supply Agreement; • Government Superannuation Fund Inform ation Matching Agreement; • Māori Trustee / Te Tumu Paeroa Information Sharing Agreement; • Massey University Information Sharing Agreement; • MyTrove Information Sharing Agreement; • National Provident Fund Information Matching Agreement; • New Zealand Marketing Association Limited Information Sharing Agreement; • University of Auckland Information Sharing Agreement; • University of Waikato Information Sharing Agreement; and • Westpac New Zeal and Limited Information Supply Agreement. The public services that this Agreement is intended to facilitate are: • the accurate and efficient assessment of eligibility for and entitlement to receive public services; • the accurate and efficient delivery of pu blic services by the Registrar -General and the other public sector agencies that are Parties; • the provision by the Registrar -General of accurate Death Information and Overseas Death Information to Parties that are New Zealand Private Sector Agencies for th eir use as per Clauses 10 to 14. • Mortality Reviews and advice on how to reduce preventable deaths; and • prevention, detection, investigation, and prosecution of offences, and the conduct of civil proceedings including judicial review The AISA is broad in t erms of the – • number and types of Parties , including broad classes of agencies and an intermediary class of agencies that may on -share the information with other entities, including overseas entities, under a separate agreement • death information fields the Parties can obtain, use, or on -share , depending on the relevant purpose ; and • purposes for which these Parties can obtain, use, or on -share information. Given this AISA’s breadth, m y focus during consultation s with DIA has been on the nature of the privacy protections built into it. 7i5kudgtnr 2023-03-23 09:21:46 2 Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs
~ Privacy Commissioner \CJ Te Mana Matapono Matatapu Classes mechanism and class es of intermediaries 9. The Privacy Act 2020 was amended to enable an authorised information -sharing agreement to apply to classes of agency by members being added to a Schedule by the Lead Agency ( in this case , DIA), and the agreement applies to each member of the class as parties to the agreement . 10. This AISA will be the first agreement to apply s 142 which allows an AISA to include classes of agencies. Under s 142(2)(g), an AISA must specify with due particularity the class(es) of agency the agreement applies to. This ensures adequate public transparenc y concerning who may be obtaining, using, and on -sharing individuals’ personal information, especially since classes can include private sector agencies and for whom DIA will be responsible for dealing with complaints if the private sector agency is unable to be held accountable . 11. Thirteen different classes of agencies are provided for under this AISA , including:1 • Charitable entities under section 4(1) Charities Act 2005; • Credit unions, friendly societies, incorporated societies, partnerships, registered limited partnerships and registered New Zealand companies; • Crown entities listed in Schedule 1 of the Crown Entities Act (other than specified organisations listed in secti on 138 of the Privacy Act); • Independent advisory committees and statutory supervisory authorities established under legislation to provide independent advice to a Minister or the Government on a matter relating to the implementation or operation of that legislation ; • Independent statutory bodies established under legislation and having a regulatory or administrative role (other than a State services agency) ; • Intermediaries – New Zealand public sector or private sector agencies whose functions or activities i nclude the collection of death information to lawfully disclose that information to a New Zealand or overseas agency in accordance with an agreement ; • Iwi organisations and other Māori organisations listed in the Schedule of the Electoral (Iwi Organisation and Other Māori Organisation) Regulations 2018 ; • Local authorities named in Schedule 1 to the Local Government Official Information and Meetings Act 1987 ; • Mortality review committees appointed under section 82 of the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022 ; • Occu pational regulatory bodies established by or under legislation to license, register, approve, provide oversight of, or otherwise regulate individuals who belong to a particular profession, calling, trade, occupation, or industry ; • Public tertiary institutio ns as defined in section 10(1) of the Education and Training Act 2020. ; and 1 The agreement has been reviewed on the basis of the proposed classes, however, the agreement has not yet been completed with the proposed members of each class as at the date of review. 7i5kudgtnr 2023-03-23 09:21:46 3 Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs
~ Privacy Commissioner \CJ Te Mana Matapono Matatapu Privacy Commissioner’s submission on the proposed information sharing agreement facilitating access to information about deaths Introduction 1. Under s 150(1)(a)(i) of the Privacy Act 2020 ( ‘Privacy Act’ ), the Department of Internal Affairs ( ‘DIA’ ), as the lead agency , has consulted me on a proposed information -sharing agreement . The agreement seek to enable twelve public sector agencies and thirteen different classes of public and private sector agencies to collect, use, and share certain personal information about deaths of individuals (‘AISA’ ) to facilitate public services . 2. Section 150(2)(a) provides that I must consider the privacy implications of the proposed agreement , and ss (2)(b) further provides that I may make any submissions that I consider appropriate. In considering the privacy implications under ss 2(a) , I have regard to the AISA’s required form and content , which is set out under s 144 , including the specified safeguards that will apply to protect the privacy of individuals and will ensure that any interference with their privacy is minimised . Background 3. When a person dies in New Zealand, the Registrar General of Births, Deaths, and Marriages (‘Registrar General’ ) must register the person’s death. This Agreement facilitates the sharing of death information the Registrar General holds to public and private agencies that have a role in updating individuals’ records when they die. Parties to this Agreement may take subsequent actions based on the update of records relating to the deceased individual or associa ted persons, such as granting benefits or entitlements. 4. This Agreement aims to ensure that personal information records held in organisations ’ databases or lists in electronic formats are updated from information held by the Registrar -General when the in dividual in question has died. The intended benefits are as follows: • Organisations having ready access to an authoritative source of registered death information in New Zealand from the Death Register, avoiding the risk of services and communications to a living individual being incorrectly discontinued; • Organisations not having to approach the survivors of the deceased individual to require them to provide information and/or a death certificate and thus placing an additional burden on people already exp eriencing other complex issues; • Avoiding the risk that incorrect or false information may be provided to an organisation; • Organisations being aware of the death so that whānau of the deceased individual do not receive official correspondence, subscription reminders, or invoices for charges which may cause significant upset or distress to the deceased’s family; and 7i5kudgtnr 2023-03-23 09:21:46 1 Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs
~ Privacy Commissioner \CJ Te Mana Matapono Matatapu in the appropriate schedule and circulate the updated schedule to all Parties. This ensures further transparency for agencies and the public. Other safeguards 16. There are important l imits on sharing personal information under this agreement. Information may only be received under this Agreement where the Registrar -General or DIA is either the providing or receiving Party. As identified, i ntermediaries can only on - share information with Clients if they have a l egal basis to do so, other than this Agreement. Other Parties may not share personal information between themselves under this Agreement. This helps to ensure that once agencies receive personal information, there are protections to ensure that it is not unnecessarily diffused to other agencies. 17. The AISA also provides that n o Party is obliged to provide any of the requested information to be shared under this Agreement. This is an important privacy protection because it allows agencies to exercise discretion or judgement concerning personal information sharing in the interest s of an individual’s privacy. An agency cannot be forced to share when they consider that sharing may constitute a breach of the agreement or a person’s privacy more generally. 18. Another protection requires that c harities, registered New Zealand companies, partnerships, registered limited partnerships, friendly societies, credit unions, incorporated societies , and intermediaries may only offer and/or commence products and services where the deceased individual had a prior relationship with the Party. I consider that this can prevent individuals’ personal information from being used in a way that could be considered potentially unethical during a time of distress for families. 19. The AISA also requires that p rocesses and procedures exist within each Party to ensure that information sent under this Agreement is transferred separately from information transferred under other agreements. This will help to ensure that p ersonal information is not inadvertently disclosed to the wrong agencies. It also means that agencies will be able to comply with privacy -protective AISA obligations that apply to the information processed under this agreement, as agencies may have other r epositories of personal information outside of this agreement. Crucially, the AISA provides that p rocesses and procedures exist within each Party to ensure that the personal information received under this Agreement is only used for the purposes specified in this Agreement and remains protected. Review 20. This AISA provides that a joint review of this Agreement must be undertaken whenever any Party not included within a Class of Agencies believes a review is necessary. Furthermore, DIA shall conduct a review annually or at intervals specified by the Privacy Commissioner as specified in section 156 of the Privacy Act 2020. On its face, the ‘intermediaries’ class has the potent ial to be very broad. However, I am satisfied that the proposed AISA includes appropriate safeguards . 13. First, intermediaries are defined as – A New Zealand Agency that is a public sector agency (other than a Department or a Specified Organisation) or a New Zealand private sector agency and whose functions or activities include the collection of death information for the purpose of lawfully discl osing that information to another New Zealand Agency or an Overseas Agency in accordance with an agreement between the Intermediary and that other agency. 14. Intermediaries may only on -share information with their clients if they have a legal basis to do so. As New Zealand agencies, intermediaries will clearly fall within the scope of the Privacy Act and must comply with the information privacy principles , including principle 5 (security of personal information) and principle 12 (disclosure of personal information outside New Zealand) . Intermediaries are allowed to disclose information to overseas agencies. However, this can only be done in accordance with an ag reement between the intermediary and other agency governing the safeguar ds for the information before the intermediary shares information they receive under this AISA with the client. My Office and the Registrar -General will review these written agreements before signing. 15. Moreover, I am pleased to see that prior to including a New Zealand Agency in the Intermediary class , DIA must consider the following : • The nature of the Intermediary’s undertaking or activity and whether the Intermediary has a genuine ne ed and lawful purpose to use the personal information in carrying out that undertaking or activity; • The Intermediary’s policies and practices in relation to the security of personal information and the privacy of individuals; and • Any other matter that DIA considers to be relevant. 2. Further, DIA will have control over the specific data fields of death information to be shared with a particular intermediary that are appropriate for the intermediary’s purpose and the permitted uses of that information when adding an intermediary party to the AISA. 3. Regarding classes other than intermediaries, while DIA may agree that an agency may become a member of a class and , therefore , a party to the AISA, DIA must obtain the Registrar -General’s consent prior to approv ing the agencies’ inclusion . This will help to ensure that sufficient checks are occurring prior to the admission of an agency. Document Oassificaoon -KPMG Conrtden tial Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs 2.3 Background The government has funded a post COVID-19 recovery initiative across New Zealand's library system, especially in public libraries. with a funding package of $58.8 million over 2 -4 years. The New Zealand Libraries Partnership Programme will support librarians a nd library services to be retained in New Zealand libraries and assist them to support community recovery. This will enable librarians and library services to play a key role in supporting their communities and people seeking jobs as part of the recovery from COVID-19. The Local Government COVI0-19 Response Unit signalled in its initial analysis that all councils expected a significant reduction in non-rate revenue in the fourth-quarter of 2019/20 and well into 2020/21. Councils that have large numbers of non-essential service businesses in their district are also more likely to face delayed collection from both commercial and residential property rates. The combined effect of lower-than-planned rates and other revenue reductions means councils are likely to reduce some operationa l expenditure and capital expenditure , which will create job losses directly or indirectly. Although all local authorities provide public library services, such services are not a legislative requirement. The National Library has received clear signals from the library sector that reductions to public library services are expected as a direct result of councils reviewing their expenditure plans. Local governme nt collective ly is the biggest employer of librarians in New Zealand. Role reductions will likely mean a permanent loss of talent to the profession and a consequent deterioration of a valued community service that will be difficult to restore to former levels once skilled workers are lost. The tertiary education sector publicly signalled it is experiencing an 11 % impact that they expect will worsen over the next year. Deficits are likely to be addressed in the short term by cutting staff salaries. Library services that can be exited to reduce costs include collaborative services provided by the National Library that are likely to impact student access to knowledge and information. This initiative is designed to support the retention of librarians in employment by public libraries over the next two years, while councils' position for recovery. The initiative will provide the opportunity to improve reading, literacy and wellbeing outcomes in communities. support building digital literacy among those who have been most excluded from online services and information during the pandemic or have lost jobs as a consequence . and create new digital resources to support online learning for students. This will primarily utilise and build the skills and experience of librarians currently employed in the local government sector. particularly where they otherwise risk losing their jobs. The programme also includes funding for specialist library services for schools and young people with the greatest need, and needs to consider 'where to from here' for all elements of the programme. The opportunities this funding presents the libraries sector are immense. therefore a key focus of the programme is to assess both the current state of the New Zealand libraries system and define the desired future state, as well as develop a strategic roadmap on how to get there. Document Classification -t<PMG Confidenti .al 10 Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs The intervention logic map for the programme as shown in the Programme Initiation Document describes the programme focus areas: Current state Intervention The programme had to be set up in a short timeframe to implement the business case and demonstrate how the National Library can help lead and support COVID-19 recovery across New Zealand's library system and public libraries. The programme has been setup with defined projects. These defined projects are supported by the central National Library project team that provide strategic direction and governance. According to the Programme Initiation Document, these projects include: Secondments Project: to evaluate and support the workforce capability of the seconded library staff. Evaluation and Monitoring Workstream: to support and monitor evaluation of secondments workstream and the programme to ensure they are meeting the defined outcomes. Workforce Capability Workstream: to build on the skills gap analysis and undertake a training provision analysis to understand what current training is available in the New Zealand market and where gaps exist. Focus on Matauranga Maori. 3. Support the communities most in need. 4. Leverage existing partnerships and initiatives. We understand from inteNiews that the National library wants to promote equitable outcomes for the sector and community. Rural and remote areas have a significant Maori population and an equity strategy is critical for the programme to achieve its strategic objectives in these areas. lnteNiews identified that the programme has limited Maori representat ion at the governance level and is struggling to hire Maori resources into the programme team. We did not see any evidence of a clear Maori and Pacific strategy that outlines how the programme plans to focus and help improve outcomes for Maori and Pacifica population in rural areas. We understand from the inteNiews that the library sector has a unique culture, operating model. and needs. This is accepted and recognised by the programme leadership . The programme team has limited resources with previous library sector experience which impacts the programme's ability to engage and relate with the public libraries effectively. Recommendations: The programme should accelerate and prioritise efforts to recruit Maori resources in the programme team and improve Maori representation at the governance level. The programme should leverage sector partnerships and relationships to hire resources with strong library experience . 3.4 Governance The NZLPP governance structure has been designed to cover both the programme governance and control, and sector reference group type approaches . The programme SRO is ultim ately accountable for the success of the programme and should ideally provide continuity of leadership throughout the programme. The SRO's role is to: Ensure that the programme is focused on achieving its objectives and benefits. Ensure the programme gives value for money, ensuring a cost-conscious approach to the programme of work. Appoint the other members of relevant governance groups and programme management team. Secure funding for the programme. Hold the programme to account for the quality of the products created for any outputs created and realising the benefits, including undertaking benefits reviews. (LIAC) Other management groups or forums that support the Programme include: Governance Groups Responsibilities Frequency Training Advisory Group A small group of representatives from partners, public libraries and Monthly ITO's are available as an advisory group to the programme director and team. They will use their expertise across training, skills enhancement and the public library sector to support and guide the programme of initiatives. The responsibil ities of the Training Advisory Group are as follows: Provide input and advice to the programme team on training and capability uplift activities. Review and comment on training related documentat ion. Support the programme by sharing knowledge and helping connect the team to resources and the wider library sector. Provide an active and positive contribution to the programme. Programme Reference Group The Programme Reference Group are individuals brought together to Monthly discuss and deal with operational issues for the programme and the workstreams w ithin. They provide advice and guidance as subject matter experts to support programme delivery. The Reference Group will: Provide input and advice to the programme team. Review and comment on draft programme documents. Ensure that the views and interests of other stakeholders are represented . Provide an active and positive contribution to the programme. NZLPP Working Group The NZLPP Working Group is made up of internal National Library and Weekly programme team members. It is an extension of the programme team and meets to discuss programme progress and seek feedback and input from relevant National library subject matter experts. We understand from our interviews and review of the NZLPP Governance Member Induction Pack that the programme has a governance structure with the defined accountabilities for the Steering Group and supporting groups (Assurance Groups, Reference Group and Training Advisory Group) described above. However, a number of responsibilities of the Assurance Group and Steering Group overlap. The stakeholders indicated that the governan ce structure could be simplified for more robust decision making and that critical feedback received from the governance is limited. Documen t Oassrhcatk,n -Client Confld,ntla l 2 Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs 1 Executive summary The results of NZLPP IOA Round Two indicate an uplift in programme management and governance since IQA Round One conduct ed in May 2021 which focused on the assessme nt of Programme Scope, Documentation, Sustainability and Programme Controls. This is primarily reflected in the stakeholders· interviews conducted during the review, during which senior programme leadership expressed a strong level of comfort in overall programme management and reporting. KPMG notes positive changes have been made to the change control process and an improved programme governance structure. In addition. the Programme has also established clear tolerance levels around time, cost, scope and risk to remain in place until 30 April 2022. From that date the Programme will be in the final weeks of programme closure activities and will adopt a zero-tolerance change threshold i.e. any/all proposed changes need to have programme board visibility. While KPMG endorses the tolerance levels being implemented, the Programme should consider reassessing the baseline date {30 April 2022) for the 'time' threshold to an ear1ier date to allow sufficient runway for implementation of any changes required. The library sector is diverse with different types of libraries such as medical, law and public etc. Public libraries have been a primary focus for the Programme. Although the Programme has had a positive impact in terms of creating benefits for the broader sector, 1t has an important role going forward to manage sector expectations around funding and the ongoing role of the National library, post the life of the Programme. Several benefits and positive community stories created by the Programme have been shared with KPMG during our review. However, these benefits and stories need to be shared more broadly w ith the sector. governmen t bodies and NZ public more proactively to gain and demonstrate sector buy in and to demonstrate the developed capabilities within the libraries to demonstrate what has been achieved over the lifetime of the Programme. Notwithstanding positive shifts in respect of the programme management and governance. we believe risk management across the Programme has been 'light' and requires manageme nt attention. In particular, project delivery and post-delivery risks e.g. reputational risk for National library and partners if they are unable to demonstrate a lasting positive impact from NZLPP, needs to be appropriately tracked and managed. We have raised a recommendation associated with risk management in section 3.3 of the report. Whilst a review of the Programme's transition or wind down planning has not been a focus for this review period the Programme is at a critical juncture where it must move foiward with certainty and complete all in-flight projects/wo rkstreams by June 2022 and develop a clear plan for the Programmes' transition into business as usual (BAU) post the end date. The Programme should consider its future resourcing requirements to include specialist resources with strategy, change manageme nt and policy backgrounds to support management w ith effective w ind down planning. KPMG have raised a number of recommendations throughout the report which require management attention to continue delivering successfully to programme outcome s. Document C~sificat\on -Client Confident ial Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs 2 Introduction 2.1 Scope The Client Services Order (CSO) dated November 2021 outlines the IQA scope as a formal programme level IOA Round Two. This is Round Two of three tranches of IOAs is planned to provide assurance over the overall health of the Programme, confirming appropriate controls, governance, and structure is in place to ensure success of the projects within it. This will certify that the sponsor receives independent feedback that the appropriate structure is in place across the Programme . Focus areas for IQA Round Two as agreed with NZLPP include: Programme Manageme nt Programme Governance Councils Progress Reporting Risk Manageme nt Sustainability 2.2 Approach Planning Before we commenced the review, we undertook a planning phase where we agreed the Programme stakeholders to be interviewed for the review to assess the Programme's progress in focus areas listed above. Fieldwork KPMG has achieved the scope through reviewing project documentat ion and interviewing relevant project stakeholders. The scope and approach form a broad review of project processes against accepted project management practices and the New Zealand Government guidelines for managing major project investments. Detailed analysis and collation of the programme data was undertaken by information gathering into specific themes/a reas highlighted for validation, to ensure facts were confirmed and the context is fully understood to determine if the programme has adequately assessed the impact and likelihood of risks and identified appropriate responses to mitigate risks. Document Oasslficatioo -Client Confidential Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs 2.3 Background The government has funded a post COVID-19 recovery initiative across New Zealand's library system. especially in public libraries. with a funding package of $58.8 million over 2 - 4 years. The New Zealand Libraries Partnership Programme will support librarians and library seNices to be retained in New Zealand libraries and assist them to support community recovery. This will enable librarians and library services to play a key role in supporting their communities and people seeking jobs as part of the recovery from COVID-19. The Local Governmen t COVID-19 Response Unit signalled in its initial analysis that all councils expected a significant reduction in non-rate revenue in the fourth quarter of 2019/20 and well into 2020/21. Councils that have large numbers of non-essent ial seNice businesses in their district are also more likely to face delayed collection. from both commerc ial and residential property rates. The combined effect of lower-than-planned rates and other revenue reductions means councils are likely to reduce some operational expenditure and capital expenditure. which will create job losses directly or indirectly. Although all local authorities provide public library seNices, such seNices are not a legislative requirement. The National Library has received clear signals from the library sector that reductions to public library seNices are expected as a direct result of councils reviewing their expenditure plans. Local government collectively is the biggest employer of librarians in New Zealand. Role reductions will likely mean a permanent loss of talent to the profession and a conseque nt deteriorat ion of a valued community service that will be difficult to restore to former levels once skilled workers are lost. The tertiary education sector publicly signalled it is experiencing an 11 % impact that they expect will worsen over the next year. Deficits are likely to be addressed in the short term by cutting staff salaries. Library seNices that can be exited to reduce costs include collaborat ive services provided by the National Library that are likely to impact student access to knowledge and information. This initiative is designed to support the retention of librarians in employment by public libraries over the next two years, while councils' position for recovery. The initiative will provide the opportunity to improve reading, literacy and wellbeing outcomes in communi ties, support building digital literacy among those who have been most excluded from online services and information during the pandemic or have lost jobs as a consequence and create new digital resources to support online learning for students. This will primarily utilise and build the skills and exper ience of librarians currently employed in the local government sector. particular ly where they otherwise risk losing their jobs. The Programme also includes funding for specialist library services for schools and young people with the greatest need and needs to consider 'where to from here' for all elements of the Programme. The opportunities this funding presents the libraries sector are immense, therefore a key focus of the Programme is to assess both the current state of the New Zealand libraries system and define the desired future state. as well as develop a strategic roadmap on how to get there. Oocum,,nt Classification -Client Confidential 8 Proa ctively released by the Department of Internal Affairs 3 Programme Raviaw Findings 3.1 Programme Management NZLPP has made good progress with uplifting its programme management, documentation maintenance and addressing recommendatio ns around programme management made in IOA Round One. Senior programme stakeholders interviewed during the review expressed overall satisfaction and comfort in programme reporting, the quality of governance papers and procurement management. As indicated in Management Response to IOA Round One Recommendatio ns, the programme has developed and maintained a Programme Execution Plan (PEP) as a core programme document which provides an overview of programme operations, managemen t, scope and contractual requirements. Since the programme was re-baselined, a change control process has also been introduced which is positive. A Change Request form (template) has been developed which requires information about change request type, description. impact analysis and cost of change etc. All change requests require SRO and Business Owner approvals. KPMG has no recomme ndations in relation to Programme Management during the IQA Round Two. 3.2 Programme Governance We understand from the Project Execution Plan that NZLPP governance structure has been established to cater for programme management, governance, delivery, and ongoing quality assurance. The Senior Responsible Officer (SRO) has the overall financial accountability and responsibility for the strategic direction of the Programme . The SRO also has the accountability for programme success and continuity of leadership througho ut the Programme. KPMG acknowledges that manageme nt has leveraged the Programme reset as an opportunity to implement the recommenda tions from IOA Round One to improve governance structure. increase Maori representation in forums and disbanding of Assurance Group and Steering Group. Since IQA Round One. the Programm e has also changed responsibilities between the Programme Director and SRO. The former Programme SRO has moved to focus on the National Librarian role and the Programme Director has taken up SRO responsibilities. This has allowed the SRO role to be completely focused on the programme delivery and enabling the National Librarian to focus their attention on sector engagement and programme governance . Governance on the Programme has improved with the development of a clear Terms of Reference (ToR) for the Sector Reference Group and Programme Board that clearly outlines members· roles and responsibilities. frequency of meetings and other forum details. We understand that Sector Reference Group has been established as a central forum with sector wide representation from various organisations e.g. LIANZA, Te RopO Whakahau, Public Libraries New Zealand and Local Governmen t New Zealand. to provide input and advice to the Programme. The benefits and engagemen t from the Sector Reference Group are recognised by the sector and we understand from stakeholders interviewed that there is a desire for it to continue beyond the Programme life and help sustain some of the benefits created by the Programme in the library sector. Given the broad library sector needs. expectations from National Library and varying operating models of different library types. dividing responsibility between two primary governance forums {Sector Reference Group and Programme Board) should enable more effective managemen t of the Programme. Notwithstanding the enhancemen ts noted above we understand at times governance members might have competing sector interests. funding expectations and lose sight of expectations and forum's purpose which is to provide advice and guidance as subject matter experts to support programme delivery. While stakeholders interviewed acknowledged that governance forums are held monthly as intended. attendance at these forums varies at times and in some instances. there is not sufficient time allocated to discuss significant programme decisions or agenda items. Recommendation 3.2.1: The chair for Sector Reference Group and Programme Board should challenge any viewpoints at the meetings to ensure the discussion is focused on the agenda, intended decision or outcome from the meeting. Any member that is unable to attend a meeting should nominate a delegate or provide the Chair and Programme SRO a clear rationale for absence. Recommendation 3.2.3: The Programme should considers increasing Maori and Pacifica representation at the governance forums, to at least two members each. While this may not be practical for Programme Board given the remaining time left till end of the Programme (June 20221. the Programme should consider this for Sector Reference Group as there is an intention for it to continue beyond the life of the Programme. 3.3 Councils Progress Reporting Since IQA Round One. NZLPP has introduced a consistent progress reporting template for reporting on quarterly progress across various councils which is positive. The template provides clear guidance on how to report on Action Statements and Delivery Objectives. We understand that definition of success is different for each library given different internal systems, processes and delivery objectives. Due to this how libraries wanted to use the funding and improve the libraries was quite varied which has resulted in variances in the level of detail reported by councils on action statements and delivery objectives. An overall view of council's performance over the length of the Programme and risks or issues are also missing, and we were unable to see evidence of an overarching reporting framework or mechanism being used to ensure consistency in the completion percentage being reported. Recommendation 3.3.1: The Programme should setup an ongoing reporting framework for councils. This is particularly important to ensure consistent and accurate sector reporting to Sector Reference Group as it is likely to continue beyond the Programme's life. The Programme Manager should challenge Councils on reporting to ensure there is a sufficient level of detail included in reports to ensure the Programme's qualitative and quantitative benefits are captured. Recommendation 3.3.2: The quarterly reporting template should be updated to include an overview of the council's performance to date and any risks and issues. 3.4 Risk Management In the IQA Round One, KPMG made a recommendation in relation to programme controls, that the Programme should review the risk register to ensure that any long-standing risks are revaluated and mitigated in a timely manner. We understand that in response, NZLPP was going to hold a delivery phase risk workshop and maintain risk registers with a clear escalation path to the Programme Board as required. Our testing indicated however that this process has not been adhered to in all cases. Examples of this include: We did not see evidence of some of the key programme risks such as; potential reputationa l risk to National Library if the Programme is unable to demonstrate a lasting positive impact and loss of benefits to sector after the Programme ends being appropriately tracked or managed . There was no evidence of mitigations or treatment plans being consistently updated or managed. Most risks are owned by the Programme Manager. Risks have been open for a significant amount of time e.g. R04 Sector Engagement raised on 16 October 2020. According to some stakeholders interviewed, the Programme has internal processes to manage risks however, the risks are not robustly discus_sed at governance or strategic meetings. Recommendation 3.4.1: Additional focus on the Programme risk management is required. All programme risks should be captured and included within the risk register. The risks should be reviewed regularly and validated and if required, escalated to issues that are required to be managed by the Programme or an appropriate owner. Critical risk management should be prioritised ahead of the regular governance forums with Treatment Plans being adequate ly documented and updated. From a Local Government system perspective , the primary concern remains whether Councils will have reliable triggers to charge development contributions, and if there will be robust enforcement mechanisms when these buildings are exempt from Building Consents and Resource Consents. Advice on Car Parking Options HUD and MfE have prepared advice to Hon Chris Bishop as Minister for/of RMA Reform and Housing on options to enable better management of carparking, as directed by Cabinet [CAB-24-MIN-0228.0 1 refers]. This is part of the Going for Housing Growth work programme. The options presented will impact councils as regulators and enforcers, as well as in their roles managing and providing on-street carparking. Implementation will also fall to councils. We have concerns about the robustness and accuracy of the cost benefit figures used in the advice to support the preferred option, particularly as they relate to the impact on councils. The briefing was planned to go to the Minister on 25 September 2024. It is likely to be forwarded to you in your capacity as Minister of Transport. We have requested that it also be forwarded to you in your capacity as Minister of Local Government. 7. ~~~(!!§( Te Tari Taiwhenua Internal Affairs Bylaws Work Programme Update: The Departmen t has begun work on a comprehens ive review of the local governmen t bylaw system with the aim of providing local government with appropriate and cost­ effective tools to: • manage and control council facilities; • regulate behaviours to manage harm; and • appropriately enforce local regulation, including considering whether there should be greater delegation to local authorities to set infringement fees. As the work has progressed , the Departmen t believes the time is now right to make initial contact with key local governmen t stakeholders. We would like to talk to them about this work, to test our assumptions and identify any gaps in our desktop analysis .. For this initial engagemen t, the Department proposes discussing the work with the Bylaws Special Interest Group (BSIG) and the Taituara Regulations and Bylaws Reference Group (RBRG). The BSIG is made up of council staff from around New Zealand who work on all aspects of bylaws (e.g. bylaw drafting and review, compliance and enforcement ). The RBRG is a group of council regulatory managers who meet quarterly to discuss and advance council regulatory practice. Engaging with these groups would provide valuable insights from those drafting and working with bylaws to find out what is not working well and what could be done to improve the system. There is a lot of interest in the bylaws work since your announcement of the local government work programme on 21 August 2024. It is important that those working with bylaws can provide the Departmen t with their knowledge and expertise . We expect to brief you on policy direction later this year, and would seek agreement at that time for a wider engagement programme (including with groups and industries who are affected by or whose activities are regulated through bylaws) around policy options. Action Required: Agree that the Department can engage with the Bylaws Special Interest Group and the Taituara Regulations and Bylaws Reference Group to test assumptions and learn from their experiences about issues with the bylaws system within councils, as part of early work on the comprehens ive review of the local government bylaws system. ~~~(!!§( Te Tari Taiwhenua Internal Affairs Engaging with affected Post-Settlement Governance Entities (PSGEs) on potential impacts of water services legislation on their settlement Acts Update: In July 2024, Cabinet agreed to the proposals i n Local Water Done Well -Stage 3 [CAB-24-MIN-0277.03] that under the Local Government Water Services Bill: • existing council or CCO obligations under the Local Government Act 2002 (LGA02) to consider iwi / Maori interests will continue to apply, regardless of service delivery model; and • existing Treaty settlement obligations relating to water services that apply to councils or their CCOs will be upheld under the new arrangements. Cabinet also agreed that you will report back as part of the LEG paper for the Local Government (Water Services) Bill on engagemen t by the Departme nt of Internal Affairs with PSGEs to ensure the potential impacts of Local Water Done Well (L WOW) on Maori interests are understood . Senior officials from the Departmen t have convened online presentations and discussions on the main elements of LWDW policy and legislation. The Departmen t has also engaged with Treaty settlement specialists to undertake analysis of LWDW policy on existing Treaty settlement arrangemen ts. lwi participating in the discussions have made it clear that these engagements have been an introduction to the main elements of the LWDW policy and legislation, and they will need more time to consider the implications of the water services reform for their Treaty settlements and other rights and interests. There are eight settlement Acts across four catchments that are reasonably complex, and LWDW will have direct impacts o n the settlement (the "category 1" settlemen ts). These are: • Waikato-Tainui Raupatu Claims (Waikato River) Settlement Act 2010; • Ngati Tuwharetoa, Raukawa, and Te Arawa River lwi Waikato River Act 201 0; • Nga Wai o Maniapoto (Waipa River) Act 2012; • Te Awa Tupua (Whangan ui River Claims Settlement ) Act 2017; • Ngati Rangi Claims Settlement Act 2019; • Te Rohe o Rongokako Joint Redress Act 2022; • Ngati Kahungunu ki Wairarapa Tamaki nui-a-Rua Claims Settlement Act 2022; and • Rangitane TO Mai Ra (Wairarapa Tamaki nui-a-Rua) Claims Settlement Act 2017. There are 20 further Treaty settlement Acts (the "category 2" settlements ) where there the impact of LWDW is limited, and any legislation to uphold those arrangemen ts should be more straightforward. 9-(2)(f)(iv) 7 Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs
~~~(!!§( Te Tari Taiwhenua Internal Affairs Local Government Funding Agency (LGFA) Update: The LGFA's AGM will be held on 19 November 2024. We are preparing advice for you in consultation with the Treasury on the business tlnat will be considered and the use of shareholding Ministers' proxy votes to be cast on your behalf. Together with MoF, shareholding Ministers hold 20 percent of voting rights. Craig Stobo, Chair of the LGFA is u for re-election. -<2Kf}{iv ne AGfVI w1llalso6e consiaering otner Board appo intments, and the following with respect to LGFA's Foundation Policies: Changes to LGFA Foundation Policies Amendments are sought to Schedule 1 of the Share Holders Agreement Foundation Policies. These amendmen ts are to: a) remove the "A" credit rating requirement , noting instead that the higher borrowing limits are available to rated councils. To assess credit quality of borrowing councils the LGFA relies upon the financial covenants and its own credit monitoring rather than the "A" rating required in the Foundation Policies. The LGFA notes the "A" rating is subjective amongst rating agencies . This change would avoid doubt as to whether the covenants would apply to "A-" ratings, with some councils' ratings potentially moving lower as council debt increases over time in response to infrastructure investment requirements. b) Allow bespoke covenants up to 350 percent Net Debt: Total Revenue ratio for rated councils on a bespoke basis at the discretion of the Board. This proposal is to support high growth counc ils that may exceed covenants to provide growth infrastructure. The expectation of the LGFA Board is that the bespoke higher covenants would not apply to more than 15-20 percent of total LGFA lending to councils. This ratio will be monitored by the LGFA Shareholders ' Council with a view to such covenants not exceeding 20 percent of total counciil lending by the LGFA. A fuller discussion of the Board's recommenda tion regarding delegation to provide bespoke covenants is provided in explanatory note 5 to the Notice of Annual Meeting. The Shareholders' Council supports the proposed amendments to the Foundation Policies. 4 Proactively released by the Department of Internal Affairs

   Figure 3: Distribution of class 4 NCGMs by low-, mid- and high-deprivation census area units, 2012 –2018 100% 90% 80% 70% 60% 49.1% 49.1% 48.9% 50.0% 49.4% 49.3% 49.6% 37.6% 12.8% 38.2% 37.8% 37.8% 38.0% 37.5% 37.7% 13.1% 13.1% 13.1% 12.9% 12.6% 12.3% High (8-10) 50% 40% Mid (4-7) 30% 20% 10% Low (1-3) 0% as of June as of June as of June as of June as of June as of June as of June 2012 2013 2014 2015 2016 2017 2018 Source: Department of Internal Affairs How do inequities come about? Inequities are not random; they are typically due to structural factors present in society and the local community that cannot be explained by biomedical differences between population groups. This means their causes are often complex and multifaceted and are outside the scope of the health system to address on its own. For example, income inequality (poverty) has been shown to be strongly associated with differences in health outcomes, including gambling (Canale et al 2017; Kolandai-Matchett et al 2017; Rintoul et al 2013 ; Tu et al 2014 ; van der Maas 2016). This means that achieving equity in gambling harm minimisation requires a strong evidence base and a strategic, integrated approach from the health sector and other sectors. The Ministry will use strategies and frameworks such as He Korowai Oranga (Ministry of Health 2014c); Equity of Health Care for Māori: A framework (Ministry of Health 2014b); ‘Ala Mo’ui: Pathways to Pacific Health and Wellbeing 2014 –2018 (Ministry of Health 2014a) and the New Zealand Health Strategy (Minister of Health 2016) to focus on minimising gambling-harm-related inequities. It will support this focus through health literacy activities. The Ministry ’s health literacy framework and guide aim to improve the quality of services delivered to individuals, families , whānau and communities by raising awareness of issues such as the importance of screening and the presence of inequities and harm in service use (Ministry of Health 2015). It has applied the approach in gambling harm minimisation services; more broadly to promote screening in drug, alcohol and mental health services; and in the ‘navigator ’ approach to accessing health services. 18 STRATEGY TO PREVENT AND MI NIMISE GAMBLING HARM 2019/20 TO 2021/22 Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs

© Crown Copyright, Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) IN-CONFIDENCE Page 1 of 15 Office of the Minister for Government Digital Service s Office of the Minister of Internal Affairs Chair, Cabinet Economic Development Committee Progressing Digital Identity: Establishing a Trust Framework Proposal 1. Digital identity can deliver significant economic and social benefits to public and private sector organisations. The Covid -19 pandemic has highlighted the role of digital identity as a foundation for accessing services and entitlements online. This paper recommends the creation of a Digital Identity Trust Framework (Trust Framework) to accelerate the development and uptake of digital identity services that are secure, trusted and intero perable. 2. This paper seeks approval for operating funding of $3.260 million in total for 2020/21 and 2021/22 to establish an interim Trust Framework and develop legislation to create a statutory Trust Framework. 3. The Trust Framework will align with trust frameworks in Australia, Canada and the United Kingdom, and is the basis for delivering on the Prime Minister’s commitment under the Single Economic Market agenda for mutual recognition of digital identity services with Australia. Executive summary 4. Digital identity is the user -consented sharing of personal and organisational information online to access services and complete transactions. Digital identity services are delivered by both public and private sector providers and rely on trusted information from sources such as government agencies and financial institutions. There is the potential for digital identity to play a larger role in New Zealand’s economy by improving service delivery and reducing inefficiencies, security risks and privacy breaches. Ther e is wide support in both the public and private sectors to ensure that digital identity services are trusted, coherent and sustainable. 5. Digital identity is a foundational element for enabling the integration of services and digital transformation across g overnment, as identified in Rautaki mō tētahi Rāngai Kāwanatanga Matihiko , the Strategy for a Digital Public Service.1 6. New Zealand has the opportunity to be a leader in digital identity. This includes delivering on the New Zealand and Australian Prime Min isters’ commitment to mutual recognition of identity services between Australia and New Zealand.2 It also includes ongoing alignment with Canada and the United Kingdom with each of these countries developing their own Trust Frameworks to clarify rules and enable interoperability. 7. © Crown Copyright, Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) Priority Routine Internal Affairs briefing Hon Brooke van Velden Minister of Internal Affairs Te Tari Taiwhenua Internal Affairs Title: Date: Options for making Class 3 gambling online payments permanent 14 June 2024 Key issues A temporary exemption allowing Class 3 operators of large-scale lotteries to take online or remote payments expires in October this year. On Thursday, 20 June 2024 you are meeting with the Chief Executives of the Heart Foundation, Coastguard, and Auckland Rescue Helicopter Trust. They will likely ask you to make the exemption permanent to make fundraising easier. These organisations are reliant on large-scale lotteries to raise money for their work in the community. Reverting to in-person or postal sales will severely hamper their fundraising efforts, especially when facing increased costs. We support making the exemption permanent , but it has been challenging to find a suitable legislative vehicle. There are essentially 2 choices to make the exemption permanent. The first is to adopt Hon Barbara Edmonds ' yet-to-dra wn Gambling (Enabling Remote Interactive Gambling for Class 3 Operator s) Amendment Members ' Bill, or the second is to seek Cabinet approval prior to the expiry date to make the exemption permanent when a suitable legislative vehicle becomes available. The likely legislation within the Internal Affairs portfolio would be the Regulatory Systems Amendment Bill or the online casino gambling legislation. Adopting the Members ' Bill and passing under urgency would ensure the permanent exemption is made before 31 October 2024. If you were to decide on a preferred option before the meeting next week, you could communicate this to the Class 3 operators at the meeting. Action sought I Timeframe Read this briefing ahead of your meeting with the Chief Executives of the Heart Foundation, Coastguar d and Auckland Rescue Helicopter Trust on Thursday, 20 June 2024. By 20 June 2024 Direct officials to draft a Cabinet paper based on your preferred option. This briefing provides options for you r consider ation , to make the exemption allowing Class 3 operators of large -scale lotteries to take online and remote payments permanent .1 In 202 0, a temporary exemption was given to Class 3 operators What is Class 3 gambling? 2. Class 3 gambling includes large -scale lotteri es, housie (otherwise known as bingo) , instant games and other forms of gambling run by incorporated societies . It is used to raise money for an ‘authorised purpose ,’ where p rizes offered exceed $5,000. Organisations that hold Class 3 licences are mostly registered charities and faith -based organisations .2 3. Under section 9 of the Gambling Act 2003 (the Act), Class 3 lotteries cannot be run online or by phone . This limit s operators to selling lottery tickets via post or in person and receiving payment by ca sh or cheque . However, New Zealanders are using cash less often to purchase goods and services and c heques are no longer an option as they have been phased out by banks. There is also a security risk of sending cash or credit card details in the mail. A temporary exemption allowing online payments expires in October 2024 4. In 2020, a s part of the COVID response , Class 3 operators were permitted to sell their tickets online and remotely . This is because in -person sales were difficult during lockdown . Due to the emergency -related nature of the COVID -related legislation, all amendments had an expiry date: in this case, October 2024 . 5. Since then, w e have tried to find a suitable legislative vehicle to make this exemption permanent. In March 2023, the Department proposed an amendment for the next Statut es Amendment Bill. However, the Ministry of Justice concluded it was not suitable for inclusion as, in its view, the proposal did not meet the criteria of being non -controversial. Another option was for the online g ambling legislative process to be utilised but that has not been progressed in time to address this issue before the temporary exemption expires. 6. Class 3 operators have been contacting us, your office, and other Ministers advocating for the change to be come permanent. They are understandably concerned about the prospect of returning to non -digital sales or being in breach of the law if they do not . 7. we do not expect the proposal to be controversial – exce pt to the extent that any changes to gambling provisions always attract some attention from those concerned about gambling harm, even from low -risk activities . Digital payments are the norm for most New Zealanders now and this change simply brings Class 3 into line with that . There is no evidence that the exemption caused an increase in gambling harm or additional workload for the regulator . Class 3 organisations rely on lottery sales for their operations 8. Organisations , such as the Heart Foundation and Coastguard, rely on large -scale lotteries to raise money for their work in the community . For the Coastguard, its lottery programme is its second largest fundraising stream . It runs 6 lotteries per year which generates ar ound $3.5m per annum (around 13% of its annual income in FY23). Last year, . This was only possible because of the temporary exemption . 9. These organisations are concerned that removing digital or remote sales will result in: • a loss of customers, both existing and new, because purchasing lottery tickets will become too hard under the old rules ,

Underlying principles: one team/k otahi te tīma The Ministry is working to build a more cohesive, integrated and collaborative approach across the health and disability system , towards shared goals and beyond organisational boundaries , to proactively help people and populations in need. Building on the experience in the addictions sector in particular (addressing harms from alcohol, tobacco and drugs), the Ministry will encourage appropriate collaborative partnerships among services providers and related stakeholders; for example, by promoting co-design and including consumer networks. Objective 8: Gambling environments are designed to prevent and minimise gambling harm There is compelling evidence that certain types of gambling are more likely to be associated with harm than others. The Ministry will continue to advocate for technological and/or environmental changes to gambling environments that are likely to have a positive effect on reducing harmful gambling behaviour and be cost-effective. It intends to focus on greater use of technology to monitor and manage gambling environments and gambling behaviours over the course of th is strategic plan, and has set aside resources to pilot new and innovative uses of technology that may include:  technology-based support for people at risk of or affected by harmful gambling, such as online self-help and support services  tools to support gamblers and host venues to monitor for signs of harmful gambling and enable gamblers to set limits on their gambling activity 30 STRATEGY TO PREVENT AND MI NIMISE GAMBLING HARM 2019/20 TO 2021/22 Proactively released by the Minister of Internal Affairs
“Contact event” was defined as contact that we would intend a contact tracing card to record by Ministry of Health contact definition [3], such as hugging, touching, and talking face-to-face. For example, two people standing within two metres back-to-back would be scored 3, but face-to-face would be scored 4 as the transmission risk is different even though the relative distance is the same. Minutes where two contacts were out-of-range (>10m) from each other were left blank. Minutes where we were unable to determine distance were scored ‘-1’ and both card and ground truth events for those minutes were removed before evaluation. Distances were verified by using floor plans as well as physically measured space between reference points such as walls and furniture.

• It would bring consistency into the digital identity ecosystem in New Zealand , enabling a high trust environment for all participants . • Unlike Option 4, which would also enable a high trust envi ronment, it can be established in the near term and at a lower cost. • It is sufficiently flexible and responsive enough to grow and develop into a larger and more complex model, if required. • Government would maintain control over compliance process, ensuring consistency across the trusted digital identity ecosy stem. • RealMe , or parts of it, could be incorporated into the Trust Framework . • Māori representation at the governance level will ensure Māori concerns and approaches to personal information (e.g. prioritising iwi affiliation over other attributes) are given appropriate consideration . • It would meet stakeholder requirements. Evidence gathered through The Department’s engagement process indicated stakeholders generally wanted a government -led intervention, that combined rules, compliance testing and legal enforceability, and could be established in a timely manner. The digital identity ecosystem is not at a level of maturity to allow for Option 4. Option 4 would involve the establishment of a larger and more complex Trust Framework regime than Option 3. Similar to Option 3, the Trust Framework would be overseen by a governance body and supported by an accreditation regime , and it would bring trust and consistency to the digital identity ecosystem . Additionally, Option 4 would allow for greater autonomy fr om government. It would still have clear lines of accountability and could react quickly to changes in industry standards. However, it could not be established in a timely fashion. Th is option could not be operationalised until a new entity had been created and resourced to support it, and until such time as a new Trust Framework Bill had been introduced, all of which will take years. Furthermore , there is a realistic possibility that it may not be fit for purpose when it does come on line. The size and complexit y of this option may be out of proportion with the market and requirements, especially as there will only likely be a small number of participants authorised to operate under the Trust Framework when it first comes online. As suc h, the cost of establishing a large and complex regime from the outset outweigh the benefits of such a regime. Approving Option 3 does not preclude the possibility to moving to an Option 4 model in the future, if the uptake and size of the ecosystem warrants such an approach. Option 3 is preferred over Option 4 as it enables responsive scalability. Options 1 and 2 will not achieve the objective of bringing trust and consistency into the digital identity ecosystem in New Zealand. Under Option 1, the digital identity ecosystem will continue to be afflicted by inefficiency and a lack of consumer control over their information. • Phase two: the formal establishment of the Trust Framework (2022 -25). In this phase, the Trust Framework is established in legislation and becomes legally enforceable. The governance board becomes formalised with its powe rs and parameters formally established in legislation. The compliance process in phase one transitions into a formal accreditation regime, where systems can be tested against legally enforceable rules, and compliance can be formally recognised. The limitat ions on the number of entities being assessed against the rules are relaxed and any entity wishing to participate in the trusted digital identity ecosystem can apply to undergo assessment. The Bill will provide the accreditation body with the power to impl ement a cost -recovery model and charge for accreditation. The anticipated cost of this phase is $3.75 million . The outyear costs of running the Trust Framework will be confirmed once cost recovery policy is confirmed . The government -led option outlined ab ove is preferred because: • The intervention outlined above would even out the digital identity playing field, increase people’s trust and confidence in digital identity services, and position the ecosystem to realise the significant potential of trusted information sharing via digital means . • There is a strong imperative to implement an intervention in the near future, especially now that Covid -19 is accelerating demand for digital identity services and solutions . • there is likely to be a reduction in revenue for sports and racing codes from the POCC removal and reductions in BI UC payments – (the racing codes collected approximately $2 million f rom POCC in the 2024 financial year and $22.8 million the 2022 financial year from BIUC agreements). The Department considers the risks of these costs outweighing the increased benefits of the monopoly are unlikely, it is not guaranteed. We also note that the racing codes support the monopoly despite these losses ; • there is likely to be a reduction in GST - as noted, the proposals will see a fall in GST paid as offshore operators exit the market. Officials estimate the amount of GST collected in 2023/24 from offshore operators that related to income from sports and racing wagering to be approximately $5.8 million. However much of the GST loss will be offset by increased TAB NZ GST revenue through the monopoly or gamblers shifting their spending to other GST registered gambling operators (e.g. casinos or pokies) or spending a similar amount of funds on other goods and services such as entertainment which are subject to GST. In addition, the payments from Entain NZ to TAB NZ that are conditional on an online mon opoly ($100m upfront should lead to additional spending in the New Zealand economy which would contribute to tax revenues. This positive impact of additional spending in the New Zealand economy could outweigh any GST losses from some NZ gamblers shifting to non -compliant offshore operators. It is therefore assumed the impact will be minimal, but this will depend on the amount of customer s returning to TAB which is difficult to estimate ; • customers may not automatically return to TAB NZ if the monopoly is established - while Entain taking o ver the day -to-day operations has resulted in improved odds and betting options, TAB NZ still offers less variety than most other online sports and racing wagering and there is a risk that a lack of competition could lower likelihood of TAB providing competitive odds and new/innovative products in future . • a black market will likely remain - while reputable operators are likely to prevent customers from New Zealand from accessing their sites, this is easy to circumvent using a VPN. Customers may also choose to bet with less reputable operators to access different products or more range, increasing the risk of gambling harm if they are using sites without adequate consumer protections and harm minimisation practices; • there is a risk that the proposed interim enforcement regime will not be sufficient for TAB NZ to receive the payments from Entain provided. … identified that when situations call for deliberation in the absence of high levels of emotion (cold cognition), such as voting, granting consent for research participation, and making autonomous medical decisions, the ability of an individual to reason and consider alternative courses of action reaches adult levels during the mid‐ teen years. When situations that involve emotionally ‐charged situations where time for deliberation and self‐ restraint is unlikely or difficult (hot cognition), such as driving, co nsuming alcohol, and criminal behaviour, impulse choices are more likely and mental processes are slower to develop, reaching adult levels into adulthood.

●Custom Bluetooth apps.​ Users would download and run such an app which would broadcast out unique keys to others in the area. If each phone is aware of other phones it has been close to for a defined time a view of close contacts can be formed. A “case report form” is submitted for every case to the national ESR EpiSurv platform and some PHUs have their own IT solutions to manage the investigation of cases and contacts. Following the interview, the PHU traces ‘close contacts’, provides self-isolation advice and monitors these persons regularly for symptoms. The PHU also provides advice to institutions and the public in higher risk situations around management of ‘casual contacts’ (e.g. flights). Since COVID-19 there have been some modifications to this process, including establishment of the National Close Contact Service (NCCS) and the National Contact Tracing Solution - an IT platform that can be used by PHUs (although is not mandatory and some PHUs have chosen not to use it) and the Ministry of Health to manage cases and contacts. The NCCS is a Ministry of Health service that aims to help find the contact details of close contacts and high-risk casual contacts (e.g. flights). The NCCS is available at the request of PHUs for the management of individuals or clusters. These two initiatives were necessitated by rapidly increasing COVID-19 cases and multiple complex clusters, which rapidly exceeded the capacity of PHUs.  The Ministry negotiated and implemented service outcome agreements, incorporating results-based accountability measures from 1 January 2018.  The Ministry prepared the Gambling Outcomes Monitoring Report 2007 –2017 (in publication) , which reviewed progress towards gambling harm outcomes since 2010. 3.1.2 Service delivery in 2016/17 to 2018/19 This section discusses service delivery during the 2016/17 to 2018/19 period in terms of public health activity, intervention activity, accessibility for and responsiveness to the needs of Māori and Pacific peoples, and research and evaluation. Public health Effective health promotion is central to the Ministry ’s national public health activity. In the context of gambling, the Ministry ’s public health promotion aims are to rais e awareness of the signs of harmful gambling and encourage more at-risk people to check whether their gambling is OK before harm escalates in severity, and to motivate those who are at risk to get help earlier (or change their behaviour through self-help). HPA’s health promotion programme focuses on encouraging positive behaviour change among at-risk gamblers and raising awareness about the signs of harmful gambling and risky gambling behaviours. H PA-led developments have included enhancing national awareness-raising campaigns, developing and implementing host responsibility policies and practices, and increasing staff knowledge of gambling harm minimisation. Over 2016/17 –2018, HPA continued to promote the Gambling Helpline, Choice Not Chance 13 and face- to-face support services. National and regional service providers delivered a variety of health promotion activities to minimise gambling-related harm in communities, including advocating and supporting hundreds of organisations and workplaces to adopt reducing gambling harm policies, run workshops and presentations on recognising gambling harm and learn how to support someone who wants help to stop gambling, and thousands of awareness-raising activities in communities. A regionally led campaign to ‘Turn Off the Pokies ’ was well supported by class 4 venues. Many service providers also provided a community perspective into the reviews of local gambling venue policies undertaken by territorial authorities. Currently about 87 percent of local authorities have either gaming machine caps or sinking-lid policies in their areas. In line with the objectives of th e strategy, the Ministry funded dedicated Māori, Pacific and Asian public health services to provide appropriate and relevant services within their communities. The national Multi Venue Exclusion Advisory Group led a review of MVE processes for gamblers who want to be stopped from entering gambling venues. As a result of the review, a pilot national standardised process for supporting this process is under way. 13 www.choicenotchance.org.nz/the-latest-campaign (accessed 25 April 2019). Together, the strategic and service plans set out the Ministry ’s approach and the range of activities it plans to undertake to minimise gambling harm from 2019/20 to 2021/22. The strategy sets out the statutory requirements for an integrated problem gambling strategy and the aim for gambling harm minimisation, and specifies 11 strategic objectives. It reflects the Ministry ’s public health approach to gambling harm minimisation and its relationship to the complementary responsibility of DIA in regulati ng gambling activity. Other key Ministry strategic documents inform the strategy and align with it. The strategic plan provides the strategic context and direction for the three-year service plan. The Ministry has made some changes to the strategic plan to reflect changes in the minimising gambling harm and wider addiction and mental health sector landscape . Section 3 outlines more substantial changes for the next three years of the service plan, to address areas highlighted by the needs assessment and outcomes monitoring summarised below. Gambling venues are one of the best environments in which to observe, identify and intervene in potentially harmful gambling. The Ministry, DIA and HPA are committed to working with operators to maximise venues ’ potential for offering safe gambling environments and detecting harmful gambling at an early stage. The Ministry will also support DIA to judicious ly and effective ly use its regulatory tools to deal with operators or venues that do not meet legal requirements. The location of EGMs in high-risk areas (most notably areas of high deprivation) is a long-standing area of concern. The Ministry will continue to support promoting awareness of safe gambling environments , to improve access to gambling harm prevention services in high-risk areas and to work with DIA on its risk-based regulatory approach that guides where regulatory actions should be applied. A particular focus in the next levy period will be NCGM locations and guidance to local authorities and other regulators. Host responsibility training will continue to be an important part of work under this objective. There will be a renewed emphasis on materials related to cultural competence, and how to effectively and appropriately engage with gamblers and their family and whānau from diverse cultural backgrounds.
